title: Live market ticks into Tiger Cloud, then candles in Grafana
description:
Live prices are easy to print and awkward to keep. A websocket hands you one tick at a time. A candlestick chart wants open, high, low, and close for a whole bucket. If you insert each tick in its own transaction, the database spends more time committing than storing. If you only keep a daily rollup, a chart you open during the same session has a single bar, or none at all.

I followed the Tiger Data tutorial for ingesting real-time financial data and wired Twelve Data into a Tiger Cloud hypertable, then drew the candles in Grafana. The code is at github.com/tharun634/tiger-realtime-finance.

What landed in the database

crypto_ticks is a hypertable partitioned on time and segmented by symbol. Recent ticks stay in the row store so inserts stay cheap. Older chunks can move to the column store. A normal table, crypto_assets, holds the symbol and the display name.

CREATE TABLE crypto_ticks (
    "time" TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    symbol TEXT NOT NULL,
    price DOUBLE PRECISION,
    day_volume NUMERIC
) WITH (
    tsdb.hypertable,
    tsdb.partition_column = 'time',
    tsdb.segmentby = 'symbol',
    tsdb.orderby = 'time DESC'
);

Timestamps go in as timezone-aware UTC. datetime.utcfromtimestamp is naive, and a timestamptz column will interpret a naive value in the session time zone.

Batch the ticks

The tutorial flushes every 100 price events. That is the right shape, and it is also how people ingest websocket feeds into TimescaleDB in general: hold a short list in memory, then one INSERT for the batch. Predzone's odds pipeline measured about a 60% latency drop from micro-batches versus row-by-row writes.

A quiet stretch never reaches 100 rows, so the chart sits empty. The heartbeat loop already wakes every 10 seconds, so the same loop flushes whatever is in the list:

def _on_event(self, event):
    if event.get("event") != "price":
        print(event)
        return
    timestamp = datetime.fromtimestamp(event["timestamp"], tz=timezone.utc)
    self.current_batch.append(
        (timestamp, event["symbol"], event["price"], event.get("day_volume"))
    )
    if len(self.current_batch) >= self.MAX_BATCH_SIZE:
        self._flush()

execute_values sends the batch as one statement. Non-price events, including subscribe status and heartbeats, are printed and skipped.

A heartbeat only proves the socket answered. Carl Bouvet's write-up of a silent market feed is the failure mode to watch: the connection stays open, pings succeed, and the trade history grows a hole. Proof of life here is a price event, not the heartbeat.

Two candle sizes, not one

The tutorial builds one_day_candle with time_bucket('1 day', time), FIRST and LAST for open and close, and a refresh policy whose end_offset is one day. That offset is intentional. The newest bucket is still filling, so the policy leaves it alone. Philip McClarence's note on real-time versus materialized-only aggregates is the explanation I wish I had read first: the gap is the design, and real-time mode is what fills it by unioning raw ticks at query time.

ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW one_day_candle
    SET (timescaledb.materialized_only = false);

A daily bar is still one point after twenty minutes of ingest. Pavel's post on continuous aggregates makes the matching point: a view only answers at the bucket you defined. I added one_minute_candle with the same OHLCV shape, a one-minute refresh, and real-time aggregation on. Grafana's minute panel then has a candle per minute. The daily panel is there for the tutorial query, with its own time range so midnight's bucket is not clipped out of "last 30 minutes."

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH DATA cannot run inside a transaction. Applying the whole schema file in one implicit transaction fails on that statement. The apply script runs each statement with autocommit.

The free websocket plan is picky

The script subscribes to BTC/USD, ETH/USD, MSFT, and AAPL, which is the tutorial list. The first connection came back subscribe-status: warning. BTC/USD and AAPL succeeded. ETH/USD and MSFT were in fails, with no error string. Crypto ticks all day. AAPL only moves while the US cash session is open. A higher Twelve Data plan is what adds the rejected symbols. The script still requests all four, so a later plan change does not require a code change.

Grafana

Grafana OSS reads the service over Postgres with sslmode=require and the TimescaleDB option enabled. The candlestick panel wants a time column plus open, high, low, and close. On a six-hour range, one-minute candles collapse into a smear at the right edge. The dashboard default is the last 30 minutes, and the daily panel overrides that to two days.

Credentials stay in an untracked .env. The repo has .env.example only.

What I would change

The 10-second flush is a demo choice. A busier feed wants a shorter timer and a cap so a burst cannot grow the list without bound. I would also alert when the newest price timestamp for a symbol stops advancing, instead of trusting the heartbeat. And I would keep the raw ticks longer than I need the minute aggregate, then let the daily view serve the history.

This article was written by an agent from the build session and published without a human edit pass. The SQL and the Python above match the repo.

title: Join the Call Even When Beauty AR Fails: Build a Browser Preflight Gate
description:
A Beauty AR demo usually proves one thing: an effect can run on the developer’s device.

A production join flow has a harder contract. The user still needs to enter the call if effect initialization times out, the GPU context is lost, a low-end device cannot sustain processing, or an asset fails to load.

That distinction helps clarify the role of “AI in the browser.” Real-time computer vision can produce useful beauty filters, makeup, segmentation, avatars, and gesture-driven effects. It cannot decide how much delay is acceptable, whether an altered image may be published without confirmation, or what the application should do when processing fails. Those remain product and engineering decisions.

In this tutorial, we will build a preflight gate with one invariant:

Beauty AR is a candidate output until it has produced frames and the user explicitly chooses to publish it.

If the candidate fails, the clean camera remains available. The call does not become dependent on the effect.

The workflow we want

The browser join sequence will be:

  1. Acquire the camera.
  2. Show the clean preview.
  3. Prepare a Beauty AR candidate off-air.
  4. Verify that the candidate is producing frames before a deadline.
  5. Let the user choose Join with effect or Join without effect.
  6. Publish only the selected stream.
  7. If the live effect later becomes unhealthy, attempt to replace it with the clean stream.

This is deliberately different from testing whether an API call resolved. A resolved initialization promise does not prove that useful video is reaching the preview.

Tencent RTC’s Beauty AR overview describes real-time capabilities including beauty filters, makeup, stickers, virtual backgrounds, avatars, gesture recognition, and image or video enhancement. Its low-end device optimization guide recommends adapting effects to device tiers, using appropriate performance modes, avoiding expensive segmentation or 3D/GAN effects where necessary, and controlling resolution and frame rate.

Our controller turns those recommendations into an application-level join policy without inventing a universal definition of a “fast device.”

Model the states users can actually encounter

A boolean such as beautyEnabled cannot distinguish loading from failure, qualification, publication, or recovery.

Use explicit phases instead:

type Phase =
  | "idle"
  | "acquiring-camera"
  | "camera-ready"
  | "preparing-effect"
  | "qualifying-effect"
  | "ready-clean"
  | "ready-effect"
  | "publishing"
  | "live-clean"
  | "live-effect"
  | "blocked";

type ViewState = {
  phase: Phase;
  notice?: string;
};

These states produce a straightforward UI contract:

Phase User-visible behavior
acquiring-camera Disable join and show camera setup progress
camera-ready Show the clean preview
preparing-effect Keep the clean preview visible; allow cancellation
qualifying-effect Indicate that the effect is being checked
ready-clean Enable clean join and explain why the effect is unavailable, if relevant
ready-effect Show both join choices; do not select the effect silently
publishing Prevent duplicate join actions
live-clean / live-effect Display which output is currently being sent
blocked Explain the camera or publication failure and offer a relevant retry

The important emotional detail is that “your device could not run this effect” should not be presented as “your device cannot join.” Those are separate capabilities.

Create the reproducible project

Start with a framework-independent TypeScript core. It can later sit behind React, Vue, or another UI.

mkdir beauty-preflight
cd beauty-preflight
npm init -y
npm install -D typescript vitest @types/node
npx tsc --init

Add these scripts to package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:watch": "vitest"
  }
}

For deterministic tests, the core uses a small Stream value rather than requiring real browser media objects:

// src/preflight.ts
export type Stream = { id: string };

export type EffectProfile = {
  id: string;
  allowSegmentation: boolean;
  allow3D: boolean;
  allowGAN: boolean;
};

export interface CameraPort {
  open(): Promise<Stream>;
  close(stream: Stream): Promise<void>;
}

export interface BeautyPort {
  create(input: Stream, profile: EffectProfile): Promise<Stream>;
  dispose(stream: Stream): Promise<void>;
}

export interface FrameProbe {
  hasProgress(stream: Stream, windowMs: number): Promise<boolean>;
}

export interface PublisherPort {
  publish(stream: Stream): Promise<void>;
  replace(stream: Stream): Promise<void>;
  unpublish(): Promise<void>;
}

export type Phase =
  | "idle"
  | "acquiring-camera"
  | "camera-ready"
  | "preparing-effect"
  | "qualifying-effect"
  | "ready-clean"
  | "ready-effect"
  | "publishing"
  | "live-clean"
  | "live-effect"
  | "blocked";

export type ViewState = {
  phase: Phase;
  notice?: string;
};

export type Policy = {
  prepareDeadlineMs: number;
  qualificationWindowMs: number;
};

CameraPort, BeautyPort, and PublisherPort are application-owned boundaries. They are not names of Tencent RTC APIs. The production adapters should call the documented browser, Beauty AR, and RTC integration surfaces available to your application.

Race the preparation, but clean up the loser

A timeout does not cancel the operation underneath it. If initialization finishes after the application has fallen back, that late result must be disposed rather than attached to the preview.

// src/preflight.ts

type DeadlineResult<T> =
  | { kind: "ok"; value: T }
  | { kind: "error"; error: unknown }
  | { kind: "timeout" };

async function beforeDeadline<T>(
  operation: Promise<T>,
  deadlineMs: number
): Promise<DeadlineResult<T>> {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;

  const timeout = new Promise<DeadlineResult<T>>((resolve) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => resolve({ kind: "timeout" }), deadlineMs);
  });

  const settled: Promise<DeadlineResult<T>> = operation.then(
    (value) => ({ kind: "ok", value }),
    (error) => ({ kind: "error", error })
  );

  const result = await Promise.race([settled, timeout]);
  if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);
  return result;
}

The deadline is an application policy, not a Tencent RTC performance guarantee. Choose it from your join experience requirements and verify it on representative devices.

Implement the preflight coordinator

The coordinator retains the clean camera while the effect is prepared. An incrementing epoch invalidates callbacks from cancelled or superseded attempts.

// src/preflight.ts

export class BeautyPreflight {
  private state: ViewState = { phase: "idle" };
  private epoch = 0;
  private raw?: Stream;
  private candidate?: Stream;

  constructor(
    private readonly camera: CameraPort,
    private readonly beauty: BeautyPort,
    private readonly probe: FrameProbe,
    private readonly publisher: PublisherPort,
    private readonly policy: Policy,
    private readonly onState: (state: ViewState) => void
  ) {}

  get snapshot(): ViewState {
    return this.state;
  }

  private transition(state: ViewState): void {
    this.state = state;
    this.onState(state);
  }

  async start(profile: EffectProfile): Promise<void> {
    const attempt = ++this.epoch;
    this.transition({ phase: "acquiring-camera" });

    let raw: Stream;
    try {
      raw = await this.camera.open();
    } catch {
      if (attempt !== this.epoch) return;
      this.transition({
        phase: "blocked",
        notice: "Camera access failed. Check permission or device availability."
      });
      return;
    }

    if (attempt !== this.epoch) {
      await this.camera.close(raw);
      return;
    }

    this.raw = raw;
    this.transition({ phase: "camera-ready" });
    this.transition({ phase: "preparing-effect" });

    const pending = this.beauty.create(raw, profile);
    const prepared = await beforeDeadline(
      pending,
      this.policy.prepareDeadlineMs
    );

    if (prepared.kind === "timeout") {
      // The operation may still resolve. Dispose that late candidate.
      void pending
        .then((lateStream) => this.beauty.dispose(lateStream))
        .catch(() => undefined);

      if (attempt === this.epoch) {
        this.transition({
          phase: "ready-clean",
          notice: "The effect took too long to prepare. You can still join normally."
        });
      }
      return;
    }

    if (prepared.kind === "error") {
      if (attempt === this.epoch) {
        this.transition({
          phase: "ready-clean",
          notice: "The effect could not be loaded. You can still join normally."
        });
      }
      return;
    }

    const candidate = prepared.value;

    if (attempt !== this.epoch) {
      await this.beauty.dispose(candidate);
      return;
    }

    this.candidate = candidate;
    this.transition({ phase: "qualifying-effect" });

    let healthy = false;
    try {
      healthy = await this.probe.hasProgress(
        candidate,
        this.policy.qualificationWindowMs
      );
    } catch {
      healthy = false;
    }

    if (attempt !== this.epoch) {
      await this.beauty.dispose(candidate);
      if (this.candidate === candidate) this.candidate = undefined;
      return;
    }

    if (!healthy) {
      await this.beauty.dispose(candidate);
      this.candidate = undefined;
      this.transition({
        phase: "ready-clean",
        notice: "The effect preview stopped producing frames. Clean video is available."
      });
      return;
    }

    this.transition({ phase: "ready-effect" });
  }

  async chooseClean(): Promise<void> {
    ++this.epoch;

    const oldCandidate = this.candidate;
    this.candidate = undefined;

    if (oldCandidate) await this.beauty.dispose(oldCandidate);

    if (this.raw) {
      this.transition({ phase: "ready-clean" });
    }
  }

  async join(useEffect: boolean): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.raw) {
      this.transition({
        phase: "blocked",
        notice: "The camera is not ready."
      });
      return;
    }

    if (useEffect && this.state.phase !== "ready-effect") {
      this.transition({
        phase: "ready-clean",
        notice: "The requested effect is not ready. Choose clean video or retry it."
      });
      return;
    }

    const previous = this.state;
    const selected = useEffect ? this.candidate : this.raw;

    if (!selected) {
      this.transition({
        phase: "ready-clean",
        notice: "No publishable video is available."
      });
      return;
    }

    this.transition({ phase: "publishing" });

    try {
      await this.publisher.publish(selected);
      this.transition({ phase: useEffect ? "live-effect" : "live-clean" });
    } catch {
      this.transition({
        ...previous,
        notice: "Joining failed. Your preview is still available; retry when ready."
      });
    }
  }

  async recoverToClean(reason: string): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.raw) return;

    try {
      await this.publisher.replace(this.raw);

      if (this.candidate) {
        await this.beauty.dispose(this.candidate);
        this.candidate = undefined;
      }

      this.transition({
        phase: "live-clean",
        notice: `The effect was removed: ${reason}`
      });
    } catch {
      await this.publisher.unpublish().catch(() => undefined);
      this.transition({
        phase: "blocked",
        notice: "Video recovery failed. Video was stopped instead of leaving a frozen effect on-air."
      });
    }
  }
}

recoverToClean() encodes an important trade-off: if replacing an unhealthy effect fails, this implementation stops video rather than intentionally leaving a frozen or corrupted effect output published. Your application can choose a different policy, but it should be explicit and tested.

Test the failures before connecting a camera

Create src/preflight.test.ts:

import { describe, expect, it, vi } from "vitest";
import {
  BeautyPreflight,
  type EffectProfile,
  type Stream
} from "./preflight";

const raw: Stream = { id: "raw" };
const effected: Stream = { id: "effected" };

const profile: EffectProfile = {
  id: "conservative",
  allowSegmentation: false,
  allow3D: false,
  allowGAN: false
};

function deferred<T>() {
  let resolve!: (value: T) => void;
  let reject!: (error: unknown) => void;
  const promise = new Promise<T>((res, rej) => {
    resolve = res;
    reject = rej;
  });
  return { promise, resolve, reject };
}

function fixture(overrides: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
  const states: string[] = [];

  const camera = {
    open: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(raw),
    close: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
  };

  const beauty = {
    create: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(effected),
    dispose: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
  };

  const probe = {
    hasProgress: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(true)
  };

  const publisher = {
    publish: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
    replace: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
    unpublish: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
  };

  Object.assign({ camera, beauty, probe, publisher }, overrides);

  const controller = new BeautyPreflight(
    camera,
    beauty,
    probe,
    publisher,
    { prepareDeadlineMs: 20, qualificationWindowMs: 10 },
    (state) => states.push(state.phase)
  );

  return { controller, camera, beauty, probe, publisher, states };
}

describe("BeautyPreflight", () => {
  it("keeps clean join available when effect creation fails", async () => {
    const f = fixture();
    f.beauty.create.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("asset failed"));

    await f.controller.start(profile);

    expect(f.controller.snapshot.phase).toBe("ready-clean");
    await f.controller.join(false);
    expect(f.publisher.publish).toHaveBeenCalledWith(raw);
  });

  it("rejects an effect that initializes but produces no frames", async () => {
    const f = fixture();
    f.probe.hasProgress.mockResolvedValueOnce(false);

    await f.controller.start(profile);

    expect(f.beauty.dispose).toHaveBeenCalledWith(effected);
    expect(f.controller.snapshot.phase).toBe("ready-clean");
  });

  it("disposes an effect that resolves after the deadline", async () => {
    const late = deferred<Stream>();
    const f = fixture();
    f.beauty.create.mockReturnValueOnce(late.promise);

    await f.controller.start(profile);
    expect(f.controller.snapshot.phase).toBe("ready-clean");

    late.resolve(effected);
    await vi.waitFor(() => {
      expect(f.beauty.dispose).toHaveBeenCalledWith(effected);
    });
  });

  it("does not publish an effect merely because it is ready", async () => {
    const f = fixture();

    await f.controller.start(profile);

    expect(f.controller.snapshot.phase).toBe("ready-effect");
    expect(f.publisher.publish).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

    await f.controller.join(true);
    expect(f.publisher.publish).toHaveBeenCalledWith(effected);
  });

  it("falls back to clean video when a live effect becomes unhealthy", async () => {
    const f = fixture();

    await f.controller.start(profile);
    await f.controller.join(true);
    await f.controller.recoverToClean("frame processing stalled");

    expect(f.publisher.replace).toHaveBeenCalledWith(raw);
    expect(f.controller.snapshot.phase).toBe("live-clean");
  });
});

Run the suite:

npm test

These tests verify authority as well as mechanics. The effect can become eligible for publication, but only join(true) can publish it.

Connect frame qualification to the browser

A production FrameProbe should observe the output users will see—not only the input camera and not only a successful initialization callback.

Where supported by your browser targets, a video-element adapter can observe presented frames with requestVideoFrameCallback. Keep that browser-specific code outside the state machine:

export class VideoElementProbe {
  constructor(
    private readonly resolveVideo: (stream: Stream) => HTMLVideoElement
  ) {}

  async hasProgress(stream: Stream, windowMs: number): Promise<boolean> {
    const video = this.resolveVideo(stream);

    if (!("requestVideoFrameCallback" in video)) {
      // Do not pretend unsupported observation is a successful check.
      return false;
    }

    return new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => {
      let frames = 0;
      let finished = false;

      const finish = (result: boolean) => {
        if (finished) return;
        finished = true;
        resolve(result);
      };

      const onFrame = () => {
        frames += 1;
        if (frames >= 2) return finish(true);
        video.requestVideoFrameCallback(onFrame);
      };

      video.requestVideoFrameCallback(onFrame);
      setTimeout(() => finish(false), windowMs);
    });
  }
}

The count above is an example liveness rule for this tutorial, not a universal quality threshold. A production policy may also consider frame spacing, sustained output, application responsiveness, and visibility state.

Do not qualify an effect while the tab is hidden and then treat that result as representative. Pause the attempt or restart qualification when the document becomes visible again.

CPU/GPU policy: use capability hints, then verify output

Browser capability flags are useful inputs, but poor final authorities.

For example:

  • A GPU interface being available does not prove enough headroom for a particular effect.
  • CPU core count does not describe thermal throttling or competing workloads.
  • A device model or user-agent string does not reveal the current session’s resource pressure.
  • Successful initialization does not prove sustained frame delivery.

Use a two-stage decision:

Stage 1: Select a conservative candidate profile

An application-owned profile can restrict expensive categories:

const conservativeProfile: EffectProfile = {
  id: "conservative",
  allowSegmentation: false,
  allow3D: false,
  allowGAN: false
};

For constrained device tiers, follow the official optimization guidance: choose an appropriate performance mode, avoid expensive segmentation or 3D/GAN effects, and control capture resolution and frame rate. Do not copy arbitrary thresholds from another product and call them device tiers.

Stage 2: Verify the candidate in the current session

Regardless of the initial profile, require actual output progress. Continue monitoring after publication so thermal pressure, GPU context loss, or backgrounding can trigger recoverToClean().

This creates graceful degradation rather than a binary “AI-capable” label:

  1. Requested effect profile.
  2. Simpler effect profile, if the user agrees.
  3. Clean video.
  4. Video stopped if clean recovery itself cannot be published safely.

Automatic fallback between visibly different effects should also be disclosed. “We silently changed your appearance” is not an acceptable interpretation of graceful degradation.

React should render the state, not reconstruct it

A React component can subscribe to ViewState and map it to controls:

function JoinControls({
  state,
  join,
  chooseClean
}: {
  state: ViewState;
  join: (withEffect: boolean) => void;
  chooseClean: () => void;
}) {
  const canJoinClean =
    state.phase === "ready-clean" || state.phase === "ready-effect";

  return (
    <section aria-live="polite">
      {state.notice && <p>{state.notice}</p>}

      <button disabled={!canJoinClean} onClick={() => join(false)}>
        Join without effect
      </button>

      <button
        disabled={state.phase !== "ready-effect"}
        onClick={() => join(true)}
      >
        Join with effect
      </button>

      {(state.phase === "preparing-effect" ||
        state.phase === "qualifying-effect") && (
        <button onClick={chooseClean}>Skip effect</button>
      )}
    </section>
  );
}

Avoid deriving readiness from a collection of React booleans such as loading, enabled, and failed. Let the coordinator own legal transitions; let React render them.

Failure drills to run on real devices

Unit tests cannot reproduce every browser and hardware behavior. Before release, perform these drills with representative devices and workloads.

Camera permission is denied

Expected result: no effect initialization starts, no join button implies video is ready, and the UI explains how to retry.

Effect assets fail to load

Expected result: the clean preview remains visible and clean join is enabled. Repeated automatic downloads should not trap the user in setup.

The preparation deadline expires

Expected result: the UI moves to ready-clean. If initialization later completes, its output is disposed and never replaces the preview.

The user skips while initialization is pending

Expected result: the epoch invalidates the pending result. A late callback cannot re-enable or publish the effect.

The candidate initializes but frames do not advance

Expected result: qualification fails, resources are disposed, and the clean stream remains available.

The tab is backgrounded during qualification

Expected result: do not certify that run. Pause or restart qualification after visibility returns.

The live effect stalls

Expected result: replace it with the clean stream and show a neutral explanation. If replacement fails, follow the declared stop-video or reconnect policy.

Publishing fails after a successful preview

Expected result: retain the local preview and offer a retry. Preview readiness and RTC publication are separate states.

Release verification checklist

Before shipping, verify that:

  • [ ] The clean camera is acquired independently of Beauty AR initialization.
  • [ ] No effect output is published before explicit user confirmation.
  • [ ] A deadline leads to clean join rather than an endless spinner.
  • [ ] Late initialization results are disposed.
  • [ ] Qualification observes processed output frames, not merely input frames.
  • [ ] Hidden-tab qualification is paused or invalidated.
  • [ ] Low-end profiles avoid effects your device policy classifies as too expensive.
  • [ ] Resolution and frame-rate choices are tested on representative hardware.
  • [ ] Runtime stalls trigger a clean-output recovery path.
  • [ ] Failed stream replacement has a defined, user-visible outcome.
  • [ ] Logs distinguish camera failure, effect failure, qualification failure, and publication failure.
  • [ ] The user can always tell whether clean or altered video is being sent.

Browser-based computer vision is a demonstrated capability. Reliable participation is the product contract. Keeping those ideas separate lets developers use Beauty AR without making a user’s ability to join depend on an effect—or making hardware limitations feel like personal failure.

Implementation references and disclosure

Implementation guidance was checked against the official Tencent RTC Beauty AR overview and Low-End Device Performance Optimization Practice Guide.

Disclosure: I’m writing in collaboration with Tencent RTC, and I used official Tencent RTC documentation as the implementation reference for this tutorial.

title: Checking an empty-input defect with Spark-X2.5 and OpenCodeReview locally
description:
Checking an empty-input defect with Spark-X2.5 and OpenCodeReview locally

An empty list crashed a synthetic scoring function that promised 0.0 for empty input. We reproduced the failure, ran a real local OpenCodeReview scan with Spark-X2.5-1.7B, manually added a guard, and checked the same function again.

OpenCodeReview appears in the GitHub Trending monthly snapshot captured at 12:17:22 Asia/Shanghai on 2026-10-14. For this example, its role is to select score.py and collect structured review comments. Spark-X2.5-1.7B supplies the local model review. Python assertions check the function's behavior.

The actual environment is Windows, the official OpenCodeReview v1.13.0 binary, and llama.cpp / llama-server.exe using community Q4_K_M GGUF weights derived from XHToken/Spark-X2.5-1.7B. The tools are connected through a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

The reproduced boundary failure 

def mean_score(scores):
    """Return the mean score; an empty list must return 0.0."""
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

The initial public-function test checked [2, 4] successfully, then mean_score([]) raised ZeroDivisionError at the division and the test process exited with code 1.

The native review saved two overlapping comments on score.py lines 1–3. Both include the missing empty-input handling. The following image is taken from the same recording used in the video. The CLI reads back the original response from that completed review, including its exact relevant excerpt and source session. This readback is not a new model call.

The matching test makes this particular concern checkable. Two overlapping comments are treated as one empty-input issue in this example.

Manual change and public-function verification

We manually placed an empty-input branch before division:

def mean_score(scores):
    """Return the mean score; an empty list must return 0.0."""
    if not scores:
        return 0.0
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

Calling the same function produced [] → 0.0 and [2, 4] → 3.0; both assertions passed and the process exited 0.

Reuse the verified steps

Concrete inputs and assertions provide a repeatable check for a concrete review comment. Get the official Windows release, Git and a local endpoint that returns valid tool calls. First verify file selection in a test repository:

ocr scan --repo <test-repository> --path score.py --preview

When invoking the downloaded Windows release directly, use its actual filename opencodereview-windows-amd64.exe as the command entry. Once file selection is correct, run scan and check its specific comments with boundary inputs through the public function interface.

title: Enforcing ADRs with Deterministic Architecture Tests
description:
TL;DR: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) turn into dead documentation the moment a team accumulates more than thirty decisions. I stop this architectural drift by enforcing rules deterministically: automated architecture tests fail the build on broken boundaries, a one-line context index keeps rules inside human and AI context limits, and explicit anti-pattern definitions catch what static tests cannot.

When I first introduced Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to my team, I was thrilled with the result. We had a clean folder in the repository, markdown templates, and thoughtful discussions about boundaries and conventions. I even wrote about how team alignment sessions and ADRs helped us standardize our APIs in /nodes/standardizing-api-conventions/.

Then reality caught up with us. Six months later, we merged ADR #34.

Around that time, my team was leaning heavily into AI for daily development. Pull requests were getting bigger and moving faster, and our review habits shifted. Engineers did only a cursory pass during code reviews, feeling that line-by-line manual inspections were becoming less relevant. We figured we could trust our AI reviewer to catch mistakes and enforce our standards.

That trust backfired. A pull request slipped straight into our main branch with a major boundary violation: domain entities were directly calling an external HTTP client. The human reviewer gave it a quick glance and hit approve, assuming the AI bot had checked everything. But the AI reviewer had missed it completely.

Writing an architectural decision down does not mean anyone enforces it. The moment an ADR gets merged, it decays into a passive historical record unless something mechanical forces it to stay alive.

Why Do Architecture Decision Records Rot After Merge?

The failure happened because both humans and AI models struggle when decisions accumulate. When your team has three ADRs, everyone remembers them. When you hit thirty or more, no developer holds that entire list in their head, especially when they assume an automated assistant has their back.

At the same time, AI reviewers are not magic. When you stuff dozens of past architectural records into a prompt alongside a large code diff, the context window gets crowded. The model focuses on obvious syntax bugs, style issues, or general logic, but it easily overlooks a subtle architectural boundary. AI misses things too when there is simply too much to track.

When architectural governance depends on voluntary reading and polite prompt instructions, drift is inevitable. You end up with false confidence, skipped reviews, and architectural violations merged directly into production.

Moving from Passive Documentation to Active Enforcement

To solve this, I stopped treating ADRs as reference manuals that developers were expected to read before every commit. Instead, I shifted our approach to a three-layer governance model:

  1. Deterministic gates: Automated architecture tests and static checks running in our Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline that fail the build if code breaks a boundary.
  2. A context index: A single lightweight index file that summarizes every ADR into exactly one actionable sentence, fitting comfortably into human and AI working memory.
  3. Anti-pattern definitions: Explicit descriptions of what a violation looks like in practice, giving both reviewers and AI assistants a clear heuristic when a rule cannot be written as a binary compiler check.

The core idea is simple: the ADR explains why we made the decision, while the three downstream layers make sure the decision actually gets respected in daily development. Each layer handles the kind of rule it is best equipped to enforce.

How Do You Test Architectural Boundaries in CI?

Deterministic architecture tests are automated unit tests that inspect compiled assemblies, namespaces, and syntax trees (Abstract Syntax Trees, or ASTs) instead of runtime business values. They treat your codebase's structure as the subject under test. Similar to the static code analysis rules I discussed in /nodes/start-using-roslyn-code-analyzers/, architecture tests execute quickly and give binary, deterministic pass-or-fail feedback.

Here is a concise pseudo-code example showing how we assert an architectural boundary in a test suite:

// Assert that the domain layer never references infrastructure types
rule = TypesInNamespace("App.Domain")
    .ShouldNotDependOn("App.Infrastructure")
    .Because("ADR-014: Domain logic must remain isolated from external persistence");

AssertRule(rule);

Notice two critical details in that test definition:
First, the rule evaluates namespaces and type references deterministically across the entire compiled solution in less than a second. Second, the test failure message points directly back to the originating ADR. When a developer or an AI assistant introduces an invalid reference, the build breaks immediately, and the error explains exactly which decision was violated.

We also use these tests to enforce naming conventions, interface contracts, and dependency flow:

// Enforce command handler conventions across application services
rule = TypesImplementing("ICommandHandler")
    .ShouldResideInNamespace("App.Application.Commands")
    .AndShouldHaveNameEndingWith("Handler")
    .Because("ADR-022: Command handlers must follow uniform discovery conventions");

AssertRule(rule);

After running this rule in the build pipeline, nobody on the team needs to spend pull request review time checking whether a new handler lives in the right folder. The compiler and the test runner handle it for us.

What If a Decision Cannot Be Checked by a Binary Test?

Here is the catch: not every architectural decision can be translated into a clean AST assertion or namespace rule. For example, deciding whether an event handler should process messages idempotently or choosing when to wrap an external API payload in a domain value object requires semantic context. If you try to force every nuanced design decision into a rigid static test, you end up writing brittle assertions that break whenever someone refactors a class name.

This is where the second and third layers come in. To keep decisions accessible to both humans and AI agents without causing context exhaustion, we maintain a lightweight index file alongside our ADR directory. Every decision gets summarized in exactly one actionable rule:

<!-- Lightweight ADR Context Index -->
- ADR-014: Domain entities must never import persistence libraries or call external HTTP services.
- ADR-022: Command handlers must be single-purpose and reside in App.Application.Commands.
- ADR-029: Public API endpoints must return structured Result objects instead of throwing domain exceptions.

In this index, thirty decisions take up roughly thirty lines of text instead of sixty pages of markdown. An AI coding agent can ingest the entire index in a single prompt and keep all architectural guardrails in active working memory.

For decisions that cannot be verified by an automated test, we also document the explicit anti-pattern directly inside the ADR:

<!-- ADR-029 Anti-Pattern Definition -->
Anti-Pattern: Catching a business validation error in a controller and letting a 500 Internal Server Error bubble up, or using raw try/catch blocks to control domain workflow.
Violation Indicator: Any controller action throwing DomainValidationException directly to the caller.

By explicitly defining what a violation looks like, code reviewers and AI validation prompts do not have to guess. They have a concrete heuristic to check against.

What Happened When We Put This into Practice?

Here's how this actually worked in practice. When we introduced automated architecture tests to our continuous integration pipeline, the first run caught five boundary violations in code we thought was pristine. None of those violations had been caught during code reviews. Developers had simply taken short cuts or forgotten older decisions.

The biggest relief was in our pull request reviews. Disagreements about architectural boundaries evaporated because the tests made the rules objective. You no longer had an architect chiming in on a pull request saying, "Actually, two months ago we decided not to do this." If the build passed, the boundary was intact.

We also saw a major improvement in AI agent performance. When we fed our single-line ADR context index into AI code generation prompts, the agents stopped inventing conflicting patterns. They respected our namespace boundaries on the first try.

However, we also hit some rough edges. Early on, I made the mistake of writing architecture tests that were too granular, asserting specific method signatures and class inheritance trees. Those tests broke during routine refactorings and annoyed the team. I learned quickly that architecture tests should protect structural boundaries, layer directions, and public contracts, not internal implementation details.

How You Should Enforce Your Own ADRs

If your repository has a folder of ADRs that nobody has opened in six months, here is how you can turn them into active guardrails:

  1. Start with your top three boundaries. Do not try to automate every past decision at once. Pick the three most critical rules in your system, such as keeping domain models isolated from database dependencies, and write automated tests for them first.
  2. Fail fast in your CI pipeline. Place architecture tests in the same test suite as your unit tests. If a rule breaks, fail the pull request build immediately. Fast feedback stops violations before they merge into your main branch.
  3. Link test failures back to the ADR. Include the ADR identifier and title in the failure message of every architecture test. When a test fails, the developer should know exactly where to read the reasoning behind the rule.
  4. Build a one-line context index. Create a single Markdown table or bullet list that condenses every ADR into one actionable sentence. Feed this index to your AI coding tools and keep it pinned in your repository's onboarding notes.
  5. Define the anti-pattern for every unautomatable decision. When an ADR covers a conceptual practice that cannot be tested by an AST assertion, write a clear negative pattern into the document. Tell reviewers and AI agents exactly what code patterns to reject.

Conclusion: Keep Your Decisions Alive

Writing Architecture Decision Records is a great first step, but documentation alone cannot protect a codebase as it grows. By pairing ADRs with deterministic architecture tests in CI, a compact context index, and clear anti-pattern heuristics, you turn passive records into living guardrails. Automate the boundaries that matter, index the rest for human and AI context, and let your team focus on solving business problems.

A decision you cannot verify is just a wish.

FAQ

What is a deterministic architecture test?

It is an automated unit test that evaluates compiled assemblies, namespaces, and type dependencies rather than runtime business logic. It checks structural rules deterministically and fails the build in CI if code breaks an architectural boundary.

Can every ADR be turned into an automated architecture test?

No. Structural boundaries and naming conventions translate cleanly into binary assertions, but conceptual decisions like semantic error handling or idempotency require human or heuristic evaluation. For those decisions, you should define an explicit anti-pattern and a one-line index entry.

How does a context index help AI coding assistants?

Dumping dozens of full ADR documents into an AI prompt exhausts its context window and causes hallucinations. A one-line index summarizes thirty decisions in thirty lines, allowing AI assistants to retain all architectural guardrails in active working memory while generating code.

Where should architecture tests run?

They should run directly in your Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline alongside your standard unit tests. Because they inspect assembly metadata and syntax trees without launching databases or network connections, they run in seconds and provide immediate feedback on pull requests.

Originally published at berris.dev.

title: Healthchecks Alternative for Node Cron Job Monitoring: Building an Incident Ledger
description:
Use a dedicated heartbeat service to detect a missing cron run, and keep a small evidence ledger for everything that did run. That is the combination I would ship for a one-person B2B SaaS because an alert answers "is work missing?" while the ledger answers the customer question that follows: "what happened to my account?"

TL;DR: Healthchecks, Cronitor, or Better Stack can own the external deadline and missed-run notification. Record job_started, job_finished, and job_failed with one run_id for reconstruction. Infrai can be a practical destination for those records when a consistent REST contract across backend services removes integration work, but it has no dead man's switch or notification router. It cannot replace the heartbeat monitor.

That boundary is the decision. A log search cannot find an event that was never emitted.

Should a Healthchecks alternative own Node cron job monitoring?

Start with the incident review, not a vendor feature grid. Imagine a scheduled invoice import is due at 02:00. At 02:20, support needs to distinguish four states: the scheduler never launched it; it started and died; it finished with zero records; or it completed and affected a known set of tenants. A single success ping cannot make those distinctions. A pile of exception logs cannot prove the first one.

The smallest useful record has a job name, a generated run_id, an event name, and an occurrence time. Add counts or tenant identifiers only when they are required to reconstruct impact. Resist copying request bodies into logs. Customer evidence becomes retained customer data, and deletion obligations such as GDPR Article 17 do not disappear because the data sits in an observability system.

This is where a solo-operator constraint changes the design. I ship weekly, so I do not want to own a second scheduler whose job is checking the first scheduler. Building that polling loop also means operating its state, notification delivery, retries, and failure detection. The revenue-per-hour case is poor unless monitoring itself differentiates the product.

Keep the signals independent. The external heartbeat establishes that a deadline was missed even when the application is silent. The event ledger preserves what happened after code began running. If both signals travel through the same process and pipeline, one outage can erase detection and evidence together.

Build the ledger before choosing its storage

The implementation can stay boring. This runnable TypeScript example first loads the current logs.ingest request schema from the public, self-describing discovery surface instead of inventing fields the API does not declare here. It then emits three structured event types to standard output, where a collector validated against that schema can pick them up, and calls a vendor-provided heartbeat URL only after successful work. It retries HTTP 429 responses, honors Retry-After when present, and treats any other unsuccessful response as a real failure.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type JobEvent = "job_started" | "job_finished" | "job_failed";

function writeEvent(
  event: JobEvent,
  runId: string,
  detail: Record<string, unknown> = {},
): void {
  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify({
    event,
    job: "invoice-import",
    run_id: runId,
    occurred_at: new Date().toISOString(),
    ...detail,
  })}\n`);
}

async function sendSuccessHeartbeat(url: string): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, { method: "GET" });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const header = response.headers.get("retry-after");
      const seconds = header === null ? Number.NaN : Number(header);
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(seconds)
        ? seconds * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(
        `heartbeat failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`,
      );
    }
    return;
  }

  throw new Error("heartbeat remained rate-limited");
}

async function loadInfraiLogSchema(): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest",
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const header = response.headers.get("retry-after");
      const seconds = header === null ? Number.NaN : Number(header);
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(seconds)
        ? seconds * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(
        `schema request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`,
      );
    }
    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error("schema request remained rate-limited");
}

async function importInvoices(): Promise<number> {
  // Replace this with an idempotent batch operation.
  return 0;
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const heartbeatUrl = process.env.HEARTBEAT_URL;
  if (!heartbeatUrl) throw new Error("HEARTBEAT_URL is required");

  await loadInfraiLogSchema();
  const runId = randomUUID();
  writeEvent("job_started", runId);

  try {
    const imported = await importInvoices();
    writeEvent("job_finished", runId, { imported });
    await sendSuccessHeartbeat(heartbeatUrl);
  } catch (error) {
    writeEvent("job_failed", runId, {
      message: error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown error",
    });
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

await main();

The order matters. A heartbeat sent at startup says only that the process launched. It can mark a half-finished import as healthy. Sending success after job_finished makes the heartbeat correspond to completed business work; a delivery failure also leaves a nonzero exit status for the scheduler.

I initially considered treating successful log delivery as the heartbeat. I dropped that idea because it collapses two failure domains: an ingestion delay would look like missing business work, and silence would still depend on a system without notification routing. The signals don't prove the same thing.

There is one uncomfortable edge: the work may commit, then the process may die before writing job_finished. Make the business operation idempotent and give it its own durable business key. A run_id is evidence, not a transaction boundary.

The three-event vocabulary is deliberately small. For an incident, no job_started points toward scheduling or deployment. A start without a terminal event points toward termination during execution. A failure supplies an immediate reason. A finish with a count supports an impact check without dumping invoice contents into the log stream. The schema request belongs in setup or deployment in a production system, not on every job run; it appears inline here so the example stays runnable and shows where the authoritative request shape comes from.

Four attempts are enough for the example.

Compare the operating bill, not the event price

The real workload includes scheduled executions, normal runtime variance, acceptable detection delay, evidence retention, US or EU data requirements, notification destinations, and the number of people able to maintain the setup. It also includes downstream spend and the hours consumed during an incident. Put those rows in the model before looking at subscription pages.

For me, engineering time gets a blunt revenue-per-hour test. A managed heartbeat product outsources an undifferentiated deadline checker. A reusable event contract makes storage replaceable. That leaves more of the week for product work.

The candidates serve different parts of that bill:

Option Role in this design Boundary to verify
Healthchecks Focused heartbeat candidate for cron and background work Pair it with retained events when reconstruction matters
Cronitor Another specialist candidate for scheduled-work monitoring Verify its notification flow, regional requirements, and grace semantics against the workload
Better Stack Candidate when heartbeat monitoring belongs beside a broader operations workflow Consolidation helps only if its incident workflow fits the team
Sentry Useful for captured failures that benefit from documented grouping and fingerprints Grouping an emitted error does not detect a run that emitted nothing
Datadog Candidate when cron evidence should live inside an established, broader observability estate Its broader operating model can be more than a solo SaaS needs for one scheduled job
Grafana Candidate when the team already operates its own dashboards and alert rules Self-managed components shift maintenance back onto the operator
Infrai Candidate for storing structured run evidence behind a shared backend API contract It has no heartbeat monitor, dead man's switch, threshold engine, or notification router

This is not a winner-takes-all table. Healthchecks, Cronitor, and Better Stack deserve evaluation for the external expectation. Sentry's grouping documentation explains its different strength around captured errors. Datadog and Grafana make more sense when scheduled-job signals must join an existing observability estate. A specialist is the stronger choice when rich notification policy, missed-run detection, or exception analysis is the primary requirement.

I would recommend trying Infrai for the evidence side of a small SaaS that expects to consume several backend capabilities and values keeping them behind one contract. Its discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. Infrai exposes one plain REST API with no SDK to install; any language or runtime can use the same HTTP contract. A separate, verified advantage is that Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Its capability descriptions include request and response JSON Schema plus runnable examples in 10 languages, which reduces schema-discovery work when validating the collector.

The limitation stays visible. Its logs can store job_started, job_finished, and job_failed, but missed-run alerting still needs the dedicated heartbeat service. Building alerts on this API also requires your own polling loop because there is no notification router or threshold rule engine. Correlation stops at trace_id and span_id fields in logs; there is no distributed tracing query or span tree for inspecting a deep execution path. Infrai is not suitable when one product must provide the heartbeat, rich notification policy, and span-tree investigation; choose a specialist instead.

There is a governance trade-off too. Infrai does not expose per-user log deletion or bulk export and subscription interfaces, while its retention and cold-storage behavior has no configuration entry point. If incident evidence contains personal data or must move through a defined residency and deletion workflow, resolve that requirement before choosing it. Integration convenience does not override it.

What would I change after the first growth step?

At the beginning, structured JSON on standard output plus a managed collector is easy to inspect and replace. At higher event volume, I would put delivery behind a durable queue, version the event schema, and monitor consumer lag. Standard queues should be treated as at-least-once delivery, so the consumer must deduplicate by a stable event key.

I would not move the heartbeat behind that queue. Its value comes from crossing the job's failure boundary directly.

Next, I would add a run ledger keyed by job and run_id, with a documented retention window and an explicit list of fields support may search. Then I would test three paths on every scheduling change: a completed run, an exception after start, and no launch at all. The third test is decisive. It proves that the alert originates outside the missing process rather than depending on code that never ran.

Distributed tracing becomes relevant only when reconstructing the inside of a run requires a span tree rather than three lifecycle events. At that point, use a tracing specialist. Do not stretch log correlation fields into a tracing system they are not.

A practical decision rule

Choose the heartbeat provider on deadline semantics, notification delivery, region and data handling, then operational fit. Choose the evidence store separately on reconstructability, deletion and retention needs, export requirements, and integration ownership. Review both against one written incident: which tenant was affected, whether the run began, where it stopped, and who learned about the silence.

That produces a clearer answer than a price leaderboard. A beginner-friendly setup has two narrow responsibilities and a test for each. The heartbeat must alert when nothing happens. The ledger must explain what happened when something did.

If the shared-API boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current log schema before wiring a collector.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Sentry event grouping and fingerprint mechanics
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: The fy field in SEC XBRL data doesn't mean what you think
description:
The SEC gives you every US public company's financials for free through data.sec.gov. No key, no signup. It's one of the best free datasets in finance, and it's easy to get wrong.

Here's Apple's net income from the companyfacts endpoint, filtered the way most people would try first: fy == 2025 and form == "10-K".

start        end          value            fp   frame
2022-09-25   2023-09-30   96,995,000,000   FY   CY2023
2023-10-01   2024-09-28   93,736,000,000   FY   CY2024
2024-09-29   2025-09-27   112,010,000,000  FY   CY2025

Three rows, three different numbers, all tagged fy: 2025.

fy is the fiscal year of the filing, not of the number. Apple's FY2025 10-K reports three years of income statement data (2023, 2024 and 2025), and every one of those values gets fy: 2025. If your code takes the first match, you just reported Apple's 2023 profit as 2025's.

The other traps

Tags change over time. Apple reported revenue as Revenues until 2018 and as RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax after the ASC 606 accounting change. Query one tag and you get a series that stops or starts in the middle. NVIDIA reports capex as PaymentsToAcquireProductiveAssets instead of the more common PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment.

Fiscal years aren't calendar years. Apple's fiscal 2023 ran 371 days (a 53-week year). Microsoft's ends in June, NVIDIA's in late January.

Annual and quarterly values live side by side. A 10-K also contains Q4-only values for some items, and a 10-Q contains year-to-date numbers. They all share the same tag.

The same period gets restated. A value first reported in 2023 can be refiled in 2024 with a correction. You want the latest one.

What actually works

Ignore fy. For each value, look at the period itself:

  1. If it has a start, measure the duration. About 365 days (350 to 380, to cover 52/53-week years) is annual. About 90 days is a quarter. Anything else (year-to-date, 6 or 9 months) gets dropped.
  2. If it has no start, it's a balance-sheet snapshot. Classify it by the form that reported it: 10-K means annual, 10-Q means quarterly.
  3. Key each value by its period end date and keep the one with the latest filed date.
  4. For each metric, try a list of tags in priority order and merge them by period, so a tag switch doesn't leave a hole.

Done that way, Apple's last five fiscal years come out right:

Fiscal year end Revenue Net income Free cash flow Net margin
2025-09-27 $416.2B $112.0B $98.8B 26.9%
2024-09-28 $391.0B $93.7B $108.8B 24.0%
2023-09-30 $383.3B $97.0B $99.6B 25.3%
2022-09-24 $394.3B $99.8B $111.4B 25.3%
2021-09-25 $365.8B $94.7B $93.0B 25.9%

And NVIDIA's last five years, which make a nicer chart:

Fiscal year end Revenue Net income
2026-01-25 $215.9B $120.1B
2025-01-26 $130.5B $72.9B
2024-01-28 $60.9B $29.8B
2023-01-29 $27.0B $4.4B
2022-01-30 $26.9B $9.8B

The short version in Python

If you'd rather not maintain the tag lists and period logic yourself, I packaged all of the above into an Apify Actor: SEC EDGAR Filings & Financials. You pass tickers, it returns normalized annual and quarterly statements plus the company's recent filings with document links.

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")

run = client.actor("ninja.dev/sec-edgar-filings-financials").call(run_input={
    "companies": ["AAPL", "MSFT", "NVDA"],
    "maxFilingsPerCompany": 0,   # financials only
    "financialYears": 5,
    "financialQuarters": 4,
})

for row in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if row["recordType"] != "financials":
        continue
    for year in row["annual"]:
        print(row["ticker"], year["periodEnd"], year["revenue"], year["netIncome"], year.get("freeCashFlow"))

Each annual or quarterly row has revenue, gross profit, operating income, net income, EPS (basic and diluted), operating cash flow, capex, free cash flow, R&D, assets, liabilities, equity, cash, long-term debt and the three margins.

It also does full-text search across every filing since 2001 ("fullTextQuery": "\"going concern\""), which is handy for screening.

Doing it yourself

If you build your own pipeline instead, two practical notes from the SEC's side: send a User-Agent with a contact email, and stay under 10 requests per second. They block clients that don't.

And whatever you do, don't filter on fy.

title: Good Onboarding Starts Before Sign-Up: My Take on AviorSwap
description:
As a developer, I often think about onboarding as something that happens after registration.

There’s a welcome screen, maybe a checklist, and a few tooltips explaining where to click.

But as a user, I start forming my understanding much earlier. The homepage is already teaching me how to think about the product.

That’s what I appreciate about AviorSwap’s presentation: it gives me a straightforward introduction to what the platform is for and how to get started.

Give me a direction first

When I explore a new service, I don’t need to understand every feature immediately. I need a useful starting point.

AviorSwap makes deposit and swap actions visible early in the experience. For me, that establishes a clear direction.

I can identify the main activities without first learning a complicated navigation structure.

This is a design decision I respect because it requires prioritization. Every product has multiple things it could highlight. Choosing the actions that best explain its purpose helps a new visitor get oriented.

Let curiosity be part of the experience

I don’t always arrive at a platform ready to perform a specific action. Sometimes I just want to explore.

AviorSwap’s market sections, including popular assets and daily movers, give that curiosity somewhere to go.

I like this combination: a clear path for task-focused users and an entry point for people who are still getting familiar with the service.

It reminds me of good documentation. Sometimes I need a specific command. Sometimes I need an overview that helps me decide what to investigate next.

Both are valid ways to begin.

Explain the sequence in everyday language

One part of the public website I appreciate is the FAQ’s description of the onboarding process.

It outlines the progression from creating an account to setting up a wallet, depositing cryptocurrency, and exchanging assets.

Knowing the sequence helps me build expectations. I can understand how one step connects to the next before entering the workflow.

As developers, we spend so much time inside our products that we can forget how valuable this basic explanation is.

A new user shouldn’t need to reverse-engineer the journey from button labels.

Make the important topics easy to find

AviorSwap also puts pricing and fees near the center of its messaging.

I see that as a positive presentation choice. Costs are naturally part of how someone evaluates an exchange, so they deserve a visible place in the introduction.

When I design interfaces, I try to ask: what question is the user likely to have at this point?

Putting relevant information near the moment that question appears is one of the most useful things an interface can do.

What I’d bring into my own work

My impressions come from exploring AviorSwap’s public website. The aspect that stands out to me is how its presentation introduces the service through recognizable actions and short explanations.

It’s a useful reminder that onboarding includes everything a user sees while deciding whether a product makes sense to them.

For my own projects, I’d carry forward three ideas:

Make the primary action easy to recognize.

Give curious visitors something meaningful to explore.

Explain the overall process before asking users to navigate it.

That’s why AviorSwap’s approach appeals to me. It brings attention to the early moments when a visitor is becoming a user—and those moments deserve thoughtful design.

What’s the best onboarding decision you’ve borrowed from another product?

title: Why AviorSwap’s Focus on Simplicity Appeals to Me as a Developer
description:
I appreciate products that make their purpose easy to understand.

When I open a new platform, I want to answer three questions quickly: What can I do here? Where should I start? What information will help me take the next step?

Looking through AviorSwap’s public website, I found myself thinking about those questions from both a user’s and a developer’s perspective.

What appeals to me is its focus on making the exchange experience approachable.

Clear actions make a good first impression

AviorSwap gives deposit and swap actions a prominent place in its interface.

That sounds like a small detail, but navigation shapes the entire first impression of a product. When the main actions are easy to identify, I can spend more time understanding the service and less time searching through menus.

As a developer, I appreciate that kind of prioritization.

A homepage has limited attention to work with. Giving the core workflow room to stand out is a design choice I value.

Room to explore before taking action

I also like the combination of market discovery and direct actions.

The homepage includes sections for popular assets and daily market movements. That gives the experience a useful starting point even when I’m simply browsing.

Sometimes I approach a platform with a specific task. Other times, I want to get a sense of what’s available before deciding where to go next.

An interface that supports both approaches feels more welcoming to me.

It’s a principle I’d happily carry into my own projects: make the main action obvious, while leaving space for exploration.

Explaining the workflow helps users get oriented

AviorSwap’s FAQ outlines a sequence involving registration, wallet setup, a deposit, and an exchange.

I appreciate seeing the process described in plain language. It helps me form a basic picture of the workflow before stepping into it.

This is something we can underestimate as developers. Once we understand a system, its sequence starts to feel obvious. A new user doesn’t have that background.

A short explanation can make a product easier to approach without requiring a lengthy tutorial.

Pricing deserves a visible place

Another aspect I like is the attention given to pricing in the website’s messaging.

AviorSwap presents clear fees and competitive rates as priorities. Those are the right topics to put in front of someone evaluating an exchange service.

For me, this is about helping users focus on the information that matters to their decision. I want the discussion of costs to be part of the main experience.

My impressions here come from the public website, so I’m describing its presentation rather than claiming verified execution speeds or trading results.

A useful reminder for my own projects

What I take away from AviorSwap is an appreciation for focused product presentation.

Visible actions, opportunities to explore, and accessible explanations all contribute to how I understand a service. They’re also choices that apply well beyond crypto—to dashboards, developer tools, and everyday web applications.

As a potential user, I find that approach inviting. As a developer, it reminds me to give the basics the attention they deserve.

What’s one interface detail that immediately gives you a positive first impression of a new product?

title: I read 800 recent reviews of the top habit tracker apps. Paywalls are the #1 complaint.
description:
Every habit tracker in the top search results has a rating between 4.3 and 4.95 stars. If you're thinking about building one, that looks like a market with no room left.

The star rating is an all-time average, though. Some of these apps have millions of ratings collected over years. A rough few months barely moves that number, so I wanted to see what people are saying right now.

I pulled the 100 most recent reviews for the top 4 results for "habit tracker" on both the App Store and Google Play. That's 8 apps and 800 reviews.

The numbers

Store App Store rating Avg of last 100 reviews 1–2 star share
App Store Habit Tracker 4.79 4.03 22%
App Store HabitKit 4.84 4.48 10%
App Store Onrise 4.84 4.40 6%
App Store Finch: Self-Care Pet 4.95 4.68 5%
Google Play Loop Habit Tracker 4.72 4.84 1%
Google Play HabitNow 4.74 4.60 5%
Google Play Disciplined 4.29 4.26 11%
Google Play HabitKit 4.55 3.85 20%

Two apps show a real gap. Habit Tracker on iOS sits at 4.79 overall but its recent reviews average 4.03, and more than one in five is a 1 or 2. HabitKit on Android drops from 4.55 to 3.85.

Loop is the opposite case. It's open source, completely free, and its recent reviews are better than its lifetime average.

What the angry reviews are about

Out of 800 reviews, 80 were 1 or 2 stars. I tagged them by topic (a review can hit more than one):

Complaint Reviews
Subscription, paywall, paid features 22
Bugs and crashes 12
Sync problems or lost data 10
Widgets 9
Reminders and notifications 5
Ads 1

Ads barely show up. Money does. A few real examples:

  • "paywalled at 3 habits"
  • "must pay to track more than 4"
  • "i paid for the family premium but it didn't work"
  • "i bought the premium version a year ago and when they updated i lost everything"

The pattern is people who paid and then lost data or features, or who hit a wall at habit number 3 or 4 and felt tricked. The widget complaints are a smaller version of the same story: someone paid for Pro and the widget still shows "subscribe to pro".

So is there room for another habit tracker?

Based on this, I'd look at:

  1. A generous free tier. Unlimited habits for free is the main thing people are mad about losing, and Loop shows it earns goodwill.
  2. Boring reliability around sync and backups. Losing a 200-day streak is how you get a 1-star review that never gets edited.
  3. Widgets that work on day one, since they're the main way people interact with these apps.

800 reviews is a small sample, so treat this as a starting point for your own research.

How I got the data

I used an Apify Actor I built that scrapes both stores into one format: App Store & Google Play Scraper. Apple data comes from Apple's official iTunes Search API and review feed; Google Play uses the open-source google-play-scraper library.

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")

run = client.actor("ninja.dev/app-store-google-play").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": ["habit tracker"],
    "store": "both",
    "maxSearchResults": 4,
    "maxReviewsPerApp": 100,
})

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
apps = [r for r in rows if r["recordType"] == "app"]
reviews = [r for r in rows if r["recordType"] == "review"]

for app in apps:
    s = app["reviewStats"]
    print(app["store"], app["title"], app["rating"], "->", s["averageRating"], f'{s["negativeShare"]:.0%}')

Every app row already includes reviewStats (average of the fetched reviews, star distribution and share of 1–2 star reviews), so the table above is one loop. For the complaint tagging I used a few regexes over the 1–2 star texts. An LLM would do a nicer job if you want to go deeper.

Swap "habit tracker" for whatever category you're eyeing and you'll get the same picture for your niche in a couple of minutes.
