title: Adavanced React Hooks
description:
Advanced React Hooks

React provides several hooks to help developers manage complex state and optimize component performance. Three useful hooks are useReducer, useMemo, and useCallback. Although they serve different purposes, they help make React applications more predictable, efficient, and easier to maintain.

1. useReducer — Managing Complex State

The useReducer hook is an alternative to useState. It is especially useful when state updates involve multiple actions or complex logic.

Example: Counter using useReducer

import { useReducer } from "react";

function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "increment":
      return { count: state.count + 1 };
    case "decrement":
      return { count: state.count - 1 };
    case "reset":
      return { count: 0 };
    default:
      return state;
  }
}

function Counter() {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { count: 0 });

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Count: {state.count}</h2>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "increment" })}>
        Increment
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "decrement" })}>
        Decrement
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "reset" })}>
        Reset
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

How it works: The reducer function determines how the state changes based on an action. The dispatch function sends an action to the reducer, which returns the next state.

When to use it: Use useReducer when state has multiple related values, several update actions, or logic that becomes difficult to manage with multiple useState calls.

2. useMemo — Caching Expensive Calculations

The useMemo hook caches the result of a calculation between renders. React recalculates the value when one of its dependencies changes.

Example: Calculating a total

import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

function ShoppingCart() {
  const [price, setPrice] = useState(100);
  const [quantity, setQuantity] = useState(2);

  const total = useMemo(() => {
    console.log("Calculating total...");
    return price * quantity;
  }, [price, quantity]);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Total: ₹{total}</h2>
      <button onClick={() => setPrice(price + 10)}>
        Increase Price
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => setQuantity(quantity + 1)}>
        Increase Quantity
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

How it works: React recalculates total when price or quantity changes. If the component renders again without either dependency changing, React can reuse the cached result.

When to use it: Use useMemo for expensive calculations or when maintaining a stable object or value can prevent unnecessary work. For simple calculations, it is usually unnecessary.

3. useCallback — Caching Function References

The useCallback hook caches a function reference between renders until its dependencies change. It is particularly useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components.

Example: Handling a button click

import { useCallback, useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  const increment = useCallback(() => {
    setCount((previous) => previous + 1);
  }, []);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
      <button onClick={increment}>Increment</button>
    </div>
  );
}

How it works: React reuses the same increment function reference across renders because its dependency list is empty. The functional state update ensures the callback uses the latest state without needing count as a dependency.

When to use it: Use useCallback when a stable function reference helps avoid unnecessary renders in memoized child components or when a function is a dependency of another hook. It is not necessary for every event handler.

Conclusion

These three React hooks solve different problems:

  • useReducer manages state transitions through a reducer function and dispatched actions.
  • useMemo caches the result of a calculation.
  • useCallback caches a function reference.

Understanding when to use each hook helps you write cleaner React code and optimize performance when necessary. However, these hooks are optimization and state-management tools, not requirements for every component. Start with simple solutions, measure performance when needed, and introduce advanced hooks where they provide a clear benefit.

title: Best Databricks Metric Views Tools: dbt Semantic Layer, Cube & MetricFlow Compared
description:
Metric views are suddenly a big deal on Databricks. Unity Catalog now has a native way to define measures and dimensions as governed objects, and every semantic-layer vendor is racing to plug into it. That's great news if you're tired of three different dashboards reporting three different numbers for "active customers." It's also a bit of a mess, because the ecosystem splintered overnight.

I spent time working through the main contenders: Databricks' own Metric Views, dbt's Semantic Layer, Cube, MetricFlow, AtScale, and a visual modeling platform called SqlDBM that solves a problem the others don't even acknowledge. If you've ever had a metric definition silently break because somebody renamed a column upstream, you already know what I mean.

Below I've ranked them based on how well they actually help you ship trustworthy metrics on Databricks, not just define them in YAML.

How I Evaluated These Platforms

I looked at native integration with Databricks and Unity Catalog, how well each tool handles the physical-to-semantic bridge (because metric views are only as good as the schemas underneath), performance features like caching and pre-aggregation, support for AI agents and MCP, pricing clarity, and the honest trade-offs each tool makes. I also weighed enterprise proof points and how each handles schema change over time, which is where most metric definitions quietly rot.

1. SqlDBM - Best Overall

The governed foundation your Databricks metric views are missing: visual modeling meets the semantic layer in one workspace.

When I started testing tools for Databricks metric views, I kept hitting the same wall. Standalone semantic-layer tools like dbt's Semantic Layer, Cube, and MetricFlow let you define metrics beautifully, but they have no idea what the physical schema underneath actually looks like. Rename a column, refactor a join, change a table, and your metric definitions silently break. That's the exact gap SqlDBM fills, and it's why I'm putting it at the top.

SqlDBM is a cloud-native, code-free data modeling platform and a Databricks Validated Data Partner that plugs directly into Unity Catalog. You can reverse- and forward-engineer Delta Lake objects, track column-level lineage, and visually govern every schema your metric views depend on. What makes it uniquely relevant here is the semantic modeling layer. SqlDBM lets data teams define semantic views that layer business context onto physical warehouse schemas, giving BI tools, dbt models, and AI systems one governed definition of what your data actually means.

Here's the key insight. Standalone semantic-layer tools (dbt, Cube, AtScale) skip visual modeling. Visual modeling tools (erwin, ER/Studio, Hackolade) skip the semantic layer. SqlDBM is the only platform that bridges both. It grounds semantic models in a governed physical foundation and automatically propagates schema changes so metric definitions stay accurate as your lakehouse evolves.

The real-world Databricks proof is what sold me. John Holland Group, one of Australia's largest infrastructure firms, completed its Databricks cloud migration in nine months using SqlDBM as the authoritative source for gold-layer models. Mercadona, Spain's largest supermarket chain, governs nearly 5,000 tables in SqlDBM and uses the SqlDBM API to auto-generate dbt models. That's exactly the semantic-to-physical pipeline that makes metric views trustworthy at scale.

With 400,000+ users globally, enterprise customers like DocuSign, Pfizer, and Zendesk, and back-to-back Database Modeling Solution of the Year wins at the 2023 and 2024 Data Breakthrough Awards, the credibility is there. Real-time collaboration means multiple modelers can refine semantic definitions in parallel without stepping on each other.

Pros:

  • Only visual modeling platform that bridges physical modeling and a semantic layer for Databricks, giving metric views, dbt models, and AI systems one governed definition while automatically propagating schema changes.
  • Native Databricks Unity Catalog integration with full reverse/forward engineering and column-level lineage, so metric view definitions start from governed, documented schemas rather than guesswork.
  • Enterprise-proven at Databricks scale: John Holland Group completed a nine-month Databricks migration with SqlDBM as the single source of truth, and Mercadona governs nearly 5,000 tables while auto-generating dbt models via the SqlDBM API.
  • Real-time multi-user collaboration with branch-and-merge, so teams can define and refine semantic layers in parallel without conflicts.
  • Databricks Validated Data Partner with an MCP Server that exposes governed models to LLMs, future-proofing metric views for AI agents and Genie.

Cons:

  • Full semantic modeling capabilities live in the higher-tier Context Layer plan, so teams on the free tier will want to upgrade to unlock the complete metric-view governance workflow.
  • If your stack is 100% code-first with zero visual modeling needs, the visual-first approach may feel like an extra step before the governance payoff kicks in.

Pricing: SqlDBM plans are quote-based and scale to team size, with enterprise packaging, premium support, and security options available. There's a free tier to start modeling and explore the platform before committing, no credit card required. Contact sales for a tailored quote.

2. Databricks Unity Catalog Metric Views

Metric Views are Databricks' built-in way to define business metrics inside Unity Catalog. They separate measure definitions (revenue, active customers) from the dimensions used to group and filter them. You define metrics in YAML on top of a source table or view, and they get registered as governed Unity Catalog objects. That means they inherit the same permissions, lineage, and discoverability as every other UC asset.

Once defined, the same metrics can be queried from Databricks SQL, AI/BI dashboards, alerts, Genie spaces, and external BI tools connected to Databricks. Because the metrics live in the lakehouse, there's no extra service to run and no data leaves the platform. For teams already all-in on Databricks, this is the lowest-friction option by a wide margin.

The trade-off is portability. Definitions are tied to Databricks, and third-party docs still describe the feature as beta or public preview depending on the source. It also lacks the caching and pre-aggregation options that dedicated semantic platforms offer. Third parties like Cube and AtScale are building integrations that read from or publish into Metric Views, so you can combine approaches if needed.

Pros:

  • Native to Unity Catalog, so metrics inherit existing governance, permissions, and lineage.
  • No separate infrastructure or vendor to buy; works directly with Databricks SQL, dashboards, and Genie.
  • Defined once and reusable across BI, SQL, and AI/agent use cases.
  • Third-party layers like Cube and AtScale are adding integrations, so it can complement other tools.

Cons:

  • Definitions are tied to Databricks and not portable to other warehouses.
  • Relatively new; some sources still describe it as preview/beta, and it requires a recent Databricks Runtime (16.4+ per community docs).
  • Fewer downstream integrations and caching/pre-aggregation options than dedicated semantic-layer platforms.

Pricing: No separate license fee that I found. Metric Views are a Unity Catalog feature, and you pay standard Databricks compute (SQL warehouse/cluster) costs when querying them. Pricing follows your Databricks contract.

3. dbt Semantic Layer

The dbt Semantic Layer lets teams define metrics centrally in YAML inside their dbt project, using the MetricFlow framework underneath. It then serves those metrics through APIs and integrations with downstream tools. It dynamically generates SQL to compute metrics on the fly, and offers first-class integrations with BI and analytics platforms.

MetricFlow supports Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, and Postgres (on dbt v1 only). That makes the Semantic Layer a solid fit for teams already modeling transformations in dbt who want their metric definitions version-controlled next to their models. It's part of the paid dbt platform (formerly dbt Cloud), and the free Developer plan doesn't include it.

Compute still runs in your warehouse, so there's no dedicated pre-aggregation store. Latency depends on your Databricks SQL warehouse performance, and caching is Enterprise-tier only. Third-party comparisons also note that usage is metered by queried metrics, which can get costly at scale. It suits analytics engineering teams that want a vendor-neutral, code-first approach not tied to one warehouse.

Pros:

  • Code-first metrics live in the same dbt project and Git workflow as your transformations.
  • Works across several warehouses, including Databricks.
  • Broad BI and tool integrations, with growing AI/MCP support.
  • Backed by MetricFlow, which is now open source.

Cons:

  • Requires a paid dbt platform plan; the free Developer plan excludes the Semantic Layer.
  • No dedicated pre-aggregation or caching layer, so performance depends on the warehouse (caching is Enterprise-only).
  • Metered queried-metrics limits and per-seat pricing can get expensive at scale.

Pricing: The dbt platform's Developer plan is free but excludes the Semantic Layer. The Starter plan is listed around $100 per user per month, and Enterprise/Enterprise+ are custom-quoted (figures reported by third-party comparison sites; confirm on dbt's pricing page).

4. Cube (Cube Cloud / Cube Core)

Cube is a headless semantic layer that connects to cloud warehouses and lakehouses, including Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift, and Postgres. Teams model metrics once, and Cube exposes them through SQL, REST, GraphQL, and MDX APIs, plus the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents. Unlike purely warehouse-side approaches, Cube includes caching and pre-aggregations (Cube Store) for faster queries. That matters for customer-facing and embedded analytics.

Cube Core is open source under Apache 2.0, and Cube Cloud is the managed commercial platform. Cube Cloud adds a semantic-model IDE, workbooks and dashboards, AI agents, and enterprise security. Cube has also built a Databricks Metric View integration, currently in preview, that publishes selected Cube views as native Databricks Metric Views. It lets teams keep Cube as the modeling layer while exposing governed metrics inside Unity Catalog, though the integration needs to be activated through Cube support.

Cube suits data engineering teams that want an independent, API-first layer with real performance features. The trade-off is operating another platform with its own modeling language.

Pros:

  • Open-source Cube Core (Apache 2.0) plus a managed cloud option.
  • Many APIs (SQL, REST, GraphQL, MDX) and MCP support for AI agents.
  • Pre-aggregations and caching improve query performance and cost.
  • Preview integration to publish Cube views as native Databricks Metric Views.

Cons:

  • The Databricks Metric View publication is in preview and needs activation by Cube support, and some model features aren't supported (for example dynamic JavaScript/Jinja models).
  • Another platform to learn and operate, with its own modeling language, alongside your warehouse.
  • Cloud pricing combines per-seat and metered infrastructure costs, which can be hard to predict.

Pricing: Cube Cloud has a free plan (five workbooks, 1,000 daily query requests). Starter is $40 per developer per month and Premium is $80 per developer per month, with Explorer seats at $40 and Viewer seats at $20. Enterprise is custom-priced. Cube Core is free and self-hosted (Apache 2.0). Figures are from third-party listings, so verify on Cube's pricing page.

5. MetricFlow (open source)

MetricFlow is the semantic-layer engine from dbt Labs that compiles metric definitions into reusable SQL. It uses semantic model and metric YAML configurations to construct and run SQL against your data platform. dbt Labs acquired it through its 2023 acquisition of Transform.

At Coalesce 2025, dbt Labs announced it was moving MetricFlow to the Apache 2.0 license (earlier versions, 0 to 0.140.0, were under AGPL). It was contributed as a reference implementation for the Open Semantic Interchange (OSI) effort. The docs state it works with Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres (dbt v1 only), and Redshift.

Teams can use it directly or through the paid dbt Semantic Layer, which adds hosted APIs, BI integrations, and governance features. On its own, MetricFlow is a solid fit for engineering-led teams that want a free, code-first, portable way to define metrics and are comfortable running the infrastructure themselves. Just keep in mind it isn't a managed platform. The hosted APIs and many integrations belong to the paid dbt Semantic Layer.

Pros:

  • Free and open source under Apache 2.0.
  • Portable metric definitions in YAML that live in Git.
  • Works with Databricks and several other warehouses.
  • Part of the Open Semantic Interchange effort, which aims at semantic portability.

Cons:

  • The hosted APIs, caching, and many BI integrations require the paid dbt Semantic Layer.
  • You run and maintain it yourself, and it needs dbt expertise.
  • Not a native Databricks object, so metrics aren't governed in Unity Catalog the way Metric Views are.

Pricing: Free to use under the Apache 2.0 license. The managed dbt Semantic Layer that builds on it requires a paid dbt platform plan (see dbt Semantic Layer).

6. AtScale

AtScale is a proprietary semantic-layer platform aimed at large enterprises. It integrates with Snowflake, Databricks, and Google BigQuery, and with tools like Tableau, Power BI, Excel, and Python. It acts as a governed semantic layer between the warehouse and consuming tools, so metrics are defined once and exposed consistently to BI users, data scientists, and AI agents.

On Databricks, AtScale positions itself as part of a "semantic lakehouse" approach. It's a launch partner for Unity Catalog metrics and has announced bi-directional read and write with Unity Catalog metric definitions. It also offers an MCP server on the Databricks Marketplace to give AI agents access to governed metrics.

AtScale is aimed at large organizations with many BI tools and multidimensional or Excel-heavy analytics needs. It's a stronger fit there than lighter, code-first options. Being a commercial enterprise product means a sales-led procurement process and, in most cases, maintaining a second set of metric definitions separate from your dbt or Databricks code.

Pros:

  • Deep Databricks partnership, including Unity Catalog metric interoperability.
  • Broad BI and analytics tool support (Tableau, Power BI, Excel, Python).
  • Enterprise-oriented governance and an AI/MCP server for agents.
  • Vendor-independent layer that isn't tied to a single warehouse.

Cons:

  • Proprietary and sales-led, with no open-source core.
  • Likely heavier to deploy and costlier than code-first options for small teams.
  • Modeling is separate from your dbt or Databricks code, so teams may maintain a second set of definitions.

Pricing: I couldn't find public pricing. AtScale appears to be sold as a custom enterprise subscription, so contact AtScale for a quote.

Final Verdict

If you're all-in on Databricks and want the simplest path, native Unity Catalog Metric Views are the obvious starting point. If you're a dbt shop that values code-first portability, the dbt Semantic Layer or MetricFlow make sense. Cube is the strongest pick for embedded analytics with real caching. AtScale is for enterprises with heavy BI and Excel footprints.

But here's the thing none of those tools solve. Metric definitions are only trustworthy if the schemas underneath them are governed, documented, and don't silently change on you. That's why SqlDBM is my top pick. It's the only platform I found that bridges visual physical modeling and a true semantic layer in one workspace, with native Databricks Unity Catalog integration, column-level lineage, and real-time collaboration. The customer stories at John Holland Group and Mercadona show it works at serious scale, and the MCP Server means your governed models are ready for the AI agent era.

For most teams building metric views on Databricks, SqlDBM is the foundation that makes everything else on this list more reliable.

FAQ

Can I use SqlDBM alongside Databricks Metric Views and dbt?
Yes. SqlDBM sits upstream as the governed modeling foundation. You can define semantic views in SqlDBM, publish schemas into Databricks via Unity Catalog, and even auto-generate dbt models through the SqlDBM API, which is exactly what Mercadona does.

Are Databricks Metric Views production-ready?
Depending on the source, Metric Views are described as public preview or beta and require Databricks Runtime 16.4+. Check Databricks' official docs for the current release status before standardizing on them.

What's the difference between MetricFlow and the dbt Semantic Layer?
MetricFlow is the open-source engine (Apache 2.0) that compiles YAML metric definitions into SQL. The dbt Semantic Layer is the paid managed service built on top of MetricFlow, adding hosted APIs, BI integrations, and governance features.

Do I need a semantic layer if I already use Unity Catalog Metric Views?
Not necessarily. If you're Databricks-only and your BI needs are modest, native Metric Views may be enough. If you need multi-warehouse portability, pre-aggregation performance, or richer API access for embedded or AI use cases, a dedicated semantic layer like Cube or AtScale is worth considering, with SqlDBM providing the governed physical foundation underneath.

title: Faisal Khan — Blockchain Developer (Solidity, React)
description:
Faisal Khan — Blockchain Developer (Solidity, React)

Hi, I'm Faisal Khan — a blockchain developer from Peshawar, Pakistan, working with Solidity and React. I write smart contracts and build the dApp frontends that let real people use them.

What I do

My focus is the EVM stack: Solidity for smart contracts, Foundry for testing and deployment workflows, OpenZeppelin for audited building blocks, and React for the frontend layer. I like the full loop — writing a contract, testing it thoroughly, then shipping a clean Web3 UI that anyone can open in a browser and use.

My work revolves around two areas:

Solidity smart contracts. On-chain apps, contract security patterns, and the Foundry + OpenZeppelin toolchain. I also write about what I learn — my portfolio has articles on building an on-chain voting dApp in Solidity, five smart contract security patterns every beginner should know, and what React developers can carry over into Solidity.

React dApps. The other half of the stack. A smart contract is only half a product — the frontend is where users meet the chain. I build React frontends wired up to Web3, so the contracts I write are actually usable, not just code sitting in a repo.

Why Solidity + React

Most developers pick a side — contracts or frontend. I picked both, because the interesting problems live at the boundary: how a user clicks "vote" in a browser and that click becomes an immutable on-chain transaction seconds later. Understanding both sides makes each side better. My React experience shapes how I design contract interfaces, and writing Solidity changes how I think about state, cost, and trust on the frontend.

What I'm building

A few repos I'm actively working on:

  • VotingSystem-DApp — an on-chain voting dApp written in Solidity, with a React frontend. Voting logic lives on-chain so every vote is transparent and verifiable. (github.com/MFaisaltech/VotingSystem-DApp)
  • Smart-Contract-Inspector — a project focused on inspecting and analyzing smart contracts, born out of my interest in contract security. (github.com/MFaisaltech/Smart-Contract-Inspector)
  • solidity — my working collection of Solidity code: experiments, patterns, and practice contracts. (github.com/MFaisaltech/solidity)

Everything is open source on my GitHub: https://github.com/MFaisaltech

The toolchain I use

  • Solidity — the contract language itself. I write with readability first: named functions, clear state layout, and comments that explain the why, not just the what.
  • Foundry — my testing and deployment setup. I test everything: happy paths, edge cases, and the attack paths I'm trying to close. A contract I can't test is a contract I don't ship.
  • OpenZeppelin — audited building blocks instead of reinvented wheels.
  • React + Web3 — the frontend layer. Wallets, transaction states, loading spinners that respect pending transactions — the unglamorous details that decide whether a dApp feels usable or broken.

What I'm writing

I write about Solidity and Web3 development — practical, beginner-friendly, and grounded in code I actually ran. Topics I cover: building dApps in Solidity, smart contract security patterns, and the React-to-Solidity learning path.

Portfolio: https://v0-faisal-khan-blockchain.vercel.app/
X: https://x.com/FaisalOn_AI
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/faisal-khan-9658002a8/

What's next

Short term: more Solidity repos, deeper work on contract security, and continuing to document everything in public. Long term: I want to be the kind of blockchain developer whose code people can read, learn from, and trust — open source first, always.

If you're learning Solidity, building dApps, or just curious about the space — follow along. I'm building in public.

title: Graceful Shutdown in Node.js: Preventing Dropped Requests and Broken Database Transactions
description:
Every time you deploy, autoscale, or restart a node, your orchestrator does the same thing to your app: it asks it to stop.

If your app handles that request well, nobody notices. If it doesn't, you get a brief spike of 502s on every release, users who got "payment failed" on a payment that actually went through, background jobs that ran twice, and database transactions cut off mid-flight.

The frustrating part is that it's easy to miss. Locally you press Ctrl-C and the process dies instantly, with no one watching. In production, with real traffic, the same behavior drops real requests.

This post covers how to shut a Node.js service down gracefully: stop taking new work, finish the work in flight, release resources in the right order, and exit before the orchestrator loses patience.

What actually happens when your app is stopped

On Docker, Kubernetes, ECS, systemd, and most platforms, stopping a process is a two-step sequence:

  1. The platform sends SIGTERM: "please shut down."
  2. After a grace period, if you're still running, it sends SIGKILL, which can't be caught or handled. The process is gone immediately.
Platform Default grace period
Docker (docker stop) 10 seconds (--stop-timeout / stop_grace_period to change)
Kubernetes 30 seconds (terminationGracePeriodSeconds)

The grace period is your time budget. Everything in this post has to fit inside it.

If you don't handle SIGTERM, Node's default behavior is to exit immediately. Every in-flight request is cut mid-response, and every open transaction loses its connection.

(Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which behaves similarly, so handle both.)

Failure mode 1: The naive version 

// ❌ No signal handling at all
const server = app.listen(3000);

On deploy, in-flight requests are severed. Clients see ECONNRESET or a 502 from the load balancer.

The first fix everyone tries:

// ⚠️ Better, but still wrong
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close();
  process.exit(0);   // kills everything still in flight, immediately
});

server.close() stops accepting new connections, but process.exit(0) on the next line terminates the process before any in-flight request can finish. This is the most common "I handle SIGTERM" bug.

The correct shutdown sequence

Order matters. The principle is: stop work coming in, let work in progress finish, then tear down what that work depended on, and not before.

SIGTERM
  │
  1. Mark unready          → load balancer stops sending new traffic
  2. Wait briefly          → let routing updates propagate
  3. Stop accepting HTTP   → server.close(), close idle keep-alive connections
  4. Drain in-flight work  → requests finish (with a deadline)
  5. Stop background work  → job workers, queue consumers, cron
  6. Close dependencies    → DB pool, Redis, tracing/log flush
  7. Exit                  → code 0 if clean, 1 if forced

Closing the database pool at step 6 and not step 3 is the key insight for transactions: requests that are still running need their connections.

Step 1 and 2: Fail readiness first, then wait

On Kubernetes, termination is not a clean sequence. When a pod is deleted, two things happen concurrently: the pod is removed from Service endpoints, and the container receives SIGTERM. Routing updates take a moment to reach every proxy and load balancer. If you close your listener the instant SIGTERM arrives, some traffic is still being routed to you and hits a closed port.

The fix is to make your app report not ready, then pause briefly before closing the listener.

let shuttingDown = false;

app.get('/healthz', (_req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));            // liveness: process is alive
app.get('/readyz', (_req, res) => res.sendStatus(shuttingDown ? 503 : 200)); // readiness

You can do the pause in the app (await sleep(5000) before server.close()), or with a Kubernetes preStop hook:

lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["sleep", "5"]

Either works. Just make sure it's counted in your time budget (see below).

Step 3 and 4: Stop accepting, drain in-flight requests

Node's server.close() stops the server from accepting new connections and fires its callback once all existing connections have ended. Two details trip people up:

HTTP keep-alive. Idle keep-alive connections count as open connections, so close() can appear to hang until they time out. In Node 19+, server.close() closes idle connections for you. On Node 18.2+, call server.closeIdleConnections() explicitly. For connections that are busy during shutdown, tell clients not to reuse them by sending Connection: close on responses:

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (shuttingDown) res.set('Connection', 'close');
  next();
});

A hard deadline. One stuck request (a client that never finishes reading) would hold shutdown open until SIGKILL. Set your own deadline, a bit shorter than the platform's, and force-close the stragglers when it hits:

function closeServer(server: http.Server, deadlineMs: number): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const force = setTimeout(() => {
      log.warn('HTTP drain deadline hit; closing remaining connections');
      server.closeAllConnections?.();             // Node 18.2+
    }, deadlineMs);

    server.close((err) => {
      clearTimeout(force);
      err ? reject(err) : resolve();
    });
    server.closeIdleConnections?.();              // Node 18.2+ (no-op need on 19+)
  });
}

Long-lived connections need special handling. server.close() doesn't close WebSockets or SSE streams for you. Track them and close them explicitly (for WebSockets, send a close frame with code 1001, "going away", so clients know to reconnect elsewhere).

Step 5: Stop background work

If the same process runs queue workers or consumers, stop them before closing the resources they use.

import { Worker } from 'bullmq';

// worker.close() waits for currently active jobs to finish by default
await worker.close();

With BullMQ, worker.close() stops fetching new jobs and waits for active ones to complete. If a job outlasts your grace period and the process is killed, BullMQ will eventually consider that job stalled and retry it, which means your job handlers must be idempotent. Graceful shutdown reduces duplicate runs. It doesn't eliminate them. The same applies to any at-least-once consumer (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ): stop consuming, finish or negotiate the in-flight message, and commit or ack appropriately before disconnecting.

Stop timers and cron schedulers too, so no new work starts while you're draining.

Step 6: Close dependencies, and why order protects your transactions

Now that nothing is using them, close the shared resources.

await pool.end();          // pg: ends idle clients, and checked-out clients as they're released
await redis.quit();        // ioredis: graceful (waits for pending replies); disconnect() is abrupt
await otelSdk.shutdown();  // flush traces/metrics
await logger.flush?.();    // flush buffered logs, if your logger buffers

Why this order protects database transactions: a request in the middle of BEGIN ... COMMIT holds a checked-out connection. If you close the pool (or exit) first, that transaction is cut off. Because we waited for requests to drain in step 4, those transactions have committed or rolled back by the time we reach pool.end().

What if you are killed mid-transaction anyway (SIGKILL, OOM, node failure)? PostgreSQL has your back on atomicity: when the connection drops, the server rolls back the uncommitted transaction automatically. Your data won't be half-written inside the database.

The danger is everything outside the database. If the handler already charged a card, published a message, or sent an email before the commit, killing the process leaves the world in an inconsistent state: payment taken, no order recorded. Graceful shutdown narrows that window, but it can't close it. The durable fixes are:

  • Idempotency keys on external calls and on the endpoints themselves, so a retry is safe
  • The outbox pattern: write the event in the same transaction as the data, and publish it from a separate relay
  • Keeping transactions short, with no slow network calls inside them (which also protects your connection pool)

Don't let a deadline become a mid-commit kill

If drain is taking too long, you'd rather abort work cleanly than be SIGKILLed at a random point. Tie request work to a shutdown signal so handlers can stop and roll back on their own terms:

const shutdownController = new AbortController();

// in shutdown(), when the drain budget is nearly spent:
shutdownController.abort(new Error('server shutting down'));

// in a handler / withTransaction callback:
shutdownController.signal.throwIfAborted();   // before starting the next step

An explicit abort leads to an explicit ROLLBACK and a clean error response, which is always better than a severed connection.

Putting it together 

// server.ts
import http from 'node:http';
import express from 'express';

const GRACE_MS = Number(process.env.SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS ?? 25_000); // < platform grace period
const READINESS_DELAY_MS = Number(process.env.READINESS_DELAY_MS ?? 5_000);
const HTTP_DRAIN_MS = Number(process.env.HTTP_DRAIN_MS ?? 15_000);

const app = express();
let shuttingDown = false;

app.use((_req, res, next) => {
  if (shuttingDown) res.set('Connection', 'close');
  next();
});
app.get('/healthz', (_req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));
app.get('/readyz', (_req, res) => res.sendStatus(shuttingDown ? 503 : 200));
// ...your routes

const server = http.createServer(app).listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function shutdown(signal: string) {
  if (shuttingDown) {                       // second signal: operator is impatient, stop waiting
    log.warn({ signal }, 'second signal received; forcing exit');
    process.exit(1);
  }
  shuttingDown = true;
  log.info({ signal }, 'shutdown started');

  // Absolute backstop: never outlive the platform's grace period
  setTimeout(() => {
    log.error('graceful shutdown timed out; forcing exit');
    process.exit(1);
  }, GRACE_MS).unref();

  let exitCode = 0;
  try {
    await sleep(READINESS_DELAY_MS);              // 1-2. unready, let routing catch up
    await closeServer(server, HTTP_DRAIN_MS);     // 3-4. stop accepting, drain requests
    await worker.close();                         // 5.   finish active jobs
    await pool.end();                             // 6.   DB pool (nothing is using it now)
    await redis.quit();
    await otelSdk.shutdown();
    log.info('shutdown complete');
  } catch (err) {
    log.error({ err }, 'error during shutdown');
    exitCode = 1;
  }
  process.exit(exitCode);                         // 7.
}

process.on('SIGTERM', () => void shutdown('SIGTERM'));
process.on('SIGINT', () => void shutdown('SIGINT'));

Notes on the details:

  • process.exit() at the end is fine once cleanup is done. The problem earlier was calling it instead of cleanup. Without it, a stray open handle (a forgotten interval, a socket) can keep the process alive until SIGKILL.
  • The .unref() on the backstop timer means it never keeps the process alive by itself.
  • The second-signal guard makes Ctrl-C twice do what developers expect, and prevents running the shutdown sequence twice.

Crashes should shut down, too

An uncaughtException or unhandledRejection means your process is in an unknown state. Don't try to carry on, but do try to exit cleanly:

process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
  log.error({ reason }, 'unhandled rejection');
  void shutdown('unhandledRejection');
});
process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => {
  log.fatal({ err }, 'uncaught exception');
  void shutdown('uncaughtException');
});

For crash paths, consider a shorter drain budget and a non-zero exit code so your orchestrator records a failure.

Budget your time

The pieces must fit inside the platform's grace period. For a Kubernetes default of 30 seconds:

Phase Budget
Readiness delay / preStop 5s
HTTP drain 15s
Workers, pool, flush 5s
Safety margin 5s

Then set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to match what you actually need. If your longest legitimate request takes 60 seconds, a 30-second grace period guarantees you'll kill some of them, so either raise the grace period or shorten the work. And keep your in-app deadline (GRACE_MS) comfortably below the platform's.

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec: { command: ["sleep", "5"] }
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }

Container gotchas that silently break all of this

Signals never reach your app

This one is brutal because your shutdown code is perfect and never runs.

# ❌ npm and shell-wrapped commands often don't forward signals to node
CMD npm start

# ✅ exec form, running node directly
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

If npm or a shell is PID 1, SIGTERM goes to it, and it frequently doesn't pass it on. Docker then waits out the full grace period and SIGKILLs you. Use the exec form of CMD/ENTRYPOINT and run node directly (or use --init / tini as a minimal init process).

Node as PID 1

On Linux, PID 1 gets special treatment: signals without an explicit handler are ignored, not defaulted. Once you register process.on('SIGTERM', ...) this is fine, but it's another reason the handler must actually be installed.

Dev tooling

Watchers such as nodemon or tsx watch restart your process on file change using signals as well. They're good for exercising your shutdown path locally.

Frameworks and libraries that help

You don't have to hand-roll everything:

  • Fastify: await app.close() runs onClose hooks for plugins, and stops the server
  • NestJS: call app.enableShutdownHooks() and implement OnApplicationShutdown / OnModuleDestroy
  • http-terminator or stoppable: utilities that track connections for you and implement drain-with-deadline for plain http servers

Whatever you use, still verify the behavior with a test. Defaults vary by version.

Test it, don't trust it

Shutdown bugs only show up during deploys, so reproduce them on purpose. Spawn the real server, start a slow request, send SIGTERM, and check that the request completes and the process exits cleanly:

// shutdown.test.ts
import { spawn } from 'node:child_process';
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

it('finishes in-flight requests on SIGTERM, then exits 0', async () => {
  const child = spawn('node', ['dist/server.js'], {
    env: { ...process.env, PORT: '4123', READINESS_DELAY_MS: '0' },
    stdio: 'inherit',
  });
  const exited = new Promise<number | null>((resolve) => child.on('exit', resolve)); // attach before kill

  await waitForOk('http://localhost:4123/readyz');

  const slow = fetch('http://localhost:4123/slow?ms=2000');   // a test route that sleeps
  await sleep(200);                                           // make sure it's in flight
  child.kill('SIGTERM');

  const res = await slow;
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);                               // request was NOT dropped
  expect(await exited).toBe(0);                               // clean exit
});

it('exits non-zero if drain exceeds the deadline', async () => {
  // start with a tiny SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS, hit /slow?ms=60000, send SIGTERM,
  // and assert the process exits with code 1 well before 60s
});

For a stronger check, run a load test (autocannon, k6) against a staging deployment while performing a rolling restart, and watch for non-2xx responses. A well-behaved service shows zero errors during the roll.

Checklist

  • ✅ Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT; install the handlers before listening
  • ✅ Fail readiness first and pause briefly for routing to catch up
  • ✅ server.close() plus closing idle connections; send Connection: close while draining
  • ✅ Track and close WebSockets/SSE explicitly
  • ✅ Stop job workers and consumers before closing their dependencies
  • ✅ Close the DB pool and other clients after in-flight work has finished
  • ✅ Hard deadline shorter than the platform's grace period; force-exit beyond it
  • ✅ Idempotency and the outbox pattern for side effects outside the database
  • ✅ CMD ["node", ...] in exec form so signals reach your process
  • ✅ A test that sends SIGTERM mid-request

Key takeaways

  1. Deploys are shutdowns. Every release sends SIGTERM to your app, then SIGKILL after the grace period.
  2. server.close() then process.exit() is a bug. Wait for the close to complete before exiting.
  3. Order is everything: unready, stop accepting, drain requests, stop workers, close the pool, exit.
  4. Close the database pool last, so in-flight transactions can finish. If the process dies anyway, Postgres rolls back uncommitted work, but side effects outside the database need idempotency or an outbox.
  5. Always have a deadline, shorter than the platform's grace period, so a stuck request can't turn a clean shutdown into a SIGKILL.
  6. Check your container. If signals never reach node, none of the above matters.
  7. Test it by sending SIGTERM during a slow request.

What's the worst shutdown bug you've seen in production? Share it in the comments.

Further reading: the Node.js docs for http.Server.close() and process signal events, and the Kubernetes documentation on pod termination.

title: Building a Transformer from Scratch: Part 1 — The Embedding Layer
description:
Before the attention mechanism computes a single dot product in an autoregressive Transformer like GPT, the model faces a fundamental problem: neural networks do not understand text, and feeding them raw token IDs introduces false mathematical assumptions.

If the tokenizer maps "cat" to index 200 and "dog" to 201, a linear layer treats "dog" as having a higher numerical value than "cat". Token IDs are discrete categorical variables, not ordinal measurements.

The embedding layer bridges this gap. It maps discrete integers into continuous vector spaces where semantic relationships and sequence ordering can actually be learned.

Here is how the embedding layer works under the hood, along with a production-grade PyTorch implementation.

The Two Problems Embeddings Must Solve

1. Semantic Representation (Token Embeddings)

A tokenizer splits raw text into tokens and assigns each one an integer ID. To eliminate arbitrary numerical ordering, we map each ID to a learned vector of dimension d_model via a token lookup matrix W_e of shape (vocab_size, d_model).

Through backpropagation, tokens that appear in similar linguistic contexts gravitate toward each other in this high-dimensional vector space.

2. Sequence Order (Positional Embeddings)

Unlike Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which process tokens step-by-step from left to right, Transformers process the entire sequence in parallel.

Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant, the model would process "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" identically without an explicit position signal. To fix this, we map each sequence position 0, 1, ..., seq_len - 1 to a positional embedding vector of dimension d_model.

PyTorch Implementation

This module combines token embeddings with learned absolute positional embeddings and dropout regularization, matching the architectural setup used in GPT-2.


python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class TransformerEmbeddings(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, d_model: int, max_seq_len: int, dropout: float = 0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model

        # Token lookup matrix: shape (vocab_size, d_model)
        self.token_embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)

        # Position lookup matrix: shape (max_seq_len, d_model)
        self.position_embeddings = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)

        # Regularization: applies dropout across the summed embeddings
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

    def forward(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Expected input shape: (batch_size, seq_len)
        batch_size, seq_len = input_ids.shape

        # Guard clause: prevent context window overflows
        if seq_len > self.position_embeddings.num_embeddings:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Sequence length ({seq_len}) exceeds maximum context window "
                f"({self.position_embeddings.num_embeddings})"
            )

        # Generate positional indices [0, 1, ..., seq_len - 1]
        # Shape: (1, seq_len), created directly on the input's target device
        positions = torch.arange(0, seq_len, device=input_ids.device).unsqueeze(0)

        # Retrieve vectors
        tok_emb = self.token_embeddings(input_ids)    # (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
        pos_emb = self.position_embeddings(positions) # (1, seq_len, d_model)

        # Combine via broadcasting: (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
        embeddings = tok_emb + pos_emb

        return self.dropout(embeddings)


# Sanity check execution block
if __name__ == "__main__":
    vocab_size, d_model, max_len = 50257, 768, 1024
    layer = TransformerEmbeddings(vocab_size, d_model, max_len, dropout=0.1)

    # Dummy batch of 2 sequences, each 8 tokens long
    dummy_input = torch.randint(0, vocab_size, (2, 8))
    output = layer(dummy_input)

    print(f"Input shape:   {dummy_input.shape}")  # torch.Size([2, 8])
    print(f"Output shape:  {output.shape}")       # torch.Size([2, 8, 768])
    assert output.shape == (2, 8, d_model), "Shape mismatch!"
    print("Embedding module ran successfully.")

title: New psychology test promises to predict athletes' performance under pressure
description:
NTangible claims its photo-based assessment test can predict athlete performance under pressure.

However, testing revealed participants could game the system for higher scores.

When college sports teams recruit new players, they typically measure physical attributes like sprinting speed and muscle strength. However, measuring mental toughness and performance in critical moments has remained a challenge until now.

NTangible founder and CEO Dan Connerty, a former professional baseball player, developed the test with psychologist Dr. Ann Levine of the University of South Florida. The tool draws inspiration from a test in which participants describe images of ambiguous situations.

According to the company, the words someone uses are analyzed through a special guide, giving a score from 0 to 1.000. Connerty claims that an athlete who scores above 750 is twice as likely to get into a top-tier school. NTangible currently supports sports in nine different disciplines.

READ ALSO

Google's Gemini accidentally revealed its internal election guidelines

However, testing showed that users can answer dishonestly in order to achieve a higher score, as an honest answer yielded a lower score compared to attempts to imitate an ideal candidate.

In addition to sports, the company plans to expand the assessment into the business sector. Through the NTerpret test, human resources departments will be able to evaluate employees.

The company's core business model involves selling its services directly to organizations and companies, rather than individual users.

title: Google Jobs results as JSON, for $1 per 1,000 jobs (no proxies, no browser)
description:
Google Jobs is the best free job index on the web. It pulls listings from LinkedIn, Indeed, company career sites and hundreds of smaller boards into one search. What it does not have is an API.

The scrapers that fill that gap tend to break: they drive a browser through Google, get blocked, and you pay for failed runs. In October 2026 the most used one on the Apify Store failed 19% of its runs and charged $0.35 to $0.90 per 100 jobs, and another succeeded in only 1 of 500 runs in a month.

So I built one that does not scrape Google from a browser at all. It reads Google Jobs through a commercial search-data API, so there are no proxies to rotate and nothing to break. This post shows how to use it.

What you get per job

You send one or more searches and a country, optionally a city. You get one record per job:

{
  "query": "data engineer",
  "country": "US",
  "position": 1,
  "title": "Senior Data Engineer",
  "company": "Acme Corp",
  "location": "Austin, TX",
  "contract_type": "Full-time",
  "salary": "$140K–$180K a year",
  "salary_min": 140000,
  "salary_max": 180000,
  "salary_currency": "USD",
  "salary_period": "year",
  "posted_ago": "2 days ago",
  "source": "LinkedIn",
  "apply_url": "https://..."
}

(Example of the output format.)

What to expect from real data: in a test of 3 US searches (30 jobs), Google showed a salary on 5 of the 30 jobs. Many apply links go straight to the company's own career site. When the apply link is on a company job board (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby), the record also includes the full job description; in a test of 79 US jobs that was 16 of them. Other jobs keep the apply_url to the original posting.

Run it

The tool is the Google Jobs Scraper Actor on Apify.

From the console

Open the Actor, type your searches, pick a country, optionally a city such as Austin,Texas, and press Start. Results appear as a table you can export to CSV, Excel or JSON.

From curl 

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/hirepulse~google-jobs-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"queries": ["data engineer"], "country": "US", "location": "Austin,Texas", "max_jobs_per_query": 50}'

From Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("hirepulse/google-jobs-scraper").call(run_input={
    "queries": ["account executive", "sales development representative"],
    "country": "GB",
    "employment_types": ["fulltime"],
})
for job in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(job["title"], "|", job["company"], "|", job.get("salary"))

From an AI agent

Add Apify's MCP server with this one tool to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client:

https://mcp.apify.com?tools=hirepulse/google-jobs-scraper

Then ask: "Which companies in Austin are hiring data engineers this week, and what do they pay?"

Pricing

  • $0.005 per search that returns jobs. Searches with no results are free.
  • $0.001 per job.
  • 100 jobs from one search cost about $0.11.

You need an Apify account. You can try it on the free Apify plan: each free run returns the first 10 jobs of your first search. Full results need a paid Apify plan, because every search has a real data cost.

Related

If you track specific companies rather than roles, the ATS Job Scraper reads every open job, with full descriptions, straight from a company's Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby or Workable board, and tells you what changed since the last run.

title: Building a Production-Ready FastMCP Server Integration for Cognee Knowledge Graphs
description:
Overview

Context fragmentation is one of the most critical bottlenecks when building autonomous AI agents. While LLMs excel at localized reasoning, they lose track of structured graph relationships across multi-turn sessions and disjointed tool calls.

To solve this, I built a production-ready FastMCP (Model Context Protocol) server integration for Cognee, allowing standard MCP clients (such as Claude Desktop and Cursor) to read from and write to persistent knowledge graphs seamlessly.

Architecture & Integration Flow

The integration lives under cognee/api/mcp/ and bridges standard MCP client requests directly into Cognee's engine.


text
+------------------------------------+
|   Claude Desktop / Cursor / Agent  |
+------------------------------------+
                 |
        (MCP Protocol via stdio)
                 v
+------------------------------------+
|     FastMCP Server (server.py)     |
+------------------------------------+
       |                     |
       v                     v
 [cognee_add_memory]   [cognee_search_memory]
       |                     |
       +---------> <---------+
                 |
                 v
   Cognee Knowledge Graph & FalkorDB
Exposed Core Tools
The server implements two deterministic async tools:

cognee_add_memory: Ingests raw text or structured document payloads into Cognee's ingestion pipeline, automatically cognifying and extracting entity relationships into the graph.

cognee_search_memory: Executes hybrid vector and graph queries across the knowledge graph to retrieve grounded context for reasoning.

Implementation Snippet (server.py)
Python
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import cognee

mcp = FastMCP("Cognee-Context-Engine")

@mcp.tool()
async def cognee_add_memory(content: str, dataset_name: str = "main") -> str:
    """Ingest context into Cognee knowledge graph."""
    await cognee.add(content, dataset_name=dataset_name)
    await cognee.cognify(dataset_name=dataset_name)
    return "Memory successfully cognified."

@mcp.tool()
async def cognee_search_memory(query: str) -> str:
    """Retrieve grounded context from the knowledge graph."""
    results = await cognee.search(query_text=query)
    return str(results)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")
Claude Desktop Configuration
To connect this integration with Claude Desktop, add the server to your claude_desktop_config.json:

JSON
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cognee": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "cognee.api.mcp.server", "--transport", "stdio"],
      "env": {
        "OPENAI_API_KEY": "your-api-key"
      }
    }
  }
}
Testing & Verification
The integration includes a full mock test suite using pytest covering:

Correct tool schema dispatching.

Graceful handling of empty queries and malformed payloads.

Case insensitivity and dataset segregation.

Result: 10/10 unit tests passed (100% green) in 0.06 seconds.

Hackathon Submission
This integration is submitted for Mergetober / Graph Hacks under Cognee Pull Request #5864.

title: Is that really a Dogecoin address? Checking D... vs 0x... before anyone loses coins
description:
I nearly lost 500 DOGE to a dropdown. A casino cashier listed Dogecoin twice, once as the native coin and once as a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain, and the BEP-20 option came first. I copied the address it gave me, pasted it into my wallet and only then saw the 0x at the start. I stopped before sending. Plenty of people don't.

I spent eight years testing payment flows, and this one's a classic edge case: two things with the same name and different rails. If you build anything that takes or sends DOGE, the cheapest fix is to check the address format before a single coin moves. Here's how, with nothing but the Python standard library.

Two families of "DOGE" addresses

Starts with What it is Format
D Native Dogecoin, pay-to-public-key-hash Base58Check, version byte 0x1E, 34 characters
9 or A Native Dogecoin, pay-to-script-hash Base58Check, version byte 0x16
0x An EVM address (BNB Smart Chain, Ethereum…), where a token borrows the DOGE ticker 0x + 40 hex characters

A native Dogecoin wallet won't send to a 0x address, and coins sent the other way land on a chain the receiving service may never look at. The first character tells you which world you're in, but the first character alone isn't validation: typos and truncated pastes start with D too.

Base58Check in a few lines

A native address is 25 bytes encoded in Base58: one version byte, a 20-byte hash, and a 4-byte checksum, which is the first four bytes of a double SHA-256 of the first 21. Decode, split, recompute, compare.

import hashlib
import re

ALPHABET = "123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz"
DOGE_VERSIONS = {0x1E: "P2PKH", 0x16: "P2SH"}   # mainnet: D... and 9.../A...
EVM_RE = re.compile(r"^0x[0-9a-fA-F]{40}$")


def b58decode(s: str) -> bytes:
    n = 0
    for ch in s:
        i = ALPHABET.find(ch)
        if i < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"not base58: {ch!r}")
        n = n * 58 + i
    raw = n.to_bytes((n.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")
    pad = len(s) - len(s.lstrip("1"))
    return b"\x00" * pad + raw


def classify(address: str) -> str:
    address = address.strip()
    if EVM_RE.match(address):
        return "evm"   # BEP-20 / ERC-20 style: not a Dogecoin address
    try:
        data = b58decode(address)
    except ValueError:
        return "invalid"
    if len(data) != 25:
        return "invalid"
    payload, checksum = data[:-4], data[-4:]
    if hashlib.sha256(hashlib.sha256(payload).digest()).digest()[:4] != checksum:
        return "invalid"
    kind = DOGE_VERSIONS.get(payload[0])
    return f"doge-{kind.lower()}" if kind else "invalid"

classify returns one of four answers: doge-p2pkh, doge-p2sh, evm or invalid. A Bitcoin legacy address passes the checksum but has version byte 0x00, so it comes back invalid, which is what you'd want in a DOGE field.

What to test

The edge cases I'd put in any test suite for this field:

  • a real D… address, and the same address with one character changed (checksum must fail)
  • a 9… or A… script address
  • 0x followed by 40 hex characters (must be flagged, not rejected silently)
  • a Bitcoin address, a Litecoin address, an empty string, a string with spaces around it
  • the characters Base58 leaves out on purpose: 0, O, I, l

What to do with the answer

Validation is half the job. The other half is what the person at the screen sees:

  1. evm in a DOGE field: say so in words. "This is a BNB Smart Chain address, not a Dogecoin one" saves more coins than a red border.
  2. Two networks for one ticker: default to the native chain, label the other one with its chain name, not just "DOGE".
  3. No memo field for native DOGE. If your form shows one for Dogecoin, people will assume something's wrong. They'll be right.
  4. Show the first and last characters back after paste, so people compare what they meant with what they copied.

None of this needs a node or an API call. It runs before the request leaves the page, and that's where a payment bug costs the least, give or take a support ticket.

I test crypto casino cashiers the way I used to test checkouts. The write-ups are at dogecasino.best, and the raw numbers are on GitHub.

title: From Chained REST Calls to Events: Kafka Microservices in Node.js
description:
A checkout looks simple. The customer clicks “Place order” and sees a confirmation. Behind that click, the order service calls inventory, then payments, then notifications, all inside one HTTP request. That works until the email provider slows down and checkout slows with it, or a payment timeout triggers a client retry and a double charge.
This guide restructures that flow as event-driven microservices using Apache Kafka, Node.js, and KafkaJS, and covers duplicates, poison messages, ordering, and lost events. The code is simplified: a starting point, not a production service.

Why synchronous chains hurt

Chained calls create two kinds of coupling. Temporal coupling means every service must be healthy at the moment of the click, so a slow notification service can degrade your most important path. Knowledge coupling means the order service must know every downstream consumer. Retries add risk: after a timeout, the caller cannot tell whether the callee ever got the request.
Synchronous calls are not wrong: a price quote needs an answer now. Events fit work that is really a notification of something that already happened.
Event-driven basics
An event is an immutable record that something happened, named in the past tense: OrderCreated, PaymentFailed. A command asks a service to act, such as ChargeCard. In event-driven design, services publish facts and let others decide how to react. Three roles appear in every design:
• A producer publishes events without knowing who listens.
• A consumer subscribes to events and reacts.
• A broker stores events durably and serves them to consumers. Here, that is Kafka.
Because the producer finishes when the broker acknowledges the write, the system is eventually consistent: POST /orders should return 202 Accepted with a PENDING order.
Why Kafka and Node.js work well together
Kafka is a distributed, append-only log, not a queue. Consumers track their own position, called an offset, and reading never deletes an event. Many consumer groups can read one topic independently, a new service can replay history, and partitions provide parallelism.
Most handlers are I/O-bound, which Node.js handles well. The caveat is CPU-heavy work: it blocks the event loop, delays heartbeats, and can trigger rebalances. Move it to worker threads or another service. If you are still shaping the API side, DevLogix’s full-stack web development overview shows how its team pairs typed Node.js back-ends with modern front-ends.
This guide uses KafkaJS, a pure JavaScript client whose latest stable release is 2.2.4. Release activity has been slow, so for production also evaluate Confluent’s @confluentinc/kafka-javascript, whose API is designed to feel familiar to KafkaJS users.
The example: an order flow
Four services take part: order, inventory, payment, and notification. None calls another directly.
order-service --OrderCreated--> orders.events
inventory-service --StockReserved | StockRejected--> inventory.events
payment-service --PaymentCompleted | PaymentFailed--> payments.events
order-service confirms or cancels; notification-service emails
This style is choreography: each service reacts to what it observes. Failures use compensating events (a saga): if payment fails, the order is cancelled and stock released. Three decisions come first:
• One topic per domain stream, keyed by orderId, so one order’s events stay in sequence.
• A consistent envelope: eventId, type, version, occurredAt, and data.
• No sensitive data in events. Publish a payment reference, never a card number. Isolating payments also limits compliance scope, as DevLogix’s guide to PCI-DSS compliant fintech architecture explains.
Building the flow with KafkaJS
You need Node.js 18+ and Docker. Start a local single-node broker (no auth, no TLS, development only) and install the client:
docker run -d -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:3.9.0
`npm install kafkajs
Create topics explicitly with admin.createTopics rather than relying on auto-creation. Then publish from the order service:
const { Kafka } = require('kafkajs');
const { randomUUID } = require('node:crypto');

const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: 'order-service', brokers: ['localhost:9092'] });
const producer = kafka.producer({ idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 1 });

async function publish(topic, type, orderId, data) {
const event = { eventId: randomUUID(), type, version: 1,
occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(), orderId, data };
await producer.send({ topic, acks: -1,
messages: [{ key: orderId, value: JSON.stringify(event) }] });
}
The key sends every event for one order to one partition. acks: -1 waits for all in-sync replicas, and idempotent: true avoids duplicates when the producer retries internally. Now consume in the inventory service:
const consumer = kafka.consumer({ groupId: 'inventory-service' });
await consumer.connect();
await consumer.subscribe({ topics: ['orders.events'], fromBeginning: true });
await consumer.run({
eachMessage: async ({ message }) => {
const event = JSON.parse(message.value.toString());
if (event.type === 'OrderCreated') await reserveStock(event);
},
});
KafkaJS commits the offset after eachMessage resolves. If the handler throws, the message is retried and may arrive again. That is at-least-once delivery, and it shapes everything below. Restart a stopped consumer and it resumes where it left off, because offsets live in Kafka.
Concepts that shape your design
Partitions and keys. Kafka guarantees order within a partition, not across a topic. Key by the entity that must be processed in order: here the order, for a ledger the account. Partition count caps parallelism, and adding partitions later changes key mapping.
Consumer groups. Each partition goes to one group member, so with three partitions, five instances leave two idle. Separate groups are independent: the notification service receives every event without affecting inventory.
Commits. Committing before processing risks lost messages; committing after risks repeats. Most systems choose repeats and tolerate them.
Reliability and failure handling
Make duplicates harmless. For events you cannot lose, use acks: -1, replication factor 3, and min.insync.replicas=2. Then make consumers idempotent by recording processed event IDs in the same database transaction as the business change:
const claim = await client.query(
INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id, consumer)
VALUES ($1, 'inventory-service') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, [event.eventId]);
if (claim.rowCount === 0) return; // duplicate: skip
// update stock in the same transaction, then COMMIT
For external calls such as card charges, pass a stable idempotency key to the provider. Expected outcomes like out-of-stock are business results: publish StockRejected rather than throwing.
Poison messages. A message that can never succeed, such as malformed JSON, blocks its partition if retried forever. Retry transient failures a bounded number of times with backoff, then publish the message to a dead-letter topic (orders.events.dlq) with the original topic, offset, and error in headers. Alert on DLQ volume, or nobody will look.
Ordering. There is none across partitions or topics, so check current state, such as ignoring PaymentFailed for an already cancelled order.
The dual-write problem. If the order service saves an order and then publishes, a crash between the two leaves an order with no event. The transactional outbox fixes this: write the business row and an outbox row in one transaction, and let a relay process publish outbox rows to Kafka.
await client.query('BEGIN');
const { rows } = await client.query(
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status) VALUES ($1, 'PENDING') RETURNING id,
[customerId]);
await client.query(
INSERT INTO outbox (message_key, topic, payload) VALUES ($1, 'orders.events', $2)`,
[String(rows[0].id), event]);
await client.query('COMMIT');
The relay may crash after publishing and send a row again, which idempotent consumers absorb. Several relays can reorder events, so run one or shard by key. Debezium-style change data capture is an alternative.
Exactly-once? Kafka transactions only cover Kafka-to-Kafka flows. Once a handler touches a database or email provider, aim for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
Security and production readiness
Never run production in plaintext. Use TLS and SASL authentication, loading credentials from a secrets manager. Give each service its own identity and least-privilege ACLs: inventory reads orders.events and writes inventory.events, nothing more.
Event-driven systems fail quietly, so watch consumer lag (alert on sustained growth), DLQ volume, and rebalance frequency. Copy a correlation ID through event headers to trace one order across services.
Events outlive their code: add optional fields, never rename existing ones, and keep a version in the envelope. As teams multiply, a schema registry with Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema can enforce compatibility in CI.
Operationally: replication factor 3, auto-creation off, deliberate retention, graceful SIGTERM shutdown, and replicas scaled by lag up to the partition count. If your consumers run on Kubernetes, DevLogix’s cloud and DevOps services page outlines its approach to Kubernetes, CI/CD, and Terraform.
When not to use Kafka
Pick something simpler for background jobs with delays or priorities (BullMQ, RabbitMQ, SQS), synchronous questions (HTTP or gRPC), a small team with one deployable (a modular monolith), or fan-out without replay (SNS with SQS, Pub/Sub). If you cannot name which Kafka property you need, start simpler.
Conclusion
Use events for facts and calls for questions. Choose keys and partitions on purpose. Assume at-least-once delivery and make every consumer idempotent. Use an outbox instead of dual writes, bound retries with a monitored DLQ, and treat security, lag monitoring, and schemas as part of the design.
Next, publish OrderCreated, consume it, kill the consumer mid-message to watch redelivery, then add processed_events and the outbox.

title: Unlocking the Power of Go: A Hands‑On Guide for Modern Developers
description:
Introduction

Go (often called Golang) has been gaining momentum since its release by Google in 2009. It blends the performance of compiled languages with the simplicity of scripting languages, making it ideal for cloud services, micro‑architectures, and command‑line tools. In this post we’ll explore why Go matters, walk through a quick setup, and dive into core language features with practical code samples.

Why Choose Go?

  1. Speed – Native compilation produces fast binaries with a tiny runtime.
  2. Simplicity – A small, orthogonal syntax reduces cognitive load.
  3. Concurrency – Goroutines and channels let you write safe concurrent code without the headaches of locks.
  4. Static Typing & Tooling – The built‑in go vet, go fmt, and go test make codebases maintainable.
  5. Cross‑Compilation – One command can target Windows, macOS, Linux, and even ARM devices.

Getting Started

Install Go from the official site or your package manager:

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install go
# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install golang

After installation, verify the version:

go version

You should see something like go version go1.22 linux/amd64.

Create a workspace:

mkdir -p ~/go/src/hello
cd ~/go/src/hello

Create main.go:

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, Go!")
}

Run it:

go run main.go

You’ll see Hello, Go! printed to the console.

Language Basics

Variables & Types

Go is statically typed, but you can let the compiler infer types using :=.

var explicit int = 42          // explicit type
inferred := "Go is fun!"      // type inferred as string

Control Flow

Standard if, for, switch work as you’d expect, but Go eliminates the classic while keyword. A for loop without a condition behaves like a while.

for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

// while‑style loop
n := 10
for n > 0 {
    fmt.Println(n)
    n--
}

Concurrency Made Easy

The hallmark of Go is its lightweight concurrency model.

Goroutines

A goroutine is a function that runs concurrently with other goroutines.

func say(message string) {
    for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
        fmt.Println(message)
        time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)
    }
}

func main() {
    go say("goroutine 1") // runs concurrently
    say("main function")   // runs in the main goroutine
}

The go keyword launches a new goroutine. Note that the program may exit before goroutines finish; we’ll address coordination next.

Channels

Channels provide a safe way to communicate between goroutines.

func worker(id int, jobs <-chan int, results chan<- int) {
    for j := range jobs {
        fmt.Printf("worker %d processing job %d\n", id, j)
        time.Sleep(time.Second)
        results <- j * 2
    }
}

func main() {
    const numJobs = 5
    jobs := make(chan int, numJobs)
    results := make(chan int, numJobs)

    // start 3 workers
    for w := 1; w <= 3; w++ {
        go worker(w, jobs, results)
    }

    // send jobs
    for j := 1; j <= numJobs; j++ {
        jobs <- j
    }
    close(jobs)

    // collect results
    for a := 0; a < numJobs; a++ {
        fmt.Println("result", <-results)
    }
}

Channels block until the other side is ready, eliminating race conditions without explicit locks.

Building a Simple Web Server

Go’s standard library includes a powerful net/http package. Let’s create a tiny JSON API.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

type Message struct {
    Text string `json:"text"`
}

func helloHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    msg := Message{Text: "Hello from Go!"}
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(msg)
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/hello", helloHandler)
    log.Println("Server listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

Run go run server.go and visit http://localhost:8080/hello – you’ll receive {"text":"Hello from Go!"}.

Testing & Benchmarking

Go treats testing as a first‑class citizen.

package mathutil

import "testing"

func Add(a, b int) int { return a + b }

func TestAdd(t *testing.T) {
    got := Add(2, 3)
    want := 5
    if got != want {
        t.Fatalf("Add(2,3) = %d; want %d", got, want)
    }
}

func BenchmarkAdd(b *testing.B) {
    for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
        Add(i, i)
    }
}

Run tests with go test ./... and benchmarks with go test -bench=..

Best Practices

  • Format before you commit – go fmt ./... ensures a consistent style.
  • Prefer interfaces over concrete types – they enable mocking and flexible APIs.
  • Avoid global variables – pass dependencies explicitly.
  • Use context for cancellation – especially in HTTP servers and long‑running goroutines.
  • Leverage modules – go.mod isolates dependencies and supports reproducible builds.

Conclusion

Go strikes a sweet spot between performance, developer productivity, and reliable concurrency. Its batteries‑included standard library lets you spin up web services, CLIs, and system tools with minimal ceremony. Whether you’re building microservices, data pipelines, or dev‑ops utilities, Go offers a pragmatic path to production‑grade software.

Give it a try: install the toolchain, write a few functions, and let the compiler do the heavy lifting. Happy coding!
