title: Java var, Records and Sealed Classes Explained Simply
description:
Java has a reputation for being wordy, and for a long time it earned it. To store a simple pair of numbers, I had to write a class with two fields, a constructor, two getters, equals, hashCode and toString. That's around forty lines for something that is just "x and y." And a line like this made my eyes tired:

Map<String, List<Integer>> scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

Modern Java fixed a lot of this. In this post, we'll learn three features that make code shorter and safer:

  • var (local variable type inference), so you stop repeating types.
  • record classes, which give you data classes in one line.
  • sealed classes, which let you say exactly which classes may extend yours.

At the end, we'll combine all three in one small program. If you read the post about streams, you'll notice that these features fit with them very well.

A quick note on versions, because each feature arrived at a different time: var came in Java 10, records are final in Java 16, sealed classes in Java 17, and the pattern-matching switch that I use with sealed types is final in Java 21. Any recent LTS version has all of them.

Unless I show a full class, the snippets go inside a main method. Records and other types are declared outside it.

Part 1: var (local variable type inference)

What is var?

var lets the compiler work out the type of a local variable from the value on the right side. This is called LVTI, short for Local Variable Type Inference.

var name = "Asha";
var count = 10;
var prices = new ArrayList<Double>();
var scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

The long line from the start of this post becomes much shorter, because the type was already written on the right side. Why say it twice?

var is NOT dynamic typing

This is the most common misunderstanding. var doesn't make Java behave like JavaScript. The variable still has one fixed type, chosen at compile time:

var name = "Asha";
System.out.println(name.toUpperCase());

name = 5;

Output:

ASHA

and then a compile error on the last line:

incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String

name is a String forever. You can call String methods on it, and you can't put a number in it.

Behind the scenes

The compiler simply replaces var with the real type while compiling. The bytecode is exactly the same as if you had written the type yourself, so var has no cost at run time.

   var count = 10;                       -->   int count = 10;
   var names = new ArrayList<String>();  -->   ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();

   The type is worked out when you COMPILE. Nothing changes when the program RUNS.

Where you can use it

var works for local variables, in several places:

var message = "Hello";                          // normal local variable

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }                 // classic for loop

for (var n : List.of(1, 2, 3)) { }              // enhanced for loop

BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add =
        (var a, var b) -> a + b;                // lambda parameters (Java 11+)

Where you can't 

   var x;                  error: cannot infer type (no initial value)
   var x = null;           error: cannot infer type (the value is 'null')
   var f = () -> 1;        error: cannot infer type (lambda needs a target type)
   var a = {1, 2, 3};      error: cannot infer type (array initializer needs a type)

   Also NOT allowed: fields, method parameters and return types.

The compiler can only infer a type when the right side makes it clear. In all these cases, there's nothing (or not enough) to infer from. Also, var is only for local variables, so it can't be used for class fields or in method signatures.

A gotcha: the diamond 

var list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("a");
list.add(1);

System.out.println(list);

Output:

[a, 1]

With a normal declaration, List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); tells the compiler to use String for the diamond <>. With var, there's no target type, so the compiler picks ArrayList<Object>, and the list accepts anything. Write new ArrayList<String>() when you use var.

Another small thing to know: var list = new ArrayList<String>(); has the type ArrayList<String>, not List<String>. If you want your variable to use the interface type (a good habit), write it out: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();.

Is var a good idea?

It depends on readability:

  • Good: the type is obvious from the right side. var users = new ArrayList<User>(); and var reader = new BufferedReader(...); need no extra explanation.
  • Not good: the right side hides the type. In var result = process(data);, a reader has to look up process to learn what result is.

A good rule: use var when it removes repetition, and use the explicit type when it adds information. And since the type is no longer visible, choose clear variable names.

Part 2: Records

The problem: so much code for plain data

Here is a simple class that just carries two numbers:

class PointClass {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    PointClass(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    int getX() { return x; }
    int getY() { return y; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof PointClass)) return false;
        PointClass other = (PointClass) o;
        return x == other.x && y == other.y;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "PointClass[x=" + x + ", y=" + y + "]";
    }
}

That's a lot of text, and every line is boilerplate (code you write only because the language requires it). A record does the same in one line:

record Point(int x, int y) { }

Point p = new Point(3, 4);

System.out.println(p);
System.out.println(p.x());
System.out.println(p.equals(new Point(3, 4)));
System.out.println(p.hashCode() == new Point(3, 4).hashCode());

Output:

Point[x=3, y=4]
3
true
true

Two points with the same values are equal, even though they are different objects. Records compare by value, not by identity.

What the compiler writes for you

The list in the parentheses, (int x, int y), is called the record's components. For them, the compiler generates:

   record Point(int x, int y) { }
            |
            |   the compiler expands it into roughly this:
            v
   final class Point extends java.lang.Record {
       private final int x;
       private final int y;

       Point(int x, int y) { ... }         // the "canonical" constructor
       int x() { return x; }               // accessors: note, NO "get" prefix
       int y() { return y; }
       boolean equals(Object o) { ... }    // compares all components
       int hashCode() { ... }
       String toString() { ... }           // Point[x=3, y=4]
   }

You can verify the hidden parts yourself:

System.out.println(Point.class.getSuperclass());
System.out.println(java.lang.reflect.Modifier.isFinal(Point.class.getModifiers()));

Output:

class java.lang.Record
true

So a record is a real class. It's final (nobody can extend it), and its parent is java.lang.Record. (Behind the scenes, the generated equals, hashCode and toString are wired up with the same invokedynamic mechanism we saw with lambdas.)

Validation with a compact constructor

What if you want to reject bad values? Write a compact constructor. It has the record's name but no parentheses. It runs before the fields are set:

record Age(int value) {
    Age {
        if (value < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
        }
    }
}

System.out.println(new Age(25));

try {
    new Age(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
}

Output:

Age[value=25]
Error: Age cannot be negative

You can also adjust a value in the compact constructor by reassigning the parameter. And records can have their own methods and static helpers:

record Person(String name, int age) {
    Person {
        name = name.trim();
    }

    String greeting() {
        return "Hi, " + name;
    }

    static Person of(String name) {
        return new Person(name, 0);
    }
}

System.out.println(new Person("  Asha ", 25));
System.out.println(Person.of("Ravi").greeting());

Output:

Person[name=Asha, age=25]
Hi, Ravi

The rules of records

  • A record is implicitly final and can't extend another class (it already extends Record).
  • It can implement interfaces, and it can be generic, like record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second).
  • The component fields are private final. You can't add extra instance fields, and there are no setters.
  • You can add methods, static methods and static fields.
  • Any extra constructor must call the canonical one with this(...).

A trap: records are shallowly immutable

The fields can't be reassigned, but if a field holds a changeable object, that object can still change:

record Team(String name, List<String> members) { }

var members = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha"));
var team = new Team("Core", members);

members.add("Ravi");
System.out.println(team);

Output:

Team[name=Core, members=[Asha, Ravi]]

The team changed even though we never touched the record! The fix is a defensive copy in the compact constructor:

record SafeTeam(String name, List<String> members) {
    SafeTeam {
        members = List.copyOf(members);
    }
}

var members = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha"));
var team = new SafeTeam("Core", members);

members.add("Ravi");
System.out.println(team);

Output:

SafeTeam[name=Core, members=[Asha]]

Now the record keeps its own unchangeable copy.

Records work nicely with streams

Because the accessors are plain methods, they fit method references:

record Student(String name, int marks) { }

List<Student> students = List.of(
        new Student("Asha", 88),
        new Student("Ravi", 72),
        new Student("Meera", 95));

students.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.marks() > 80)
        .map(Student::name)
        .forEach(System.out::println);

Output:

Asha
Meera

Records are ideal for small data carriers: results that return several values, map keys, DTOs (objects that carry data between layers) and test data.

Part 3: Sealed classes

The problem: inheritance is too open

Normally, if you write interface Shape, anyone can implement it, anywhere, at any time. That's flexible, but sometimes it's a problem. Imagine you want to say "a Shape is only a Circle or a Rectangle, nothing else." With normal inheritance, you can't say that, and the compiler can never be sure it has seen every possible shape.

A sealed class or interface solves this. It lists exactly which classes may extend or implement it, using the permits keyword:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle { }

record Circle(double radius) implements Shape { }
record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape { }

   Normal hierarchy:    Shape  <---  anyone can extend it (unknown subclasses)

   Sealed hierarchy:    Shape  <---  ONLY Circle and Rectangle
                                     the compiler knows ALL the cases

If another class tries to join the family uninvited:

final class Triangle implements Shape { }

class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Shape (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)

The three choices for a subclass

Every class that is permitted by a sealed class must declare what happens next in the family, with one of three keywords:

  • final: no more subclasses. The family ends here.
  • sealed: it restricts its own subclasses again, with its own permits list.
  • non-sealed: it opens the hierarchy back up, so anyone may extend it. 
sealed class Vehicle permits Car, Truck, Bike { }

final class Car extends Vehicle { }

sealed class Truck extends Vehicle permits Pickup { }
final class Pickup extends Truck { }

non-sealed class Bike extends Vehicle { }

              Vehicle  (sealed)
             /    |     \
          Car   Truck    Bike
        final  sealed   non-sealed
                  |
               Pickup
                final

Records are automatically final, which is why they pair so well with sealed interfaces. A few more rules:

  • A permitted subclass must directly extend the sealed class.
  • It must be in the same module (or the same package, if your project doesn't use modules).
  • If all the subclasses are in the same file as the sealed class, you can leave out permits, and the compiler works it out.

The payoff: exhaustive switch

Because the compiler knows every possible subtype, a switch over a sealed type doesn't need a default:

static double area(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c    -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
        case Rectangle r -> r.width() * r.height();
    };
}

System.out.println(area(new Circle(1)));
System.out.println(area(new Rectangle(3, 4)));

Output:

3.141592653589793
12.0

(This pattern-matching switch needs Java 21 or newer.) The best part comes later. Imagine you add a Triangle to the permits list but forget to update area. The code stops compiling:

the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

The compiler found the bug for you, long before a user would. That's the real value of sealed types: when the set of cases changes, every place that must handle them is flagged.

In Java 21 and newer, you can even take a record apart inside the case:

case Circle(double radius)             -> Math.PI * radius * radius;
case Rectangle(double width, double height) -> width * height;

A practical example: success or failure

A common use is a result type that is either a success or a failure:

sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure { }
record Success(String data) implements Result { }
record Failure(String error) implements Result { }

static String describe(Result r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Success s -> "OK: " + s.data();
        case Failure f -> "Error: " + f.error();
    };
}

System.out.println(describe(new Success("saved")));
System.out.println(describe(new Failure("timeout")));

Output:

OK: saved
Error: timeout

Behind the scenes

The permits list is stored inside the .class file. When a class is loaded, the JVM checks it, so the rule is enforced both by the compiler and at run time. You can even read it with reflection:

System.out.println(Shape.class.isSealed());

for (Class<?> c : Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
    System.out.println(c.getSimpleName());
}

Output:

true
Circle
Rectangle

Sealed vs enum vs final

These three often get confused:

  • final means no subclasses at all.
  • enum means a fixed set of objects (like MONDAY, TUESDAY), each created once.
  • sealed means a fixed set of types, and each type can have many objects, usually with different data (a Circle has a radius, and a Rectangle has a width and height).

Putting it all together

Let's use everything in one small program: a tiny calculator that models expressions as a sealed hierarchy of records, walks them with a switch, and uses var for the local variables.

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { }
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }
record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }

public class Calculator {
    static int eval(Expr e) {
        return switch (e) {
            case Num n -> n.value();
            case Add a -> eval(a.left()) + eval(a.right());
            case Mul m -> eval(m.left()) * eval(m.right());
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var expr = new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Num(3), new Num(4)));

        System.out.println(eval(expr));
        System.out.println(expr);
    }
}

Output:

14
Add[left=Num[value=2], right=Mul[left=Num[value=3], right=Num[value=4]]]

Look at how each feature helped:

  • Records gave us four tiny data types in four lines, and a readable toString for free.
  • Sealed told the compiler that Expr is only Num, Add or Mul, so eval needs no default.
  • switch with patterns unpacked each case without casts.
  • var kept the long type name out of main.

Try adding a Sub record to the permits list, and watch the compiler point at eval.

Which one should I use?

  • var or the explicit type? Use var when the right side already shows the type (new ArrayList<String>(), a constructor call, a clearly named factory). Use the explicit type when it helps the reader, or when you want an interface type like List<String>.
  • Record or class? Use a record for plain, unchangeable data carriers: DTOs, map keys, multiple return values, test data. Use a class when you need changeable state, inheritance, hidden internal data or behavior that doesn't revolve around the data. Many frameworks that need changeable, proxied objects (such as JPA entities) don't fit records.
  • Sealed, enum or open interface? Use an enum for a fixed set of constants. Use a sealed hierarchy for a fixed set of types that carry different data. Use a normal open interface when other people should be able to add their own implementations (a plugin system, for example).
  • Records and sealed together? This is a great combination for modeling "one of several shapes of data," like results, events, commands and expressions.

Common mistakes

  1. Using var when the type becomes unclear. If a reader can't tell what the variable is without hunting, write the type. Also remember var list = new ArrayList<>() gives you ArrayList<Object>.
  2. Thinking var makes Java dynamic. The type is fixed at compile time. You can't assign a different type later, and you can't use var for fields, parameters or return types.
  3. Assuming records are fully immutable. If a component is a list or another changeable object, it can still change. Make a defensive copy in the compact constructor, and remember that you can't add instance fields or setters.
  4. Using the wrong accessor name. A record's accessor is p.x(), not p.getX(). And equality is based on values, so two records with the same data are equals.
  5. Forgetting what a permitted subclass must say. Each one has to be final, sealed or non-sealed, and it must sit in the same module (or package). Otherwise, the code won't compile.
  6. Adding a default branch to a switch over a sealed type. It silences the compiler's exhaustiveness check. When you add a new subtype later, it falls into default without any warning. Leave default out so the compiler can protect you.

Quick recap

  • var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable. The type is still fixed at compile time, and the bytecode is the same as if you'd written it out.
  • var needs an initial value that shows the type. It can't be used for fields, parameters, return types, null or lambdas without a target type. Use it when it removes repetition, not when it hides the type.
  • A record is a one-line data class. The compiler generates the final fields, canonical constructor, accessors like x(), and equals, hashCode and toString. It's implicitly final, extends java.lang.Record and can't have extra instance fields.
  • Use a compact constructor for validation, and make a defensive copy of changeable components.
  • A sealed class or interface lists its allowed subclasses with permits. Each one must be final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Sealed types give you an exhaustive switch with no default, so the compiler tells you when you forget a case.
  • Records plus sealed interfaces plus pattern-matching switch is a powerful modern-Java pattern.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: model a payment system. Create a sealed interface Payment permits Card, Upi, Cash, with a record for each, such as Card(String number, int amount), Upi(String id, int amount) and Cash(int amount). Write a method fee(Payment p) that returns a different fee for each, using a switch with no default. Use var for your local variables in main.

For a bonus experiment, add a new record NetBanking to the permits list, and read the compiler error on your switch. Then handle the new case and see it compile again.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

That wraps up this two-part series on modern Java.

title: There Is Already an Object Named 'X' in the Database: What EF Core Is Really Telling You
description:
You run dotnet ef database update against a database that already has a schema,
and it stops with this:

Msg 2714, Level 16, State 1, Line 5
There is already an object named 'BlogPosts' in the database.

The instinct is to go and look at the migration. That is the wrong place. The migration is
almost certainly fine. What has gone wrong is that EF Core's record of what it has already
applied no longer matches the migration files sitting in your project, so it is trying to
run something for the second time.

This happened on this site's own database, and the evidence is still in the table as I write
this. I will show you the real rows further down.

The same bug wears three different faces

Which error message you get depends entirely on what the migration being re-run happens to do.
That is why this problem is so hard to search for - three people hit the identical bug and go
looking for three unrelated strings.

I captured all three from a live SQL Server 2022 rather than quoting them from memory, using a
temporary table so nothing real was touched:

Migration operation Error Message
CreateTable 2714 There is already an object named 'X' in the database.
AddColumn 2705 Column names in each table must be unique. Column name 'ResumeUrl' in table 'SiteSettings' is specified more than once.
CreateIndex 1913 The operation failed because an index or statistics with name 'IX_BlogPosts_Slug' already exists on table 'BlogPosts'.

One quirk worth knowing if you ever try to reproduce this: 2714 is raised when the batch is
compiled, not when it runs, so a TRY...CATCH in the same batch will not catch it. The
other two will. It is a small detail, but it is the kind that makes you think your error handling
is broken when it is working exactly as designed.

What __EFMigrationsHistory actually is

EF Core has no magic here. Its entire memory of your database is one small table that it
creates itself:

SELECT MigrationId, ProductVersion FROM __EFMigrationsHistory ORDER BY MigrationId;

Two columns. MigrationId is the filename of the migration without the extension -
a 14-digit timestamp, an underscore, and the class name. ProductVersion is the EF
version of the tooling that applied it.

When you run database update, EF reads every MigrationId out of that
table, compares the list against the migration classes compiled into your assembly, and runs
whatever is in the assembly but not in the table. That is the whole algorithm.

Which means the error is not really "this object exists". It is "I have no row saying I created
this object, so I am going to create it".

The real cause: your file and your history row drifted apart

Here is the actual history table behind this site, trimmed to the interesting part:

MigrationId                                    ProductVersion
---------------------------------------------  --------------
20260719093058_AddLogoDarkUrlToSiteSettings     9.0.0
20260920154152_AddResumeToSiteSettings          9.0.9
20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings          9.0.9
20260922181332_AddLeadFieldsToContactMessages   9.0.9

Look at the middle two. The same migration name, twice, with timestamps one minute and forty
seconds apart. There is only one file on disk -
20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings.cs. The 154152 row is a ghost.

What happened is mundane and extremely common: the migration was generated, applied, then
something about it was wrong, so it was deleted and generated again. The regenerated file got a
fresh timestamp, because the timestamp is simply the moment migrations add ran. As
far as EF is concerned that is a completely different migration which has never been applied - and
its Up method said AddColumn("ResumeUrl") against a table that already
had the column.

That is error 2705, and this is the version of the story where it was caught. Run the same
mistake on a migration that creates tables instead and you get 2714.

Other routes to the same state, all of which I have run into:

  • The database was built by hand or restored from a backup, and the first migration tries to create what is already there.
  • Two branches each added a migration, both were applied in different environments, and the merge left one environment's history out of step.
  • A migration was applied, then reverted in source control but never reverted in the database.
  • Someone ran database update against the wrong connection string. On shared hosting, with staging and production on one instance, this is easier than it sounds.

Why dotnet ef migrations list will not show you this

This is the part that cost the most time, so I will be blunt about it. The obvious diagnostic
does not work.

dotnet ef migrations list --project MyApp.Core --startup-project MyApp.Api

On the database above, that command printed eighteen migrations. The ghost row was not one of
them. It cannot be: the command builds its list from the migration classes in your assembly and
then annotates which of them are pending. A history row with no matching class is not in the
assembly, so there is nothing to annotate and it never appears.

So migrations list answers "which of my files have been applied". It does not
answer "what does the database think it has applied", and the second question is the one you need.
You have to go and ask the table yourself.

The diagnosis, in one query

Read the history table and compare it with your files. Nothing here writes anything, so it is
safe to run against production:

SELECT MigrationId, ProductVersion
FROM   __EFMigrationsHistory
ORDER  BY MigrationId;

Then list the files:

ls Migrations/*.cs | grep -v Designer | grep -v Snapshot

Three outcomes, and each one has a different fix:

  • A file with no row. EF will try to apply it on the next update. If the schema it creates is already there, that is your error.
  • A row with no file. Harmless on its own - EF ignores rows it does not recognise - but it is a loud signal that a migration was regenerated, and the replacement is probably case 1.
  • Duplicate names with different timestamps. The two above, together. This is the regenerated-migration case and it is the most common one by a distance.

Check ProductVersion while you are in there, too. Mixed values across rows mean
different machines with different EF tooling versions have been applying migrations to the same
database, which is its own source of surprises.

Fixing it without dropping the database

The fix depends on which of two things is true, and you have to decide which before you type
anything.

If the schema is already correct and only the history row is missing - the
usual case - you do not want to run the migration at all. You want to tell EF it has already been
run. Insert the row yourself, idempotently, so re-running the script is harmless:

IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM __EFMigrationsHistory
               WHERE MigrationId = N'20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings')
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO __EFMigrationsHistory (MigrationId, ProductVersion)
    VALUES (N'20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings', N'9.0.9');
END

The MigrationId must match the filename exactly, timestamp included.
ProductVersion should match the EF version you are running; it is informational, but
getting it wrong makes the table lie to the next person who reads it.

If the history row exists but the schema does not - someone restored an older
backup over a newer history, say - then deleting the row is what lets EF apply the migration
properly. Take a backup first. This is the direction in which guessing loses data.

If you have an orphan row and no corresponding file, leaving it alone is a
legitimate choice. EF will not trip over it. The 154152 row is still in this site's
database for exactly that reason: it is harmless, and it documents what happened. If it bothers
you, delete it - but delete it because you have confirmed no file matches it, not because it looks
untidy.

To generate the SQL without applying it, and read what EF intends to do first:

dotnet ef migrations script 20260719093058_AddLogoDarkUrlToSiteSettings 20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings --idempotent --output check.sql

--idempotent wraps every operation in a check against the history table, which
makes the script safe to run more than once. On a production database it is the only form worth
running.

Three fixes to not reach for

dotnet ef database drop ends the error by destroying the data. It is the right
answer on a local development database you can reseed in a minute, and the wrong answer everywhere
else. The two commands sit next to each other in the documentation, which is how accidents
happen.

Deleting the Migrations folder and starting again feels like a reset. It is not -
the history table survives, so a fresh InitialCreate immediately collides with the
existing schema and you are back at 2714 with less information than before.

Adding --ignore-changes, or hand-emptying the Up method to make the
error go away, is the one that causes real damage later. You end up with a migration that claims
to do something and does nothing, and the next environment you deploy to is missing the schema
with no error to tell you.

Keeping it from happening again

One rule covers most of it: never regenerate a migration that has already been applied
anywhere. Once a migration has run against a database you cannot reach and fix by hand,
its timestamp is a fact about the world. If the migration is wrong, add a new one that corrects
it. migrations remove is only safe while the migration is still unapplied
everywhere.

Three more habits that have earned their place:

  • Script the deployment with migrations script --idempotent rather than running database update against production. You get to read it first, and it is safe to run twice if a deploy is interrupted.
  • Check __EFMigrationsHistory as part of a release, not as part of an incident. The query above takes two seconds.
  • Be deliberate about which connection string is active. On shared hosting, where staging and production often sit on the same instance, the only thing between you and the wrong database is which appsettings file happened to load.

If you are working on the same stack, the post
on indexes and idempotency covers why idempotent scripts matter well beyond migrations, and
the ASP.NET Core deployment errors post
covers the failures that show up immediately after this one, when the application starts but the
database will not cooperate.

The short version: when EF says an object already exists, it is not describing your schema. It
is telling you it has lost track of its own history. Read the table, find the disagreement, and
fix the record rather than the migration.

FAQ

Can I just delete the migration file and create a new one?

Only if the migration has never been applied to any database. Once it has run somewhere you cannot reach and correct by hand, regenerating it creates a second migration with a new timestamp that EF treats as unapplied - which is the exact cause of this error. Add a corrective migration instead.

Is it safe to insert rows into __EFMigrationsHistory manually?

Yes, when you have confirmed the schema that migration creates is already present. You are recording a fact that is already true. Use an IF NOT EXISTS guard so the script can be run twice, and make MigrationId match the filename character for character, including the timestamp.

Why does dotnet ef migrations list not show the extra row?

Because it builds its list from the migration classes compiled into your assembly and then marks which ones are pending. A history row with no matching class is not in the assembly, so it never appears in the output. You have to query __EFMigrationsHistory directly to see it.

What is the difference between error 2714, 2705 and 1913?

Nothing, as far as the cause goes - they are the same re-applied migration hitting different operations. 2714 comes from CreateTable, 2705 from AddColumn and 1913 from CreateIndex. Searching the message text sends three people with one problem to three unrelated places.

Does --idempotent fix this error?

It prevents it rather than fixing it. An idempotent script wraps every operation in a check against the history table, so operations EF has already recorded are skipped. It will not repair history that has already drifted - do that first, then use idempotent scripts so it does not drift again.

My database was created by hand and now the first migration fails. What now?

That is case 1: the schema exists, the history row does not. Generate the script for InitialCreate and read it against your actual schema. If they match, insert the history row and skip the migration. If they differ, reconcile the differences in a new migration before recording anything as applied.

Should I run dotnet ef database update against production?

Prefer migrations script --idempotent and apply the SQL deliberately. You get to read exactly what will run, the script is safe to re-run if a deploy is interrupted, and you are not relying on a build machine holding a production connection string.

Originally published on knowledgemarkg.com.

title: Two posts, one output file: the static-site bug that deletes a page (and a zero-dependency linter)
description:
A static site generator can drop one of your pages and still exit 0. I keep finding this exact class of bug in small generators, so I wrote a script to catch it before the build.

The bug

Two source posts compute the same output path. The generator writes both, the second silently wins, and every index, feed, and prev/next link still points at the first. Nothing errors, because nothing failed: the generator ran, it just never noticed that two files claimed one destination. Your tests pass for the same reason.

I have hit this in two forms:

  1. Two posts declaring the same slug:.
  2. A post with an explicit permalink: (say /note.html) colliding with a post whose derived path is also /note.html. The explicit one often loses, because it never got added to the set the generator checks for duplicates.

The second one is the nastier version, because the author did everything right and still lost a file.

The linter

sluglint reads your source posts, works out the output path each one will get, and reports any path claimed by more than one file. One Python file, standard library only.

curl -O https://lumen-198.surge.sh/sluglint.py
python3 sluglint.py content/ --pattern '{year}/{month}/{slug}.html'

Given a clean tree it says so:

$ python3 sluglint.py content/
sluglint: 2 file(s), no output collisions.

Given the collision above:

$ python3 sluglint.py fx_permalink/content
sluglint: 2 file(s), 1 colliding output path(s):
  /note.html
    <- fx_permalink/content/note-followup.md (pattern)
    <- fx_permalink/content/note.md (permalink)

Exit code is 1 on a collision and 0 on a clean tree, so it drops straight into a pre-commit hook or CI step.

Honest edges

It understands a small subset of front matter (slug, permalink, date) and does not render templates or run your generator. If your path logic lives in code, pass the matching --pattern. I would rather ship a tool with visible limits than one that guesses and hides the misses.

Get it

Full page, the script, and a test file: https://lumen-198.surge.sh/sluglint.html

If your generator is eating a page and you want the deeper hunt, I do reproducible code reviews: I find the break, hand you the one-command repro, then the fix.

title: Node.js Express Images: Strip EXIF Location Data Before Publishing
description:
The page fires because a Node.js Express upload did not strip EXIF location data before publishing a customer-support image thumbnail. By then, the privacy boundary has already failed: a user-facing URL exists, caches may hold the object, and an incident responder is proving exposure instead of preventing it.

TL;DR: put a re-encoding worker between the Express upload handler and public storage, because copying or renaming an image does not remove metadata. Keep the source object private only when a documented retention reason requires it, generate the thumbnail from decoded pixels, then read the derivative back and reject publication if an EXIF marker remains. Alert on that rejected publication, not on a dashboard ratio that can stay green while one sensitive image escapes.

Infrai fits early in this design when processing and metadata inspection should use the same REST contract as other backend work. Its public discovery schema is useful here because the worker can inspect the current image.process contract instead of embedding an assumed request shape; the privacy decision and publication gate remain application responsibilities.

For a customer-support system, this is also the useful cost boundary. The workload is uploads, pixel decoding, thumbnail encoding, private source retention, public derivative storage, cache fills, and verification reads; a per-image transformation quote covers only one line of that bill.

What page should fire?

The actionable page is thumbnail_publish_blocked: the worker produced a derivative, the verification pass found metadata that violates policy, and the object was not published. It should carry the upload identifier, derivative identifier, encoder version, output format, attempt count, and the failed policy check. It should not carry the original filename or metadata values into a broad alert channel.

Work backward from there. The earlier signal is not “image processing latency increased.” It is a counter at the publication boundary: derivatives attempted, derivatives verified clean, derivatives rejected, and originals retained under an explicit policy. Those numbers describe a state transition an operator can act on. A latency chart does not answer the question I ask first during an incident: what page fired, and did the unsafe object cross the publication boundary?

The control flow should be small enough to audit:

  1. Express accepts the upload and assigns an opaque job ID.
  2. The source enters access-controlled storage, never the public cache path.
  3. A worker decodes pixels and creates the responsive thumbnail by encoding a new file.
  4. A separate read-back check inspects the exact bytes intended for publication.
  5. Only a clean derivative moves to the publish and cache stage.

Do not treat a successful encoder exit as verification. Those are two different signals.

How should Node.js strip EXIF location data before publishing?

The following Go program is deliberately narrow: it accepts JPEG input, decodes the image, scales it to a bounded width, writes a fresh JPEG, reopens that derivative, and fails if it finds an APP1 segment beginning with the EXIF identifier. It uses only the standard library, so the resampling is nearest-neighbor; for visual quality, substitute a reviewed resampler without changing the verification boundary.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "bytes"
    "encoding/binary"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "image"
    "image/jpeg"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 4 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: thumbnail input.jpg output.jpg max-width")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    maxWidth, err := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[3])
    if err != nil || maxWidth < 1 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "max-width must be a positive integer")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    must(checkProcessSchema())

    in, err := os.Open(os.Args[1])
    must(err)
    src, err := jpeg.Decode(in)
    in.Close()
    must(err)

    dst := resize(src, maxWidth)
    out, err := os.OpenFile(os.Args[2], os.O_CREATE|os.O_EXCL|os.O_WRONLY, 0600)
    must(err)
    must(jpeg.Encode(out, dst, &jpeg.Options{Quality: 82}))
    must(out.Close())

    derived, err := os.Open(os.Args[2])
    must(err)
    hasEXIF, err := containsEXIF(derived)
    derived.Close()
    must(err)
    if hasEXIF {
        must(errors.New("publication blocked: derivative contains EXIF"))
    }
    fmt.Println("verified: derivative contains no EXIF APP1 segment")
}

func checkProcessSchema() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/image.process"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("schema request failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        if !bytes.Contains(body, []byte(`"path":"/v1/image/process"`)) {
            return errors.New("discovery response did not describe /v1/image/process")
        }
        return nil
    }
    return errors.New("schema request remained rate-limited after four attempts")
}

func resize(src image.Image, maxWidth int) image.Image {
    b := src.Bounds()
    width := b.Dx()
    if width <= maxWidth {
        maxWidth = width
    }
    height := b.Dy() * maxWidth / width
    if height < 1 {
        height = 1
    }
    dst := image.NewRGBA(image.Rect(0, 0, maxWidth, height))
    for y := 0; y < height; y++ {
        for x := 0; x < maxWidth; x++ {
            sx := b.Min.X + x*width/maxWidth
            sy := b.Min.Y + y*b.Dy()/height
            dst.Set(x, y, src.At(sx, sy))
        }
    }
    return dst
}

func containsEXIF(r io.Reader) (bool, error) {
    b := bufio.NewReader(r)
    soi := make([]byte, 2)
    if _, err := io.ReadFull(b, soi); err != nil || !bytes.Equal(soi, []byte{0xff, 0xd8}) {
        return false, errors.New("not a JPEG")
    }
    for {
        prefix, err := b.ReadByte()
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if prefix != 0xff {
            continue
        }
        marker, err := b.ReadByte()
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if marker == 0xda || marker == 0xd9 {
            return false, nil
        }
        if marker == 0x00 || marker == 0xff || marker == 0xd8 || (marker >= 0xd0 && marker <= 0xd7) {
            continue
        }
        var rawLength [2]byte
        if _, err := io.ReadFull(b, rawLength[:]); err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        length := int(binary.BigEndian.Uint16(rawLength[:]))
        if length < 2 {
            return false, errors.New("invalid JPEG segment length")
        }
        payload := make([]byte, length-2)
        if _, err := io.ReadFull(b, payload); err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if marker == 0xe1 && bytes.HasPrefix(payload, []byte("Exif\x00\x00")) {
            return true, nil
        }
    }
}

func must(err error) {
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Run it as a worker after the Node.js handler has durably queued the opaque source reference:

go run ./thumbnail.go private-source.jpg candidate-thumbnail.jpg 640

The create-exclusive output and file mode are intentional safeguards for this local example, but production idempotency belongs at the job and object-name boundary too. A retry should address the same derivative key, and publication should be a state transition after verification, rather than a second upload that can produce two cacheable objects.

This checker targets EXIF in JPEG APP1 segments because location commonly arrives there. A real acceptance policy must enumerate every output format you allow and the metadata containers relevant to those formats. The safer simplification is to allow a small derivative-format set and test each encoder version with fixtures containing GPS metadata, orientation, comments, and color profiles. Decide deliberately which non-location data, such as an ICC profile, the product needs to preserve.

Where does the full operating bill come from?

Start with counts, not vendor price cards. For each day, record original bytes received, retained-source byte-days, derivative pixels encoded, derivative bytes stored, verification bytes read, cache egress, failed jobs, and retries. Multiply those by the system's current billing dimensions, then add the engineering surface: credentials, SDK upgrades, queue behavior, observability, and the labor involved in proving that publication is gated.

Suppose one upload creates three responsive sizes. That is three encodes and three verification reads, not “one image transformation.” If the original is retained indefinitely by accident, storage grows even when the public-thumbnail cache works perfectly. If cache keys include unstable query parameters, egress and transformation volume can rise together. None of those failure modes appears in a unit-price leaderboard.

Retention deserves its own decision. Keep the original only for a documented purpose such as an authorized support workflow or a defined reprocessing window, under access control and with a deletion rule. Otherwise discard it after the verified derivatives are committed. “We may need it” is not a retention policy.

Which implementation boundary earns its keep?

There are at least four credible choices, and they optimize different parts of the workload.

Option Boundary you operate Cost and control trade-off
Sharp in the Node.js worker Your application owns decode, resize, encode, verification, queueing, storage, and cache behavior Strong control over bytes and deployment; your team carries native dependency updates, capacity planning, and the entire incident path.
Cloudinary A specialist image service becomes the transformation and delivery boundary Attractive when image workflow depth and managed delivery dominate; validate metadata behavior on the delivered derivative and model storage, transformations, and delivery together.
imgix A specialist image delivery and transformation layer sits in front of source assets Attractive when URL-driven variants and delivery are central; source governance and an explicit read-back privacy check still need an owner.
ImageKit A managed image optimization and delivery service handles variants outside the application worker Attractive when managed optimization and delivery reduce application work; verify the final delivered bytes and include source storage and cache behavior in the model.
Infrai Image processing and metadata inspection share a REST contract with other backend modules Attractive when integration breadth reduces credential, client, and billing surfaces; a specialist remains the better choice when its image-specific workflow is the main product requirement.

I would try Infrai for the processing and metadata-check portion of a support-thumbnail pipeline when the same team also expects to add other backend capabilities, because its verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key and a consistent REST surface. The supporting benefit is operational: its public discovery surface exposes full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, which gives build-time validation a stable source instead of adding another SDK-specific integration. Keep the recommendation bounded. The supplied image workflow still owns private-original policy, publication gating, cache keys, and the acceptance tests.

Sharp is the cleanest fit when byte-level control and in-process execution matter more than outsourcing operations. Cloudinary or imgix can be the better fit when a specialist's image transformation and delivery model is the workload, rather than one module in a broader backend. Infrai is credible when the marginal integration is the expensive part. That is a workload decision, not a universal ranking.

Instrument the boundary before tuning the alert

Emit one structured event when the candidate derivative is written, one when verification completes, and one when publication commits. Join them with the opaque job ID. The useful service-level invariant is exact: every published derivative has a successful verification event for the same content identity and encoder version.

Then test the monitor by feeding a fixture with EXIF GPS data through the actual deployment path. The expected result is a newly encoded derivative with no EXIF marker and a successful publication; separately, inject a deliberately noncompliant candidate after encoding and confirm that publication stops and the page contains the identifiers needed to retry or quarantine it. A synthetic check that never exercises storage and publication proves too little.

Be conservative with paging thresholds. Paging on any blocked publication catches the privacy control doing its job, but one corrupt customer upload can wake someone even though no unsafe image became public. Paging only on a high rejection ratio reduces noise and can miss a single policy regression. A practical split is to record individual user-input rejections for investigation, while paging immediately when the publish-without-verification invariant is violated or when known-clean canary fixtures fail. The exact volume threshold needs production traffic and an error budget; inventing it in advance creates a confident-looking alarm with no evidentiary basis.

The false-positive cost is real. An alert that fires whenever malformed input is safely rejected trains responders to ignore the channel, while the event that matters is sharper and rarer: the system cannot prove that a public derivative passed the metadata policy. Page on loss of the guardrail.

Further reading

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations documentation
  • imgix image rendering documentation
  • ImageKit documentation
  • ExifTool tag names and metadata reference
  • Infrai documentation

If this integration boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before wiring the worker.

title: pg_vectorsearch Claims 6 ms at 100M Vectors. Filtered Queries Can Come Back Short
description:
• Book: Database Playbook
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If your RAG app keeps its embeddings in Postgres, the index behind it is probably pgvector's HNSW. pgvector's own README says HNSW "has slower build times and uses more memory" than its other index type, IVFFlat, in exchange for a better speed-recall trade-off.

On October 13, Tiger Data, the company behind TimescaleDB, announced pg_vectorsearch, an open-source Postgres extension with a new index called PRISM. Its headline: 6 ms median latency at 95% recall on 100 million vectors, on a machine where pgvector's HNSW build did not finish. On October 14 it drew a Hacker News thread.

Two things decide whether this matters to you yet. The numbers come from Tiger Data's own benchmark. And the alpha has a gap right where most RAG queries live: the WHERE clause.

What Tiger Data shipped

PRISM stands for Partitioned Routing Index for Similarity Matching, and it is a native Postgres index access method, so there is no separate service to run. Instead of HNSW's graph, it groups vectors into k-means clusters and, per the announcement, "stores each vector as a RaBitQ code of roughly one bit per dimension."

A query walks a centroid tree to the nearest clusters, scans their posting lists, filters candidates with RaBitQ error bounds, then reranks them with full-precision vectors from the table (README). The README describes it as "conceptually similar" to pgvector's IVFFlat.

The practical details, all from the README:

  • It needs PostgreSQL 18 or later.
  • It ships its own vec32 and vec16 types, and they are binary-compatible with pgvector's vector and halfvec.
  • It can index an existing pgvector column without rewriting the table, and the two extensions can sit side by side.
  • It is under the PostgreSQL License.

The pitch is one sentence in the announcement: "We built pg_vectorsearch so you can stay in PostgreSQL."

The numbers are Tiger Data's, so read the conditions

Every result in Tiger Data's announcement comes from its public benchmark tool, rekall. Recall is recall@10 against exact brute-force results, and every HNSW run used pgvector's halfvec. Here is the 100-million-vector run, on Cohere embeddings, as the post reports it:

Machine Index Build Size p50 @95% p50 @99%
r8i.4xlarge (128 GB) PRISM 1 h 40 min 25 GB 6 ms 21 ms
r8i.4xlarge (128 GB) HNSW did not finish n/a n/a n/a
r8i.16xlarge (512 GB) PRISM 49 min 25 GB 4 ms 19 ms
r8i.16xlarge (512 GB) HNSW 42 h 180 GB 8 ms not reached

At 1 million vectors, the same post reports PRISM at 15 ms median for 99% recall on a 2 GB c8g.medium, against 392 ms for HNSW on a 4 GB c8g.large. It says the HNSW build on the 4 GB machine took about 21.7 hours and thrashed.

What the announcement doesn't give you: the dimensionality of either dataset, throughput (queries per second), or a direct IVFFlat comparison. Multi-client throughput testing is listed as still pending. In the HN thread, one commenter asked for exactly that: "qps and precision/recall, please." I haven't run pg_vectorsearch myself, so treat the table as the vendor's claim, which rekall lets you check on your own data.

What the alpha doesn't do yet

Tiger Data is upfront about this. "This is the first public release of pg_vectorsearch, and we're calling it an alpha," the announcement says, and the 0.1.0-rc1 release notes call it "alpha quality and meant for testing, not production." The known issues in those notes are the part to read before you plan anything:

  • Filtered queries can return fewer rows than LIMIT. If the rows that pass your WHERE aren't among the candidates the scan ranked, it doesn't look further (issue #188). A multi-tenant query like WHERE tenant_id = 7 ... LIMIT 10 can come back with fewer than 10 rows.
  • Large ordered scans can return partial results without an error. With no LIMIT, or a LIMIT larger than work_mem lets it rank, you get only what that budget covers. Raising work_mem fixes the budget case.
  • At most 1,968 dimensions, and no unlogged tables or expression indexes.
  • Upgrades between prereleases may not work, so plan to drop and recreate the extension and its indexes.

The announcement adds the rest. There is no automatic rebalancing, so recall can drift under heavy churn until you run prism_rebalance or REINDEX. Space from deleted rows isn't reclaimed until REINDEX, and replication and backup/restore testing is still pending. Filtered "streaming search" is planned for GA.

The dimension cap is the one to check first. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large returns 3,072 dimensions by default (OpenAI docs), and pgvector's HNSW can index halfvec up to 4,000 (pgvector README). If that's your setup, you'd need to shorten the vectors before PRISM could index them: re-embed with OpenAI's dimensions parameter, or truncate the stored vectors and re-normalize, which OpenAI's guide also describes.

pgvectorscale moves to maintenance mode

If you adopted Tiger Data's earlier extension, pgvectorscale, this is the news for you. Tiger Data's announcement says it is stable and runs production workloads, but will enter maintenance mode, and that its DiskANN-inspired graph index could lose recall on low-dimensional datasets. A pgvectorscale author said the same in the HN thread.

The post doesn't say what pgvectorscale users should do next. As of October 14, the pgvectorscale README carries no maintenance notice, and Tiger Cloud's extension list still includes it. The announcement doesn't mention Tiger Cloud support for pg_vectorsearch, and a commenter in the HN thread noted it isn't on managed providers' extension lists yet.

Try it next to HNSW, on a copy

You need Postgres 18 for this anyway, so do it on a staging copy of the table, not your production database. The README shows indexing an existing pgvector column directly. Pick the operator class that matches your column type and distance: vec32_* for vector, vec16_* for halfvec, with _l2_ops, _ip_ops or _cosine_ops.

CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch;

CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_prism
  ON documents
  USING prism (embedding vec32_cosine_ops);

-- 40 is the README's example value.
-- 0 = auto (~0.95 recall); raise for recall,
-- lower for speed.
SET prism.nprobe = 40;

On the copy, drop the HNSW index so the planner can only pick PRISM, then confirm it does:

EXPLAIN
SELECT id FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding <=> (
  SELECT embedding FROM documents WHERE id = 1
)
LIMIT 10;

For recall, run the same query with index scans off, which gives you the exact top 10, and compare the two lists of IDs:

BEGIN;
SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off;
SET LOCAL enable_indexonlyscan = off;
SELECT id FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding <=> (
  SELECT embedding FROM documents WHERE id = 1
)
LIMIT 10;
ROLLBACK;

Do that for a few hundred real queries, including your filtered ones, before you trust a number. Short results on filtered queries are issue #188, not your setup.

So, would you switch?

Vectors that fit in RAM, with HNSW fast enough? The alpha gives you little reason to move today. If your HNSW builds take a day, or your index no longer fits in memory, it is worth a weekend on a copy. Selective WHERE filters, like a per-tenant query, are where the alpha comes back short, so those are the queries to watch when GA lands.

What's stopping you: the Postgres 18 upgrade, the filtering gap, or your managed provider's extension list?

If this was useful

Picking between HNSW, IVFFlat and a new index type is the same call as picking a store: you trade memory, build time and query shape against each other, and the benchmark only tells you about someone else's data. The Database Playbook walks through those trade-offs for Postgres, SQLite, Redis, DynamoDB and the rest, so you can make that call for your own system.

I also build Hermes IDE (GitHub), free and source-available for macOS, Windows and Linux, where each coding-agent task can run on its own branch and worktree. That helps if you hand an experiment like this one to an agent. It's my project, so weigh that.

title: "We had good coverage" is the weakest answer in the round
description:
what deserves a test, what does not, and how you know the suite is telling you the truth. Coverage percentages answer none of that.

Written after an answer that was a number and nothing else. Updated October 2026. 7 min read

Where the tests should live
end to end, few
integration
unit, many and fast
WHAT THEY ASK
what would you test here?
what would you not test?
how do you test the failure?
what makes a test flaky?
The short version: say what you would test and what you deliberately would not, put most tests at the fast end, test the failure paths rather than only the happy one, and have an opinion about flaky tests. A candidate who can say what is not worth testing sounds far more experienced than one quoting coverage.

Team practices vary widely. Defend your own with reasons rather than rules.

The number that answered nothing
"Our coverage was around eighty percent."

It was true and it told the interviewer nothing. Coverage measures which lines ran, not whether anything was checked. The follow up, which I had no answer for, was simple: which part of that system were you most afraid of, and what did you do about it.

Coverage says what was executed. The interview is about what was verified.
What to say instead
Risk first, shape second.

1
Name the risk
Which part would
hurt most if it
broke quietly?
2
Pick the level
Unit for logic,
integration for
wiring, end to end
sparingly.
3
Test the failure
Timeouts, bad input,
partial writes.
4
Keep it honest
Delete tests that
never fail and fix
ones that fail
randomly.
Four moves that turn a coverage answer into a judgement answer.
What not to test
The part that signals experience.

Usually worth testing
Business rules and edge cases
Data transformations
Error and retry paths
Anything that has broken before
Usually not worth it
Framework behaviour
Simple getters and setters
Exact log strings
Private methods through reflection
Flaky tests are a trust problem
Say that out loud.

One test that fails randomly teaches an entire team to rerun the pipeline without reading it. That habit then hides a real failure. Quarantine first so trust survives, then fix the cause, which is nearly always time, test ordering or shared state between tests.

Testing the failure path
The question candidates skip.

Timeouts
What does your code do when the dependency never answers?
Partial writes
Half the batch succeeded. Is that state recoverable?
Bad input
Not just invalid, but plausible and wrong.
Retries
Does retrying twice produce two of something?
If your current team has no tests
Answer honestly and move to the plan.

Saying that your team ships without tests, followed by which single path you would cover first and why, reads far better than inventing a culture you did not have. Interviewers are mostly checking whether you have an opinion and whether you would improve things without demanding a rewrite.

How I practised the discussion
Out loud, on real code.

I took functions from my own projects and talked through what I would test and skip, with a timer. For the rest of the loop, the algorithm round and the behavioral round, I used Phantom Code AI[https://www.phantomcodeai.com/] nightly, attempting first and comparing second. Having coding, system design, SQL and behavioral practice in one place meant the craft discussions above were the only thing I had to rehearse separately.

Common questions
Short answers.

Unit versus integration?
Is high coverage a good goal?
How do you handle flaky tests?
What if your job has no tests?
Have an opinion, not a percentage
The strongest testing answers I have heard were specific about what the person chose not to test. That is the sentence that separates judgement from compliance.

Take one function you wrote this week and say out loud what deserves a test and what does not.

Written after learning that eighty percent is not an answer

What is the most useful test you ever wrote?

Mine caught a timezone bug that would have been invisible.

title: Database Indexes and Idempotency: What They Fix, and How to Get Them Wrong
description:
Two things quietly decide whether a small application survives being used: whether its reads
are indexed, and whether its writes can be repeated safely. They are usually taught as separate
subjects - one belongs to databases, the other to API design. They are the same subject seen
twice. An index is how reads survive scale. Idempotency is how writes survive retries.

Every example below is from the application that serves this page, including a failure that
happened while it was being written.

Part one: what an index actually is

The mental model that gets people into trouble is "an index makes the table faster". It does
not. An index is a second, ordered copy of some of your columns, with a pointer back to the
row. Adding one gives the query planner a new route to the data. It does not change the table.

Two consequences follow immediately, and both matter more than the speedup:

  • Every index is paid for on write. An insert into a table with four indexes is five writes, not one. An index nobody reads is a pure tax.
  • An index only helps if the query can use it. Wrapping the indexed column in a function - WHERE YEAR(PublishedAt) = 2026 - throws the ordering away and the planner scans anyway. So does a leading wildcard in a LIKE.

The problem an index solves, concretely

This site lists blog posts. The query behind that list is, in effect:

SELECT ... FROM BlogPosts
WHERE IsPublished = 1 AND PublishedAt IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY PublishedAt DESC;

Without a useful index the database reads every row to find the published ones, then sorts
the survivors. At a hundred rows nobody notices. At fifty thousand you are reading fifty thousand
rows and sorting most of them to return ten.

With the right index the database walks a structure that is already filtered and already in
the right order, takes the first ten entries, and stops.

Composite indexes, and why column order is the whole game

These three indexes shipped with this application:

IX_BlogPosts_IsPublished_PublishedAt             (IsPublished, PublishedAt)
IX_BlogPosts_IsPublished_IsFeatured_PublishedAt  (IsPublished, IsFeatured, PublishedAt)
IX_BlogPosts_AuthorId_IsPublished                (AuthorId, IsPublished)

Look at the first one. The order is not arbitrary and it is not alphabetical. A composite
index is sorted by its first column, then within that by its second - like a phone book sorted by
surname, then first name.

(IsPublished, PublishedAt) puts all the published rows together, and inside that
group they are already in date order. The query above filters on the first column and sorts on
the second, so the database seeks to the published section and reads straight down it. No sort
step at all.

Reverse it to (PublishedAt, IsPublished) and the same index is nearly useless
for the same query. The rows are now ordered by date first, with published and unpublished
interleaved throughout. There is no contiguous block of published rows to seek to.

Same two columns. Same table. One arrangement answers the query without a sort; the other
does not. The rule worth memorising: columns you filter by with equality come first,
the column you sort or range-scan on comes last.

Why the third index exists separately

(AuthorId, IsPublished) could look redundant next to the others. It is not,
because of the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (A, B) can serve queries filtering
on A, or on A and B - but not queries filtering on
B alone. The author page filters by author first, so it needs an index that leads
with AuthorId. No amount of indexes leading with IsPublished will help
it.

When not to add one

Indexes are not free and the instinct to add one per column is how tables get slow at writing
without getting faster at reading. Skip them on small tables, on columns with very few distinct
values, and on anything you have not actually seen in a slow query. Add them from evidence -
an execution plan, a slow query log - rather than from intuition.

Part two: idempotency, and the problem it actually solves

An operation is idempotent when doing it twice leaves the same result as doing it once.
Reading is naturally idempotent. Setting a value is idempotent. Appending is not. Charging a card
is emphatically not.

The problem it solves is narrower and more common than "duplicate clicks". It is this:
a network gives you no way to tell a request that failed from a response that was
lost. Your client sends a request, waits, and gets a timeout. Did the server do the
work? You cannot know from the client. And the moment you retry - and every HTTP client, load
balancer and message queue retries - you are betting the outcome on that unanswerable
question.

Idempotency removes the question. If the operation is safe to repeat, the retry is safe. You
stop needing to know whether the first attempt landed.

The pattern, in SQL

The simplest form is to make the write describe the destination rather than the change. This
is not idempotent:

UPDATE Posts SET ViewCount = ViewCount + 1 WHERE Id = 42;   -- runs twice, counts twice

This is:

UPDATE Posts SET ViewCount = 981 WHERE Id = 42;             -- runs twice, same result

When you genuinely need an increment, the idempotency has to come from somewhere else -
usually a record of which events you have already counted.

For inserts, the equivalent is to check before writing. The script that published this post
runs as an upsert, so running it a second time edits the post rather than creating a duplicate:

IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM BlogPosts WHERE Slug = @slug)
    UPDATE BlogPosts SET Title = @title, Content = @content WHERE Slug = @slug;
ELSE
    INSERT INTO BlogPosts (Title, Slug, Content) VALUES (@title, @slug, @content);

That is a small habit with a large payoff: any script written this way can be re-run after a
failure without anyone having to work out how far it got.

Idempotency keys, and when you need one

Checking before writing works when the row has something naturally unique - a slug, an email,
an order reference. When it does not, the client supplies the uniqueness instead: a key generated
per intended operation, sent with the request, and stored by the server alongside the result.

The server's logic becomes: if this key has been seen, return the stored response and do
nothing. If not, do the work and record the key with the outcome, in the same transaction. Stripe
popularised the pattern with its Idempotency-Key header, and it is the right answer
for anything that moves money or sends a message.

Two details decide whether an implementation works. The key must be stored in the same
transaction as the work - store it afterwards and a crash in between gives you the duplicate
you were preventing. And the stored response has to be returned on a repeat, not just a bare
200, or the caller cannot tell what happened.

Where the two ideas meet: EF Core's migration history

Entity Framework's __EFMigrationsHistory table is an idempotency ledger, though
nobody calls it that. It exists so that running dotnet ef database update twice does
not apply the same migration twice. Each applied migration's ID is the key.

Which makes its failure mode instructive - and it happened on this project while this article
was being drafted. A migration had been applied under one generated ID. Later the migration file
was regenerated and picked up a new timestamp in its name. The change was already in the database;
the ledger held the old key. EF compared files to history, saw an ID it had no record of,
and tried to apply it again:

Column names in each table must be unique.
Column name 'ResumeUpdatedAt' in table 'SiteSettings' is specified more than once.

The schema was correct. Only the bookkeeping was wrong. The fix is to record the key that
should have been there - itself written idempotently, so re-running it is harmless:

IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM __EFMigrationsHistory
               WHERE MigrationId = '20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings')
    INSERT INTO __EFMigrationsHistory (MigrationId, ProductVersion)
    VALUES ('20260920154332_AddResumeToSiteSettings', '9.0.0');

The lesson generalises past EF. An idempotency mechanism is only as good as the stability of
its key. Change how the key is derived and the ledger stops protecting you - silently, until
something tries to run twice.

What to take from this

Indexes answer a question about reading: can the database find these rows without looking at
all of them? Get the column order right and most of the work disappears; get it backwards and
the index is decoration you pay for on every insert.

Idempotency answers a question about writing: if this runs twice, is the result the same?
Make it so, and the entire category of bug that begins "the request timed out and then
everything was duplicated" stops existing.

Neither is advanced. Both are the difference between an application that works in testing and
one that works in production.

FAQ

What is a database index, in simple terms?

A second, ordered copy of some of your columns with pointers back to the rows. It gives the query planner a faster route to the data without changing the table itself. The cost is that every insert and update has to maintain it as well.

Why does column order matter in a composite index?

A composite index is sorted by its first column, then by its second within that - like a phone book by surname then first name. An index on (IsPublished, PublishedAt) lets a query filter on IsPublished and read the results already in date order. Reverse the columns and the same query gains almost nothing.

When should I not add an index?

On small tables, on columns with very few distinct values, and on anything you have not seen in a slow query. Every index is paid for on every write, so one nobody reads is a pure tax. Add them from an execution plan, not from intuition.

What does idempotent mean?

Doing the operation twice leaves the same result as doing it once. Setting a value is idempotent; incrementing one is not. It matters because a network cannot tell you whether a request failed or the response was simply lost.

What problem do idempotency keys actually solve?

They remove the need to know whether a timed-out request landed. The client sends a key with the operation; the server stores it with the result. A repeat of the same key returns the stored response instead of doing the work again - so a retry cannot charge a card or send an email twice.

How do I make an SQL script safe to re-run?

Write the destination rather than the change, and check before inserting. An upsert - IF EXISTS then UPDATE, ELSE INSERT - can be run any number of times without creating duplicates, which means a failed run can simply be repeated.

Originally published on knowledgemarkg.com.
