title: Brotli for WASM and ONNX Models: Cutting First-Run Downloads From 72MB to 13MB, and the Compatibility Call We Made on Purpose
description:
We build ClearPix, a set of media cleanup tools that run entirely in the browser. That means every engine we ship — the ONNX Runtime WebGPU backend (a 27MB jsep.wasm plus a 14MB core), the ffmpeg core for video (30.7MB), and the model zoo behind our inpainting, upscale, and detection tools (up to a 198MB LaMa) — is downloaded into a stranger's browser tab before anything useful happens. The download path is the product experience. This post is about the delivery layer we ended up with: pre-compressed brotli objects on Cloudflare R2, why we compress WASM hard and ONNX barely, the progress-bar bug that fell out of it, and the compatibility decision we made consciously instead of by default.

What actually constrains model delivery

Three hard facts shaped everything:

  1. Cloudflare Pages has a 25MB per-file limit. Our biggest files (27–198MB) can't even live in the deploy bundle. The build strips them, so a "mirror chain" isn't an optimization — it's the only way the product works at all.
  2. Public mirrors are a fallback, not a source. We learned this in production on 2026-09-26: huggingface.co was unreachable from some networks, and hf-mirror's CORS headers were inconsistent (sometimes Access-Control-Allow-Origin, sometimes nothing), so model downloads simply failed for real users. Everything large now lives in an R2 bucket we control — 10GB free, zero egress fees, one controllable origin.
  3. The fallback path gets real traffic. For the ORT runtime binaries we probe jsDelivr first (measured roughly 7× the throughput of our R2 custom domain) and fall back to R2 when the CDN is blocked — which happens in entire network regions. So the R2 path is not a theoretical safety net; for a slice of users it is the path. We measured our own access too: the default pub-*.r2.dev URL crawls at 75–110 KB/s, while a same-zone custom domain (static.clearpix.org) sustains ~2.3 MB/s — a 20–30× difference that has nothing to do with compression.

Brotli: compress at upload, not at request time

R2 doesn't transcode on the fly. You store bytes; it serves bytes. So we compress at upload time in the setup script, using nothing but Node's built-in zlib:

const br = brotliCompressSync(readFileSync(p), {
  params: { [BROTLI_PARAM_QUALITY]: 11 },
});
// wrangler r2 object put ... --content-encoding br --content-type application/wasm

The object key doesn't change, Content-Type stays application/wasm, and the browser transparently decodes Content-Encoding: br before the bytes ever reach ONNX Runtime or our model loader. Zero runtime changes — the URLs are identical, SHA-256 pins validate the decoded bytes, and IndexedDB caches the decoded bytes.

Measured ratios at quality 11, on our real files:

File Raw Brotli Ratio
ort-wasm-simd-threaded.jsep.wasm 27.0 MB 3.8 MB 14%
ort-wasm-simd-threaded.wasm 14.2 MB 2.2 MB 16%
ffmpeg-core.wasm 30.7 MB 6.9 MB 22%
migan.onnx (inpainting) 28.2 MB 23.1 MB 82%
yolo11_watermark_det.onnx 10.6 MB 8.8 MB 84%
lama_fp32.onnx 198.4 MB 179.2 MB 90%
real_esrgan_x4.onnx 63.9 MB 58.6 MB 92%
ppocr_v5_mobile_det.onnx 4.5 MB 4.2 MB 93%

The pattern is physics, not tuning: WASM is code — structured, repetitive, full of zeros — and crushes to 14–22%. ONNX models are mostly float32 weights, which are close to entropy-maximal noise; brotli shaves 8–18% and that's the ceiling. (Worth knowing before you promise "50% smaller models" somewhere.) The full archive, all ten files, drops from 384MB to 293MB — but the number users feel is the first-run set: ORT WASM + ffmpeg went from 71.9MB to 13.0MB, an 82% cut on the critical path. Upload-side cost is a one-time ~10 minutes of q11 compression; quality 11 matters for a file served a million times, not for one.

The bug this introduced: progress bars that lie

Compression broke one thing, and it's worth calling out because it's subtle. When a response carries Content-Encoding: br, the Content-Length header is the compressed size, but a streaming reader in JavaScript receives decoded bytes. Our model loader's progress bar counted decoded bytes against the compressed total — so a 198MB model served as 179MB of brotli would blow straight past "100%" and keep climbing.

The fix is three lines: if Content-Encoding is present, ignore Content-Length and use the spec's known original size (expectedSize) as the denominator. Decoded bytes over original size — progress is honest again. Integrity checking was never affected: we hash the decoded bytes against pinned SHA-256s, so a compressed mirror and an uncompressed mirror are interchangeable.

The decision: br-only, no negotiation, on purpose

Here's the call we get asked about. An object uploaded with content-encoding: br is served that way to every request — R2 stores the encoded bytes and doesn't do content negotiation. A client that can't decode brotli gets undecodable bytes. We could have stored two variants (identity + .br) and put a ~50-line Worker in front of the custom domain to switch on Accept-Encoding, with Vary headers and doubled storage.

We didn't. The reasoning, in one table:

Brotli support Our runtime baseline
Chrome 50 (2016) WebGPU since 113 (2023)
Firefox 44 (2016) WebGPU since 141 (2025)
Safari 11 (2017) WebGPU since 26 (2025)
Edge 15 (2017) 113 (2023)

A browser that can't decode brotli is from 2016 or earlier. A browser that can run ONNX Runtime Web with WASM SIMD and WebGPU is from 2023 or later. The intersection of "can't decode br" with "can boot our app" is empty — the fallback we'd be building serves users who are stopped two checkpoints earlier anyway. Building dual-variant + negotiation to protect a theoretical client is solving a problem we don't have, at the cost of a Worker in the request path and an ops surface we have to maintain forever. If that ever changes — say, a genuinely non-br embedded client appears — the dual-variant design is a clean add-on, and we wrote down exactly how we'd do it.

The honest caveat, for your own tooling rather than users: anything that fetches from R2 with plain curl needs brotli support (curl --compressed), or it saves compressed bytes to disk. Fine for scripts, worth documenting.

One thing we still don't love: ORT WASM has no persistent cache

Our ONNX models and ffmpeg core have a two-level cache: immutable HTTP headers plus IndexedDB with self-healing SHA-256 verification — download once, keep forever, survive releases. The ORT runtime WASM is different: ONNX Runtime fetches it internally, so we can't feed it from IndexedDB, and its only cache layer is the browser's HTTP cache. Mobile browsers evict that under storage pressure, and our release cadence happens to match the eviction cadence — which is why "every release makes users re-download the WASM" is an illusion we'd like to kill properly with a Service Worker and Cache Storage. That's the next post in this layer of the stack.

Try it

Everything described here runs in production: the dual-engine MI-GAN/LaMa watermark remover at clearpix.org/remove-watermark (the 198MB LaMa is the opt-in HQ engine — never prefetched), the Real-ESRGAN upscaler at clearpix.org/upscale-image, and the WebCodecs/ffmpeg pipelines that motivated the ffmpeg core over at clearpix.org/remove-video-watermark. Open devtools on any of them: the only bytes on the wire are the engines and models themselves.

Part 9 of the ClearPix engineering series — how we build free, private, in-browser media tools at clearpix.org.

title: Realtime WebRTC Message Limits — Failure Recovery for Node.js Video Consults
description:
A video consultation room should treat message size as a negotiated runtime constraint, not a constant hidden in a client library. Read the WebRTC data-channel limit, reserve bytes for the envelope, split only payloads that are safe to reassemble, and make an oversized message observable and recoverable. Keep media on the media path; keep typing indicators and read receipts small enough to survive reconnects.

Short answer: cap application messages below the channel's advertised maximum, reject or chunk oversized payloads before send(), and backfill durable receipt state after reconnect instead of replaying every transient keystroke.

Decision Pick this when Failure behavior
Single bounded message Typing or a receipt fits the negotiated limit Send once with an idempotent event id; record success or rejection
Chunked payload A document or audit bundle must cross the same channel Add a transfer id and sequence; expire incomplete transfers
Durable backfill A receipt affects the room's shared truth Store the state server-side and fetch from the last revision after reconnect

The room in this guide is a logistics call between a driver and a dispatcher. A typing signal can disappear. A read receipt cannot silently move backward because a phone changed networks.

What should a realtime video consultation room do about message size limits and failure handling?

Start with the value exposed by the browser. The W3C WebRTC Recommendation defines RTCSctpTransport.maxMessageSize, which represents the maximum size for a message sent over the SCTP transport. It is a property of the negotiated connection, so two rooms or two browser pairs may produce different values. Do not bake one number into a shared constant and call it a protocol.

The diagram in words: application event -> envelope budget check -> data channel -> receiver reassembly -> reducer -> durable reconciliation. The envelope is part of the budget. If a JSON object is 900 bytes in one language and 1,200 after UTF-8 encoding, a character count is the wrong measurement.

A practical envelope carries a stable event id, room id, kind, revision when the event is durable, and the payload. The client measures encoded bytes, not JavaScript string length. It rejects before send() so the transport exception does not become the user's failure message.

type RoomEvent = {
  eventId: string;
  roomId: string;
  kind: "typing" | "read_receipt" | "attachment_chunk";
  revision?: number;
  payload: unknown;
};

function encodedBytes(event: RoomEvent): number {
  return new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(event)).byteLength;
}

function channelLimit(channel: RTCDataChannel): number {
  const limit = channel.transport?.maxMessageSize;
  if (typeof limit !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(limit)) {
    throw new Error("SCTP message limit is unavailable");
  }
  return limit;
}

export function sendBounded(
  channel: RTCDataChannel,
  event: RoomEvent,
  safetyBytes = 256,
): "sent" | "rejected" {
  const budget = channelLimit(channel) - safetyBytes;
  if (budget <= 0 || encodedBytes(event) > budget) return "rejected";
  channel.send(JSON.stringify(event));
  return "sent";
}

The safety margin is local policy, not a WebRTC requirement. I use it to leave room for a future envelope field, then measure rejection rates. Your mileage may vary; the right margin depends on whether the channel carries only tiny control events or also carries occasional structured records.

Keep typing ephemeral and receipts durable

Typing indicators are presence-like hints. Give them a short expiry, coalesce repeated updates, and drop them while the channel is backpressured. A dispatcher does not need ten typing=true events queued behind a stale network path. A single typing event with a timestamp is enough to render a temporary state.

Read receipts are different. Persist the highest message sequence each participant has read, or persist an equivalent monotonic marker, then publish a compact notification. On reconnect, the client asks for the authoritative receipt revision and applies it only if it is newer than its local value. That is backfill, not replay.

type Receipt = {
  participantId: string;
  messageSeq: number;
  revision: number;
};

export function applyReceipt(current: Receipt | undefined, incoming: Receipt): Receipt {
  if (!current) return incoming;
  if (incoming.revision <= current.revision) return current;
  if (incoming.messageSeq < current.messageSeq) return current;
  return incoming;
}

export function shouldQueue(kind: RoomEvent["kind"], buffered: number): boolean {
  if (kind === "typing") return false;
  return buffered < 64 * 1024;
}

One early implementation queued both event types in the same FIFO. It looked orderly in a test room, then a brief disconnect made the queue contain old typing pulses ahead of a receipt. The receipt arrived late, the UI appeared to un-read a message, and the only useful clue was a rising bufferedAmount. Separate the semantics before you add retries.

Instrument the rejection path before shipping

A failed send() is not enough telemetry. Record the event kind, encoded byte length, negotiated limit, channel label, connection state, and a pseudonymous room identifier. Never record consultation text or a full attachment while diagnosing a size problem. The useful metric is a ratio: rejected bytes or events divided by attempted events, split by browser and release.

Emit counters for message_rejected_size, message_dropped_backpressure, receipt_backfill_requested, and receipt_revision_gap. Add a duration for reconnect-to-convergence. An alert should fire on a sustained increase in receipt gaps, not on one driver's laptop losing Wi-Fi.

type SizeObservation = {
  kind: RoomEvent["kind"];
  bytes: number;
  limit: number;
  connectionState: RTCPeerConnectionState;
  roomKey: string;
};

export function observeSize(o: SizeObservation): void {
  metrics.increment("message_rejected_size", 1, {
    kind: o.kind,
    browserLimit: String(o.limit),
    connectionState: o.connectionState,
  });
  logs.info("realtime message rejected", {
    ...o,
    roomKey: hashForMetrics(o.roomKey),
  });
}

const metrics = {
  increment(name: string, value: number, labels: Record<string, string>) {
    void [name, value, labels];
  },
};

const logs = {
  info(message: string, fields: unknown) {
    void [message, fields];
  },
};

function hashForMetrics(value: string): string {
  return value.slice(0, 8);
}

That hash is a placeholder for an application-approved pseudonymization function, not a security primitive. The point is to keep the metric joinable without putting a room identifier into every dashboard label.

One useful drill is a three-step reconnect with a dispatcher tablet. First, send a read receipt at revision 41, then cut the data channel while the tablet is offline and let the driver read two more messages. The tablet must not manufacture revisions 42 and 43 from local timestamps; it should mark its receipt as stale and request the authoritative marker. Next, deliver a duplicate notification and a notification whose payload is larger than the current budget. The duplicate should be harmless, while the oversized event should be rejected before transport and counted with the negotiated limit that was observed for that room. Finally, restore the channel with a smaller maxMessageSize than the previous connection, apply the backfilled receipt, and confirm that the UI converges once. This sequence exercises the awkward ordering that happy-path demos skip: a local queue, a changed transport capability, a revision gap, and a duplicate can all coexist. Logs should make each transition legible without storing the consultation itself, so an on-call engineer can explain why the receipt moved forward even though a typing indicator vanished.

Keep the signal small.

Test reconnects, limits, and partial transfers

The catch is scope. A data channel is not a durable log, and maxMessageSize does not give you a server-side history. This design is unsuitable when a consultation needs guaranteed delivery of large clinical or legal artifacts; use an authenticated upload or durable message store and send only its reference through realtime. It is also a poor fit if your target browsers do not expose a dependable SCTP limit, because guessing creates silent fragmentation failures.

Test with the smallest observed negotiated limit, a payload exactly at the budget, one byte over, a channel with a growing bufferedAmount, a disconnect between chunks, duplicate chunks, and a reconnect after the receipt revision has advanced. Verify that an incomplete transfer expires, that a duplicate event id is harmless, and that the final screen converges to the durable receipt state.

I am not sure a single chunk size will remain optimal as browser implementations and network paths change. Capture the negotiated limit at connection time, keep the policy configurable, and review the distributions after each release. The operational win is clarity: a driver sees a temporary typing gap, while the dispatcher and driver eventually agree on the same read receipt.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/RTCSctpTransport/maxMessageSize

title: Letting an LLM press buy: idempotency keys, fsync and process groups
description:
We recently shipped a way for AI agents (Claude Code, Codex, anything that takes a prompt and reads stdin, or speaks MCP) to act on the live trades of Polymarket wallets and place orders of their own. The data side streams fills to the agent; the trading side is a command the agent calls:

pmwallets-copytrade order buy <tokenId> --usdc 5 --max-price 0.45 --key <eventId>

The happy path needs little code. Most of what we wrote handles failures that could cost money; those are the cases I'll cover here.

The failures we planned for were ordinary ones:

  • The agent retries a command after it seemed slow.
  • The model misspells an argument.
  • The process crashes, or the machine loses power, halfway through something.
  • The agent CLI starts child processes that outlive it.

Each of those, unhandled, turns into either a second order or an order without the limit you meant to set.

1. A spend ceiling that's actually a ceiling

--usdc 5 reads as "spend $5". What we wanted was "never spend more than $5".

A BUY is fill-or-kill at a limit price, and the share count is computed at that limit, not at the current ask:

// usdc is a ceiling: sized at the limit, the order cannot cost more than it whatever it matches
shares = roundBuyShares((microToward(req.usdc, 'down') * UNIT) / limit, limit);

If the ask is 0.40 and the agent sets --max-price 0.45, it gets 5 / 0.45 shares. If the book moves up to 0.45 between the check and the match, the cost is still at most $5. A loose --max-price buys fewer shares, but keeps the order within the budget.

The rounding took more thought than expected. Prices and amounts are integers in millionths, and the caller's numbers come in as JavaScript floats. Rounding to nearest turns usdc 1.9999999 into 2.00 and minPrice 0.3800001 into 0.38, both of which loosen the caller's limit slightly. So every caller number is rounded in the direction that can't loosen it: a budget, a max price or a share count down, a min price up. It's done on the number's shortest decimal string, exactly, so no binary floating-point digit decides the direction:

export function microToward(x: number, dir: 'up' | 'down'): bigint {
  const m = /^(\d+)(?:\.(\d+))?(?:e([+-]?\d+))?$/.exec(String(x));
  if (!m) throw new Error(`cannot read ${x} as a decimal`);
  const digits = BigInt(`${m[1]}${m[2] ?? ''}`);
  const shift = Number(m[3] ?? 0) - (m[2]?.length ?? 0) + 6;
  if (shift >= 0) return digits * 10n ** BigInt(shift);
  const div = 10n ** BigInt(-shift);
  const q = digits / div;
  return dir === 'down' || digits % div === 0n ? q : q + 1n;
}

The same rule applies to the market's tick size: a BUY limit is rounded down onto the tick grid, a SELL floor up, and a floor above the highest price the market accepts is refused rather than lowered.

2. The idempotency key is written before the order leaves

A claude -p run that saw a slow response may run the same command again. --key prevents that retry from sending a second order; the fill's eventId is a suitable choice.

The key is claimed on disk and synced before the order is sent:

claim(key: string): boolean {
  mkdirDurable(this.dir);
  let fd: number;
  try {
    fd = openSync(this.file(key), 'wx');        // exclusive create: two callers can't both win
  } catch (e) {
    if ((e as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === 'EEXIST') return false;
    throw e;
  }
  try {
    writeSync(fd, JSON.stringify({ status: 'sending', key, claimedAt: new Date().toISOString() }));
    fsyncSync(fd);
  } finally { closeSync(fd); }
  syncDir(this.dir);                             // the directory entry too
  return true;
}

These details each came from a specific failure case:

  • wx (O_CREAT | O_EXCL) means two concurrent calls with the same key can't both claim it.
  • fsync on the file isn't enough for a new file. Its directory entry also has to reach the disk, or a power cut can lose the file entirely. Hence syncDir, and mkdirDurable, which syncs each directory level it creates into its parent.
  • If the claim can't be synced, it throws and nothing is sent.
  • A claim with no recorded result (the process died while sending) comes back to the next caller as status: unknown, verify: true, not as "free". The order may have filled; the agent is told to check trades first.

To record the result, we write a temporary file, fsync it, rename it and sync the directory. A crash between the claim and the send means that key won't order again, even though nothing was sent. We accepted that missed-trade risk to avoid sending the same order twice.

3. Handing fills to the agent at most once

pmwallets watch --exec "<agent command>" holds a WebSocket to the fill stream and runs the agent once per batch of fills. The stream itself delivers each fill once, in order, and replays gaps. The question was what happens between the stream and the agent.

At-least-once is the usual choice for queues. Here, if the agent placed an order and then the process crashed, running the batch again could place it again. We hand each batch over at most once:

  1. A fill is appended to queue.jsonl and synced before the stream cursor moves past it.
  2. To run a batch, the batch is written to batch-<id>.jsonl, the queue is rewritten without it, and the batch's eventIds are appended to handed.txt and synced. Only then is the batch renamed to running-<id>.jsonl and the command started.
  3. If the command exits 0, the file is deleted. If it fails or times out, it moves to failed/.
  4. At startup, any running-* file means the previous process died while the agent ran. It moves to failed/ and is never run again. A batch-* file that was never started goes back to the front of the queue, unless its ids are already in handed.txt, in which case it also goes to failed/ for a human.

A fill whose eventId is in handed.txt is never queued again, even if the stream replays it because the cursor wasn't saved before a crash. handed.txt is trimmed occasionally, but only of ids at or before the stream cursor as it is on disk (synced first), since those are the only ones the stream can never replay.

A crash can leave fills in failed/ that nobody acted on. We log those for manual checking and accept that risk with this design.

4. Stopping the agent means stopping everything it started

An agent CLI is rarely one process. claude -p and codex exec start their own children, and a child left running after a timeout might still be about to call order buy.

The command runs in its own process group:

child = nodeSpawn(this.o.exec!, { shell: true, env, stdio: ['pipe', 'inherit', 'inherit'], detached: process.platform !== 'win32' });

A timeout or a stop sends SIGTERM to the whole group (process.kill(-pid, ...)), then SIGKILL five seconds later. On Windows it's taskkill /T /F. When the command exits normally, the group is killed anyway, because a grandchild may still be running.

Two things went wrong here before they were fixed:

  • The pending SIGKILL timers weren't cancelled when the command ended on its own. Five seconds later they could hit a different process that had been given the same pid.
  • A process can leave its group (setsid), and after a crash of the watcher itself, there's no parent left to remember the group.

For the second, every batch's command gets PMW_BATCH_FILE=<absolute path> in its environment. That doubles as a marker. On Linux, startup scans /proc/*/environ for the marker of any running-* batch and stops those groups before handing anything new out. On other systems, where that can't be checked, a running batch with no pid record makes startup refuse with instructions, instead of guessing.

5. Lock files that are never reused

We need one watcher per directory to avoid sending every fill to the agent twice. The classic pid lock file (create it, delete it on exit, take it over if the pid is dead) has a race. Starter A reads the lock, sees a dead pid, and pauses. Starter B also sees it dead, deletes it, creates its own and starts running. A wakes up, deletes B's live lock and creates its own, leaving two watchers running.

The fix was to stop reusing names. Locks are generations, watch.lock.0, watch.lock.1, and so on. The highest number is the lock. A new one is created with exclusive create, as highest + 1, only when the current highest is released or its owner is dead. Releasing writes { released: true } into the file instead of deleting it, and old generations are never removed. A starter that paused on an old scan tries to create a number that already exists and gets EEXIST. Each file is a few bytes, one per start.

6. Rejecting misspelt arguments

Over MCP, a model calls order_buy with a JSON object. If it sends max_price instead of maxPrice, a lenient server ignores the unknown field and the order goes out with the default limit, which is the current ask, whatever that is. MCP hosts don't have to validate against the schema, so the server does, strictly:

for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(args)) {
  const p = props[k];
  if (!p) throw new Error(`unknown argument ${JSON.stringify(k)} (allowed: ${Object.keys(props).join(', ') || 'none'})`);
  // ...type checks; null is rejected with "leave it out instead"
}

The error lists the allowed names so the model can fix the call. The command line also rejects unknown flags such as --max_price. A flag with no value, like --key --all, returns an error; otherwise it could place an order under the key --all.

7. Secrets are removed before anything is serialized

Exchange errors sometimes echo the request back, and the request can contain credentials. Anything written to a key record, a log line or stderr goes through redact() first. It walks the whole value, keys included, and replaces every known secret value plus anything shaped like an API key or a user:pass@ URL. It runs on the object before JSON.stringify, so field names are covered as well as values.

Finding failure cases in review

Many of the failure cases above came out of an adversarial review loop with Codex over the diff. We asked it specifically for crash windows, races and partial writes, and successive rounds found more cases to fix. The data CLI went from 0.6.0 to 0.6.5 on the day it shipped:

  • 0.6.1: cancel pending SIGKILLs once the command is over; keep a batch recorded as handed but never started in failed/.
  • 0.6.2: sync the stream cursor before forgetting handed ids; new-fills moves its cursor only once the answer is complete.
  • 0.6.3: a new queue or handed file is created durably, directory synced, before a fill counts as queued.
  • 0.6.4: cut a half-written last line off the queue and the handed record at start (otherwise the next append is glued onto the fragment and lost with it); one new-fills queue per file however its path is spelt.
  • 0.6.5: on Linux, find a batch's processes by the environment marker even when there's a pid record, and stop any that left the group when the batch ends.

The trading CLI's 0.4.1 was the redaction fix in section 7.

None of those would show up in a normal test run. They need a crash at one specific line, or two processes starting within milliseconds of each other. What made the review useful was asking a narrow question: where can a crash between two lines cause an order to be sent twice, or a fill to be handed over twice?

Does it work

In a production test, 57 real fills reached the agent command between 0.01 and 0.16 seconds after they were pushed. A headless claude -p took about 11 seconds to read a fill, look up the market and place a dry-run order; codex exec took about 27. Most of the time went into the model run. That delay is another reason we start the trading side in dry-run mode, where orders are simulated against the live book and nothing is sent.

For a similar setup, I'd check the following:

  • Make the money limit a hard ceiling, computed at the limit price, and round caller numbers in the safe direction.
  • Claim idempotency keys durably before the side effect, and report a claim with no recorded result as "unknown", never as free to reuse.
  • Pick at-most-once when the consumer has side effects, and keep what fell through somewhere a human will look.
  • Stop the whole process group and leave a marker you can find after the watcher crashes.
  • Use a new lock file name for each generation.
  • Reject unknown arguments so a model's typo can't silently change an order.

The code is MIT-licensed: src/watch.ts and src/mcp.ts in polymarketwallets/pmwallets-node, and src/agent.ts in polymarketwallets/polymarket-copy-trading-bot on GitHub.

Nothing here is financial advice, and Polymarket's regional restrictions apply to placing orders.

I help maintain PMWallets.

title: Web Accessibility (a11y): Building UIs Everyone Can Use
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Most accessibility is free if you start with semantic HTML: a real button beats a div-button every time. Use the POUR principles, keyboard support, and contrast, and remember the first rule of ARIA is don't use ARIA.

Contents

  • The button that isn't a button
  • Accessibility is just usability, for everyone
  • How assistive tech actually sees your page
  • The four POUR principles
  • Div-button vs. real button
  • The first rule of ARIA
  • Common mistakes that lock people out
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The button that isn't a button

Here is a "button" that ships to production every day. It looks perfect. It has hover states, a nice gradient, and the click handler works:

DivButton.tsx

<div className="btn" onClick={handleCheckout}>
  Checkout
</div>

Now try to use it without a mouse. Press Tab, your focus skips right past it, because a div is not focusable. Press Enter or Space, nothing happens, because a div has no built-in click behavior for the keyboard. Turn on a screen reader and it announces… nothing useful. It is just "Checkout, group." A blind user, a keyboard-only user, someone with a tremor using switch control, none of them can check out. You did not mean to lock them out. The markup did it for you.

📌 Who this is for: Frontend developers who can build a working UI but have never thought hard about who can't use it. No prior accessibility knowledge assumed. By the end you will know what to do, what not to do, and how to check your work.

Accessibility is just usability, for everyone

Accessibility is not a feature you bolt on for a minority. It is usability, for everyone, and most of it is free if you start with semantic HTML.

The web was born accessible. A plain HTML document with headings, links, and form controls works with a screen reader, a keyboard, voice control, and a braille display out of the box. We break that accessibility ourselves, by replacing <button> with <div>, by removing focus outlines because they "look ugly," by choosing grey-on-grey text that looks elegant in Figma. Accessibility work is mostly not breaking what the browser already gives you.

In the real world In tech
A curb cut (the ramp in a sidewalk) was built for wheelchairs Semantic HTML was built for screen readers
But it also helps strollers, luggage, delivery carts, and cyclists But it also helps keyboard users, voice control, SEO, and automated tests
Nobody complains the sidewalk has a ramp Nobody complains your button is a real <button>

Accessibility helps the people you designed for too.

This is the curb-cut effect: design for the edge and you improve the center. Captions help deaf users and anyone watching on a muted phone in a quiet office. Good contrast helps low-vision users and anyone outside in sunlight. Keyboard support helps motor-impaired users and power users who never touch the mouse. Accessibility is not charity, it is good engineering with a wider blast radius.

How assistive tech actually sees your page

To reason about accessibility you need one mental model: the accessibility tree. When the browser parses your HTML it builds the DOM, and alongside it, a second, simplified tree describing what each element is and does: its role (button, link, heading), its name ("Checkout"), and its state (pressed, disabled, expanded). Screen readers and other assistive tech read that tree, not your CSS.

Semantic HTML feeds the accessibility tree, which is what assistive tech reads.

A <div onClick> shows up in the DOM, so it renders and clicks. But in the accessibility tree it has no role, no name, and no keyboard behavior, so the screen reader and keyboard paths simply have nothing to grab onto. A real <button> populates all three. That single difference is most of accessibility.

  1. You write semantic HTML: Use the element that means what you intend: for actions, for navigation,

    -

    for structure, for inputs.
  2. The browser builds the accessibility tree: Each element gets a role, an accessible name, and state, derived automatically from the tag and its content.
  3. Assistive tech reads the tree: A screen reader announces "Checkout, button." The Tab key stops on it. Enter and Space activate it. You wrote none of that logic.
  4. The user acts: They hear what the control is, reach it with the keyboard, and operate it, exactly like a sighted mouse user, through a different door.
    5.

The four POUR principles

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) organize everything under four principles, abbreviated POUR. You do not need to memorize the spec, you need the gist of what each one asks of your UI.

Principle The question it asks In practice
Perceivable Can users sense the content? Alt text on images, captions on video, enough color contrast, never rely on color alone to convey meaning
Operable Can users drive the UI? Everything works by keyboard, focus is visible, no keyboard traps, enough time to act, no seizure-inducing flashes
Understandable Can users make sense of it? Clear labels, predictable behavior, helpful error messages, a declared page language
Robust Will it work with their tools? Valid HTML and correct roles/names/states so any browser or assistive tech can interpret it

POUR, what each principle means at the keyboard.

💡 A pocket test: Unplug your mouse and use your app with the keyboard alone. Then zoom the browser to 200%. Those two checks surface the majority of Operable and Perceivable failures in minutes.

Div-button vs. real button

Let us fix the opening example. The naive instinct is to patch the div until it behaves like a button. Watch how much code that takes, and how much the right element gives you for free.

Inaccessible.tsx

// Inaccessible: a div pretending to be a button
<div className="btn" onClick={handleCheckout}>
  Checkout
</div>

// "Fixing" the div means re-implementing the browser:
<div
  className="btn"
  role="button"            // 1. fake a role
  tabIndex={0}             // 2. make it focusable
  onClick={handleCheckout}
  onKeyDown={(e) => {       // 3. wire up keyboard yourself
    if (e.key === "Enter" || e.key === " ") handleCheckout();
  }}
>
  Checkout
</div>

Accessible.tsx

// Accessible: just use the element that already does all of that
<button className="btn" onClick={handleCheckout}>
  Checkout
</button>

// Focus is visible by default, keep it, style it, never delete it:
.btn:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #0d9488;   /* teal */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

// Icon-only button? Give it an accessible NAME or it announces nothing:
<button onClick={handleClose} aria-label="Close dialog">
  <XIcon aria-hidden="true" />
</button>

The <button> is focusable, keyboard-operable, and announced as "Checkout, button", with zero extra code. Two things worth calling out: never delete the focus outline (use :focus-visible to style it instead of removing it), and an icon-only button needs an accessible name via aria-label, because there is no visible text for the accessibility tree to use. Mark the decorative icon aria-hidden="true" so it is not announced twice.

The first rule of ARIA

The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA. If a native HTML element gives you the role and behavior you need, use it instead.

WCAG ARIA Authoring Practices

ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of role, aria-*, and state attributes that describe elements to assistive tech. The catch: ARIA changes only what is announced, never how the element behaves. Adding role="button" to a div makes a screen reader say "button," but it does not make Tab stop on it, and it does not make Enter fire the handler. You still have to build all of that yourself, and forget one piece, and you have shipped a control that claims to be a button but is broken. A real <button> is honest by construction.

So when is ARIA the right tool? When HTML genuinely has no element for what you are building: a tabbed interface, a custom autocomplete combobox, a tooltip, a aria-live region that announces async updates. There ARIA is essential, but follow a recipe (the ARIA Authoring Practices patterns), do not improvise. The rule of thumb: reach for the HTML element first, and only add ARIA when you have proven nothing native fits.

⚠️ Bad ARIA is worse than no ARIA: An incorrect role or a stale aria-state actively lies to screen-reader users. <button role="link"> or an aria-expanded that never updates is more confusing than plain markup. If you are not sure the ARIA is correct and kept in sync, leave it off.

Common mistakes that lock people out

  1. Div buttons and div links. <div onClick> is not focusable or keyboard-operable. Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation, the choice signals intent to the accessibility tree.
  2. Deleting focus styles. outline: none with no replacement leaves keyboard users with no idea where they are. Style :focus-visible instead, never remove it.
  3. Low color contrast. Grey-on-white that looks sleek can fail WCAG. Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text). Check it with your DevTools or a contrast tool.
  4. Color as the only signal. "Required fields are red" is invisible to colorblind users. Pair color with an icon, text, or an asterisk.
  5. Images without alt text. Every meaningful <img> needs alt describing its content. Decorative images get alt="" (empty, not missing) so screen readers skip them.
  6. Misused or stale ARIA. Inventing roles, or an aria-expanded / aria-pressed that never updates, lies to users. Prefer native HTML; keep any ARIA state in sync with reality.
  7. Inputs with no label. A placeholder is not a label, it vanishes on typing and is poorly announced. Wire every input to a real <label> (or aria-label).

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • Accessibility is usability for everyone, and mostly free if you start with semantic HTML.
  • Assistive tech reads the accessibility tree (role · name · state), not your CSS.
  • Use the right element: <button> for actions, <a href> for links, <label> for inputs, headings for structure.
  • POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust, the four questions every UI must answer.
  • Keep focus visible (:focus-visible), hit 4.5:1 contrast, and never use color as the only signal.
  • First rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA, it changes announcements, not behavior. Reach for HTML first.
  • Test it: unplug the mouse, tab through, zoom to 200%, run a screen reader.

Where to go next

Accessibility is a thread that runs through everything else on the Frontend Engineer path, it is not a separate module so much as a quality bar for all the UI you build. Two sibling articles connect directly to it.

  • CSS Fundamentals: The Box Model & Layout, where you will style :focus-visible outlines and make sure contrast survives your color palette.
  • Component Architecture & Design Systems, build accessibility into your shared Button, Input, and Dialog components once, and every screen inherits it.

Then practice the pocket test on your own app: unplug the mouse, tab through a full flow, and fix the first thing that traps or hides your focus. That one habit will teach you more than any checklist.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: Assemble 24fps Clips into a 30fps Remotion Composition
description:
Generating the shots was one stage. Making the product name, transitions and sound land on the intended frames was another.

This implementation note records the inputs, failure modes and checks needed to make the workflow reviewable.

Place sound on the same timeline

Music and effects were placed at frame positions, with fades where needed. The final mix in this record measured about -17.5 LUFS and -2.7 dB peak; these are project measurements rather than universal loudness targets. Review speech and music together after export, as a correct source track does not establish a correct final mix.

Keep copy and motion editable

We used Composition for the complete timeline and Sequence for the cuts, with exact text and diagrams rendered as code. Letter animations were offset by three frames. Where clip duration differed from the allotted cut, playback rate was adjusted from the source duration and cut length. Preserve the approved wording outside the generated footage so revisions do not require a new video generation.

Define the output timeline

Our fictional coffee sample uses five cuts in a 30-second film. Input clips were 24fps at 1080p; the output composition was 30fps and 900 frames, exported as H.264. The recorded environment was Node 24, Remotion 4.0.532 and Apple Silicon. Fixing the duration and frame rate first made the other timings explicit.

Checks to carry into the next project

  • Fix duration and fps before timing the layers.

  • Keep approved copy in an editable layer.

  • Inspect the exported file with audio enabled.

Keep a reproducible record of the configuration and inspect the final exported artifact. An automation success message is not a content review.

title: Room booking app with Next.js and Prisma
description:
The room booking tutorial ends with "check again on the server". This one builds that server. You get a Next.js App Router app where rooms and bookings live in Postgres through Prisma, the calendar is Resource Scheduler in a client component, and the route handlers decide whether a booking is allowed.

Every file is in the steps below, so you can copy them in order. The finished app is also in the repository as the resource-scheduler-rooms-starter folder; fetch just that folder with npx degit mdobaid311/resource-scheduler/resource-scheduler-rooms-starter rooms.

See the browser side running live: interactive demo (it has no server, so its data resets on reload).

Drag across free time on a room to open the form. The app you build adds three things to it: the data comes from a database, a save can be refused by the server, and a refused save rolls back on screen.

Versions. The snippets are written for Next.js 15 (in 14, params in a route handler is not a Promise) and Prisma 6 with Postgres. Newer Prisma majors changed how the client is generated and how the connection is configured, so follow the Prisma docs for that part. The queries and the transaction do not depend on it.

How the pieces fit

  1. The server component app/page.tsx reads rooms and bookings with Prisma and passes them as plain strings.
  2. The client component app/board.tsx renders ResourceScheduler and sends changes to the API.
  3. The route handlers under app/api/bookings call one function, which re-checks the placement with isPlacementAllowed inside a transaction.
  4. The browser and the server share one object, bookingRules, so they cannot disagree about what "free" means.

1. Create the app 

npx create-next-app@latest rooms --ts --app
cd rooms
npm install resource-scheduler @prisma/client
npm install -D prisma@6
npx prisma init --datasource-provider postgresql

Put your Postgres connection string in .env as DATABASE_URL. Any Postgres works, local or hosted.

2. The schema

Store times as DateTime. Prisma saves them in UTC, and the end is exclusive: a booking that ends at 10:00 does not collide with one that starts at 10:00.

prisma/schema.prisma

generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client-js"
}

datasource db {
  provider = "postgresql"
  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
}

model Room {
  id       String    @id @default(cuid())
  name     String
  seats    Int
  bookings Booking[]
}

model Booking {
  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
  title     String
  roomId    String
  room      Room     @relation(fields: [roomId], references: [id])
  startsAt  DateTime
  endsAt    DateTime
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())

  @@index([roomId, startsAt])
}

Create the tables and two rooms to play with:

npx prisma migrate dev --name init

prisma/seed.ts

import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client";

const prisma = new PrismaClient();

async function main() {
  await prisma.room.createMany({
    data: [
      { name: "Atlas", seats: 8 },
      { name: "Borealis", seats: 4 },
    ],
  });
}

main().finally(() => prisma.$disconnect());

npx tsx prisma/seed.ts

3. Shared code

One Prisma client for the whole dev server (Next.js reloads modules, and without this every reload opens a new connection pool):

lib/db.ts

import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client";

const globalForPrisma = globalThis as unknown as { prisma?: PrismaClient };

export const prisma = globalForPrisma.prisma ?? new PrismaClient();

if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production") globalForPrisma.prisma = prisma;

The rule, in one place. The client spreads it onto the component, and the server hands the same object to isPlacementAllowed:

lib/rules.ts

export const bookingRules = { eventOverlap: false as const };

A booking crosses the server boundary and the network as JSON, where a Date becomes a string. This is the shape on the wire:

lib/dto.ts

import type { Booking } from "@prisma/client";

export type BookingDTO = {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  roomId: string;
  startsAt: string;
  endsAt: string;
};

export const toDTO = (b: Booking): BookingDTO => ({
  id: b.id,
  title: b.title,
  roomId: b.roomId,
  startsAt: b.startsAt.toISOString(),
  endsAt: b.endsAt.toISOString(),
});

4. The page loads rooms and bookings

A server component can read the database directly. It loads the rooms and a window of bookings around now (for a long range, fetch per visible range with onRangeChange, see Loading and control). It also passes the current time as a string, so the first render on the server and in the browser start on the same day. See Next.js and SSR.

app/page.tsx

import { prisma } from "@/lib/db";
import { toDTO } from "@/lib/dto";
import { Board } from "./board";

export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"; // read the database per request, not at build time

const DAY = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

export default async function Page() {
  const now = new Date();
  const [rooms, bookings] = await Promise.all([
    prisma.room.findMany({ orderBy: { name: "asc" } }),
    prisma.booking.findMany({
      where: {
        endsAt: { gt: new Date(now.getTime() - DAY) },
        startsAt: { lt: new Date(now.getTime() + 14 * DAY) },
      },
    }),
  ]);

  return (
    <main style={{ padding: 16 }}>
      <Board
        rooms={rooms.map((r) => ({ id: r.id, name: `${r.name} (${r.seats} seats)` }))}
        initial={bookings.map(toDTO)}
        initialDate={now.toISOString()}
      />
    </main>
  );
}

5. The server decides

This is the file the whole tutorial is for. A booking is allowed only if isPlacementAllowed says so for the room's current bookings, and the check and the write happen in one Serializable transaction, so two requests that both read "free" cannot both commit.

lib/bookings.ts

import { Prisma } from "@prisma/client";
import { isPlacementAllowed } from "resource-scheduler/headless";
import type { Resource } from "resource-scheduler/headless";
import { prisma } from "./db";
import { bookingRules } from "./rules";

export class Conflict extends Error {}
export class NotFound extends Error {}

type Slot = { roomId: string; start: Date; end: Date };

const inTransaction = <T>(run: (tx: Prisma.TransactionClient) => Promise<T>) =>
  prisma.$transaction(run, { isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable });

// Throws Conflict unless the booking `id` (none, for a new one) may take this slot.
async function assertFree(tx: Prisma.TransactionClient, id: string | undefined, { roomId, start, end }: Slot) {
  const room = await tx.room.findUnique({
    where: { id: roomId },
    include: { bookings: { where: { startsAt: { lt: end }, endsAt: { gt: start } } } },
  });
  if (!room) throw new NotFound();

  const resource: Resource = {
    id: room.id,
    name: room.name,
    events: room.bookings.map((b) => ({ id: b.id, title: b.title, startDate: b.startsAt, endDate: b.endsAt })),
  };
  const moving = { id: id ?? "new", title: "", startDate: start, endDate: end };

  if (!isPlacementAllowed(moving, { resourceId: roomId, start, end }, [resource], bookingRules)) {
    throw new Conflict();
  }
}

export const createBooking = (slot: Slot & { title: string }) =>
  inTransaction(async (tx) => {
    await assertFree(tx, undefined, slot);
    return tx.booking.create({
      data: { roomId: slot.roomId, title: slot.title, startsAt: slot.start, endsAt: slot.end },
    });
  });

export const moveBooking = (id: string, slot: Slot) =>
  inTransaction(async (tx) => {
    if (!(await tx.booking.findUnique({ where: { id } }))) throw new NotFound();
    await assertFree(tx, id, slot); // the booking's own old time is ignored: its id is `id`
    return tx.booking.update({
      where: { id },
      data: { roomId: slot.roomId, startsAt: slot.start, endsAt: slot.end },
    });
  });

The query already narrows to bookings that overlap the slot, and isPlacementAllowed applies the same overlap rule the browser used, including ignoring the booking being moved. Under Serializable, Postgres aborts one of two conflicting transactions when it commits; Prisma reports that as error P2034, which the next file also turns into a 409 (retrying once is an equally good answer).

Two small helpers turn requests into slots and errors into responses:

lib/http.ts

import { Prisma } from "@prisma/client";
import { Conflict, NotFound } from "./bookings";

// body comes from request.json(), so nothing in it is trusted.
export function parseSlot(body: { roomId?: unknown; startsAt?: unknown; endsAt?: unknown }) {
  const start = new Date(body.startsAt as string);
  const end = new Date(body.endsAt as string);
  if (typeof body.roomId !== "string" || !(start < end)) return null; // also catches Invalid Date
  return { roomId: body.roomId, start, end };
}

export function fail(error: unknown) {
  if (error instanceof Conflict || (error instanceof Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError && error.code === "P2034")) {
    return Response.json({ error: "That time was just booked." }, { status: 409 });
  }
  if (error instanceof NotFound) return Response.json({ error: "Not found." }, { status: 404 });
  throw error;
}

The route handlers are thin:

app/api/bookings/route.ts

import { createBooking } from "@/lib/bookings";
import { toDTO } from "@/lib/dto";
import { fail, parseSlot } from "@/lib/http";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const body = await request.json().catch(() => ({}));
  const slot = parseSlot(body);
  const title = typeof body.title === "string" ? body.title.trim() : "";
  if (!slot || !title) return Response.json({ error: "Invalid booking." }, { status: 400 });

  try {
    return Response.json(toDTO(await createBooking({ ...slot, title })), { status: 201 });
  } catch (error) {
    return fail(error);
  }
}

app/api/bookings/[id]/route.ts

import { moveBooking } from "@/lib/bookings";
import { toDTO } from "@/lib/dto";
import { fail, parseSlot } from "@/lib/http";

export async function PATCH(request: Request, { params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const slot = parseSlot(await request.json().catch(() => ({})));
  if (!slot) return Response.json({ error: "Invalid booking." }, { status: 400 });

  try {
    return Response.json(toDTO(await moveBooking(id, slot)));
  } catch (error) {
    return fail(error);
  }
}

This app has no sign-in. Anyone who can reach these routes can book and move anything. Before real use, check the user in each handler, and let a person change only their own bookings.

6. The calendar, with optimistic updates

The client component keeps the bookings in state and renders them through the flat events prop, each with a resourceId, which maps straight onto database rows. The key idea of an optimistic update: show the change at once, send it, and undo it if the server says no. A booking that is still being saved is drawn grey and has a temporary id.

app/board.tsx

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { ResourceScheduler, ViewType } from "resource-scheduler";
import type { SchedulerEvent, SlotSelection } from "resource-scheduler";
import "resource-scheduler/dist/resource-scheduler.css";
import type { BookingDTO } from "@/lib/dto";
import { bookingRules } from "@/lib/rules";

type Room = { id: string; name: string };

const PENDING = "pending-";

const toEvent = (b: BookingDTO): SchedulerEvent => ({
  id: b.id,
  title: b.title,
  resourceId: b.roomId,
  startDate: new Date(b.startsAt),
  endDate: new Date(b.endsAt),
});

async function send(url: string, method: "POST" | "PATCH", body: unknown): Promise<BookingDTO> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method,
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body), // a Date becomes an ISO string
  });
  if (response.status === 409) throw new Error("Someone just booked that time.");
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("The booking could not be saved.");
  return response.json();
}

export function Board({ rooms, initial, initialDate }: { rooms: Room[]; initial: BookingDTO[]; initialDate: string }) {
  const [bookings, setBookings] = useState(() => initial.map(toEvent));
  const [start] = useState(() => new Date(initialDate));
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState<SlotSelection | null>(null);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState("");

  async function book(slot: SlotSelection, title: string) {
    const tempId = PENDING + crypto.randomUUID();
    setMessage("");
    setBookings((all) => [
      ...all,
      { id: tempId, title, resourceId: slot.resourceId, startDate: slot.start, endDate: slot.end, color: "#94a3b8" },
    ]);
    try {
      const saved = toEvent(await send("/api/bookings", "POST", { roomId: slot.resourceId, title, startsAt: slot.start, endsAt: slot.end }));
      setBookings((all) => all.map((b) => (b.id === tempId ? saved : b)));
    } catch (error) {
      setBookings((all) => all.filter((b) => b.id !== tempId)); // roll back
      setMessage((error as Error).message);
    }
  }

  async function reschedule(event: SchedulerEvent, roomId: string, startDate: Date, endDate: Date) {
    if (event.id.startsWith(PENDING)) return; // not saved yet, so there is nothing to patch
    const before = bookings.find((b) => b.id === event.id);
    setMessage("");
    setBookings((all) => all.map((b) => (b.id === event.id ? { ...b, resourceId: roomId, startDate, endDate } : b)));
    try {
      await send(`/api/bookings/${event.id}`, "PATCH", { roomId, startsAt: startDate, endsAt: endDate });
    } catch (error) {
      if (before) setBookings((all) => all.map((b) => (b.id === event.id ? before : b))); // roll back
      setMessage((error as Error).message);
    }
  }

  return (
    <>
      {draft && (
        <form
          onSubmit={(e) => {
            e.preventDefault();
            book(draft, String(new FormData(e.currentTarget).get("title")));
            setDraft(null);
          }}
        >
          <input name="title" aria-label="Title" placeholder="Meeting title" required autoFocus />
          <button type="submit">Book</button>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => setDraft(null)}>Cancel</button>
        </form>
      )}
      {message && <p role="alert">{message}</p>}
      <div style={{ height: 440 }}>
        <ResourceScheduler
          {...bookingRules}
          resources={rooms}
          events={bookings}
          initialDate={start}
          initialView={ViewType.Day}
          allowViewChange={false}
          slotDuration={30}
          dayStartHour={8}
          dayEndHour={18}
          ariaLabel="Meeting room bookings"
          onSlotSelect={setDraft}
          onEventDrop={(event, _from, to, s, e) => reschedule(event, to, s, e)}
          onEventResize={(event, roomId, s, e) => reschedule(event, roomId, s, e)}
        />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

Why it holds together:

  • Board passes callbacks and holds state, so it has to be a client component. The scheduler's own bundle already starts with "use client".
  • The browser refuses overlaps before the drop (the place turns red), so most conflicts never reach the server. The ones that do, from two people at once or from someone who skips the UI, come back as 409 and are rolled back with a message.
  • reschedule serves both moving and resizing: both end with a room and a new start and end. Without onEventResize there would be no resize handles.
  • The rooms are plain { id, name } rows. The bookings are the single flat list in events, so no room carries its own events.

7. Try it 

npm run dev

Open the page, drag across free time on Atlas and book it. Then ask the server directly, with the same body twice, to see the guard work without the UI (replace the room id with one from npx prisma studio):

curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/api/bookings -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"roomId":"ROOM_ID","title":"Standup","startsAt":"2026-10-20T09:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-20T09:30:00Z"}'

The first call answers 201, the second 409. Open the page in two windows, book the same free slot in both, and the second window shows the grey block disappear with "Someone just booked that time."

Going further

  • A second line of defence in the database. Postgres can refuse overlapping rows by itself with an exclusion constraint on a tsrange of the two columns (CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist, then EXCLUDE USING gist ("roomId" WITH =, tsrange("startsAt", "endsAt") WITH &&)), added to a migration you create with npx prisma migrate dev --create-only. It is optional here, because the transaction already covers the normal case.
  • Rules beyond overlap (office hours, a seat limit, no booking in the past): put them in isValidDrop inside bookingRules. The browser and the server then both apply them. See Conflict control.
  • Recurring bookings: store the rule next to the booking and let expandEvents produce the occurrences. See Recurring events.
  • Rooms in several time zones: Time zones.
  • React 19 has useOptimistic. The plain useState version above does the same job and works on React 18 too.

Where next

  • The front-end only version: React room booking calendar.
  • The finished room booking recipe, with business hours, capacity and recurring bookings.
  • Next.js and SSR and Build your own UI for the server entry point.

Originally published at https://resource-scheduler-docs.vercel.app/tutorials/react-room-booking-nextjs-prisma/.

title: React Frontend Feature Flags: 3 Polling API Fallback Rules
description:
Short answer: Poll feature flags for presentation changes in a React dashboard, and keep defaults in the application so a delayed or failed fetch cannot stop operators from inspecting a nightly fintech pipeline. Do not use a browser flag to authorize a payment or change billing behavior. If the real goal is searching structured pipeline logs and attributing their costs, treat flags as a small part of the operator interface, not as a substitute for log search, alerts, or an audit trail.

Keep the dashboard readable.

Pick this When it fits the job Recovery boundary
Infrai An existing backend already uses several services and wants flags and log ingestion behind one REST contract Poll flags; build separate alerting and compliance reporting
LaunchDarkly Flag evaluation, targeting, and experimentation drive the product decision Keep authoritative checks on the server
Unleash The team wants control over a dedicated feature-management deployment Operate its own service and integration
OpenFeature The team wants a portable evaluation interface across providers Supply and operate a provider; it is not a flag service
Datadog Pipeline log search and alerting are the primary job Assess log indexing and retention against compliance needs
Grafana Existing observability data sources need shared dashboards Arrange the underlying log store and flag service separately
Sentry Application errors and debugging dominate the workflow Use a separate system for structured pipeline log search

How should a React frontend recover when feature flags API polling fails?

Imagine an operator opening a React view while the overnight settlement pipeline is being reviewed. The page should still show its core status and let the operator find the relevant run even if its optional presentation flag has not loaded. A useful flag might switch the layout of a cost-attribution panel; it must never decide whether a settlement is valid. The backend owns that decision.

The failure mode is mundane: the first request is slow, or a refresh fails after the page has opened. Start from defaults compiled into the client. Fetch the current values on load, then refresh on an interval. On a failed refresh, retain the last known values during that session; on a fresh load without a successful fetch, use the compiled defaults. This is a client policy, not a claim that the flag provider delivers offline evaluation. Choose the refresh interval against the acceptable time for a presentation change to appear, and avoid synchronized retries across every open tab.

One tempting shortcut is to make the entire operator page wait for the remote flag read. It turns an optional layout setting into a dependency for inspecting a time-sensitive pipeline run. Render from defaults first. The flag read should update presentation after it succeeds; failed reads must not clear the operator's current view. This is a deliberate trade: an operator can briefly see the default layout, but can still inspect the underlying run while a configuration service is unavailable.

Try Infrai for the dashboard's non-sensitive flags and pipeline log ingestion when your backend already benefits from one contract across multiple modules. Its published surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key, so adding a capability need not mean adding another service integration. The same public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, which helps an operator verify a contract before wiring a recovery path. Neither advantage turns browser polling into realtime evaluation or supplies a missing alerting service.

What evidence links a pipeline run to its cost?

The flag snapshot explains which layout an operator saw. It does not explain which nightly run produced a transaction, which log entries belong to that run, or where the cost was incurred. For cost attribution, design the backend record first: give each run a stable identifier in your own system, correlate its structured events with that identifier, and reconcile the underlying charge or usage records at the source that owns them. The dashboard can then display the result without calculating financial truth from a client-side toggle. Keep financial and personal fields out of presentation flags.

This is the line between a pleasant control and an auditable record.

Implement the recovery path before the rollout

The following TypeScript read probe is runnable with a current Node runtime and a configured INFRAI_API_KEY. It checks the response before parsing, honors Retry-After for rate limits, and prints the returned JSON so you can inspect the documented schema before mapping any fields into React state. It does not guess the shape of a flag response or put a private API key in browser code. Run the poll from a trusted backend and expose only non-sensitive, validated presentation values to the frontend.

const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!key) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY");

const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/flags/get_all";
for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
  const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
  });
  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
    const seconds = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const delay = Number.isFinite(seconds) && seconds >= 0
      ? seconds * 1000
      : 1000 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
    continue;
  }
  const body = await response.text();
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Flag read ${response.status}: ${body}`);
  console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body), null, 2));
  break;
}

The probe is intentionally a read, not a browser hook: its output needs a schema check before anything is shipped to a public client. Keep a boolean default such as showCostPanel = false in the application. After validating the actual flag response, map only the specific presentation value into the UI; don't pass an entire remote configuration payload through to the browser. A refresh error leaves the previous validated snapshot in place. The backend's cost records and security decisions remain independent of that snapshot.

No secret belongs in the bundle.

Think of the data flow as a short chain: compiled defaults, then a successful flag read, then the next scheduled refresh. Only a validated response replaces the current snapshot. If a read fails, the UI keeps working. The server independently enforces any sensitive rule. This order gives operators a stable dashboard without pretending that a client-side setting is a source of authority.

For the nightly pipeline, make the panel label identify the run being inspected and show whether its cost attribution is available from your own backend. A flag can choose a compact or expanded presentation of that information. It cannot manufacture attribution data. Likewise, instrument the flag-fetch failure count and the age of the last successful read in your own telemetry, but avoid per-run or per-user metric labels that explode cardinality. A structured log entry for a failed read should carry a stable operation name and correlation identifier, without secrets or raw financial records.

Retries deserve a separate rule. On rate limiting, honor Retry-After when available and use exponential backoff; do not let an interval tick start a second request while the first is still pending. For a read, a retry does not double-apply a change. For any separate write or publish action in the pipeline, use a client-supplied idempotency key and verify the server's contract before retrying. Keep those two recovery policies distinct.

Which option fits the operating model?

Choose LaunchDarkly when evaluation and experimentation are the project, especially if you need a dedicated feature-management workflow. Its documentation is the right place to check the SDK and targeting model against your requirements. A browser-only gate remains inappropriate for security or billing, regardless of vendor.

Choose Unleash when running a dedicated flag service and controlling that deployment is an acceptable operational trade. It is a different decision from adding a modest UI switch to an existing backend. OpenFeature helps when the application should depend on a provider-neutral evaluation API, but it does not host your flags or make provider-specific data available by itself.

For log-first teams, compare Datadog's log management and alerts, Grafana's observability dashboards backed by selected data sources, and Sentry's application error investigation. These solve different pieces of the pipeline review. Datadog is a stronger fit when managed alerting and log search are the main procurement decision. Grafana fits an existing metrics and logs stack; it does not remove the need to select and operate those data sources. Sentry helps with application failures, but it is not a replacement for a run-oriented structured log search workflow. If the cost attribution evidence must be reconciled across overnight runs, inspect how each candidate identifies a run in stored events, what data it keeps, and how operators recover after a missing or delayed batch. A feature-flag service cannot answer those questions for the log store.

Infrai fits the narrower case of a polled configuration source alongside existing backend capabilities. There is no flag evaluation-statistics or change-audit history here; product experiments and compliance reporting require separate tooling. For a regulated workflow, that distinction matters more than the convenience of a shared key. Log search also has a boundary: documented search-filter parameters are not declared in discovery, so verify a concrete search query against the contract before designing a run-id drill-down. Do not promise arbitrary filters on the strength of a route name.

Pick the evidence trail first.

Where does this stop?

Polling cannot prove that an overnight job ran at all. Use a heartbeat monitor for silent missed runs, and a dedicated alerting system if an operator needs threshold notifications: Infrai does not provide alert or notification routes. Its logs can carry trace and span identifiers for correlation, but there is no distributed trace-query or span-tree view. There is also no per-user log deletion or bulk export/subscription interface; confirm retention and deletion requirements before putting regulated data in those logs.

For experiments needing evaluation counts or for compliance processes requiring an audit history, choose a specialist and test its evidence trail before launch. If the narrower polling boundary suits your application, start with the Infrai capability documentation and verify the current flag contract there.

Sources

  • Infrai capability documentation
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • OpenFeature documentation
  • Datadog log management
  • Grafana documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Logback appender documentation
