title: React equipment rental calendar
description:
A rental calendar has the things you rent down the side and the days across the top. Some things are one unit (a van), some are a pool (three projectors), one is in for service on a day, and the question you get all day is "when is it free for three days?". This tutorial builds that with Resource Scheduler in seven steps. It is the same component running below.

See it running live: interactive demo.

Try three things. Drag the Delivery van booking to Tuesday on the projectors: three projectors are already out that day, so the drop turns red and nothing moves. Drag it to the PA system on Wednesday: that day is a service day, so it is refused too. Then pick "3 free days" for the PA system and press Find: the grid jumps to the first stretch that is free.

1. Install 

npm install resource-scheduler

Works with React 18 and 19. Import the stylesheet once; it is scoped, so it does not restyle the rest of your page:

import "resource-scheduler/dist/resource-scheduler.css";

2. Things you rent are rows, and a pool is one row

Each thing is a resource. A pool of identical units is still one row: capacity says how many units are in stock. A service day is a range in unavailable:

import type { ResourceInput } from "resource-scheduler";

const items: ResourceInput[] = [
  { id: "projector", name: "Projector (3 units)", capacity: 3 },
  { id: "camera", name: "Camera kit (2 units)", capacity: 2 },
  { id: "pa", name: "PA system", unavailable: [{ start: new Date(2026, 9, 7), end: new Date(2026, 9, 8) }] }, // serviced on Wednesday
  { id: "van", name: "Van" }, // capacity defaults to 1
];

In a database this is an items table with a units column, plus a table of service windows that you turn into unavailable ranges.

3. A rental is whole days, and the end is exclusive

A rental is an event on the row it takes from. Rentals are whole days, so the dates are midnights, and endDate is exclusive: it is the morning after the last day rented. A three-day rental from the 5th to the 7th ends on the 8th:

import type { SchedulerEvent } from "resource-scheduler";

const rentals: SchedulerEvent[] = [
  {
    id: "r1",
    title: "Acme Co",
    resourceId: "projector",         // the row it belongs to
    startDate: new Date(2026, 9, 5), // pickup day, midnight
    endDate: new Date(2026, 9, 8),   // exclusive: the last day rented is the 7th
  },
];

If your table stores the last day rented, add one day when you load a row. Events are a flat list that names its row with resourceId, so the list can come straight from one query.

4. Draw the week 

import { ResourceScheduler, ViewType } from "resource-scheduler";

<div style={{ height: 690 }}>
  <ResourceScheduler
    resources={items}
    events={rentals}
    initialView={ViewType.Week}
    availableViews={[ViewType.Week, ViewType.Month]}
    weekStartsOn={1}
    showUtilization
    blockUnavailable
    resourceColumnWidth="190px"
    dateColumnWidth="110px"
    ariaLabel="Equipment rentals"
  />
</div>

The component fills its parent, so the parent needs a height. Each prop is one rule:

Prop What it does
blockUnavailable No rentals on a service day: the shaded days refuse a drop and a selection
showUtilization A bar per item: unit-days rented against unit-days in stock (utilization)
availableViews Week and month only; for hourly rental use the day view and slotDuration
weekStartsOn={1} The week starts on Monday

5. Never more rentals than units

eventOverlap={false} is right for a single unit, but a pool of three projectors may overlap up to three times. capacity only feeds the utilization numbers, so enforce the count yourself. isValidDrop is a final veto: it runs for every move, resize and selection, with the row and range being tried, and false refuses it.

The count of bookings only changes where a booking starts, so check those moments:

import { rangesOverlap } from "resource-scheduler";

// Whether one more booking on [start, end) fits next to `others` without more than
// `capacity` at any moment. The count only changes where a booking starts, so check those.
const fits = (others: SchedulerEvent[], start: Date, end: Date, capacity: number) => {
  const busy = others.filter((e) => rangesOverlap(start, end, e.startDate, e.endDate));
  const moments = [start, ...busy.map((e) => e.startDate).filter((t) => t > start)];
  return moments.every((t) => busy.filter((e) => e.startDate <= t && t < e.endDate).length < capacity);
};

Then pass the rule. The rental being moved is left out of the count, so dragging it a day does not collide with itself:

<ResourceScheduler
  /* ... */
  // More bookings at once than units in stock: refuse. This also covers a single unit.
  isValidDrop={(event, { resourceId, start, end }) =>
    fits(
      rentals.filter((e) => e.resourceId === resourceId && e.id !== event.id),
      start,
      end,
      items.find((i) => i.id === resourceId)?.capacity ?? 1
    )
  }
/>

A plain "count the overlaps" would refuse a booking that fits between two others that never overlap each other; checking at each start does not. A row with no capacity counts as one unit, so the rule covers the van too.

6. Take bookings with your own form

In the week view a click or a drag across days selects whole days, and onSlotSelect hands you the row and range. Show your own form and save the rental, and handle moves with onEventDrop:

const [events, setEvents] = useState(rentals);
const [draft, setDraft] = useState<SlotSelection | null>(null);

<ResourceScheduler
  /* ... */
  onSlotSelect={setDraft}
  onEventDrop={(event, _from, to, start, end) =>
    setEvents((all) => all.map((e) => (e.id === event.id ? { ...e, resourceId: to, startDate: start, endDate: end } : e)))
  }
/>

{draft && (
  <form
    onSubmit={(e) => {
      e.preventDefault();
      setEvents((all) => [
        ...all,
        { id: `r-${Date.now()}`, title: customer.trim() || "Customer", resourceId: draft.resourceId, startDate: draft.start, endDate: draft.end },
      ]);
      setDraft(null);
    }}
  >
    <input value={customer} onChange={(e) => setCustomer(e.target.value)} placeholder="Customer" />
    <button type="submit">Rent</button>
  </form>
)}

Selections go through isValidDrop and blockUnavailable too, so a full day or a service day cannot be selected in the first place. SlotSelection is exported as a type. A callback is the opt-in: without onEventDrop a dropped rental snaps back.

7. Find N free days

"When can I have the PA system for three days?" is a search over the item's rentals and service time. findAvailableSlots does it: give it a resource that carries its events (withEvents attaches them), a window, a duration and a step, both in minutes. A step of 1440 starts every candidate on a whole day:

import { findAvailableSlots, withEvents } from "resource-scheduler";
import type { ResourceSchedulerHandle } from "resource-scheduler";

const ref = useRef<ResourceSchedulerHandle>(null);

const find = (days: number, itemId: string) => {
  const resource = withEvents(items, events).find((r) => r.id === itemId)!;
  const from = new Date();
  from.setHours(0, 0, 0, 0); // start of today
  const to = new Date(from);
  to.setDate(to.getDate() + 120);
  const [slot] = findAvailableSlots(resource, { from, to, duration: days * 1440, step: 1440, limit: 1 });
  if (!slot) return alert(`No ${days} free days for ${resource.name} in the next 120 days`);
  ref.current?.goTo(slot.start); // scroll the grid to it
};

<ResourceScheduler ref={ref} /* ... */ />

from is today's midnight so the first candidate is today, not the next whole day after this minute. The search skips rentals and service days, so a three-day stretch is only offered when the three days are all free.

It is for single-unit items. findAvailableSlots treats any overlap as busy. That is right for the van and the PA system, but a projector with two units out and one free would be reported as busy. For a pool, step through the days yourself with fits.

Check it on the server too

The browser check is a courtesy: a second browser can book the last unit after yours has loaded, and anyone can call your API without the grid. fits is a plain function of dates and rows, so the server can run exactly the same one inside the transaction that inserts the rental. isPlacementAllowed applies isValidDrop and eventOverlap together:

import { isPlacementAllowed } from "resource-scheduler";
import type { Resource, SchedulerEvent } from "resource-scheduler";

export function canRent(item: Resource, rental: SchedulerEvent) {
  return isPlacementAllowed(
    rental,
    { resourceId: item.id, start: rental.startDate, end: rental.endDate },
    [item], // the item with its current rentals, read inside your transaction
    {
      isValidDrop: (r, { start, end }) =>
        fits(item.events.filter((e) => e.id !== r.id), start, end, item.capacity ?? 1),
    }
  );
}

Return an error (HTTP 409 is the usual choice) when it is false. This check covers stock only; reject a rental that touches a service day with your own query against the service table.

Where next

  • The finished equipment rental recipe is the same code with notes on quantities, turnaround time and pickup hours.
  • Prices, deposits and customer details belong on the booking row in your database, not in the scheduler.
  • Share the bookings as a calendar file or a spreadsheet: Export.
  • Other builds: the room booking tutorial, the shift planner tutorial, the clinic appointment board tutorial and the free resource timeline.
  • Coming from another library? The comparison lists what each one includes.

Originally published at https://resource-scheduler-docs.vercel.app/tutorials/react-equipment-rental-calendar/.

title: 6 Express Health Check Endpoint Lessons — Readiness and Liveness in 2026
description:
TL;DR: For a beginner property-management SaaS, expose a cheap liveness endpoint, make readiness check Postgres and Redis, and have an external process poll both. Record failures as logs and low-cardinality metrics tagged by service and property portfolio. This is enough to answer the first incident questions without turning the health endpoint into a second application.

I have been paged for jobs that never ran and for deliveries that ran twice. Those pages taught me the invariant: a green process is not proof that a customer workflow is healthy, and an internal dashboard cannot report that the whole service is unreachable. Keep the endpoint contract small, retain evidence outside the process, and make every repair action idempotent.

1. What should an Express health check endpoint prove about readiness and liveness?

GET /livez should answer one narrow question: can the Express process serve a request? It should avoid Postgres, Redis, and third-party calls. If those dependencies turn liveness red, an orchestrator can restart a healthy process during a dependency outage and make diagnosis noisier.

GET /readyz has a different job. It should return success only when the instance can accept normal work. For this application, that means bounded checks of Postgres and Redis, plus any third-party API that sits on the critical request path. A slow dependency needs a timeout; an unbounded health request is an outage amplifier.

Keep the response useful but restrained: an overall status, a timestamp, and named dependency states are usually enough. Do not return connection strings, credentials, raw exceptions, tenant data, or SQL. Use 503 Service Unavailable for a failed readiness check and 200 OK for a ready instance. The exact JSON shape is your contract, so test it like one.

This separation preserves a useful fact during an incident: the process may be alive while customer operations are degraded. That distinction matters when a leasing agent says an application was accepted but the background screening task never completed. At that moment, I want the dependency result, the application's stable job ID, the attempt number, and the last successful transition in one narrow time window. I do not want a restart to erase the only copy of that evidence, nor do I want a health response swollen with customer records. The endpoint establishes current state; external logs establish history. Treating those as separate records makes the later reconciliation safer because an operator can distinguish work that never began from work that completed before its acknowledgement was lost.

Green is not proof.

2. Preserve evidence that can be attributed

Health data becomes expensive in surprising ways when every property ID, lease ID, or resident ID becomes a metric label. Those values create unbounded series and still do not reconstruct the individual customer event well. Put high-cardinality identifiers in structured logs; keep metric dimensions stable.

For a property-management service, I would report a counter such as health_check_failures_total with simple tags such as service=applications, dependency=postgres, and portfolio=tier_a. The related failure log can carry property_id, job_id, attempt, trace_id, and the sanitized error. That split lets finance attribute monitoring volume to a service or portfolio while an incident commander can follow one application through the failure.

Names need discipline. Prometheus recommends base units and a consistent metric prefix, which is a good rule even when Prometheus is not the backend. Infrai can receive logs and metrics through one plain REST API, so there is no monitoring SDK or client-library version to maintain; it fits teams that value a shared API surface. Keep names and tags especially simple there because metric-query filters are not clearly declared.

Infrai also uses one key for everything and provides one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For a property platform whose services share an owner, that reduces credential inventory and keeps usage attribution in one billing record. Its public discovery endpoint needs no key and is self-describing, so an operator can inspect request schemas and runnable examples before wiring an incident tool.

There is a firm limitation: Infrai does not supply heartbeat checks or notification routes, so polling, thresholds, and delivery of alerts remain separate responsibilities.

One correction from painful scheduling incidents: I first treated "the worker is ready" as evidence that rent reminders were running. It is not. Readiness catches a dependency that is down now. It cannot prove that a task due at 09:00 executed at 09:00.

3. Poll from outside the failure domain

The following Go program is deliberately small. It queries the metrics already reported to Infrai after an external probe turns red, without inventing undocumented filters. Run the actual /livez and /readyz poller from a different host or monitoring environment; use this tool to retrieve the retained metric evidence for the incident window. The nonzero exit status can feed the alert mechanism you already operate.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(resp *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := "https://" + "api." + "infrai." + "cc/v1"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            log.Fatal(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            log.Fatalf("metrics query returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    log.Fatal("metrics query remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

The API call retries only a 429, honors an integer Retry-After, and otherwise backs off exponentially. It uses the query route without filters because those parameters are not declared. That constraint is inconvenient, but guessing a query string would make the example look more capable than the documented contract.

The health probe itself should not retry. A scheduler can run it repeatedly, while the alert rule can require several consecutive failures. Retrying inside one probe blurs a four-second failure into a much longer and harder-to-attribute event. Choose the interval and consecutive-failure threshold from the response-time objective, not from a vendor default.

For scheduled work, add a separate dead-man signal. Each successful rent-reminder run should check in with an external heartbeat service using a stable job identity. Retries must use the same delivery or operation key so that recovery does not send a resident two reminders. Quiet failures are the dangerous ones.

4. Compare products by the missing failure mode

No single product choice removes the endpoint design work. The useful comparison is which evidence and detection path each option adds around it.

Option Best fit here Boundary to plan for
Prometheus Scraping numeric service metrics and applying its established naming model An unreachable target can be observed, but a business task still needs an explicit completion signal
Healthchecks.io Dead-man monitoring for cron and queue jobs that should check in It complements rather than replaces Express liveness, readiness, and dependency logs
Better Stack External uptime checks when a team wants a hosted monitoring path Keep detailed customer-incident evidence in structured application logs
Datadog Teams consolidating service monitoring in an existing observability program Define tag cardinality and cost ownership before sending tenant-shaped dimensions
Infrai Sending logs and metrics from small services through one REST interface Build the alert poller separately; distributed trace queries, source-map processing, and session replay are outside this fit

That is a fair split of responsibilities. The trade-off is operational ownership: a small team might pair Better Stack with structured logs, while a scheduler-heavy system might prioritize Healthchecks.io. An organization already operating Prometheus or Datadog usually gains more from consistent labels and runbooks than from adding another destination. Infrai is not a fit when the team requires built-in alert notifications, distributed trace-tree queries, source-map processing, or session replay; choose a product that owns those workflows instead.

Tool count is not the objective.

5. Turn a red check into a reconstruction runbook

When readiness turns red, capture four times: the external probe failure, the dependency-check failure, the last successful customer job, and the next successful recovery. Then correlate by service, portfolio, job ID, and trace ID. This produces a bounded incident window and an answer to "which properties were affected?" without encoding every property into a metric.

The runbook should ask, in order: Was the process reachable? Which dependency failed? Did queued work stop, retry, or complete? Were retries deduplicated? Which customer operations fall inside the failure window? Reconciliation comes before replay. Replaying first can turn missing work into duplicate deliveries.

There are cases where this design is too small. If one request crosses many services, logs carrying trace and span IDs do not substitute for a queryable distributed trace tree. Browser crashes need source maps or symbolization. A customer-support workflow that depends on session replay needs a different tool. Admit those boundaries early.

6. Ship the smallest system that can falsify "healthy"

Start with two Express routes, one external probe, one job heartbeat, structured failure logs, and a small metric vocabulary. Test Postgres and Redis readiness with strict timeouts. Keep liveness local. Attach customer identifiers to logs and cost-allocation dimensions to metrics.

Then stage three failures: stop Redis, block Postgres, and suppress a scheduled job without stopping its worker. The first two should make readiness fail while liveness stays green; the third should trip the heartbeat even though both HTTP endpoints remain healthy. If the evidence identifies the affected portfolio and prevents duplicate replay, the system is doing useful work.

That is enough to begin. Add tracing, replay, or a broader platform only when an incident question proves the need.

References

  • Express health-check discussion: https://expressjs.com/en/advanced/healthcheck-graceful-shutdown.html
  • Kubernetes liveness, readiness, and startup probes: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/
  • Prometheus metric and label naming: https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/
  • Healthchecks.io documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • Better Stack uptime monitoring documentation: https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/
  • Datadog tagging guidance: https://docs.datadoghq.com/getting_started/tagging/

Sources

  • https://expressjs.com/en/advanced/healthcheck-graceful-shutdown.html
  • https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/
  • https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/
  • https://docs.datadoghq.com/getting_started/tagging/

title: React clinic appointment board
description:
A clinic board has clinicians down the side and the day across the top. Every visit is the same length, each clinician works their own hours, nobody is booked back to back, and reception wants to ask "who is free next?". This tutorial builds that with Resource Scheduler in seven steps. It is the same component running below.

See it running live: interactive demo.

Try three things. Drag Tanaka (Dr Brown, 9:00) to Nurse Cho at 9:30: that is right after Singh, so the gap is missing and the drop turns red. Drop it at 9:45 and it moves. Then pick "Anyone" and press "Book it" to book the next free visit.

1. Install 

npm install resource-scheduler

Works with React 18 and 19. Import the stylesheet once; it is scoped, so it does not restyle the rest of your page:

import "resource-scheduler/dist/resource-scheduler.css";

2. Clinicians are rows, with their own hours

Each clinician is a resource. Their working days and hours are businessHours, and one-off gaps such as lunch or training are unavailable. Both are shaded in the grid:

import type { ResourceInput } from "resource-scheduler";

const everyDay = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; // use [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] for a Monday to Friday clinic

const clinicians: ResourceInput[] = [
  {
    id: "ahmed",
    name: "Dr Ahmed",
    businessHours: { daysOfWeek: everyDay, startHour: 8, endHour: 17 },
    unavailable: [{ start: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 12), end: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 13) }], // lunch
  },
  { id: "brown", name: "Dr Brown", businessHours: { daysOfWeek: everyDay, startHour: 8, endHour: 13 } }, // mornings only
  {
    id: "cho",
    name: "Nurse Cho",
    businessHours: { daysOfWeek: everyDay, startHour: 9, endHour: 17 },
    unavailable: [{ start: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 15), end: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 16) }], // training
  },
];

daysOfWeek counts Sunday as 0. In a database this is a clinicians table with hours, plus a table of blocked time that you turn into unavailable ranges for the day on screen.

3. A visit is an event with a fixed length

Three numbers describe the clinic. Keep them in one place, because every step below uses them:

const SLOT = 15; // the grid: a booking starts on a quarter hour
const VISIT = 30; // every appointment is the same length
const BUFFER = 15; // minutes to write up and reset between patients
const MINUTE = 60_000;

A booked visit is a plain event. It names its row with resourceId:

import type { SchedulerEvent } from "resource-scheduler";

const visits: SchedulerEvent[] = [
  { id: "v1", title: "Patel", resourceId: "ahmed", startDate: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 8, 30), endDate: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 9) },
  { id: "v2", title: "Okafor", resourceId: "ahmed", startDate: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 9, 30), endDate: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 10) },
  { id: "v4", title: "Reyes", resourceId: "brown", startDate: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 8), endDate: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 8, 30) },
];

The list is flat, so it can come straight from one query on your appointments table.

4. Draw the day 

import { ResourceScheduler, ViewType } from "resource-scheduler";

<div style={{ height: 330 }}>
  <ResourceScheduler
    resources={clinicians}
    events={visits}
    initialView={ViewType.Day}
    allowViewChange={false}
    slotDuration={SLOT}
    dayStartHour={8}
    dayEndHour={17}
    blockUnavailable
    ariaLabel="Clinic appointments"
  />
</div>

The component fills its parent, so the parent needs a height. Each prop is one rule:

Prop What it does
slotDuration={SLOT} The grid is quarter hours, so a click or a drop lands on one
dayStartHour / dayEndHour The hours shown, 8:00 to 17:00
blockUnavailable Nothing can be booked outside a clinician's hours or in their lunch

Because onEventResize is not passed, the resize handles stay off and a visit keeps its length. See views and slots.

5. One rule: no double booking, with a gap

eventOverlap={false} would stop two visits overlapping, but it cannot ask for a gap between them. Give each booked visit some padding instead, and ask whether the new visit fits in what is left:

import { findAvailableSlots, withEvents } from "resource-scheduler";

// Each booked visit holds its clinician for BUFFER minutes either side. A free slot in this
// padded copy is a visit plus its gaps, and the padding never shows on screen.
const padded = (all: SchedulerEvent[], ignoreId?: string): SchedulerEvent[] =>
  all
    .filter((e) => e.id !== ignoreId)
    .map((e) => ({
      ...e,
      startDate: new Date(e.startDate.getTime() - BUFFER * MINUTE),
      endDate: new Date(e.endDate.getTime() + BUFFER * MINUTE),
    }));

// The one rule: hours, lunch, no double booking and the gap, all answered by findAvailableSlots.
// The window is exactly the range asked about, so it returns that slot or nothing.
const canBook = (all: SchedulerEvent[], clinicianId: string, start: Date, end: Date, ignoreId?: string) => {
  const clinician = withEvents(clinicians, padded(all, ignoreId)).find((c) => c.id === clinicianId);
  return (
    !!clinician &&
    findAvailableSlots(clinician, { from: start, to: end, duration: (end.getTime() - start.getTime()) / MINUTE, step: SLOT }).length > 0
  );
};

withEvents puts the flat list onto the clinicians. findAvailableSlots treats a slot as free when it overlaps no event, misses unavailable time and sits inside the clinician's businessHours, so one call covers all four rules. Times that only touch do not overlap, so a visit that starts exactly 15 minutes after the last one ends is allowed. The visit being moved is left out with ignoreId, so it does not block its own new place.

Pass it as isValidDrop, and book through your own form:

<ResourceScheduler
  /* ... */
  onSlotSelect={setDraft} // a click on a free slot: open your form
  onEventDrop={(visit, _from, to, start, end) =>
    setEvents((all) => all.map((e) => (e.id === visit.id ? { ...e, resourceId: to, startDate: start, endDate: end } : e)))
  }
  isValidDrop={(visit, { resourceId, start, end }) => canBook(events, resourceId, start, end, visit.id)}
/>

isValidDrop runs for every move and every new selection, and the refused place turns red before the drop. A callback is the opt-in: without onEventDrop a dropped visit snaps back.

A click selects one slot, a visit is two. A click selects a single 15 minute slot, so the grid only checks that slot. The form then books a full 30 minute visit and runs canBook on the whole range before it adds it, saying so when it does not fit. The full code is in the demo source.

6. The next free slot

Reception rarely picks a time first. They ask who is free next. suggestResources answers that: give it a window and a length, and it returns the earliest free slot of each clinician, best first. Hand it the same padded events, so the gap is respected:

import { suggestResources } from "resource-scheduler";

const [next] = suggestResources(
  withEvents(clinicians, padded(events)),
  { from: new Date(), to: new Date(2026, 9, 7, 17), duration: VISIT, step: SLOT },
  { resourceIds: who === "any" ? undefined : [who], limit: 1 }
);
// next = { resourceId, start, end, ... }, or undefined when nobody is free before 17:00

Pass resourceIds to ask about one clinician, or leave it out to ask about all of them. For a single clinician, findAvailableSlots(clinician, { from, to, duration: VISIT, step: SLOT, limit: 3 }) lists the next three free slots to offer the patient. See Availability.

7. Check it on the server too

The browser check is a courtesy: anyone can call your API without the board. The rule is a plain function of dates and events, so the server runs it again before it saves. isPlacementAllowed applies isValidDrop for you:

import { findAvailableSlots, isPlacementAllowed } from "resource-scheduler";
import type { Resource, SchedulerEvent } from "resource-scheduler";

export function canBookVisit(clinician: Resource, visit: SchedulerEvent) {
  return isPlacementAllowed(
    visit,
    { resourceId: clinician.id, start: visit.startDate, end: visit.endDate },
    [clinician], // the clinician with their hours and current visits, read inside your transaction
    {
      isValidDrop: (v, { start, end }) =>
        findAvailableSlots(
          { ...clinician, events: padded(clinician.events, v.id) },
          { from: start, to: end, duration: (end.getTime() - start.getTime()) / MINUTE, step: SLOT }
        ).length > 0,
    }
  );
}

Return an error (HTTP 409 is the usual choice) when it is false, and run the check and the insert in one transaction. See Conflict control.

Where next

  • Add recurring events for a standing weekly slot, such as a patient seen every Tuesday.
  • A clinic in another time zone from the browser: Time zones.
  • Share the day as a calendar file or a spreadsheet: Export.
  • Other builds: the room booking tutorial, the shift planner and the free resource timeline.
  • Coming from another library? The comparison lists what each one includes.

Originally published at https://resource-scheduler-docs.vercel.app/tutorials/react-clinic-appointment-board/.

title: How I made quality non-negotiable in an Expo app
description:
React Native apps don't usually fail loudly. They rot quietly. A refactor leaves a screen that return null and ships a blank page. A "temporary" stub passes lint, type-check, and unit tests because nothing renders it. A business rule everyone agreed on — "the wallet changes when you spend" — is never actually asserted, so it silently breaks three releases later.

Tests don't catch these because tests check logic, and these are integration truths. So I made them impossible to skip, with two build gates that fail npm run check and CI.

Gate 1 — a "screens gate": a screen must actually be a screen

A stub screen (returns null, or renders nothing) is invisible to logic tests. This gate walks src/ui/screens and asserts every file is a real, default-exported component that renders markup:

// src/__tests__/screens.gate.test.tsx
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

const SCREENS_DIR = path.join(__dirname, '..', 'ui', 'screens');
const MIN_LINES = 20;
const files = fs.existsSync(SCREENS_DIR)
  ? fs.readdirSync(SCREENS_DIR).filter((f) => f.endsWith('Screen.tsx'))
  : [];

describe('every screen is a real implementation (not a stub)', () => {
  it('has screen files', () => expect(files.length).toBeGreaterThan(0));

  files.forEach((file) => {
    it(`${file} is implemented`, () => {
      const src = fs.readFileSync(path.join(SCREENS_DIR, file), 'utf8');
      expect(src.split('\n').length).toBeGreaterThan(MIN_LINES);
      expect(src).not.toMatch(/return\s+null\s*;/);
      expect(src).toMatch(/export\s+default/);
      expect(src).toMatch(/return\s*\(|<[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9.]*[\s/>]/);
      const mod = require(path.join(SCREENS_DIR, file));
      expect(typeof mod.default).toBe('function');
    });
  });
});

It's ~25 lines, and it has caught a black-screen launch more than once.

Gate 2 — an acceptance-contract gate: no unproven invariants

Instead of hoping people remember to test the important things, you declare them as a machine-checkable contract (contract/acceptance_spec.json):

{
  "invariants": [
    { "id": "INV-PERSIST-1", "assertion": "settings round-trip through storage unchanged" },
    { "id": "INV-STATE-1",   "assertion": "changing a setting leaves unrelated fields untouched" }
  ],
  "journeys": [
    { "id": "J-SETTINGS-1", "name": "settings persist, reload, and reset" }
  ]
}

Then a gate test fails the build unless every id is referenced by at least one test — and it rejects fake coverage: tests that only assert on literals they defined themselves don't count, and contract-tagged test files must import real code.

// src/__tests__/contract.gate.test.tsx  (excerpt)
it('every invariant/journey id is proven by a test', () => {
  const c = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(CONTRACT, 'utf8'));
  const ids = [...c.invariants, ...c.journeys].map((x) => x.id);
  const missing = ids.filter((id) => !corpusText.includes(id));
  expect(missing).toEqual([]);
});

The effect: "we should test that" becomes a red build. You can't ship an unproven invariant.

The point

Both gates are cheap and boring — which is exactly why they work. They turn quality from a habit into a property of the build. npm run check (strict TS + ESLint + Jest) stays green because it has to.

The free baseline — typed navigation, deep links, theme tokens, MMKV persistence, and native modules mocked for tests — is on GitHub: https://github.com/nwebersoftware/expo-starter

The production gates above, plus CI and local iOS/Android release scripts, are packaged up in a Pro kit — link in the first comment.

title: A reader picked apart my benchmark. Here is what survived, and what changed
description:
Last week I published a study of 181 real code changes, and one sentence in it was wrong. A reader found it by re-adding my numbers. This is what they found, what I changed, and what is still open.

The sentence

I'd written that in 10% of agent-written pull requests every test failed on the old code only because the test file imports a name the change adds (so the file can't even load), and that "no maintainer commit in my sample looked like that."

The reader re-derived my results files before reading the write-up. Every sum held. Then they pointed at a line I'd skipped: the maintainer file lists 9 tests with the verdict WEAK out of 212 (4%), while the agent file lists 79 out of 591 (13%). So the pattern isn't absent on the maintainer side.

I went and looked. All nine come from one marshmallow feature commit that added a new keyword argument. Its test file loads fine, and the same commit also has tests that do prove the change. So the sentence was about "every test is WEAK", and the fix was to say what the maintainer data actually contains. By change, 14 of 91 agent PRs contain a WEAK test, against 1 of 71 maintainer commits.

The split that made it more interesting

The reader's next question: does the import pattern show up even when something else already proves the change, or only when nothing does? Splitting the 91 agent PRs by whether they have a proving test:

  • With a proving test: 5 of 80 carry a WEAK test (6.3%, 95% interval 2.7 to 13.8).
  • Without one: 9 of 11 (81.8%, interval 52.3 to 94.9).

If WEAK tests were written at the same 6.3% rate everywhere, you'd expect about 0.7 of the 11 to carry one. There are 9. So most of it sits exactly where nothing else proves the change. The reader also pointed out the catch: my change-level rule never calls a change Proven if it carries a WEAK test, so part of that is the aggregation rule read back. The 5 of 80 is the only number that isn't, because those PRs ship a proof and still add a WEAK test. That's an authoring rate, and it's small but not zero.

I checked their statistics myself (Wilson intervals, Fisher exact tests). They hold. The maintainer side is a different story: 1 of 71 is one event, so it can't tell anyone the base rate, however clean the contrast looks.

What changed

  • The study doc now says all of the above, with the intervals, and one definition of "weak only" everywhere (my generator and two results files disagreed with the doc).
  • Receipts, the tool, now prints how each PROVEN test failed on the old code. A different reader, on Reddit, said "it went red" isn't enough: you want to see that the test reached its assertion, not that it died on an import. The tool knew that and wasn't showing it.
  • I wrote down the next step before running it: a few hundred more maintainer commits, as their own row, with one selection rule applied to both sides. The reader predicted the maintainer rate would move up toward the agent rate, because the one maintainer event is itself a churn-shaped commit. That prediction is in the doc now, so whatever comes back gets read against it.

What I took from it

Two things. One: re-derive someone's sums before you argue with their sentence, because the sentence is where it's loose. Two: a nice headline number ("10% of agent PRs") can be a fact about your verdict rules as much as about the code, and the only way I found that out was a reader who wasn't invested in the answer.

The tool is open source and free: https://github.com/syntaxixr/receipts. The study with every change linked: https://github.com/syntaxixr/receipts/blob/main/docs/study.md

Heads up: I drafted this post with an AI assistant. The numbers are from the study files in the repo and from the comment thread under the original post.

title: SaaS Health Checks — Readiness, Liveness, and Reliable Incident Reconstruction
description:
TL;DR: For a beginner B2B SaaS, ship two small health endpoints: liveness says the process can answer, while readiness tests the dependencies needed to serve useful work. Add low-cardinality metrics and structured failure logs, then use an external check for the nightly pipeline. An internal endpoint cannot report that a task never started.

Need First choice Why
Restart a stuck process Lightweight liveness It does not turn a brief database problem into a restart loop
Stop routing work to a degraded instance Dependency-aware readiness It tests Postgres, Redis, and critical third-party reachability
Reconstruct a missed nightly run Structured logs plus simple metrics Timestamps and stable tags preserve the sequence of events
Detect a job that never ran External heartbeat or polling check There may be no process event to log

The recommendation is deliberately boring: implement /health/live and /health/ready, record every failed dependency check, and report a tiny set of consistently named metrics. Pair that with Healthchecks, Uptime Kuma, or another external scheduler-aware monitor for the silent-failure case. Do not begin with distributed tracing or a large agent configuration. Neither answers the first question during an incident: did the nightly import run, and where did it stop?

How should an Express health check endpoint split readiness and liveness?

Liveness and readiness answer different operational questions. Liveness should be cheap and local. If the event loop can serve the request, the process is alive. Readiness is deeper: it checks whether this instance can do useful work right now. For the pipeline in this example, that means Postgres and Redis, plus any third-party API whose absence must block the job.

Mixing those signals creates a nasty failure mode. Suppose Postgres has a 20-second interruption. If the liveness route waits for Postgres, an orchestrator may restart healthy application processes while the database is already recovering. More churn. Less evidence.

Keep the split sharp. A readiness failure should remove an instance from service or mark it degraded. A liveness failure can justify restarting the process. A third-party dependency can be required or advisory, but make that decision explicitly; otherwise a nonessential API outage can take the whole SaaS offline.

Two signals. Two jobs.

The response body should be useful to an operator without leaking credentials, SQL, Redis URLs, or upstream response bodies. Return dependency names, a small status vocabulary, and elapsed milliseconds. Log the detailed failure on the server with the pipeline run ID. That ID is the join key when the nightly job crosses several workers.

The two criteria that actually matter

The first criterion is incident reconstruction. At 08:10, “database was unhealthy” is weak evidence. You want a sequence: run run_2026_10_14 started, Postgres passed, Redis failed after a bounded check, readiness changed to degraded, and the run did not reach its completion marker. Structured events make that sequence searchable. A counter and duration metric show whether it was isolated or part of a wider degraded period.

Names matter more than clever queries. Use stable metric names such as pipeline_runs_total, pipeline_run_duration_seconds, and dependency_check_failures_total. Keep tags constrained to values such as dependency=postgres and outcome=failed; never put a customer ID, error message, or run ID into metric tags. Those values grow without bound and belong in logs.

The second criterion is time to first useful signal. I benchmark this as integration work, not a vendor latency claim: count required SDKs, keys, config files, and glue modules before the first check is visible. A plain endpoint plus one reporting path is easier to audit than a stack of collectors for a small app. It also gives you fewer places to lose the run ID.

This is where Infrai can fit: its public discovery surface describes each capability with request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts by reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. Infrai uses a single API key and a single bill across 295 routes in 20 modules; for this pipeline, that means later scheduling or storage work does not require another vendor credential, invoice path, and client library for each backend task. Its observability surface can ingest logs and report metrics under that same credential. The boundary is important, though. It does not provide alert or notification routes, synthetic checks, heartbeat monitoring, distributed span-tree queries, source-map symbolication, or Session Replay. Query filters for log search and metric queries are not declared in discovery, so keep names and tags simple and validate the current discovery schema before building query-dependent automation.

A minimal TypeScript implementation

Before sending logs or metrics, inspect the live discovery document instead of guessing a payload. This call is runnable, uses the required environment variable, sets the method explicitly, checks real errors, and backs off on rate limiting. Discovery is public, but using the standard credential path here makes the helper reusable for authenticated capability reads.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function loadDiscovery(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const origin = ["https://api", "infrai", "cc"].join(".");
  const response = await fetch(`${origin}/v1/discovery`, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return loadDiscovery(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

void loadDiscovery().then((document) => {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(document));
});

Read the relevant capability's request schema and runnable TypeScript example from that document before adding a report call. This matters because log-search and metric-query filters are not declared; a plausible-looking filter is still an invented contract.

The health server below is intentionally small. It assumes existing pg and redis clients, applies an 800 ms timeout to each dependency check, and never makes liveness depend on the network. A concrete failure drill is easy: start the server, stop Redis, request readiness, and confirm that the response becomes 503 while liveness stays 200. Then restore Redis and verify readiness returns to 200. That three-step check is more useful than a polished green dashboard because it tests the exact routing semantics operators will depend on.

import express, { type Request, type Response } from "express";
import { Pool } from "pg";
import { createClient } from "redis";

const app = express();
const postgres = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });

type Check = {
  name: "postgres" | "redis";
  status: "ok" | "failed";
  elapsedMs: number;
};

async function within<T>(promise: Promise<T>, timeoutMs: number): Promise<T> {
  let timer: NodeJS.Timeout | undefined;
  const timeout = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("dependency check timed out")), timeoutMs);
  });

  try {
    return await Promise.race([promise, timeout]);
  } finally {
    if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

async function check(
  name: Check["name"],
  operation: () => Promise<unknown>,
): Promise<Check> {
  const started = performance.now();

  try {
    await within(operation(), 800);
    return { name, status: "ok", elapsedMs: Math.round(performance.now() - started) };
  } catch (error) {
    const elapsedMs = Math.round(performance.now() - started);
    console.error(JSON.stringify({
      event: "dependency_check_failed",
      dependency: name,
      elapsed_ms: elapsedMs,
      error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown error",
    }));
    return { name, status: "failed", elapsedMs };
  }
}

app.get("/health/live", (_request: Request, response: Response) => {
  response.status(200).json({ status: "alive" });
});

app.get("/health/ready", async (_request: Request, response: Response) => {
  const checks = await Promise.all([
    check("postgres", () => postgres.query("SELECT 1")),
    check("redis", () => redis.ping()),
  ]);
  const ready = checks.every((item) => item.status === "ok");

  response.status(ready ? 200 : 503).json({
    status: ready ? "ready" : "degraded",
    checks,
  });
});

async function start(): Promise<void> {
  await redis.connect();
  app.listen(3000);
}

void start();

The 800 ms budget is an application choice, not a universal default. Set it below the caller's timeout and test it under dependency failure. Also cap how often infrastructure polls readiness; an expensive health route can become its own load test.

It can bite hard.

For the nightly job, emit explicit start and completion events. Report one duration and one outcome per run, with the unique run ID in the log only. The crucial detector remains outside the job: a polling script or heartbeat service should expect completion within a defined window. No completion event means something even if every server is currently ready.

Where do the alternatives win?

Prometheus is the stronger runner-up when the team wants a mature metrics model and can operate scraping, storage, and alerting around it. Its naming guidance is also the right baseline for any backend: one unit per metric and consistent suffixes. Choose it when metrics are the primary product and the operational overhead is acceptable. It will not, by itself, prove that a scheduled task which emitted nothing was supposed to run.

Healthchecks is narrower and therefore useful. It is built around jobs signaling success, start, or failure to an external service. Choose that shape for the nightly pipeline's dead-man switch, especially when “no event” is the incident. It is a complement to readiness, structured logs, and dependency metrics rather than a replacement for them.

Uptime Kuma fits teams that want a self-hosted monitor for endpoint polling and visible status. It can watch the public readiness URL from outside the application boundary. The trade-off is ownership: the monitor, its network path, and its storage become systems your team operates.

Grafana is the natural dashboard layer when the team already has metrics and logs in compatible data sources and wants to correlate them visually. It wins on flexible visualization around an existing observability stack; it does not replace the external heartbeat that notices an absent nightly run.

Datadog is the better fit when one integrated commercial suite and broad operational workflows matter more than minimizing config and SDK surface. A team already standardized on it will usually gain more from consistent dashboards and process than from adding another observability backend. For a first pipeline monitor, though, validate that the extra integration work buys an incident question you cannot answer with two endpoints, structured events, and a heartbeat.

These are not interchangeable products. Benchmark the setup against one forced Redis failure and one deliberately skipped nightly run. Record how many minutes and configuration artifacts it takes to identify each cause. That test exposes the boundary quickly.

The decision rule

Start with the two endpoints when the application is small, Postgres and Redis are the critical dependencies, and the immediate goal is simple uptime plus reconstructable nightly runs. Add an external heartbeat on day one. Silent failure is common enough to deserve its own detector.

Pick Prometheus when metric depth and control justify operating the stack. Add Healthchecks when scheduled-job absence is the dominant risk. Use Uptime Kuma when self-hosted external polling is the desired model, or Datadog when the organization already values a unified managed suite. Consider Infrai when a self-describing REST surface and low glue count are more important than built-in alerting and tracing; plan to poll queries and deliver alerts through your own service.

Do the failure drill before polishing a dashboard. Kill Redis. Skip one run. Then ask whether the evidence names the failed dependency, preserves the run sequence, and detects the missing completion. If all three answers are yes, the first version is done.

References

  • Prometheus metric and label naming
  • Express health checks and shutdown guidance
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Uptime Kuma repository and documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Datadog API tests documentation

title: React shift planner (employee roster)
description:
A shift planner has people down the side and days across the top. The standing rota repeats every week, people have contracted days and leave, someone covers a shift now and then, and there is a house rule about hours. This tutorial builds that with Resource Scheduler in six steps. It is the same component running below.

See it running live: interactive demo.

Try three things. Drag Cy's Friday shift to Ann: she already works 32 hours, so the drop turns red and nothing moves. Drag Cy's Monday shift to Dee instead and it is covered for that day only. Click an empty day in Dee's row to add a shift with your own form.

1. Install 

npm install resource-scheduler

Works with React 18 and 19. Import the stylesheet once; it is scoped, so it does not restyle the rest of your page:

import "resource-scheduler/dist/resource-scheduler.css";

2. People are rows, with a contract and leave

Each person is a resource. Their contracted days and hours are businessHours, and leave is unavailable. Both are shaded in the grid:

import type { ResourceInput } from "resource-scheduler";

const staff: ResourceInput[] = [
  { id: "ann", name: "Ann Lee", businessHours: { daysOfWeek: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], startHour: 7, endHour: 15 } },
  {
    id: "cy",
    name: "Cy Ortiz",
    businessHours: { daysOfWeek: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], startHour: 7, endHour: 15 },
    unavailable: [{ start: new Date(2026, 9, 7), end: new Date(2026, 9, 9) }], // leave
  },
  { id: "bo", name: "Bo Kim", businessHours: { daysOfWeek: [3, 4, 5, 6], startHour: 11, endHour: 19 } },
];

daysOfWeek counts Sunday as 0, so [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] is Monday to Friday. In a database this is a people table with contract and leave columns.

3. The standing rota is one row per series

You do not store a shift for every week. A shift is one event with a weekly recurrence, and the component expands it into the weeks on screen. Give it the first occurrence and the weekdays it repeats on:

import type { SchedulerEvent } from "resource-scheduler";

const shifts: SchedulerEvent[] = [
  {
    id: "ann-early",
    title: "Early",
    resourceId: "ann",                              // the row it belongs to
    startDate: new Date(2026, 8, 21, 7),            // the first Monday, 7:00
    endDate: new Date(2026, 8, 21, 15),             // 15:00
    recurrence: { freq: "weekly", byWeekday: [1, 2, 3, 4] },   // Monday to Thursday
  },
];

Events are a flat list that names its row with resourceId, so the list can come straight from one query. See recurring events for ending a series and skipping days.

4. Draw the week and refuse bad shifts 

import { ResourceScheduler, ViewType } from "resource-scheduler";

<div style={{ height: 530 }}>
  <ResourceScheduler
    resources={staff}
    events={shifts}
    initialView={ViewType.Week}
    allowViewChange={false}
    weekStartsOn={1}
    showUtilization
    blockUnavailable
    eventOverlap={false}
    ariaLabel="Shift roster"
  />
</div>

The component fills its parent, so the parent needs a height. Each prop is one rule:

Prop What it does
showUtilization A bar per person: rostered hours against contracted hours (utilization)
blockUnavailable No shifts on days off or leave
eventOverlap={false} Nobody works two shifts at once
weekStartsOn={1} The week starts on Monday

5. Cover a shift for one day

Dragging a shift hands your handler one occurrence of the series, with an id such as ann-early::2026-10-07 and a seriesId of ann-early. Covering that one day means skipping it in the series and adding a one-off shift for the new person:

onEventDrop={(shift, _fromId, toId, start, end) =>
  setEvents((all) => {
    if (!shift.seriesId) {
      return all.map((e) => (e.id === shift.id ? { ...e, resourceId: toId, startDate: start, endDate: end } : e));
    }
    const skipped = all.map((e) =>
      e.id === shift.seriesId
        ? { ...e, recurrence: { ...e.recurrence!, exceptions: [...(e.recurrence!.exceptions ?? []), shift.startDate] } }
        : e
    );
    return [...skipped, { ...shift, id: crypto.randomUUID(), seriesId: undefined, resourceId: toId, startDate: start, endDate: end }];
  })
}

A callback is the opt-in: without onEventDrop a dropped shift snaps back. To change the series for good instead, edit the original event.

6. Add a rule: at most 32 hours a week

isValidDrop is a final veto for anything the other props cannot say. It gets the event and where it would land, and returns false to refuse. A weekly cap needs the hours the person already has that week, so count the shifts you hold. expandEvents turns a series into real shifts for a date range, which is the expansion the grid uses:

import { expandEvents, rangesOverlap } from "resource-scheduler";

const MAX_WEEK_HOURS = 32; // four eight-hour shifts

const hoursBetween = (start: Date, end: Date) => (end.getTime() - start.getTime()) / 36e5;

// Hours already rostered for one person in the Monday to Sunday week containing `day`.
const rosteredHours = (all: SchedulerEvent[], personId: string, day: Date, ignoreId?: string) => {
  const from = new Date(day);
  from.setHours(0, 0, 0, 0);
  from.setDate(from.getDate() - ((from.getDay() + 6) % 7));
  const to = new Date(from);
  to.setDate(to.getDate() + 7);
  return expandEvents(all.filter((e) => e.resourceId === personId), from, to)
    .filter((e) => e.id !== ignoreId && rangesOverlap(e.startDate, e.endDate, from, to))
    .reduce((sum, e) => sum + hoursBetween(e.startDate, e.endDate), 0);
};

Then pass the rule. The shift being moved is left out of the count (ignoreId), so moving someone's own shift to another day in the same week is not charged twice:

<ResourceScheduler
  /* ... */
  isValidDrop={(shift, { resourceId, start, end }) =>
    rosteredHours(events, resourceId, start, shift.id) + hoursBetween(start, end) <= MAX_WEEK_HOURS
  }
/>

The refused place turns red before the drop. Ann has four eight-hour shifts, so any shift dropped on her week is refused; Dee has none, so she can take cover.

New shifts come from your form. In the week view a click selects a whole day, so the placement of a new shift is the day, not the eight hours your form will add. The demo therefore applies isValidDrop to moves of existing shifts, and checks a new shift in the form with the same rosteredHours before it adds it. The full code is in the demo source.

Check it on the server too

The browser check is a courtesy: anyone can call your API without the grid. The rule is a plain function of dates and ids, so the server can run exactly the same one before it saves. isPlacementAllowed applies eventOverlap and isValidDrop together:

import { isPlacementAllowed } from "resource-scheduler";
import type { Resource, SchedulerEvent } from "resource-scheduler";

export function canRoster(person: Resource, shift: SchedulerEvent) {
  return isPlacementAllowed(
    shift,
    { resourceId: person.id, start: shift.startDate, end: shift.endDate },
    [person], // the person with their current shifts, read inside your transaction
    {
      eventOverlap: false,
      isValidDrop: (s, { resourceId, start, end }) =>
        rosteredHours(person.events, resourceId, start, s.id) + hoursBetween(start, end) <= MAX_WEEK_HOURS,
    }
  );
}

Return an error (HTTP 409 is the usual choice) when it is false, and run the check and the insert in one transaction. For rest rules, such as at least 11 hours between shifts, write the same kind of function against the neighbouring shifts. See Conflict control.

Where next

  • The finished shift roster recipe is the same code with notes on night shifts and time zones.
  • A site in another time zone: Time zones.
  • Share the rota as a calendar file or a spreadsheet: Export.
  • Other builds: the room booking tutorial and the free resource timeline.
  • Coming from another library? The comparison lists what each one includes.

Originally published at https://resource-scheduler-docs.vercel.app/tutorials/react-shift-planner/.

title: Compare Video Models with the Same Image and Motion Brief
description:
The useful question was not which model won. It was whether the shot kept the coffee berries in frame while the morning light changed.

This implementation note records the inputs, failure modes and checks needed to make the workflow reviewable.

Include the delivery route and price

Through Higgsfield, the recorded five-second Kling 3.0 Pro estimate was USD 0.84 and the Seedance 720p estimate was about USD 2.31. The resolutions differ, and a provider route can change available settings and prices. Record input, prompt, route, model, resolution and estimate together. Recheck pricing when you run the next test.

Compare the actual outputs

In this test, Seedance made the light warmer and kept the red berries visible. Kling moved forward enough that the berries left the frame. The Kling output was 1920 by 1080, while Seedance was 1280 by 720. These were individual attempts; repeated generation can produce a different movement, so neither result establishes a universal ranking.

Describe the required shot

We used one image of a highland coffee farm and asked for a slow forward camera movement, drifting mist and growing sunrise light. Defining those visible changes made the output easier to judge than a broad request for a cinematic result. When commissioning a shot, name the subject that must stay visible as well as the movement you want.

Checks to carry into the next project

  • Write down what must remain visible.

  • Test the same image and movement with a small shortlist.

  • Compare revision effort as well as the quoted generation cost.

Keep a reproducible record of the configuration and inspect the final exported artifact. An automation success message is not a content review.

title: Check the Model ID Before Migrating a Veo Integration
description:
A model migration starts with an exact identifier. A product screen that only says Veo does not tell you which retirement notice applies.

This implementation note records the inputs, failure modes and checks needed to make the workflow reviewable.

Test the output contract

Record the provider, model ID, request settings and expected output before switching. Check resolution, duration, audio, download handling and estimated cost with a small test. In our Omni test, audio was generated with the video, so a workflow that creates music separately needed to mute or replace that track in editing.

Keep a small comparison reproducible

We tried the same input image and motion prompt with two Veo outputs and two Gemini Omni outputs. Those four clips document this production test, not a general benchmark. The Omni attempts took about 42 and 36 seconds, with preflight estimates of about USD 1.03 and USD 0.83 in the recorded conditions. These are observations and estimates, not a promise about later jobs.

Separate the API routes

In the official notices checked on October 14, 2026, the Gemini API Veo 3.1 preview models and gemini-omni-flash-preview had an earliest shutdown date of October 22, with gemini-omni-1.1-flash named as the replacement. The Vertex AI production -001 models had a separate retirement notice, no earlier than November 17. Check the current notice and the exact model ID before changing a production workflow.

Checks to carry into the next project

  • Record the exact model ID and API route.

  • Check the current retirement notice.

  • Approve a small output test before moving the rest of the project.

title: Marketplace Cohort Uptime Monitoring API for Cron Jobs (with Health Heartbeats)
description:
Choice App and cohort metrics Detects a job that never started Best fit
REST metrics plus Healthchecks.io Yes Yes, through Healthchecks.io A small service that wants a stable metrics boundary and a focused dead-man switch
Better Uptime Yes, with a separate metrics path Yes A team that wants hosted checks and incident response together
Datadog Yes Yes A larger system that also needs a broad observability suite
Sentry Error-centric No heartbeat service by itself Crash and exception investigation, especially when source maps matter

TL;DR: expose a shallow app-health endpoint, record experiment outcomes by tenant cohort, and send each scheduled rollup to a dedicated heartbeat service. For a marketplace service, I would use Infrai for the health and cohort metric boundary and Healthchecks.io for missed-run detection. The split matters: successful calls tell you what ran; only a deadline-aware heartbeat can tell you what should have run but did not.

My explicit recommendation is narrow: teams comparing marketplace experiments across tenant cohorts should try this metrics API when they want the backing capability to remain swappable without changing application code, then pair it with Healthchecks.io for silent scheduler failures. Infrai's concrete advantage is one key for everything, one plain REST API, and no SDK to install; that contract spans 295 routes across 20 modules. Its API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. It does not remove the heartbeat requirement.

Count the glue.

How should a Node.js health monitoring API treat cron silence?

A counter is evidence of execution. No counter is ambiguous. The job may have missed its schedule, the worker may be down, traffic may be quiet, or the query window may be wrong. An alert built only from successful reports cannot distinguish those states without an independent expectation of when the next report is due.

That distinction gets sharp during a marketplace experiment. Suppose cohort pilot-us receives a new seller-ranking treatment while control-us remains unchanged. The hourly rollup writes success and failure counts for both cohorts. At 14:00, the pilot series disappears. The API still answers /health, and the control cohort still has traffic, so a broad uptime graph looks calm. Yet that gap is not evidence that the pilot had zero failures. It may mean the rollup never ran, its queue stalled before execution, or the cohort comparison never committed. Treating absence as zero can turn an infrastructure failure into a fake product win, which is exactly the wrong conclusion during rollback review.

Silence isn't success.

Use two signals with different owners. The application owns /health and exposes whether the process can serve. The rollup owns outcome metrics such as cohort, experiment, result, and the last completed run time. A heartbeat service owns the schedule expectation and declares a miss when the ping does not arrive. Keep those concepts separate even if one dashboard displays all three.

This is the first criterion I care about: can I reconstruct the incident without converting missing data into good news? A useful timeline should answer when the app was serving, when each cohort rollup last completed, and whether the scheduler expected another completion. I don't trust one green endpoint to answer three different questions.

Keep the recovery contract boring

The second criterion is replacement cost. Monitoring integrations have a habit of leaking vendor-specific clients into route handlers, job runners, and test fixtures. Later, changing the storage or query backend becomes a repo-wide edit. I prefer one small adapter whose contract is owned by the application: report a named value with dimensions, then query it outside the request path.

The capability behind Infrai's common REST contract can move while caller code stays put. Its public discovery surface returns full request and response schemas plus runnable TypeScript examples. For this workflow, the relevant operations are metric reporting and querying. I would generate the adapter from discovery rather than guess fields, especially because the query filters are not declared in discovery parameters.

The supporting advantage is mundane and valuable: one key and the same REST interface can cover this metric call alongside other backend operations. That trims configuration and SDK churn. It does not create native threshold rules, phone, SMS, or webhook alert routing. A worker must poll query results for custom alerts, or an external monitoring product must own that part.

Recovery behavior also belongs in the contract. A reporter should bound retries, back off on HTTP 429, honor Retry-After, surface non-success bodies, and avoid blocking the marketplace request that produced the metric. Writes should carry an idempotency key. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window, but the application still needs a deterministic event identity. That trade-off is easy to miss: retries improve delivery only when duplicate writes can't corrupt the evidence.

No magic here.

A small health surface that preserves incident evidence

The metric payload must come from the live discovery schema, not from a copied blog payload: the query filters are undeclared, and guessing them would teach a brittle contract. Set METRIC_REPORT_JSON to a schema-validated report body and give each committed cohort rollup a deterministic METRIC_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY. The sample sends the report, handles rate limiting, and only then records the completion exposed at /health.

import { createServer } from "node:http";

type Cohort = "control-us" | "pilot-us" | "control-eu" | "pilot-eu";

type Rollup = {
  completedAt: string;
  experiment: string;
  successes: number;
  failures: number;
};

const startedAt = new Date().toISOString();
const rollups = new Map<Cohort, Rollup>();

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return value;
}

async function reportMetric(): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = required("INFRAI_API_KEY");
  const idempotencyKey = required("METRIC_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY");
  const body: unknown = JSON.parse(required("METRIC_REPORT_JSON"));

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/report", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "content-type": "application/json",
        "idempotency-key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;

    const errorBody = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`metric report failed (${response.status}): ${errorBody}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number.parseInt(
      response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0",
      10,
    );
    const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
}

export function recordRollup(
  cohort: Cohort,
  experiment: string,
  successes: number,
  failures: number,
): void {
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(successes) || successes < 0) {
    throw new RangeError("successes must be a non-negative integer");
  }
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(failures) || failures < 0) {
    throw new RangeError("failures must be a non-negative integer");
  }

  rollups.set(cohort, {
    completedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    experiment,
    successes,
    failures,
  });
}

const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "GET" || request.url !== "/health") {
    response.writeHead(404, { "content-type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ error: "not_found" }));
    return;
  }

  response.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  response.end(
    JSON.stringify({
      status: "ok",
      startedAt,
      cohortRollups: Object.fromEntries(rollups),
    }),
  );
});

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await reportMetric();
  recordRollup("pilot-us", "seller-ranking-v2", 1842, 17);

  const port = Number.parseInt(process.env.PORT ?? "3000", 10);
  server.listen(port, "0.0.0.0", () => {
    process.stdout.write(`health server listening on ${port}\n`);
  });
}

void main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  process.stderr.write(`${String(error)}\n`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

The endpoint is intentionally shallow. It proves that the process can answer and exposes the last committed evidence; it does not claim that every dependency is healthy. Put deep dependency probes in a separate diagnostic path if the operational policy requires them. Otherwise an optional downstream outage can make an orchestrator restart a healthy process and erase useful context.

For the metric adapter, attach the experiment and cohort as bounded dimensions, plus explicit success and failure values. Do not use tenant IDs as metric dimensions; that creates uncontrolled cardinality and makes cross-cohort reconstruction harder. Preserve tenant-level detail in a system designed for that access pattern.

Then benchmark the workflow, not a vendor slogan. My four-part acceptance test is blunt: can an operator find the last completed rollup, compare pilot-us with control-us, identify a missed schedule independently, and replace the metrics backend by changing one adapter? I time the first successful call and count credentials, packages, and retry implementations. Those are reproducible DX measurements. Invented latency numbers aren't.

When is the runner-up the better tool?

Choose Healthchecks.io as the center of the design when cron and scheduler deadlines are the whole problem. Its job is the negative signal: a ping was expected and did not arrive. You will still need somewhere else to compare experiment outcome metrics, but the mental model is small and direct.

Better Uptime is the stronger choice when hosted uptime checks, heartbeat monitoring, and incident response need to live in one operational product. That reduces the number of consoles. The trade-off is a wider vendor boundary than a tiny heartbeat companion.

Datadog fits when this marketplace already needs a broad observability platform and the team can support its instrumentation and configuration surface. It is a more coherent choice than assembling narrow tools when metrics, monitors, and deeper cross-service investigation share one operating team. For a two-service experiment, I would make it earn that configuration cost in a trial before adopting it.

Pick Sentry when the incident starts with an exception and the real requirement is source-map crash analysis. Infrai does not provide source-map resolution, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, distributed span-tree queries, or session replay. Logs may carry trace_id and span_id, but correlation fields are not a tracing product.

Those limits are decisive. The split stack supports basic US/EU SaaS dashboards and cohort rollups. It is not a substitute for synthetic probing, a tracing backend, or a client-session debugger. There is also no native alert-routing layer, so a team unwilling to own a polling worker should select a product with alert rules and notification delivery built in.

The decision rule

Use the split stack when incident reconstruction depends on a few application-owned metrics, the scheduler needs independent missed-run detection, and keeping provider details behind one REST adapter matters. The stable contract is the reason to consider it; reduced credential and SDK glue is the second reason.

Use a specialist as the primary product when the missing capability is the investigation itself. Heartchecks favor Healthchecks.io. Hosted checks and incident response favor Better Uptime. A broad platform favors Datadog. Source-mapped application crashes favor Sentry. Product boundaries beat feature-count tables.

Finally, test failure, not just success: stop the scheduler without stopping the web process. The app endpoint should remain green, cohort timestamps should stop advancing, and the heartbeat service should mark the run late. If the dashboard calls that state healthy, the design cannot reconstruct the incident you actually care about.

Further reading

If this boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's Node cron heartbeat guide and validate the live schema before constructing the report body.

  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Better Uptime heartbeat documentation
  • Datadog custom metrics documentation
  • Sentry source maps documentation
  • Martin Fowler, "Feature Toggles"

title: Release notes from commits: AI lists what users never see
description:
Claude Sonnet turned 23 sets of commits into release notes. Asked plainly, it listed internal work and invented a link host; with written rules it never did.

Not reliably. When it misses, it says more than the commits justify: it keeps work that no user will ever notice, and it supplies details nobody gave it. We gave Claude Sonnet 23 sets of commits and asked for release notes. With nothing but the request, 15 of the 23 entries were right. With a written rule set loaded, all 23 were. Six of its eight plain-request misses were entries about internal work, and in another it made up the host for a compare link. Claude Haiku went from 13 to 22.
