title: GitHub App least privilege for SaaS repo creation and access
description:
A SaaS product may need to create a customer repository during onboarding, or add an existing repository to an already installed GitHub App. Those are legitimate product workflows, but asking a customer for a broad organization personal access token can make the integration difficult to approve and hard to constrain.

GitHub announced two fine-grained permissions for both GitHub Apps and fine-grained personal access tokens: repository_creation:write for creating a repository in the account where the app or token has access, and installation_repositories:write for adding or removing repositories from an installation. GitHub says repository creation no longer needs the broader repository_administration:write, which can also allow deletion and transfer. The announcement is the GitHub App least-privilege update.

For a SaaS builder, the practical change is to match each operation to the smallest permission and approval path it needs. Separate “make a new repo” from “manage which repos an installation can access.” Then explain the remaining organization approval requirements plainly. Narrower permissions reduce unnecessary access; they do not remove GitHub’s installation or organization controls.

Start with the customer action

Write down the operation in customer language before selecting permissions. “Connect GitHub” is too broad to guide a request. Ask whether the user wants to create a new repository, attach an existing repository to an installed app, or both.

For repository creation, the app needs the new repository_creation:write permission. GitHub also makes the new permission available to fine-grained personal access tokens, though a SaaS integration should use the credential model appropriate to its product and customer workflow. GitHub’s announcement says this permission can create a repository in an account where the app or token is granted access. It also explains that the new permission avoids requesting repository_administration:write just to create a repository. That distinction matters: a create-only workflow should not imply that your product needs permissions to delete or transfer repositories.

For an existing repository, use installation_repositories:write only when your workflow adds or removes repositories from an app installation. GitHub says those APIs previously required the broader repo scope for personal access tokens; the fine-grained permission now narrows that request for supported callers. This controls the set of repositories the installation can access; it is not a substitute for the separate permission to create a repository.

Some products need both operations. Request both only if the customer-facing workflow actually offers both. A user who only connects an existing repository should not be pushed through a request for repository creation.

Keep the permission request understandable

Permission review is part of onboarding. Tell the customer what the app will do, when it will do it, and which repositories are in scope. If you need repository creation, say that clearly. If you need to update an installation’s repository selection, explain that separately.

The new permission names make a narrower request possible, but they do not make approval automatic. GitHub notes that organization-level permissions, repository-administration permissions, and repository-creation permissions require organization-owner approval. Plan for that approval in the product flow. Do not describe a repository administrator as able to approve every request, or imply that a customer can avoid an organization owner when GitHub requires one.

Also keep app installation distinct from selecting repositories. An organization must install the GitHub App before it can operate through that installation. The announcement says that when an app is already installed at the organization level, repository administrators can add it to a repository without a new organization-owner approval. That is useful for the existing-installation path, but it does not eliminate the initial organization-level installation decision.

Build two explicit workflows

A reliable integration can present two choices instead of one vague “connect” button.

One repository is created after the organization-owner approval checkpoint. Conceptual illustration; no product UI is shown.

Create a repository. Explain the name and purpose that will be used, request the relevant repository-creation permission, and tell the user if an organization owner must approve it. After GitHub returns the created repository, show its name and link and let the user continue setup. Keep the operation idempotent: if the browser retries after a timeout, check whether the intended repository was created before trying to create another one.

Add an existing repository. First establish that the app is installed for the organization. Then let an authorized user choose the specific repository and use the installation-repository permission to add it to the installation. Confirm the selected repository in the UI. Avoid presenting access to every organization repository as the default when the customer is choosing one.

One selected repository is added to an already installed app; the other repositories remain outside its scope.

If the same product supports both, make the choice visible before the permission screen. A user should understand why the app asks for a permission, and what happens if their organization requires an owner to approve it.

Design for approval and failure

Permission scoping does not replace operational safeguards. Use a clear audit trail for who initiated the action, the customer account, the repository, the requested operation, and the outcome. Keep enough context to diagnose a denied request or a retry without storing credentials in logs.

Handle approval states as normal product states. If an organization owner needs to approve a permission, explain what the user can do next and preserve their setup progress. If the app is installed but a selected repository is not part of its installation, guide the user to the repository-access step rather than returning a generic failure.

Test at least four cases before launch: a personal account that can grant the requested access; an organization where an owner must approve; an app already installed with a repository that is not yet selected; and a repeated request after a network timeout. Verify that the product asks only for the permission needed by each path and that it does not silently broaden access after a denial.

For related GitHub integration risk, see our guide to protecting repositories from leaked keys. Keep those concerns distinct: secret scanning protects credentials committed to source; least-privilege app permissions control what your integration can do.

Check the boundary before launch

Review the permission list against product actions whenever you add a GitHub workflow. A useful review question is: if this permission were denied, which exact button or automated step would stop working? If the answer is “nothing,” remove the permission from the request. If several unrelated features depend on it, split those features into separate customer choices where possible.

For repository creation, verify that the app creates only the repository the customer asked for and records the resulting repository identity. For installation repository changes, verify that adding one repository does not expand access to all repositories. Test the denied and partially approved states, not only the successful path. Make the requested permissions visible in your setup copy so a customer can compare them with the workflow they initiated.

This review also helps support teams answer “why does the app need this?” with a concrete explanation. Tie each permission to a named action, show the relevant approval status, and avoid implying that a successful app installation means every repository is already accessible.

What this means for a small SaaS

The improvement is most useful when your product automates customer setup or provisions a repository as part of a project workflow. A narrow create permission can make that request easier to explain than a broad administration permission. A separate installation-repository permission can support a deliberate “choose the repositories” step.

Neither permission means your app has access without a customer granting it, nor does it bypass organization-owner approval where GitHub requires approval. Keep the product copy precise, request only the operations you ship, and provide an escape route when the customer cannot approve the request themselves.

The SaaS Dashboard kit can serve as an optional UI and authentication starting point for a custom review flow. It does not include a GitHub App integration; the permission request, GitHub API work, and approval handling remain implementation work for your team.

Sources

  • GitHub Changelog: GitHub App improvements for least privilege and management (October 13, 2026)

title: I Filled sqlite_stat1 and Six Query Plans Did Not Change
description:
This blog's articles are no longer served from files but from a single SQLite file: every deploy renders all the MDX into content.db, and the server opens it read-only. Today I asked that file a simple question — is the planner working with no statistics at all?

$ sqlite3 -readonly /opt/mustafaerbay/dist/content.db \
    "select coalesce((select group_concat(name) from sqlite_schema
       where name like 'sqlite_stat%'),'NO STAT TABLES');
     select count(*) from posts;"
NO STAT TABLES
2676

The answer is unambiguous: not a single statistics row in the live database. There is none in the repository either — the words ANALYZE, PRAGMA optimize and analysis_limit appear nowhere in the scripts, the deploy files or the application code. A 2,676-row, 58 MiB database has been telling SQLite's query planner "you figure it out" since the 29 June cutover, three and a half months now.

I did not fill those statistics in production — every measurement below ran on locally rebuilt copies of the same database, and the live file still has no stat tables as I write this. Filing that as a gap and adding ANALYZE to the pipeline would have taken ten minutes. But I wanted a measurement first, because "collect statistics and the planner decides better" is as true as it is empty: does any decision actually change in this schema, for these queries? An hour in the lab answers it: four statistics rows written, 80 histogram rows produced, and all six plans came back identical.

That is where the real subject begins. A "nothing changed" result counts as silence, not as a finding, until your measurement rig has proven it can see a change.

The rig: what was measured, and with what

I wrote nothing to the live database. Running node scripts/migrate-content.mjs in the repo rebuilt the same file locally — 2,676 rows (1,338 Turkish, 1,338 English) in 34.5 seconds, 60,690,432 bytes. Each phase got a fresh copy of that file, so the only difference between "before" and "after" was the ANALYZE statement.

The signal is the plan, not the clock: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. There is a measured reason for that choice near the end of this article, but briefly: on a 2,676-row table, wall time reports the mood of the page cache more than the shape of the plan.

The queries are not invented. The six read queries on the serving path came out of the code one by one: four in the data layer (src/lib/content-db.ts: the list, lookup by id, lookup by slug, category counts), one in the newsletter notifier (a date range), one in the search-index generator (a full scan). Five of them have a live caller; the category count does not — something this lab turned up, and I come back to it below. The write queries inside the migrate script that builds the database (a full scan to read source hashes, an UPDATE, a DELETE, batched INSERTs) are not in this set; they run at deploy time with no reader waiting on them. The whole schema is one table and three hand-written indexes:

CREATE INDEX idx_posts_lang_date ON posts(lang, publish_date DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_category  ON posts(category);
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_slug      ON posts(url_slug, lang);

There is a fourth, sqlite_autoindex_posts_1, created automatically by id TEXT PRIMARY KEY — a text primary key on a rowid table means a separate index, the small side discovery of this lab.

Plans without statistics: blind but lucky

On the fresh copy, the six plans came out like this:

Query Plan (no statistics)
List (lang + ORDER BY publish_date DESC) SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?)
Single row by id SEARCH posts USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_posts_1 (id=?)
slug + language SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_slug (url_slug=? AND lang=?)
Category counts (GROUP BY) SEARCH ... idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?) + USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY
Newsletter window (date range) SEARCH ... idx_posts_lang_date (lang=? AND publish_date>? AND publish_date<?)
Search index (WHERE draft = 0) SCAN posts

Five of the six picked the best of the indexes available. The sixth — the full scan — is also right, because draft = 0 selects every row and the columns it needs live in the table; there is nothing else to narrow.

Reading these lines is a small skill of its own, so a short detour. SCAN means the table is read end to end, SEARCH means SQLite dives in through an index, and the part in parentheses shows which conditions were handed to that index. USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY means "the index could not provide the ordering, so a temporary tree went up in memory" — wherever that line appears, there is work being done.

There is also an invisible word: COVERING. A slightly modified query on the same database shows it:

SELECT publish_date FROM posts WHERE lang='tr' ORDER BY publish_date DESC LIMIT 20
  → SEARCH posts USING COVERING INDEX idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?)

SELECT title FROM posts WHERE lang='tr' ORDER BY publish_date DESC LIMIT 20
  → SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?)

The only difference is the selected column. publish_date lives inside the index, so SQLite never touches the table; ask for title and every row costs one more hop into the table. My list query asks for 21 columns, which means 1,338 table lookups for 1,338 rows. Statistics do not change that cost — the column list does. The presence or absence of COVERING on a plan line is usually a far bigger deal than statistics.

And that table taught the main lesson: the planner needs statistics where it has to choose between two indexes. If an equality condition points at a single index, statistics only refine the cost estimate; they do not change the decision. In my schema lang, url_slug, id and category never compete with each other.

ANALYZE: one millisecond, 20 kibibytes, four rows 

ANALYZE duration : 1 ms
File             : 60,690,432 → 60,710,912 bytes (+20 KiB)
sqlite_stat1     : 4 rows
sqlite_stat4     : 80 rows

The cost debate ends right there. Thinking about whether one millisecond and 20 kibibytes are worth it takes longer than measuring them. What is interesting is not the cost but how readable the written rows are:

idx_posts_category        2676 669
idx_posts_lang_date       2676 1338 7
idx_posts_slug            2676 2 1
sqlite_autoindex_posts_1  2676 1

SQLite's file format documentation explains the list: the first integer is the approximate number of rows in the index, and the Nth integer is the average number of rows whose first N-1 columns match. So those four rows are the blog's own fact sheet:

  • 2676 2 1 — each url_slug maps to exactly two rows. Correct: every article has a Turkish and an English version, so all 1,338 slugs appear twice. The trailing 1 says the (url_slug, lang) pair is unique.
  • 2676 1338 7 — 1,338 rows per language, and an average of 7 rows sharing the same (lang, publish_date) pair. The seven is rounding at work: there are 430 distinct (language, date) pairs, 2,676 / 430 = 6.22, and SQLite rounds the average up. What pushes the average near six is April's bulk import: 17 April carries 31 articles in one language, 62 across both. Today's pace of three a day will drag that average down over the years.
  • 2676 669 — four categories, 669 rows per category on average. The real distribution is 940 / 784 / 536 / 416.

The histogram table's distribution teaches something too: of the 80 rows, 24 belong to idx_posts_lang_date, 24 to idx_posts_slug, 24 to the automatic primary key index, and only 8 to idx_posts_category. The documentation says an index typically gets 10 to 40 samples; the category index sits below that range because it only carries four distinct values — the sample count is bounded by the variety in the index.

This is why reading sqlite_stat1 is pleasant: there are no guesses in it, only counts. A table built for the planner hands you a summary of your corpus as a side effect.

And the plans? All six identical, line for line. The category count still builds its temporary B-tree, the list still uses the same index, the full scan is still a full scan. Repeating the comparison with statistics produced by PRAGMA optimize and by analysis_limit=100 gave the same answer: no difference.

"Is the rig broken?" — testing it with a deliberate positive

It would have been easy to stop here and publish "ANALYZE is unnecessary". But a measurement that shows nothing has two explanations: there is no effect, or the instrument is broken. The only way to separate them is to prove the instrument can see a known positive.

So a deliberately bad index went onto a copy of the same database. The draft column holds a single value (all 2,676 rows are draft = 0), so the index filters nothing at all:

CREATE INDEX idx_draft_test ON posts(draft);

Plans without statistics:

SELECT count(*) FROM posts WHERE draft = 0 AND lang = ?
  → SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_draft_test (draft=?)
SELECT id FROM posts WHERE draft = 0 AND category = ?
  → SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_draft_test (draft=?)

The planner walked into the trap. With no statistics, SQLite assumes every equality condition narrows the row set meaningfully; draft = 0 looked like a filter, so both queries bound themselves to a useless index. After ANALYZE:

sqlite_stat1: idx_draft_test  2676 2676
  → SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?)
  → SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_category (category=?)

The row 2676 2676 says "one value of this index returns 2,676 rows", and the planner abandoned it instantly, moving to two different correct indexes. The rig works. Which means the stillness across those six queries is a real finding.

The second check is built on one sentence from the documentation: statistics are loaded into memory when the schema is read, and manual changes to those tables are not noticed right away. Writing the unordered flag into sqlite_stat1 by hand tells the planner, in the documentation's words, to use that index neither for a range query nor for sorting:

UPDATE sqlite_stat1 SET stat = '2676 1338 7 unordered'
 WHERE idx = 'idx_posts_lang_date';

On the same connection, the plan did not move a muscle. After ANALYZE sqlite_schema forced a reread, the sorting cost surfaced:

SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?) | USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY

A freshly opened connection gave the same plan. So the documented "loaded when the schema is read" line is a concrete trap for any script that writes statistics and then expects the effect in the same process: the statistics you just wrote will not change that connection's plans.

PRAGMA optimize: the 2000 that is not in the docs

The modern advice is not ANALYZE but PRAGMA optimize: short-lived connections should run it just before closing, long-lived ones should run PRAGMA optimize=0x10002 on open and then repeat it periodically. Neither works in my pipeline, because the application opens the database read-only:

PRAGMA optimize    → SqliteError: attempt to write a readonly database
PRAGMA optimize(-1) → ANALYZE "main"."posts"

The dry run (-1) works even on a read-only connection and reports what it would do — a useful split for diagnosis: I can read the recommendation, I just cannot apply it. The recommendation is not an accident either; the documentation requires five conditions to hold before a table is analyzed, and what opens the gate here is that indexes have no sqlite_stat1 entry at all. Once the statistics are in place that gate closes and the dry run comes back empty.

More interesting is that the statistics PRAGMA optimize produces are not the same as a full ANALYZE:

Index Full ANALYZE PRAGMA optimize
idx_posts_category 2676 669 2676 501
idx_posts_lang_date 2676 1338 7 2676 1001 6
sqlite_stat4 rows 80 0

Why did the numbers get coarser? The documentation says that since 3.46.0 PRAGMA optimize sets its own temporary scan limit, but it does not say what that limit is. Setting limits by hand and matching the output pins it down: the four rows produced by analysis_limit=2000 are byte-for-byte what PRAGMA optimize writes, and three separate fresh copies gave the same result. The source agrees — the SQLITE_DEFAULT_OPTIMIZE_LIMIT macro is 2000, and the comment beside it explains the choice: it was picked empirically so that the worst case on a Raspberry Pi 4 stays under 100 milliseconds. The same comment adds that an analysis limit of 2000 is almost always enough for the planner to characterise an index fully. The limit is scaled down further when a schema holds more than 100 b-trees; mine has one table and four indexes, far below a hundred, so the full 2000 applied.

Which matches my own finding: the numbers got coarser, the decision did not change.

There is a quiet side effect too. Whenever analysis_limit is non-zero, sqlite_stat4 is never computed. Trying 100, 500, 1000, 2000, 2676 and 5000 gave zero histogram rows in all six cases. Only the default limit (analysis_limit = 0, meaning a full scan) produced the 80 rows. Histograms are what help with LIKE prefixes and skewed distributions, so whoever sets a limit "to keep it fast" is quietly switching off the most detailed statistics available.

Going stale: nobody tells you

Writing statistics once and relaxing is tempting, so the next thing on the bench was how long that lasts. After ANALYZE, adding 60 rows left PRAGMA optimize(-1) with nothing to propose. Pushing the row count to 26,736 — 9.99 times 2,676 — produced the recommendation:

2,736 rows  → PRAGMA optimize(-1) → (empty)
26,736 rows → PRAGMA optimize(-1) → ANALYZE "main"."posts"
sqlite_stat1 → still "2676 1338 7"

The documented condition is explicit: a table is re-analyzed if an index is missing its sqlite_stat1 entry, or if the row count has changed tenfold since the last ANALYZE. That tenfold is not exactly ten. Scanning the threshold by adding rows: at 25,422 and 25,449 rows (9.50 and 9.51 times) no recommendation came; at 25,690 (9.60 times) it did. The reason sits in the source — the comparison runs through const LogEst iRange = 33; /* 10x size change */, and a LogEst is one tenth of a base-2 logarithm, so 33 means 2^3.3 ≈ 9.85 times, on top of a table size that is itself a rounded estimate. In practice the gate opens around nine and a half. A blog that publishes three articles a day takes years to get there. In my pipeline, PRAGMA optimize would be a watchman that does nothing ever again after its first round.

On top of that there is the pipeline's own behaviour. A deploy does not rebuild content.db from scratch; it takes the previous file as a baseline and re-renders only the changed MDX. The statistics travel along with that baseline copy — measured: handing an analyzed file in as the baseline, the new database inherited all four sqlite_stat1 rows and all 80 sqlite_stat4 rows without re-rendering a single article. So once ANALYZE runs, those statistics ride from deploy to deploy for months, and nothing attaches a note saying "measured when this table held 2,676 rows".

The SQLite documentation has a recipe for exactly this, and it fits my pipeline surprisingly well: applications that want stable plans should run ANALYZE during development, save the contents of sqlite_stat1 as a script, replay it into deployed copies, and not run a full ANALYZE or PRAGMA optimize inside the application. My database is a build artefact — regenerated on every deploy, then mounted read-only. "Measure in development, replay on deployment" is precisely what the migrate script does.

Why timing misleads here

Here is the measured reason for picking the plan as the signal. Running the six queries 31 times each against the unanalyzed and the fully analyzed copies, comparing medians, the first run said:

Q6 search (2,676 rows)  no statistics 1.243 ms   ANALYZE 0.774 ms

A 38 percent "improvement" — with identical plans. Running the same script again immediately:

Q6 search (2,676 rows)  no statistics 0.750 ms   ANALYZE 0.747 ms

The difference evaporated. What the first run captured was a freshly copied file entering the page cache for the first time, which is by definition not reproducible. For the other five queries the noise is larger than any effect: the list query sits at roughly 5 ms on both sides (a separate run put the medians at 5.4 and 5.6 ms, with individual samples wandering between 4.9 and 7.7), and the single-row lookups are in the microsecond band.

The rule I take from this: if you can measure a timing difference from an intervention that did not change the plan, the thing you measured is not the intervention. The EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output, by contrast, is reproducible — the same statistics always yield the same lines. The run where I measured this blog's WAL file carried a similar distinction: what the counters count and what you are curious about are not obliged to be the same thing.

The real gap the measurement exposed

Going hunting for statistics and coming back empty-handed had a pleasant side effect: reading the plans line by line exposed a schema gap. The category count query filters on lang and groups by category, and there is no index holding both, which is why every call builds a temporary B-tree. Trying it:

CREATE INDEX idx_lang_cat ON posts(lang, category);

before     : SEARCH ... idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?) | USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY
after index: SEARCH ... idx_lang_cat (lang=?)
median     : 0.331 ms → 0.204 ms

The temporary tree is gone and the median of 31 runs drops from 0.33 milliseconds to 0.20. The new index's sqlite_stat1 row reads 2676 1338 335 — 1,338 rows per language, 335 per language-category pair. Before and after ANALYZE the plan was the same again; the gain comes from the index, not from statistics.

So will the index go in? No — and the reason is more embarrassing than the measurement. Looking for the query's caller turned up nothing: category counts on the pages are computed in JavaScript over the cached article list rather than in SQL — getAllCategories is called from seven places across both languages, from the footer and the home page to the blog listing and the category pages. The GROUP BY query sitting in the data layer is dead code right now. Adding an index would have sped up a query nobody calls.

That may be the most practical lesson of this run: before deciding to improve a query's plan, verify that the query is called at all. The gain was computed as 130 microseconds per call, and 130 microseconds multiplied by zero calls is zero. The price would have been one more index written for 2,676 rows on every deploy. It stays as a note: if the count ever moves back to the SQL path, this line is where to look first.

One more detail: the new plan has no COVERING, because draft = 0 sits outside the index and every row still needs a table hop. A three-column index would have closed that too — at the cost of writing three columns for the gain measured here.

Which binary runs ANALYZE, and what it writes

A last detail that can bite in mixed-binary environments. The application uses the SQLite embedded in better-sqlite3; the version installed locally is 3.53.0, compiled with ENABLE_STAT4. macOS ships its own sqlite3 at 3.51.0, built without ENABLE_STAT4. Running both against the same file:

  • ANALYZE with the Apple binary: the same four sqlite_stat1 rows, and no sqlite_stat4 table at all.
  • ANALYZE with better-sqlite3 first (80 histogram rows), then with the Apple binary: the histogram rows are cleared, not left stale.

The second result is a relief, because stale histograms lying around was the scenario I feared. They do not linger; a build without STAT4 support empties the table. The server's sqlite3 is 3.45.1 — older than 3.46, so a hand-run PRAGMA optimize there would not set its own temporary limit. Nothing is at risk today: nobody invokes that shell for maintenance, and the serving process uses the SQLite embedded in better-sqlite3. Still, knowing which binary performs your maintenance is the same thing as knowing what the maintenance does.

Trying the line I recommend

Saying "I will put an ANALYZE at the end of migrate" is easy; whether that line gets along with the rest of the pipeline is a separate question. When the migrate script finishes writing it calls wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) and switches the journal mode to DELETE, and the file is then mounted read-only. Imitating that exact order — ANALYZE → checkpoint → journal_mode = DELETE → open read-only:

journal_mode         : delete
sqlite_stat1         : 4 rows
sqlite_stat4         : 80 rows
plan (list query)    : SEARCH posts USING INDEX idx_posts_lang_date (lang=?)

The statistics survive the journal switch and are read on a read-only open. The placement is settled too: before the checkpoint, otherwise the analysis writes land in the journal and have to be moved afterwards.

The cost claim deserves more than one data point as well. One millisecond is the price for a 2,676-row table. On the 25,690-row copy left over from the staleness experiment, the same ANALYZE took 25.1 ms — ten times the rows, twenty-five times the duration. Building histograms means a full scan, and the bill grows faster than linearly; at hundreds of thousands of rows the "run it on every build" advice needs re-measuring, while at my scale it is not worth a debate.

One more fear went onto the bench. Since the incremental pipeline copies a baseline, does a dropped index leave its statistics row haunting the file? Creating a temporary index, analyzing, then issuing DROP INDEX: the sqlite_stat1 row left with the index. SQLite does that cleanup itself; what goes stale is the content of the rows, not their existence.

Which suggests a monitoring rule: after migrate finishes, check that the sqlite_stat1 row count equals the index count. There is no other way to notice an ANALYZE that quietly did not run — no plan changes, so nothing gets slower, your insurance is simply cancelled.

If you want to repeat it: a ten-line rig

SQLite's own shell is enough to repeat this measurement on your database. Leave the live file alone and work on copies:

cp app.db /tmp/before.db && cp app.db /tmp/after.db

# 1) are there any statistics
sqlite3 /tmp/before.db \
  "select coalesce((select group_concat(name) from sqlite_schema
     where name like 'sqlite_stat%'),'NONE');"

# 2) let the planner say what it would do (without touching the app)
sqlite3 -readonly /tmp/before.db "pragma optimize(-1);"

# 3) capture the unanalyzed plan into a file
sqlite3 /tmp/before.db ".eqp on" "select ... ;" > /tmp/plan-before.txt

# 4) analyze, capture the same query again
sqlite3 /tmp/after.db "ANALYZE; select idx||' = '||stat from sqlite_stat1;"
sqlite3 /tmp/after.db ".eqp on" "select ... ;" > /tmp/plan-after.txt

# 5) decision: an empty diff means statistics change no decision here
diff /tmp/plan-before.txt /tmp/plan-after.txt

Keeping the plan output from .eqp on in a file in the repository has a second benefit: when the schema or a query changes, diff tells you the plan changed too. The plan lines from this run are now noted for comparison at the next schema change; wiring the same diff into continuous integration amounts to the same thing. Cases where adding an index quietly breaks a plan — a query losing its covering index, for instance — are only caught this way.

A decision framework

For anyone about to look at their own setup, in order:

  1. Check whether they exist at all. select name from sqlite_schema where name like 'sqlite_stat%' — if that is empty, the planner has been working from its own assumptions rather than your measurements.
  2. Record the plan rather than the clock. Pull the queries the application actually runs out of the code and write the EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output to a file. That file becomes your regression test later.
  3. Run ANALYZE, capture the plans again, diff them. If there is no difference, test the rig with a deliberate positive: index a single-valued column, watch the plan move, then drop the index.
  4. Work out where write access lives. PRAGMA optimize cannot run against a read-only database; put the statistics step into whatever builds the database.
  5. Re-run it on every build. When the cost is a millisecond, never having to ask "when did this go stale" is cheaper. In incremental pipelines that copy a baseline, statistics travel silently.
  6. Refresh statistics when the schema changes. A new index increases the number of candidates the planner weighs — and that is the one case where statistics genuinely change a decision. The documentation calls out CREATE INDEX specifically.
  7. Do not set a limit if you want histograms. With a skewed distribution, leave analysis_limit at zero, or sqlite_stat4 is never produced.
  8. Verify that it ran. After the build step, compare the sqlite_stat1 row count against the index count; an ANALYZE that was silently skipped trips no alarm.

What is going into my own pipeline is items 4 and 5 of that list: one ANALYZE line at the end of the migrate script, before the journal mode is switched. I know by measurement that it changes none of today's plans. It is there for tomorrow, when a non-selective index joins the schema — and the assumption that an index helps every query is one of the costlier assumptions around — so the planner has counts in hand.

Conclusion

What this lab taught is not really about SQLite. Collecting statistics is not a performance tweak but insurance against the planner: the premium is one millisecond, and the risk covered is the bad index your schema will acquire later. Cancelling the policy because "nothing changed" treats the absence of a claim as evidence that no claim will come.

The second lesson is about measuring. Output showing that nothing changed is the least exciting result to publish and the most reassuring one to own — provided you first proved your rig could see a change. I no longer believe a "no difference" sentence of my own unless there is a deliberate positive next to it.

Official Sources

  • SQLite — ANALYZE
  • SQLite — PRAGMA optimize and analysis_limit
  • SQLite — File format: sqlite_stat1 and sqlite_stat4
  • better-sqlite3

title: Your tokens are correct and dark mode still broke the screen
description:
The token file was clean. Two tiers, aliased, no copied values, reviewed by two people. Then somebody added a dark theme and 127 places on the screen did not move.

None of them looked wrong before that. That is the part worth sitting with. A value that was typed in and a value that resolved through a role are visually identical. The difference only exists in what happens next.

This is not a tooling problem. You can hit it with Style Dictionary, Tokens Studio, native Figma variables, plain CSS custom properties, or all four. It is a binding-tier problem, and it stays invisible until it is expensive.

The one rule that decides whether dark mode is a switch or a rebuild

Two tiers, each with one job.

Primitive holds raw values and no opinions. Colour ramps, spacing scale, type sizes, radii. It is the only file you edit to rebrand.

Semantic holds roles. What a value is for. This is the only tier with modes.

// 1-primitive.json: no opinions, no modes
{
  "color": {
    "brand": { "500": { "$value": "#6366F1", "$type": "color" } },
    "slate": { "900": { "$value": "#0F172A", "$type": "color" } }
  }
}

// 2-semantic.json: roles, and the only tier that knows about modes
{
  "color": {
    "action": {
      "primary": {
        "background": {
          "$value": "{color.brand.500}",
          "$type": "color",
          "$description": "Fill of the single primary action on a screen. Not for links, not for selected rows, not for status."
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Bind a button to color.brand.500 and dark mode has nothing to swap. It is a fixed value. It will stay that exact indigo on a dark surface whether or not anybody can read the label on it.

Bind it to color.action.primary.background and the swap happens underneath. The button follows for free, in both modes, forever.

That is the whole rule, and almost nobody disputes it. The reason it gets broken constantly is that reaching past a layer always works in the moment. The screen looks right. The rule only earns its keep later, when a value has to mean something different in a different context and there is nothing in the file that knows the difference between this blue and the colour a primary action uses.

An alias tier that mirrors primitives 1:1 is two names and one decision

Here is the version that passes review and still breaks.

// This looks like two tiers. It is one.
"color.surface.raised": { "$value": "{color.slate.50}" },
"color.surface.default": { "$value": "{color.white}" },
"color.surface.sunken": { "$value": "{color.slate.100}" }

Three roles, three primitives, one-to-one, forever. Nothing is wrong on the page. But a tier only earns its place when it can refuse something. If every semantic name maps to exactly one primitive and no role ever absorbs a decision, you have two files and one decision, and the second file is a rename.

The test I use: can this role say no? color.surface.raised has to be able to refuse a case that color.surface.default takes. If it cannot, nothing stops a component reaching past it to the raw value for convenience, because the role is not carrying any information the primitive did not already carry.

And when a layout genuinely needs a value the scale lacks, the answer is to add the semantic role, then point at it, not to let one component resolve straight to a primitive. A component reaching past semantic for convenience is how a token set quietly loses the ability to change anything centrally.

The pairs nobody listed

Now the half that bites hardest, because it survives every check.

Contrast is a property of a pair. Your token file holds colours, one at a time. So the pairs get measured from a list somebody wrote down, and building the screen invents pairs that were never on it.

  • A label on a tinted chip
  • An initial on an avatar ground
  • A caption on the far end of a gradient
  • White on a status fill

If your built list is the same length as your planned list, it was copied rather than enumerated.

Three specific failures worth naming, because each one passes with both tokens individually correct:

1. The worst ground is the one nearest the text colour, not the darkest one. Dark text is hardest on the darkest stop. Light text is hardest on the lightest. A table that measures both modes against the same background has measured one of them not at all.

2. Text on a status fill flips with the mode. Your amber gets lighter in dark mode, white on it drops under 3.0, and nothing in the token file says so because both values are fine on their own. A colour used as a fill and the same colour used as text are two different roles, even at the same hex: the fill is measured against what sits on it, the text against every ground it can land on.

3. A translucent surface makes the text's background a computation. The colour actually behind the text is in no token file and changes as the page scrolls.

/* The real background here is a composite, not a token */
.card {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.72);
}

Composite the fill over the worst ground stop and measure that. And note the consequence: a translucent surface is only valid over the ground it was measured against. Move the same card so it overlaps a hero image or another card, and the percentage showing through is no longer the canvas, and its overlapping strip goes muddy while every number still checks out.

Opacity is not how text gets de-emphasised

This one is short and it is the most common.

/* measured 5.2, renders 2.8 */
.caption { color: var(--color-content-primary); opacity: 0.55; }

/* measure this instead */
.caption { color: var(--color-content-secondary); }

The compositor applies opacity after the measurement. So the number in your audit is right and the pixels on the screen are not. Opacity is legal on a surface, measured through. It stays illegal on text.

The half a token set cannot hold

A token set holds colour, spacing, radius, type size, elevation. That is a real and useful floor.

It cannot hold:

  • what leads the screen
  • the size contrast between the largest block and the smallest type
  • how much of the screen is empty
  • how many distinct block shapes there are

So token wins every conflict has a consequence nobody intends: what a token can express gets decided, and what it cannot express nobody decides at all. The screen reads as basic while every value is correct.

A locked type scale is the clearest case. It gives you correct sizes. It is not a hierarchy. Every value on the page can be right while the largest type sits in the middle of it, which leaves the screen with no head and makes every local fix break something else.

The cheap fix is a ladder per screen, head down to caption, stepping down once at each level. Ten lines before any markup. It turns hierarchy into something a screen can fail, rather than something you eyeball.

Make the rules mechanical, or they get forgotten silently

Every rule in here has the same shape: it can be satisfied at magnitude zero unless something fails without it.

Two checks that cost almost nothing:

The toggle is a test, not a convenience. Build one mode and reach the other with a toggle in the file. One click forces every colour through a semantic variable, so a value that fails to change is a hard-coded defect, and you fix it in the tokens, never on the screen. Building both modes by hand doubles the work, lets the two drift, and hides exactly what the toggle would have exposed.

Give every token a failing condition. One line per token saying what it must not be used for. Not usage guidance, an exclusion.

"$description": "Fill of the single primary action on a screen.
                 Not for links, not for selected rows, not for status."

A linter cannot check that sentence. A reviewer can, and it is the difference between a variable and a decision. A rule with no failing condition cannot be broken, so nobody notices when it is used in the wrong place, and consistency in the wrong role is the expensive failure, because it is the quiet one.

There is a side effect I did not expect when we started doing this. A request that cannot be refused by any existing rule is almost always a genuine gap. So the exclusions end up working as an intake filter too: either a new case falls inside a stated boundary, or it names something nobody has ruled on yet, which is the honest version of a new decision.

What this does not solve

A closed, exclusion-carrying token set stops invention. It says nothing about whether the set is any good. Constrain a team, or an agent, to a badly designed system and you get consistent, coherent, thoroughly wrong output, delivered fast.

And it is work. Every genuinely new requirement now needs a decision instead of an improvisation. That is the point, and on a small project it can cost more than the drift would have.

The set I use, free

The two-tier set this is written from is public: 698 tokens, W3C DTCG format with alias syntax, Light and Dark already paired on every mode-aware role, plus a Figma plugin that imports both as Variables in dependency order. Free for commercial work, no attribution. It also feeds Style Dictionary and Tokens Studio, since the format is standard.

Free 2-tier design tokens + Figma Variables import plugin

If you import it, I am curious which semantic role you had to add first. That answer usually says more about a product than its brief does.

And if you have ever run the dark-mode toggle on a build you thought was clean, I would like to know what your number was. Mine was 127, and I did not see it coming.

title: LocalStorage in JavaScript for Beginners 💾
description:
When I started learning JavaScript, I learned how to store data in variables. But I had one question: What happens to the data when we refresh the webpage?

Normally, data stored only in variables is lost when the page reloads. That's where localStorage becomes useful!

What is LocalStorage?

localStorage is a browser feature that allows us to store data in the user's browser.

The best part? The data stays saved even after refreshing or closing the browser, until it is removed by the user or the application.

  1. Store Data Using setItem()

We can save data using localStorage.setItem().

localStorage.setItem("name", "Narasimma");

Here:

"name" is the key.

"Narasimma" is the value.

  1. Get Data Using getItem()

We can retrieve the saved data using getItem().

let name = localStorage.getItem("name");

console.log(name);

Output:

Narasimma

  1. Remove Data Using removeItem()

Want to remove a particular item?

localStorage.removeItem("name");

This removes the data stored with the key "name".

  1. Clear All Data Using clear()

localStorage.clear();

This removes all entries from the website's local storage. Use it carefully!

  1. Store Objects and Arrays

One important thing to remember is that localStorage stores values as strings.

To store an object or array, we can use JSON.stringify().

let student = {
  name: "Arun",
  age: 21
};

localStorage.setItem("student", JSON.stringify(student));

To retrieve the object, use JSON.parse().

let data = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("student"));

console.log(data.name);

Output:

Arun

Where Can We Use LocalStorage?

Saving a user's theme preference

Remembering form data

Storing shopping cart information

Saving simple application settings

Building small projects without a backend

title: Matching the Same Esports Match Across 27 Bookmakers: Entity Resolution in Go
description:
An arbitrage scanner is only as good as its answer to a boring question: are these two listings the same match? Our scanner reads esports odds from 27 books — sportsbooks, crypto sportsbooks, Polymarket and Kalshi. The same CS2 match shows up with different team spellings, different IDs, different tournament names and start times that disagree by minutes. Get the match wrong in one direction and you miss arbs. Get it wrong in the other and you show an "arb" between two different matches — and someone bets real money on it. A false merge is worse than a split, and most of the design follows from that.

The pipeline is a pure function

Every tick, the resolver hands the matcher the full current snapshot of all books and gets back a world of clusters plus proposals for a human. The matcher does no I/O, reads no database, and does not look at the clock. The same input always produces the same world.

That was not always true. The previous core kept a long-lived index in Postgres, mutated it during the cycle and minted IDs into it, so the result depended on event order and on what had already been written. Recomputing the world from scratch every tick turned out to be cheaper to reason about and fast enough: the whole working set is in memory anyway.

The stages: normalize names → resolve discipline → apply identity rules → group into time slots → find splits by anchor → decide → merge for this tick only.

1. Normalize names, but not too much

Team names go through Unicode NFKD, combining marks are stripped, full case-folding is applied, punctuation becomes spaces, and whitespace is collapsed. Then a small set of organisation tokens that do not identify a roster is removed — esports, esport, gaming, team, club — so "PaiN" and "PaiN Gaming" meet. Duo-team connectors ("A x B" vs "A & B") are dropped, and different conventions for women's rosters are mapped to one marker.

Just as important is what is not removed: academy, junior and digits stay, because they mean a different team. Normalization is cached, with the cache reset when it overflows — keys come from third-party feeds, and one broken feed can stream unique strings forever. One small performance lesson: creating a Unicode case-folder per call cost 1.47 s in a resolver profile; pooling them removed it.

2. Time slots anchored to the first event

Within a pair of normalized names, events are cut into time slots with a 90-minute window. The slot boundary is measured from the slot's anchor, not chained from event to event; otherwise events an hour apart would chain into one slot of unbounded width.

Live events get a directional tolerance of six hours backwards, because some books report a live match without an honest start time. That tolerance created a subtle bug: with "first slot that fits", the live leg of game two landed in game one's slot, and the cluster combined prematch odds from one game with live odds from another. The fix is to choose the nearest compatible slot, which also means the normal window always beats the tolerance.

3. Find splits by a shared opponent, not by similar names

String similarity fails in both directions. "NAVI" vs "Natus Vincere" is 18% similar and obviously the same team. "Evil Geniuses" vs "Evil Geniuses GC" is 81% similar and a different roster.

So the matcher first looks for evidence that does not depend on spelling: two groups with a common opponent, the same discipline and close start times, but different names on the other side. That is almost certainly one match listed two ways. Each group is registered under both of its canonical keys in an inverted index, so finding candidates is two hash lookups — a team plays one or two matches at a time. The previous implementation scanned the whole index on every miss, every tick.

Two rules keep the anchor honest:

  • Placeholders are never anchors. "TBD" and "Bye" appear in every unfilled bracket slot; letting them in made the candidate check quadratic and proved nothing.
  • If one book shows both sides, they are two events (games of a series), not a split.

4. Similarity only decides how fast to merge

Once an anchor says "probably the same match", similarity decides whether to merge now or ask a human. It is deliberately conservative:

  • an initialism matches only if one name's token equals the initials of all tokens of the other ("ic" does not match "inner circle academy");
  • both names must be at least 5 characters;
  • a differing token from a block list — academy, junior, youth, women, colour markers like blue/white — means a different team;
  • a one-sided addition (all tokens of one name contained in the other, like "gc") is vetoed;
  • a diff made only of organisation suffixes is fine;
  • otherwise, normalized Levenshtein similarity of at least 0.7.

5. Let automation write rules — with guardrails

Merges from a single tick are ephemeral. The durable truth about team identity is one rules file with exactly one writer, the resolver. Humans add rules through bot buttons; automation may also add one, but only with strong evidence that does not depend on spelling:

  • starts within 5 minutes — on a sample of 185 multi-book clusters, 90% of real matches started within five minutes of each other across books and 53% in the same minute, while repeated games of the same pairing are about a quarter of an hour apart;
  • the books agree on a meaningful tournament token;
  • at least two independent feed groups on each side (mirrors of one vendor's line do not count twice);
  • at most 20 automatic writes per hour, and a human "never" is an absolute veto.

The one-sided-addition veto exists because of an incident: two names, one being the other plus a regional suffix, were merged and split back and forth, rewriting the file 86 times per second. With the veto, that pair is never auto-merged; and structurally, after a real merge both sides normalize to the same key, so there is nothing left to flip.

6. Decide on the outcome, not on the intention

One last lesson cost us a silent failure. The matcher used to suppress the "please confirm this merge" question whenever it decided an automatic merge would happen. But between that decision and the file on disk sit the hourly limit, the human veto and the write itself — any of them can refuse. When one did, nobody got a question or a summary, and the split stayed invisible. Now the proposal is always created, and it is suppressed only after the write is confirmed.

What it powers

The matched world feeds a server-side arb engine that recomputes every market each cycle, with exchange fees applied per market. Per-book and per-pair statistics from the result are public and update daily: bookmakers, pairs. Why mirrors of one vendor are kept apart: feed groups. The exchange side of the pipeline is in our earlier post on streaming Polymarket and Kalshi order books.

Dozor is an esports arbitrage scanner covering 25 sportsbooks plus Polymarket and Kalshi. It is an information tool, not a bookmaker. 18+.

title: I stopped diffing my Go structs against the schema by hand. Now CI does it.
description:
A while ago I wrote about a column that changed type 8 days after I mapped it. int NOT NULL became decimal(19,2) NULL, my hand-written struct still said int64, and nothing complained. The fix back then was to point a code generator at the live database and diff its output against what I had.

That worked. It also had a weak spot I didn't want to admit: I had to remember to run it. The generator lived in an IDE plug-in and talked to the database over JDBC. Great on my machine, useless in a pipeline. A check that depends on a human remembering it is a check that runs on good days.

So I rewrote the generator in Go.

One binary, no JVM 

go install github.com/panedrone/go-sdm/cmd/sdm@latest

It's called go-sdm. One static binary, no runtime dependencies, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite. Same idea as before: an XML manifest says what to generate, the live database says what it actually looks like, and the generator writes the models and DAO in Go.

The part that matters for this story is one command:

sdm val

It generates everything in memory, compares it with the files in the repo, and exits 1 if anything differs:

out of date: internal/dbal/models/asset.go

That's the whole trick. If someone runs a migration and nobody regenerates, the build goes red. Not three weeks later as "why is this value off by a few cents" — on the next push.

# GitHub Actions, roughly
- run: go install github.com/panedrone/go-sdm/cmd/sdm@latest
- run: sdm val
  env:
    SDM_PWD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}

The honest caveat: sdm val needs a database to read. I don't parse DDL, on purpose — the database knows things the DDL doesn't show: views, the real column types of a query's result set, procedure parameters, ref-cursors. So CI needs a reachable database with the current schema: a staging one, or a container you migrate right before the check.

Starting from an existing database

The first post was about a DB-first rewrite: eighteen tables already there, nobody planning to redesign them. Writing the manifest by hand for that is exactly the kind of busywork that makes people skip the whole idea. So:

sdm xml -orm sqlx > start.xml

reads every table and view and prints a starting manifest: a model per table and a DAO per table, named after it, with CRUD and the lookups by foreign key already in place:

<dto-class name="sqlx-Task" ref="tasks"/>

<dao-class name="TasksDao">
    <crud dto="sqlx-Task" table="tasks"/>
    <query-dto-list dto="sqlx-Task" method="getTasksByGroup(gID)" ref="tasks(g_id)"/>
</dao-class>

Run it again after a new table appears and it prints only the new one — whatever is already in the manifest is skipped. -orm picks plain database/sql, sqlx or gorm for the models, and it's required on purpose: I'd rather type six characters than find out later that a default chose for me.

This week I pointed it at a Postgres database with 21 tables: one command for the manifest, one sdm gen, and the data layer compiled. Most of the time went into reading the output.

DAO as variables, not structs

One more thing I changed compared to the usual generated DAO. There's no repository struct to construct and pass around, and no interface to mock. Each DAO function is a package-level variable:

var GetTestRating = func(ctx context.Context, tID int32) (res float64, err error) { ... }

A unit test swaps the one it needs and puts it back:

saved := dbal.GetTestRating
dbal.GetTestRating = func(ctx context.Context, tID int32) (float64, error) { return 4.5, nil }
t.Cleanup(func() { dbal.GetTestRating = saved })

No mocking library, no database in unit tests. The database shows up exactly once — in sdm val, which is the one place where it's supposed to be the source of truth.

The point, again

Last time the conclusion was: stop hand-maintaining the mapping between a table and a struct, regenerate it from the table. This time it's the second half of that sentence: and make the build fail when you forget. A generator you have to remember to run is just a nicer way to hand-maintain things.

go-sdm is here: github.com/panedrone/go-sdm. A working example with a generated data layer: sdm_todolist_go_react_vue_npm_sqlite3.

title: I Gave My Coding Agent a Server of Its Own. Here's How to Do It Safely.
description:
My coding agent writes the app, writes the tests, and fixes the bug I missed. Then it stops and hands me a list of deploy commands. The most capable collaborator I've ever had turns into an intern who isn't allowed near production. Why is the last mile still mine?

In this post, I'll walk through agentic-hosting, an open-source tool that turns a server you own into a place your AI agent can safely ship apps to on its own. By the end, you'll be able to set it up, let an agent deploy an app and add a database, and drive the whole loop from your agent with simple commands.

⭐ agentic-hosting is open source — star it on GitHub: https://github.com/dennisonbertram/agentic-hosting

🤖 Give this to your agent: point it at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dennisonbertram/agentic-hosting/main/llms.txt and it can set everything up for you.

I don't think the problem is that agents can't be trusted. It's that hosting was built for humans clicking through dashboards. So when an agent shows up, we give it nothing or everything: no access, or root.

agentic-hosting is a third option. It's a self-hosted PaaS (platform-as-a-service, like a Heroku you run yourself) whose main user is an agent talking to a REST API. There's a dashboard, but it's for you to look over the agent's shoulder.

The idea: a small, safe set of verbs

The README's design principles read like a philosophy of delegation:

  1. Agentic-first. Agents call the API directly.
  2. One happy path per primitive. One build system (Nixpacks, which turns source code into a container image with no config), one router (Traefik, a reverse proxy), one engine per database type (Postgres, Redis).
  3. Multi-tenant. Each agent or team is a tenant, with its own API key, its own resources, and its own rate limits.
  4. Secure by default. Every container runs under gVisor, a sandbox that intercepts system calls before they reach the host kernel. Root filesystems are read-only, Linux capabilities are dropped, privilege escalation is blocked, and secrets are encrypted with AES-256-GCM.

The second principle is my favorite. For humans, choice is a feature. For agents, choice is surface area for mistakes. With one way to build, route, and provision, an agent can't get creative in ways you'll regret at 2 a.m. You're not building a platform for agents so much as a grammar.

Under the hood it's refreshingly boring: one Go binary, ah, runs as a systemd service on 127.0.0.1:8080. Traefik sits in front on ports 80/443, and two SQLite databases hold state and metering.

Setting it up

You need a Linux server (Ubuntu 22.04+ recommended). The README has the full script; here's the shape.

1. Install the pieces: Docker, gVisor's runsc, Go 1.25, and Nixpacks. Register gVisor as a Docker runtime:

cat > /etc/docker/daemon.json <<'JSON'
{
  "runtimes": { "runsc": { "path": "/usr/bin/runsc" } },
  "default-address-pools": [{"base":"172.20.0.0/14","size":24}]
}
JSON
systemctl restart docker

2. Start the infrastructure: a traefik-public network, Traefik (copy its docker run command from the README), and a local image registry bound to loopback:

docker network create --driver bridge traefik-public

docker run -d --name paas-registry --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 127.0.0.1:5000:5000 \
  -v /var/lib/ah/registry:/var/lib/registry \
  registry:2

3. Build ah and create its secrets:

git clone https://github.com/dennisonbertram/agentic-hosting /agentic-hosting
cd /agentic-hosting
CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -o bin/ah ./cmd/ah
cp bin/ah /usr/local/bin/ah

mkdir -p /var/lib/ah/builds /var/lib/ah/backups
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | xxd -p -c 64 > /var/lib/ah/master.key
chmod 600 /var/lib/ah/master.key

openssl rand -hex 32   # your bootstrap token

4. Run it: put the token in /etc/default/ah as AH_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN=..., install deploy/ah.service, and start it:

systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now ah
curl -H 'X-Forwarded-Proto: https' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/system/health
# → {"status":"ok"}

Just kicking the tires? Run locally in dev mode: ./bin/ah --dev --open-registration --port 8080.

Handing the keys to an agent

Now the fun part. Register a tenant — think of it as giving one agent its own apartment in the building:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/tenants/register \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Bootstrap-Token: <bootstrap-token>' \
  -d '{"name": "my-agent", "email": "me@example.com"}'
# → {"tenant_id": "ten_...", "api_key": "keyid.secret"}

That key is all the agent needs: Authorization: Bearer <api_key>. Two operator endpoints are worth knowing. POST /v1/system/bootstrap-token/validate with {"token":"…"} returns {"valid":true|false}. POST /v1/tenants/{tenantID}/reactivate restores a suspended tenant and issues a fresh key.

Deploy from git. Create a service (image is required, so the git flow passes the placeholder "pending"), then start a build:

POST /v1/services
{ "name": "my-app", "image": "pending", "port": 3000 }

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/builds
{ "source_type": "git", "source_url": "https://github.com/org/repo", "source_ref": "main" }

Builds pull from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, sr.ht, and Codeberg over HTTPS. The agent can stream build logs (/builds/{buildID}/logs?follow=true) and runtime logs (/v1/services/{serviceID}/logs?follow=true&tail=100). That matters: an agent that can read its own failure can fix it.

Add a database.

POST /v1/databases
{ "name": "my-db", "type": "postgres" }   # or "redis"

GET /v1/databases/{dbID}/connection-string

Wire it in with POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/env. Env vars are encrypted at rest and masked unless you ask for ?reveal=true.

Services live at http://{serviceID}.localhost, or at https://{dns_label}.example.com if you start ah with --base-domain example.com. ah writes Traefik's routing config itself and sets traefik.enable=false on containers, so an image's own labels can't hijack routing.

Even easier: let Claude Code drive

The repo ships a Claude Code skill and slash commands, so nobody writes curl:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/agentic-hosting
cp .claude/skills/agentic-hosting/SKILL.md ~/.claude/skills/agentic-hosting/SKILL.md
cp .claude/commands/ah-*.md ~/.claude/commands/

That gives you six commands:

Command What it does
/ah-register <tenant-name> <email> Register a tenant and get an API key
/ah-deploy <git-url-or-image> <service-name> [port] Deploy from a git URL or Docker image
`/ah-db <postgres\ redis> [db-name]`
/ah-logs <service-name> [build-id] Stream runtime logs, or build logs for a build
/ah-status Health, services, databases, circuit breakers
/ah-snapshot <service-name> [snapshot-name] Snapshot a running service

In practice:

/ah-deploy https://github.com/org/my-app web 3000
/ah-db web postgres
/ah-logs web
/ah-status

The first time I watched the loop — agent writes code, deploys, reads logs, fixes the crash, redeploys — it felt less like using a tool and more like managing someone. (No Claude? The same flows exist as bash scripts in scripts/.)

The guardrails are the product

What makes me comfortable isn't the agent. It's the boring stuff around it:

  • A reconciler checks every 30 seconds that what the database thinks is running matches what Docker is actually running.
  • A circuit breaker stops restarting a service after 5 crashes in 10 minutes. Resetting it is an explicit API call.
  • Disk watermarks warn at 80% and block new deploys, builds, and databases at 90%.
  • Rate limits per tenant (100 req/s, burst 200) and globally.
  • Idempotency keys (scoped to tenant, method, path, and body, with a 10-minute TTL) mean a retried request doesn't deploy twice.
  • ah backup takes safe SQLite snapshots and keeps the last 10.

Each one is built for a user who is fast, tireless, and occasionally wrong. That describes an agent. It also describes a junior engineer — and we learned long ago that the answer there isn't withholding access. It's making mistakes cheap.

What this changes

We're moving from operating software to supervising it. The valuable skill is less "do you know the right docker run flags" and more "did you set boundaries so the thing doing the work can't hurt you." Infrastructure becomes management: define the verbs, the limits, and the escape hatches, then get out of the way.

agentic-hosting is an early, opinionated version of that idea. It isn't trying to be Kubernetes. Known gaps include HKDF key separation, billing (metering is query-only today), Prometheus export, and multi-node SQLite.

If you try it:

  • Start in --dev mode locally, then move to a real box.
  • Give each agent its own tenant and key — isolation is the point.
  • Install the Claude Code skill; it's the fastest way to feel the loop.
  • Read the README's security model before handing over a key.

Wrapping up

We covered why agents need infrastructure built for them, how to set up agentic-hosting on your own server, and how an agent can register, build from git, add a database, and read its own logs — all inside guardrails like sandboxing, circuit breakers, and idempotency keys. The bigger idea: infrastructure is becoming a management problem. You design the boundaries; the agent does the work.

If that resonates:

  • ⭐ Star agentic-hosting on GitHub — it genuinely helps other people find it.
  • 🤖 Give this to your agent: point it at llms.txt to set everything up, or install the Claude Code skill so it knows how to run things day to day.
  • 🚀 Try the quickstart in the README — --dev mode is the fastest way to feel the loop.
  • 💬 Open an issue with feedback or what you'd want your agent to do next.

I'd love to hear what you build with it.

title: Your AI agent wrote its own log. That's the problem.
description:
A value showed up in a staging table that shouldn't have been there. Benign on its face — recoverable, nothing critical. But it didn't quite make sense to me, and I needed to know how it got there.

I checked the agent's log. Nothing. No write, no read, no mention of that table at all.

I checked the database logs. The change was there, and the timing lined up. But the connection was the shared service account, the one the whole deploy pipeline uses, and there's no per-session identity attached to it. So the database knew a write happened. It couldn't tell me which process made it, or which run.

Two records. Neither one could tell me what I needed to know.

Which meant I had a strong feeling I knew what happened and no way to prove it. Not to a teammate, not to a reviewer, not even to myself. I spent the morning in that gap.

The log is written by the thing you're checking

Every agent framework has logging. Claude Code has telemetry. Cursor shows you what's happening. MCP servers log their calls. There's no shortage of visibility.

But all of it is produced inside the agent's process. The agent writes directly to its own history. There's no separate observer in the loop — the record you read afterward was authored by the thing you're trying to check.

That's the part I couldn't get past. I can't trust the integrity of a record whose only author is a hallucinating agent on a strong dose of overconfidence. Not because it's lying. Because it isn't. It reports what it believes it did, and it believes it did the right thing. A confident record that's wrong reads exactly like a confident record that's right.

When the agent is right, that's fine. When it's confused, when the model is wrong, when something goes somewhere you didn't expect — the record is coming from the exact thing you're trying to verify. If it's compromised, the log is compromised. If it's wrong, the log is confidently wrong. And if it simply didn't notice what it did, the log is silent.

This isn't a new problem. It's the problem every evidence-producing domain solved decades ago. You don't accept a company's own security report as a SOC 2. You don't accept a company's own financial statement without an audit. The reason is the same everywhere: a record produced by the entity being observed is a claim, not evidence.

Agent tooling hasn't caught up to that.

And you can't just re-run it

My first instinct was the obvious one: if I don't know what happened, run it again and watch.

That doesn't work. Agents aren't deterministic. Same input, different path. Same task, different files touched. The run you're trying to understand is gone, and re-running gives you a different run.

So you're left with two bad options. Trust the agent's own record, or have no record at all.

The part I couldn't unsee

It wasn't the wrong value.

Once I was in that gap, the thought went further. If I can't account for this — one staging table, low stakes, recoverable — what about the environments where I don't get a second chance? Payment endpoints. Customer records. Anything with real consequences and an audit trail someone else would eventually read.

But that's the smaller realization. Here's the one that changed how I work.

I'd been writing prompts with full confidence. Detailed instructions, clear boundaries, "don't touch X" and "only do Y." Reading the agent's summaries and signing off. Confident the whole time.

Underneath that, I had no idea what was actually happening.

The confidence in my instructions didn't match what I actually knew. I was writing authoritative prompts into a void and calling the output a result. And the reason I couldn't tell the difference was that every piece of evidence I had about the agent's behavior came from the agent.

That's the thing I couldn't unsee.

What an independent record actually requires

The fix isn't better logging. It's where the record lives.

The record has to be produced outside the agent's process. Separate process, separate identity, separate storage, separate code path. The agent can't write to it, because there's nothing persistent running for it to write to. It starts when the agent starts and it's gone when the agent ends.

That's the same trust topology audit converged on everywhere else. The observer has to be independent of the observed.

The second requirement is that anyone can check it. Not "trust the vendor's dashboard" — actually verify it. Locally, offline, without an account, without a network call. A hash-chained ledger and a verifier that imports nothing from the tool that wrote it. Two independent implementations agreeing is a stronger claim than one program checking its own work.

What I built

Centrol is a free, local flight recorder for AI agents. It's a single Go binary, no daemon, no cloud, no account, no telemetry. It covers the paths agents act through — the filesystem, MCP tool calls, shell, and outbound network — and logs what it sees to an append-only, hash-chained ledger.

Two commands do most of the work:

centrol guard wraps an agent run. It takes a snapshot first, records every action out-of-band while the run is happening, and leaves you with a state you can return to. No slowdown, no change to how the agent works — one word in front of the command you were already running.

centrol proxy sits in front of your MCP servers. Every tool call passes through it before anything executes, which is where allowlists and blocks happen. A call that violates policy doesn't run, and it's recorded as having been refused.

Setup for the proxy path is one command. centrol proxy install <client> rewrites the MCP config so every server launches through the proxy. You run it once. It backs up your original config first, and it's safe to re-run — anything already wrapped is left alone.

What it doesn't do

I'd rather tell you the limits up front than have you find them the hard way.

It's not a sandbox. It records and reverses governed actions. It doesn't prevent a determined agent from acting outside the governed interfaces.

Guard and proxy enforce differently, on purpose. centrol guard never blocks a filesystem write — not even one to ~/.ssh or ~/.aws. A filesystem watcher sees writes after they've landed, so there's nothing left to block. It logs those as violations and lets them through. centrol proxy is different: the call hasn't reached the server yet, so a tool call that resolves to a protected path is genuinely never forwarded. If you need a hard guarantee that a credential path is never touched, that guarantee exists on the proxy path, not the guard path.

Rollback has honest scope. centrol undo restores tracked git state and untracked files that existed at snapshot time. It doesn't restore ignored files, databases, or other external state. And it doesn't guess — when it finds files it can't account for, it lists them and lets you decide what happens to them instead of deleting on your behalf.

Quickstart 

# Install (macOS/Linux)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baitelmal/centrol/main/install-centrol.sh | sh

# Install (Windows, PowerShell)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baitelmal/centrol/main/install-centrol.ps1 | iex

# Wrap an interactive agent session
centrol guard -- claude

# Or front a stdio MCP server
centrol proxy --target "npx @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /path/to/allow"

# See what happened
centrol audit

# Confirm the record hasn't been tampered with
centrol audit --verify

# Roll back the most recent run
centrol undo

The ledger is written locally and never transmitted. centrol-verify is a standalone binary that checks a ledger's hash chain without importing anything from centrol — so you can verify a record without trusting, or even building, the tool that produced it.

Why I'm posting this

I built it for myself, because I wanted something to boost trust in my agents and mitigate the obscurity of their black box designs. The record needs to be independent, it has to work offline as well, and it has to be verifiable without taking my word for it. Those three constraints ruled out everything I looked at.

If you've given an agent real access to something that matters and you've had a similar experience — give it a spin. I hope it's useful to someone.

Repo: https://github.com/baitelmal/centrol

If you try it, I'd like to hear how it goes — your experience with it, and any edge cases you run into.
