title: Farmora: my Next.js shop stalled up to 6s a page, so I made it local-first
description:
What Farmora is

Farmora ("From Local Farms to Your Door") is a farm-to-door marketplace. Farmers list what they've harvested and customers buy straight from them. Every order is delivered within three days, with a live tracker. Behind the shop there's an admin side where the platform keeps a 10% commission on each sale.

  • Live demo: https://farmora-smoky.vercel.app
  • Code: https://github.com/Fehan999/Farmora

Fehan999 / Farmora

Farmora 🌱

From Local Farms to Your Door

Farmora is a farm-to-table marketplace I built with Next.js. Farmers list what they've harvested, customers buy it straight from them, and every order arrives within three days with a live tracker that follows it from the farm to the front door. Behind that there's an admin side where the platform keeps a 10% commission on each sale. It started as a portfolio project, but I wanted it to behave like a real shop: real sign-ups, a real database, photo uploads for farmers, and pages that still load when the backend is having a bad day.

Live demo: farmora-smoky.vercel.app

Try it

No sign-up and no passwords needed. Open the login page and:

  1. Pick Customer or Farmer.
  2. Click View demo account to jump straight in, or Create your own account if you'd rather start fresh.
  3. Curious about the business side? Click View admin…
View on GitHub

I designed and built it on my own. It has 27 page routes plus 6 blog article pages, 40 products in 8 categories, 8 partner farms with full profiles, 12 sample customers and 18 sample orders. All of it is sample data. There are no real farms, customers or payments behind it.

There are three roles:

  • Customers search and filter the shop and fill a cart. Delivery is free over $50 and $4.99 otherwise. They can apply coupons and check out with a demo card or cash on delivery.
  • Farmers get a dashboard with gross sales, the 10% platform fee, net earnings, a 7-day earnings chart and a product editor with photo upload.
  • Admins see platform revenue, a sales table with CSV export, product moderation, user management and a contact inbox. They don't get a cart or "My Orders", because they aren't shoppers.

Why I built it

I wanted a portfolio project that behaves like a real shop, and a marketplace forces questions a single-vendor store never has to answer. Who can see which order? What counts as the platform's revenue? What does a farmer see that an admin doesn't? What happens when the backend is down?

The farm angle gave every product a source, too. Each item shows the farm it came from, and each farm has its own profile page.

Architecture

I kept the stack small on purpose:

  • Next.js 14.2 with the App Router and React 18, in plain JSX (no TypeScript)
  • Tailwind CSS 3
  • Firebase 10 for Authentication, Firestore and Analytics
  • Supabase Storage for farmer photo uploads
  • Pexels CDN for product photos
  • Vercel for hosting
  • Playwright and GitHub Actions for screenshots and image checks

Seed farms, products, orders and photo ids live in data/. Most of the code in this post is in lib/.

1. A data layer that never makes the page wait

In the first version, getProducts() started with await readCollection("products"), and the page sat on a loading state until that came back. Now every getter in lib/db.js answers immediately. It merges three sources by id: the seed data, the last Firestore snapshot cached in localStorage, and any changes made in this browser. Firestore only refreshes that data in the background.

Every Firestore call in db.js goes through a timeout, now 4 seconds instead of 6:

const withTimeout = (p, ms = 4000) =>
  Promise.race([p, new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej(Object.assign(new Error("timeout"), { code: "timeout" })), ms))]);

remote() returns whatever is cached right now. If that cache is more than a minute old, it also starts a refresh. refresh() does the fetch, but skips it when Firestore is already known to be down, when the collection is locked, or when a request for that collection is already in flight:

function refresh(name) {
  if (!isBrowser || remoteDown || deniedCollections.has(name) || inflight.has(name)) return;
  const job = (async () => {
    try {
      const { db, sdk } = await getDb();
      const snap = await withTimeout(sdk.getDocs(sdk.collection(db, name)));
      const data = snap.docs.map((d) => ({ id: d.id, ...d.data() }));
      memory.set(name, { data, at: Date.now() });
      local.set(CACHE_PREFIX + name, data);
      notify();
    } catch (err) {
      markFailure(name, err);
    } finally {
      inflight.delete(name);
    }
  })();
  inflight.set(name, job);
}

function remote(name) {
  if (!isBrowser) return [];
  let entry = memory.get(name);
  if (!entry) {
    entry = { data: local.get(CACHE_PREFIX + name), at: 0 };
    memory.set(name, entry);
  }
  if (Date.now() - entry.at > REMOTE_TTL) refresh(name);
  return entry.data;
}

getProducts() merges the three sources in one line:

let all = mergeById(PRODUCTS, remote("products"), local.get("farmora_products"))

Failures go one of two ways. A permission-denied on one collection keeps only that collection local. Anything else, like a timeout or a disabled API, marks Firestore as down for the rest of the session, so no other page waits out the same four seconds:

function markFailure(name, err) {
  const code = err?.code || "";
  if (code === "permission-denied") {
    deniedCollections.add(name);
    return;
  }
  remoteDown = true;
  try { sessionStorage.setItem(STATUS_KEY, "1"); } catch {}
}

When fresh data arrives, notify() fires a window event:

function notify() {
  if (isBrowser) window.dispatchEvent(new Event("farmora:data"));
}

On the React side, components/useData.js listens for that event and re-runs the page's loader in silent mode, so the page updates without a spinner. A request counter drops the result of an older run that finishes late:

const run = useCallback(async (silent) => {
  const request = ++requestRef.current;
  if (!silent) setLoading(true);
  const result = await loaderRef.current();
  if (request !== requestRef.current) return;
  setData(result);
  setLoading(false);
}, deps);
...
useEffect(() => {
  const onChange = () => run(true);
  window.addEventListener("farmora:data", onChange);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("farmora:data", onChange);
}, [run]);

The home page, product pages and farm profiles pass seed data to useData as the initial value, so their first render already has content. Writes follow the same pattern. They're saved to localStorage first, then sent to Firestore in the background.

2. Loading Firebase when the browser is idle

The other cost was bundle size. The first lib/firebase.js imported firebase/auth and firebase/firestore at the top of the file, so every page shipped the SDK whether it used it or not. In the build output, that was about half of the shared JavaScript on every page.

Now each service is a cached promise around a dynamic import():

export function getDb() {
  if (!dbPromise) {
    dbPromise = Promise.all([getFirebaseApp(), import("firebase/firestore")]).then(([app, sdk]) => ({
      db: sdk.getFirestore(app),
      sdk,
    }));
  }
  return dbPromise;
}

The auth listener in context/AuthContext.jsx doesn't start until the browser is idle:

const idle = window.requestIdleCallback || ((fn) => setTimeout(fn, 200));
idle(start);

start prefetches the products, users and orders collections, starts Analytics and subscribes to onAuthStateChanged. The saved session in localStorage is read before any of that, so a returning user sees their name in the navbar straight away.

Shared first-load JS per page went from about 215 KB to about 106 KB.

Supabase got the same treatment. getSupabase() in lib/supabase.js is a lazy import("@supabase/supabase-js"), so the client only downloads when a farmer uploads a photo.

3. Commission math in one place

The business rule is short. Farmora keeps 10% of the product subtotal (price × quantity) of every order that wasn't cancelled. Delivery fees and tax don't count. An order with $42.00 of produce earns the platform $4.20 and the farmer $37.80.

My first admin dashboard got this wrong. Its "Total revenue" card added up full order totals, delivery and tax included. The platform never keeps that money, so the biggest number on the page was misleading.

Now the rate lives in one constant in lib/format.js:

export const COMMISSION_RATE = 0.1;
export const itemsSubtotal = (items = []) => items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
export const commissionOf = (amount) => amount * COMMISSION_RATE;

And lib/stats.js builds every order-level number from it:

export const FEE_PCT = Math.round(COMMISSION_RATE * 100);
export const PAYOUT_PCT = 100 - FEE_PCT;

export const isActiveOrder = (o) => o.status !== "cancelled";
export const orderGross = (o) => itemsSubtotal(o.items || []);
export const orderCommission = (o) => commissionOf(orderGross(o));
export const orderPayout = (o) => orderGross(o) - orderCommission(o);

The admin overview, the 7-day commission chart, commission by category, the Sales table, its CSV export and the farmer dashboard all read from these two files, so the numbers always agree. Even the labels use FEE_PCT. Change the rate and the "Commission (10%)" column header changes with it.

The admin side still shows sales volume and farmer payouts, labelled as context so nobody mistakes them for revenue.

4. A delivery tracker with no background job

Every order moves through five stages over 72 hours. I didn't want a cron job or a cloud function moving statuses along, so lib/delivery.js works out the stage from the order's timestamp:

export const DELIVERY_HOURS = 72;

export const STAGES = [
  { key: "placed", label: "Order Placed", at: 0, icon: "📝" },
  { key: "packed", label: "Packed at Farm", at: 6, icon: "📦" },
  { key: "shipped", label: "Shipped", at: 24, icon: "🚚" },
  { key: "out", label: "Out for Delivery", at: 60, icon: "🛵" },
  { key: "delivered", label: "Delivered", at: 72, icon: "🏡" },
];

export function deliveryStatus(order, now = Date.now()) {
  ...
  const created = new Date(order.createdAt).getTime();
  const hours = Math.max(0, (now - created) / 36e5);
  const percent = Math.min(100, (hours / DELIVERY_HOURS) * 100);
  let stageIndex = 0;
  STAGES.forEach((s, i) => { if (hours >= s.at) stageIndex = i; });
  ...
}

The DeliveryTracker component updates now every 30 seconds, which moves the progress bar and the countdown.

Because it's plain math on a timestamp, no server has to keep it current. Sample orders work too, since the seed creates them relative to the current time. And the public /track page can show any order's progress from its order number, with no login. Customers can cancel until the order ships, and each order has a printable invoice.

The trade-off is that a stage isn't a real event. A real delivery system would need scans from the farm and the courier, and the timestamp math would only be the estimate shown until those scans arrive.

5. Images: srcset, fallbacks, and a workflow that checks every photo

The first version used placeholder images from a random-image service. They were slow and often showed the wrong food, so I replaced them with 125 curated Pexels photos.

data/photos.js stores the Pexels ids. lib/images.js builds a srcset from each URL, so a phone never downloads a desktop-sized photo:

const WIDTHS = [320, 480, 640, 960, 1280];
...
export function srcSetFor(src) {
  if (!isPexels(src) || !/[?&]w=\d+/.test(src)) return undefined;
  return WIDTHS.map((w) => `${resize(src, w)} ${w}w`).join(", ");
}

SafeImage wraps every product photo. It lazy-loads unless the image is marked priority, which the hero images are. When a photo fails, it falls back in two steps: first to an optional fallbackSrc, then to an inline SVG placeholder.

function onError() {
  setStage((s) => {
    const from = s === 0 && !src ? 1 : s;
    return from === 0 && fallbackSrc ? 1 : 2;
  });
}

Fallbacks hide broken images from me as well as from visitors. So I added a GitHub Action that builds the site, starts it and runs scripts/screenshots.mjs with Playwright.

The script screenshots every page, with the right demo session in place where a page needs one. It also requests every photo URL in data/photos.js. A photo passes only on a 200 response whose content type, if there is one, is an image:

entry.ok = entry.status === 200 && (!entry.contentType || entry.contentType.startsWith("image/"));

The results go to image-report.json. The script also renders contact sheets: grids of every photo, each captioned with the product or page it belongs to, with failures outlined in red. The workflow uploads all of it as an artifact and pushes the screenshots to a separate screenshots branch.

The URL check caught 10 broken photo URLs.

The contact sheets caught something a status code never will: several photos that loaded fine but didn't match their product. When I couldn't find a matching photo, I renamed the product rather than show a misleading picture. "Rainbow Carrots" became "Farm Fresh Carrots".

6. SEO with JSON-LD and generated OG images

A pageMeta() helper in lib/seo.js gives each public page its own title, description, canonical URL and Open Graph/Twitter tags.

The root layout adds a JSON-LD graph with WebSite (including a SearchAction that points at /shop?q=), Organization, Person for me as the author, and SoftwareSourceCode linking to the repo.

Product pages get a Product graph with offers, price, stock, delivery time and rating, plus a breadcrumb list. The product page itself is a client component, so the JSON-LD goes in a server layout that looks the product up in the seed data:

export default function ProductLayout({ children, params }) {
  const { product, farmer, category } = lookup(params.id);
  return (
    <>
      {product && <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: toJsonLd(productJsonLd(product, farmer, category)) }} />}
      {children}
    </>
  );
}

toJsonLd escapes <, so a product description can never close the script tag early:

export const toJsonLd = (data) => JSON.stringify(data).replace(/</g, "\\u003c");

Product pages start from seed data, so the h1, price and description are in the server-rendered HTML too. Blog articles get BlogPosting data. app/sitemap.js lists every product, farm and blog post, and app/robots.js tells crawlers to skip the cart, checkout, orders, account, wishlist and dashboards. There's also a web manifest and a humans.txt.

The share image is generated with next/og. app/opengraph-image.jsx returns a 1200×630 ImageResponse with the logo, the tagline, my name and the stack. There's no separate design file to keep in sync with the site.

7. Demo accounts for visitors

Nobody reviewing a portfolio wants to sign up just to see a dashboard. The login page asks one question: Customer or Farmer? Then you can click "View demo customer account" (or the farmer version), or create your own account with Firebase email/password. A separate "View admin demo" option opens the business side.

The demo login doesn't wait on Firebase. It writes a session and tells the auth listener to ignore Firebase for it:

async function demoLogin(role) {
  const acc = DEMO_ACCOUNTS[role];
  const session = {
    uid: `demo-${role}`, id: `demo-${role}`, email: acc.email, name: acc.name,
    role: acc.role, farmerId: acc.farmerId || `demo-${role}`, demo: true,
  };
  ignoreFirebase.current = true;
  setUser(session);
  ...
  return session;
}

The demo button also prefetches its destination route as soon as it renders.

The demo farmer is Robert Hayes from Green Valley Farm. His dashboard opens with products, orders and earnings already in it.

How I tested it

Besides the screenshot workflow, I crawled every route with Playwright at desktop and mobile widths. No route had page errors or horizontal overflow. I checked 79 internal links and ran the main flows end to end: each demo login, checkout through to the tracker, and the admin access rules. The layout holds up on phones down to 390 px wide.

Lessons learned

A timeout doesn't help if the page still waits for it. The first version had a timeout and a fallback to sample data. Every page still sat through six seconds before it got to use that fallback. Rendering from local data first, and treating the network as an update, is what fixed it.

Read the build output before optimizing. I only found out Firebase was half of every page's JavaScript because I looked at the numbers. Moving it behind dynamic imports was a small change with a big result.

Write down what "revenue" means before building the dashboard. My first admin overview led with the wrong number because I hadn't defined what the platform keeps. One constant and a few small helpers fixed it.

A 200 status doesn't mean the image is right. The HTTP check found the broken URLs. Only the contact sheets showed me the photos of the wrong food.

Make the demo the front door. For a portfolio project, a one-click demo account matters more than any feature hidden behind a sign-up form.

Limitations and what's next

Checkout is a demo. No real payments happen, and the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242 charges nothing.

Next on my list:

  • Real payments with Stripe
  • Moving the background sync to Firestore real-time listeners, and tightening the security rules
  • Delivery slots per farm, instead of one 72-hour timeline for everyone
  • A proper end-to-end test suite (the screenshot script already does half the clicking)

Try it

Open the login page, pick a role and click the demo button.

A few other things to try:

  • Track a sample order without signing in at /track. Try ORD-10241.
  • Use the coupons FRESH10, FARMORA20 and WELCOME5 at checkout.

If something breaks, or you'd have built the data layer differently, leave a comment here or open an issue on GitHub. I'd like to hear it.

title: Apple is testing a black and white icon for Apple Music in iOS 18.2
description:
Apple Music is refreshing its visual identity by replacing its 13-year-old red icon with a black-and-white design, as observed in iOS 27.2 beta 4.

The update introduces a slightly tilted logo, oval-shaped notes, a drop shadow, and dark mode variants, alongside removing red accents from widgets and the app interface.

The new icon retains the classic note shape, but is slightly tilted to the left, has more oval notes, and a subtle shadow. The company also created a dark version with a white design on a black background, as well as options with a transparent or colored appearance. Along with removing the red color from the icon, Apple also removed red from the widgets on the home screen, and changed the interior color of the app from red and pink to blue.

Reactions from users on social media have been mostly negative. Many have called the new look boring and uninteresting, arguing that the change was unnecessary, although there have also been some users who found the change positive.

As the app is still in the testing phase, Apple reserves the right to change its mind before the final version is released.

title: Supabase bought Turso. Now comes the hard part.
description:
Disclosure up front: I've used both Supabase and Turso. I've evaluated both for real projects, and I recommend both. That's part of why I have an opinion here. I want both of them to keep being great.

Two databases I actually like just became one company

Supabase announced it is acquiring Turso. Glauber Costa, Turso's cofounder and CEO, joins Supabase as Head of Agentic Services, along with cofounder Pekka Enberg and the rest of the team. No price was disclosed.

If you haven't followed both products: Turso rebuilt SQLite from the ground up in Rust and built a cloud platform around a "many databases" architecture. One database per user, per agent, per task, provisioned on demand, on a WAL-on-S3 design, in their cloud or yours through BYOC. Supabase is the leading Postgres platform: database, auth, storage, and a broad integration ecosystem, launching over a million databases a week.

Two of the best commercial open source companies in the database space, and one just bought the other. COSS is alive and well, and that's worth celebrating on its own.

Why this deal makes sense on paper

The strategic logic is actually good. AI agents are creating a new workload shape: one agent, one task, one user, millions of small databases that come online instantly and get created at a rate infrastructure has never seen. SQLite is the natural fit for that. Postgres is what you want when the application outgrows it. Supabase's own announcement says it plainly: "SQLite is well suited to these small, on-demand workloads. Postgres is what you want as your application scales."

And the migration story isn't hand-waving. Turso is building a Postgres frontend on the same Rust core as its SQLite engine. Their framing is "the LLVM of databases": one modern core, many frontends. A "seamless path to Postgres when an application outgrows them" is credible engineering, not marketing. Teams like Superhuman, Sauna.ai, and Mastra already run agent workloads on Turso at scale.

So yes: on paper, this is a smart acquisition. Start small on Turso, scale into Supabase, stay in one ecosystem the whole way. I get it. I'd make a version of that pitch myself.

The instinct will be to consolidate

Here's the part I'll believe when I see.

The announcements promise continuity. Supabase: "For existing users, nothing changes." Also Supabase: "Turso will continue operating, with a clear path into the broader Supabase ecosystem as workloads grow."

Take those seriously, but read them carefully. "Nothing changes" is exactly what you say to calm users and avoid churn in the weeks after an acquisition closes. It's churn management, not a strategy guarantee. And "Turso will continue operating" is a lower bar than it sounds. A product can keep operating and still get absorbed: same dashboard, same billing, same sales team, same brand slowly dissolving into the parent platform. Operating and independent are not the same thing.

I've watched this pattern from the inside of enough companies to recognize it. The business instinct after any acquisition is consolidation: one brand, one platform, one toolset, one sales team. It feels efficient. It demos well to a board. And for products that are actually different, it's usually a mistake — the buyer gets confused about what to buy and which solution to use, the value props get muddied, and you end up chasing multiple ideal customer profiles with one muddled message. Salesforce and Adobe built empires on the monolith M&A pattern, and even there, the products that kept their identity thrived while the absorbed ones became feature checkboxes.

Neither company has said they'll do this. I'm not predicting they will. I'm saying the pressure will exist, especially from business leaders who may not understand what makes COSS companies valuable in the first place, and resisting it is the actual hard part of this deal.

Why these two can't merge

Could Supabase and Turso converge into one platform? I won't say it's impossible. I'll say it would be challenging, and it would almost certainly cost something from one or both.

They're different technologies. Turso is SQLite rebuilt for server workloads: concurrent writes, millions of small databases, per-user economics, BYOC. Supabase is platform Postgres: fewer, larger, more powerful databases with an ecosystem around them. Those aren't two flavors of the same problem. They're two different problems.

The communities are different too. Turso runs an open-contribution model — the full test suite is open, contributions welcome — and its engine is MIT licensed. Supabase's community is the Postgres ecosystem. Smash the two together under one brand and one roadmap, and you don't get a bigger community. You get two communities wondering which one they belong to.

Convergence would mean one of these products stops being fully itself. That's the sacrifice. It would be a shame, because both are great at what they actually do.

The winning play: loose coupling

The best version of this deal is the least dramatic one: keep Turso Turso.

Separate brand, separate pricing, separate community. Turso keeps solving its problem its way, Supabase keeps solving its problem its way, and the connection between them is a bridge, not a merger. Real migration and scaling tooling, cross-promotion, and maybe shared services like billing and identity behind the scenes where the buyer never has to think about them.

That preserves two clear value propositions and two clear customer profiles instead of muddying both. It's the difference between a portfolio and a monolith. Portfolios compound; monoliths average.

To be clear, this isn't me telling Supabase how to run their company. They've earned the benefit of the doubt, and they've been one of the most disciplined open source companies in the space. It's me naming what I'll be watching.

What I'm watching

The next 12–24 months will tell the story. The signals are observable:

  • Good outcome: Turso keeps shipping as its own product, with its own branding, pricing, and community. The SQLite-to-Postgres path stays a bridge between two platforms.
  • Warning signs: a shared sales motion appears, "Turso" becomes a feature inside the Supabase dashboard, the brand starts dissolving into unified platform messaging.

And I'll hold myself to the same standard: if Turso is still independent and both platforms are thriving through 2027 and 2028, my caution was overweighted. I'll be glad to be wrong.

Both of these are great platforms solving real problems, built by teams that have earned their communities. COSS is alive and well. The question now is whether this deal becomes the example of how to combine strengths without collapsing identities, or one more data point for the monolith rule.

I'm rooting for the exception.

title: Add an Emoji Favicon with One Line of HTML (Next.js, Astro, Vue, WordPress) Plus Dynamic Tab Notifications
description:
Favicons used to mean a ZIP of PNGs, an ICO, an apple-touch icon, and a half-remembered manifest.json. For a lot of sites, that is still the right approach. For many others — a side project, a docs site, a staging deploy, a dashboard that needs a notification badge — you only need one emoji in the tab, and you need it today.

EmojiFavicons is a URL-based emoji favicon service from FindUtils. You point a normal <link rel="icon"> at an emoji slug, and the API returns an SVG (under 200 bytes for a plain emoji, per the docs). No signup, no API key, no build step. This article sticks to what the site documents and what the endpoints actually return when you request them.

The one-line install

Drop this in your HTML <head>:

<link rel="icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/fire">

Replace fire with any emoji name. The homepage and docs state that EmojiFavicons covers 3,773 Unicode emojis, searchable by 11,550 keywords. Names and keywords are case-insensitive. You can also use a keyword (/hot resolves to fire), a URL-encoded emoji character, or a country code for flags (/US, /TR).

A live request to https://emojifavicons.com/fire returns image/svg+xml — a tiny SVG wrapping the 🔥 glyph. Safari is a special case: the how-it-works page explains that Safari has limited SVG favicon support, so the service auto-serves a PNG (Twemoji) for Safari User-Agents. You can force a format with ?svg or ?png.

If you later want a classic downloadable package instead of a live URL, the docs also expose GET /download/:emoji — for example https://emojifavicons.com/download/rocket returns a ZIP of standard sizes. That is the honest self-host path when you do not want a third-party dependency at runtime.

Customize with URL parameters

Every favicon endpoint accepts query parameters. A documented example that works today:

https://emojifavicons.com/fire?size=64&bg=1a1a1a&animate=pulse

That request returns image/svg+xml with a 64×64 viewBox, a dark background, and a CSS pulse animation. Useful parameters from the docs (not an exhaustive list):

Parameter What it does (per docs)
size SVG size in pixels (16–512; default 48)
bg Background hex without #
shape e.g. circle, rounded, hexagon, …
animate e.g. pulse, bounce, spin, and many others
badge Notification overlay: 1–99 or dot
theme Branded presets such as github-dark, vercel-dark, tailwind
png / svg Force output format

Combine freely. Combos put 2–10 emojis side by side with a +:

<link rel="icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/fire+rocket">

That endpoint returns a single SVG with 🔥 and 🚀 next to each other — useful for “shipping fast” vibes without designing an icon.

For a red unread count without JavaScript:

<link rel="icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/bell?badge=3">

Framework installs (verified against the official guides)

The frameworks index lists 19 tutorials. Below are the four most common, copied from the site’s own guides. In every case, remove or rename any default favicon.ico / favicon.svg in public/ so the external URL wins.

Next.js (App Router)

From the Next.js guide:

// app/layout.tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'next';

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  icons: {
    icon: 'https://emojifavicons.com/rocket',
    apple: 'https://emojifavicons.com/apple-touch-icon/rocket',
  },
};

Pages Router: put the <link> tags in pages/_document.tsx inside <Head>. The guide notes that Vercel may cache an old favicon for up to 24 hours; append ?v=2 if you need a cache bust.

Astro

From the Astro guide, in your shared layout:

<head>
  <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="https://emojifavicons.com/rocket" />
  <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/apple-touch-icon/rocket" />
</head>

Delete public/favicon.svg if the starter left one. Keep the tags in the persistent layout so View Transitions do not thrash the tab icon.

Vue 3 + Vite / Nuxt 3

From the Vue guide:

Vite: edit root index.html:

<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="https://emojifavicons.com/rocket" />
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/apple-touch-icon/rocket" />

Nuxt 3: in nuxt.config.ts:

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  app: {
    head: {
      link: [
        { rel: 'icon', type: 'image/svg+xml', href: 'https://emojifavicons.com/rocket' },
        { rel: 'apple-touch-icon', href: 'https://emojifavicons.com/apple-touch-icon/rocket' },
      ],
    },
  },
});

WordPress

From the WordPress guide, append to the child theme’s functions.php (or a site-wide snippets plugin):

add_action('wp_head', function () {
  echo '<link rel="icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/rocket" type="image/svg+xml">';
  echo '<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/apple-touch-icon/rocket">';
});

Clear the Customizer Site Icon if WordPress still serves its own. Hard-refresh after saving.

Dynamic tab notifications with the JS SDK

Static badges are fine for marketing sites. Apps need the tab to react. Include the SDK once:

<script src="https://emojifavicons.com/sdk.js"></script>

https://emojifavicons.com/sdk.js returns application/javascript. The homepage and docs show the core surface; the script itself exposes:

EmojiFavicon.set('rocket');
EmojiFavicon.animate('fire', 'pulse');
EmojiFavicon.notify('bell', 3000); // flash, then restore
EmojiFavicon.restore();
EmojiFavicon.setBadge('bell', 5);
EmojiFavicon.clearBadge();

A practical pattern for “you have new messages while the tab is in the background”:

function onUnread(count) {
  if (count > 0) {
    EmojiFavicon.set('bell', { badge: Math.min(count, 99) });
  } else {
    EmojiFavicon.restore();
  }
}

notify(emoji, durationMs) temporarily swaps the icon, then restores the previous href — handy for a one-shot alert without managing state yourself.

Trade-offs (be honest)

Depends on a third-party URL. If emojifavicons.com is unreachable, the tab falls back to whatever the browser does without a favicon. The compare page itself lists this as a con of URL-based services, mitigated by CDN caching (docs: 7-day CDN cache, 24-hour browser cache) and by downloading the SVG/PNG/ICO (or the ZIP from /download/:emoji) and hosting it yourself.

Rate limits. The FAQ on the homepage says normal use has a 300 requests per minute limit, with no signup or credit card required. That is generous for a favicon, but it is still a shared free resource — do not hammer it from a CI loop that rebuilds thousands of pages per minute.

Not a full custom-image favicon studio. If you need a hand-drawn mark or a photo crop, generate and self-host assets instead. For that workflow, FindUtils’ favicon generator is a useful browser-side companion when you already have an image file. EmojiFavicons and the FindUtils generator solve different problems: emoji-as-URL vs. image-to-package.

Caching surprises. CDNs and browsers cache favicons aggressively. After a change, hard-refresh or bump a query string.

Quick health check

Before you ship, run your domain through the Favicon Health Checker. It scores icon / SVG / apple-touch / manifest coverage and offers copy-paste fixes. Pair that with the interactive generator if you want to preview size, shape, animation, and badge before pasting a URL into production.

Wrap-up

  1. Add <link rel="icon" href="https://emojifavicons.com/fire"> (or your emoji of choice).
  2. Optionally tune with ?size=, ?bg=, ?animate=, ?badge=, or a combo like /fire+rocket.
  3. Follow the framework guide for Next.js, Astro, Vue, or WordPress.
  4. For runtime swaps, load sdk.js and call set / animate / notify.
  5. If you outgrow a third-party URL, download the ZIP and self-host.

Start at emojifavicons.com, browse the docs, and if you need more free browser-only utilities beyond favicons, FindUtils has a large catalog of client-side tools that never upload your files.

title: WebGL Basics
description:
Unveiling the Magic: Your Casual Guide to WebGL Basics

Ever scrolled through a website and stumbled upon a mesmerizing 3D animation, a mind-bending interactive game, or a data visualization so slick it made you do a double-take? Chances are, you’ve witnessed the power of WebGL in action. But what exactly is this sorcery, and how does it conjure such wonders directly in your browser?

Fear not, intrepid explorer of the digital realm! This article is your friendly, in-depth guide to the basics of WebGL. We’re ditching the jargon-heavy textbooks and diving into a casual exploration of this incredible technology that brings 3D graphics to life on the web. So, grab a virtual coffee, settle in, and let’s embark on this exciting journey together.

Introduction: What in the World is WebGL?

Imagine the internet as a giant canvas. Historically, this canvas was mostly for flat, 2D content – text, images, and the occasional animated GIF. Then came HTML5, bringing with it <canvas>, a magical element that allowed for 2D drawing. But what about depth? What about things that spin, twist, and immerse you in a virtual world?

Enter WebGL (Web Graphics Library). It’s essentially a JavaScript API that lets you render 2D and 3D graphics and images within any compatible web browser without the need for plugins. Think of it as a direct pipeline to your computer's graphics processing unit (GPU), the powerhouse responsible for all those stunning visuals in your favorite games and design software. WebGL leverages the OpenGL ES (Embedded Systems) graphics library, a standard used in countless devices, making it incredibly efficient and widely supported.

In simpler terms, WebGL empowers web developers to harness the raw graphical might of your machine to create experiences that were once confined to desktop applications.

Prerequisites: What Do You Need to Know Before Diving In?

Before we start conjuring triangles, let’s make sure you’ve got the right tools in your mental toolbox. While WebGL might seem intimidating, you don’t need to be a rocket scientist to get started. Here’s what will make your WebGL journey smoother:

  • JavaScript Fundamentals: This is your primary language. You should be comfortable with variables, data types, functions, loops, conditional statements, and basic object-oriented concepts. If you can build interactive web pages with vanilla JavaScript, you’re in good shape.
  • HTML & CSS Basics: You’ll be working within an HTML document, and understanding how to structure your page and style elements will be helpful. The <canvas> element, which is where WebGL magic happens, is an HTML tag.
  • A Glimpse of Linear Algebra (Optional but Helpful): This is where things can get a bit mathy, but don’t panic! Understanding basic concepts like vectors (directions and positions) and matrices (transformations like rotation, scaling, and translation) will significantly deepen your understanding of how 3D objects are manipulated. You don’t need to be a math whiz, but a conceptual grasp will be your best friend.
  • A Modern Web Browser: Most modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) have excellent WebGL support. Just ensure you’re not using a browser that’s older than your favorite flip phone.

Advantages: Why Should You Care About WebGL?

So, why bother with WebGL when there are other graphics libraries out there? Here are some compelling reasons:

  • No Plugins Required: This is a huge one! Unlike Flash or Java applets of the past, WebGL is a web standard. Users don't need to download and install anything extra. It just works, making your applications accessible to a broader audience.
  • Leverages Hardware Acceleration: WebGL talks directly to your GPU. This means it can render complex scenes at high speeds, delivering smooth animations and incredibly detailed graphics that would bog down a CPU-only solution.
  • Cross-Platform Compatibility: WebGL works across different operating systems and devices. Your WebGL application will look and perform similarly whether it's running on a Windows PC, a Mac, or even a mobile device (with some performance considerations, of course).
  • Rich and Interactive Experiences: From immersive 3D games and product configurators to dynamic data visualizations and architectural walkthroughs, WebGL opens the door to a world of engaging and interactive content that was previously impossible on the web.
  • Open Standard and Community Support: As a web standard, WebGL is constantly evolving. There's a thriving community of developers sharing knowledge, tools, and libraries, making it easier to learn and build complex applications.
  • Integration with Existing Web Technologies: WebGL seamlessly integrates with the rest of the web. You can easily combine your 3D scenes with HTML elements, CSS styling, and JavaScript interactions.

Disadvantages: The Double-Edged Sword

As with any technology, WebGL isn't a magic bullet for every scenario. Here are some of its limitations:

  • Steep Learning Curve: Compared to simpler 2D drawing APIs, WebGL can have a steeper learning curve, especially if you’re new to 3D graphics concepts and linear algebra.
  • Performance Variability: While it leverages the GPU, performance can still vary significantly depending on the complexity of your scene, the user’s hardware, and the browser’s implementation. Optimizing for performance is crucial.
  • Browser and Device Compatibility (Edge Cases): While generally well-supported, there can be subtle differences in how different browsers and devices handle WebGL. Older devices or browsers with limited GPU capabilities might struggle.
  • Security Considerations: As with any technology that interacts with hardware, there are potential security implications to be aware of, though these are generally well-managed by browser sandboxing.
  • Debugging Can Be Tricky: Debugging GPU-related issues can sometimes be more challenging than debugging standard JavaScript.

Features: The Building Blocks of WebGL Magic

Let's peek under the hood and see what makes WebGL tick. At its core, WebGL operates on a pipeline of rendering stages, processing data to create the final image you see. Here are some key concepts and features:

The Canvas Element: Your Digital Drawing Board

Every WebGL adventure begins with the humble HTML <canvas> element. This is where your 3D world will be rendered.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My First WebGL Scene</title>
    <style>
        body { margin: 0; overflow: hidden; } /* Remove default margin and scrollbars */
        canvas { display: block; } /* Ensure canvas takes up available space */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <canvas id="webglCanvas"></canvas>
    <script src="script.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

The Rendering Context: Your Gateway to the GPU

To draw on the canvas using WebGL, you need to get a special "rendering context" from the canvas element. This context is your interface to the WebGL API.

// script.js

const canvas = document.getElementById('webglCanvas');
let gl; // Declare gl variable

try {
    // Try to get the WebGL rendering context
    gl = canvas.getContext('webgl') || canvas.getContext('experimental-webgl');
} catch (e) {
    console.error("Unable to initialize WebGL. Your browser may not support it.");
}

if (gl) {
    console.log("WebGL context successfully obtained!");
    // Now you can start using 'gl' to interact with the GPU
} else {
    console.error("Failed to get WebGL context.");
}

Shaders: The Pixel-Level Painters

This is where the real artistry happens. WebGL uses two types of programs called shaders, written in a specialized language called GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language). Think of them as tiny programs that run directly on the GPU, controlling how individual pixels are drawn.

  • Vertex Shader: This shader deals with vertices – the points that define your 3D objects. It transforms these vertices in 3D space, determining their position on the screen. For example, it can rotate, scale, or move your objects.
  • Fragment Shader (or Pixel Shader): This shader determines the color of each individual pixel on your screen. It takes the information processed by the vertex shader and decides what color each pixel should be, considering things like lighting, textures, and material properties.

Here’s a super simplified example of a vertex and fragment shader. Note that in a real WebGL application, these are typically loaded as strings and compiled by the WebGL context.

Vertex Shader (Simplified GLSL):

attribute vec4 a_position; // Input vertex position

void main() {
    gl_Position = a_position; // Output the transformed position
}

Fragment Shader (Simplified GLSL):

void main() {
    gl_FragColor = vec4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); // Output a solid red color (R, G, B, Alpha)
}

You'll then combine these shaders to create a shader program that the GPU executes.

Buffers: Storing Your Geometric Data

To draw anything, you need to tell the GPU about the geometry. This is done by storing vertex data (positions, colors, texture coordinates, etc.) in buffers. You’ll typically use Float32Array to represent this data.

// Example of creating a buffer for vertex positions
const vertexBuffer = gl.createBuffer();
gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, vertexBuffer); // Bind the buffer to the ARRAY_BUFFER target

const vertices = new Float32Array([
    // Triangle 1
    0.0, 0.5, // Top
    -0.5, -0.5, // Bottom-left
    0.5, -0.5, // Bottom-right

    // Triangle 2 (example, not connected to the first for simplicity)
    -0.5, 0.0, // Left
    0.5, 0.0, // Right
    0.0, -0.5  // Bottom
]);

gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, vertices, gl.STATIC_DRAW); // Upload data to the buffer

Attributes and Uniforms: Passing Data to Shaders

  • Attributes: These are variables within your vertex shader that receive per-vertex data (like position, color, normals). You'll link your buffers to these attributes.
  • Uniforms: These are variables that have the same value for all vertices in a single draw call. They are used to pass global data to both vertex and fragment shaders, such as transformation matrices, lighting parameters, or texture samplers.

Textures: Adding Detail and Realism

Textures are images that you can wrap around your 3D objects to add intricate details, patterns, and realism. Think of them as wallpaper for your models. WebGL allows you to load and apply these textures.

Matrices and Transformations: Moving and Shaping Your World

As mentioned earlier, linear algebra plays a crucial role. You’ll use matrices to:

  • Model Matrix: Transforms an object from its local coordinate system to world space. This is how you position, rotate, and scale individual objects.
  • View Matrix: Defines the camera's position and orientation in the world. It essentially transforms world space to view space.
  • Projection Matrix: Defines how the 3D scene is projected onto the 2D screen. This includes setting up perspective (objects further away appear smaller) or orthographic (no perspective) views.

These matrices are often multiplied together to form a model-view-projection (MVP) matrix, which is a uniform variable passed to your vertex shader to perform all the necessary transformations.

Depth Testing: Ensuring Objects are Rendered Correctly

In a 3D scene, objects can overlap. Depth testing (also known as the Z-buffer) is a crucial feature that ensures that objects closer to the camera obscure objects further away, creating a realistic sense of depth.

A Tiny Glimpse of Code in Action

While a full WebGL application is a bit more involved, here’s a conceptual snippet demonstrating how you might set up a basic scene with a single colored triangle:

// This is a simplified conceptual example.
// Actual WebGL code involves more setup, shader compilation, etc.

// ... (Previous code for canvas and gl context) ...

function initShaders() {
    // Code to load, compile, and link vertex and fragment shaders
    // This is a significant part of WebGL development.
    // For brevity, we'll assume shaders are already compiled and linked
    // into a 'shaderProgram'.

    // Get attribute and uniform locations
    const positionAttributeLocation = gl.getAttribLocation(shaderProgram, 'a_position');
    const matrixUniformLocation = gl.getUniformLocation(shaderProgram, 'u_matrix');

    // Create and configure the vertex buffer
    const positionBuffer = gl.createBuffer();
    gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, positionBuffer);

    // Define vertices for a triangle
    const positions = new Float32Array([
        0.0, 0.5,
        -0.5, -0.5,
        0.5, -0.5,
    ]);
    gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, positions, gl.STATIC_DRAW);

    // Enable the attribute
    gl.enableVertexAttribArray(positionAttributeLocation);
    gl.vertexAttribPointer(positionAttributeLocation, 2, gl.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);

    // Create a simple transformation matrix (e.g., identity matrix for now)
    const matrix = mat4.create(); // Assuming you're using a math library like gl-matrix
    mat4.identity(matrix);

    // Set viewport and clear color
    gl.viewport(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
    gl.clearColor(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); // Black
    gl.clear(gl.COLOR_BUFFER_BIT | gl.DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT);

    // Use the shader program
    gl.useProgram(shaderProgram);

    // Set the uniform matrix
    gl.uniformMatrix4fv(matrixUniformLocation, false, matrix);

    // Draw the triangle
    const primitiveType = gl.TRIANGLES;
    const offset = 0;
    const count = 3; // 3 vertices for a triangle
    gl.drawArrays(primitiveType, offset, count);
}

// Call initShaders after setting up canvas and gl
// initShaders();

Note: This code snippet is highly simplified and assumes the existence of shaderProgram and a math library like gl-matrix for matrix operations. A real WebGL application would involve more detailed shader compilation, buffer setup, and drawing calls.

Beyond the Basics: Libraries and Frameworks

While you can build everything from scratch with raw WebGL, it’s a lot of work. Fortunately, the ecosystem has blossomed with powerful libraries and frameworks that abstract away much of the complexity:

  • Three.js: This is arguably the most popular WebGL library. It provides a high-level API for creating and displaying animated 3D computer graphics in the browser. It handles much of the boilerplate, making it easier to create scenes, load models, apply materials, and implement lighting and animation.
  • Babylon.js: Another robust and feature-rich framework for building 3D web applications. It offers a comprehensive set of tools for game development, visualizations, and more.
  • PlayCanvas: A cloud-powered, collaborative platform for creating 3D web experiences, with a strong focus on game development.

These libraries empower developers to focus on the creative aspects of their projects rather than getting bogged down in low-level graphics details.

Conclusion: Your Gateway to Interactive 3D on the Web

WebGL is a powerful technology that has revolutionized what's possible on the web. It allows us to move beyond static pages and experience dynamic, immersive, and interactive 3D content directly in our browsers.

While the initial learning curve might seem a little daunting, with a solid understanding of JavaScript and a willingness to explore the concepts of 3D graphics, you can begin your journey into this exciting world. Libraries like Three.js and Babylon.js are excellent starting points for building impressive 3D experiences without reinventing the wheel.

So, are you ready to unleash your creativity and bring your 3D ideas to life on the web? The canvas is waiting, and with WebGL, the possibilities are truly boundless. Happy coding, and may your pixels always be vibrant!
