title: Circuit Breakers Protect Callers from Failing Dependencies
description:
A payment service slows down. Checkout continues sending requests and waiting for timeouts. Lab 14 places a circuit breaker before the payment client so repeated failures can stop subsequent attempts.

A circuit breaker protects the caller; it does not repair the dependency.

The lab uses real local HTTP through an httptest fake server. It does not perform real payments, balance mutations, or production gateway integration.

The implemented path

Checkout calls Breaker.Execute, whose callback calls payment.Client.ProcessPayment. The client sends POST /pay. The fake server supports HEALTHY (200), DOWN (500), and SLOW (sleep, then 200).

The README motivates the pattern with cascading resource exhaustion. The tests demonstrate narrower behavior: state transitions, callback rejection, HTTP request counts, timeout errors, and recovery probes. They do not measure thread exhaustion, memory pressure, or a platform-wide outage.

CLOSED counts consecutive failures

The breaker starts CLOSED and admits callbacks. A successful completion resets its failure count. A nonnil error increments it; reaching the threshold opens the circuit:

// circuit_breaker.go: onFailureLocked excerpt
b.failures++
if b.failures >= b.cfg.FailureThreshold {
    b.state = Open
    b.openedAt = now
    b.generation++
}

This is a consecutive-error counter, not a sliding-window failure rate. With concurrent calls, valid completion order determines the counter updates.

Defaults are three failures, a 300 ms cooldown, and one HALF_OPEN call. New substitutes defaults for nonpositive values. These are lab settings, not universal production recommendations.

Callbacks execute outside the mutex. CLOSED has no general in-flight limit, so a concurrent burst can dispatch more requests than the threshold before the first failures complete. A circuit breaker is not automatically a bulkhead.

OPEN rejects before invoking the callback 

// circuit_breaker.go: Execute state branch
case Open:
    b.mu.Unlock()
    return ErrCircuitOpen

During OPEN before cooldown expires, no callback runs. When the callback wraps the payment client, that rejected call produces no new network request. TestOpenDoesNotCallDownstream checks one initial failed callback followed by five rejections, with the callback count remaining one.

Already admitted calls are not canceled. “No downstream calls while rejecting” is different from claiming no older request is still running.

Cooldown advancement is lazy

There is no background timer that sleeps and sends a probe. Both State() and Execute() call advanceLocked. Once enough time has elapsed since openedAt, the state becomes HALF_OPEN, the probe counter resets, and the generation increases.

Calling State() can therefore mutate state. An expired cooldown does not itself dispatch a recovery request; a later admitted Execute does that.

HALF_OPEN limits admission, not the number of successes required 

// circuit_breaker.go: HALF_OPEN branch
case HalfOpen:
    if b.halfOpenIn >= b.cfg.HalfOpenMaxCalls {
        b.mu.Unlock()
        return ErrCircuitOpen
    }
    b.halfOpenIn++

Extra calls receive the same ErrCircuitOpen used for OPEN. The error alone does not distinguish an open circuit from a full probe allowance.

One successful probe closes the breaker. One failed probe reopens it and restarts cooldown. When the configured allowance exceeds one, the implementation does not wait for every admitted probe to succeed: the first state-changing result advances the generation, making remaining old results stale.

That is a specific recovery policy, not a requirement for N consecutive successful probes.

Generation guards separate old work from new state

Execute captures a generation before releasing the mutex to run the callback. Result bookkeeping begins with this guard:

// circuit_breaker.go: result bookkeeping guard
if b.generation != gen {
    return
}

A trailing request from an earlier generation cannot reset or reopen a newer state. The trailing-in-flight test starts a slow CLOSED request, opens the circuit using another request, advances to HALF_OPEN, and checks that the old failure does not corrupt HALF_OPEN.

The old callback still runs and its error still returns to its caller. Generation filtering changes its authority to update breaker state; it is not cancellation.

Panic cleanup does not swallow panic

Deferred bookkeeping treats a callback panic as a failure, including reopening HALF_OPEN. The panic continues to the caller rather than becoming an ordinary returned error. The test recovers outside the breaker and checks that a later recovery probe can run.

This prevents a probe panic from leaving the breaker permanently stuck with its allowance consumed, while preserving the panic's normal propagation.

Timeouts remain necessary

The HTTP client has a configured timeout. Checkout(ctx) passes the caller's context into the payment request; the two demo helpers use context.Background().

Breaker.Execute itself has no context argument or execution deadline. An admitted callback can still wait indefinitely without its own timeout, including a HALF_OPEN probe occupying a slot.

Retry and exponential backoff are discussed in the README but not implemented in this client or checkout service. The breaker does not schedule retries or automatically control an external retry loop. It only admits or rejects each callback evaluation.

The fake SLOW handler sleeps without checking request cancellation. A client timeout is therefore not proof that the server has stopped its work.

Failure classification is intentionally broad

The client accepts only HTTP 200. Every other status becomes ErrPaymentFailed; transport errors, timeouts, and cancellation also return errors. The breaker counts all nonnil errors without classification, so a 4xx or canceled request can affect the threshold if it reaches this path.

A 200 response is not decoded to validate payment business semantics. A successful probe means this client returned nil, not that a real transaction was completed correctly.

Read the demo as four scenarios, not one benchmark

The first scenario uses SLOW with a 200 ms server delay and a 100 ms client timeout, making three sequential calls without a breaker. The second uses DOWN responses, a threshold of three, and six sequential calls with a breaker.

Those are different failure modes. They should not be presented as a controlled latency benchmark of an identical workload. The N × timeout approximation describes sequential waiting, not general concurrent request latency.

The third scenario makes the server HEALTHY before probing and demonstrates HALF_OPEN → CLOSED. The fourth keeps it DOWN and demonstrates HALF_OPEN → OPEN.

Nanosecond or microsecond durations shown in the README are example output, not a latency guarantee or a newly measured result here.

Fallback must preserve business meaning

The implemented checkout returns an error on payment failure or rejection. It has no cached success, queue, or automatic alternative payment flow.

The README's CMMS and PPOB examples discuss critical versus noncritical dependencies. Invoice creation, WhatsApp delivery, provider fulfillment, queue retention, and debit protection are architectural discussion, not implemented workflows in this folder.

A fast payment rejection still means checkout has failed. The breaker reduces futile attempts; it does not manufacture a successful payment during an outage.

What the tests and instrumentation establish

Unit tests cover thresholds, success resets, rejected callbacks, cooldown, both probe outcomes, probe limits, panic cleanup, stale generations, and concurrent access. Integration tests use the HTTP fake server to check 500 responses, recovery, request counts, and slow-call timeouts.

The general concurrency test checks a valid final state. The interleaved test waits for goroutines without additional semantic assertions. A race-detector run can provide evidence about executed paths, but does not independently prove every interleaving or policy.

Production gauges, open/rejected counters, and dependency latency percentiles are recommendations in the README. This implementation exposes state and the fake server's request counter, not a production metrics exporter.

cd labs/14-circuit-breaker
go test -v ./...
go test -race ./...
go run ./cmd/demo

The module declares Go 1.22. Go is unavailable in this authoring environment, so I inspected code and assertions rather than rerunning the tests. No new passing-test result or benchmark is claimed.

The reusable lesson is to bound permitted calls and interpret recovery precisely: timeout limits waiting, the breaker controls subsequent admission, and probes decide whether that path should reopen.

Source

Software Engineering Lab 14, snapshot commit 82af988b89439fa92b1200406c5afbd59ce72a56: README, circuit breaker implementation/tests, payment client/fake server, checkout service, integration tests, demo, and go.mod. Excerpts belong in their existing package context.

title: Your AI Agent Is Smart. So Why Shouldn't You Trust It?
description:
Why AI Agents Should Preview Changes Before Executing Them

Because understanding a request and safely executing it are two different things.

Imagine building an AI assistant that manages calendar events.

A user asks:

“Clear my Tuesday and move everything to next week.”

The AI understands the instruction. It identifies the events and proposes new dates. Everything seems fine.

But should the application immediately update the calendar?

Not necessarily.

AI Agents Can Make Real Changes

Modern AI assistants can do much more than answer questions. They can modify records, create tasks, delete information, and trigger workflows.

That makes them powerful. It also means mistakes can have real consequences.

What if the assistant moves an important meeting? What if the user meant only personal tasks? What if the proposed schedule conflicts with another commitment?

Even when an AI generates a reasonable plan, executing it without review can lead to unexpected results.

The Human-in-the-Loop Pattern

At ByDesign, AI scheduling follows a preview-first approach.

Instead of immediately applying generated changes, the application presents a proposed schedule for the user to review.

The workflow looks like this:

User Request → AI Generates a Plan → Preview Changes → User Reviews → Accept and Schedule

The user can inspect the proposed changes before they are applied. This creates a clear separation between generating a plan and committing changes to persistent data.

The AI can suggest what should happen, while the user remains in control of whether those changes should be applied.

Why This Pattern Matters

Human-in-the-loop design provides three important benefits.

1. Transparency

Users can see what the AI intends to change before those changes take effect.

2. Control

Users can review the proposed schedule, identify mistakes, and adjust the plan before accepting it.

3. Trust

Important changes are not silently applied. Users have a clear opportunity to understand and approve the outcome.

ByDesign also includes undo behavior and confirmation for destructive actions, helping users recover from mistakes and make important changes more deliberately.

The Bigger Lesson

Not every AI action needs manual approval. Low-risk actions may be handled automatically when the user has clearly authorized them.

However, when an AI agent can modify important user data, it is worth considering whether an action should be previewable, reversible, or explicitly confirmed.

The right approach depends on the impact of the action, the user's intent, and the consequences of getting it wrong.

A reliable AI agent isn't one that acts without hesitation. It's one that knows when to ask.

title: TanStack Start 1.0 + tanstack-fetch: 6 Real-World Data Fetching Patterns
description:
TanStack Start is officially stable. If you have been waiting for the 1.0 release before building a production application, now is a good time to explore the framework.

But getting a full-stack React application running is only the first step. The more interesting engineering decisions come later:

  • Where should an API request run: in a route loader, on the server, or in the browser?
  • How do you avoid fetching the same data twice?
  • How should server-side rendering handle cookies and authorization?
  • How do mutations update the existing Query cache?
  • What happens when an API returns an HTTP error?
  • How can a page combine REST data with live server-sent events?

In this tutorial, we'll explore these scenarios using TanStack Start, TanStack Router, TanStack Query, and tanstack-fetch.

I'm the creator of tanstack-fetch, an HTTP client designed to work with TanStack Query's server-state model. It is an independent community package, not an official TanStack project.

1. Start with the right mental model

These libraries solve different problems:

  • TanStack Start provides the full-stack application framework, including server rendering and server functions.
  • TanStack Router coordinates routes, navigation, search parameters, and loaders.
  • TanStack Query manages server-state caching, freshness, mutations, and background updates.
  • tanstack-fetch handles HTTP requests, typed responses and errors, and reusable request behavior.

The important distinction is that an HTTP client and a server-state manager should not compete for the same responsibilities.

TanStack Query owns the cache. The HTTP client executes requests.

Install the core dependencies:

npm install tanstack-fetch @tanstack/react-query

Follow the current TanStack Start and Router documentation for the framework-specific setup and SSR integration:

  • TanStack Start documentation
  • tanstack-fetch documentation

2. Pattern one: Fetch data directly

Not every request needs a complicated abstraction.

For a simple client-side request, create a reusable API client:

// src/lib/api.ts
import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'

export const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl: '/api',
})

Then use it in a component or a query function:

import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'
import { api } from '~/lib/api'

type User = {
  id: string
  name: string
}

export function Users() {
  const usersQuery = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['users'],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
      api.get<User[]>('/users', { signal }),
  })

  if (usersQuery.isPending) {
    return <p>Loading users...</p>
  }

  if (usersQuery.isError) {
    return <p>Could not load users.</p>
  }

  return (
    <ul>
      {usersQuery.data.map((user) => (
        <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

Three details matter here:

  1. The response is typed as User[].
  2. The query function passes Query's AbortSignal to the HTTP client.
  3. HTTP failures should reject the query so Query can represent them through its error state.

Passing the signal also allows an obsolete request to be cancelled when appropriate.

When to use this pattern: Client-side widgets, independent requests, and pages that do not need route-level preloading.

3. Pattern two: Share route loaders and Query cache

This is where TanStack Router and TanStack Query become particularly useful together.

A common implementation fetches data in a loader, then makes another request when the component mounts. Another implementation stores loader data separately from Query's cache.

Both approaches can be valid, but they introduce extra synchronization work when the same resource is used across routes or components.

Instead, define reusable query options:

// src/queries/users.ts
import { queryOptions } from '@tanstack/react-query'
import { api } from '~/lib/api'

export const usersQueryOptions = queryOptions({
  queryKey: ['users'],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
    api.get<User[]>('/users', { signal }),
  staleTime: 30_000,
})

Use the same options in the route loader and component:

import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router'
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'
import { usersQueryOptions } from '~/queries/users'

export const Route = createFileRoute('/users')({
  loader: ({ context }) =>
    context.queryClient.ensureQueryData(
      usersQueryOptions,
    ),
  component: UsersPage,
})

function UsersPage() {
  const { data: users } = useQuery(usersQueryOptions)

  return (
    <ul>
      {users?.map((user) => (
        <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

The router must expose the appropriate queryClient through its typed context, and the application must configure the Query provider and, when using SSR, the appropriate Router–Query integration.

The result is a shared contract:

  • The loader can ensure that data is available before the route renders.
  • The component reads from the same Query cache.
  • Other components can reuse the same query options.
  • Query controls freshness and subsequent refetching.

This does not mean a network request can never happen again. A stale query, invalidation, or an explicit refetch can legitimately trigger one. The goal is to avoid unnecessary duplicate fetching and separate caches.

When to use this pattern: Lists, detail pages, nested routes, dashboards, and resources shared across multiple components.

4. Pattern three: Handle SSR and authenticated requests

Server-side rendering introduces a different problem: the server does not automatically inherit the browser's request context when it calls an external API.

If an upstream API requires the incoming request's cookies or authorization headers, the HTTP client needs an explicit server-side strategy.

tanstack-fetch supports an ssr-forward plugin for forwarding request context.

A server-aware client can be configured like this:

// Illustrative server-side setup
import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'

export const createServerApi = (
  apiOrigin: string,
  cookie: string | undefined,
) =>
  createFetch({
    baseUrl: `${apiOrigin}/api`,
    source: 'ssr',
    plugins: ['ssr-forward'],
    incoming: () => ({ cookie }),
  })

This example illustrates the configuration pattern. Obtain the cookie from the actual incoming request using the relevant TanStack Start server API, and create the client in the request's server-side execution context.

For a real application:

  • Use an absolute API origin on the server.
  • Read credentials from the incoming request, not from a global variable.
  • Never expose private environment variables or server-only credentials to the browser.
  • Avoid sharing user-specific API clients or Query caches across SSR requests.
  • Forward only the headers that the upstream service actually needs.

A server-side request may also need to preserve an authorization header or request ID. Those should be forwarded deliberately rather than copying every incoming header.

When to use this pattern: Personalized SSR pages, authenticated dashboards, and applications whose API uses cookie-based sessions.

5. Pattern four: Mutations and cache invalidation

Fetching data is only half of a data layer. The other half is keeping the UI consistent after writes.

Suppose an application creates a user. The mutation should use the same HTTP client and invalidate the query that represents the user list.

import {
  useMutation,
  useQueryClient,
} from '@tanstack/react-query'
import { api } from '~/lib/api'

type CreateUserInput = {
  name: string
}

type User = {
  id: string
  name: string
}

export function CreateUserButton() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient()

  const createUser = useMutation({
    mutationFn: (input: CreateUserInput) =>
      api.post<User>('/users', { body: input }),

    onSuccess: () =>
      queryClient.invalidateQueries({
        queryKey: ['users'],
      }),
  })

  return (
    <button
      disabled={createUser.isPending}
      onClick={() =>
        createUser.mutate({ name: 'New user' })
      }
    >
      {createUser.isPending ? 'Creating...' : 'Create user'}
    </button>
  )
}

The example assumes the application has already configured the appropriate Query provider.

Invalidation marks matching cached queries as stale and allows active queries to refetch according to Query's behavior. It does not blindly replace every cached copy of the data.

For more responsive interfaces, optimistic updates may be appropriate. However, they need a rollback strategy when the mutation fails and careful handling when concurrent updates are possible.

When to use this pattern: Forms, CRUD screens, admin panels, and any UI where a write affects previously fetched data.

6. Pattern five: Centralize HTTP errors and authentication behavior

HTTP errors should have predictable semantics across the application.

A 401 Unauthorized response might indicate that a session has expired. A 403 Forbidden response generally means that the caller is authenticated but lacks permission. A 404 means the resource was not found.

These conditions should not all trigger the same recovery action.

A reusable HTTP client gives you a place to configure error handling and interceptors instead of repeating that logic in every query function.

For example, a refresh-token interceptor can coordinate token refresh and retry eligible failed requests:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'
import {
  createRefreshTokenInterceptor,
} from 'tanstack-fetch/plugins'

const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl: '/api',
})

api.use(
  'refresh-token',
  createRefreshTokenInterceptor({
    refresh: async () => {
      // Refresh the session using your authentication flow.
      // Store updated credentials according to your
      // application's security model.
    },
  }),
)

The refresh implementation is application-specific. It must actually obtain and persist or update the new credential before a retry can succeed.

A production implementation should also consider:

  • Concurrent requests that fail while a refresh is in progress.
  • Refresh failure and session expiry.
  • Avoiding recursive refresh requests.
  • Which HTTP methods are safe to retry.
  • Cross-tab session changes.
  • Whether credentials are stored in secure, HttpOnly cookies or another appropriate mechanism.

Do not redirect to login on every error. In particular, a 403 should not automatically trigger logout, and a 404 should not be treated as an expired session.

When to use this pattern: Applications with authentication, protected APIs, consistent error handling, and several features that share the same backend.

7. Pattern six: Combine REST queries with live SSE updates

Some pages need both an initial snapshot and a stream of updates.

Examples include notifications, order tracking, live dashboards, and operational monitoring.

A useful architecture is:

  1. Load the initial resource through REST or another regular API.
  2. Use TanStack Query to cache and manage that resource.
  3. Open a server-sent events connection in the browser.
  4. Update the cache when an event arrives, or invalidate the relevant query when the event is incomplete.

tanstack-fetch provides SSE support through its tanstack-fetch/sse integration.

The exact event handling depends on the shape of your API. For a complete entity update, you may be able to update the cache directly:

queryClient.setQueryData(
  ['order', orderId],
  updatedOrder,
)

If the event only tells you that an order changed, invalidating the query is usually safer:

queryClient.invalidateQueries({
  queryKey: ['order', orderId],
})

An SSE reconnect does not prove that no events were missed. If you need reliable recovery, design the protocol around event IDs, replay or resume support, and a strategy for reconciling the current snapshot.

For authenticated streams, verify how credentials are transported. The browser's native EventSource API does not provide a general option for setting arbitrary authorization headers; a fetch-based SSE client can be useful when those headers are required.

When to use this pattern: Live dashboards, event-driven interfaces, and pages where server state changes without a user action.

8. What about Server Functions?

TanStack Start Server Functions are useful for server-only logic that your own application invokes across the client/server boundary.

For example, they can wrap a database operation or access server-only environment variables.

They are not interchangeable with a generic HTTP client.

Use a Server Function when the operation belongs to the application's server logic. Use an HTTP client when communicating with a REST API or another HTTP service. Use Server Routes when you need endpoints intended to be called externally or across origins.

If you combine Server Functions with TanStack Query, keep validation, authorization, and cache invalidation explicit. The server boundary does not remove the need for security checks.

9. A practical project structure

One possible structure is:

src/
  lib/
    api.ts
  queries/
    users.ts
    orders.ts
  routes/
    users.tsx
    orders.$orderId.tsx
  components/
    create-user-button.tsx

The exact folders are less important than keeping responsibilities clear:

  • lib/api.ts owns reusable HTTP configuration.
  • queries/ owns shared query keys, options, and request functions.
  • routes/ owns navigation and route-level data requirements.
  • components/ owns UI behavior and presentation.

For SSR, keep request-specific clients and caches scoped to the request. Do not turn a convenience singleton into a cross-user data leak.

10. How should you choose?

Requirement Recommended approach
Simple browser request createFetch + useQuery
Route-level preloading queryOptions + ensureQueryData
Authenticated SSR Request-scoped client + ssr-forward
Writes and stale cached data useMutation + invalidation
Shared HTTP error policy Client configuration and plugins
Live server updates SSE + Query cache
Server-only application logic TanStack Start Server Functions
Public HTTP endpoint Server Routes or a dedicated API

You do not need to adopt every pattern at once. Start with one API client and shared query options. Add SSR forwarding, mutation strategies, and live updates only when the application needs them.

Final thoughts

TanStack Start 1.0 makes this a good moment to evaluate a full-stack React architecture, but a stable framework does not automatically give you a maintainable data layer.

The important part is choosing clear boundaries: Router coordinates navigation, Query owns server-state caching, the HTTP client owns transport concerns, and the server owns privileged operations.

That's the problem space tanstack-fetch is designed to address. It is not a replacement for TanStack Query or TanStack Start; it is an option for standardizing HTTP behavior alongside them.

Explore the project:

  • tanstack-fetch documentation
  • TanStack Start documentation
  • TanStack Query integration guide

If you're building with TanStack Start, which part of the data layer has required the most work in your project: SSR, authentication, caching, or real-time updates?

title: Java Stream API for Beginners: From Loops to Pipelines
description:
For a long time, my Java code for "take this list, keep the long names, make them uppercase, collect the result" was six lines of loop, an if and a temporary list. Then I saw this:

names.stream().filter(n -> n.length() > 2).map(String::toUpperCase).toList();

One line. It read almost like English, but it also raised questions. What is a stream? What does String::toUpperCase mean? And why do some methods in this style return something called Optional instead of just the value?

In this post, we'll answer those questions in order: method references and constructor references (the :: syntax), the Stream API, and the Optional class. They fit together, so by the end you'll be able to read and write the one-liner above with confidence. If you haven't read about lambdas, skim that first, because everything here builds on them.

All the snippets assume these imports and go inside a main method unless I show a full class:

import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

Part 1: Method references and constructor references

A method reference is a shorter way to write a lambda that does nothing except call one existing method. You write the class (or object), then ::, then the method name, with no brackets.

s -> s.length()         // lambda
String::length          // method reference, same meaning

There are four kinds. Here they are with their lambda twins:

   KIND                          REFERENCE              SAME AS THIS LAMBDA
   1. static method              Integer::parseInt      s -> Integer.parseInt(s)
   2. method of a given object   prefix::concat         s -> prefix.concat(s)
   3. method of "any" object     String::length         s -> s.length()
      of a type
   4. constructor                Person::new            n -> new Person(n)

Let's see them one by one:

// 1. static method
Function<String, Integer> parse = Integer::parseInt;
System.out.println(parse.apply("42") + 1);

// 2. method of a specific object we already have
String prefix = "Hello, ";
Function<String, String> greet = prefix::concat;
System.out.println(greet.apply("Asha"));

// 3. method of an object that will be given to us later
Function<String, Integer> len = String::length;
System.out.println(len.apply("lambda"));

BiFunction<String, String, Boolean> same = String::equalsIgnoreCase;
System.out.println(same.apply("Java", "JAVA"));

Output:

43
Hello, Asha
6
true

Kind 3 is the one that confuses people. In String::length, no object is named, so where does the string come from? From the first parameter of the functional interface. Function<String, Integer> gives us one String, and Java calls .length() on it. In String::equalsIgnoreCase, the first parameter is the object, and the second is the argument: (a, b) -> a.equalsIgnoreCase(b).

Constructor references

A constructor reference uses ::new. It's a lambda that creates an object:

class Person {
    private final String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Person(" + name + ")";
    }
}

Function<String, Person> maker = Person::new;
Supplier<List<String>> listMaker = ArrayList::new;
IntFunction<int[]> arrayMaker = int[]::new;

System.out.println(maker.apply("Asha"));

List<String> list = listMaker.get();
list.add("x");
System.out.println(list);

System.out.println(arrayMaker.apply(3).length);

Output:

Person(Asha)
[x]
3

How does Java know which constructor Person::new means? It looks at the functional interface. Function<String, Person> takes a String, so Java picks Person(String). Supplier<List<String>> takes nothing, so ArrayList::new means the no-argument constructor. The same words, ArrayList::new, can mean different constructors depending on the target type.

Behind the scenes

Method references work like lambdas. The compiler doesn't create a separate class for them. It writes an invokedynamic instruction, and the JVM builds the function object at run time. The compiler picks the method by matching the parameter types of the functional interface. If two methods could fit, you get an "ambiguous method reference" error, and the fix is to write a normal lambda.

Use a method reference when it makes the code shorter and clearer. If the lambda does more than one call, or the reference looks cryptic, keep the arrow form.

Part 2: The Stream API

What is a stream?

A stream is a pipeline for processing a sequence of data, usually from a collection. It's not a data structure. It doesn't store anything, and it never changes the original collection. Think of a factory conveyor belt: items come in, pass through stations and come out the other end.

Every stream pipeline has three parts:

   SOURCE            INTERMEDIATE operations           TERMINAL operation
   (where data   -->  (each one returns a stream)  -->  (produces a result
    comes from)                                          and starts the work)

   list.stream()  --> filter(...) --> map(...) --> sorted() --> collect(...) / count() / forEach(...)
  • Source: list.stream(), Arrays.stream(array), Stream.of(...), IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5) and others.
  • Intermediate operations: filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, flatMap. Each one returns a new stream, so you can chain them.
  • Terminal operation: collect, toList, forEach, count, sum, reduce, min, max, findFirst, anyMatch and others. It ends the pipeline.

From a loop to a stream

Here's the task from my intro, done the old way and the stream way:

List<String> names = List.of("Meera", "Jo", "Ravi", "Asha", "Jo");

// the old way
List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
for (String n : names) {
    if (n.length() > 2) {
        result.add(n.toUpperCase());
    }
}

// the stream way
List<String> result2 = names.stream()
        .filter(n -> n.length() > 2)
        .map(String::toUpperCase)
        .toList();

System.out.println(result2);

Output:

[MEERA, RAVI, ASHA]
  • filter keeps the items where the condition is true (a Predicate).
  • map transforms each item into something else (a Function).
  • toList() collects the result into a list. (It needs Java 16 or newer. In older versions, write .collect(Collectors.toList()).)

The stream version says what you want. The loop says how to do it step by step.

The operations you'll use most 

List<Integer> nums = List.of(5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 9, 8);

System.out.println(nums.stream().distinct().sorted().limit(4).toList());
System.out.println(nums.stream().filter(n -> n > 4).count());
System.out.println(nums.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum());
System.out.println(nums.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum));
System.out.println(nums.stream().max(Integer::compare));
System.out.println(nums.stream().anyMatch(n -> n > 8));

Output:

[1, 3, 5, 8]
4
37
37
Optional[9]
true

Let's read them:

  • distinct().sorted().limit(4) removed duplicates, sorted, then kept the first four.
  • count() counted the numbers bigger than 4 (5, 8, 9, 8).
  • mapToInt(...).sum() and reduce(0, Integer::sum) both add everything up. reduce repeatedly combines two values into one, starting from 0.
  • max(...) returns an Optional, which we'll meet in the next part. Here it printed as Optional[9].
  • anyMatch checks whether at least one item passes. (allMatch and noneMatch work the same way.)

A tip: for numbers, prefer mapToInt(...) and the primitive streams (IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream). They avoid the boxing cost we discussed in the wrapper classes topic, and they give you sum(), average() and similar methods for free.

Collecting results: Collectors

collect takes a collector, a recipe for building the final result:

List<String> names = List.of("Meera", "Jo", "Ravi", "Asha", "Jo");

System.out.println(names.stream().distinct()
        .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]")));

Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength = names.stream().distinct()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
System.out.println(byLength);

Map<String, Long> frequency = names.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(n -> n, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
System.out.println(frequency);

Output:

[Meera, Jo, Ravi, Asha]
{2=[Jo], 4=[Ravi, Asha], 5=[Meera]}
{Asha=1, Jo=2, Meera=1, Ravi=1}
  • joining glued the names into one string.
  • groupingBy made a map from each key (the length) to the list of items that share it.
  • counting counted the items in each group.

Look closely at TreeMap::new. That's a constructor reference from earlier, used to say "put the result in a TreeMap," so the keys come out sorted.

flatMap: flattening nested lists

When each item turns into several items, or you have a list of lists, use flatMap:

List<List<Integer>> nested = List.of(List.of(1, 2), List.of(3), List.of(4, 5));

List<Integer> flat = nested.stream()
        .flatMap(List::stream)
        .toList();

System.out.println(flat);

Output:

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

map would give you a stream of streams. flatMap merges them into one.

Streams are lazy

This is the most surprising thing about streams. Intermediate operations do nothing until a terminal operation starts the pipeline:

Stream<String> s = Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
        .filter(x -> {
            System.out.println("filter " + x);
            return x.length() > 1;
        });

System.out.println("Nothing printed yet");
s.forEach(x -> System.out.println("got " + x));

Output:

Nothing printed yet
filter a
filter bb
got bb
filter ccc
got ccc

Two lessons are hidden here:

  1. Nothing ran when we built the pipeline. The filter code only ran after forEach, the terminal operation, started the work.
  2. Each item travels through the whole pipeline before the next one starts. It's not "filter everything, then print everything." It's item by item: 
   "a"    -> filter (fails)  -> stops here
   "bb"   -> filter (passes) -> forEach prints "got bb"
   "ccc"  -> filter (passes) -> forEach prints "got ccc"

Laziness also allows short-circuiting. Operations like findFirst and limit can stop early:

Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
        .filter(n -> {
            System.out.println("check " + n);
            return n % 2 == 0;
        })
        .findFirst()
        .ifPresent(n -> System.out.println("first even: " + n));

Output:

check 1
check 2
first even: 2

It never even looked at 3, 4 or 5.

Streams can be used only once

After a terminal operation, the stream is finished:

Stream<Integer> s = Stream.of(1, 2, 3);
s.forEach(System.out::println);
s.forEach(System.out::println);

1
2
3
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed

If you need it again, create a new stream from the source.

Behind the scenes

When you chain filter(...) and map(...), Java doesn't process any data. It just builds a chain of stages, like a recipe. Only when the terminal operation runs does it pull items from the source through all the stages. Because of this, the stages can be fused into one pass over the data, and short-circuit operations can stop early. A few operations, like sorted(), need to see all items before they can pass any on, so they act as a wall in the pipeline.

Also, the lambdas you write become the standard functional interfaces we learned about: Predicate for filter, Function for map, Consumer for forEach.

Two rules keep streams safe: don't change the source while a pipeline runs, and avoid side effects inside the lambdas (like adding to an outside list). Use collect to build results instead.

You may also see .parallelStream(), which splits the work across several threads. It can speed up big, CPU-heavy jobs, but for small data it's usually slower, and shared mutable state can cause bugs. Don't reach for it by default.

Part 3: The Optional class

The problem: null

You've probably met this error many times:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException

It happens when a method returns null ("no result") and the caller forgets to check. The method signature String findEmail(String user) doesn't tell you that null is possible. You only find out when the program crashes.

Optional<T> fixes this by making "maybe no value" visible in the type. It's a small container that either holds one value or is empty. When you see Optional<String> as a return type, you know right away: "there might be nothing here, and I must deal with that."

Creating an Optional 

Optional<String> a = Optional.of("Asha");           // value must NOT be null
Optional<String> b = Optional.ofNullable(null);     // null becomes "empty"
Optional<String> c = Optional.empty();              // explicitly empty

System.out.println(a);
System.out.println(b);

Output:

Optional[Asha]
Optional.empty

Use ofNullable when the value might be null. Optional.of(null) throws a NullPointerException immediately.

Using an Optional

Don't pull the value out and test it by hand. Use the methods that handle both cases for you:

Optional<String> name = Optional.of("Asha");
Optional<String> none = Optional.empty();

System.out.println(name.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("unknown"));
System.out.println(none.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("unknown"));

name.ifPresent(n -> System.out.println("Hello " + n));
none.ifPresentOrElse(
        n -> System.out.println("Hello " + n),
        () -> System.out.println("No name"));

Output:

ASHA
unknown
Hello Asha
No name

The main tools:

  • map(...) transforms the value if there is one, and does nothing if empty.
  • filter(...) keeps the value only if it passes a test.
  • orElse(default) gives the value, or a default.
  • orElseGet(supplier) gives the value, or calls a supplier to make a default.
  • orElseThrow(...) gives the value, or throws an exception you choose.
  • ifPresent(...) and ifPresentOrElse(...) run code depending on the case.
  • isPresent() and isEmpty() check without reading.
  • get() returns the value, but throws NoSuchElementException if empty. Avoid it.

A real example: a method that returns Optional 

static Optional<String> findEmail(String user) {
    Map<String, String> emails = Map.of("asha", "asha@example.com");
    return Optional.ofNullable(emails.get(user));
}

System.out.println(findEmail("asha").orElse("no email"));
System.out.println(findEmail("ravi").orElse("no email"));

findEmail("ravi").ifPresentOrElse(
        e -> System.out.println("Email: " + e),
        () -> System.out.println("Missing"));

Output:

asha@example.com
no email
Missing

Notice that the caller can't forget the empty case. The type forces the question.

Chaining instead of nested null checks

Optional shines when you chain steps that each might fail:

static String clean(String input) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(input)
            .map(String::trim)
            .filter(s -> !s.isEmpty())
            .map(String::toUpperCase)
            .orElse("EMPTY");
}

System.out.println(clean("  hi "));
System.out.println(clean("   "));
System.out.println(clean(null));

Output:

HI
EMPTY
EMPTY

The same logic with if (input != null) { ... } would take several nested checks. Here, if any step fails (null, or blank after trimming), the whole chain turns into "empty" and falls to orElse.

orElse vs orElseGet: a hidden trap 

static String expensive() {
    System.out.println("computing default");
    return "default";
}

Optional<String> present = Optional.of("value");

System.out.println(present.orElse(expensive()));
System.out.println(present.orElseGet(() -> expensive()));

Output:

computing default
value
value

Even though the Optional had a value, the first line still ran expensive(). With orElse, Java computes the argument before the call, whether it's needed or not. With orElseGet, you pass a Supplier, and it runs only if the Optional is empty. For cheap constants, orElse is fine. For anything that does real work, use orElseGet.

Optional and streams

You already met Optional in the stream section: findFirst, max, min and reduce (the version without a starting value) all return one, because a stream might be empty:

List<Integer> nums = List.of(5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 9, 8);

System.out.println(nums.stream().filter(n -> n > 100).findFirst());
System.out.println(nums.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).average());
System.out.println(nums.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).average().orElse(0));

Output:

Optional.empty
OptionalDouble[5.285714285714286]
5.285714285714286

Primitive streams have their own versions: OptionalInt, OptionalLong and OptionalDouble.

Behind the scenes

Optional isn't magic. It's a small final class with one field holding the value, which is null when empty. The empty case is one shared object, so Optional.empty() doesn't create a new one each time.

   Optional.of("Asha")   ->  [ Optional | value --> "Asha" ]
   Optional.empty()      ->  the shared EMPTY object [ Optional | value = null ]

Because it's an extra object, it has a small cost. And it's meant for one job only: return types that mean "might have no result." That leads to a few guidelines:

  • Don't use Optional for fields, method parameters or items inside collections. Just use normal types, or overloads.
  • Don't return an Optional of a collection. Return an empty list instead.
  • Never return null from a method whose return type is Optional.
  • Don't write if (opt.isPresent()) { opt.get() }. That's just a null check in disguise. Use map, orElse or ifPresent.

Which one should I use?

  • Lambda or method reference? Use a method reference when the lambda only calls one method and the result is clearer (String::toUpperCase). Use a lambda when there's more logic.
  • Loop or stream? Use a stream for transform-filter-collect jobs, since it reads clearly. Keep a loop when you need break, an index, several changing variables or the simplest possible code. Don't force a stream into a job where it makes the code harder to read.
  • toList() or collect(Collectors.toList())? On Java 16 or newer, toList() is shorter, but the result can't be modified. If you need a changeable list, use collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new)).
  • map or mapToInt? For numeric work (sums, averages), mapToInt avoids boxing and gives you sum() and average().
  • orElse, orElseGet or orElseThrow? orElse for cheap defaults, orElseGet for computed ones and orElseThrow when "empty" is truly an error.
  • Optional or null? Use Optional as a return type when "no result" is a normal answer. Don't use it everywhere.

Common mistakes

  1. Forgetting the terminal operation. list.stream().filter(...).map(...) alone does nothing, because the pipeline never starts. Always end with toList(), collect, forEach, count or similar.
  2. Reusing a stream. After a terminal operation, it's closed. You'll get IllegalStateException. Make a new stream from the source.
  3. Changing things from inside a stream. Adding to an outside list in forEach, or modifying the source collection, causes confusing bugs. Let collect build your result.
  4. Calling get() on an Optional without checking, or using Optional.of(null). Both throw exceptions. Prefer orElse... and ofNullable.
  5. Using orElse with an expensive call. It always runs, even when the value is present. Use orElseGet.
  6. Writing huge, unreadable chains, or using parallelStream() by default. If a pipeline needs a comment to explain it, split it into named steps. Parallel streams help only for large, CPU-heavy work.

Quick recap

  • A method reference (Class::method) is a short lambda. There are four kinds: static, specific object, "any object of a type" and constructor (::new).
  • A constructor reference picks the constructor that matches the functional interface's parameters.
  • A stream is a lazy pipeline: source → intermediate operations → terminal operation. It doesn't store data or change the source, and it can be used only once.
  • Nothing runs until the terminal operation starts, and each item flows through the whole pipeline in turn.
  • Common tools: filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit, reduce, collect with Collectors like groupingBy, counting and joining.
  • Optional<T> is a container that holds one value or nothing. It makes "maybe no result" visible in a method's return type.
  • Use map, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow and ifPresent instead of get(). Use orElseGet when the default is expensive.
  • Use Optional for return types, not for fields, parameters or collection items.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: take a list of words, such as the lines of a short paragraph split by spaces. Use a stream to remove blanks, make everything lowercase, count how often each word appears with groupingBy and counting into a TreeMap, and print them sorted. Then write a method Optional<String> longestWord(List<String> words) that returns the longest word, and print it with orElse("none").

For a bonus experiment, add a System.out.println inside a filter and a map, and watch how the items flow one by one. Then add .limit(2) and see how many items get processed.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

Next in this series: var, records and sealed classes.

title: Java Collections Framework Explained Simply
description:
When I first saw Collection and Collections in the same Java file, I thought one of them was a typo. Then I found Arrays, Objects and Collectors and was sure the Java team had a thing for confusing names.

On top of that, I had a bigger problem. Arrays were fine until I needed to add an item to the middle, remove one, avoid duplicates or look something up by name. I kept writing the same helper code over and over, and every version had its own bugs.

The Collections Framework is Java's answer to all of this. It's a ready-made toolbox of data structures and algorithms. In this post, we'll learn the big idea, the Collection interface, the Collections class (and why they're different), the built-in algorithms, and the most popular collections you'll use every day. I've drawn the key pictures in text so you can see how things connect.

All the snippets assume import java.util.*; at the top, and they go inside a main method unless I show a full class.

The concept: what is the Collections Framework?

A collection is an object that holds a group of other objects. The Collections Framework is the set of classes and interfaces in java.util that gives you the common ways to group objects: lists, sets, queues and maps.

Why use it instead of plain arrays?

  • Arrays have a fixed size. A collection grows and shrinks as needed.
  • Ready-made operations. Adding, removing, searching, sorting and checking for duplicates are already written, tested and fast.
  • Different shapes for different needs. Need order? A list. No duplicates? A set. Look up by key? A map.
  • Swappable parts. Code written against an interface works with any implementation.

The framework has three parts. This is the most useful way to remember it:

   1. INTERFACES        the contracts: what a list, set, queue or map CAN DO
                        (List, Set, Queue, Map ...)

   2. IMPLEMENTATIONS   the real classes that do the work
                        (ArrayList, HashSet, HashMap ...)

   3. ALGORITHMS        ready-made methods that work on any collection
                        (sort, search, shuffle ... in the Collections class)

The family tree

Here's how the main interfaces and classes are related. Spend a minute on this picture, because everything else hangs on it:

                      Iterable
                         |
                     Collection                         Map   (separate tree!)
            /------------+-------------\                 |
          List          Set           Queue          +---+----------+
           |             |              |            |   |          |
      ArrayList      HashSet        PriorityQueue  HashMap LinkedHashMap TreeMap
      LinkedList     LinkedHashSet  ArrayDeque
                     TreeSet        (also LinkedList)

Two details in this picture trip people up:

  • Map is not a Collection. A map stores key-value pairs, not single items, so it has its own tree. It's still part of the framework.
  • Iterable sits at the very top. Anything that is Iterable can be used in a for-each loop.

The Collection interface

Collection<E> is the root contract for groups of single items. Lists, sets and queues all extend it, so they all share the same basic methods:

  • add(item) and addAll(otherCollection)
  • remove(item) and removeAll(otherCollection)
  • contains(item) and containsAll(otherCollection)
  • size(), isEmpty() and clear()
  • iterator() to walk through the items
  • removeIf(condition), stream() and toArray()

Because they share this contract, you can write code against Collection and not care which kind you get:

Collection<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Asha");
names.add("Ravi");
names.add("Asha");

System.out.println(names.size());
System.out.println(names.contains("Ravi"));
names.remove("Asha");
System.out.println(names);

Output:

3
true
[Ravi, Asha]

remove("Asha") removed only the first match. Now change one word, the implementation on the first line:

Collection<String> names = new HashSet<>();
// ...the same add calls as above...
System.out.println(names.size());

Output:

2

Everything else stayed the same, but a set ignores the second "Asha", so the size is 2. That's the power of programming to an interface: the rest of your code doesn't change when the structure does.

Looping and removing safely

Because every Collection is Iterable, you can loop with for-each. Behind the scenes, the compiler turns it into an iterator loop, using iterator(), hasNext() and next().

Here's a trap that almost everyone falls into: changing the collection while looping over it.

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));

for (Integer n : nums) {
    if (n == 2) {
        nums.remove(n);
    }
}

Output:

Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException

Most collections are fail-fast. They count how many times they've been changed. The iterator remembers that count, and if it sees a different number, it throws this exception, instead of continuing with confusing data.

There are two safe ways:

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));

Iterator<Integer> it = nums.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next() % 2 == 0) {
        it.remove();          // removes through the iterator: allowed
    }
}
System.out.println(nums);

Output:

[1, 3]

Or, shorter, with removeIf: nums.removeIf(n -> n % 2 == 0);

The Collections class (with an "s")

Now the name that causes the most confusion. Let's separate them clearly:

  • Collection (no s) is an interface. It's the contract for a group of items.
  • Collections (with an s) is a utility class. It holds only static helper methods for working on collections. You never create an object of it.

A simple memory trick: the plural-named classes in Java are usually toolboxes of static methods. Collections works on collections, Arrays works on arrays, and Objects works on objects. You call their methods like Collections.sort(list).

   Collection<E>       interface   "what a group of items can do"      (you implement/use it)
   Collections         class       "helpers that work on collections"  (you just call its methods)

Algorithms

In the framework, an algorithm is a ready-made, reusable method that works on collections. They're all static methods in the Collections class, and the nice part is that they work on any List, whether it's an ArrayList or a LinkedList.

Here are the most useful ones:

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 2, 9, 1, 7));

Collections.sort(nums);
System.out.println(nums);

System.out.println(Collections.binarySearch(nums, 7));

Collections.reverse(nums);
System.out.println(nums);

System.out.println(Collections.max(nums) + " " + Collections.min(nums));

Collections.swap(nums, 0, 4);
System.out.println(nums);

System.out.println(Collections.frequency(nums, 5));

Output:

[1, 2, 5, 7, 9]
3
[9, 7, 5, 2, 1]
9 1
[1, 7, 5, 2, 9]
1

What each one did:

  • sort put the list in ascending order.
  • binarySearch found 7 at index 3. The list must be sorted first, or the result is meaningless.
  • reverse flipped the order.
  • max and min found the biggest and smallest.
  • swap exchanged the items at positions 0 and 4.
  • frequency counted how many times 5 appears.

Others worth knowing: shuffle (random order), rotate, fill, nCopies, emptyList and addAll.

Sorting your own way

By default, sort uses the items' natural order (numbers ascending, strings alphabetical). For anything else, pass a Comparator, which is a rule for comparing two items:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Meera", "Jo", "Ravi", "Asha"));

Collections.sort(names);
System.out.println(names);

Collections.sort(names, Comparator.comparing(String::length));
System.out.println(names);

Collections.sort(names, Collections.reverseOrder());
System.out.println(names);

Output:

[Asha, Jo, Meera, Ravi]
[Jo, Asha, Ravi, Meera]
[Ravi, Meera, Jo, Asha]

Look at the second line. Asha and Ravi both have 4 letters, and they kept their earlier order. That's because the sort is stable: equal items don't swap places.

Behind the scenes

  • Collections.sort(list) simply calls list.sort(...). For objects, Java uses TimSort, a fast and stable algorithm that takes about n log n steps. (For arrays of primitives, Arrays.sort uses a different algorithm, called dual-pivot quicksort.)
  • binarySearch repeatedly cuts the search range in half, so it takes about log n steps. It's very fast on an ArrayList, but slower on a LinkedList, which can't jump to the middle.

Read-only views and thread-safe wrappers

Collections can also wrap a collection to change its behavior:

List<String> original = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
List<String> readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(original);

original.add("c");
System.out.println(readOnly);

try {
    readOnly.add("d");
} catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
    System.out.println("Read-only!");
}

Output:

[a, b, c]
Read-only!

An unmodifiable list is a view, not a copy. You can't change it through readOnly, but when someone changes original, the view shows the change. If you want a real, independent, unchangeable copy, use List.copyOf(original). There's also Collections.synchronizedList(...) to make a list safe for several threads (although for new code, the classes in java.util.concurrent are usually a better choice).

Well-known collections

Now the real workers. Let's visit the four families.

List: ordered, with duplicates, accessed by position

A List keeps items in the order you add them, allows duplicates and lets you use an index.

ArrayList is the everyday choice. Behind the scenes, it keeps an array. When the array fills up, it creates a bigger one (about 1.5 times larger) and copies everything over.

List<String> fruits = new ArrayList<>();
fruits.add("Apple");
fruits.add("Banana");
fruits.add("Apple");
fruits.add(1, "Mango");

System.out.println(fruits);
System.out.println(fruits.get(2));
System.out.println(fruits.indexOf("Apple"));

Output:

[Apple, Mango, Banana, Apple]
Banana
0

   ArrayList is an array inside:

   [ Apple ][ Mango ][ Banana ][ Apple ][  ][  ]     size = 4, capacity = 6
      0        1        2        3
   get(2) jumps straight to slot 2. Adding in the middle shifts the items after it.

LinkedList stores each item in a small node that points to the previous and next ones:

   head --> [ prev | Apple  | next ] <--> [ prev | Mango | next ] <--> [ prev | Banana | next ] <-- tail

Adding or removing at the ends is very quick. But get(i) must walk node by node, so it's slow for big lists.

Set: no duplicates

A Set never holds the same item twice. add returns false if the item was already there:

Set<Integer> ids = new HashSet<>();

System.out.println(ids.add(10));
System.out.println(ids.add(10));
System.out.println(ids.size());

Output:

true
false
1

There are three common sets, and the only real difference is the order:

List<String> input = List.of("pear", "apple", "fig", "apple");

System.out.println(new LinkedHashSet<>(input));
System.out.println(new TreeSet<>(input));

Output:

[pear, apple, fig]
[apple, fig, pear]
  • HashSet: fastest, but the order is not guaranteed.
  • LinkedHashSet: keeps the order you inserted (pear, apple, fig).
  • TreeSet: keeps items sorted (apple, fig, pear).

Map: key to value

A Map stores pairs. Each key is unique, and it points to a value.

Map<String, Integer> marks = new HashMap<>();
marks.put("Asha", 88);
marks.put("Ravi", 72);
marks.put("Asha", 91);

System.out.println(marks.get("Asha"));
System.out.println(marks.size());
System.out.println(marks.getOrDefault("Meera", 0));

Output:

91
2
0

Putting "Asha" a second time replaced her old value. And getOrDefault gave 0 for a missing key, instead of null.

A very common job is counting. Here's a word counter that uses merge:

String text = "to be or not to be";
Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>();

for (String word : text.split(" ")) {
    counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);
}

System.out.println(counts);

Output:

{be=2, not=1, or=1, to=2}

Maps come in the same three flavors as sets: HashMap (fastest, no order), LinkedHashMap (insertion order) and TreeMap (sorted by key).

Behind the scenes: how HashMap finds things

A HashMap keeps an array of buckets. When you put a key, Java calls the key's hashCode(), turns it into a bucket number and stores the entry there. To find it again, it repeats the same steps, then uses equals() to pick the right entry if a bucket holds several.

   put("Asha", 91)
        |
   "Asha".hashCode()  -->  a number  -->  bucket index 3

   buckets:   [0] [1] [2] [3: Asha=91 -> Ravi=72] [4] [5] ...
                               ^
                   two keys landed in the same bucket (a "collision"),
                   so equals() decides which one you meant

This is why lookup is so quick (about one step on average, not a search through everything). A few details:

  • It starts with 16 buckets, and doubles when it's 75% full.
  • Since Java 8, a bucket that gets too crowded switches from a chain to a balanced tree, so even bad cases stay fast.
  • If you use your own class as a key, you must override both equals() and hashCode(), and keep them consistent. Otherwise, lookups will fail even for identical-looking objects.
  • A HashSet is secretly a HashMap (the items are the keys). In the same way, TreeSet is backed by a TreeMap, and LinkedHashSet by a LinkedHashMap.

Queue and Deque: waiting lines and stacks

A Queue processes items in order: first in, first out (FIFO). A Deque (double-ended queue) can add and remove at both ends, so it works as a stack too (last in, first out, LIFO).

Queue<String> line = new ArrayDeque<>();
line.offer("A");
line.offer("B");
line.offer("C");

System.out.println(line.poll());
System.out.println(line.peek());

Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push(1);
stack.push(2);
stack.push(3);

System.out.println(stack.pop());

Output:

A
B
3
  • offer adds, poll removes and returns the front, and peek looks at the front without removing.
  • For a stack, prefer ArrayDeque over the old Stack class.

A PriorityQueue doesn't use arrival order. It always gives you the smallest item first (or whatever your comparator says is first):

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 3));

System.out.println(pq.poll());
System.out.println(pq.poll());

Output:

1
3

Don't print the whole queue to check the order. Inside, it's a heap, and only the front is guaranteed to be the smallest.

How fast is each one?

Here is a rough guide to the speed of the common operations (n is the number of items):

  • ArrayList: get(i) is instant (O(1)). Adding at the end is fast (O(1) on average). Inserting or removing in the middle, or searching with contains, takes O(n).
  • LinkedList: adding or removing at the ends is O(1). get(i) and contains are O(n).
  • HashSet / HashMap: add, remove and lookup are O(1) on average.
  • TreeSet / TreeMap: add, remove and lookup are O(log n), and the items stay sorted.
  • ArrayDeque: adding and removing at either end is O(1).
  • PriorityQueue: add and poll are O(log n), and peek is O(1).

Which one should I use?

Start from what you need, and the choice is usually clear:

   Need to look things up by a KEY?          -> Map
        default: HashMap     sorted keys: TreeMap     insertion order: LinkedHashMap

   Need NO DUPLICATES?                       -> Set
        default: HashSet     sorted: TreeSet          insertion order: LinkedHashSet

   Need first-in-first-out, a stack,
   or "smallest first"?                      -> Queue / Deque
        ArrayDeque  or  PriorityQueue

   Otherwise, an ordered group?              -> List
        default: ArrayList

Some extra advice:

  • Default to ArrayList and HashMap. They're the best general-purpose choices. In practice, ArrayList beats LinkedList in most real cases, even for inserts, because arrays are friendly to the CPU.
  • Declare variables with the interface: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();. Then you can swap the implementation by editing one word.
  • Collections hold objects, not primitives. Write List<Integer>, not List<int>. (This is where wrapper classes and autoboxing come in.)
  • Sorted data you keep changing? Use a TreeSet or TreeMap. Sorted once? Keep an ArrayList and call Collections.sort once.

Common mistakes

  1. Mixing up Collection, Collections and Arrays. Collection is the interface. Collections and Arrays are classes of static helper methods.
  2. Changing a collection while looping over it. It throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use an Iterator with remove(), or removeIf.
  3. Using your own class as a key without equals() and hashCode(). Lookups fail, and duplicates sneak into sets. Also, don't change a key's fields after you've put it into a map or set.
  4. Relying on the order of a HashSet or HashMap. It looks stable in small tests, then changes. If you need an order, choose LinkedHash... or Tree....
  5. Calling get(i) in a loop over a LinkedList. Each call walks the list, so the loop becomes slow (O(n²)). Use for-each, or an ArrayList.
  6. Forgetting that some lists can't be changed. List.of(...), List.copyOf(...) and Collections.unmodifiableList(...) throw UnsupportedOperationException on changes. Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3) has a fixed size, so add also fails. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(...) when you need a normal list.

Also remember Collections.binarySearch only works on a list that's already sorted in the same order.

Quick recap

  • The Collections Framework is Java's ready-made toolbox in java.util: interfaces, implementations and algorithms.
  • Collection is the root interface for groups of items (List, Set, Queue). Map is separate, because it stores pairs.
  • Every Collection is Iterable, so for-each works, but don't change a collection while looping over it.
  • Collections (with an s) is a utility class of static methods: sort, binarySearch, reverse, shuffle, max, min, frequency, swap and wrappers like unmodifiableList.
  • List: ArrayList (array inside, the default) and LinkedList (nodes). Set: HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet. Map: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap. Queue/Deque: ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue.
  • HashMap uses hashCode() to find a bucket and equals() to pick the entry, so your key classes need both.
  • Choose by need: key lookup, no duplicates, queue behavior or an ordered list. When unsure, start with ArrayList and HashMap.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: build a tiny contact book. Store contacts in a Map<String, String> (name to phone number) and print them sorted by name using a TreeMap. Then add every name to a List, sort it with Collections.sort by name length, and use Collections.binarySearch to find one name.

For a bonus experiment, create a Student class without equals() and hashCode(), and add two students with the same data to a HashSet. Notice that both get in. Then add the two methods and watch the duplicate disappear.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Java Được Sử Dụng Để Làm Gì?
description:
Java là một ngôn ngữ lập trình mạnh mẽ và linh hoạt, được sử dụng rộng rãi trong nhiều lĩnh vực khác nhau. Dưới đây là một số ví dụ cụ thể về những gì Java có thể làm:

Phát triển ứng dụng web

↳ Java là ngôn ngữ phổ biến nhất cho phát triển ứng dụng web back-end, sử dụng các framework như Spring MVC, Struts, JSF.

↳ Java cũng được sử dụng để phát triển các ứng dụng web front-end với các thư viện như GWT, JavaFX Script.
