title: Using AG Grid in server side mode with Spring Data JPA
description:
Documentation — every feature with a live grid you can click through

ag-grid-jpa-adapter — the library source

Showcase backend — the Spring Boot app all the code below is taken from

In AG Grid’s server side row model, the grid posts a request describing what it wants and expects the backend to answer it. ag-grid-jpa-adapter builds that query for you with the JPA Criteria API, against the entities you already have — no native SQL, no string concatenation. You define the columns once and hand the request to a QueryBuilder.

The data model 

@Entity
@Table(name = "trade")
@Getter @Setter
public class Trade {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    @Column(name = "trade_id")
    private Long tradeId;

    // self-reference -> tree data
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "parent_trade_id")
    private Trade parentTrade;

    @OneToMany(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, mappedBy = "parentTrade", orphanRemoval = true)
    private Set<Trade> childTrades = new HashSet<>();

    @Column(name = "product")
    private String product;
    @Column(name = "portfolio")
    private String portfolio;
    @Column(name = "book")
    private String book;
    @Column(name = "deal_type")
    private String dealType;
    @Column(name = "bid_type")
    private String bidType;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
    @JoinColumn(name = "submitter_id")
    private Submitter submitter;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
    @JoinColumn(name = "submitter_deal_id")
    private SubmitterDeal submitterDeal;

    @Column(name = "current_value")
    private BigDecimal currentValue;
    @Column(name = "previous_value")
    private BigDecimal previousValue;

    @Embedded
    private Statistics statistics;

    @Column(name = "birth_date")
    private LocalDate birthDate;
    @Column(name = "is_sold")
    private Boolean isSold;
    // materialised path, "1/7/12" -> tree data filtering and child counts
    @Column(name = "data_path")
    private String dataPath;
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "submitter")
@Getter @Setter
public class Submitter {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    // the detail rows of a master/detail grid
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "submitter")
    private Set<Trade> trades = new HashSet<>();
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "submitter_deal")
@Getter @Setter
public class SubmitterDeal {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "name")
    private String name;

    @Column(name = "created_at")
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "submitterDeal")
    private Set<Trade> trades = new HashSet<>();
}

@Embeddable
public record Statistics(
        @Column(name = "pl1")
        BigDecimal pl1,
        @Column(name = "pl2")
        BigDecimal pl2,
        @Column(name = "gain_dx")
        BigDecimal gainDx,
        @Column(name = "sx_px")
        BigDecimal sxPx,
        @Column(name = "x99_out")
        BigDecimal x99Out
) {}

The metamodel generator

Columns are declared with static metamodel attributes so you need a generator on the build:

<annotationProcessorPaths>
    <!-- Lombok first, if you use it -->
    <path>
        <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
        <artifactId>hibernate-jpamodelgen</artifactId>
        <version>${hibernate.version}</version>
    </path>
</annotationProcessorPaths>

${hibernate.version} comes from spring-boot-starter-parent.

The QueryBuilder 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.smolcan</groupId>
    <artifactId>ag-grid-jpa-adapter</artifactId>
    <version>1.1.7</version>
</dependency>

QueryBuilder<E, E_ID, D> — entity, id type, detail entity (Void unless you use master/detail). It is immutable and built once, so it belongs in the service constructor (It works just as well as a @Bean in a @Configuration class, autowired into the service.).

@Service
public class TradeService {

    private final QueryBuilder<Trade, Long, Void> queryBuilder;

    public TradeService(EntityManager entityManager) {
        this.queryBuilder = QueryBuilder.builder(Trade.class, Trade_.tradeId, entityManager)
                .colDefs(
                        ColDef.builder(Trade_.tradeId)
                                .filter(new AgNumberColumnFilter<>())
                                .build(),
                        ColDef.builder(Trade_.product)
                                .filter(new AgTextColumnFilter())
                                .enableRowGroup(true, key -> key)
                                .build(),
                        ColDef.builder(Trade_.portfolio)
                                .filter(AgSetColumnFilter.forString())
                                .enableRowGroup(true, key -> key)
                                .build(),
                        ColDef.builder(Trade_.currentValue)
                                .filter(new AgNumberColumnFilter<>())
                                .enableValue(true)
                                .build(),
                        ColDef.builder(Trade_.birthDate)
                                .filter(AgDateColumnFilter.forLocalDate())
                                .build(),
                        // dot walk into related entities, the column comes back as "submitter.name"
                        ColDef.builder(FieldPath.of(Trade_.submitter).to(Submitter_.name))
                                .filter(new AgTextColumnFilter())
                                .build()
                )
                .build();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public LoadSuccessParams getRows(ServerSideGetRowsRequest request) {
        return this.queryBuilder.getRows(request);
    }
}

The controller 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/trades")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class TradeController {

    private final TradeService tradeService;

    @PostMapping("getRows")
    public ResponseEntity<LoadSuccessParams> getRows(@RequestBody ServerSideGetRowsRequest request) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(this.tradeService.getRows(request));
    }
}

ServerSideGetRowsRequest is what AG Grid posts — startRow/endRow, sortModel, filterModel, rowGroupCols, groupKeys, valueCols, pivotCols, pivotMode. Everything the grid can ask for arrives in that one body, and one getRows call answers all of it.

Sorting

Sorting is enabled on column by default. Turn it off per column, and a sort request on it is rejected:

ColDef.builder(Trade_.product)
        .sortable(false)
        .build()

Grid sorted by Trade ID column

sortModel becomes order by

Sorting docs →

Filtering

Say the grid needs a text filter on product, a set filter on portfolio, a number filter on currentValue and a date filter on birthDate:

QueryBuilder.builder(Trade.class, Trade_.tradeId, entityManager)
        .colDefs(
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.product)
                        .filter(new AgTextColumnFilter())
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.portfolio)
                        .filter(AgSetColumnFilter.forString())
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.currentValue)
                        .filter(new AgNumberColumnFilter<BigDecimal>())
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.birthDate)
                        .filter(AgDateColumnFilter.forLocalDate())
                        .build()
        )
        .build();

Text filter on Portfolio

contains “port” becomes condition in where clause

Filtering docs →

Row grouping and aggregation

Group by portfolio and product, aggregate currentValue and previousValue:

QueryBuilder.builder(Trade.class, Trade_.tradeId, entityManager)
        .colDefs(
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.portfolio)
                        .enableRowGroup(true, key -> key)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.product)
                        .enableRowGroup(true, key -> key)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.currentValue)
                        .enableValue(true)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.previousValue)
                        .enableValue(true)
                        .build()
        )
        .build();

Grouped by Portfolio and Product, aggregated average on current and previous value. Expanded group “Portfolio 7”

Group key becomes where, value columns become aggregation function (avg)

Row grouping docs →

Aggregation docs →

Pivoting

Pivot book into columns, grouped by product and portfolio, averaging currentValue and previousValue:

QueryBuilder.builder(Trade.class, Trade_.tradeId, entityManager)
        .colDefs(
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.product)
                        .enableRowGroup(true, key -> key)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.portfolio)
                        .enableRowGroup(true, key -> key)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.book)
                        .enablePivot(true)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.currentValue)
                        .enableValue(true)
                        .build(),
                ColDef.builder(Trade_.previousValue)
                        .enableValue(true)
                        .build()
        )
        .build();

Book pivoted into column groups

One query finds the columns, one fills them

Two queries: select distinct book to find out which columns exist, then one aggregate with a case per generated column.

Pivoting docs →

Pagination 

QueryBuilder.builder(Trade.class, Trade_.tradeId, entityManager)
        .colDefs(/* ... */)
        .paginateChildRows(true)
        .build();

The total count comes from a separate call — make it when the grid state changes the count, such as on a filter change:

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public long countRows(ServerSideGetRowsRequest request) {
    return this.queryBuilder.countRows(request);
}

@PostMapping("countRows")
public ResponseEntity<Long> countRows(@RequestBody ServerSideGetRowsRequest request) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(this.tradeService.countRows(request));
}

100,000 rows, one block fetched

getRows fetches the block

countRows fills the pager

Same timestamp, two endpoints: getRows fetches the block, countRows fills in the pager.

Pagination docs →

Tree data

Trade points at its own parent, so the table is already a tree:

QueryBuilder.builder(Trade.class, Trade_.tradeId, entityManager)
        .colDefs(/* ... */)
        .treeData(true)
        .isServerSideGroupFieldName("hasChildren")
        .treeDataParentReferenceField(Trade_.parentTrade)
        .treeDataStringToParentIdTypeConverter(Long::valueOf)
        .treeDataDataPathFieldName(Trade_.dataPath)
        .treeDataDataPathSeparator("/")
        .build();

A self-referencing table as a tree (with expanded node with id 1)

hasChildren is an exists subquery, where children of node 1

hasChildren is the case when exists (...) subquery; expanding a node sends its key back as groupKeys and the children are fetched with where parent_trade_id = ?.

Tree data docs →

Master detail

A submitter on the master row, its trades in the detail grid:

QueryBuilder.builder(Submitter.class, Submitter_.id, Trade.class, entityManager)
        .colDefs(
                ColDef.builder(Submitter_.id).build(),
                ColDef.builder(Submitter_.name).build()
        )
        .masterDetail(true)
        .masterDetailParams(
                QueryBuilder.MasterDetailParams.<Submitter, Long, Trade>builder()
                        .detailClass(Trade.class)
                        .detailColDefs(
                                ColDef.builder(Trade_.tradeId).build(),
                                ColDef.builder(Trade_.product).build(),
                                ColDef.builder(Trade_.portfolio).build()
                        )
                        .detailMasterReferenceField(Trade_.submitter)
                        .build()
        )
        .build();

Detail rows are loaded when a row is expanded, through a second endpoint:

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<Map<String, Object>> getDetailRowData(Map<String, Object> masterRow) {
    return this.queryBuilder.getDetailRowData(masterRow);
}

@PostMapping("getDetailRowData")
public ResponseEntity<List<Map<String, Object>>> getDetailRowData(@RequestBody Map<String, Object> masterRow) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(this.submitterService.getDetailRowData(masterRow));
}

A submitter expanded into its trades

Masters only

Details on expand

Expanding a row posts the master row itself, and the detail rows come back from where submitter_id = ?.

Master detail docs →

title: The 11-year-old premise inside Rust's memory-safety proof
description:
"If it compiles, the memory is safe."

That is Rust's brand — not a slogan, a machine-checked proof: the borrow checker refuses unsafe lifetimes at compile time, host-enforced, the strongest rung any language has claimed. Yesterday, issue #164250 landed on the rust-lang tracker: an unsoundness in the borrow checker, reproducing on current stable, with variants compiling since 1.18.0 (2017) — and one version traced back to 1.4. Eleven years inside the proof.

I ran the reproduction tonight on the official playground — stable channel. The output, verbatim:

read after scope: hello world, this is long enough
the stack slot is freed. the string still printed.

A short-lived reference escaped a T: 'static bound through field assignment after construction, survived a Drop that assumed the bound held, and was read after its stack slot was freed. On stable. Same result on nightly. The receipts are one click away — the playground permalink runs it in seconds.

The mechanics, in three sentences

struct Q<T: 'static + Send> demands its payload outlive the program. Assigning a field after construction (q.0 = Some(&l), where l is stack-local) unifies the types covariantly — and that unification does not re-check the 'static bound. A Drop impl that pushes the value into a static list assumes the bound held; it leaks the reference out; a downcast_ref::<&'static String>() reads freed stack memory. With AddressSanitizer, per the issue, the same program crashes with stack-use-after-scope.

The number that matters is not 11

It is the severity call: P-high, downgraded from P-critical. The pinned note from lcnr is explicit — it would have been P-critical regardless of whether anyone encountered it in the wild, and it is P-high only because it has been latent for eleven years with "very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident." The exploit requires, per the issue, "an intentionally malicious Drop implementation."

Read that as an auditor, because it is a premise confession, and it is not Rust-specific. The compiler's proof descends a ladder: borrow check → variance rules → trait bounds → and at the floor, an assumption nobody executes — Drop implementations respect the bounds they inherit. The type system verified everything it could check and rested on the one thing it could not: the honesty of every Drop impl ever written by every hand that touched every crate. Eleven years, that premise held by accident of nobody aiming at it. This week someone aimed.

Sound familiar? It is the QGIS conscience test — "did you in good conscience write the code yourself" — inside a compiler. It is the authority ladder — rung 0, "the caller's argument": a claim the impl author makes, unverifiable by the checker below. Every soundness proof, every security certification, every "guaranteed" has a floor like this. The floor is not a scandal. An unlabeled floor is.

Credits, because the finder's method is the receipts

  • jsnell filed it October 13, with the reproduction that compiles and prints freed memory.
  • theemathas added the I-unsound label, a minimal core repro, and traced a variant compiling "ever since 1.18.0 (2017)" — and asked the question in the thread: "How on earth was this not found before this???"
  • maxdexh contributed a version going back to 1.4, and the generalization: "unification just generally doesn't check lifetime bounds of the type" — including via mem::swap, no field assignment needed.
  • lcnr pinned the severity reasoning and the linkage to the next-gen trait solver and Project Zero rework. PR #164277 is the fix in motion.

Four people, four contributions, each with its own denominator. That is what a healthy process looks like from the outside — and it is also, per the issue, a thread that was briefly locked as too heated before being unlocked and re-locked to collaborators. Soundness conversations run hot.

What to steal

  • Audit the premises under your proofs. Every guarantee you rely on — a type system, a SOC 2 report, a DCO sign-off, a "tested and measured" claim — rests on unlabeled assumptions the guarantee cannot check. Name one. The table is the audit.
  • Label your severity calls with their reasons. P-high because eleven years latent because it needs a malicious Drop — that reasoning is the difference between a decision and an assertion. Rust's team did this in the pinned note; copy the format.
  • Permalinks for reproductions. The playground link makes my claim one click from being your claim. If your repro needs setup, ship the setup.

Two honest limits

The exploit requires a malicious Drop by design, and the team's downgrade is defensible. Eleven years without an accidental hit is evidence of something — either the premise held because nobody aimed, or because honest Drops overwhelmingly dominate. Both readings favor the team's call. My point is narrower: the premise existed, was unlabeled, and now is labeled — by the issue, in public.

And my run is a playground snapshot, not a forensic audit. Stable and nightly, debug profile, no AddressSanitizer in my harness — the stack-use-after-scope confirmation cited in the issue comes from their ASAN run, not mine. One compiler family, one evening. The issue's own denominators are better than mine; use theirs.

Your turn

The reproduction is twenty lines, the playground is free, and here is the whole thing — paste it into the playground, hit Run, and compare your output to mine:

static KEPT: std::sync::Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn std::any::Any + Send>>> =
    std::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new());

struct Q<T: 'static + Send>(Option<T>);

impl<T: 'static + Send> Drop for Q<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(v) = self.0.take() {
            KEPT.lock().unwrap().push(Box::new(v));
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let l = String::from("hello world, this is long enough");
    {
        let mut q = Q(None);
        q.0 = Some(&l);
    } // <- Drop here: the short-lived reference escapes as if 'static

    let kept = KEPT.lock().unwrap();
    let s = kept[0].downcast_ref::<&'static String>().unwrap();
    println!("read after scope: {}", s);
    println!("the stack slot is freed. the string still printed.");
}

Run it on your rustc, your channels, your edition, and post your output — the issue's variants reach back to 1.4, and every data point sharpens the map. Then pick one guarantee you ship or rely on, and write down the premise under it that nobody executes. That list is where the next eleven-year bugs live.

title: How Do You Secure API Keys in an AWS Application?
description:
A developer finishes a weekend project, pushes it to a public repository, and goes to bed. Somewhere in a configuration file is an API key for a paid third-party service. By morning, someone has found it, and the usage dashboard looks nothing like it did the night before.
Nobody had to "hack" anything. The key was sitting in plain text, and anyone who found it could use it. Depending on what that key allowed, the fallout might be an unexpected bill, access to someone's data, or misuse of a connected service under your name.
This happens to experienced engineers as well as beginners, which is exactly why secrets management deserves attention early. The core idea is simple: an API key is a credential, and credentials need a secure way to be stored, accessed, rotated, and monitored. AWS gives you several tools for that. Using them well takes a bit more thought than just knowing their names.

What Is an API Key, and Why Does It Need Protection?

An API key is a string that an application sends along with a request so the service on the other end knows who is calling. Your app might use one to fetch weather data, send email, process payments, or call an AI model. The provider uses the key to track usage, apply limits, and decide what that caller is allowed to do.
It helps to separate three ideas that often get blurred together. Identification says "this request comes from this project or client." Authentication says "this caller is who they claim to be." Authorization says "this caller is allowed to do this specific thing." Many API keys mostly handle identification, and some also grant real permissions. The more a key can do, the more damage it can cause when exposed.
Not all keys carry the same risk. A key restricted to read-only access on public data is a very different problem from a key that can send messages, move money, or delete resources. Treat the risk as a function of what the key can do, not just the fact that it exists.
One more clarification: API keys, AWS access keys, IAM credentials, database passwords, and tokens are not interchangeable. Each has its own lifecycle and its own best practices. An AWS access key, for example, can authorize actions across your cloud account, so exposure there is usually far more serious than exposure of a low-privilege third-party key. The tools below apply to all of them in different ways, but you should always know what kind of secret you are dealing with.

Common Ways Developers Accidentally Expose API Keys

Most leaks are not sophisticated. They come from ordinary habits, and each has a safer alternative.
Hardcoding keys in source code. It is the fastest way to get something working, and it is the fastest way to leak it. Anyone with repository access, including future teammates and contractors, can read it. Keep secrets outside the code and load them at runtime.
Committing credentials to public repositories. Even a private repository can become public later, or be cloned somewhere less protected. Automated scanners watch public platforms constantly, so exposed keys are often found quickly.
Embedding secrets in frontend JavaScript. Anything shipped to the browser is visible to the user. More on this below.
Committing configuration files with secrets. A file named something like "environment settings" feels private, but if it is tracked by version control, it travels with the repository. Keep such files out of version control and store real values in a proper secret store.
Sharing keys in screenshots, chats, or documentation. A cropped screenshot in a team chat or a wiki page can outlive its context. Share access through a managed system, not through messages.
Printing secrets in logs. Debug logging that dumps a full request, including headers, can quietly write a key into a log system many people can read. Be deliberate about what gets logged, and keep sensitive values out of error messages.
Reusing one key across development and production. If a test environment leaks, production goes with it. Use separate credentials per environment.
Granting excessive permissions. A key with broad access turns a small leak into a large one. Scope each credential to what the application actually needs.
Leaving unused credentials active. Old keys from abandoned projects are quiet liabilities. Disable and remove what is no longer needed.

Why Secret API Keys Do Not Belong in Frontend Code

The browser is the user's environment, not yours. Whatever JavaScript you send, the user can open, read, and run. Minifying or bundling the code makes it harder to read, but not impossible. Anyone curious can inspect the network traffic or the loaded files and find the key.
Imagine a web page that shows live product recommendations from an external service. If the page calls that service directly with a secret key in the browser, every visitor effectively receives that key.
A safer design puts a backend in between:
User Browser
↓
Application Backend
↓
Secure Secret Retrieval
↓
External API

The browser asks your backend for what it needs. The backend retrieves the credential from a secure store, calls the external service, and returns only the result. The secret never travels to the user's device.
There is an important nuance here. Some services deliberately issue public, client-side keys, designed to be visible in the browser and limited by restrictions such as allowed domains or narrow permissions. Those are a different category from confidential secret keys. The question to ask is always: what does this specific key allow, and did the provider intend it to be public?

How AWS Secrets Manager Helps

AWS Secrets Manager is a service built for storing and managing sensitive values such as API keys, database credentials, and tokens. Instead of placing a secret in your code or configuration, you store it in the service, and your application retrieves it when it needs it.
Conceptually, the flow looks like this: the application starts up or needs a credential, it asks Secrets Manager for the value, AWS checks whether the caller has permission through IAM, and if so, returns the secret over an encrypted connection. The secret is encrypted at rest using AWS Key Management Service.
Several features make this useful in practice:
Separation from code. Secrets live outside the repository, so rotating or changing them does not require redeploying application code.
Access control through IAM. You decide exactly which roles or users can read which secrets.
Rotation support. For supported services and configurations, Secrets Manager can help rotate credentials automatically on a schedule. Rotation depends on the type of secret, and for some third-party API keys you may need to design your own rotation process.
Environment separation. You can keep distinct secrets for development, testing, and production, with different access rules.
Auditing. Access to secrets can be tracked through AWS logging services.

A few practical considerations matter as well. Retrieving a secret on every request adds latency and cost, so many applications cache it for a short time, balancing freshness against performance. The application also needs a sensible plan for when the service is briefly unavailable or when a secret rotates mid-operation. And the application itself must avoid leaking the value after retrieval, for example through logs or error messages.
It is also worth being clear about what Secrets Manager does not do. Storing a secret there does not secure the whole application. If the application's permissions are too broad, or if its code writes the secret to a log, the protection weakens considerably. It is one layer of a larger approach.

How IAM Roles Help Applications Access Secrets Securely

AWS Identity and Access Management, or IAM, controls who and what can do things in your AWS account. It is the foundation underneath most of the other tools here.
At a conceptual level, an IAM user represents a person or application with long-term credentials, while an IAM role is an identity that a workload can assume to receive temporary credentials. When an application runs on AWS compute, such as a virtual server, a container task, or a serverless function, you can attach a role to that workload. AWS then supplies short-lived credentials automatically, with no need to put keys in your code.
This matters because hardcoding long-lived AWS access keys in an application is one of the riskiest habits in cloud development. If those keys leak, they stay valid until someone notices and revokes them. Role-based credentials expire on their own and rotate automatically, which sharply narrows the window of exposure.
IAM policies then define what the role can do. This is where least privilege comes in: grant only the permissions the application genuinely needs. A service that reads one specific secret should not have permission to read every secret in the account, and certainly should not have broad administrative access.
Consider an application that only needs to read a payment provider's key. Its role should be allowed to read that one secret and nothing else. If the application is ever compromised, the damage stays contained to what that role could do.
Concepts like roles and policies tend to click only after you have set them up yourself. If you are comparing an AWS cloud training institute in Indore, it is worth asking whether the labs let you practice roles, policies, and secret retrieval in a sandbox account instead of only walking through slides.

Rotating Credentials

Even well-protected secrets should not live forever. Rotation means replacing a credential with a new one on a regular schedule, so a leaked or forgotten key eventually stops working.
Rotation takes some planning. The new credential has to be created at the provider, stored securely, and picked up by the applications that use it, ideally without downtime. Some services support automated rotation, and Secrets Manager can orchestrate it for supported types. For other third-party keys, rotation may be partly manual, and the process should still be documented and practiced.
It also helps to rotate on events, not just schedules. When a team member with access leaves, when a system is migrated, or when anything suspicious appears, rotating the affected credentials is sensible housekeeping.

Monitoring and Detecting Misuse

Prevention is not enough, because eventually something will slip through. Monitoring lets you notice quickly.
AWS CloudTrail records API activity in your account, including requests to retrieve secrets, so you can see who accessed what and when. Amazon CloudWatch can collect logs and metrics and trigger alarms when behavior looks unusual. Billing alerts and budgets can warn you when spending jumps unexpectedly, which is often the first visible sign of a misused key. AWS also offers threat detection services that flag suspicious account activity.
On the third-party side, many API providers offer usage dashboards and alerts. Setting usage limits and notifications there is worth the few minutes it takes. A sudden spike in calls from an unfamiliar location is a signal worth investigating.

What To Do If a Key Is Exposed

If a key leaks, speed matters more than perfection. A rough order of operations:
Revoke or disable the key right away. Do this at the provider, and in AWS if it is an AWS credential. Do not wait to understand the full story first.
Create a replacement and update the application. Store the new value securely, not in the place the old one leaked.
Do not assume deleting it from the repository is enough. Version control keeps history, and the key may already have been copied. Removing it from history is useful cleanup, but the key should be treated as compromised regardless.
Review activity. Check provider usage logs and, for AWS credentials, CloudTrail, to see whether the key was used and what it did.
Assess the impact. Consider what the key could access, what was actually accessed, and whether customers or data are affected. Depending on your obligations, you may need to notify others.
Learn from it. Work out how the leak happened and close the gap, whether that means better scanning, tighter permissions, or changed habits.

A Practical Checklist

Pulling the ideas together, a reasonable baseline looks like this:
Keep secrets out of source code and out of version control.
Never place confidential keys in frontend code.
Store secrets in a managed service and retrieve them at runtime.
Use IAM roles for workloads instead of long-lived access keys.
Apply least privilege to every role and credential.
Use separate credentials for each environment.
Rotate credentials, and know how you would do it in a hurry.
Monitor access and spending, and set alerts.
Keep secrets out of logs, error messages, screenshots, and chats.
Have a written plan for what to do when a key leaks.

Final Thoughts

Securing API keys on AWS is less about one clever tool and more about layers that support each other. A secret manager keeps credentials out of code. IAM roles control who can read them. Least privilege limits the damage if something goes wrong. Rotation and monitoring shorten the window in which a leaked key is useful to anyone.
None of these layers is perfect alone, and none replaces careful habits. But together they turn a single exposed key from a potential disaster into a manageable incident, which is the real goal.
For students and freshers in the city, structured practice can make these habits stick faster. An AWS cloud training institute in Indore such as Vector Skill Academy is one place to work through AWS fundamentals, IAM, and security basics with guidance. Whatever route you take, build the habit early: keep secrets out of code, give every credential the least access it needs, and assume that sooner or later one of them will leak.

title: Why Rust Is a Great Fit for Browser-Based Creative Apps
description: Creative desktop software has been dominated by the same few proprietary suites for two decades, and the alternatives that emerged were mostly Electron shells: huge, memory-hungry, and the same performance ceiling underneath. Rust plus WebAssembly is quietly changing that equation, and a new wave of browser-based creative tools shows why. ## Why Rust compiles well to this problem Image editing, vector rendering, and video processing are all compute-heavy, allocation-sensitive workloads. Rust gives you C-class performance without the memory bugs, and wasm-bindgen makes it straightforward to expose that performance to a browser UI. No server round-trips means your edits happen at native speed on the user's machine. ## A concrete example ArtCraft Suite is a good case study: a collection of creative apps - PhotoCraft for image editing, VectorCraft for vector graphics, FilmCraft for video, plus PDF and other tools - all written in pure Rust and running entirely in the browser. No install, no account, and the source is open. The interesting part is not any single app; it is that the whole suite holds one architectural stance: everything local, everything Rust, everything in the browser. ## What this unlocks - Distribution collapses to a URL. No installers, no updater infrastructure, no platform certification. - Privacy becomes default. Files never leave the device, which matters for client work. - Open source is practical. Rust's ecosystem makes community contributions tractable in a way large C++ codebases never were. None of this means Electron or native apps are dead - offline-first desktop apps with deep OS integration still need them. But for the enormous category of everyday creative tasks, Rust-in-the-browser is now good enough, and it is getting better fast. Try ArtCraft Suite if you want to feel where this is heading.

title: Go Generics in Production: Real Use Cases After 2 Years
description:
Go 1.18 shipped generics in March 2022. The community's reaction ranged from cautious optimism to outright skepticism. Two years of production code later, the picture is clearer: generics solve a handful of specific problems well and introduce complexity everywhere else. Here is what actually made it into production codebases—and what should stay out.

What Actually Works: Generic Collections

Before generics, you either wrote type-specific implementations or used interface{} (now any) and paid a casting tax everywhere. Generic containers eliminate this tradeoff entirely:

type Stack[T any] struct {
    items []T
}

func (s *Stack[T]) Push(item T) {
    s.items = append(s.items, item)
}

func (s *Stack[T]) Pop() (T, bool) {
    var zero T
    if len(s.items) == 0 {
        return zero, false
    }
    item := s.items[len(s.items)-1]
    s.items = s.items[:len(s.items)-1]
    return item, true
}

func (s *Stack[T]) Len() int {
    return len(s.items)
}

This compiles to efficient code with no runtime allocation overhead from boxing. We use this pattern for work queues, AST-like tree structures, and processing pipelines where the element type varies per service but the container logic is identical.

Functional Helpers That Actually Belong in Your Codebase

The slices package (Go 1.21) handled a lot of this, but for domain-specific transformations, generic helpers cut boilerplate without code generation:

func Map[T, U any](items []T, fn func(T) U) []U {
    result := make([]U, len(items))
    for i, item := range items {
        result[i] = fn(item)
    }
    return result
}

func Filter[T any](items []T, predicate func(T) bool) []T {
    var result []T
    for _, item := range items {
        if predicate(item) {
            result = append(result, item)
        }
    }
    return result
}

// Real usage
userIDs  := Map(users, func(u User) int64 { return u.ID })
active   := Filter(users, func(u User) bool { return u.Active })

Before Go 1.18, this required either go generate templates or []interface{} casts that the compiler could not check. Now it is type-safe and readable.

A Generic Retry That Earned Its Place in Production

This is the generic pattern that removed the most code from our codebase. We had three nearly identical retry wrappers for different return types. This replaced all three:

func Retry[T any](ctx context.Context, maxAttempts int, fn func() (T, error)) (T, error) {
    var (
        result T
        err    error
    )
    for i := 0; i < maxAttempts; i++ {
        if ctx.Err() != nil {
            return result, ctx.Err()
        }
        result, err = fn()
        if err == nil {
            return result, nil
        }
        backoff := time.Duration(1<<uint(i)) * 100 * time.Millisecond
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return result, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(backoff):
        }
    }
    return result, fmt.Errorf("after %d attempts: %w", maxAttempts, err)
}

// Usage
user, err := Retry(ctx, 3, func() (*User, error) {
    return repo.FindByID(ctx, userID)
})

The zero-value initialization (var result T) works cleanly for pointer types, slices, and structs alike. Context cancellation is respected at every step.

Repository Patterns: Less Boilerplate, Real Savings

If you build CRUD-heavy services, you write the same repository interface boilerplate repeatedly. Generics make a real dent here:

type Repository[T any, ID comparable] interface {
    FindByID(ctx context.Context, id ID) (*T, error)
    FindAll(ctx context.Context) ([]T, error)
    Save(ctx context.Context, entity *T) error
    Delete(ctx context.Context, id ID) error
}

The shared pagination logic, soft-delete, and upsert patterns move into a base implementation. Concrete types only implement the scan function for their specific columns. We reduced repository boilerplate by roughly 40% across a mid-sized service mesh.

What Went Wrong

Over-generalization is a real trap

The first weeks after enabling generics in a codebase, there is a temptation to generalize everything. We refactored a readable HTTP handler pipeline into a Pipeline[Input, Output any] abstraction. It took 200 lines to express what 60 concrete lines did before, and the compiler error messages were incomprehensible.

The rule we now follow: if you do not have two distinct concrete types that need the same logic today—not hypothetically—generics are not justified.

Complex type constraints become unreadable fast

Go's union constraints work fine for numeric types:

type Numeric interface {
    ~int | ~int32 | ~int64 | ~float32 | ~float64
}

func Sum[T Numeric](items []T) T {
    var total T
    for _, v := range items {
        total += v
    }
    return total
}

But the moment you need to constrain behavior rather than representation, you are better served by a plain interface with methods.

Stack traces in generic code are verbose

When something fails at runtime inside a generic function, the stack trace shows the instantiated type name: Retry[*github.com/myorg/myapp/domain.User]. It is accurate but noisy. Short type aliases in packages where you instantiate generics most help significantly.

The Verdict

Go generics remove one specific category of duplication: typed container and algorithm code. They do not replace interfaces, embedding, or code generation for other purposes, and they were never meant to.

Use generics for: collection types, typed utilities (Map/Filter/Reduce/Retry), and shared service layer contracts where two or more concrete types share identical behavior today.

Avoid generics for: request/response pipelines, middleware chains, or any abstraction that adds more lines than it removes.

If you are adopting generics in an existing codebase, start with your utility packages. Look for interface{} casts—those are the highest-signal targets. For teams building security-sensitive Go services, pairing these refactors with a thorough security hardening checklist helps surface edge cases that type systems alone cannot catch.

The Takeaway

Two years in, Go generics have settled into a narrow but genuinely useful role. The standard library adopted them thoughtfully (slices, maps, cmp). Production codebases that adopted them selectively are cleaner. The ones that went generic-first are harder to debug.

Write less code, not more abstract code.

I run AYI NEDJIMI Consultants, a cybersecurity consulting firm. We publish free security hardening checklists — PDF and Excel.

title: Amazon EC2 Explained: Instance Types, Sizing, Pricing, and High Availability
description:
Amazon EC2 is often the first AWS service people use, and it is also one of the services that leaves the most infrastructure decisions to the user.

Knowing how to select an instance, choose the right resources, control costs, and design for failures is the foundation for building reliable workloads on AWS.

1. WHAT: Understanding Amazon EC2

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) provides virtual servers that can be configured to meet an application's requirements.

An EC2 instance is a virtual server running on AWS infrastructure. Launching one involves several important decisions:

  1. Amazon Machine Image (AMI): A template that provides the operating system and may include preinstalled software.
  2. Instance type: Determines the available compute resources, including vCPUs, memory, networking capabilities, and sometimes specialized hardware.
  3. Storage: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) provides persistent block storage volumes that can be attached to EC2 instances. Some instance types also provide local instance-store storage.
  4. Security group: A virtual firewall that controls inbound and outbound network traffic associated with the instance.

You must also select a network configuration, an AWS Region, and an Availability Zone or placement configuration.

An EC2 instance runs in a single Availability Zone. This matters because an instance alone does not provide protection against an Availability Zone failure.

Reading an EC2 Instance Type

An EC2 instance type name communicates its family, generation, processor option, and size.

For example, consider m7g.2xlarge.

  • m — Family: General-purpose instances designed to balance compute, memory, and networking resources.
  • 7 — Generation: Identifies the generation of the instance family. Newer generations often improve price-performance, but the actual benefit depends on the workload.
  • g — Processor option: Indicates AWS Graviton, AWS's Arm-based processor family.
  • 2xlarge — Size: Specifies the capacity within the family.

Notice that the meaning of a letter depends on its position and the instance family. In m7g, the final g indicates Graviton. In g5, the initial g identifies the GPU-oriented family.

Instance sizes generally offer increasing capacity as you move from smaller sizes to larger ones. However, the exact vCPU count, memory, network bandwidth, and other resources depend on the specific instance family and size.

The right instance type is therefore not simply the one with the largest number. It is the one that provides the resources your workload actually needs.

2. WHY: Why EC2 Configuration Matters

Applications need compute resources that match their requirements, but incorrect sizing and configuration can increase costs or create performance and availability problems.

Before cloud computing, organizations often had to purchase physical servers, wait for delivery, and estimate future capacity in advance.

EC2 allows teams to provision virtual servers on demand, adjust capacity, and select from different instance families without purchasing physical hardware.

However, EC2 does not eliminate infrastructure management. It changes how that infrastructure is provisioned and operated.

Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model

AWS manages the underlying physical infrastructure and virtualization layer. Customers remain responsible for the guest operating system, application software, instance configuration, and appropriate security controls.

Depending on the workload, customer responsibilities include:

  • Operating system patching and updates.
  • Application deployment and maintenance.
  • Identity and access management.
  • Security group and network configuration.
  • Monitoring and incident response.
  • Capacity planning and scaling.

This division of responsibility is important: AWS manages the infrastructure beneath the instance, but customers still need to secure and operate what runs on it.

Two Common EC2 Design Risks

1. Availability risk

An EC2 instance runs in one Availability Zone. If the instance fails, the application may become unavailable. If the entire AZ experiences an outage, workloads dependent on that AZ may also be affected.

For critical applications, distributing instances across multiple AZs can reduce the impact of an AZ-level failure.

2. Sizing risk

An instance that is too large may leave expensive capacity unused. An instance that is too small may become constrained by CPU, memory, network throughput, or storage performance.

Selecting the wrong instance family can also create bottlenecks. For example, a memory-intensive application running on an instance with insufficient memory may perform poorly even if additional CPU capacity is available.

The solution is to measure the workload, understand its limiting resource, and select the instance accordingly.

3. WHEN: Choosing the Right EC2 Configuration

Choose EC2 when an application needs server-level control, specific software compatibility, specialized hardware, or a continuously running compute environment.

Requirement Likely fit
Operating system control, custom software, or specific licensing requirements EC2
Existing application migration with minimal changes EC2
Specialized hardware, such as supported GPU instances EC2
Steady, continuously running workload EC2 or containers, depending on requirements
Short-running, event-triggered tasks with long idle periods Lambda may be a better fit
Containerized application without a desire to manage EC2 instances ECS or EKS with Fargate, where supported

EC2 is particularly useful when the team needs direct control over the server environment. But choosing EC2 is only the first step. The instance family, processor, size, and purchasing model must also fit the workload.

Choosing an Instance Family

Different EC2 families are designed around different resource requirements.

Family Designed for Typical workloads
M — General purpose Balanced compute and memory Web servers, application servers, smaller databases
T — Burstable general purpose Low baseline CPU usage with the ability to burst Development environments, low-traffic applications
C — Compute optimized High CPU performance relative to memory Batch processing, compute-heavy applications, video encoding
R — Memory optimized Larger memory capacity relative to compute In-memory caches, memory-intensive databases, analytics
I — Storage optimized High storage performance and throughput Storage-intensive databases and data-processing workloads
P and G — GPU accelerated Parallel processing using GPUs P: demanding GPU computing and ML training; G: graphics and supported inference workloads

These are broad categories, not guarantees of suitability. The precise specifications and supported use cases vary by instance generation.

General-purpose instances: M

M-family instances are a sensible starting point when the application needs a balanced amount of CPU and memory.

They are commonly used for application servers, web servers, and workloads that do not have a strongly CPU-bound or memory-bound profile.

Burstable instances: T

T-family instances are designed for workloads that typically use relatively little CPU but occasionally need bursts of processing capacity.

Depending on the specific T instance and its operating mode, CPU credits allow the workload to exceed its baseline CPU performance. Credit behavior and costs should be checked for the selected configuration.

T instances can be cost-effective for development environments and low-traffic applications, but sustained high CPU demand may make another family a better fit.

Compute-optimized instances: C

C-family instances are designed for workloads that benefit from higher compute performance relative to memory.

Examples include CPU-intensive processing, batch workloads, and certain application servers.

Memory-optimized instances: R

R-family instances provide higher memory capacity relative to compute.

They can be appropriate for in-memory processing, memory-intensive databases, and analytics workloads where insufficient RAM is the main bottleneck.

Storage-optimized instances: I

I-family instances are designed for storage-intensive workloads requiring high local storage performance.

Check whether the application requires local instance-store storage or persistent EBS volumes. Local instance-store data has different persistence characteristics and should not be treated as a replacement for persistent storage.

GPU instances: P and G

GPU-accelerated families serve different use cases.

P-family instances are designed for demanding GPU computing, including machine-learning training and high-performance computing workloads. G-family instances target workloads such as graphics processing and supported machine-learning inference.

Select GPU instances only when the software can use GPU acceleration and the performance benefit justifies the additional cost.

Choosing the Processor Architecture

EC2 offers instances based on different processor architectures.

AWS Graviton (Arm): Graviton instances can offer attractive price-performance for compatible workloads. However, the application, dependencies, runtime, and any third-party software must support the Arm architecture.

Intel and AMD (x86): These options are useful when an application or its dependencies require x86 compatibility.

Do not choose a processor based on the name alone. Validate software compatibility and benchmark the actual workload before making a production decision.

Choosing the Instance Generation

Newer instance generations often deliver improved performance, efficiency, or price-performance compared with earlier generations.

However, the newest generation is not automatically the best choice in every situation.

Consider:

  • Availability of the instance type in the chosen Region.
  • Application and operating system compatibility.
  • Performance under realistic workloads.
  • Total cost for the required capacity.
  • Availability of the required processor architecture and features.

Use current-generation instances as a starting point, then validate the decision against actual requirements.

Choosing an EC2 Purchasing Model

Instance selection determines the compute resources. The purchasing model determines how those resources are paid for.

On-Demand Instances

Pay for compute capacity without a long-term commitment. These are useful for initial testing, unpredictable workloads, and applications where flexibility is important.

Savings Plans

Commit to a specified amount of eligible compute usage, generally measured in dollars per hour, for a one- or three-year term in exchange for discounted pricing on eligible usage.

Savings Plans provide pricing benefits but do not, by themselves, reserve physical instance capacity.

Reserved Instances

Reserved Instances provide a pricing discount for eligible configurations in exchange for a commitment, typically for one or three years. They are distinct from Savings Plans and have different flexibility and applicability rules.

Spot Instances

Spot Instances use spare AWS capacity at a discount. AWS can interrupt them when it needs that capacity, typically providing a two-minute warning when an interruption notice is issued.

Spot is suitable for interruption-tolerant workloads such as fault-tolerant batch processing, distributed jobs, and certain testing workloads. Applications must be designed to handle interruptions.

A practical strategy is to begin with a suitable flexible purchasing option, measure actual usage, and then evaluate commitment-based pricing once the workload's baseline demand is understood.

4. HOW: Selecting and Deploying EC2 for a Real Workload

Identify the workload's bottleneck, choose a suitable instance family and processor, size it using measured usage, and design for failure.

Consider migrating an on-premises inventory application to AWS.

Step 1: Measure the Existing Workload

Review current CPU utilization, memory consumption, storage performance, network usage, and peak demand.

  • Consistent CPU pressure may point toward a compute-optimized instance.
  • High memory utilization may indicate a memory-optimized instance.
  • Balanced resource usage may suit a general-purpose instance.
  • Low baseline CPU usage with occasional spikes may suit a burstable instance.

These observations provide a starting point. Validate the choice through workload testing rather than relying on a single metric.

Step 2: Select the Processor

Determine whether the application and its dependencies support Arm-based processors.

If they do, test an appropriate Graviton instance against a comparable x86 instance. Otherwise, choose a compatible Intel- or AMD-based instance.

Compare actual performance and cost before deciding.

Step 3: Select the Generation and Size

Choose a suitable current-generation instance available in the target Region.

Start with a size that meets measured resource requirements and provides reasonable headroom for peak demand. Avoid excessive overprovisioning, but do not size solely around average utilization.

Step 4: Configure Storage and Network Security

Choose the appropriate EBS volume type and capacity based on the application's storage requirements.

Configure security groups to permit only the necessary inbound and outbound traffic. Avoid exposing administrative access or application ports unnecessarily.

Use appropriate IAM roles, encryption, logging, and patching practices as part of the broader security design.

Step 5: Design for Availability

For an application that requires resilience to an AZ failure, consider a design such as:

Users → Application Load Balancer → EC2 instances in AZ-A and AZ-B

Configure the load balancer's target group health checks so traffic is directed to healthy targets.

Use Auto Scaling where appropriate to maintain the desired capacity and replace unhealthy instances. Ensure that application state and dependencies are designed to support multi-AZ operation.

For example, a database may need its own high-availability design, such as Amazon RDS Multi-AZ. Simply placing two application servers in separate AZs does not protect a single-AZ database or other shared dependency.

The goal is to avoid a single infrastructure dependency that can take down the entire application.

Step 6: Select the Purchasing Model

Use On-Demand capacity during development, testing, or early production when usage is not yet predictable.

Once usage becomes stable, evaluate Savings Plans or eligible Reserved Instance options. For suitable fault-tolerant jobs, consider Spot Instances.

The correct decision depends on workload stability, interruption tolerance, commitment flexibility, and total cost.

Step 7: Monitor and Right-size

After deployment, monitor CPU, memory, network activity, storage performance, and application response times.

Amazon CloudWatch provides monitoring and metrics for supported AWS resources. AWS Compute Optimizer can analyze supported resource usage and provide rightsizing recommendations.


Review the recommendations alongside real application performance, business requirements, and expected growth.

If the instance is consistently underutilized, a smaller size may reduce costs. If a resource is saturated, investigate whether resizing, changing families, or improving the application is the better solution.

Estimating EC2 Costs

An EC2 cost estimate depends on more than the instance's hourly rate.

Consider:

  • Instance type and size.
  • Hours running and expected utilization.
  • Purchasing model and eligible discounts.
  • EBS storage and provisioned performance.
  • Data transfer charges.
  • Load balancers, monitoring, and other supporting services.
  • Additional instances needed for high availability.

A single-instance estimate may look inexpensive but fail to represent the actual cost of a production architecture. Estimate the complete design, including resilience and supporting services.

5. Conclusion: The EC2 Design Principle

Amazon EC2 gives teams substantial control over the server environment, but that control comes with operational responsibility.

A sound EC2 design starts by understanding the workload, selecting the right instance family and processor, sizing capacity using real measurements, and choosing an appropriate purchasing model.

For production workloads, availability must also be designed deliberately. Multiple instances across Availability Zones, health checks, appropriate scaling, and resilient dependencies help reduce the impact of infrastructure failures.

The key principle: Match the instance to what limits the workload, validate it with real usage, optimize the total cost, and design for failure rather than assuming a server will always be available.

title: After Building StoreFrame in NEXT.js, Headless Magento Will Make a Big Comeback
description:
PWA Studio, Vue Storefront, GraphCommerce, Rapidez, Breeze and Hyva: why headless Magento kept losing to cost, and why AI that writes JavaScript fluently may finally flip the verdict.

Headless Magento had a moment, and then it had a funeral. Ask my ex-colleagues about it. Magento developers have been chasing Lighthouse scores and a faster frontend since 2013, and most of us went back to the stack we already knew.

I was one of them: a Magento frontend developer stuck in the PHP world, knowing only a tiny bit of jQuery. NEXT.js was a foreign object. Then I built StoreFrame’s hub, and this site, www.storeframe.io, in NEXT.js. It is my first NEXT.js project. No joke. Somewhere in that build I changed my mind about the old headless debate, and the reason is sitting in my own codebase.

To explain why, we have to start with the original attempt, and why every attempt after it ran into the same wall.

Venia and PWA Studio: the original headless Magento

When Magento shipped PWA Studio with Venia as its reference storefront, it was the official answer to a slow Luma frontend: a React application, talking to Magento through GraphQL, with its own build pipeline and its own deploy. On paper it was the clean architecture. Magento becomes a commerce API, the storefront becomes a modern JavaScript app.

In practice, the complaint from web developers was always the same: you now needed two experienced developers. One who knows React, webpack and GraphQL. One who knows PHP, dependency injection and Magento’s module system. And those two people had to agree on every field, every resolver and every checkout step.

It got worse with extensions. The Magento module ecosystem was built for Luma. Every payment method, every shipping rule, every third-party module you bought had to expose its data over GraphQL and get a React counterpart before it worked in Venia. Many never did, so somebody wrote that bridge, by hand, store by store.

Adobe has since moved on. PWA Studio still gets maintenance and compatibility releases, but new storefront projects are pointed toward Edge Delivery Services instead. The original headless Magento is not dead. It is just no longer where anyone is building.

Vue Storefront: the community’s answer

Vue Storefront came out of the same frustration, from developers who wanted the Magento frontend fast and flexible, in Vue instead of React. For a while it was the exciting option, with a busy community and agencies building on it.

But it inherited the same bill: a separate JavaScript application, its own release cycle, and an integration layer to keep in sync with Magento. Over time the project went platform-agnostic, added a React kit, and in March 2024 rebranded as Alokai, positioned as a commercial frontend platform for many commerce backends. That may be a sound business. As the default way to build a Magento frontend, it never happened.

The alternatives that stayed

After those two, the ecosystem split into tools that chose a side: either fully decoupled, or as close to Magento’s own templates as possible.

GraphCommerce

GraphCommerce is a React and NEXT.js storefront that talks to Magento through GraphQL only. It runs as a separate application and is the most modern take on the Venia idea. It is also, honestly, still two stacks: you need the React side and the Magento side, and the GraphQL contract in between.

Rapidez

Rapidez takes a different route: Laravel, Blade and Vue, reading catalog data straight from Magento’s database and Elasticsearch, with GraphQL for the rest. PHP developers feel at home in it. But it is still a second application next to Magento, with its own deploy and its own upgrade path.

Breeze

Breeze goes the other way. It keeps Luma’s templates and layout and swaps the heavy JavaScript underneath, RequireJS and Knockout, for a much lighter runtime. Most Luma-compatible modules keep working. No second application, no second team.

Hyva

Hyva is the one that won, at least this round. Tailwind and Alpine.js, a fraction of the bytes, a good Lighthouse score out of the box, and the .phtml and XML layout every Magento developer already knew. One lean stack instead of two. Since November 2025 the theme itself is free and open source.

There is a reason everyone in this industry knows Willem Wigman, Hyva’s founder. In fifteen years, only a handful of people have been able to show real work on both sides, frontend and backend. Hyva won because it did not ask every team to find one of those people.

Why headless died: cost, not architecture

So let’s be honest about why decoupled Magento didn’t win. A fast frontend talking to Magento purely as a commerce API is a good architecture. It died on cost and complexity, which is how most good architectures die.

Most PHP developers don’t do JavaScript. Most frontend developers who know a bit of PHP don’t do React either. And plenty of experienced Magento backend developers can’t centre a div inside a div. So headless meant two hires, two skill sets and two codebases to keep in step, forever. Hyva gave most of the speed for one. Why on earth run two stacks when one gets you nearly there?

What changed: AI speaks JavaScript fluently

Here is why I think the funeral was premature. Ask the obvious question: what is an AI agent almost unfairly good at? JavaScript. TypeScript. React. NEXT.js. Tailwind. The exact stack a decoupled frontend is built from.

That is not an accident. JavaScript and TypeScript sit at the top of GitHub’s language rankings year after year, and the frontend world has rewritten itself every few years: jQuery, Backbone, Angular, React, Vue, Svelte, NEXT.js. Each wave left behind millions of public repositories, tutorials, Stack Overflow answers and migration guides. Models learned from all of it. Magento’s XML layout and .phtml conventions are a small corner of the internet by comparison.

For a frontend developer, that is a relief. The churn that used to drive us crazy, a new framework, a new router, a new build tool every two years, is exactly what the agent has already read. You describe the component; it knows the idiom of whichever version you happen to be on.

Web fundamentals: the copy-paste Lighthouse 100

This is the part nobody wanted to say out loud. With a headless NEXT.js frontend, getting an almost, if not perfect, 100 Lighthouse score is close to mechanical. Run Lighthouse. **__Copy the report*__. *Paste it into the prompt. The agent fixes what it lists: the LCP image without priority, the font that isn’t preloaded, the image without dimensions that shifts the layout, the JavaScript that ships but never runs. Run it again.

It works because in a headless frontend you own every byte on the page. Every Lighthouse finding points at code in your repository, in a framework the agent knows inside out. In a classic Magento theme the same report points into RequireJS bundles, third-party module templates and inline scripts you don’t own and can’t safely change. That loop is how I tuned this site, and it took minutes, not a sprint.

The fundamentals didn’t change: ship less JavaScript, size your images, load fonts properly, don’t block the main thread. What changed is the cost of applying them. It used to take a frontend specialist a weeks or months tweaking everything and breaking it over an upgrade. Now it takes an agent a coffee break.

Frontend and backend can finally work together

Remember the two-developer problem from Venia: two people, two stacks, and a GraphQL contract nobody wanted to own. That contract is where most headless projects bled time.

Now creating an API is a few prompts away. Need a GraphQL resolver for a custom module, or a REST endpoint for a checkout field? Describe it, let the agent write it, read the diff. Need the frontend to consume it? The same agent reads the schema and writes the typed client and the component. The backend developer doesn’t have to learn React, and the frontend developer doesn’t have to learn dependency injection. They meet at the contract, and the contract is cheap.

That is what happened to me. A Magento frontend developer with a bit of jQuery built a full NEXT.js product, with its API, websockets and dashboard, because the agent filled the half of the stack I never learned.

Claude Design: the Figma handoff disappears

The last piece is design. Claude Design, which Anthropic launched in April 2026, turns a prompt, a screenshot or your existing design system into a working prototype. Personally, I think it is a Figma killer, and the market briefly seemed to agree: Figma’s stock fell about 7% on launch day.

The reason matters more than the stock price. A Figma file is a picture of an interface that somebody still has to rebuild in code. What Claude Design produces is already HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and it hands off to Claude Code. Turning that into React components for a NEXT.js storefront is a short step, because it was never a drawing in the first place. Design, frontend and the API it calls now sit in one loop.

Why I picked NEXT.js over anything else

If AI writes the JavaScript, why NEXT.js and not something else? Fair question. Here is my honest answer, in four parts.

  1. Shadcn, nothing more and nothing less. shadcn/ui is the component library I am sworn to. It was born in React and NEXT.js; the Svelte and Vue versions are ports. I want to be on the original, not the copy.
  2. The ecosystem is more polished. Animation libraries like Motion (which started life as Framer Motion), frameworks, starter kits and tooling all land in React and NEXT.js first, and they are more finished there than anywhere else.
  3. Explicit beats clever when AI writes it. Svelte might be easier, and Nuxt might be a lot better in many ways, if I were writing the JavaScript myself. But the agent writes most of it. When the agent writes and reads every line, an explicit, even verbose component it can see all of matters more than an elegant abstraction that hides what is going on.
  4. The AI tools already speak React. Guess what v0, Vercel and Claude Design produce? React. When the tools that generate interfaces all default to the same stack, that is a strong hint about what the models know best.

And StoreFrame’s NEXT.js app isn’t another Hello World portfolio site. It isn’t even a simple CRUD app wrapped in auth and payments. Most of what happens inside it runs over websockets: live consoles, live deploy logs, live metrics streaming in from every store.

Almost nobody in the PHP world builds websockets. Magento leans on caching, and real-time is the exact opposite of a cache. So after taming that beast with an agent at my side, I am more than confident that NEXT.js is a solid choice when AI is writing the JavaScript.

Is this Hyva’s peak?

Every Magento frontend has had its period. Luma had one. PWA Studio had one. Vue Storefront had one. So it’s fair to ask whether Hyva will have its period too, and whether that is something to worry about.

Not tomorrow. Hyva is still a safe, fast choice for most merchants today, and nobody needs to panic about a store running on it. I’m not telling anyone to re-platform onto a headless build this afternoon.

But I’m skeptical it is the endgame. Every Magento frontend so far has been a bet on a niche skill: Knockout for Luma, React wired into GraphQL for Venia, .phtml with Alpine for Hyva. The pool of developers, and the training data behind every AI model, is overwhelmingly JavaScript. When the cost of a JavaScript frontend collapses, a stack built to avoid JavaScript loses its main reason to exist. At times, I'm as skeptical as staying on Magento too.

I’m on the headless bandwagon, 1000%

The thing that buried headless was economics, not architecture, and the economics just changed. When an agent can write the decoupled frontend, the API between the two halves and the design it starts from, the overhead stops being the dealbreaker it was. AI writes JavaScript like Magnus Carlsen plays blindfold chess.

So yes, I’m definitely on the bandwagon. StoreFrame’s own frontend already is: a NEXT.js app with the backend behind an API. Give the agents a few more turns of the crank, and a split frontend-and-backend Magento stops being the brave choice and becomes the sensible one.

I said in an earlier post that this was a story for another day. This is me starting to tell it. It isn’t mainstream yet. But for the first time in years, I’m betting on it.

We build StoreFrame’s own frontend in NEXT.js and run Magento underneath it — so when the headless math flips for real, we’ll be ready. Curious how we think about the stack?

See how StoreFrame works

title: I Wasted Half My /24s Before I Learned VLSM
description:
I ran an office network. The engineering floor had 60 machines, marketing had 25, finance had 15, and the executive floor had 4. Each team "just needs its own subnet," so I handed out four fresh /24s. That's 4 x 254 usable addresses — more than 1,000 — for a building with about 100 machines total. I was using roughly 10% of what I allocated and calling it good practice.

The same scene repeats everywhere: a /24 with 20 devices on it, a /26 holding 15, a VLAN with a printer and a door controller. Each one feels harmless, until you actually run out of address space and have to renumber the whole floor.

The fix is VLSM — Variable Length Subnet Masking. And it's a one-sentence rule once you see the word.

The one-sentence rule

VLSM means different subnets inside the same network can use different prefix lengths, so each subnet is sized to what it actually contains — instead of forcing every subnet to share the same width.

Without VLSM, if you're working inside 192.168.0.0/24, every subnet you carve out of it has the same size. Two /25s, each 126 usable addresses. A team of 15 gets 126 addresses and the other 111 sit idle. Then you run out of /24s and wonder where all the space went.

With VLSM, you mix the sizes freely: one /26 (62 usable) for engineering's 60 machines, a /27 (30 usable) for the 25-person team, another /27 (30 usable) for the 15-person team, and a /28 (14 usable) for the executive floor — all carved from a single /24.

A worked example (this is the whole trick)

Let's split 192.168.10.0/24, which gives 254 usable addresses, into four segments: 60 devices, 25 devices, 15 devices, and 4 devices.

For each, round the host count up to the next power of two, then subtract 2 for the network and broadcast addresses, then pick the prefix that matches:

Segment Prefix Addresses Usable hosts Assign to
192.168.10.0 /26 64 62 Engineering (60)
192.168.10.64 /27 32 30 Marketing (25)
192.168.10.96 /27 32 30 Finance (15)
192.168.10.128 /28 16 14 Exec (4)

Add up the usable hosts: 62 + 30 + 30 + 14 = 136 total — still barely half of the 254 the /24 could hold, but every team gets only as much as it needs.

The subtle part: VLSM doesn't mean "make every subnet as small as possible." It means "choose each subnet's size from the same /24 based on its need."

A quick reference for picking the prefix

You don't want to redo the subtraction every time you plan a segment, so here's the lookup I actually use:

Hosts needed Block Prefix Usable
2 4 /30 2
6 8 /29 6
14 16 /28 14
30 32 /27 30
62 64 /26 62
126 128 /25 126
254 256 /24 254

To read it: "I need room for 60 machines" → 60 fits in the 64-size block → that's a /26, giving 62 usable.

That's the whole skill: memorize the "next power of two minus 2" ladder, and VLSM becomes table lookup instead of head-scratching.

When you should NOT use VLSM

  1. Routing gets more complicated. Every width you mix in means the router carries more entries.
  2. Future growth is harder. If "25 devices" becomes "80 next quarter," you're renumbering that subnet.
  3. The next person has to read your mind. The cleverest allocation is the hardest to maintain.
  4. You're still learning the basic power-of-two math. Flat equal-sized subnets are a fine starting point.

Build the plan without doing arithmetic in your head

When you're laying out several real segments, the subtraction slips — a /26 becomes a /28, or two blocks overlap. I keep a VLSM calculator that takes the network and the list of host counts, and returns a minimal, non-overlapping layout, showing the network, usable range, and hosts for each segment side by side. It's free, runs entirely in the browser, and makes the plan verifiable instead of vibes.

For the longer reasoning — why variable-length works and a fuller worked example — I've written it up in VLSM explained.

The takeaway is short: the /24 you give to a 4-person team isn't "playing it safe" — it's burning the exact thing that eventually runs out. VLSM keeps one clean address budget, gives each segment only what it needs, and leaves room for the next request. It stopped me from asking for "another /24 for five people," and it'll save your address space the same way.
