title: Designing a Political Quiz UI as an Explicit State Machine
description:
A questionnaire UI looks simple until the unhappy paths arrive. A user changes an earlier answer, reloads halfway through, reaches the final question with one response missing, or expects a “private” flow to work without a network round trip. At that point, a stack of booleans becomes harder to reason about than the questionnaire itself.

This article treats a public 48-question political test as a black-box product example. It does not claim access to its source code, private architecture, analytics, or production implementation. The goal is to extract reusable frontend questions from what the interface publicly promises.

Start with states, not screens

The visible journey suggests a compact domain model:

type QuizState =
  | { kind: "intro" }
  | { kind: "answering"; index: number; answers: Answer[] }
  | { kind: "review"; answers: Answer[] }
  | { kind: "result"; axes: AxisScore[] }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

type Answer = -2 | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2;

type AxisScore = {
  id: string;
  value: number;
  leftLabel: string;
  rightLabel: string;
};

This is a design proposal, not an observation of internal code. Its benefit is that invalid combinations become harder to represent. There is no separate isFinished, showResult, and hasError trio that can accidentally all become true.

Test Ideologia Politica is a useful reference surface because its public promise is unusually concrete: 48 statements, a five-point agreement scale, 12 result axes, no account requirement, and scoring performed on the device.

Make every transition explicit

A transition table is more useful than a component tree when product behavior is still being defined.

Current state Event Guard Next state
intro START questions loaded answering(0)
answering ANSWER valid scale value answering(next)
answering BACK index > 0 answering(previous)
answering FINISH every item answered result
answering FINISH answer missing review
review EDIT valid question id answering(index)
result RESTART always intro

The important rule is that one user event causes one documented transition. “Answer and maybe finish and maybe calculate and maybe navigate” is a cluster of behaviors that deserves decomposition.

For a fixed sequence grouped by axis, the UI should also define whether going back overwrites the previous response, whether progress shows questions seen or questions answered, and whether a neutral answer counts as complete. These are product rules, not implementation details.

Treat local scoring as a verifiable contract

“Calculated on your device” is both a privacy promise and an architectural constraint. A QA plan should be able to verify it without reading source code:

  1. Complete the flow with the network disabled after the initial page load.
  2. Observe whether answers trigger requests.
  3. Reload and check whether partial answers persist, disappear, or are explicitly recoverable.
  4. Confirm that clearing site data removes locally stored responses.
  5. Check that the result can be reproduced from the same answer vector.

The public Test Ideologia Politica interface says answers are not sent to a server and that the result is shown in the browser. That statement should be covered by regression tests because privacy copy becomes a product contract the moment it is published.

Separate scoring from interpretation

Multi-axis products need at least three layers:

  • Answer normalization: convert the five choices into stable numeric values.
  • Axis calculation: aggregate the relevant items, including reverse-scored questions where defined.
  • Presentation: turn scores into labels, charts, explanatory text, and comparisons.

Keeping those layers separate makes tests clearer. A copy change should not alter a score. A chart redesign should not change party affinity. A revised scoring rule should be visible in versioned fixtures rather than hidden inside a component.

The same separation helps with political neutrality. A nearest-party comparison is an editorial reference based on a chosen coordinate set; it should not be represented as a deterministic truth about the user. The UI needs language such as “indicative,” “closest on these dimensions,” and “not a voting recommendation.”

Accessibility is part of the state model

For each new question, focus should land on the question heading, not remain on the button from the previous screen. The five choices should form a radio group with an accessible name. Progress needs text—“Question 17 of 48”—rather than color alone. Keyboard users should be able to choose, continue, return, and review without a pointer.

Result charts also need a nonvisual equivalent. A radar or map can be attractive, but every axis should have a text label and value. Opposing pole labels must not rely on spatial position alone.

Tests that catch real failures

Before shipping a similar interface, cover these cases:

  • starting without JavaScript or with question data unavailable;
  • selecting each of the five answer values;
  • changing an earlier response and recalculating;
  • finishing with the first, middle, or last answer missing;
  • reloading at question 1, 24, and 48;
  • navigating with keyboard only;
  • reduced-motion mode and narrow mobile view;
  • deterministic results for a fixed answer fixture;
  • no answer payload in network traffic when local-only processing is promised;
  • clear restart behavior with no stale scores.

The deeper lesson is that a questionnaire is not a form with a fancy result page. It is a small stateful application handling sensitive opinions. Model it with the same care you would give checkout, onboarding, or account recovery—especially when the copy makes privacy and interpretability part of the product promise.

title: Our header is 48 pixels tall, every page offsets by 56, and the root layout renders no header at all
description:
notifio.app is the marketing site for a desktop app that watches rental search pages and alerts you when a new listing appears. The site is 38 URLs. Its header is one component, 70 lines, and the three most interesting things in it are a pair of pointer-events classes, a number that is wrong on purpose, and the fact that app/layout.tsx does not render it.

The layout renders fonts and a JSON-LD block, and then stops

Here is everything inside <body> in the root layout:

<body className="bg-[#0a0a0a] text-[#fafafa] antialiased font-sans">
  {/* Who is behind this site, in the form a crawler reads. */}
  <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ ... }} />
  {children}
</body>

No nav. No footer. Both are imported and rendered by each page:

$ grep -rl --include="*.tsx" "<Nav" src | wc -l
15

Fifteen files, each opening with the same three lines. The App Router's whole pitch is that shared chrome belongs in a layout, so this needs a reason, and the honest one is a shape rather than a rule: a layout wraps every route under it, and opting out of a layout means moving a route into a different segment. Putting the header in the page means a page that should not have one simply does not import it.

Today, all fifteen import it. The payment success page imports it, the maintenance page imports it, and so the opt-out I am describing is currently used by nothing, which makes the duplication a cost with a hypothetical benefit. The part that keeps it from being a real problem is that fifteen files is not 38 pages: one of them is ArticleLayout, which renders all eight long-form pages, the five listed at notifio.app/guides plus three audience pages, and two more are dynamic routes covering the fifteen entries at notifio.app/alerts and the five at notifio.app/compare. The number of files that would need editing to change the chrome is fifteen; the number of pages is 38.

If I were starting again I would put it in the layout and use a route group for anything that needs to escape. I am writing down the trade rather than the conclusion, because the version in the repo works and has never once been the reason a change was hard.

Two classes so a transparent header does not eat clicks

The header is fixed, full width, and centres its contents:

<div
  className={`fixed top-0 inset-x-0 z-50 flex justify-center pointer-events-none transition-all duration-300 ease-out ${
    scrolled ? "pt-3 px-4" : "pt-0 px-0"
  }`}
>
  <nav className="pointer-events-auto w-full ...">

pointer-events-none on the outer div, pointer-events-auto on the nav inside it. This is the entire reason the design works.

Once scrolled, the nav is a rounded pill with max-w-6xl and 12px of padding above it. The outer div is still the full width of the viewport and roughly 60 pixels tall, sitting at z-50 above everything. Without those two classes, that invisible rectangle swallows every click and hover in the top strip of the page, including the ones aimed at the gap either side of the pill. Nothing in the UI tells you why. You just find a dead zone at the top of a page, usually on a wide monitor, usually weeks later.

The pair is the smallest fix available: the container keeps its layout job and gives up its hit-testing job, and the one child that needs to be clickable takes hit-testing back. Worth remembering as a shape, because every floating or inset fixed element has this problem: a fixed positioning container is as clickable as it is wide, not as wide as it looks.

The scroll state is a boolean, and that is a throttle 

const [scrolled, setScrolled] = useState(false);

useEffect(() => {
  const onScroll = () => setScrolled(window.scrollY > 20);
  window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });
  return () => window.removeEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
}, []);

No requestAnimationFrame, no debounce, no IntersectionObserver sentinel. The listener runs on every scroll event, which during a trackpad flick is a lot of events, and it reads window.scrollY each time, which is a layout read.

What it does not do is re-render. setScrolled(false) while the state is already false is a no-op as far as the rendered output goes, because React bails out when the next state is identical to the current one. The component re-renders when the value flips, so a long scroll down the pricing page produces one state change rather than four hundred. The derived class strings change at exactly the moment the appearance is supposed to change, and the CSS transition does the 300ms of work between the two states.

That leaves the cost of the handler itself, which is why { passive: true } is there: it promises the browser that this listener will never call preventDefault, so scrolling is not blocked waiting to find out. A boolean threshold plus a passive listener is enough for this. The version with a rAF-throttled handler and a ref holding the last value is more code that produces the same pixels.

The one thing I would change: the handler never runs on mount. Load the page already scrolled, which happens on a refresh or when following a link to an anchor, and the header renders in its unscrolled state until you move. One extra onScroll() call before the addEventListener fixes it, and it is a genuine bug rather than a trade.

The number 56, seventeen times

The nav's inner row is h-12, which is 48 pixels. When scrolled it gains pt-3, 12 more, for 60. Every page then pushes its content down by this:

<main className="pt-14">

pt-14 is 56 pixels. Not 48, not 60, in between.

$ grep -rn --include="*.tsx" "pt-14" src | wc -l
16
$ grep -rn --include="*.tsx" "100vh-56" src | wc -l
2

Fifteen of those sixteen pt-14 matches are a page clearing the header, the sixteenth is the footer's own padding, and the two calc matches are this, on the success and maintenance pages:

<main className="pt-14">
  <section className="flex min-h-[calc(100vh-56px)] items-center justify-center px-6 py-20">

The same constant written twice in two notations, in two files, for pages whose single card is supposed to be vertically centred in whatever is left under the header. Seventeen places that know how tall the header is, and the one match that is not about the header at all is the footer, which is its own small hazard: the string is not searchable for the thing it means.

The defensible part is that the header is position: fixed, so it is out of flow and the gap under it has to come from somewhere. The indefensible part is the value. 48 and 60 are both real heights depending on scroll position, 56 is neither, and the reason it works is that pages have 80 pixels of their own top padding under it so an 8 pixel error is invisible.

A CSS variable, --nav-height, set once and used by both the component and the pages, would make the relationship explicit and let the two states disagree honestly. The reason it has not happened is the reason most of these do not: nothing has gone wrong yet. Writing it down is the cheap half of fixing it.

Three links out of 38 URLs 

<Link href="/alerts">Sites</Link>
<Link href="/pricing">Pricing</Link>
<Link href="/download">Get Notifio</Link>

That is the whole menu, with no mobile variant because three short links fit. The hub pages for guides and comparisons are not in it, which is deliberate: the header carries the path a visitor is on, which is "what does it watch", "what does it cost", "give me the app". Everything else is reachable from the footer, which has its own set of trade-offs that I wrote up in the footer post, and from in-page links.

The one detail in the markup worth copying:

<Image src="/icon-light.svg" alt="" width={18} height={18} priority className="opacity-90" />
Notifio

alt="" on the logo, because the word "Notifio" is right there in the same link as text. An alt="Notifio" here makes a screen reader announce the brand twice for one link. The priority is because this is the only image above the fold on every route.

What the component is, in total

A fixed container that does not take clicks, a pill inside it that does, one boolean of state, three links, and a hardcoded offset repeated in every page. The interesting work in a site header is almost never the markup. It is the two classes that keep an invisible rectangle from stealing input, and the constant that quietly knows how tall everything is.

The 38 URLs it sits on are mostly generated rather than written, which is a different post: our sitemap is 38 URLs and only ten of them are typed out by hand. The app the header is advertising is at notifio.app/download.

title: 40 font-face blocks, 10 files, and the word bold appears nowhere: three typefaces reaching a Next.js site and an Expo app
description:
Munchable uses three typefaces, and each has exactly one job. Fredoka, which is round and friendly, is allowed on the wordmark and hero headlines and nowhere else. Outfit does every other heading. Nunito does body text. The sizes come from a tokens package shared by the website, the phone app and the renderer that produces our video, so a heading is 27/33 in all three.

Two of those consumers load the fonts in completely different ways, and the second one surprised me more than it should have.

The web half, and why it is self-hosted 

const nunito = Nunito({
  subsets: ['latin'],
  weight: ['400', '500', '600', '700'],
  variable: '--font-nunito',
  display: 'swap',
});

Three of those, one per family, each exposing a CSS variable that globals.css consumes through role names rather than family names:

--font-display: var(--font-outfit), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
--font-body: var(--font-nunito), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
--font-brand: var(--font-fredoka), var(--font-nunito), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;

--font-brand falling back to Nunito before the system stack is deliberate: if the display face fails, the wordmark should land on the font the rest of the page is already using rather than on whatever Helvetica the device has.

next/font/google downloads the font files at build time and serves them from our own origin. That is a privacy decision before it is a performance one. A <link> to fonts.googleapis.com means every page load reports the visitor's IP address to a third party, and this is a site where the page somebody is reading can be the IBD page or the SIBO page. The URL is a health disclosure. There is no third-party request in the critical path of any page here, and the privacy policy says so, which means the fonts had to come along.

What that actually ships

You can count this yourself on any page of the site. Pull the stylesheet and look at the @font-face blocks:

  • 40 @font-face blocks
  • 10 distinct .woff2 files
  • 3 of the blocks are not web fonts at all

The three odd ones are named Nunito Fallback, Outfit Fallback and Fredoka Fallback. They are synthetic faces pointing at a local system font with adjusted metrics, generated so that the text drawn before the real font arrives occupies close to the same space. That is the mechanism that keeps display: swap from shoving your layout sideways, and it is the main reason to use the font loader rather than hand-writing the @font-face rules.

Forty blocks for ten files because the same file is declared under several weights and several unicode ranges. The browser then fetches only the ones a page actually asks for. On the homepage, in a fresh profile:

performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
  .filter(r => /\.woff2/.test(r.name))
  .map(r => [r.name.split('/').pop().slice(0, 12), r.encodedBodySize]);

Three files, 101,084 bytes in total, all from munchable.app.

The audit this led to

Eleven weights are declared across the three families: four of Nunito, four of Outfit, three of Fredoka.

The public stylesheet contains exactly three numeric weights: 600, 700 and 800. Body copy inherits 400 and never says so. Grep it and that is the whole list, inline SVG demos included.

Which means at least two declared weights are never referenced by the site: font-weight: 500 appears nowhere in the public CSS at all. It appears in exactly one file in the repository, the admin panel's own stylesheet, which is behind authentication and noindexed.

The honest accounting here matters, because it explains why nobody noticed. A declared and unreferenced weight costs a visitor nothing in bandwidth: no rule asks for it, so the file is never fetched. It costs build output, a slightly bigger stylesheet, and a wrong answer to the question "which weights does this product use". It is a one-line fix in each of three calls, and the reason to make it is tidiness rather than speed, which is worth saying out loud instead of dressing it up as a performance win.

The React Native half, where weight is not a number

Here is the part that trips up anybody moving a design system onto React Native. On the web, you ask for a family and a weight and the browser picks a face. In React Native with custom fonts, the weight is part of the family's name:

export const fontMap = {
  Fredoka_600SemiBold,
  Fredoka_700Bold,
  Outfit_500Medium,
  Outfit_600SemiBold,
  Outfit_700Bold,
  Nunito_400Regular,
  Nunito_600SemiBold,
  Nunito_700Bold,
};

Eight named faces, handed to expo-font's useFonts. Then the type scale attaches a family to each variant rather than a weight:

export const typography = {
  brand: { fontFamily: 'Fredoka_700Bold', ...typeScale.brand },
  hero: { fontFamily: 'Fredoka_700Bold', ...typeScale.hero },
  display: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_700Bold', ...typeScale.display },
  h1: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_700Bold', ...typeScale.h1 },
  h2: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.h2 },
  title: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.title },
  body: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_400Regular', ...typeScale.body },
  bodyStrong: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_700Bold', ...typeScale.bodyStrong },
  label: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_700Bold', ...typeScale.label },
  caption: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.caption },
};

fontWeight appears nowhere in the app. Not in the tokens, not in a component, not in a screen. Grep returns nothing, and that is the design: setting fontWeight: '700' on a custom family asks the platform to synthesise a bold, which on Android is a smeared version of the regular face and on iOS is sometimes ignored entirely. Two platforms, two different wrong answers. Naming the face is the only portable instruction.

The ...typeScale.h2 spread is where the two halves meet. The sizes and line heights live in a platform-free package, so h2 is 21/27 on a phone, in the browser build of the same app, and in the rendered video frames, without anybody retyping a number.

One <Text variant="h2"> component reads that table. No screen picks a family, so there is no screen that can pick the wrong one.

Boot, briefly

Fonts block the splash screen, because the app's first screen is a scanner and text reflowing under somebody's thumb in a supermarket aisle is worse than a slightly longer splash. But the gate is fontsLoaded || fontError: a font that fails to load must not hold the app hostage, and the fallback stack exists precisely so that case is merely uglier rather than broken.

Where to see all three

The homepage is the only page with the brand face at full size, so munchable.app is where Fredoka actually earns its place. A content page such as the congee recipe is the ordinary case: Outfit for the headings, Nunito for everything you read, and nothing from a third-party domain in the network panel.

title: A 3% zoom hid a one-pixel rounding gap for 372 cards, then cut the first letters off the 373rd
description:
A while ago I wrote about
putting a real screenshot at the top of 372 practice test cards:
a dev-only capture route, a crop script, and a manifest the build generates so a
card can never point at a file that is not there.

This post is what happened when a second kind of content needed the same
treatment, which is the point at which you find out which of your decisions were
decisions and which were coincidences.

The frame, and the arithmetic in it

The screenshot does not sit flush at the top of the card. It sits inset, like
the screen of a handheld console, with the card acting as the case around it:

<div className="shrink-0 p-2 pb-0">
  <div className="bg-muted ring-border relative aspect-[16/10] overflow-hidden rounded-[12px] ring-1">
    <div className="absolute -inset-px">
      <Image src={src} alt={alt} fill sizes={sizes} className="object-cover" />
    </div>
    {badge && <div className="absolute top-2.5 right-2.5 shadow-sm">{badge}</div>}
  </div>
</div>

The radius is not a taste choice, it is subtraction. The card is
rounded-[20px]. The frame around the screen is p-2, so 8px. A rounded corner
inset by 8px only stays parallel to its parent if its own radius is 8px smaller:
20 - 8 = 12, hence rounded-[12px]. Use the same radius for both and the inner
corner looks tighter than the outer one; use a bigger one and the gap between
the curves visibly fattens at 45 degrees. This is the single most common
giveaway in nested rounded rectangles and it costs one subtraction to get right.

The aspect ratio is 16/10 because that is the capture ratio, so the box and
the image agree and object-cover has nothing to crop. I did try a shorter box
on phones, on the theory that a card is mostly text. It cut off the bottom strip
of the screen, which in most of our tests is where the answer controls live, so
the screenshot stopped showing the thing it was there to show.

The bug the extraction exposed

Look at that inner wrapper again:

<div className="absolute -inset-px">

A negative one pixel inset on every side, so the image overhangs its box by a
pixel all round and gets clipped by overflow-hidden. It used to be this:

className="scale-[1.03] object-cover"

Both exist to solve the same real problem. At some card widths the browser
rounds the image's layout box a fraction short of its container and leaves a
one-pixel grey sliver down the right edge. A 3% scale buries the sliver under
overflow, and for 372 game screenshots it was invisible and fine.

Then the same component rendered an assessment centre exercise, whose brief
panel starts hard against the left edge of the screen, and 3% of 1280 pixels is
about 19 pixels of horizontal zoom. The first letters of the panel went missing.

The two fixes look equivalent and are not. A scale is proportional, so it costs
you a percentage of the content at every edge, and the percentage you need is a
guess about rendering you cannot measure. A one-pixel bleed is absolute: it
covers exactly the sub-pixel rounding that caused the problem and nothing else.
I had reached for the proportional fix because it was one class, and it survived
only because no content was near enough to the edge to notice.

The general version, which I keep relearning: a fix sized in percent for a
problem measured in pixels works until the content changes.

Extracting it

Both surfaces now render the same component:

export function CardScreenshot({ src, alt, sizes, badge }: {
  src: string;
  alt: string;
  sizes: string;
  /** Pinned to the screen's top right corner. */
  badge?: ReactNode;
}) { /* ... */ }

Four props, and the choice of which four is the whole design. src and alt
are obviously the caller's. sizes is too, and it has to be, because
next/image needs a sizes string that describes the card's width at each
breakpoint and the two grids are different:

// game cards, three columns from lg
sizes="(min-width: 1024px) 400px, (min-width: 768px) 50vw, 100vw"
// exercise format cards, two columns from sm
sizes="(min-width: 896px) 440px, (min-width: 640px) 50vw, 100vw"

A shared component that guessed sizes for its callers would silently serve one
of them the wrong image width forever, and next/image gives you no warning
because it has no idea how wide your card is.

What is deliberately not a prop: the padding, the ratio, the radius, the ring,
the bleed, the badge position. Those are the frame. If a caller needed a
different one of those, it would not be this component.

The docstring carries the constraint the component cannot enforce:

The card must be overflow-hidden rounded-[20px]: the screen's corners are the
card's 20px less the 8px frame, so the curves run parallel.

That is a contract a type cannot express, so it is written where whoever breaks
it will be looking.

916 is not a round number

Generalising the capture script meant turning its constants into a record with
one entry per content type:

const TARGETS: Record<'game' | 'exercise', Target> = {
  game: {
    viewportHeight: 800,
    headerHeight: 64,
    footerHeight: 0,
    // ...
  },
  exercise: {
    // The e-tray's three panes run the full width, so a 16:10 trim would cut
    // text off both edges. 916 is 800 plus ExerciseContainer's h-14 header and
    // the workspace's 60px "Finish & score" bar, which leaves an area of exactly
    // 1280x800 to keep whole between them.
    viewportHeight: 916,
    headerHeight: 56,
    footerHeight: 60,
  },
};

Games capture at 1280x800 and the default crop takes a 16:10 box from the middle
of the play area. That works because most games are roughly centred.

An e-tray exercise is three panes side by side across the full width. Trimming
it to 16:10 from the centre would cut text off both edges, so these captures use
the mode that keeps the whole area and pads it instead. But "the whole area" has
to actually be 16:10 to avoid padding bars, and the area is the viewport minus
the chrome. So the viewport height is derived backwards from the area you want
to keep: 800 for the content, plus 56 for the header, plus 60 for the bottom
action bar, is 916.

Which means footerHeight had to exist as a concept at all. The game target has
footerHeight: 0 and the crop maths is the same for both:

const bottom = viewport.height - target.footerHeight;
const areaHeight = bottom - header;

Three fields and two subtractions where there used to be two constants. Adding a
second target to a script written for one is almost always this: the constants
you hardcoded were not wrong, they were just unnamed.

The ids are not the filenames

One detail worth a paragraph because it bit me. The generated manifest lists the
captures that exist:

/**
 * Exercises with a card screenshot at public/exercises/screenshots/<id>.webp.
 * Generated by `pnpm tsx scripts/game-screenshots.ts manifest`; do not edit by hand.
 */
export const EXERCISE_SCREENSHOTS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
  'etray-product-launch',
  'group-discussion-scenarios',
  'intray-office-manager',
  'presentation-board-strategy',
  'roleplay-difficult-client',
  'written-recommendation-report',
]);

Four of those six do not match the source file they are defined in.
etray-marketing-launch.ts exports an exercise whose id is
etray-product-launch; written-consulting-report.ts is
written-recommendation-report. The files were named during drafting and the
ids were named for the reader.

Generating the manifest from the output directory rather than from the content
library is what makes that harmless. The capture is written as <id>.webp, the
manifest is read back from the filenames, and the card looks up its own id. At
no point does anything have to know what the file on my disk is called. Had I
written the list by hand from the content folder, four of the six would have
pointed at nothing.

And one line of selection logic

The public page shows one captured scenario per format:

/**
 * One captured scenario per format for the top of its card, the first in
 * library order, so the e-tray card shows the free sample. A format with no
 * capture keeps its icon.
 */

"The first in library order" is doing real work there. The library is ordered
with the free sample first, so the card for the format you can try without an
account shows the scenario you would actually get. And a format with no capture
is not broken, it keeps the icon treatment, which is also why the card's radius
is conditional: rounded-[20px] with a screenshot, rounded-xl without, because
the nested radius arithmetic only applies when there is something nested.

The game cards are live now, so you can see the frame on any provider page, for
example Aon's, where the cards lead with a
capture of the test they open. The exercise cards on the
assessment centre practice page
still show icons at the time of writing; the six captures above go out with the
next deploy. The free e-tray scenario on that page runs in full without an
account either way.

title: "4200subscribers": the content said "black" and the renderer believed it
description:
Our numerical reasoning practice shows you source material (a table, a bar
chart, a line graph) and asks you questions about it. The content that drives
those charts carries a unit alongside each value, because "4200" on its own
means nothing and "4200 subscribers" does.

For a while, several of our charts rendered that as:

4200subscribers

Which is the single most recognisable bug in the genre. Here is the code that
produced it, and if you have written a dashboard you have written this line:

<span className="font-semibold">
  {hasValue ? `${value}${unit}` : '-'}
</span>

Template literal, value, unit. Correct for 45 and %. Wrong for 4200 and
subscribers. And the fix is not "add a space", because then you get:

4200 %
£ 286000

Worse, the currency case is not a spacing problem at all. A pound symbol is a
prefix, so gluing it on in either direction gives you 286000£, which is not
how anyone writes money in English.

Three shapes, one function

The unit strings in our content fall into three groups, and they want three
different treatments:

shape examples rendering
currency £, $, £m symbol leads, remainder trails
symbol or one letter %, k, % per year attach directly
word or multi-letter hours, MWh, thousand households space between

So the concatenation became a function. All 32 lines of it, docstring included:

/**
 * Join a data value to the unit a question bank gives for it.
 *
 * Bank units come in three shapes, and gluing them straight on reads wrong for
 * two of them: "4200subscribers", "£4200" rendered as "4200£".
 */
export function formatWithUnit(value: number | string, unit = ''): string {
  if (!unit) return String(value);

  if (/^[£$€]/.test(unit)) {
    const symbol = unit[0];
    const rest = unit.slice(1);
    const n = typeof value === 'number' ? value : Number(value);
    // "-£5", not "£-5".
    return Number.isFinite(n) && n < 0
      ? `-${symbol}${Math.abs(n)}${rest}`
      : `${symbol}${value}${rest}`;
  }

  if (unit.startsWith('%') || unit.startsWith(' ') || unit.length === 1) {
    return `${value}${unit}`;
  }

  return `${value} ${unit}`;
}

Some notes on the decisions in there, because every branch is a judgement call
someone will want to argue with.

Currency is split, not matched whole. The unit £m is a symbol plus a
magnitude, and they go on opposite sides of the number: £12m. Taking
unit[0] as the symbol and unit.slice(1) as the remainder handles £, $m
and €bn with one branch.

Negative numbers move the sign outside the symbol. £-5 is the kind of
output that makes a reader stop and squint at a chart, which in a timed practice
test is a cost I am imposing on them for nothing. Three lines to produce -£5.

% per year attaches, per year would not. The rule is "starts with %",
not "is %", because a percentage of something still wants the sign tight
against the number: 2.5% per year.

length === 1 catches k and m without a list. Any one-character unit
attaches directly. It is a heuristic and I am comfortable with it: there is no
single-letter unit in English that wants a space.

A unit that already begins with a space is left exactly as written. This is
the escape hatch. If a piece of content needs spacing this function would not
give it, the content can say so and the function will not second-guess it.

The test file is all cases, which is the right shape for a pure function like
this:

expect(formatWithUnit(4200, 'subscribers')).toBe('4200 subscribers');
expect(formatWithUnit(1840, 'MWh')).toBe('1840 MWh');
expect(formatWithUnit(2.5, '% per year')).toBe('2.5% per year');
expect(formatWithUnit(12, '£m')).toBe('£12m');
expect(formatWithUnit(-5, '$')).toBe('-$5');
expect(formatWithUnit(7, ' units')).toBe('7 units');
expect(formatWithUnit('n/a', '')).toBe('n/a');

That last one is why the signature takes number | string. A value is not
always a number; sometimes a table cell says n/a, and Number('n/a') is NaN,
which is how you end up shipping a chart that reads "NaN%".

Two components were doing their own concatenation across five call sites, and
both now call this instead. The interesting part was not writing the function,
it was that the same mistake had been written twice independently, because
${value}${unit} looks so obviously right that nobody reviews it.

The same bug wearing a different hat

In the same commit, this:

const SHAPE_COLORS: Record<KFLogicalShape['color'], string> = {
  red: '#ef4444',
  blue: '#3b82f6',
  green: '#22c55e',
  yellow: '#eab308',
  black: '#1f2937',
};

Four of those are colours. The fifth is a role. Red means red, but "black"
means ink, and #1f2937 is a very dark grey that was effectively invisible
against the dark card those shapes are drawn on. In dark mode, the item that
the content called black was the one you could not see.

  // "Black" is the ink colour, so it follows the theme's foreground: a fixed
  // #1f2937 vanished into the dark card the frames sit on.
  black: 'currentColor',

With className="text-foreground" on the SVG, so currentColor resolves to
whatever the theme says text is. One word in a lookup table, and the shape is
dark on light and light on dark.

The thing both bugs have in common

Our content banks store descriptive strings: a unit, a colour name, a label.
Both of these bugs came from a renderer taking one of those strings literally.
unit was treated as a suffix because it usually is. black was treated as a
hex value because it usually is. In both cases the right move is for the
renderer to interpret the string as a declaration of intent rather than as
output.

That is an easy sentence to write after the fact and an annoying one to act on
in advance. The practical version: when a data field's name is a noun from the
problem domain rather than from the view layer, do not pipe it into the view
unexamined.

Both fixes are on live pages if you want to look at them. The charts and tables
that carry these units are what
numerical reasoning practice
is made of, the tabbed source documents are listed on
Aon's practice page, and the abstract shape
sequences whose "black" is now ink are the Elements Logical test on
Korn Ferry's. Each page says which of
its tests are free.

title: A loading skeleton is a second implementation of your layout, and mine was lying about four things
description:
A route-level loading.tsx in Next.js is the cheapest good thing you can add to
a slow page. It is also a duplicate of your layout written in grey boxes, and
like every duplicate it drifts.

Here is the skeleton I had for our assessment centre exercise list. It looks
fine:

function ExerciseCardSkeleton() {
  return (
    <div className="border-border bg-card flex h-full flex-col gap-3 rounded-xl border p-5">
      <div className="flex items-start justify-between gap-3">
        <div className="flex min-w-0 items-center gap-3">
          <Skeleton className="h-11 w-11 shrink-0 rounded-xl" />
          <Skeleton className="h-5 w-32" />
        </div>
        <Skeleton className="h-5 w-16 shrink-0 rounded-full" />
      </div>
      <div className="flex-1 space-y-2">
        <Skeleton className="h-4 w-full" />
        <Skeleton className="h-4 w-3/4" />
      </div>
      <div className="flex flex-wrap gap-3">
        <Skeleton className="h-3 w-20" />
        <Skeleton className="h-3 w-12" />
        <Skeleton className="h-3 w-14" />
        <Skeleton className="h-3 w-20" />
      </div>
      <div className="border-border/60 mt-1 border-t pt-3">
        <Skeleton className="h-4 w-28" />
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Now the card it is standing in for. An icon tile of h-14 w-14, not h-11
w-11. A title that is two lines, not one. shadow-sm and no border. Padding of
px-3 py-6 sm:p-6, not a flat p-5. A meta row of a clock, a duration and a
sector label, which is three items, not four. And no footer divider at all.

Every one of those is a small lie, and the sum of them is a page that reflows
the moment the real content lands. That is a Cumulative Layout Shift you
authored on purpose and then forgot about.

The rule I settled on

A skeleton earns its place only if swapping it for the real component changes
nothing about the box model. So it stops being a drawing of a card and starts
being a measurement of one:

/** Mirrors ExerciseCard: icon tile beside a two-line title, description, then time and sector. */
function ExerciseCardSkeleton() {
  return (
    <div className="bg-card h-full rounded-xl shadow-sm">
      <div className="space-y-3 px-3 py-6 sm:p-6">
        <div className="flex items-start justify-between gap-3">
          <div className="flex min-w-0 flex-1 items-center gap-3">
            <Skeleton className="h-14 w-14 shrink-0 rounded-xl" />
            <div className="w-full space-y-2">
              <Skeleton className="h-5 w-3/4" />
              <Skeleton className="h-5 w-1/2" />
            </div>
          </div>
          <Skeleton className="h-5 w-16 shrink-0 rounded-full" />
        </div>
        <div className="space-y-2.5 py-0.5">
          <Skeleton className="h-4 w-full" />
          <Skeleton className="h-4 w-4/5" />
        </div>
      </div>
      <div className="px-3 py-3 sm:px-6 sm:py-4">
        <div className="flex h-5 items-center gap-2">
          <Skeleton className="h-4 w-4 rounded-full" />
          <Skeleton className="h-4 w-14" />
          <Skeleton className="h-4 w-32" />
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

The two title bars at w-3/4 and w-1/2 are not decoration. The real title is
long enough to wrap to two lines on most cards, and if the skeleton shows one,
every card in the grid grows by 28px when the data arrives.

The description is line-clamp-2 in the real card, so the skeleton is allowed
to be exactly two bars. A clamp is the one case where you know the height in
advance, which makes it the easiest thing in the world to match and an
embarrassing thing to get wrong.

Text lines need a line box, not just a bar

The first thing I needed and did not have was a way to stand in for a line of
small text. A Skeleton with h-3.5 is 14px tall. A line of 14px text occupies
a 20px line box. Stack four of them and the skeleton is 24px shorter than the
paragraph, which is a quarter of a card.

So every stand-in for text is a bar inside a line box of the right height:

/**
 * One line of small body text: a 20px line box around a bar, so stacked lines
 * take the height the real text does. `phoneOnly` lines stand in for the extra
 * lines the text wraps onto on a narrow screen.
 */
function TextLine({ width, phoneOnly = false }: { width: string; phoneOnly?: boolean }) {
  return (
    <div className={`flex h-5 items-center${phoneOnly ? ' sm:hidden' : ''}`}>
      <Skeleton className={`h-3.5 ${width}`} />
    </div>
  );
}

h-5 is the line box, h-3.5 is the ink. The bar is centred in the box, so
stacked lines get the real leading between them for free.

The phoneOnly flag is the part I am actually pleased with

Here is the thing nobody tells you about skeletons: the real content wraps
differently at different widths, so a single skeleton cannot be correct at both.
A sentence that is one line on a laptop is four lines on a 320px phone. A
skeleton with one bar is then 60px short, which on a phone is most of the
viewport's worth of shift.

The fix is to let the skeleton wrap too, by declaring the extra lines and hiding
them above the breakpoint:

<div className="mt-0.5">
  <TextLine width="w-full max-w-xl" />
  <TextLine width="w-full" phoneOnly />
  <TextLine width="w-full" phoneOnly />
  <TextLine width="w-1/3" phoneOnly />
</div>

One line from sm up, four lines below it, and the last of the four is a third
of the width because that is roughly where the sentence ends. The same trick
appears in the page description:

{/* The description wraps to three lines on a phone, one from sm up. */}
<div className="flex flex-col gap-2 py-1">
  <Skeleton className="h-5 w-full max-w-2xl" />
  <Skeleton className="h-5 w-full sm:hidden" />
  <Skeleton className="h-5 w-1/4 sm:hidden" />
</div>

This is only maintainable because the comment says what it is claiming. "Wraps
to three lines on a phone, one from sm up" is a falsifiable statement about
the copy above it. If someone shortens that sentence, the comment is visibly
wrong, which is the best you can hope for from a duplicate.

Chips have to wrap in the same places

The sector filter is a row of pill buttons: "All sectors" plus one per sector,
with a count on each. They wrap. If the skeleton's pills are a different set of
widths, the row occupies a different number of lines and the whole grid below it
moves.

/** Approximate widths of the five sector chips, so the row wraps where the real one does. */
const SECTOR_CHIP_WIDTHS = ['w-[118px]', 'w-[118px]', 'w-[160px]', 'w-[186px]', 'w-[128px]'];

Five hardcoded pixel widths, in order, measured off the real thing. Not elegant.
Correct, which beats elegant in a file whose entire job is to be the same shape
as another file.

Their height is the one number in here I can derive rather than measure:

<Skeleton key={i} className={`h-[30px] rounded-full ${width}`} />

The real chip is text-sm inside px-3 py-1 with a 1px border. That is a 20px
line box, plus 4px of padding top and bottom, plus 1px of border top and bottom.
20 + 8 + 2 = 30. An h-[30px] with a comment pointing at the arithmetic is more
honest than py-1 on a Skeleton that has no text in it to make the line box.

The thing that triggered the rewrite

I added a UK/US spelling toggle to this page, which I wrote about
yesterday.
It sits at the right of the title line on wide screens and under the description
on narrow ones:

<div className="flex items-center gap-3 lg:shrink-0">
  <Skeleton className="h-4 w-14 shrink-0" />
  <Skeleton className="h-[54px] flex-1 rounded-full sm:h-[46px] sm:w-[214px] sm:flex-none" />
</div>

Those two heights come out of the same arithmetic as the chips. The real
toggle's segments are 44px on phones and 36px from sm up, inside a p-1
wrapper with a 1px border: 44 + 8 + 2 = 54, and 36 + 8 + 2 = 46.

A new control meant the skeleton's header had to change, and once I was in the
file I noticed how little the rest of it resembled the page. That is the
practical lesson, such as it is: a loading.tsx has no tests, nothing imports
it, and nothing will ever tell you it has gone stale. It only gets looked at
when something else drags you into the file. So when something does, re-measure
the whole thing rather than the bit you came for.

Worth saying out loud

If your page does not shift, nobody notices any of this. If it does, people
notice without being able to say why, and they trust the page less. For a
product whose whole proposition is "this feels like the real assessment", a page
that jumps while it settles is the wrong first impression.

The dashboard this skeleton belongs to needs an account, but the public page it
mirrors is the
assessment centre practice hub,
where the free e-tray scenario runs in full without signing in. The same card
pattern, with screenshots on top, is what the
practice test library is built from.

title: How to Improve Blogger Website Performance with Practical HTML and CSS Optimizations
description:
How to Improve Blogger Website Performance with Practical HTML and CSS Optimizations

A Blogger website can look beautiful and still perform poorly on mobile devices. Large images, unnecessary JavaScript, layout shifts, and oversized widgets can make a page slower and harder to use.

The good news is that you do not always need to replace your entire Blogger template to improve performance. Start by measuring the problem, identifying the biggest bottlenecks, and making small, testable changes.

This tutorial covers several practical techniques for improving Blogger website performance using HTML, CSS, image optimization, and browser tools.

1. Measure Performance Before Changing Your Template

Before editing your template, establish a baseline.

Use Google PageSpeed Insights to test both your homepage and an individual article. Mobile results deserve particular attention because mobile devices may have slower network connections and less processing power.

Focus on three Core Web Vitals metrics:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): measures how quickly the main content becomes visible. A good target is 2.5 seconds or less.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): measures how responsive a page is to user interactions. A good target is 200 milliseconds or less.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): measures unexpected layout movement. A good target is 0.1 or less.

These targets are evaluated at the 75th percentile of real-user visits, not from a single laboratory test.

Record the results before making changes. This will help you identify which optimizations actually improve the experience.

2. Make Images Responsive

Images that exceed their container can cause horizontal scrolling on mobile devices. Large image files can also delay the display of important content.

A simple CSS rule can prevent many image overflow problems:

.post-body img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

This allows images inside .post-body to shrink to fit their container while preserving their aspect ratio.

You can also reserve space for images by specifying their dimensions in HTML:

<img
  src="blogger-tutorial.webp"
  alt="Blogger template customization example"
  width="800"
  height="450">

Replace the example filename with your actual image URL.

Providing dimensions helps the browser calculate the image's layout before it finishes downloading, which can reduce unexpected layout shifts.

Should you use lazy loading?

For images far below the initial viewport, lazy loading can reduce unnecessary downloads:

<img
  src="tutorial-step.webp"
  alt="Example of a responsive Blogger layout"
  width="800"
  height="450"
  loading="lazy">

However, avoid applying loading="lazy" indiscriminately to the main hero image or another image responsible for LCP. Delaying the most important image can make the page feel slower.

3. Reduce Unnecessary CSS and JavaScript

Blogger templates sometimes accumulate scripts and styles from old widgets, sliders, social sharing buttons, and external libraries.

Review your template and ask three questions:

  1. Does this script provide a feature visitors actually use?
  2. Is the same library loaded more than once?
  3. Can the feature be loaded only on pages where it is needed?

Remove unused components carefully. A widget that looks redundant may still provide navigation or functionality required elsewhere.

For an external script that does not need to execute before HTML parsing finishes, defer may be appropriate:

<script defer src="https://example.com/script.js"></script>

The URL is illustrative only. Replace it with a real script you control or trust.

The defer attribute allows a classic external script to download while HTML parsing continues, then executes it after parsing is complete. Check script dependencies before applying it because execution order can matter.

Avoid adding third-party scripts merely to display decorative effects. Every additional dependency can introduce network requests, processing work, and potential reliability or privacy concerns.

4. Prevent Horizontal Overflow on Mobile

Tables, embedded videos, and code examples can make an otherwise responsive article wider than the screen.

For article content, a starting point is:

.post-body {
  max-width: 100%;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

.post-body iframe,
.post-body video {
  max-width: 100%;
}

.post-body table {
  display: block;
  max-width: 100%;
  overflow-x: auto;
}

This approach helps constrain common content elements. A horizontally scrollable table can preserve its columns without forcing the entire page to become wider than the viewport.

Test the result at different screen widths. If your template already defines styles for these elements, merge the rules carefully instead of creating conflicting declarations.

5. Improve the Structure of Your HTML

Semantic HTML helps browsers, assistive technologies, and search engines interpret page content.

A simplified article structure might look like this:

<main>
  <article>
    <header>
      <h1>How to Optimize a Blogger Website</h1>
      <p>A practical guide to improving website performance.</p>
    </header>

    <section>
      <h2>Optimize Images</h2>
      <p>Resize images and provide their dimensions.</p>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Improve Mobile Layout</h2>
      <p>Ensure content fits smaller screens.</p>
    </section>
  </article>
</main>

This is an illustrative structure, not a complete replacement for a Blogger template. Blogger themes may already generate these elements through their XML and widget structure.

Before changing your theme, inspect the rendered HTML and check whether the article title, navigation, and main content already use appropriate elements.

Avoid adding a second main heading simply to insert extra keywords. Clear document structure is more useful than repetitive keyword placement.

6. Optimize Fonts and Layout Stability

Custom fonts can improve visual consistency, but loading multiple font families and weights can increase page weight.

Consider using a system font stack when a custom typeface is not essential:

body {
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont,
    "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

This allows the browser to use an available system font, reducing dependence on external font downloads.

Also inspect banners, advertisements, embedded widgets, and image placeholders for unexpected movement. Reserve space for elements when their dimensions are known.

Do not remove useful content simply to improve a laboratory score. The objective is to improve the real user experience while preserving the features readers need.

7. Test Each Change Separately

A reliable optimization workflow is more useful than making dozens of changes at once.

Use this sequence:

  1. Save a backup of your Blogger theme.
  2. Record the original PageSpeed Insights results.
  3. Make one change, such as optimizing images.
  4. Test the same pages again.
  5. Check the mobile layout and important functionality.
  6. Keep or revert the change based on the results.
  7. Continue with the next optimization.

For real-user search performance, use Google Search Console to monitor indexing, search impressions, clicks, and Core Web Vitals reports when sufficient field data is available.

A better laboratory score does not automatically guarantee higher rankings. Content quality, relevance, crawlability, competition, and many other factors also matter.

8. Continue Learning and Documenting Your Changes

When working with Blogger, document the template changes you make. Keep a copy of the original code and record which CSS or JavaScript changes solved a particular problem.

This makes future troubleshooting easier, especially when a theme update or a new widget changes the layout.

For additional tutorials about Blogger, SEO, website customization, and digital tools, you can also explore ANAKSMANDA.COM. Use the tutorials that are relevant to the specific problem you are trying to solve.

Conclusion

Improving a Blogger website does not always require a new theme. Start with measurable problems: oversized images, unnecessary scripts, mobile overflow, layout shifts, and poorly structured content.

Make small changes, test them carefully, and use real performance data to evaluate the outcome. A fast, responsive website should remain useful, accessible, and easy to navigate—not merely achieve a high score in a testing tool.

Disclosure: This article was prepared with assistance from AI and should be reviewed and fact-checked by the author before publication.

title: RTL in practice: CSS logical properties, bidi text, icons, numerals and a testing checklist
description:
The second layer of right-to-left work: the properties that don't flip, the strings that reorder themselves, and how to test so regressions don't come back.

Key takeaways

  • dir belongs in HTML, not CSS. Set dir on <html> (and on islands of other-direction content) so the browser's bidi algorithm, form controls and accessibility tree all agree.
  • Logical properties cover most layout, but not everything. transform, box-shadow, background-position, gradients and SVG coordinates are physical. Handle them with :dir().
  • Isolate every inserted value. <bdi>, dir="auto" and unicode-bidi: isolate in markup; FSI/PDI control characters in plain-text contexts like title, notifications and document.title.
  • Mirror icons by meaning, not by default. Arrows and "progress" icons flip; logos, checkmarks, media controls and clocks don't.
  • Format numerals with Intl, normalize input yourself, and avoid type="number" for codes and phone numbers.
  • Test RTL as a first-class configuration: lint for physical properties, run visual snapshots in both directions, and keep a bidi torture-string fixture.

I'm Mohammadreza Alamnejad, a UI/UX designer and developer, programmer and the founder of Arka Studio in Tehran. Everything my studio ships, including the café and restaurant platform NABZA, is Persian-first and right-to-left by default.

In an earlier article I covered the basics: lang="fa" dir="rtl" on the root, margin and padding logical properties, Jalali dates and digit normalization. This post is the follow-up for when the basics are done and the remaining bugs are the subtle ones.

1. Direction: HTML attribute first, CSS second

There are two ways to set direction: the dir attribute and the CSS direction property. Use the attribute.

<html lang="fa" dir="rtl">
  …
  <pre dir="ltr"><code>npm install</code></pre>
  <blockquote lang="en" dir="ltr">Quoted English paragraph…</blockquote>
</html>

Why the attribute wins:

  • It's semantic: screen readers, the :dir() pseudo-class, form controls and the bidi algorithm all use it.
  • CSS direction can be lost when styles fail to load, and it doesn't carry meaning into the accessibility tree.
  • dir is inherited, so you only set it at boundaries: the root, code blocks, embedded content in another language, and user-generated content (dir="auto").

Also set lang together with dir on foreign-language islands. lang affects font selection, hyphenation, quotes and screen reader pronunciation; dir affects layout and bidi. They are different things and you usually need both.

2. Logical properties: the full map

Most teams start with margin-inline-start and stop. Here is the wider set worth adopting everywhere:

Physical Logical
margin-left / margin-right margin-inline-start / margin-inline-end
padding-left / padding-right padding-inline-start / padding-inline-end
left / right inset-inline-start / inset-inline-end
border-left border-inline-start
border-top-left-radius border-start-start-radius
border-top-right-radius border-start-end-radius
text-align: left text-align: start
float: left float: inline-start
clear: left clear: inline-start
width / height inline-size / block-size
overflow-x overflow-inline (support is still limited, keep overflow-x as fallback)

A component written fully logically:

.toast {
  position: fixed;
  inset-block-end: 1rem;
  inset-inline-end: 1rem;          /* bottom-left in RTL, bottom-right in LTR */
  padding-block: 0.75rem;
  padding-inline: 1rem 1.25rem;    /* start, end */
  border-inline-start: 4px solid var(--accent);
  border-start-end-radius: 12px;
  border-end-end-radius: 12px;
  text-align: start;
  max-inline-size: 28rem;
}

Flexbox and grid already follow direction. flex-direction: row lays out from the inline start, so in RTL the first child is on the right. justify-content: flex-start and grid column lines follow too. A common bug is "fixing" this with flex-direction: row-reverse in RTL, which double-flips and puts things back in LTR order. If you find row-reverse in an RTL stylesheet, it's probably a bug.

Tailwind

Tailwind CSS (v3.3+) ships logical utilities: ms-*/me-* (margin start/end), ps-*/pe-* (padding), start-*/end-* (inset), rounded-s-*/rounded-e-*, border-s/border-e, and text-start/text-end. It also has rtl: and ltr: variants for the cases logical utilities can't express.

<button class="ps-4 pe-3 rounded-e-lg border-s-4 text-start">
  <svg class="rtl:-scale-x-100 …">…</svg>
  ادامه
</button>

Rule of thumb for a code review: ml-, mr-, pl-, pr-, left-, right-, text-left, text-right in a component are red flags unless there's a comment explaining why.

3. What logical properties don't cover

These are physical, and they're where most remaining RTL bugs live.

Transforms. translateX(100%) moves right in both directions. Drawers, carousels, slide-in toasts and "swipe to reveal" all need direction-aware transforms.

.drawer          { transform: translateX(-100%); }  /* hidden off the left (LTR) */
.drawer:dir(rtl) { transform: translateX(100%); }   /* hidden off the right (RTL) */
.drawer[open]    { transform: none; }

A trick that avoids duplicating every rule is a direction custom property:

:root            { --dir: 1; }
:root:dir(rtl)   { --dir: -1; }

.drawer          { transform: translateX(calc(-100% * var(--dir))); }
.chevron-next    { transform: scaleX(var(--dir)); }

Shadows and gradients. box-shadow: 4px 0 8px … casts to the right in both directions. linear-gradient(to right, …) is physical too. Use :dir(rtl) overrides or the --dir multiplier (calc(4px * var(--dir))).

Background position. background-position: left 1rem center for an input icon won't move. Prefer an inline element positioned with inset-inline-start, or override in :dir(rtl).

SVG and canvas. Coordinates are always left-to-right. Charts are the big case: does time run right-to-left in your Persian dashboard? There's no universal answer. Many Persian-speaking users are used to left-to-right time axes from international products, while others expect RTL. Decide deliberately, document it, and keep axis labels and tooltips in RTL text either way.

JavaScript positioning. Popover and tooltip libraries computing left from getBoundingClientRect() must know the direction. Check getComputedStyle(el).direction or the closest [dir], and prefer libraries with RTL support built in. Also watch scrollLeft: in RTL, modern browsers report 0 at the starting (right) edge and negative values as you scroll left. Code written assuming positive values will break horizontal carousels.

const isRTL = getComputedStyle(scroller).direction === 'rtl';
const distanceFromStart = isRTL ? -scroller.scrollLeft : scroller.scrollLeft;

4. Bidi text: why your punctuation jumps

The Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9) decides the visual order of characters with different directions. Strong characters (Persian letters, Latin letters) have a direction; neutral characters (spaces, punctuation, many symbols) take direction from their surroundings. Digits are "weak" and have their own rules. Problems appear when an LTR fragment sits at the edge of an RTL sentence, or when neutrals sit between the two.

Classic broken examples:

  • سفارش PO-1048 ثبت شد can render with the hyphen or the number in an unexpected position.
  • An English product name ending with ! or ) inside a Persian sentence: the punctuation attaches to the wrong side.
  • A phone number +98 912 … in a Persian paragraph shows the + at the wrong end.

In HTML: isolate 

<p>سفارش <bdi>PO-1048</bdi> ثبت شد.</p>
<p>کاربر <bdi>{{ userName }}</bdi> نظر داد.</p>
<span dir="ltr">+98 912 000 0000</span>
<div dir="auto">{{ userComment }}</div>
  • <bdi> isolates a value whose direction you don't know: user names, product names, IDs.
  • dir="ltr" on a span forces a value you know is LTR (phone, email, URL, code).
  • dir="auto" picks direction from the first strong character; ideal for comments, messages and search queries.
  • In CSS, unicode-bidi: isolate gives a component the same behaviour as <bdi>; unicode-bidi: plaintext makes each paragraph pick its own direction, which is useful in chat-like lists.

In plain text: FSI and PDI

Some strings never become DOM elements: title attributes, document.title, alert(), push and system notifications, <option> text in some environments, CSV exports. There you can't use <bdi>, but you can use the Unicode isolate control characters:

const FSI = '\u2068'; // First Strong Isolate
const PDI = '\u2069'; // Pop Directional Isolate
const LRI = '\u2066'; // Left-to-Right Isolate

export const isolate = (s) => `${FSI}${s}${PDI}`;
export const isolateLtr = (s) => `${LRI}${s}${PDI}`;

document.title = `${isolate(productName)} | نبضا`;
new Notification('سفارش جدید', { body: `میز ${isolateLtr(tableCode)} سفارش داد` });

Prefer isolates (LRI, RLI, FSI + PDI) over the older embedding controls (LRE, RLE, PDF) and over sprinkling RLM/LRM marks. Isolates don't leak their effect into surrounding text. Strip these characters before comparing or storing values that will be searched, since they are invisible but real.

In i18n libraries

If you use ICU MessageFormat-style libraries, check whether interpolated arguments are isolated automatically. Some libraries can wrap arguments with isolates for you; others leave it to you. Either way, write one test with an LTR argument in an RTL message (see the torture strings below).

5. Icons: mirror by meaning

A short decision table I use with designers:

Mirror in RTL Don't mirror
Back / forward arrows, chevrons Logos and brand marks
Breadcrumb separators Checkmark, plus, close (×)
"Next step", "send" when it implies direction Play, pause, fast-forward (media follows tape direction)
Text alignment icons, list indent/outdent Clocks and most refresh/sync circles
Progress or "reading" metaphors (book, open door) Photos, maps, real objects
Sidebar toggle, drawer open Numbers and letters inside icons

A few icons have no universal answer (undo/redo, the search magnifier, a phone handset). Design systems differ on them, so decide once, write it down, and apply it everywhere.

Implementation:

[dir="rtl"] .icon--directional { transform: scaleX(-1); }
/* or */
.icon--directional:dir(rtl)    { transform: scaleX(-1); }

Mark icons as directional in your icon component's API (<Icon name="chevron" directional />) instead of adding CSS at each call site. That keeps the decision in the design system, where it belongs. And if an icon contains text or numbers, never mirror it; ship a separate RTL variant.

6. Numerals: display, input and alignment

Display with Intl 

const nf = new Intl.NumberFormat('fa-IR');
nf.format(48250000);             // Persian digits with Persian grouping
new Intl.NumberFormat('fa-IR', { style: 'percent' }).format(0.25);
new Intl.DateTimeFormat('fa-IR-u-ca-persian', { dateStyle: 'medium', timeZone: 'Asia/Tehran' })
  .format(new Date());

Use Intl instead of hand-written digit replacement for display. It handles separators, percent placement and calendars consistently. Use digit replacement only for normalization of input (below).

Input: avoid type="number" for codes

<input type="number"> is meant for quantities. For phone numbers, OTPs, postal codes and card numbers, it causes problems: leading zeros, spin buttons, scroll-wheel changes, and inconsistent handling of non-Latin digits across browsers and keyboards. Use text inputs with the right keyboard hint:

<label for="otp">کد تأیید</label>
<input id="otp" type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code"
       dir="ltr" maxlength="6" pattern="[0-9۰-۹٠-٩]*">

<label for="mobile">شماره موبایل</label>
<input id="mobile" type="tel" inputmode="tel" autocomplete="tel" dir="ltr">

Then normalize before validation, in one shared function used by every form and by the server:

const PERSIAN = '۰۱۲۳۴۵۶۷۸۹';
const ARABIC  = '٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩';

export function normalizeDigits(s: string): string {
  return s.replace(/[۰-۹٠-٩]/g, (d) => {
    const i = PERSIAN.indexOf(d);
    return String(i >= 0 ? i : ARABIC.indexOf(d));
  });
}

export function normalizeMobile(raw: string): string | null {
  const s = normalizeDigits(raw).replace(/[\s\-()]/g, '');
  const m = s.match(/^(?:\+98|0098|98|0)?(9\d{9})$/);
  return m ? `0${m[1]}` : null;   // canonical 11-digit form
}

Alignment

In tables, align numeric columns to the end of the cell and use tabular figures, so digits of the same place value line up and amounts are easy to compare:

.table td.num { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; text-align: end; }

Check that your Persian font actually supports tnum; some don't, and you'll need a font that does for financial tables.

7. Forms, focus and caret details

  • Inputs inherit direction. A Persian form has RTL inputs by default. Email, URL, phone, code and password fields should be dir="ltr" so the caret and selection behave predictably; their labels stay RTL.
  • Search boxes should use dir="auto" because users search in both scripts.
  • Placeholders follow the input's direction. An LTR input with a Persian placeholder looks odd; consider ::placeholder { direction: rtl; text-align: end; } or put the hint in a visible help text instead.
  • Focus order follows DOM order, not visual order. Don't reorder elements visually with order or absolute positioning if it breaks keyboard navigation.
  • Select and date-picker popovers must open aligned to the inline start of the field.

8. Testing: make RTL a first-class configuration

Lint

Use stylelint-use-logical (from the csstools project) to flag physical properties in CSS, and an ESLint rule or code-review check for physical Tailwind classes.

{
  "plugins": ["stylelint-use-logical"],
  "rules": { "csstools/use-logical": ["always", { "except": ["float"] }] }
}

Visual snapshots in both directions

With Playwright, run key pages and components in both directions and compare screenshots:

// rtl.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

for (const dir of ['rtl', 'ltr'] as const) {
  test(`checkout layout (${dir})`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.evaluate((d) => document.documentElement.setAttribute('dir', d), dir);
    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(`checkout-${dir}.png`, { fullPage: true });
  });
}

Even if you ship RTL only, the LTR snapshot is useful: a layout that breaks when direction flips usually has hidden physical properties.

A bidi torture-string fixture

Keep a fixture of strings and render them in every text-bearing component in Storybook or a test page:

export const bidiFixtures = [
  'سفارش PO-1048 ثبت شد.',
  'محصول iPhone 15 Pro (نسخهٔ ۲۵۶) موجود است!',
  'تماس: +98 912 000 0000',
  'ایمیل: someone@example.com را تأیید کنید.',
  'Order #۱۲۳ was paid',            // LTR sentence with Persian digits
  'می‌شود',                          // ZWNJ must survive
  '۲۵٪ تخفیف تا ۱۵ مهر',
  'نام خیلی خیلی خیلی طولانی محصول که باید در دو خط بشکند و دکمه را خراب نکند',
];

Manual checks before release

Automated tests catch regressions; a short manual pass catches meaning. On a real phone:

  • [ ] <html lang dir> correct; LTR islands marked
  • [ ] No physical properties in components (lint passes)
  • [ ] Drawers, toasts, carousels slide from the correct side
  • [ ] Shadows, gradients and input icons sit on the correct side
  • [ ] Horizontal scrollers start at the inline start; scrollLeft logic handles negatives
  • [ ] Directional icons mirrored; logos, media and checkmarks not
  • [ ] IDs, names, phones and emails isolated in sentences, titles and notifications
  • [ ] Numbers formatted with Intl; inputs accept and normalize any digits
  • [ ] Code, phone, email and OTP fields are dir="ltr" with RTL labels
  • [ ] Tables use tabular numerals and end alignment
  • [ ] Focus order matches reading order
  • [ ] Bidi fixture renders correctly in every text component
  • [ ] Charts have a documented time-axis direction

Closing

The first 80% of RTL is easy and well documented. The last 20% is a list of exceptions: physical transforms, invisible bidi rules, icons with meaning, and numbers that are both text and data. Write those exceptions down once, encode them in your design system and lint rules, and test them like any other configuration. Then RTL stops being a recurring bug category.

About the author

Mohammadreza Alamnejad is a UI/UX designer and developer, programmer and network security professional, and the founder of Arka Studio, a design and development studio in Tehran. He built NABZA, a Persian-first café and restaurant operations platform, along with Avenya, Natureio and Radepa. More on his founder page at Arka Studio.

title: Designing a Political Quiz UI That Shows Its Assumptions
description:
Scope of this review

This is a black-box review of the public interface. It does not describe source code, a private scoring algorithm, or a verified psychometric model. The visible page presents 48 statements on a five-point scale, grouped by axis, and describes a 12-axis result. It also says that answers are calculated in the browser. These are public interface claims, not independently audited implementation facts.

That distinction matters for political self-assessment. A polished chart can look more authoritative than the questions behind it. The interface should make its model and limits easy to inspect.

Keep three states visible

A useful questionnaire UI needs to communicate at least three different things:

Answer state: which items the person has answered, skipped, or changed.

Interpretation state: how answers relate to each displayed axis.

Context state: which parts of the result depend on a country-specific reference.

If the interface compresses all three into one label, users cannot tell whether a result reflects their answers, the test’s categories, or a localized comparison. A map with separate axes is easier to question than a single unexplained badge.

Treat political labels as interpretations

The page includes comparisons with PSOE, PP, VOX, and Sumar, described as editorial references for Spain. A test result should distinguish this kind of comparison from a poll, endorsement, or recommendation. The UI should also make it possible to read the underlying positions before displaying a party match.

For a design review, ask whether users can answer these questions without leaving the result screen: What does each axis mean? Which end of the scale is represented? Is a percentage a similarity score or a vote prediction? Which country and reference date does a party comparison assume?

A compact acceptance matrix

Area

Example check

Expected behavior

Completion

One answer is skipped

The result does not silently present an incomplete profile as complete

Revision

An answer changes

The displayed axes update or explain when recalculation occurs

Interpretation

A party match is visible

The page labels it as an editorial comparison, not advice

Context

A reader is outside Spain

The geographic scope remains clear

Privacy

The page claims local calculation

The actual network behavior should be checked separately

The last row is intentionally a test question. A visible privacy statement is useful, but an interface inspection alone cannot prove network behavior. If privacy is a release requirement, verify it with a network-level test and document the result.

A useful public example

12ejes organizes its explanation around 12 axes, including economy, rights, borders, ecology, taxation, Europe, work, digital policy, housing, and security. That breadth can help readers notice that two positions may point in different directions.

The Test Ideologia Politica also illustrates a key UX boundary: its party comparison is explicitly framed as indicative, and the page tells readers to consult official proposals before deciding. That boundary belongs close to the result, where people are most likely to overread a score.

Questions to carry into implementation

Before building a similar product, define how incomplete answers work, how uncertainty is communicated, how country references are updated, and how a user can inspect the scoring model. Then test the language with people who hold mixed views, not only with people who already identify with a familiar label.

The interface is not neutral merely because it uses numbers. Its question wording, axes, examples, and defaults all shape what users see. Make those choices inspectable, and treat every result as a conversation starter rather than an identity assignment.
