title: I diffed GNU coreutils against its Rust rewrite with auto-generated tests
description:
"Rewrite it in Rust" is easy to say. The hard part is proving the rewrite does what the old
tool did, including on input nobody thought about: an empty stdin, a file without a trailing
newline, --output-delimiter -1, a directory where a file should be.

So I built behave, a small Go tool that treats
a command-line program as a black box:

  1. probe: read --help and the man page, find the flags, and generate cases: each flag alone, flag pairs, value edge cases (0, -1, abc, empty, missing), stdin samples (empty, unicode, CRLF, 5,000-character line, no trailing newline), the same samples as file arguments, unknown flags and missing files.
  2. record: run each case three times in a fresh temp directory with a fixed environment. If the runs disagree, the case is marked flaky (hello sort --random-sort).
  3. diff: replay every case against another binary and show what changed, per case and per flag. 
behave probe sort                       # ~290 cases into ./behave-sort/
behave diff behave-sort --impl ~/uu/sort --skip-tag meta --ignore-stderr

What it found: GNU coreutils vs uutils 0.12.0

tool matching cases differences
wc 63/63 none
head 51/51 none
uniq 100/100 none
tr 63/63 none
cut 172/175 --output-delimiter -1 is rejected as if -1 were a flag
base64 31/36 -d on invalid input: GNU writes the bytes it decoded before failing, uutils writes nothing
sort ~260/290 usage errors exit with 1 instead of 2; --debug underline width; --check --merge

That's a strong result for uutils: four tools fully match on everything generated. The rest are
small and some are likely deliberate, but you would want to know about them before swapping
binaries in a script that checks $? -eq 2.

jq vs gojq

gojq is a well-known Go implementation of jq that documents its differences. behave finds them
quickly: 331 of 596 cases match (ignoring error wording). The per-flag table shows the reasons:
gojq drops --seq, --ascii-output, --sort-keys (it always sorts keys) and a few others, and
formats huge numbers differently (1e1000 vs 1E+1000).

Making output comparable

Raw byte comparison doesn't work across implementations, so behave normalizes before comparing:

  • the program name (jq: error vs gojq: error)
  • temp directory paths, timestamps, ANSI colors, hex addresses
  • your own regex rules in behave.yaml

Specs are plain YAML, one file per case, so you can commit them next to your port and review
changes in PRs. behave run / behave diff exit non-zero on failures, so they work in CI.

For porting with a coding assistant

behave mcp exposes behave_exec, behave_probe, behave_add_case, behave_list_cases and
behave_diff over MCP, so an assistant porting a tool can check its work after each change
instead of guessing.

Limits

The flag parser is heuristic (tested so far on GNU coreutils and jq help output),
interactive/TTY programs aren't supported yet, and tools that need a meaningful positional
argument (a jq filter, a sed script) need a few samples via --arg.

It's MIT and a single binary for Linux and macOS:
https://github.com/emirmrkaljevic/behave. If you're porting a CLI, I'd like to hear what it
gets wrong.

More of my projects: github.com/emirmrkaljevic

title: A good application doesn't start with code
description:
Introduction

When you're a developer, it's natural to start a project with the technology.

Which stack? Which architecture? Which database? Which API?

These are important questions. But they often come too early.

Before thinking about code, you need to understand what you're trying to build, for whom, and why.

An application can be technically excellent yet solve the wrong problem.

Conversely, a simple solution can have enormous value when it precisely meets a real need.

A good application starts with a problem to understand, not with code to write.

01 — Start with the problem

Before drawing a screen or creating a database, one question must be clear:

What problem are we trying to solve?

A user generally doesn't think in features.

They don't say:

« I need a dynamic form with conditional logic. »

They say instead:

« My sink is clogged. I need to find someone to help me. »

This difference is fundamental.

The product must understand the user's need, rather than asking them to understand how the product works.

02 — Complexity must belong to the system

It's a principle I place a lot of importance on:

Complexity must belong to the system, not to the user.

Let's take a simple example: a person wants to have their phone repaired.

The system may need to know the brand, model, screen condition, battery, or whether the device powers on.

But that doesn't mean you should immediately present ten fields to fill out.

The user can simply write:

« My Samsung fell and the screen no longer turns on. »

The system must then transform this description into useful information.

The user expresses their problem. The system gradually structures the information.

03 — Design the journey before the screens

Another mistake is to start directly with the interface.

We design a welcome screen, a form, a results page, a profile…

But several coherent screens do not guarantee a coherent journey.

I prefer to start with another question:

What should happen between the moment the user expresses their need and the moment their problem is actually solved?

We can then represent the journey simply:

Need → understanding → qualification → matchmaking → choice → intervention → confirmation

Each step must have a reason to exist.

Each requested piece of information must also have a purpose.

04 — The MVP is not an incomplete application

An MVP is not simply a large application from which features are removed.

It's rather:

the smallest version capable of validating an important hypothesis.

This sometimes means accepting not to build everything.

Integrated payment? Later.

Advanced automation? Later.

Complex dashboard? Later.

The initial goal is to build what allows us to verify that the product truly delivers value.

05 — Technology comes next

Once the problem, journey, and scope are defined, technical choices become much simpler.

We can then think about:

  • the architecture;
  • the data;
  • the business rules;
  • the automations;
  • artificial intelligence;
  • scalability.

Technology then becomes what it should be:

a means to build the product correctly, not the product itself.

It is easy to fall in love with a technology.

It is much more important to stay focused on the user's problem.

06 — AI does not replace design

Artificial intelligence today allows rapid generation of code, interfaces, or even architectures.

But producing something quickly does not mean producing the right thing.

An AI can perfectly solve a poorly defined problem.

That is why I consider AI a powerful tool for design and execution, but not a replacement for product thinking.

First, you must know what to build.

Only then can AI help determine how to build it more efficiently.

07 — Designing also means managing uncertainty

In the real world, not all information is always available.

The user may not know the answer.

A situation can evolve.

A professional may need to confirm certain information.

A good system must be able to function despite this uncertainty.

It should not necessarily block the user simply because information is missing.

A well-designed product knows how to move forward even when all information is not yet known.

08 — Code remains essential

All of this obviously does not mean that development is secondary.

Good design without good execution remains a good idea.

Development turns journeys, rules, and product decisions into a real, reliable, and scalable system.

But code must serve a clear intention.

A few hours of design can sometimes prevent several days of unnecessary development.

09 — Building an application is building a system

An application is not just an interface.

Behind every screen there are:

  • users;
  • data;
  • rules;
  • decisions;
  • states;

title: When Should You Stop Adding Features?
description:
Introduction — The temptation to keep adding more

When designing an application, ideas never seem to run out. A new option, an additional dashboard, an automation, an integration… Every idea seems capable of improving the product.

So we add one feature. Then another. And another, until the application becomes harder to understand, use, and maintain.

Yet one question deserves to be asked before every new addition: does this feature genuinely bring value to the user?

1. The trap of a product that tries to do everything

An application can gradually drift away from its original purpose. By trying to meet every possible need, it accumulates options, screens, and rules.

User journeys become longer. Choices multiply. Some features are rarely used, yet they continue to weigh down both the interface and the codebase.

The problem is not having lots of features. It is losing sight of which ones truly matter.

2. A feature does not automatically add value

An interesting idea is not automatically a priority. Before developing it, we need to understand what problem it solves, for whom, and in what situation.

A feature can be technically impressive without being essential to everyday use. Conversely, a small improvement that removes an unnecessary step can transform the user experience.

A product’s value is therefore not measured by the number of options it offers, but by its ability to help users achieve their goals.

3. Prioritizing means making choices

Prioritizing is not simply about ranking a long list of requests. It means deciding what deserves to be built now, what can wait, and what perhaps should never be developed.

For each idea, a few questions can help:

  • What real need does this feature address?
  • How often does this need arise?
  • How does it contribute to the product’s main goal?
  • What costs will it add in design, development, testing, and maintenance?
  • Is there a simpler way to achieve the same result?

These questions do not always lead to an immediate answer. However, they force us to justify our choices instead of turning every suggestion into a development task.

4. The MVP brings us back to what matters

A minimum viable product (MVP) is neither a rushed version nor an application designed to frustrate users. It is a focused version that helps determine whether a solution addresses an important need.

Its scope should be small enough to make progress and learn, yet coherent enough to deliver real value.

Adding too many secondary features too early can delay the reality check: do users actually have this problem? Does the solution help them?

Sometimes, it is better to launch a simple user journey, observe how people use it, and improve it based on concrete feedback than to spend months building every possibility we can imagine.

5. Saying no without closing the door to future improvements

Rejecting a feature today does not mean it will never be useful. It simply means it may not be the right decision at this stage of the product.

An idea can be saved for later, tested in the future, or replaced with a simpler approach. Needs evolve, and the product should evolve with them without losing sight of its purpose.

The role of product design is not to anticipate every possibility from the outset. It is also to create a clear enough foundation for future decisions to be made at the right time.

Conclusion — Do less, but do it better

Adding a feature is often visible. Deciding not to add one can require even more thought.

A good product is not one that responds to every request. It is one that understands its priorities and helps users accomplish what matters effectively.

Before asking “What can we add?”, let’s get into the habit of asking: “What problem are we still trying to solve, and is this really the best way to solve it?”

Product quality is built as much through the choices we make as through the features we decide to leave out.

title: When Does a Rust Rewrite Actually Pay Off? A Decision Checklist
description:
"Should we rewrite it in Rust?" is one of the most expensive questions an engineering team can answer wrongly in either direction. Say yes too easily and you spend six months re-implementing features users already had. Say no out of habit and you keep paying for servers, incidents and latency that a focused rewrite would have removed. This article gives you a way to decide on evidence, plus a checklist you can score your own system against.

First: what Rust actually buys you

Strip away the hype and Rust gives you three concrete things:

  1. Predictable performance. No garbage collector, so no GC pauses. Compiled to native code with control over memory layout, so CPU-bound code typically runs at C/C++ speed.
  2. Memory safety without a runtime. Whole classes of bugs (use-after-free, data races, buffer overflows) are rejected at compile time.
  3. Small, efficient deployables. A single static binary with low memory use, which matters at scale and at the edge.

Everything else, like "it's modern" or "developers like it", is a bonus and not a business case.

When a rewrite pays off

1. You're CPU-bound on a hot path

If profiling shows most time is spent in your own code (parsing, serialization, pricing, matching, compression, image or signal processing) rather than waiting on a database or network, Rust can turn that path from a bottleneck into a non-issue. Typical candidates: market data handlers, risk calculations, rule engines, ETL transforms.

2. Your problem is tail latency, not average latency

Garbage-collected runtimes can have excellent averages and ugly p99s. If your SLO is about the slowest 1% of requests (trading, real-time bidding, game servers, anything interactive), removing GC pauses can matter more than raw speed. Discord's often-cited move of its "Read States" service from Go to Rust was driven by exactly this: periodic latency spikes from garbage collection, which went away after the rewrite.

3. Infrastructure cost is a real line item

At small scale, a 3× efficiency gain saves a few hundred euros a month and isn't worth a rewrite. At large scale it's different: Cloudflare reported that Pingora, its Rust-based proxy that replaced its NGINX setup, used about 70% less CPU and 67% less memory for the same traffic. If compute is one of your biggest costs, run the numbers.

4. Correctness failures are expensive

Parsers handling untrusted input, financial calculations, concurrent state machines: places where a memory bug or race condition becomes a security incident or a wrong trade. Rust's compiler catches categories of these before they ship.

5. You need to run where runtimes are a burden

Edge devices, embedded systems, WebAssembly in the browser, CLI tools you distribute to customers: one small binary with no runtime to install is a genuine advantage.

When it doesn't pay off

  • The system is I/O-bound. If requests spend 95% of their time waiting on Postgres or a third-party API, a faster language makes the remaining 5% faster. Fix the queries, add caching, batch the calls.
  • The product is still changing weekly. Rust rewards knowing what you're building. Before product-market fit, iteration speed beats runtime speed.
  • Nobody will own it. If the team that maintains the system won't learn Rust, you're creating an island. Budget for training or a partner, or don't do it.
  • The real problem is architecture. A chatty microservice design, N+1 queries or a missing queue will be just as slow in Rust.
  • "Rewrite everything" is the plan. Big-bang rewrites of working systems are where projects go to die, regardless of language.

The approach that works: rewrite the hot path, not the system

In practice the best return comes from replacing the 5–10% of the code where the time goes, and leaving the rest alone:

  1. Profile production-like load. Flame graphs, not intuition. Find where CPU time and allocations actually go.
  2. Put a boundary around the hot path. Define its inputs and outputs precisely. This step alone often reveals simplifications.
  3. Rewrite that component in Rust and call it from the existing code. Rust integrates well with other stacks: PyO3 for Python, napi-rs for Node.js, a C ABI with P/Invoke for C#/.NET, or a separate service over gRPC/HTTP.
  4. Prove equivalence. Run old and new side by side on recorded production inputs and diff the outputs. Property-based tests help here.
  5. Measure, then decide on the next piece. Gradual replacement (the "strangler fig" pattern) lets you stop as soon as the remaining gains aren't worth it.

This keeps risk low, gives you real numbers within weeks instead of quarters, and often delivers most of the benefit of a full rewrite.

The checklist

Score each statement 0 (not true), 1 (partly) or 2 (clearly true) for the system you're considering:

# Statement Score
1 Profiling shows we're CPU-bound in our own code, not waiting on I/O.
2 Tail latency (p99/p999) or latency jitter is a business problem.
3 Compute or memory cost for this component is significant and growing.
4 Correctness or memory-safety failures here are costly (money, security, trust).
5 The component's behaviour is well understood and fairly stable.
6 We can isolate it behind a clear interface.
7 We have, or can get, people to build and maintain Rust code.
8 We can test the new version against real production inputs.

How to read your score:

  • 0–6: Not now. Look at architecture, queries and caching first.
  • 7–11: Run a time-boxed proof of concept on the single hottest path and measure.
  • 12–16: A targeted rewrite is very likely worth it. Plan it incrementally.

Statements 1–4 are the why; 5–8 are the can we. A high "why" with a low "can we" means: fix the prerequisites first (interfaces, tests, people) before touching the code.

What a proof of concept should answer

Keep it to two to four weeks and make it answer three questions with numbers: how much faster or cheaper is the hot path under realistic load, how hard was it to integrate with the existing system, and what will it cost to maintain. If the answers are good, you have a business case. If not, you've spent a few weeks instead of a few quarters.

We help teams with exactly this: profiling, isolating the hot path, building the Rust component and integrating it. See Rust development, legacy modernization and proof of concept development, or start with an independent build vs. buy evaluation.

title: Shipping Desktop Software to People Who Will Never Read the Docs
description:
Rueda de Actos has a README. It's long, half technical documentation and half user manual, and it's accurate: the data model, every feature, where the backups live, what to do after a bad close.

Nobody who uses the app will ever read it.

That isn't a complaint about users. It's the most important design constraint the app has, and it took me two versions to treat it as one.

Rueda de Actos is the Windows desktop app I built for a festival group in Alcoy, Spain: five events, eleven spots each, and a rotating turn that has to stay fair year after year. The person who runs it is a volunteer on the group's board. They aren't technical, they open the app once a year, and on the night that matters there's no store to reinstall from, no support line and nobody to call. For most of the year I'm not in the room.

So every instruction that matters has to be somewhere they'll actually look, at the moment they need it. This is the last article in the series about this app, and it's about the unglamorous part: getting software into the hands of people who will never read the docs, and keeping it working there.

Before the app exists: the installer

The first moment is the only one where the app can't speak for itself, because it isn't running yet.

The installer is a standard Windows setup wizard, in Spanish, the language of the people who use it. And it isn't code-signed, so the first time it runs, Windows shows a blue warning: Windows protected your PC. The button that runs it anyway is hidden behind a More info link.

I went through the economics of a signing certificate in an earlier article. What matters here is what that screen does to someone who isn't technical. It reads as "this is a virus", and the software has failed before it has opened.

Nothing inside the app can fix that. So the explanation travels with the file: before anyone double-clicks, the person who will install it is told that a blue warning is coming and exactly which two things to press, in the words Windows will show them, Más información and then Ejecutar de todas formas.

The difference is all in the timing. A warning you didn't mention looks like a problem. A warning you predicted looks like proof that the instructions were right, and that buys trust for everything that comes after.

The first screen: an empty state that says what to do

The database is created empty. There's no demo data and no sample list. An earlier build seeded the table from a bundled file, and it turned out to fire whenever the table was empty, not only on the first run, so it went.

An empty table is a dead end, though. A grid of headers with nothing under it doesn't tell you what to do next. So when there's nobody in the list, the table isn't shown at all. In its place, translated from Spanish:

No members yet

Load the full list with Import, in the header, or add them one by one with Add member.

The event buttons stay disabled until there's someone to choose from. In an earlier build they didn't, and starting an event on an empty list produced empty backups and blocked the rota.

An empty state is the first page of the manual, and it's the only page that's guaranteed to be read.

Getting the data in: their spreadsheet, and errors that name the row

Every association already has a spreadsheet. The alternative to importing it is typing everyone in by hand, which is how a tool dies before its first use.

So Import takes the spreadsheet the group already had, Excel or JSON, with a single condition: the first row holds the headers, and one of them is Nombre. Headers are matched with or without accents, by their visible or internal name, abbreviations are accepted, and columns the app doesn't know are ignored. The details of that leniency are in the September article on real use.

What matters for people who won't read the docs is what happens when the file is wrong. If any record fails validation, the whole import is rejected, the data already in the app isn't touched, and the message says how many records failed and which rows, with the reason for each.

All or nothing is deliberate. A failed import is obvious. A half-done import looks exactly like a list, and nobody counts the rows to check that they all arrived.

And then the step that would be in bold in any manual: after importing, you have to press Save. Which brings me to the one rule in this app that has to be impossible to miss.

One button that makes it real

The data model is strict on purpose. The app always starts from the last saved state, and Save is the only thing that commits anything. Closing without saving is a clean undo of the whole evening, which is exactly what you want after a session that went sideways.

A rule like that is invisible unless the interface shows it, so it shows it all the time. The status bar along the bottom always says one of two things, Saved or Unsaved changes, and hovering the second one tells you to press Save. The comment above that element is the whole argument:

<!-- What isn't saved is lost on close, so the state has to be on screen at
     all times, not just in the exit warning. -->

The exit warning exists too. Closing with something pending asks first, with three buttons: Save and exit, Exit without saving, Cancel. Clicking outside doesn't dismiss it. And if saving fails, the app stays open:

// If Save fails, we don't carry on: that would be exactly the case where it hurts most.
if (result.isConfirmed) return guardarDatos()
return result.isDenied === true

For the close that happens anyway (the wrong button, a flat battery, someone tidying up the cables), there's an escape hatch: Settings → Data management → Load temporary version (session) brings back the last thing that was on screen, saved or not, with the date of each version next to it.

None of that is documentation in the usual sense. But the status bar, the three buttons and the recovery option explain the data model better than any paragraph could, and they do it at the only moments the user is thinking about it.

Backups that live on the same disk

The app backs itself up: a full copy of the database every thirty minutes, keeping the last ten. It's a real safety net, for one specific failure: I've just broken the data.

It does nothing for the other one, the laptop died, because those copies sit on the same disk as the original. I said that in the offline-first article, and it bears repeating, because automatic backups are exactly the kind of feature that makes people stop worrying, and this is the one case where they should keep worrying.

What actually protects the group's history is an export saved somewhere else: a USB stick, an external drive, an email. JSON and Excel both re-import without losing anything, so with that file a brand-new installation gets everything back through the same Import as on the first day.

The trouble is that nobody thinks about this until it's too late, and nobody reads the paragraph telling them to. So the export sits where the data is worth the most. The final summary, the screen that appears when the fifth event closes, has the export buttons on it, and the highlighted one is the JSON export. At that moment the evening's work is done, someone is still at the keyboard, and a copy is one click away.

Updating without losing a year

The database doesn't live next to the program. It's in the user's Windows profile, so installing a new version over the old one never touches it. What does change is its shape, and the database a new version finds is, by design, a year old.

So the schema is versioned. Every change to it ships as a migration that runs on first launch, each one inside a transaction, so a failure stops the chain instead of leaving the database half converted. The migrations that move existing data have their own tests, because the database they will meet on that machine is the real one, with years of history and no copy on any server. I wrote about how those tests work in the testing article.

From the user's side, all of that has to collapse into a sentence they already believe without being told: the new version keeps my data.

A year later: the guide

The hardest user to design for is the same person, twelve months later. They used the app once, last year, and have forgotten all of it: where Import is, what the amber card means, why some cells are striped.

For that person, the app carries its own guide, one click away inside the app: nineteen short numbered sections, from managing members and choosing people for an event to verifying or skipping, reopening, the gender rules, squad leaders, search, saving and recovering, export and import, the final summary and how windows and notices behave.

A few rules make it usable rather than merely complete:

  • It uses the screen's words. Every button is named exactly as it appears, in bold, and every path is the real one: Settings → Data management → Load temporary version (session).
  • Each section is a handful of short sentences. Nobody reads a guide from the top. People scan it for the one thing they're stuck on.
  • It changes with the app. When version 2 added search, reopening and the new event states, the guide grew in the same release. A feature isn't finished until its section is written.

A guide inside the app has one advantage over every other kind of documentation: it's the only one guaranteed to still be there, on the right machine, a year from now.

The interface is the documentation

Look at where the instructions in this app actually live: a heads-up that travels with the installer, an empty state, an error that names the rows, a status bar, a dialog with three buttons, the export buttons on the last screen of the night, and a guide written in the words of the screen.

That's the documentation. For someone who isn't technical, the documentation that exists is the interface itself. Everything else, the README, the FAQ, this article, gets read by people who no longer need it.

This is the last article I'll write about Rueda de Actos for a while. The case study, with screenshots made from test data, is on my site: ancer.es/en/project/rueda-ligeros.

title: Let the designer's spec be the test: a bounded UI change request for game UI
description:
"The quest reward toast feels cramped and is hard to read on phones."

That's a fair complaint, and a hard thing to hand to an engineer. "Cramped" and "hard to read" are real observations, but nobody can finish them. The engineer guesses, the designer looks at the result, and the next round starts with "closer, but still not quite."

This tutorial turns that sentence into a request the engineer can finish and the designer can accept without either of them arguing about taste. The trick is small: the designer writes the spec as a data file, and a short script runs that same file as the test. I built the whole thing as a toy fixture (one HTML toast, one CSS file, the spec, and a checker run in headless Chrome) so every result below comes from an actual run.

Who does what

Three roles, decided before anyone touches CSS:

  • Prepares the work: the UI designer. They know what's wrong and what "fixed" looks like. They write the intent in one sentence and the spec below.
  • Executes it: the UI engineer, in their own checkout, with their own tools. If they hand the CSS to a coding agent, that agent runs under the engineer's account and the engineer owns the diff.
  • Judges acceptance: the designer again. They read the check report and look at two screenshots. The engineer reviews the code, but doesn't decide whether the toast is right.

This split matters more once agents are involved. Human AI collaboration in game development tends to go wrong when the person who knows what "right" means isn't the one who checks the result, so the check has to be something the designer wrote.

Step 1: replace taste words with properties

Go through the complaint word by word and ask what you would measure.

  • "Cramped" becomes padding, the gap between icon and text, and icon size.
  • "Hard to read" becomes font size, line height and contrast against the toast background.
  • "On phones" becomes a viewport width (360px) and a rule that the toast stays on screen.

The designer also adds the case they worry about: the German string, which is the longest one in the localization sheet.

Step 2: write the spec as data

This is the whole template. It's the designer's file, written in the units they already use in their design tool:

{
  "change": "Quest reward toast: readable at phone width, roomier, nothing cut off",
  "requestedBy": "UI designer",
  "page": "toast.html",
  "viewports": [360, 1280],
  "checks": [
    { "name": "toast stays fully on screen with 8px to spare", "selector": ".toast", "insideViewport": 8 },
    { "name": "padding is 12px top/bottom, 16px left/right", "selector": ".toast",
      "style": { "padding-top": "12px", "padding-bottom": "12px", "padding-left": "16px", "padding-right": "16px" } },
    { "name": "12px between icon and text", "selector": ".toast", "style": { "column-gap": "12px" } },
    { "name": "icon is 40 x 40", "selector": ".toast__icon", "box": { "width": 40, "height": 40 } },
    { "name": "title is 18px on a 24px line", "selector": ".toast__title", "style": { "font-size": "18px", "line-height": "24px" } },
    { "name": "title contrast is at least 4.5:1", "selector": ".toast__title", "minContrast": 4.5, "against": ".toast" },
    { "name": "title shows all its text in at most 2 lines", "selector": ".toast__title", "maxLines": 2, "noClipping": true }
  ]
}

Each check has a plain-language name, because the designer reads the report, not the code. The selectors are the only part the designer needs help with, and the engineer can fill those in during a two-minute call.

Note what isn't in the spec: no CSS approach, no flexbox-or-grid, no "make it pop." The spec says what must be true on screen, and the engineer chooses how.

Step 3: a checker that reads the spec

The checker is one HTML page. For each viewport it loads the component in an iframe of that exact width, then runs every check against computed styles and layout boxes. The core loop, trimmed:

for (const el of doc.querySelectorAll(c.selector)) {
  const cs = win.getComputedStyle(el), box = el.getBoundingClientRect();
  for (const [prop, want] of Object.entries(c.style ?? {})) {
    const got = cs.getPropertyValue(prop);
    if (got !== want) failures.push(`${prop} is ${got}, want ${want}`);
  }
  if (c.insideViewport !== undefined && (box.left < c.insideViewport || box.right > vw - c.insideViewport))
    failures.push(`spans ${Math.round(box.left)}-${Math.round(box.right)}px, viewport is ${vw}px`);
  if (c.maxLines && Math.round(box.height / parseFloat(cs.lineHeight)) > c.maxLines)
    failures.push(`uses more than ${c.maxLines} lines`);
  if (c.noClipping && el.scrollWidth > el.clientWidth)
    failures.push(`text is cut off (${el.scrollWidth}px of text in ${el.clientWidth}px)`);
  // box sizes and WCAG contrast work the same way
}

A shell script serves the folder, renders the page with chrome --headless=new --dump-dom, and prints the JSON the page wrote. One detail cost me time: headless Chrome won't lay out a window narrower than its minimum, so the 360px viewport has to be an iframe inside a wider window rather than the window itself.

Step 4: the worked handoff

Before. Against the original CSS, 3 of 14 checks passed (7 checks at 2 viewports). The report said, among other things, .toast spans 16-412px, viewport is 360px, padding 6px/8px instead of 12px/16px, and title contrast 3.50:1.

Attempt 1. The engineer changed exactly the values the spec listed: padding, gap, icon, font size, line height, and a lighter title color. 11 of 14 passed. The three failures were the interesting ones:

  • At 360px the toast ran to 428px. Bigger padding on a fixed 380px content-box width made it wider than before.
  • At both widths the German title was cut off: 361px of text in 328px. The original CSS used white-space: nowrap with an ellipsis, which was harmless at 15px and clipped at 18px.

Nobody had asked for those to change, and both were caught without the designer opening a browser. Matching the listed numbers wasn't enough to fix the actual complaint.

Attempt 2. box-sizing: border-box, a width of min(380px, calc(100% - 32px)), and the title allowed to wrap instead of ellipsizing. 14 of 14 passed, with title contrast now 7.25:1.

Acceptance. The designer reads the report, then looks at the screenshot at 360px. This is where the last judgment happens, and the spec can't make it: in attempt 2 the short English title also wraps onto two lines at phone width, where it fit on one before. The spec allows that. Whether it's acceptable is the designer's call. If it isn't, that's a new check ("English title fits on one line at 360px") and a new round, not a vague "closer, but."

Limits

  • It checks what you wrote, nothing more. Seven passing checks don't mean the toast looks good. The screenshot review stays with the designer.
  • Computed styles aren't pixels. The checker would pass a toast hidden behind another element. Overlap, animation and z-order need a visual check.
  • One font, one browser. The fixture uses Arial in desktop Chrome. Real game UI with a custom font on a phone can wrap differently, so run the check where the font actually loads.
  • Contrast is only computed against a solid background. Toasts over the game scene need a worst-case background, which a static check can't pick for you.
  • Selectors are brittle. Rename a class and the check silently matches nothing. A real version should fail when a selector matches zero elements; this toy version doesn't yet.

If your studio splits work this way, with one person knowing what "done" looks like and another able to build it, Wagglet's write-up on closing team skill gaps with AI task handoffs covers the same prepare, execute, verify split for tasks beyond UI.

title: Exodus: move an app to Google Cloud Run with the coding agent you already use
description:
Exodus is on Product Hunt today: Exodus by elim.io.

Exodus is a free web cabinet and an open-source CLI. Together with the coding agent you already use, such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Gemini CLI, it audits an app on your machine. It shows what the app costs today and on Google Cloud Run, lists every change the move needs with its file and line, and gives the agent a plan to work through. It can also design a new product for Cloud Run from an idea.

Why we built it

Cloud Run suits most web apps: it scales to zero, bills only for the time your code runs, and includes 2 million requests a month in its free tier. Moving an app there from a platform such as Heroku, Railway or Render is rarely about the container. It is about four habits a platform with long-running processes lets you keep and Cloud Run does not.

  1. Timers inside the process. An instance has CPU only while it answers a request, and there may be several instances, so a cron in your server fires late, twice or never. Each schedule moves to Cloud Scheduler: short work calls an endpoint, long work starts a Cloud Run job.
  2. A worker waiting on a queue. For the same reason the jobs stall between requests. Each job becomes an HTTP task in Cloud Tasks that posts to a handler, and the queue keeps the retries and the rate limits.
  3. Files on local disk. The disk lives in the instance's memory and disappears when the instance stops; other instances never see it. Uploads go to a Cloud Storage bucket through a signed URL, and the app keeps only the key.
  4. Sessions in memory. The next request lands on another instance and the user is signed out. The session goes into a signed cookie or a table of the database the app already has.

We met all four while moving our own apps and wrote 59 guides about them along the way. Exodus is those guides turned into a tool.

How it works

  1. Sign up at app.exodus.elim.io and install the CLI once: curl -fsSL exodus.elim.io/install | sh
  2. Give your agent the one line from the cabinet. It runs exodus init and exodus audit in your repository, answers the questions it can from the code and asks you the rest.
  3. exodus send uploads the findings and the answers, and the cabinet builds the report: today's bill against Cloud Run at Google's list prices, the changes, and a plan. Exodus never receives your source code.
  4. The agent works through the plan task by task, and each new send updates the report.

A sample report

exodus.elim.io/demo opens the report of a sample project, lumen-api: a Rust API with a worker, timers and uploads on Railway, $48.00 a month today against $10.83 on Cloud Run after 4 changes, with 4 of 9 plan tasks done.

Links

  • Site and guides: exodus.elim.io
  • CLI, Apache-2.0: github.com/elim-io/exodus
  • Product Hunt: Exodus by elim.io

We would like to hear where the audit gets your app wrong. Comments here or on Product Hunt both reach us.

title: The Borrow Checker Gaps That Let Unsafe Code Compile
description:
Two soundness bugs in Rust's borrow checker have been open since 2013 and 2014. They allow code that violates aliasing rules to compile without unsafe blocks. If you write libraries that expose safe APIs over unsafe internals, or if you rely on the borrow checker to enforce invariants in complex data structures, these holes can let undefined behavior slip into production.

You'll learn:

  • Which code patterns trigger the unsoundness
  • How to audit your crate for the affected constructs
  • Practical workarounds that keep your API safe today

What the Bugs Actually Are

The first bug (issue #164250 tracks both) involves two-phase borrows and reborrowing through raw pointers. When you create a raw pointer from a mutable reference, then reborrow that pointer as a shared reference, the borrow checker can lose track of the original mutable borrow. This lets you hold a &mut T and a &T to the same location simultaneously — the exact aliasing violation Rust promises to prevent.

The second bug concerns closure capture analysis. When a closure captures a mutable reference and also captures a shared reference derived from it, the borrow checker sometimes fails to see the conflict. The closure compiles, but calling it creates overlapping mutable and shared borrows.

Both bugs stem from the borrow checker's MIR (Mid-level Intermediate Representation) analysis not fully modeling how raw pointers and closures interact with the stacked borrows model.

How They Manifest in Real Code

The patterns look innocent. Here's a simplified version of the two-phase borrow case:

fn extend_vec(vec: &mut Vec<i32>, value: i32) {
    let ptr = vec.as_mut_ptr(); // raw pointer from &mut
    let len = vec.len();        // shared borrow of vec
    // borrow checker thinks `vec` is only shared-borrowed here
    unsafe {
        *ptr.add(len) = value;  // but we write through the raw pointer!
        vec.set_len(len + 1);   // and mutate vec again
    }
}

The borrow checker sees vec.len() as a shared borrow and vec.set_len() as a separate mutable borrow. It doesn't connect the raw pointer ptr back to the original &mut Vec. The write through ptr happens while len holds a shared reference to vec's metadata.

The closure variant:

fn process_with_closure(data: &mut [i32]) {
    let shared = &data[..];           // shared borrow
    let mut closure = || {
        data[0] = 42;                 // mutable borrow captured
        println!("{:?}", shared);    // shared borrow captured
    };
    closure(); // compiles, but creates &mut and & to data[0] simultaneously
}

The closure captures both data (mutably, for the assignment) and shared (shared). The borrow checker treats these as separate captures and misses the overlap.

Detecting Affected Patterns in Your Codebase

You won't find these with cargo clippy or cargo check. The code compiles cleanly. You need to search for the structural patterns:

  1. Raw pointer derived from &mut followed by any shared borrow of the same value
  2. Closures that capture both a mutable reference and a shared reference derived from it

A quick grep pattern for the first case:


## Look for as_mut_ptr / as_ptr followed by .len(), .is_empty(), or deref

rg 'as_mut_ptr\(\).*\.(len|is_empty|first|last|get)' --type rust

For closures, there's no reliable static search. Review any closure that captures multiple references to the same data structure, especially when one capture is &mut and another is &.

If you maintain a crate with unsafe internals, add a test that runs under Miri (the Rust interpreter that detects UB):

cargo +nightly miri test

Miri implements stacked borrows and will flag both bug patterns at runtime. It's the only reliable detection today.

Workarounds While Fixes Land

The Rust team is working on fixes, but they require changes to the borrow checker's core logic and must pass the full test suite. Until then, restructure the affected code.

For the two-phase borrow case: split the operation so the raw pointer and the shared borrow don't overlap.

fn extend_vec_fixed(vec: &mut Vec<i32>, value: i32) {
    let len = vec.len();           // shared borrow ends here
    let ptr = vec.as_mut_ptr();    // raw pointer from &mut, no overlap
    unsafe {
        *ptr.add(len) = value;
        vec.set_len(len + 1);
    }
}

The fix is mechanical: compute all shared-borrow-derived values before creating the raw pointer. The borrow checker correctly sees the shared borrow end before the mutable borrow (via raw pointer) begins.

For the closure case: avoid capturing both reference types. Restructure so the closure only needs one:

fn process_with_closure_fixed(data: &mut [i32]) {
    let shared = &data[..];
    let value = shared[0];         // copy what you need
    let mut closure = move || {
        data[0] = 42;
        println!("{}", value);    // use the copy, not the shared ref
    };
    closure();
}

If you must keep the shared reference alive, use RefCell or Cell to make the borrowing dynamic and checked at runtime:

use std::cell::RefCell;

fn process_dynamic(data: &RefCell<Vec<i32>>) {
    let shared = data.borrow();    // runtime checked
    let mut closure = || {
        data.borrow_mut()[0] = 42; // panics if shared still alive
        println!("{:?}", shared);
    };
    // closure() would panic here — the bug becomes a loud crash
}

This trades compile-time soundness for runtime safety. The panic is loud and testable; silent UB is not.

What the Fixes Change for You

When the borrow checker fixes land (tracked in rust-lang/rust#164250 and linked issues), code that currently compiles but is unsound will start producing hard errors. Your crate will fail to compile.

This is the correct outcome. The borrow checker will finally enforce the guarantees it always promised. But it means:

  • No deprecation window — these are soundness holes, not lint-worthy patterns
  • No #[allow] escape hatch — you must fix the code
  • Miri becomes mandatory in CI — if you don't run it, you'll discover breaks at update time

Add Miri to your CI now:


## .github/workflows/miri.yml

name: Miri
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  miri:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install Miri
        run: rustup component add miri && rustup override set nightly
      - name: Run tests under Miri
        run: cargo miri test

Run it locally first. Fix what it finds. Then when the compiler catches up, your crate sails through.

Key Takeaways

  • Two 11-year-old borrow checker bugs let aliasing violations compile as safe code
  • The patterns: raw pointers from &mut overlapping with shared borrows, and closures capturing both &mut and & to the same data
  • cargo check and Clippy won't catch them — only Miri reliably detects the UB
  • Workaround: reorder operations so shared borrows end before raw pointers are created; avoid dual-reference closure captures
  • Fixes will be hard errors with no migration path — add Miri to CI today

Source

11 year old unsoundness bugs found in Rust borrow checker — added working code examples for both bug patterns, detection strategies using grep and Miri, concrete workarounds that compile on stable Rust, and a CI configuration to catch regressions early.

title: October 13, 2026
description:
BigQuery

Feature

The AI.AGG function is generally available (GA). You can use this function to semantically aggregate unstructured input data based on natural language instructions.

Feature

BigQuery generative AI functions now support the gemini-4-argon model. This model is generally available.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend
  • Limitations of spend cap budgets
  • Configure a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

  • Using the Cloud Billing Budget API for spend cap budgets
  • Spend cap budget concepts and limitations
  • Create a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap
  • Cloud Billing Budget API REST reference

Cloud SDK

Breaking

589.0.0 (2026-10-13)

Breaking Changes

  • (Google Cloud CLI) Deprecated the skaffold component in Google Cloud CLI. The component will be removed from Google Cloud CLI releases after January 15, 2027. A portion of gcloud components install skaffold attempts now return an error. Please install Skaffold following the instructions at https://skaffold.dev/docs/install/.

Google Cloud CLI

  • Updated Linux and Windows bundled Python to install cryptography 46.0.7 from the official PyPI wheels instead of custom builds.
  • Updated the Alpine-based Docker images (:alpine, :VERSION-alpine) to use a bundled Python and no longer include a system python3.
  • Updated bundled Python to 3.14.8 on Linux and Windows, and in the Alpine-based Docker images. This updates the OpenSSL that Python uses for TLS to 3.5.9.

AlloyDB

  • Added --enable-express flag to gcloud beta alloydb clusters create|update.

Apigee

  • Promoted gcloud apigee apis delete to GA. The command deletes an API proxy and all of its revisions. Every command in gcloud apigee apis now serves GA.
  • Fixed an issue where gcloud apigee apis import --from-template discarded a template's endpoints and targets whenever the template referenced a feature. A template that declared its own topology and used features only for policies compiled to a proxy with no ProxyEndpoint, and the import failed. A template's endpoints and targets now seed the proxy, and features are applied on top of them.

App Engine

  • Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run dropped the Serverless VPC Access connector for deployed versions.
  • Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run mapped App Engine Flexible instance_ip_mode to Cloud Run ingress.
  • Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run did not route all egress through Direct VPC for internal-only App Engine Flexible apps.

App Lifecycle Manager

  • Hid the deprecated gcloud beta saas-runtime command group. Existing commands continue to work and print a deprecation warning. Use gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager instead.

Beyondcorp

  • Deprecated gcloud beta beyondcorp app command group.

BigLake

  • Added --service-directory-name flag to gcloud biglake delta-sharing catalogs update.

BigQuery

  • Added support for Azure Data Lake Storage URIs (abfs:// and abfss://) in inline external table definitions (--external_table_definition).
  • Added --dataplex_entry_group flag to bq mk --transfer_config and bq update --transfer_config to allow integration with Dataplex Entry Groups.
  • Added support to filter Transfer Configs by Dataplex Entry Group using --filter="metadata_destination.dataplex_configuration:*" for bq ls --transfer_config.

Cloud Alerting

  • Promoted gcloud monitoring alerts command group to GA.

Cloud Composer

  • Updated gcloud composer environments storage dags export, gcloud composer environments storage data export, gcloud composer environments storage plugins export, gcloud beta composer environments storage dags export, gcloud beta composer environments storage data export, and gcloud beta composer environments storage plugins export to skip, with a warning, objects that would be written outside of the local --destination directory.

Cloud DNS

  • Added gcloud beta dns outbound-endpoints command group.
  • Added --outbound-endpoints flag to gcloud beta dns managed-zones and gcloud beta dns policies.

Cloud Firestore

  • Promoted gcloud firestore change-streams commands to GA.

Cloud Storage

  • Added server-side hash validation by default for resumable uploads in gcloud storage cp, gcloud storage mv, and gcloud storage rsync. To disable this behavior, run gcloud config set storage/enable_server_side_hash_validation False.

Compute Engine

  • Optimized gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances by passing --limit and --page-size to the backend API and terminating page fetching early when the limit is reached.
  • Added CMEK_ENCRYPTION option to --local-ssd-encryption-mode flag of gcloud beta compute instances create to encrypt Local SSDs with customer-managed encryption keys.
  • Fixed gcloud beta compute disk-types list returning no results when --zones or --regions is specified. Deprecated NAME positional argument and --regexp flag of this command. Use --filter instead.
  • Promoted loadBalancingScheme value EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH to GA in import and export schemas for gcloud compute backend-services.
  • Promoted IPAddresses and loadBalancingScheme value EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH to GA in import and export schemas for gcloud compute forwarding-rules.
  • Promoted gcloud compute advice capacity to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud compute advice capacity-history to GA.

Database Migration

  • Updated --ssl-flags flag documentation and parsing for gcloud database-migration connection-profiles commands to support custom delimiter syntax (^DELIM^) for values containing commas (e.g. server_certificate_dn).
  • Added --dbm-port flag to gcloud database-migration connection-profiles create sqlserver and gcloud database-migration connection-profiles update commands to specify the Database Mirroring (DBM) port for SQL Server Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations.
  • Added --sqlserver-dag-source-ag and --sqlserver-dag-linked-server flags to gcloud database-migration migration-jobs create and gcloud database-migration migration-jobs update commands to configure SQL Server Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations.

Device Run

  • Removed gcloud beta device-run sessions submit xctest. The command remains available in the alpha release track.

GKE Hub

  • Added --prioritized flag to gcloud beta container fleet rolloutsequences upgrade and gcloud beta container hub rolloutsequences upgrade.

Kubernetes Engine

  • Added --wiz-sensor-api-key-secret-uri, --wiz-sensor-proxy-secret-uri, and --wiz-sensor-registry-secret-uri flags to gcloud container clusters create, create-auto, and update commands to configure Wiz Sensor.

Looker

  • Fixed gcloud looker instances update --linked-lsp-project-number sending an empty update mask and failing.

Oracle Database

  • Added update command to the following gcloud oracle-database command groups to support adding, updating, removing, and clearing labels using --update-labels, --remove-labels, and --clear-labels flags:
    • gcloud oracle-database cloud-exadata-infrastructures update
    • gcloud oracle-database cloud-vm-clusters update
    • gcloud oracle-database db-systems update
    • gcloud oracle-database exascale-db-storage-vaults update
    • gcloud oracle-database goldengate-connections update
    • gcloud oracle-database goldengate-connection-assignments update
    • gcloud oracle-database goldengate-deployments update
    • gcloud oracle-database odb-networks odb-subnets update

Workbench

  • Fixed --nic-type flag choices in gcloud workbench instances create to use VIRTIO_NET instead of VIRTIGO_NET.

Subscribe to these release notes at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/google-cloud-sdk-announce.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for SQL Server instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud Storage

Feature

Object enrichments is now available in Preview. When you configure object enrichments, Cloud Storage applies Google's pre-trained machine learning models to eligible images and PDF documents in your buckets and attaches the resulting metadata to your objects as object contexts. You can inspect enrichments on individual objects or query them at scale in BigQuery by using Storage Insights datasets. For more information, see About object enrichments and Configure object enrichments.

Feature

Object contexts with extended data are available in Preview. Google services attach these contexts to your objects during automated analysis, such as machine learning labeling. To retrieve a context and its extended data, use the viewFullContext JSON API method.

Feature

Storage Insights datasets include the Object Contexts Catalog view (object_contexts_catalog_view), which you can use to analyze object contexts in BigQuery. For more information, see Object contexts catalog and Analyze object contexts.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can query regional views of global Compute Engine project and OS image resources by using the regional read-only projectViews and imageViews endpoints. Querying regional views isolates your control-plane read requests to a specific region, helping your workloads stay available during global API disruptions. For more information, see Use regional views for resilient control-plane reads and Access global resources regionally for high availability.

Dataform

Feature

You can use Developer Connect to connect Dataform repositories to Secure Source Manager repositories. This feature is in Preview.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. Gemini 4 Argon is supported in the web app and mobile app, but isn't available in Workflow Builder. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Argon. For instructions, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce

You can connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce to search data and automate actions across these third-party apps.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon is available in AlphaEvolve

AlphaEvolve experiments can generate candidate programs with Gemini 4 Argon in the global, us, and eu regions. To use it, specify gemini-4-argon in the models field of generationSettings. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Supported models and AlphaEvolve limitations.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Argon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-argon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation tokens on the GenerateContent API, and agentic video understanding in GA.

Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive (gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive), a version of Gemini 4 Argon for defensive cybersecurity use cases, is also available in GA behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

  • Known issue (long decodes): Long decoding (continuation_token) on the GenerateContent API (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path.

For more information, see Get started with Gemini 4 and the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Data Engineering Agent is now available in the asia-northeast1 (Tokyo) regional endpoint and supports the gemini-3.5-flash model. For more information, see Where Gemini in BigQuery processes your data.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running MySQL version 8.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

For more information, see Enable the integration of Knowledge Catalog on an existing Cloud SQL instance.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running PostgreSQL version 14.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

For more information, see Enable the integration of Knowledge Catalog on an existing Cloud SQL instance.

  • Data type mappings in BigQuery

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 5, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) instances running Looker 26.18. Feature enablement for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Feature

Looker now includes built-in support for the Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) dialect. The Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) uses the bundled Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver, so that you don't have to install unpackaged custom JDBC driver JAR files. See the Dremio documentation page for more information.

Feature

The AI-Assisted Quick Starts feature, called Starter questions in the new Explore experience, is now generally available.

Feature

The new Diagnose & Repair tool evaluates your LookML project repository across eight diagnostic test checks in either your personal development environment or the shared production environment. When issues are found, Looker can automatically perform repairs (such as removing stale lock files, fixing file permissions, or repairing corrupted object indexes) or rebuild damaged repositories while safeguarding uncommitted changes on a dedicated recovery branch.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now includes the Style Validator, which enforces LookML coding standards, naming conventions, and structural best practices across your LookML project. You can run the Style Validator with the default built-in ruleset or customize rule severities, file exclusions, path overrides, and custom rules by adding an lkmlstyle.yaml configuration file to your project repository.

Feature

Now available in preview, Conversational Analytics agentic workflows support scheduled agentic workflows in addition to triggered agentic workflows. You can use scheduled agentic workflows to schedule recurring deliveries of AI-generated insights summaries, data tables, visualizations, and PDF reports to email or Slack by using natural language. Recipients can select Investigate in a workflow notification to open a private, persistent conversation with the data agent.

Users and admins can manage workflows on the updated Manage Workflows user page and Manage Workflows admin page, respectively, and Looker admins can monitor scheduled workflow runs and troubleshoot errors on the new Workflow Executions admin page.

Workflows that were created in versions earlier than Looker 26.14 appear on the Legacy Workflows tab and must be recreated.

Feature

Now available in preview, Looker Data Apps are freeform canvas dashboards that are built by local AI coding agents, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or Cursor, from natural-language prompts. Data Apps give you complete visual layout control (including absolute positioning, overlapping elements, and custom web components) while remaining bound to Looker's governed LookML semantic layer and user permissions.

Change

In Conversational Analytics, the default question mode is now Fast rather than Thinking. Fast mode is intended for answering quickly, and it directly maps your query to underlying LookML definitions without generating reasoning steps. You can still select Thinking mode from the question mode drop-down menu when asking complex, multi-step analytical questions about Explores or dashboards.

Change

The Modern User Interface preview feature toggle now defaults to ON.

Change

The Modern visualization theme now supports map charts (static map points and regions), word cloud charts, and donut multiples. While support for donut multiples was previously documented, it is now officially available with this release. These additions expand the range of visualization options that are available with the modern theme.

Feature

Looker now supports connections to the ClickHouse 26+ dialect. ClickHouse 26+ uses modernized JDBC drivers and introduces support for symmetric aggregates. See the ClickHouse documentation page for more information.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor includes enhanced prompt injection and jailbreak protection for Workspace data. This capability improves detection accuracy and minimizes false positives when screening Workspace content, such as emails, documents, and files.

This capability is available on multi-region endpoints in the US (us) and EU (eu) for templates and floor setting configured with filter version v3 or later, including the Stable and Latest aliases.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports global access. You can enable this feature when creating a Secure Web Proxy instance to make sure that clients from any Google Cloud region can connect to your proxy.

With global access, you can route your outbound traffic through specific regions to meet regulatory compliance or cost requirements. You can also use this option to simplify your network administration by managing outbound traffic from a centralized location.

This feature is available in Preview.

Security Command Center

Feature

Using gcloud CLI, the securitycenter REST API, or client libraries, you can configure Pub/Sub and BigQuery continuous export to receive notifications when findings are deleted from Security Command Center due to data retention policies.

For more information, see the following:

  • Enable finding notifications for Pub/Sub
  • Stream findings to BigQuery for analysis
  • Enable real-time notifications
  • Creating and managing Notification Configs

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Overages must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model.
