    m.keySet().stream().map(Object::toString).sorted().forEach(k -> System.out.println("  " + k));

    // An Iceberg schema. Columns are matched by the numeric field id, not by name.
    Schema schema = new Schema(
        Types.NestedField.required(1, "id", Types.LongType.get()),
        Types.NestedField.optional(2, "name", Types.StringType.get()));

    // A local file to write to; an engine would get an object store path from FileIO.
    File out = new File(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "/tmp/ffa-demo.parquet");
    out.delete();

    // 3a. Write. (PARQUET, Record.class) is the registry key; build() does the lookup
    //     and hands back the Parquet model's writer, or throws if the pair is missing.
    System.out.println("== write via FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)");
    DataWriter<Record> writer =
        FormatModelRegistry.<Record, Object>dataWriteBuilder(
                FileFormat.PARQUET, Record.class,
                EncryptionUtil.plainAsEncryptedOutput(Files.localOutput(out)))
            .schema(schema)
            .spec(PartitionSpec.unpartitioned())  // required even without partitioning
            .overwrite()
            .build();

    // Record is Iceberg's generic row type; copy(name, value, ...) makes a row.
    GenericRecord rec = GenericRecord.create(schema);
    for (long i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
      writer.write(rec.copy("id", i, "name", "row-" + i));
    }
    writer.close();

    // toDataFile() returns the manifest entry an engine would commit, statistics included.
    DataFile df = writer.toDataFile();
    System.out.println("  wrote " + df.path() + " format=" + df.format() + " records=" + df.recordCount()
        + " bytes=" + df.fileSizeInBytes() + " valueCounts=" + df.valueCounts());

    // 3b. Read. Same key, other direction. An engine would also set a filter and a split.
    System.out.println("== read via FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)");
    try (CloseableIterable<Record> rows =
        FormatModelRegistry.<Record, Object>readBuilder(
                FileFormat.PARQUET, Record.class, Files.localInput(out))
            .project(schema)
            .build()) {
      for (Record r : rows) {
        System.out.println("  " + r);
      }
    }

    // 4. A valid format and a valid row type, but iceberg-orc is not on the
    //    classpath, so nobody registered the pair. The error names it.
    System.out.println("== ask for a model that is not registered (ORC with generic Record, no iceberg-orc on classpath)");
    try {
      FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(FileFormat.ORC, Record.class, Files.localInput(out));
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
      System.out.println("  " + e.getMessage());
    }
  }
}

And its output:

== FileFormat enum values
  PUFFIN splittable=false
  ORC splittable=true
  PARQUET splittable=true
  AVRO splittable=true
  METADATA splittable=false
== registered format models on this classpath (core + data + parquet)
  (AVRO, class org.apache.iceberg.deletes.PositionDelete)
  (AVRO, interface org.apache.iceberg.data.Record)
  (PARQUET, class org.apache.iceberg.deletes.PositionDelete)
  (PARQUET, interface org.apache.iceberg.data.Record)
== write via FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)
  wrote .../out.parquet format=PARQUET records=3 bytes=684 valueCounts={1=3, 2=3}
== read via FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)
  Record(1, row-1)
  Record(2, row-2)
  Record(3, row-3)
== ask for a model that is not registered (ORC with generic Record, no iceberg-orc on classpath)
  Format model is not registered for format ORC and type interface org.apache.iceberg.data.Record

Reading the output top to bottom:

  • The map holds Parquet and Avro, each paired with the generic Record and with the position-delete row type, and nothing else.
  • Avro is present without being asked for, because its model ships inside iceberg-core.
  • ORC is absent because the iceberg-orc jar is not on the classpath, and the error names the exact pair the registry could not find.
  • The write returned valueCounts: the writer filled in the DataFile statistics without the program doing anything.
  • One thing the program cannot express at all is a request for a format outside the five names. There is no FileFormat.LANCE to pass, and converting the string "lance" to a FileFormat throws "Invalid file format: lance" before the registry is ever reached.

The row-type side is open. The format side is closed.

The same call, from Spark

To connect this back to the level you already know: when you run spark.read.table("demo.orders").show() with the Iceberg connector, Spark loads the table through the catalog, plans which data files each task should scan, and then, for every file, makes exactly the call the program made by hand. Here is the Spark connector's version at 1.12.0, from BaseRowReader in the iceberg-spark module:

// Same call as the program above, with Spark's row type and all the options set.
ReadBuilder<InternalRow, ?> reader =
    FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(format, InternalRow.class, file);
return reader
    .project(projection)          // columns the query asked for
    .idToConstant(idToConstant)   // partition values, not stored in the file
    .reuseContainers()
    .split(start, length)         // this task's byte range
    .caseSensitive(caseSensitive())
    .filter(residual)             // what is left of the WHERE clause
    .withNameMapping(nameMapping())
    .build();

The format variable is the FileFormat recorded in the manifest entry for that file, and InternalRow.class is the row type Spark registered for itself in SparkFormatModels at startup. The query you type at the top level becomes, at the bottom level, one registry lookup per file. Everything between the two is planning.

Exploring pluggability

The extension point is relatively easy to grokk and doesn't take a ton of code. This section covers what an engine supplies, what the format model owns, and what "pluggable" therefore means in practice.

Here is how the generic Parquet model is registered, with each argument labeled:

// data/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/data/GenericFormatModels.java (1.12.0)
FormatModelRegistry.register(
    ParquetFormatModel.create(
        Record.class,          // the row type
        Schema.class,          // the engine schema type
        (icebergSchema, fileSchema, engineSchema) ->              // how to write a Record
            GenericParquetWriter.create(icebergSchema, fileSchema),
        (icebergSchema, fileSchema, engineSchema, idToConstant) ->  // how to read one
            GenericParquetReaders.buildReader(icebergSchema, fileSchema, idToConstant),
        new RecordVariantShreddingAnalyzer(),                      // see below
        (Function<Schema, UnaryOperator<Record>>) ignored -> Record::copy));  // how to copy a row

The engine supplies two functions. The writer function, given a schema, builds something that writes a row's values into Parquet. The reader function builds something that reads values out of Parquet into a row; its idToConstant argument is a map from column ids to values that come from metadata rather than from the file, mostly partition columns. ParquetFormatModel wraps those two functions in the builders every caller uses, and everything else lives in the model, once, for every engine:

The engine supplies The format model owns
the row class and the engine schema type schema conversion between Iceberg's schema and the file's
a writer function (row values into the file) filter pushdown: skipping chunks of the file that cannot match
a reader function (file values into a row) splits: reading one byte range of a large file
a shredding analyzer (which variant fields to shred) encryption
a row-copy function the statistics that end up in the DataFile
the shredded write path itself

Table 6. Division of labour between an engine and a format model.

The engine never touches anything in the right-hand column.

[!note] The analyzer argument
Variant is Iceberg's type for semi-structured data such as JSON. Shredding is Parquet's technique of storing some of a variant's fields as ordinary columns so they can be filtered and read quickly. The Parquet model owns the shredded write path; each engine supplies an analyzer that says which fields to shred for its row type. There is one for Record here, and a Spark one and a Flink one in their modules. It is a small example of how the labour divides: the format owns the mechanism, the engine owns the choice.

So if you maintain an engine, or anything with its own idea of a row, this is your plugin point, and it is a good one. Register your row type against Parquet, Avro and ORC, and your engine reads any Iceberg table through the same builders Spark uses, without changing anything in the Iceberg project.

And the engines really do all go through it now, which is the part of the announcement that is simply true. Every reader in the 1.12.0 source that opens a data file (in Spark, Flink, the generic Java path, the MapReduce input format and the Arrow reader) gets its reader from the registry; none of them calls the old per-format Parquet.read, ORC.read or Avro.read directly any more. One implementation per format, shared by every engine, chosen by (format, row type).

Put that next to the dotted lines in the read diagram and "pluggable" comes into focus. What was scattered and is now unified is the engine side. What was fixed and is still fixed is the format side. That is not a flaw so much as a boundary, and the next section is about what sits on the other side of it.

Where formats come into play and the compatibility kit

This section answers two questions: how does a new file format get into Iceberg today, and what does it have to pass once it is there?

Adding a format: the Vortex example

A new format enters Iceberg the way the project's own showcase does. Vortex is a newer columnar file format, and its integration (issue 15416) has a pull request (#15915) that shows every step. The PR has been open since April, and the table shows where it lands:

Layer What a new format needs there Does the Vortex PR touch it?
iceberg-api a new FileFormat value yes, first file in the change list
a format module the format model, readers and writers yes, new iceberg-vortex module
each engine a registration of its row type against the new format yes, Spark readers and tests
the compatibility kit an entry so the whole test matrix runs against it not yet
the table spec a fifth name in the file_format sentence no

Table 7. Where a new file format has to land, and how far the Vortex PR gets.

The first file in the PR's change list is FileFormat.java, adding VORTEX to iceberg-api, the module with the strongest compatibility promises in the project; every change there is checked by a tool called Revapi and has to be acknowledged on purpose. What the PR does not touch is as telling as what it does. Iceberg's table spec is the document every implementation follows, in Java or any other language. It lists each data file in a manifest with a file_format field, and the spec at 1.12.0 defines that field as "String file format name, avro, orc, parquet, or puffin." The Vortex PR changes nothing in the spec. The Java enum is moving ahead of the spec text, which is a normal order of events in this project, but it means adding a format has two halves: the constant in iceberg-api, and the spec sentence that would need a fifth name before PyIceberg or iceberg-rust were obliged to know about it.

What a format has to pass

Behind the implementation sits the Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK). A compatibility kit is a test suite that a new component must pass to count as equivalent to the existing ones. Here, it is the set of tests a new format has to pass to be held to the same standard as Parquet. The announcement lists the TCK as in progress; the issue's author said in August that it is "more-or-less finished" apart from some v3 types and vectorized paths, which I'll take at face value and no further, since it's one comment.

The path for a format today is therefore:

  1. Get into the enum.
  2. Implement a format model.
  3. Get every engine to register its row type against it.
  4. Pass the TCK.

That is a project roadmap item, not a plugin. A closed enum is also how the DataFile metadata, the manifest field above, and every reader that switches on format stay consistent with one another, so I'd be surprised if it opened casually.

Inside the kit

Since the kit is what a format or an engine actually has to pass, it is worth looking at what it is, because it is smaller and more concrete than the name suggests.

The kit is two abstract test classes in the test folder of the iceberg-data module. Abstract means they are templates: they contain every test but leave a few blanks for an engine to fill in. ReadFormatModelTests covers reading, and BaseFormatModelTests extends it with writing. An engine joins by writing a small subclass that fills in the blanks:

  1. What its row class is.
  2. How to turn an Iceberg schema into its own kind of schema.
  3. How to turn a generic Record into one of its rows.
  4. How to compare two of its rows.
  5. How to convert a single constant value.

Spark's subclass is about a page, Flink's about the same. Everything else is inherited from the template.

What gets inherited is every test, run for every file format the kit knows about, times every data generator (a small class that produces a schema and some random rows for it). The generators cover primitives, UUID, fixed, binary, decimals, a struct, a list and a map of primitives, nanosecond timestamps and variant. The tests cover round trips in both directions (including delete files), every read builder option, default values at every nesting, statistics in each collection mode, the metadata columns, schema evolution and name mapping.

The part I find most useful is that the kit is also where the exceptions get written down. Each engine's subclass declares the Iceberg types it cannot hold, and each format declares the features it is missing. Tests for those are skipped rather than failed, so the kit doubles as the honest table of who supports what:

Cannot hold / is missing
Spark time, timestamp_ns
Flink time
Avro filter pushdown, splits, column statistics, native encryption
ORC reader-side defaults, variant, container reuse
Parquet AES stream encryption

Table 8. Exclusions declared in the compatibility kit at 1.12.0.

The nanosecond timestamp I mentioned above is a one-line entry in Spark's exclusion set, which is the clearest statement anywhere in the repository that the gap is in the engine and not in the format or the API.

The kit was not in 1.11.0. It arrived as a series of separate PRs through the year, several from contributors outside the original design group, and the last open piece is vectorized reads.

That is what sits behind the "more-or-less finished" comment, and it also tells you how a new format gets in: add an entry for it to the kit's list of formats, run the whole matrix, and write down what it cannot do in the missing-features map. That list is the contract.

Implications for native multimodal in Iceberg

Multimodal data means images, audio, video and documents, plus the embedding vectors a model produces from them. If formats are fixed, then multimodal data has to come into Iceberg through the formats it already has, and that is exactly what is happening, one level down and one project over. Two new column types are being defined in the Parquet format spec first, and then mirrored into Iceberg's table spec as part of the v4 revision. (The table spec is versioned; v3 is current, and v4 is being drafted in the open PRs below.)

Both new types are Parquet logical types. A logical type is a label on top of a physical storage type that says how to interpret the bytes: a string is bytes labeled as UTF-8, a date is an integer labeled as days since the epoch.

FILE

FILE is a column type for "bytes that live somewhere." Parquet got a FILE logical type in parquet-format PR 585, merged in July and released in 2.14.0 in September. Iceberg's FILE type proposal (Talat Uyarer, Alex Stephen, Sung Yun and Gaurav Soni; spec in PR 17918) defines the Iceberg file type by reference to it. A value is a reference with optional fields:

Field Meaning
uri where the bytes live
offset, size a byte range inside that object
content_type what the bytes are
checksum integrity check
inline the bytes themselves, for small payloads

Table 9. Sub-fields of the proposed Iceberg file type.

So a small image can sit inline inside the data file, and a large one can be a byte range inside an external object. The table carries the reference, statistics on the sub-fields, and mappings for Parquet, Avro and ORC.

Whether an engine can actually go and fetch those bytes without holding cloud credentials is a separate question, handled on the catalog side with pre-signed URLs: links that carry their own temporary permission. PR 18080 adds that to the REST catalog spec, and PR 18079 teaches the readers to use the links the catalog hands back (both by Sung Yun, both open). That is where the design is still moving.

VECTOR

VECTOR follows the same pattern, a few months behind. parquet-format PR 624 proposes a VECTOR(D) logical type, meaning a list of exactly D numbers, on top of Parquet's existing list storage. Iceberg's vector type proposal with its spec PR 18416 defines vector(E, D), a fixed-length list of D numbers of element type E, and maps it onto the three formats Iceberg has:

Iceberg v4 type Parquet Avro ORC Rules
vector(E, D) Parquet's standard nested list encoding, annotated VECTOR(D) (per parquet-format #624); element required, Parquet mapping for E array, elements non-null array, elements non-null E in int, long, float, double; exactly D non-null elements; no NaN or infinities; no type promotion to or from vector; no lower/upper bounds

Table 10. The proposed vector type and its format mappings.

What the two proposals have in common

Read those two proposals next to the registry and the shape is clear. Neither one routes embeddings or media around Parquet. Both extend Parquet to carry them, and then teach Iceberg's schema, statistics and three existing format mappings about the new type. Neither needs a new FileFormat. That was the part I didn't expect going in: the announcement talks about new formats, and the multimodal column types are being written into Parquet, the format the new formats were meant to sit beside.

The File Format API helps here, but less than you might hope, and it is worth being exact about how much. What the Parquet model shares across engines is the schema conversion, splits, filters, encryption and statistics. Turning a vector column into a Spark row field or a Flink row field is still the job of each engine's own reader and writer function, the two functions from the registration code in "Exploring pluggability." So a new type is one change in the Parquet module plus one in each engine's value readers, not one change total. (Both spec PRs are open; if either is withdrawn, or Iceberg defines the type without reference to Parquet, this section is dated.)

A useful way to hold all of this: a column type has to clear three layers before you can use it from a given engine, and the File Format API only touches the middle one. The table spec has to define it; each file format has to store it; each engine has to have somewhere to put the value. Table 11 shows four types at 1.12.0, two shipped and two proposed:

Type Table spec Parquet Avro ORC Spark Flink
timestamp_ns v3 yes yes yes no yes
geometry, geography v3 yes yes no 4.1 and later no
file v4, proposed released in parquet-format 2.14.0 mapping in the proposal mapping in the proposal no no
vector v4, proposed proposed mapping in the proposal mapping in the proposal no no

Table 11. Where four column types stand across the three layers. A "no" in the engine columns means the engine has no in-memory type to hold the value, whatever the file can store.

The nanosecond timestamp row is a keen example. The spec has it, every format stores it, and Spark's own timestamp is microseconds, so Iceberg's converter has no case for it. No change to the registry could fix that, meaning unsupported types in an engine don't suddenly become supported by this new API. Spark is in the middle of fixing it from its own side: an open proposal, SPIP: Timestamps with nanosecond precision, adds nanosecond timestamp types to Spark SQL, the types are already on Spark's main branch, and a steady stream of PRs is teaching each function about them. Once a Spark release ships them, the Iceberg side is a converter case and a one-line removal from that exclusion set, so do expect this row to change.

State of the work and future

Everything above is a reading of the Java implementation at 1.12.0 and of spec PRs that are open on the day I'm writing. It says nothing about PyIceberg or iceberg-rust, which I didn't read, and it benchmarks nothing; the run exists to show what the registry contains and what it says when a model is missing, not how fast anything is. The Vortex PR could merge in any form, and the Java enum could grow a value before the spec sentence does, as that PR already shows. If the enum is opened in some more general way, the "formats are a project change" half of this is dated. The types half stands on its own, because the FILE and vector types are defined in Parquet regardless of what the Java registry does.

Piece Status Where to look
File Format API shipped in 1.11.0; every engine in 1.12.0 reads through it announcement, proposal
Compatibility kit "more-or-less finished" per its author; vectorized reads open issue 15415
Vortex as a new format open PR, adds VORTEX to the enum PR 15915
Parquet FILE type released in parquet-format 2.14.0 PR 585
Iceberg file type (v4) open spec PR issue 17919, PR 17918
Pre-signed data access open spec and reader PRs PR 18080, PR 18079
Parquet VECTOR type open proposal PR 624
Iceberg vector type (v4) open spec PR issue 18297, PR 18416

Table 12. Status of every moving part, as of writing.

Keeping up with the Joneses: What your next step is

  • You have images or embeddings in Iceberg today. Keep the reference as a string and the embedding as a list, which the current readers handle, and plan a schema migration to file and vector when v4 is adopted rather than a storage migration to another format.
  • You want to follow the decisions. Watch the two Iceberg spec PRs, the Parquet VECTOR PR, and the two pre-signing PRs, because that is where the capability is being decided.
  • You are an engine author with your own row type. Register it. The API is for you, it works, and the run above is the whole recipe.
  • You want a new format in Iceberg. Start from the TCK issue and the Vortex PR, and budget for it as a contribution to the project, because that is what it is.

Further reading

  • Introducing the Apache Iceberg File Format API, the announcement, and the proposal issue
  • FILE type proposal and spec PR; parquet-format FILE; pre-signed data access PR 18080 and PR 18079
  • Vector type proposal and spec PR; parquet-format VECTOR
  • Vortex integration PR and the TCK issue; the kit itself is ReadFormatModelTests and BaseFormatModelTests, first merged in PR 15441
  • The run: Iceberg 1.12.0, iceberg-core + iceberg-data + iceberg-parquet, Java 17; the full program and its output are in the Usage section above

title: An Idiot's Guide to Spark Connect Clients
description:
Spark Connect is a new concept for many of us, especially given the long history of how managing Spark clusters has traditionally worked. Spark Connect in a nutshell separates your application from Spark: your code becomes a small client, Spark runs as a server somewhere else, and the two talk over the network. The primary benefit of Connect for most users is getting rid of the headaches around SparkContext, installing a package from your notebook, your Python version not mattering, or a typo failing on the line you typed it, which Connect very kindly obfuscates for us. Honestly, it's a pretty overdue upgrade for Spark as an engine and a pretty intuitive direction: decouple client sessions from the server, and make the server and its configuration as dead easy as possible for your customers.

The mindset shift away from having your PySpark setup share the same process as your Spark driver is not a super hard jump, but it does mean there are some adjustments to make in how you set things like configurations or write jobs. This becomes even more intense once you get into the meat of Spark Connect, which is the language agnosticism and running multiple clients and servers, particularly for those of us dabbling in Rust or Go.

So this guide, written for idiots by an idiot, starts with a tour of how Spark itself works and how that changes with a Connect setup. From there it's practical: how to run a server, how to connect to it from Python and other languages, what changes in your code, and how to do some basic debugging. Note that after the inclusion of session tracing in 4.3, and hopefully an eventual Spark Connect Gateway, the latter will be much, much easier.

Every example comes from spark-demos, where each one is a runnable script, and I ran every snippet here against Spark 4.2.0, the current release.

How Spark works

Spark lets you write code as if you were working with one table on one machine, and then runs it across however many machines you have; Connect's whole trick is moving part of the machinery that makes that possible somewhere else, so it's worth having a picture of that machinery first. A running Spark application has a few kinds of pieces:

  • The driver is the brain. It holds your SparkSession, works out what your code actually means, decides how to run it, and coordinates everything else. Inside it:
    • the analyzer, which resolves the tables and columns you named, using the catalog (the registry of what tables exist and what's in them);
    • the Catalyst optimizer, which rewrites your query into a cheaper equivalent (skipping columns you never use, filtering before joining, and so on);
    • the planner, which turns the optimized query into physical operations;
    • the schedulers, which cut that physical plan into stages (at every point where data has to be reshuffled between machines) and each stage into tasks, one per slice (partition) of the data.
  • The cluster manager hands out machines: Spark's own standalone master, YARN, or Kubernetes.
  • Workers are the machines (or containers) the cluster manager gives you.
  • Executors are the processes on those workers that actually run tasks, read and write data, hold cached data, and exchange data with each other during a shuffle.

Following one line of code through all of that:

orders.filter(orders.total > 20).groupBy("region").count().show()
Step What happens Where
1 Your code describes the query: filter, group, count your program
2 That becomes an unresolved logical plan: a tree of operations naming tables and columns that haven't been checked yet the driver
3 The analyzer checks orders, total and region against the catalog and fills in types the driver
4 Catalyst optimizes the plan (here it reads only the two columns it needs) the driver
5 The planner picks physical operators and generates code for them the driver
6 The schedulers split the work into stages (before and after the shuffle groupBy needs) and tasks the driver
7 Executors run the tasks against their slices of the data the executors
8 The counts come back to the driver, and on to you the driver, then your program

Nothing actually runs until step 8 is needed; until you call something that wants a result (show(), count(), writing a table), Spark is only building the plan, which is what people mean by lazy evaluation. Classic Spark does run step 3 straight away (it checks your names the moment you define a DataFrame), and that small difference ends up mattering a lot once Connect is involved, so keep it in your back pocket for the debugging section.

The detail that matters most for this guide is where the driver runs. In classic PySpark (in the default "client" mode) the driver runs inside your program: your Python process starts a Java virtual machine next to it and talks to it through a bridge called Py4J, and that JVM is the driver, with the analyzer, the catalog connection, Catalyst and the schedulers all living in it.

Your code and Spark's brain share a process, a machine, a set of installed libraries, and a fate, such that if one of them crashes it takes the other down with it.

What the shared driver costs you

Sharing a process is fine when it's one person on one laptop, and it causes a surprising number of problems as soon as more than one person (or more than one program) uses the same Spark:

  • You need Java and all of Spark on every machine that runs your code, including your laptop, a CI runner, or a web service that just wants to run one query.
  • Your application and Spark are upgraded together. Upgrading Spark means changing the environment every job runs in, whether the job was ready or not.
  • Everyone's code shares the driver. One badly behaved notebook can take the driver down for everyone attached to it.
  • Only JVM languages and Python can talk to Spark, because they're the ones that can live inside or next to the JVM.
  • Credentials go everywhere the driver goes, so catalog passwords and storage keys end up on every machine that runs a job.

Spark Connect fixes all of these with one change, which is that it splits the driver in two. The part you write against, the DataFrame API, stays in your program; everything that thinks (the session, the analyzer, the catalog, Catalyst, the schedulers) moves into a long-running Spark Connect server, with a network connection in between. Your program builds step 2, the unresolved plan, as a small protobuf message, sends it over gRPC and gets results back as Arrow, and steps 3 to 8 all happen on the server.

Piece by piece, this is what moves and what stays put:

Piece Classic PySpark Spark Connect
Your code and the DataFrame API your process your process (the client)
Building the unresolved plan the driver JVM, via Py4J the client, as a protobuf message
SparkSession and its state (temp views, settings, artifacts) the driver, in your process the server
Analyzer and catalog connection the driver, in your process the server
Catalyst, physical planning, code generation the driver, in your process the server
Stage and task scheduling the driver, in your process the server
Cluster manager, workers, executors the cluster the cluster, unchanged
Results Py4J and a local socket into your process Arrow batches over gRPC
Catalog and storage credentials wherever the driver runs the server only

The cluster itself doesn't change at all, and executors run tasks exactly as they did before. What changes is that your program no longer contains a driver, so it doesn't need Java, it can be written in any language that speaks gRPC and Arrow, and it can be upgraded on its own schedule rather than the server's. Connect first appeared in Spark 3.4, and since 4.0 the server has shipped in the standard Spark download.

Pretty much every confusing thing about Connect is this split showing up somewhere you didn't expect it. explain() shows you a plan your laptop didn't make, because Catalyst is on the server; a typo in a column name fails late, because the analyzer is on the server and only sees your plan once you ask for a result; sparkContext is gone, because it belonged to the driver. Anything that used to live in your program (the JVM, your files, your Python version, your credentials) now lives on the other side of a network connection, and most of the rest of this guide is working through the consequences of that.

Connecting from Python

From Python it's two steps: install the thin client (pyspark-client),

pip install pyspark-client

and create your session with .remote(...) instead of .master(...):

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
print(spark.version)            # the *server's* Spark version

orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("metro", "pizza", 24.0), ("metro", "sushi", 40.0), ("urban", "pizza", 18.0)],
    "region string, item string, total double",
)
orders.groupBy("region").agg(F.round(F.avg("total"), 2).alias("avg_ticket")).show()

Everything after the session line is ordinary PySpark, the same code you'd run in classic mode. Your program builds the plan and the server optimizes and runs it, so if you call .explain() you're reading the server's plan (your laptop doesn't have an optimizer anymore).

Before and after: setting up a session

A real classic session usually does a lot more than pick a master; it pulls in packages, sets SQL extensions, turns on Hive support and quiets the logs. A typical one looks something like this:

# Before: Spark Classic. Everything is configured by the program that runs the driver.
spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .master("spark://my-cluster:7077")
    .config("spark.jars.packages", "org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")
    .enableHiveSupport()
    .getOrCreate()
)
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")

Under Connect that one block splits in two, because some of those settings describe the driver, and the driver isn't yours anymore. Anything the server reads once when it starts (packages and JARs, spark.sql.extensions, catalog implementations, Hive support) moves to the command that starts the server:

# After, part 1: the server owns its JVM, so it gets the packages and static settings.
./sbin/start-connect-server.sh \
  --master spark://my-cluster:7077 \
  --packages org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0

and the client keeps only what can change per session:

# After, part 2: the client names the server and sets runtime options.
spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")   # runtime settings still work from the client
    .getOrCreate()
)

The log level moves to the server as well (its conf/log4j2.properties), since the logs are the server's now. The sneaky part is that Connect doesn't stop you from setting a startup-only setting from the client; it warns and carries on without it. Asking for a package from the client gets you this, and no package:

UserWarning: Failed to set spark.jars.packages to Some(org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0)
due to [CANNOT_MODIFY_CONFIG] Cannot modify the value of the Spark config ...

enableHiveSupport() does the same thing (with CANNOT_MODIFY_STATIC_CONFIG) and hands you a session without Hive, which you might not notice until a table you expected isn't there. The rule of thumb I've landed on is that if a setting describes how the server starts, it belongs wherever the server starts.

You can also leave the URL out of your code entirely by setting SPARK_REMOTE, and a plain SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate() will connect to it:

export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost:15002"

Before and after: the rest of your code

Most DataFrame code doesn't change at all. What does change is anything that reached into the driver, and accumulators are a good example:

# Before: an accumulator, counted on the executors and read on the driver
bad_rows = spark.sparkContext.accumulator(0)
orders.foreach(lambda row: bad_rows.add(1) if row.total is None else None)
print(bad_rows.value)

# After: an Observation, collected alongside a query you were running anyway
from pyspark.sql import Observation

obs = Observation("quality")
checked = orders.observe(obs, F.count(F.when(F.col("total").isNull(), 1)).alias("bad_rows"))
checked.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("orders_checked")
print(obs.get["bad_rows"])

I'd argue the Observation is the better pattern anyway, since the metric rides along with a write you were already doing instead of needing its own pass over the data. The rest of the common swaps, side by side:

Before (Classic) After (Connect)
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN") set the level in the server's conf/log4j2.properties
df.rdd.zipWithIndex() df.zipWithIndex() (4.2+)
spark.read.json(rdd_of_strings) spark.read.json(df) on a string column (4.2+)
sc.accumulator(0) df.observe(Observation(...), ...)
sc.addPyFile("lib/geo.py") spark.addArtifact("lib/geo.py", pyfile=True)
sc.broadcast(lookup) a broadcast join, F.broadcast(lookup_df), or a literal column
spark.newSession() SparkSession.builder.remote(url).create()
spark-submit job.py python job.py with SPARK_REMOTE set

All of that assumes there's a server sitting at localhost:15002, which brings us to running one.

Running a Connect server

There are three ways to get one, roughly in order of effort.

1. Inside your own Python process, for trying things out. Full PySpark can start a Connect server in-process:

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("local[*]").getOrCreate()

This needs full pyspark (not pyspark-client) and Java installed, because the server still has to run somewhere; it's the Connect code path without a separate server, which makes it great for tests and for learning.

2. From a Spark download, on your machine or a server. Download Spark from spark.apache.org (you'll need Java 17 or newer) and start the server that ships with it:

./sbin/start-connect-server.sh        # listens on port 15002
./sbin/stop-connect-server.sh         # when you're done

By default it runs Spark locally on that one machine; to have it run jobs on a cluster instead, point it at the cluster's master:

./sbin/start-connect-server.sh --master spark://my-cluster:7077

One thing that surprised me is that by default the server listens on every network interface, so anything that can reach your machine can reach the server the moment it starts. On a laptop on shared Wi-Fi, restrict it with --conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.address=127.0.0.1. (You'll see spark.connect.grpc.binding.host in plenty of examples, including some of mine; it isn't a real setting, and Spark silently ignores it.)

3. In Docker. The official apache/spark image includes Spark, Java and Python; add PyArrow and pandas on top, since Python UDFs use Arrow by default as of Spark 4.2:

FROM apache/spark:4.2.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
USER root
RUN python3 -m pip install --no-cache-dir pyarrow pandas
USER spark

Then start the server with --wait, which keeps it in the foreground (what a container needs):

services:
  spark-connect:
    build: .
    entrypoint:
      - /opt/spark/sbin/start-connect-server.sh
      - --wait
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:15002:15002"   # Spark Connect
      - "127.0.0.1:4040:4040"     # Spark UI

The image's Python is 3.10, which matters for your client (more on that below).

For production, Connect servers also run on Kubernetes (the Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator deploys one as an ordinary Spark application) and, since Spark 4.2, inside YARN. The repo's topology guide walks through six ways to deploy one and when each makes sense.

Before you share a server with other people, know that a single server holds many sessions, each isolated from the others but all sharing the server's memory and executors; if people need stronger isolation than that, they need separate servers.

Running a job

There's no separate "submit" step for a Connect job, because your program is the job, and running it sends the work:

export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost:15002"
python my_pipeline.py

(SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate() picks up SPARK_REMOTE from the environment, so the same script runs against whichever server the variable names.) A few other routes are worth knowing about.

An existing job, almost unchanged. spark.api.mode switches a classic job to Connect: Spark starts a Connect server for the job and runs your code as its client. Set it in the session builder and keep your existing master:

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .master("spark://my-cluster:7077")
         .config("spark.api.mode", "connect")
         .getOrCreate())

This is the gentlest way to try Connect on real work, since you can move one job, watch it, and move it back if something breaks. The documentation also shows passing it to spark-submit as --conf spark.api.mode=connect; on 4.2.0 that failed for me with TypeError: 'JavaPackage' object is not callable while the builder setting worked, so for now, set it in code.

A declarative pipeline. Tell the spark-pipelines CLI which server to use with --remote:

spark-pipelines run --spec spark-pipeline.yml --remote sc://localhost:15002

Don't rely on SPARK_REMOTE here; the CLI ignores it and quietly starts a local server of its own. The spark-pipelines command comes with full PySpark, and with only the thin client it's the other way round: run python -m pyspark.pipelines.cli run --spec spark-pipeline.yml, which has no --remote option and connects to whatever SPARK_REMOTE names.

Code your job depends on. If your functions import your own modules, the server doesn't have them, so ship them with the session using addArtifact:

spark.addArtifact("lib/geo.py", pyfile=True)        # importable by your UDFs
spark.addArtifact("model.tar.gz", archive=True)     # unpacked on the executors
spark.addArtifact("lookup.csv", file=True)          # copied as is

JARs for catalogs and extensions are the exception; those have to be installed on the server.

What you need locally

Much less than before, which is kind of the point:

You need Why
Python, the same minor version as the server's Python functions you send run in the server's Python. The 4.2 client needs Python 3.10 or newer
pyspark-client The thin client
Its dependencies: pyarrow, pandas, numpy, grpcio They come with it; this is most of the install
No Java, no Spark download, no SPARK_HOME That all lives on the server

The thing actually worth getting right is which package you install, because there are four with nearly identical names:

Package What you actually get Java needed locally?
pyspark Full PySpark: about 470 MB, most of it some 280 JAR files yes
pyspark[connect] Full PySpark plus the Connect extras yes
pyspark-connect A tiny package that installs full pyspark (and makes Connect its default) yes
pyspark-client The thin client: about 15 MB, no JARs no

pyspark-connect sounds like the Connect client and isn't; the thin client is pyspark-client. Don't judge by the size of your environment either: with its dependencies a pyspark-client environment is about 330 MB against about 780 MB for pyspark[connect], because pyarrow, pandas and numpy are most of it, so what the thin client really saves you is Java, not disk space. To check which one you actually have:

import importlib.util, pathlib, pyspark

print((pathlib.Path(pyspark.__file__).parent / "jars").exists())  # thin client: False
print(importlib.util.find_spec("py4j") is not None)               # thin client: False

If either prints True, you're on full PySpark. And if you have a full Spark installed elsewhere on the machine, clear SPARK_HOME and PYTHONPATH before you start, or they can quietly shadow the thin client.

Clients in other languages

Because the client only has to build a plan and read Arrow, it doesn't have to be Python, or even a JVM language, and the same server takes all of these:

Language Client Latest release
Python pyspark-client (in apache/spark) 4.2.0
Scala and Java spark-connect-client-jvm (in apache/spark) 4.2.0
Go apache/spark-connect-go v0.1.0
Swift apache/spark-connect-swift 0.7.0
Rust apache/spark-connect-rust 4.2.0
Anything with JDBC spark-connect-client-jdbc, URL jdbc:sc://host:15002 since 4.1

They all start the same way, with a connection string. In Scala:

val spark = SparkSession.builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
spark.range(10).filter("id % 2 = 0").show()

In Go:

spark, err := sql.NewSessionBuilder().Remote("sc://localhost:15002").Build(ctx)
df, err := spark.Sql(ctx, "SELECT 'apple' AS word, 123 AS count")
df.Show(ctx, 100, false)

(At the time of writing, the Go client's only release, v0.1.0, can't be fetched with go get because of a module-path mismatch; go get github.com/apache/spark-connect-go@master works.)

Rust is where it gets fun for me, because results arrive as Arrow and can go straight into a native Rust tool. This program from the repo has Spark aggregate five million rows down to seven and then hands them to Polars for local work:

let spark = SparkSession::builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").get_or_create()?;
let e = |c: Column| c.expression().clone();   // aggregate expressions, unwrapped

let summary = spark
    .range(5_000_000)?
    .with_column("bucket", col("id") % lit(7))
    .group_by([col("bucket")])
    .agg(vec![e(f::count(col("id")).alias("n"))]);

let batches = summary.collect_record_batches()?;   // Arrow RecordBatches, ready for Polars

That division of labour, with Spark doing the part that needs a cluster and your language of choice doing the rest, is the part of Connect I find most interesting. The clients aren't equally complete yet, though (the Python and JVM ones cover the most, the newer ones less), so check that the one you pick supports what you need before you build on it.

Debugging

Most Connect problems come from forgetting that there are now two sides, so when something goes wrong I work through these in roughly this order.

1. Am I talking to the server I think I am? Print spark.version first, every time, since nothing in sc://localhost:15002 says which Spark is supposed to answer. I learned this one the hard way: an old Spark 4.1 server was still sitting on port 15002 on my machine when I pointed newer tools at it, and it answered, misunderstood a request it had never heard of, and gave me an error convincing enough that I wrote it up as a Spark bug. (The full story is in Hosting an Entire Open Lakehouse on Port 8080.) Two related traps:

a = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://server-a:15002").getOrCreate()
b = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://server-b:15002").getOrCreate()
assert b is a    # getOrCreate() returned the existing session; use .create() for a new one

and connection strings that look fine but aren't; the part after the port has to be empty, and parameter values can't contain /:

sc://localhost:15002/;user_agent=myapp/setup
PySparkValueError: [INVALID_CONNECT_URL] ... The path component '/;user_agent=myapp/setup' must be empty.

2. Read the error's name. Connect errors carry an error class in square brackets, and a handful of them cover most of what you'll hit early on:

Error What it means What to do
JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED You used something that lived in the local JVM: spark.sparkContext (and so everything reached through it, like sparkContext.setLogLevel), _jvm, df.rdd Use the DataFrame replacement: df.zipWithIndex(), spark.read.json(df), df.observe(...) for counters, addArtifact for files
PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH Your Python and the server's differ (e.g. 3.12 vs 3.10) Match your Python minor version to the server's
ModuleNotFoundError inside a UDF The server's Python is missing a package your function needs Ship it with addArtifact, or install it on the server
UNSUPPORTED_LOCAL_CONNECTION_STRING You called .create() with local[*] Use .getOrCreate() for local
INVALID_CONNECT_URL The connection string is malformed Empty path, no / in parameter values

One that doesn't raise at all is enableHiveSupport(), which prints a warning and gives you a session without Hive, so read your warnings.

3. Errors arrive late. Classic Spark checks your DataFrame the moment you define it (that step 3 from earlier); Connect doesn't send anything to the server until it needs an answer, so a typo in a column name fails at the show() or write rather than on the line with the typo, and a try/except around the definition catches nothing. The same thing has two quieter consequences:

a.createOrReplaceTempView("brands")
first = spark.table("brands")
b.createOrReplaceTempView("brands")
first.count()     # Classic: rows of a    Connect: rows of b

A DataFrame built on a temp view reads whatever the view points to when it runs, and a Python function that reads a variable sees that variable's value when it runs, so give temp views unique names and pass values into functions explicitly.

4. Look at the server's side. The server has the Spark UI (port 4040 by default), where you can see the jobs your client triggered along with a Connect tab listing every client session and request, and it has its logs (in logs/ under the Spark directory, or docker logs for a container). df.explain() shows you the plan the server actually built.

5. Check your client isn't newer than your server. The supported direction is an older client talking to a newer server, and the other way round can fail in odd ways: a 4.2 client can't even build a DataFrame from a three-row Python list on a 4.1 server, because the 4.1 server reports a size limit as 3221225472b and the 4.2 client chokes on the b.

6. Let a script check for you. The repo includes a doctor that checks the client you installed, whether the server is reachable, its version, and whether Python functions actually run on it:

python tools/doctor.py --remote sc://localhost:15002 --expect-version 4.2

The whole guide, on one page

  • Spark splits big data work across many machines.
  • Spark Connect moves the driver out of your program; your code becomes a client that sends plans to a server.
  • Use it with pip install pyspark-client and SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002").
  • Get a server in-process with local[*], from a Spark download with start-connect-server.sh, or from the apache/spark Docker image (plus PyArrow).
  • Send a job by running your program; ship your own modules with addArtifact.
  • Locally you need Python matching the server's version and pyspark-client, and nothing else.
  • Other languages (Scala, Go, Rust, Swift, JDBC) use the same server and the same connection string.
  • When it breaks, check which server answered, read the error's name, remember errors arrive late, and look at the server's side.

Nearly all of it comes back to the one change at the start, which is that the driver moved out of your program; once you know which side of the network a thing lives on, most of Connect stops being surprising.

title: Freelancing from Pakistan as a Web Developer in 2026: The No-Fluff Playbook
description:
Pakistani freelancers pulled in a record $1.76 billion in foreign exchange
during FY26, up 78% from the year before, with IT freelancers contributing
$1.16 billion of it. Nearly three million Pakistanis now freelance, making
the country the world's fourth-largest freelance market. This post is the
no-fluff version of how a web developer actually gets into that number:
which platform to pick, what the fees really cost, how the 0.25% tax works,
how to get paid, and what to do in your first 90 days.

The short answer

Start freelancing as a web developer from Pakistan in 2026 by picking one
niche (Next.js builds, e-commerce, or AI integrations), building two or three
portfolio projects that look like paid work, opening on Fiverr (free to start,
20% commission) or Upwork (variable 0-15% fee, ~10% typical, plus $0.15
Connects per bid), registering with PSEB to qualify for the 0.25% final tax
rate on IT export income, and receiving payments through Payoneer or Wise.
Expect your first client in 30-90 days of daily effort.

Why 2026 is genuinely a good year to start

Most "start freelancing" guides lean on vibes. The State Bank of Pakistan
numbers do not need any:

  • $1.76B freelance earnings in FY26 (State Bank of Pakistan data, reported by Dawn, The News, TechJuice, July 2026)
  • 78% year-on-year growth (Up from $984 million in FY25 - SBP figures)
  • ~3M freelancers in Pakistan (Industry estimates (PAFLA) - fourth-largest freelance workforce in the world)

The breakdown matters more than the headline. IT freelancers generated $1.16
billion (up 49%), while non-IT freelance earnings tripled to $592 million -
writing, design, marketing, and virtual assistance. Two readings of that: the
demand for technical work keeps compounding, and clients are buying wider
skill bundles than before. A web developer who can also ship the landing
page, wire up the analytics, and write the launch copy sells a bigger ticket
than one who ships code alone.

Where these numbers come from
Freelance remittance figures are from State Bank of Pakistan data released
in July 2026 and reported by Dawn, The News, Pakistan Today, TechJuice,
and ProPakistani. The 0.25% tax extension comes from coverage of the
Finance Act 2026 by Business Recorder, TechX, and PhoneWorld. Platform fee
figures are 2026 published rates; confirm the current number on each
platform's official fee page before you quote it to yourself, because these
change without notice.

Pick your platform: the 2026 fee reality

Your platform choice is a tax on your income, so do the math before you fall
in love with anyone's marketing. Here is what each major platform actually
costs a Pakistani web developer in 2026:

Platform Freelancer fee Bidding cost Best for
Fiverr Flat 20% on every order None (gig-based) Zero-capital starts, packaged services
Upwork Variable 0-15% per contract (most report ~10%) $0.15 per Connect, ~2-16 Connects per proposal Custom projects, long-term clients
Freelancer.com 10% (or $5 minimum) Free bids on plan tiers Contest-style and budget work
Toptal 0% to the freelancer Screening, not bidding Senior devs who can pass the vetting

Two practical conclusions. First, Fiverr's 20% is the highest headline rate
in the table, but it costs you nothing before you earn, which makes it the
only rational first platform when you are bootstrapping from zero. A $100
order nets you $80 from day one with no ad spend. Second, Upwork's effective
rate is lower than Fiverr's for most freelancers, but the Connects system
means you spend $3-5 per proposal with no guarantee of a reply. If you burn
through 50 Connects a week at $0.15 each with weak proposals, Upwork is a
hole you pour money into.

The right sequence for most Pakistani beginners: Fiverr first for the first
client and first reviews, Upwork second once you can afford to bid on ten
jobs a week, and direct clients third once you have a portfolio worth
showing off-platform. Never build your entire income on one platform - an
account flag, a fee change, or an algorithm shift can take 100% of your
revenue overnight.

The six things you need before your first client

Nothing on this list costs more than a few evenings. Every item you skip
becomes a delay later, so treat it as a checklist, not advice.

One niche, not five

"Web developer" is not a niche, it is a commodity listing. Pick one: Next.js
marketing sites, Shopify/WooCommerce builds, SaaS MVPs, or AI integrations
(chatbots, RAG, MCP tools). Your niche decides your gig titles, your
portfolio, and which jobs you bid on. Everything below compounds from this
choice.

Three portfolio projects that look like paid work

Build three projects in your niche as if a client paid for each one: real
brief, real deadlines, live deployment link, GitHub repo, and a short
case-study writeup explaining the problem and your decisions. Clients do not
read code on a first pass, they look at the live thing and the writeup.
Three strong projects beat ten tutorial clones every time.

One platform profile done properly

Profile photo (real face, decent light), headline with your niche and one
outcome ("Next.js sites that load in under 2s"), a description written for
buyers not recruiters, and your portfolio projects linked. On Fiverr, build
2-3 gigs with tiered packages (Basic/Standard/Premium). On Upwork, pick 10-15
skills that match your niche exactly. Generic profiles get generic results.

One payment rail, verified with a small withdrawal

Set up Payoneer or Wise (Elevate Pay is worth comparing as a
Pakistani-built option) before you need it, and run one small test
withdrawal to your local bank. Discovering your payout path is broken the
day a $500 client payment lands is a special kind of panic you only need
once. PayPal is still not functional in Pakistan, so do not plan around it.

PSEB registration on your 90-day list

Registration with the Pakistan Software Export Board is what qualifies your
IT and IT-enabled service export income for the 0.25% final tax rate under
Section 154A, instead of normal income-tax treatment. It is a government
portal process, not a lawyer's job. Do it once your income is real and
before filing season, not after.

A written proposal template, not a begging letter

Your template: one line naming the client's actual problem, two lines on
how you would solve it, one line of proof (a link), and the price. Custom
beats clever every time. Send 3-5 tailored proposals a day on Upwork or
answer every Fiverr inquiry within the hour. Volume of quality attempts is
the whole game at the start.

What web developers actually charge

Rate anxiety kills more freelancing careers than competition does. The
numbers below are indicative ranges seen across platforms for Pakistani
developers in 2026 - not guarantees, and your niche, reviews, and how well
you sell all move you up or down the band:

Service Starter range With reviews + niche
Landing page / marketing site $100-300 $500-1,500
Full website (Next.js / WordPress) $300-800 $1,000-3,000
E-commerce build $500-1,200 $1,500-5,000
SaaS MVP $1,000-2,500 $3,000-10,000+
Hourly dev work $15-30/hr $40-80/hr
AI integration / chatbot build $400-1,000 $1,500-4,000

Price for take-home, not for the platform
These are gross figures. Run every quote through your platform's cut before
you accept it: a $1,000 Fiverr order is $800 in your account, and a $1,000
Upwork contract at a 10% fee is $900 minus whatever Connects you spent
winning it. The section below works the math on a real example so you stop
doing it in your head mid-proposal.

The money math: what a $1,000 project leaves you

Concrete example, because fee percentages stay abstract until you lose real
money to them. You win a $1,000 fixed-price website build:

  • On Fiverr: 20% commission = $200 to the platform, $800 to you. No bidding cost, 14-day clearance hold before withdrawal.
  • On Upwork: ~10% service fee = ~$100 to the platform, ~$900 to you, minus Connects. Say you spent 12 Connects ($1.80) across two rounds of bidding to win it: you keep ~$898, minus withdrawal fees depending on your method.

Then the tax layer: if you are PSEB-registered and the income qualifies as
IT export proceeds under Section 154A, the 0.25% final tax on $900 is $2.25,
and that is the whole tax bill on that income. Without PSEB registration,
the same income can fall under normal tax treatment - a difference of
hundreds of dollars on a $1,000 project. This is why the paperwork section is
not bureaucratic decoration.

The lesson is not "Upwork always wins." It is that Fiverr's simplicity costs
about $100 per $1,000 project versus Upwork's cheaper-but-pay-to-bid model,
and that the tax setup dwarfs both. A freelancer who fixes their tax
registration earns more from a Fiverr order than one who ignores it earns on
Upwork.

The tax setup nobody explains properly

Pakistani freelancers get two pieces of tax news in 2026, one good and one
demanding attention. The good: the Finance Act 2026 extended the 0.25% final
tax rate on IT and IT-enabled service export income for PSEB-registered
exporters through June 30, 2029. It is a final tax - once it is deducted
from your export proceeds, you owe nothing more on that income.

The part that needs attention is qualification. The 0.25% rate applies to
export proceeds from computer software, IT, or IT-enabled services where the
exporter is registered with and certified by PSEB, received through proper
banking channels. Receiving money from a foreign client does not
automatically make every service PSEB-qualified, and non-filers face higher
withholding on top. Keep client invoices, bank records, and your PSEB
registration in one folder. Filing season runs on its own calendar - the
September 30 deadline catches first-timers every year.

Register with PSEB, get paid through banking channels, file your return.
Everything else about freelancer tax in Pakistan is detail around that sentence.

-- The one-sentence version

Getting paid: pick one rail and verify it

Three rails matter for Pakistan in 2026. Payoneer is the default most
platforms integrate with natively. Wise usually wins on exchange rates for
direct client transfers. Elevate Pay is the Pakistani-built option designed
for cheaper direct transfers and keeps your dollars in a foreign-currency
account with local withdrawals. Each has different fee structures and payout
speeds, and the cheapest rail for a $50 gig is not always the cheapest for a
$5,000 contract - that comparison deserves its own post, and it is coming.

For now, the rules: one primary rail plus one backup, a test withdrawal
before you need it, and never your entire balance sitting on a platform.
Withdraw on a schedule, keep payment screenshots with your invoices, and
remember every withdrawal is also your tax documentation.

Your first 90 days, week by week

Days 1-14: build the machine

Pick your niche, finish one portfolio project end-to-end with a live URL and
a writeup, set up your payment rail, and complete your platform profile.
No proposals yet. A half-built profile sending proposals is how beginners
burn their first 100 Connects for nothing.

Days 15-45: ship and propose daily

Finish portfolio projects two and three. Start sending 3-5 tailored
proposals a day on Upwork, or launch your Fiverr gigs and share them where
your buyers are (LinkedIn, relevant communities - not spam, answers). Target
small jobs first: clients hire beginners for $100-300 test projects, not
$5,000 builds.

Days 46-90: convert, deliver, repeat

Your goal is 3-5 completed jobs with 5-star reviews, not one big win. Over-
deliver on the first ones - fast communication, clean handoff, a short Loom
walkthrough. Each review multiplies your next proposal's reply rate. Start
your PSEB registration the week your second client pays.

The fluff version:

  • "Just create an Upwork profile and wait for clients!"
  • "Charge $5/hour to get started!"
  • "Taxes? Worry about that when you're rich."
  • One generic profile, copied proposals, rage-quitting at week six.

The version that works:

  • Niche down, build three projects that look like paid work.
  • Price at the starter band of your niche, raise every 5 reviews.
  • PSEB registration + banking channels + invoices from the second client.
  • Daily proposals, weekly shipping, 90 days of patience.

FAQ

How much can a Pakistani web developer earn from freelancing?
Ranges vary by niche, but Pakistani web developers on international platforms
commonly report $15-40/hour starting out and $50-150/hour with specialization
and reviews. In FY26, Pakistani freelancers earned a record $1.76 billion,
with IT freelancers contributing $1.16 billion, so the demand side is real -
your earnings depend on niche, positioning, and how consistently you ship.

Is Upwork or Fiverr better for beginners in Pakistan in 2026?
Fiverr costs nothing to start: no bidding fees, you build gig listings and
clients come to you, but you pay a flat 20% commission on every order. Upwork
charges a variable 0-15% fee per contract (most report around 10%) plus $0.15
Connects to bid, so it costs money before you earn. Start with Fiverr if you
have zero capital, add Upwork once you can afford to bid strategically.

Do I need PSEB registration to freelance legally from Pakistan?
You can start freelancing without it, but registering with the Pakistan
Software Export Board is what unlocks the 0.25% final tax rate on IT and
IT-enabled service export income under Section 154A. Without registration,
the reduced rate does not apply to you, so the tax difference is large enough
that registration should be on your 90-day list.

What is the freelancer tax rate in Pakistan in 2026?
For PSEB-registered IT and IT-enabled service exporters, the rate is 0.25%
final tax on eligible export proceeds received through banking channels,
extended by the Finance Act 2026 through June 30, 2029. Other export income
under Section 154A is taxed at 1%. The 0.25% rate is final - you owe nothing
more on that income.

How do Pakistani freelancers receive money from foreign clients?
The common rails are Payoneer, Wise, and Elevate Pay, with bank withdrawals
into local accounts. PayPal still does not work properly in Pakistan, so do
not plan around it. Pick one rail, verify it with a small withdrawal before a
big one, and keep client payments and personal spending separated for clean
tax records.

How long does it take to get your first freelancing client?
With daily effort - 3-5 quality proposals a day on Upwork or a few well-built
Fiverr gigs - most beginners land a first small project in 30-90 days. The
first client is the slowest because you have no reviews; after five completed
jobs with ratings, reply rates climb sharply. There is no shortcut here that
does not involve sending proposals and shipping work.

The tools worth bookmarking

Tool What it does Link
Fiverr Gig-based marketplace, zero cost to start https://www.fiverr.com
Upwork Proposal-based marketplace for custom projects https://www.upwork.com
Payoneer Receive international payments, local bank withdrawal https://www.payoneer.com
Wise Multi-currency transfers, usually best exchange rates https://www.wise.com

Want the freelancer playbook applied to your project? If you are a
founder who needs a Next.js site, a store, or an AI integration shipped by
someone who understands both the code and the business math, reach out
through my about page. I take on a small number of projects at a
time, and I answer every serious inquiry personally.

title: Spark's Modules, Seen Through Spark Connect
description:
Spark is moving its centre of gravity out of the JVM. Spark Connect, introduced in 3.4, lets a client drive Spark over gRPC without running a JVM of its own, and in the 4.x line that thin client has become the thing new features are built for: pip install pyspark-client gets you the DataFrame API with none of the JARs full PySpark carries. That gives a simple way to tell which parts of Spark have a future. The state of each Spark module is best read through a single test: can you reach it from a thin Python client over Spark Connect? The modules getting sustained investment were either built for that world (SQL, Declarative Pipelines) or are being rebuilt to reach it (Structured Streaming, MLlib, the Python UDF path); the ones fading (GraphX, SparkR, DStreams, the RDD-based spark.mllib) are exactly the ones that can't cross it.

I learned to read Spark this way by accident. In February I tested Real-Time Mode on open-source Spark 4.1, and the first obstacle wasn't latency; it was Python. The real-time trigger existed in Scala, PySpark had no way to ask for it, and to run the pipeline at all I wrote a helper that reached through the Py4J gateway and built the Scala trigger object by hand:

def with_real_time_trigger(dsw, checkpoint_interval="5 minutes"):
    jvm = dsw._spark._jvm
    jTrigger = jvm.org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.RealTimeTrigger.apply(
        checkpoint_interval
    )
    dsw._jwrite = dsw._jwrite.trigger(jTrigger)
    return dsw

It worked, and it's exactly the kind of code that has no future. It only runs in classic mode, because a Spark Connect client has no JVM to reach into; the PySpark 4.2 Connect session refuses _jvm by name, along with _jsc, sparkContext, and the rest of the Py4J surface. Five months later the helper was obsolete anyway. Spark 4.2 added trigger(realTime=...) to PySpark, so the same pipeline runs from a thin client, and the 4.3 branch lets that Python code run aggregations and deduplication in real time too. A feature that existed but couldn't be reached from Python became real the moment it crossed the client boundary, and that is the story of nearly every module below.

Crossing isn't free, and part of this post is what it cost me when I tried. It's written against Spark 4.2.0 (released July 14, 2026). Spark 4.3 is close but not out: its first release candidate was tagged on August 31, and the vote on it failed on September 6, so where 4.3 matters I describe what's on the release branch, not what has shipped.

What "reachable over Connect" actually means

Spark Connect splits the application from the engine. The client builds an unresolved logical plan, serializes it as protobuf, sends it over gRPC, and gets results back as Arrow batches; everything that plans and runs the query lives on the server.

That contract is the whole test. Anything expressible as a logical plan travels; anything that assumes the client and the driver share a JVM doesn't. The line falls in a predictable place:

Over Spark Connect Status
DataFrame operations, Spark SQL, catalog operations, temp views Supported
Structured Streaming Supported
Python, Pandas, and Arrow UDFs; UDTFs Supported
pyspark.ml pipelines (fit / transform) Supported, via a server-side model cache
SparkContext, RDDs, broadcast variables, accumulators Not supported

RDDs are the dividing line because an RDD isn't a plan; it's a handle to partitioned data and closures living in the driver's JVM. Every module built on RDDs inherits that limitation, which is most of the reason the left-hand column of the diagram above looks the way it does.

The payoff for crossing the line is a client with no JVM. pyspark-client ships only the gRPC client, the protobuf definitions, and the DataFrame API; it installs none of the roughly 277 jars that full pyspark carries. When I measured the 4.2.0 packages, Spark's own Python payload dropped from roughly 480 MB to about 20 MB and the jar directory to zero.

The common "1.5 MB client" line is misleading, though: 1.60 MB is the wheel, and a working thin-client virtualenv still came to roughly 360 to 380 MB across my installs, because pyarrow, pandas, and numpy are hard requirements and dwarf Spark itself. The honest headline is no JVM, no JDK, no jars, not small.

Package What it is
pyspark-client The thin client: pure Python, no JDK, remote only (sc://...)
pyspark[connect] Full PySpark plus Connect extras; can also start a local server
pyspark-connect A small shim that depends on full pyspark (so not thin)
pyspark Classic Py4J by default; talks to a Connect server via .remote() with the extras installed

The classic/Connect choice is controlled by spark.api.mode, whose default is still classic; the proposal to make Connect the default (SPARK-50411) is open. So the direction is clear, but for now you opt in, and what that means for someone choosing today is simple: anything you write that touches sparkContext or _jvm is a bet against where the project is going.

Built for it: SQL and Declarative Pipelines

Spark SQL passes the test almost by definition, because a Connect request is a logical plan and Spark SQL is the machinery that turns logical plans into execution. Every DataFrame call, every spark.sql() string, and every Structured Streaming query goes through the same pipeline:

That's why SQL keeps absorbing features that used to live in application code. Across the 4.x line it gained procedural scripting (generally available in 4.1, with cursors added in 4.2), recursive common table expressions (a request that sat open as SPARK-24497 from 2018), the VARIANT type for semi-structured data (shredded into typed Parquet columns from 4.1), collations, and pipe syntax. None of these needs anything from the client beyond the text of the query, which is the point: the more logic moves into SQL, the less it matters what language or process the client is.

-- Recursive CTE: walk an org chart without a loop in application code
WITH RECURSIVE reports (id, name, manager_id, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT * FROM reports;

The most interesting 4.2 addition, and the one I spent the most time probing, is metric views (SPARK-54119): a semantic layer declared with CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS, where measures such as a conversion rate are defined once and re-aggregated correctly at whatever grain you query.

The problem they solve is real. In an example I built on synthetic session data, the true monthly conversion rate was 0.0923, while the naive average of the five regional rates was 0.2384, 2.6 times too high, because an average of ratios gives a region with 200 sessions the same weight as one with 50,000. A metric view makes that mistake hard to write.

What it doesn't yet do is fail gracefully.

I ran a grammar probe of 87 statements against the official apache/spark:4.2.0 image (once in classic mode and twice over Connect, all three runs identical), and six invalid statements didn't produce a clean error; they crashed the planner with INTERNAL_ERROR, the message that begins "You hit a bug in Spark":

Statement (abridged) Result on 4.2.0
SELECT * FROM <metric view> INTERNAL_ERROR at planning
Selecting a measure without MEASURE() INTERNAL_ERROR at planning
Joining a metric view on a dimension INTERNAL_ERROR at planning
MEASURE() over an ordinary table INTERNAL_ERROR
CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS without LANGUAGE YAML, and a metric view defined over another metric view INTERNAL_ERROR

The numbers are protected; the person writing the query isn't, yet.

Declarative Pipelines (SDP) extend the same idea from queries to whole pipelines: you declare what each table should contain, and Spark resolves dependencies, orders execution, and manages checkpoints and writes. Pipelines are defined in Python or SQL and run over Spark Connect by design, so SDP was born on the right side of the line.

It arrived in 4.1; 4.2 added AUTO CDC for applying change feeds as SCD Type 1, and the 4.3 branch adds SCD Type 2 end to end and a SQL form, CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC. I tested the 4.2 behaviour in detail in AUTO CDC: Turning an event log into current state.

Concept Python API Behavior
Materialized view @dp.materialized_view Batch table, recomputed each run
Streaming table @dp.table Incremental ingestion with managed checkpoints
Flow @dp.append_flow Named writer into a streaming table
AUTO CDC flow (4.2) dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(...) Applies a change feed as SCD Type 1

For someone choosing today: push as much logic as you can into SQL and declarative definitions. It's the part of Spark that works identically from every client, it's where new features land first, and it's the part least likely to strand you in a migration.

Rebuilt to reach it: streaming, ML, and Python UDFs

The second group are modules that predate Spark Connect and are being reworked to pass the test. Each has made real progress, and each still has a visible seam.

Structured Streaming and Real-Time Mode

Spark has had three streaming engines, and the history is a clean illustration of the thesis. DStreams (described by Matei Zaharia and colleagues in 2012 and 2013) modelled a stream as a sequence of small RDDs; Structured Streaming (Spark 2.0, 2016; written up by Michael Armbrust and colleagues at SIGMOD 2018) rebuilt streaming on DataFrames, as an unbounded table queried with the same API as batch; and Real-Time Mode, added in 4.1, replaces the micro-batch loop with a continuous pipeline:

Real-Time Mode is also where I learned how wide the gap between a feature's design and its open-source reality can be. The widely quoted single-digit-millisecond figures come from Databricks' own deployments.

On open-source 4.1, a stateless Kafka-to-Kafka passthrough I measured (500 events per second on a single 16-core machine, six runs of roughly two thousand events each) had a p50 of about 17 ms and a p99 of 21 to 26 ms. That's fast; it's also a different number, measured on a much smaller setup, and I'd treat both figures as specific to where they came from. The limits mattered more than the latency:

  • Stateless only. The 4.1 operator allowlist permitted projections, filters, and broadcast joins; aggregations, shuffles, and state store operators were off it.
  • No Python UDFs. BatchEvalPythonExec wasn't on the allowlist.
  • No PySpark trigger, hence the Py4J helper at the top of this post.
  • Every stage runs concurrently, so a 16-partition Kafka source needs 16 task slots just to read.

Spark 4.2 fixed the Python gap (the realTime trigger in PySpark) but, per the 4.2 source, left the operator allowlist unchanged, so on 4.2 it's still a stateless engine:

# Spark 4.2+: Real-Time Mode from PySpark, no JVM access needed.
# The argument is the checkpoint interval, not a latency target.
query = (
    events.select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("e"))
    .select("e.*")
    .filter(col("amount") > 0)                      # stateless: allowed
    .selectExpr("to_json(struct(*)) AS value")
    .writeStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:9092")
    .option("topic", "payments_clean")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/payments_clean")
    .outputMode("update")
    .trigger(realTime="5 minutes")
    .start()
)

The 4.3 branch is where it becomes a general engine. It adds stateful Real-Time Mode (umbrella SPARK-54699): streaming aggregations including windowed ones, dropDuplicates, the JVM transformWithState, and pipelined shuffles, and it removes the @Experimental marker from the trigger APIs.

The branch documentation is just as clear about what remains out of scope: stream-stream joins, flatMapGroupsWithState, session windows, and the PySpark transformWithState APIs are unsupported; Python UDFs are still not allowed (SPARK-57237 is open); Kafka is the only source; and stateful queries need enough cores to run both stages at once.

Notice where the seam is. When I built the 4.3 branch and ran it against my own stack, the stateful operators that are ordinary DataFrame operations worked from PySpark in Real-Time Mode: a streaming aggregation and a dropDuplicates both ran at about 40 ms median latency (against about 600 ms for the same query as a one-second micro-batch), with no duplicates getting through. What's still missing is Python's own stateful API: PySpark transformWithState isn't supported in Real-Time Mode, and on the branch today it fails with a misleading checkpoint-metadata error (STDS_FAILED_TO_READ_OPERATOR_METADATA) rather than the documented unsupported-operator one. Custom state in real time is still a Scala feature.

The rest of Structured Streaming is further along. transformWithState (SPARK-46815) replaced the older mapGroupsWithState APIs in 4.0 with typed, evolvable state, and it has a Python API, which ended the era when complex stateful streaming meant writing Scala. RocksDB is the default state store in 4.x, and 4.1 enabled adaptive query execution for stateless streaming queries (SPARK-53941).

For someone choosing today: on 4.2, use Real-Time Mode from Python for stateless transforms where the latency matters, and micro-batch Structured Streaming for anything stateful. On 4.3, aggregations and deduplication move into Real-Time Mode from Python as well; if you need custom state (transformWithState) at real-time latency, that's still Scala.

MLlib on Connect

MLlib's problem was more fundamental than streaming's.
