In classic PySpark, model.fit(df) returns a model object that lives in the driver's JVM, and the Python client just holds a Py4J reference to it. A Connect client has no JVM to hold anything, so ML over Connect required moving model state to the server:

The server keeps fitted models in a cache and hands the client an ID; fit, transform, evaluation, attribute lookup, and save/load become RPCs. This is the one rebuild that's essentially finished. pyspark.ml on Connect shipped in 4.0 (SPARK-50812); 4.1 brought it to general availability with model cache offloading, model size and cache limits, and summaries that survive eviction (SPARK-51236); 4.2 re-enabled FPGrowth (SPARK-54574); and the 4.3 branch adds model-size estimation for around twenty model types (umbrella SPARK-58181) plus a fix for size overcounting (SPARK-57521).

What it hasn't done is grow: the estimators, transformers, and evaluators registered for Connect are the same list from 4.0 through the 4.3 branch, a few known gaps remain open (SPARK-51473, SPARK-51478), and the ML guide still has no section on Connect at all.

Meanwhile the DataFrame-based spark.ml has been the primary API since Spark 2.0, when the RDD-based spark.mllib entered maintenance mode; spark.mllib doesn't pass the Connect test and isn't going to. For deep learning, the path is TorchDistributor (SPARK-41589), which uses Spark to launch distributed PyTorch training rather than reimplementing it.

For someone choosing today: spark.ml pipelines over Connect are safe for the algorithms MLlib already has; don't expect the catalogue to expand, and use TorchDistributor or an external framework for anything modern.

Python UDFs on Arrow

The Python UDF path is the rebuild I've measured most closely. Its history is a long march away from pickling one row at a time: Pandas UDFs (2018) moved data in Arrow batches but converted them to pandas; useArrow=True (from 3.5) put ordinary scalar UDFs on Arrow transport; and @arrow_udf (public in 4.1, SPARK-53014) hands your function a pyarrow.Array with no pandas conversion at all.

In my benchmark on Spark 4.1, what decided the cost of a UDF was mostly what the function received, not how the bytes travelled. useArrow=True was worth 1.4x to 2.4x over pickle depending on the workload; the vectorized UDFs were faster again; and @arrow_udf beat @pandas_udf by about 1.6x on strings but only 5 to 9% on numeric work, because a numeric pandas Series is cheap to build from Arrow while strings are not. The details, and a correction to my own benchmark, are in Stop Blaming Serialization for Slow Python UDFs.

Getting Arrow on by default took two tries. SPARK-48516 flipped the default for Spark 4.0, and Hyukjin Kwon reverted it in March 2025, before 4.0 shipped. Spark 4.2 finally turned it on (SPARK-54555), for regular Python UDFs, UDTFs, and the pandas conversions, and raised the minimum PyArrow to 18.0.0.

The 4.3 branch drops Python 3.10 (SPARK-56889) and adds an opt-in pipelined UDF transfer (spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled, off by default, SPARK-56642); pandas 3 still isn't fully supported even there (SPARK-55139 is open).

The same Arrow-first direction shows up in the Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), which lets you write a connector entirely in Python and, since 4.1, receive pushed-down filters. That removes one of the last reasons a Python team needed Scala.

For someone choosing today: on 4.2, plain @udf already gets Arrow transport for free; write new UDFs as @arrow_udf when the logic maps onto pyarrow.compute (especially strings), and @pandas_udf when you need pandas or SciPy.

What crossing the boundary cost me

Everything above argues that Connect is where Spark is going. It's worth being equally concrete about the price of getting there, because I paid it in two ways this month.

Migrating a real pipeline. I moved the pipelines in my lakehouse-stack project to Spark Connect and started with an audit script over the repository. It reported 27 findings across 24 files, and 21 of them were the same line: spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN").

That single call was the entire blocking surface, and it has no client-side equivalent, because the log level belongs to the server's JVM; the fix is to configure logging where the Connect server starts and delete the call.

The migration itself was almost mechanical, and after it all ten tables matched their pre-migration versions on schema, row count, and an order-independent content hash (that parity result is recorded in my migration notes rather than as a saved log).

The real blocker was the ecosystem. Apache Iceberg doesn't publish a Spark 4.2 runtime; the newest on Maven Central targets 4.1. And the 4.1 jar can't simply be reused, because Spark 4.2 changed the catalog interfaces it implements: View became a class, so loading the old runtime fails with

java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class org.apache.iceberg.spark.source.SparkView
can not implement org.apache.spark.sql.connector.catalog.View, because it is not an interface

and because that failure happens while the catalog loads, it takes down tables, reads, and writes along with views. 4.2 also requires catalogs that serve both tables and views to implement a new RelationCatalog interface. I built a local Iceberg runtime for 4.2 to keep going, which is fine for a demo and not something I'd run in production.

The general lesson is that a Spark minor version can break connectors, and your upgrade schedule is set by your slowest connector, not by Spark.

Mixing versions. Connect's promise is that client and server can be upgraded independently. I tested all four combinations of 4.1.2 and 4.2.0 clients and servers, running each fourteen-operation matrix twice, with identical results:

Client → server Result
4.2.0 → 4.2.0 Everything works
4.1.2 → 4.2.0 Works; newer APIs simply don't exist in the old client
4.1.2 → 4.1.2 Works
4.2.0 → 4.1.2 createDataFrame from a local list fails; GetStatus returns UNIMPLEMENTED

The createDataFrame failure is worth spelling out, because it's so small. A 4.2 client checks the size of local data against a limit it reads from the server (SPARK-55047); a 4.1.2 server reports that limit as 3221225472b, with a unit suffix, and the new client's integer conversion fails on the b:

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3221225472b'

So a new client can't build a three-row DataFrame on an old server. Independent upgrades hold in one direction only: upgrade the server first, and pin clients to it.

Left behind: GraphX, SparkR, and the RDD APIs

The last group fails the test for the same structural reason: each is built on RDDs or on a pre-Connect bridge, and none has a path across.

GraphX was one of Spark's original libraries (Spark 0.9, 2014), built entirely on RDDs and never given a Python API. Between September 30 and October 8, 2024, the dev list voted on Holden Karau's proposal to officially deprecate it in Spark 4; she noted that it "hasn't been updated meaningfully in several years" and was already "de-facto deprecated," and was explicit that it was "not a vote to remove GraphX." The proposal passed, although the 4.2.0 GraphX programming guide still carries no deprecation notice.

The clearest verdict came from outside the project. GraphFrames, the DataFrame-based graph library that Berkeley and Databricks released as an external package in 2016, had gone quiet for years; its maintainers revived it, moved it to the io.graphframes namespace, added Spark 4 support, and, starting with 0.10.0, stopped depending on Spark's GraphX at all, shipping their own "internal modified and updated fork of the Apache Spark GraphX" instead.

Because GraphFrames stores vertices and edges as DataFrames, graph queries go through Catalyst, work from Python, and pass the Connect test's premise:


# pip install graphframes-py==0.12.2
# pyspark --packages io.graphframes:graphframes-spark4_2.13:0.12.2
from graphframes import GraphFrame

g = GraphFrame(vertices, edges)          # two DataFrames: id, and src/dst
ranks = g.pageRank(resetProbability=0.15, maxIter=20)

# Motif finding: patterns become DataFrame joins that Catalyst can plan
triangles = g.find("(a)-[]->(b); (b)-[]->(c); (c)-[]->(a)")

SparkR was contributed in Spark 1.4 (2015) by Shivaram Venkataraman and the AMPLab team. Hyukjin Kwon committed its deprecation (SPARK-49347) in August 2024, and since 4.0 starting a SparkR session prints a warning that it "is deprecated from Apache Spark 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version." It uses its own JVM bridge and was never ported to Connect, and most R users had already moved to sparklyr, which is maintained by Posit and supports Spark Connect.

DStreams were deprecated in 3.4 (SPARK-42075), and spark.mllib has been in maintenance mode since 2.0; both are RDD APIs with DataFrame successors that do pass the test.

For someone choosing today: don't start anything new on these. Use GraphFrames for graphs (it's the only option from Python), sparklyr for R, Structured Streaming for streams, and spark.ml for ML, and treat existing code on the old APIs as migration work with a deadline you don't control.

Choosing, module by module

Module Verdict Reachable over Connect What I'd do
Spark SQL Built for it Yes Default choice; push logic here
Declarative Pipelines Built for it Yes Use for multi-table pipelines; AUTO CDC for change feeds
Structured Streaming Rebuilt Yes Micro-batch for stateful work
Real-Time Mode Rebuilding Yes from 4.2 (stateless) Stateless only until 4.3; check Python gaps
MLlib (spark.ml) Rebuilt Yes (since 4.0) Fine for existing algorithms
Python UDFs Rebuilt Yes @arrow_udf first; Arrow transport is default in 4.2
GraphX Left behind No Migrate to GraphFrames
SparkR Left behind No Migrate to sparklyr
DStreams, spark.mllib Left behind No Migrate to DataFrame APIs

The part of this that surprised me most is how little of the sorting is about quality. GraphX isn't fading because its algorithms were bad, and SparkR isn't fading because R users were wrong; they're fading because they sit on the wrong side of a client boundary the project has decided to build everything else around.

My Py4J helper was on that side too; it still works in classic mode, and on 4.2 nothing needs it.

Further reading

  • SPARK-54633: Quarterly release cadence SPIP.

title: AUTO_CDC: Turning an event log into current state with Spark Declarative Pipelines
description:
The question an event log can't answer cheaply

The dataset I use for most of my pipeline demos is a simulated ghost kitchen (a delivery-only restaurant operation), and like most operational data it arrives as an append-only log. Every order produces a lifecycle of events, each stamped with a time and a per-order sequence number, and a day of it is about a million events. The generator deliberately injects a few percent of late and duplicated events, because real streams do that.

Logs like this are excellent at answering what happened and awkward at answering what operations people actually ask: which orders are live right now, and where is each one?

The usual answer is to recompute it. Group the whole history by order, take the latest event for each, drop the cancelled ones, and repeat on every refresh, paying for the entire history every time and getting it subtly wrong whenever "latest" means latest to arrive rather than latest to happen.

The better answer depends on noticing something that sounds obvious once it's said: an append-only lifecycle log is already a change data capture feed. Each event is a change to the current state of one entity (the order), keyed by order id, sequenced by when it happened, and a cancellation is simply a delete.

Here is an illustrative order (simplified; the real sequence is described below), first as the lifecycle log records it, then as the change feed it implies:

seq event_type as a change to orders_live
1 order_created UPSERT order 1042, status = order_created
2 kitchen_started UPSERT order 1042, status = kitchen_started
3 order_ready UPSERT order 1042, status = order_ready
4 driver_picked_up UPSERT order 1042, status = driver_picked_up
5 driver_ping UPSERT order 1042, status = driver_ping
6 delivered UPSERT order 1042, status = delivered

An order that ends in order_cancelled produces a DELETE as its last change instead, and disappears from the table. Once the log is seen this way, "current status of every order" stops being an aggregation problem and becomes the problem of applying a change feed to a table, which is exactly what AUTO CDC was built to do.

My argument is that AUTO CDC is worth adopting less because it saves code (though it does, a lot) than because it moves the hard parts of change application into the engine, and leaves you with a small, explicit contract: a sequence column that is unique and never null, a target that genuinely supports row-level operations, and deletes expressed as events. Most of what goes wrong with hand-rolled CDC is the engine's side of that contract done badly; most of what can still go wrong with AUTO CDC is your side of it.

What AUTO CDC is, and where it stands

AUTO CDC began as APPLY CHANGES in Databricks' Delta Live Tables and was contributed to Apache Spark under its own SPIP (SPARK-56249), as part of Spark Declarative Pipelines. In Python it's create_auto_cdc_flow.

Release AUTO CDC status
Spark 4.2.0 (July 2026) Shipped. SCD Type 1 via the Python / Spark Connect API
Spark 4.3.0 (release candidate) Adds SCD Type 2 (history with validity ranges)
main branch (5.0.0-SNAPSHOT) Ongoing work under SPARK-56249

Everything I tested was SCD Type 1 (the target holds only the current state per key, and updates overwrite in place), on a build of the main branch from late May 2026, before 4.2 was released.

Applying a change feed correctly means doing several things at once:

  • matching each change to its row by key
  • keeping the version with the highest sequence per key, not the last to arrive
  • honouring deletes, but only when the delete is the latest thing that happened to that key
  • staying idempotent when a streaming source redelivers after a failure

The hand-rolled version is usually a foreachBatch with windowed deduplication feeding a MERGE, and it tends to get the cross-batch cases wrong without throwing errors. A late update that lands in the micro-batch after a newer one quietly overwrites it, and nobody notices until the numbers disagree with something else.

The code

The projection from lifecycle log to change feed is ordinary Spark. This is the core of what my test harness does: every event becomes an UPSERT of the order's current status, a cancellation becomes a DELETE, and the sequence is made unique per order.

feed = events.select(
    F.col("order_id"),
    F.col("event_type").alias("status"),
    F.col("location_id").cast("int").alias("location_id"),
    F.col("ts_seconds").alias("event_ts"),
    F.when(F.col("event_type") == "order_cancelled", F.lit("DELETE"))
     .otherwise(F.lit("UPSERT")).alias("op"),
    # unique per-key ordering: event time, broken by per-order sequence
    (F.col("ts_seconds") * F.lit(100) + F.col("sequence")).alias("seq"),
)

Then the pipeline itself is three declarations: a streaming source, a target streaming table, and the flow.

from pyspark import pipelines as dp

@dp.table(name="order_cdc_source")
def order_cdc_source():
    return spark.readStream.schema(ORDER_SCHEMA).json("file:///data/order_cdc/*.json")

dp.create_streaming_table("ice.gold.orders_live")

dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="ice.gold.orders_live",
    source="order_cdc_source",
    keys=["order_id"],                  # how a change finds its row
    sequence_by="seq",                  # highest sequence per key wins, whatever the arrival order
    apply_as_deletes="op = 'DELETE'",   # which events delete the row
    except_column_list=["op", "seq"],   # bookkeeping columns to leave out of the target
    stored_as_scd_type=1,
)

The engine handles what the hand-rolled version gets wrong: deduplication across micro-batches by sequence_by, the generated upsert and delete, exactly-once checkpointing, and the auxiliary state table that remembers the latest sequence per key across runs.

That table is what lets a late event arriving in a later batch resolve correctly.

Recompute from the log AUTO CDC
Cost per refresh re-aggregates the entire history processes only new events
Out-of-order events "latest" by arrival is wrong resolved by sequence_by
Cancellations a row every query must remember to filter the row is deleted
Code bespoke foreachBatch + dedup + MERGE three declarations

Running it on messy data

I ran the order-status projection on a sample of the ghost-kitchen stream: a little under five thousand orders and roughly 125,000 of their lifecycle events, including the injected late and duplicate ones. AUTO CDC collapsed them into one row per live order:

gold.orders_live rows
delivered 4,601
driver_ping (mid-delivery) 84
order_ready 3
order_created 1
kitchen_started 1
driver_picked_up 1
total live orders 4,691
cancelled orders removed by apply_as_deletes 308

To check it, I recomputed the same table from scratch the naive way and compared the two in both directions:

w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("seq"))
naive = (feed.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1")
             .filter("op != 'DELETE'").select("order_id", "status"))
pairs = spark.table("ice.gold.orders_live").select("order_id", "status")
match = naive.subtract(pairs).count() == 0 and pairs.subtract(naive).count() == 0
# match = True

They matched exactly.

It's worth being precise about what that proves: it compares the two columns the table exists to answer, as sets, rather than every column byte for byte.

Two details of the run also deserve honesty, because they're the kind of thing that makes a demo look cleaner than it was. The sample was drawn by sorting order ids and taking the first five thousand, and because the raw data contains events with a null order id (which Spark sorts first), the sample was really 4,999 orders.

And the projection joined each event to its order's creation event, so orders with duplicated creation events fanned out into duplicate rows in the feed. AUTO CDC handled both without complaint, since duplicate copies of an event carry the same sequence value and resolve to the same row, but a pipeline that quietly processes inputs it wasn't meant to receive is a reminder to look at your inputs before trusting your outputs.

The second scenario was the textbook one: keeping a dimension current as kitchens relocate, rename, and close. These are the exact changes streamed into silver.dim_locations_current, on top of an initial load of four locations at sequence 1:

changes = [
    {"id": 2, "city": "Los Angeles - Arts District", "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 5},
    {"id": 1, "city": "San Francisco - SoMa",        "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 4},
    {"id": 3, "city": "Chicago",                      "op": "DELETE", "seq": 6},   # kitchen closed
    {"id": 2, "city": "Los Angeles (STALE)",          "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 3},   # arrives late, older
]
id after AUTO CDC why
1 San Francisco - SoMa rename at seq 4 applied
2 Los Angeles - Arts District rename at seq 5 kept; the stale seq 3 edit ignored
3 (no row) closure at seq 6 deleted it
4 Austin unchanged

A nightly full reload would eventually reach the same names, but it copies every unchanged row to get there and has no way at all to express that a location no longer exists.

That's the more general lesson: an append-only or aggregate pipeline can only add facts, so "this was cancelled" becomes another row every downstream query has to remember to filter. In a CDC pipeline a terminal business event can be the delete itself, and the same mechanism propagates hard deletes for compliance.

Edge cases, and how Type 1 resolves them

I put SCD Type 1 through a battery of adversarial cases, and it behaved correctly in every one. The behaviours are worth knowing precisely, because this is where intuition tends to be wrong. These are the cases from my stress harness, with the events in arrival order; | separates micro-batches.

Case Events for one key Result
Upsert to a key that never existed UPSERT@1 row inserted
Delete of a key that never existed DELETE@1 no-op
Several updates in one batch UPSERT@1, UPSERT@2, UPSERT@3 row has the @3 values
Stale delete UPSERT@1 | UPSERT@3 | DELETE@2 row stays, with the @3 values; the update is newer
Stale insert after a delete UPSERT@3 | DELETE@5 | UPSERT@2 row stays deleted
Delete arrives before an older insert DELETE@5 | UPSERT@2 row stays deleted
Resurrection UPSERT@1 | DELETE@2 | UPSERT@3 row present, with the @3 values
Volume, out of order 500 keys, each UPSERT@1, @3, @2 shuffled across 5 batches, plus DELETE@5 for 100 of them exactly 400 rows, all with the @3 values
Tie (probe, not pass/fail) UPSERT@5 "Boston", UPSERT@5 "Denver" in one batch one of them, chosen arbitrarily

Your side of the contract

The sequence. A null in the sequence_by column fails the micro-batch with AUTOCDC_MICROBATCH_VALIDATION.NULL_SEQUENCE rather than guessing, which is the right behaviour, and means the column has to be non-null by construction.

Ties are worse, because they don't fail: two changes to the same key with the same sequence in one micro-batch are resolved arbitrarily, as the programming guide itself warns. A coarse timestamp is the classic way to produce ties, so sequence on something strictly increasing per key, like a log offset or commit LSN. My composite of timestamp times 100 plus the per-order sequence works only because no order in this data has more than 99 events; it's a local trick, not a general recipe. The ties that did occur in my data were all injected exact duplicates, the one case where an arbitrary choice is harmless.

The target. AUTO CDC needs a connector that implements Spark's DataSource V2 row-level operation interface (SupportsRowLevelOperations), and "supports MERGE" is not the same thing:

Target Result in my testing
Plain Parquet rejected immediately: AUTOCDC_TARGET_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_MERGE
Delta did not work: Delta's table implementation doesn't expose SupportsRowLevelOperations, despite supporting MERGE elsewhere
Iceberg, Hadoop catalog worked
Iceberg, JDBC (Postgres) catalog worked
Iceberg, Hive Metastore catalog worked
Iceberg, Gravitino REST catalog worked
Iceberg, Glue catalog (emulated) worked
Iceberg, Unity Catalog OSS REST failed: the catalog is read-only
Any ephemeral / in-memory catalog unsuitable: the aux state table must persist across restarts

Two smaller surprises: the target carries a hidden __spark_autocdc_metadata column that shows up in SELECT *, and Iceberg's own changelog is batch-only in open-source Spark for now, so you can't stream one Iceberg table's changes straight into AUTO CDC as a source.

A correction. I originally reported that running an AUTO CDC pipeline through the spark-pipelines CLI failed at registration with InvalidPlanInput: RELTYPE_NOT_SET, and called it a bug. It wasn't.

The CLI connects to the default Spark Connect endpoint, and an old Spark 4.1 Connect server was still listening there, so my pipeline was being sent to a server that had never heard of AUTO CDC. Against a server of the right version the CLI works correctly. If you see that error, check what's actually listening on sc://localhost:15002 before anything else.

What changes

With a hand-rolled pipeline, the question you're left with is whether you've correctly implemented cross-batch deduplication, sequenced deletes, and idempotent merges, and the honest answer is usually that you won't know until something disagrees. With AUTO CDC that part belongs to the engine, which is tested against exactly the cases people get wrong.

The question becomes whether you've given it a sequence that is unique and never null, a target that really supports row-level operations, and a delete for everything that should be allowed to disappear. That's a much better question to be left with, and the first step is often not a new data source at all; it's noticing that the event log you already have has been a change feed all along.

Further reading

  • Test harnesses and results: lakehouse-stack/scripts/pipelines/autocdc-scd1 (Spark main branch, 5.0.0-SNAPSHOT at 06ffa273, with an Iceberg runtime ported to Spark 5.0).

title: Java Variables in GenAI Applications
description:
Introduction

Java variables are essential for storing and managing data in applications. In Generative AI (GenAI), variables can store user prompts, AI responses, and configuration values. They help Java applications communicate with AI models and process generated content.

What Are Java Variables?

A variable is a named storage location used to hold data in a Java program.

Syntax / Example 

String prompt = "Explain Generative AI";
String aiResponse = "GenAI generates new content.";

System.out.println(prompt);
System.out.println(aiResponse);

Practical Example

In a Java-powered AI chatbot, a prompt variable stores the user's question, while an aiResponse variable stores the response returned by the AI model.

Key Takeaways

  • Variables store data in Java applications.
  • String stores prompts and text responses.
  • int stores whole numbers, such as token counts.
  • Variables help manage AI inputs and outputs.
  • Meaningful variable names improve code readability.

Conclusion

Java variables provide a simple way to manage data in GenAI applications. They help developers handle prompts, AI responses, and other application values. Understanding variables is a useful first step toward building AI-powered Java applications.

How would you use Java variables in your own GenAI project?

Thanks for reading! 🚀

Follow me on DEV Community for more Java, GenAI, and software development tutorials.

Follow me: @manikandan4411
