title: Explaining the Python-JVM Boundary in Spark, and What Arrow Changed
description:
Arrow's real contribution to PySpark isn't speed at any one API but a shared memory format at every boundary between the JVM and Python; each release removed one conversion at one boundary, what each one left behind explains the next, and the conversion that remains now lives inside Spark's own engine rather than at the Python edge.

That crossing is the oldest problem in PySpark, and the most persistent attempt to fix it started in February 2016, when Wes McKinney (the creator of pandas) filed a Spark ticket with a modest title: SPARK-13534, "Implement Apache Arrow serializer for Spark DataFrame for use in DataFrame.toPandas." It asked for one method to stop using pickle.

It took two years to ship. And over the decade that followed, the same idea went through every other door between Spark's JVM and Python: UDFs, partition-level APIs, the network protocol of Spark Connect, custom data sources, until in Spark 4.1 a Python function could receive Spark's data as an Arrow array and never touch pandas at all, and in Spark 4.2 the Arrow paths finally became the defaults.

The wall

PySpark is not a Python reimplementation of Spark. It's a Python client for a JVM engine. When you write df.filter(col("x") > 5).groupBy("y").count(), Python builds a query plan and hands it to the JVM, which optimizes, distributes, and executes it; Python never touches the data, which is why DataFrame code runs at the same speed in PySpark and Scala.

The trouble starts the moment your own code needs the data: a UDF, toPandas(), createDataFrame(pandas_df), a custom data source. Then data has to physically cross from the JVM into a Python process, and for most of Spark's history the only way across was pickle, one row at a time:

Every row pays four serialization steps and a function call. For a UDF like return x * 1.1, the arithmetic is nanoseconds and the machinery around it is microseconds, three orders of magnitude of overhead wrapped around almost no work.

That was PySpark from 2015 to 2018.

Why the fix was a memory format, not a faster pickle

Arrow was conceived in late 2015 by people who had hit the same wall from different directions. McKinney had spent years fighting pandas' memory model; his 2017 essay "Apache Arrow and the 10 Things I Hate About pandas" lists the grievances, including a rule of thumb that pandas users needed "5 to 10 times as much RAM as the size of your dataset."

Jacques Nadeau, building a query engine at Dremio, saw every data system inventing its own internal format and paying to translate between them at every boundary. Marcel Kornacker, who created Impala at Cloudera, saw the same copying across the Hadoop ecosystem. They met at Strata NYC in September 2015, and Arrow was announced as an Apache top-level project in February 2016, skipping the incubator entirely, which is unusual and reflected how many companies wanted the same thing.

The idea was not a faster serializer. It was to agree on the bytes themselves: a language-independent, columnar, in-memory layout specified down to byte alignment, null bitmaps, and buffer order, so that two Arrow-aware systems can hand each other data without converting it.

Within a process, or with shared memory, that's genuinely zero-copy; across a socket it's still a copy, but with no per-row decoding on either side, because the bytes on the wire are already the bytes in memory.

Columnar mattered as much as standard. In a row layout, values from one column are interleaved with everything else in the row:

row layout:     [id=1, name="Alice", age=30] [id=2, name="Bob", age=25] [id=3, name="Carol", age=35]
columnar:       id:   [1, 2, 3]
                name: ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
                age:  [30, 25, 35]

With columns stored contiguously, a 64-byte cache line holds eight useful int64 values instead of one row's mixed fields, and SIMD instructions can process a run of values at once.

The database literature had already shown what this buys: the MonetDB/X100 work (CIDR 2005) argued that pushing batches of around a thousand column values through each operator, instead of one row at a time, is an order of magnitude or two faster. Arrow's batch-oriented design was built around exactly that model.

The rest of this post is the story of Spark adopting it, one door at a time.

Boundary one: the driver (2018)

The first door was the smallest. DataFrame.toPandas() collected results to the driver by pickling every row and rebuilding each one as Python objects before pandas could wrap them, and it was notoriously slow. McKinney's ticket, filed on February 28, 2016, three weeks after the first commit to the Arrow repository, asked to replace that path. It stayed open for over a year. Bryan Cutler, at IBM's Spark Technology Center, resolved it on June 23, 2017, and it reached users in Spark 2.3.0 in February 2018.

Two years, for one method.


# Spark 2.3 name, later renamed; on by default since Spark 4.2
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")

The reverse direction, createDataFrame(pandas_df), got the same treatment (SPARK-20791). What made this matter wasn't the one method; it was the plumbing Cutler built to do it (Arrow converters on the JVM side, pyarrow integration on the Python side), which every later boundary reused.

What it removed: pickle for collecting data to the driver. What it left: everything that happens on executors. UDFs still crossed row by row.

Boundary two: UDFs, in batches (2018)

The second door was the one that mattered for performance, and it came from outside Databricks. The proposal, SPARK-21190 ("SPIP: Vectorized UDFs in Python"), was filed by Reynold Xin, but most of the implementation was done by Li Jin, an engineer at the quantitative investment firm Two Sigma and an Arrow committer, on top of Cutler's serializer. It shipped in the same Spark 2.3.0 release. Instead of calling your function once per row, Spark would send a batch of rows (10,000 by default, spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch) as an Arrow RecordBatch and call your function once per batch, with a pandas Series:

# Before: once per row, pickle both ways
@udf(returnType="double")
def add_tax(price):
    return price * 1.1 if price else None

# After: once per batch, a pandas Series in and out
@pandas_udf("double")
def add_tax(price: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return price * 1.1

Li Jin's post introducing the feature in October 2017 reported speedups from around 3x on simple arithmetic to around 100x on a cumulative-probability function, and the spread is the point: the simpler the function, the more of its cost was the crossing, and the more complex the function, the more it also benefits from running as vectorized NumPy instead of Python bytecode.

My own measurements, eight years and many releases later, land in the same shape. At 50 million rows, a pandas UDF did the arithmetic workload in 0.79 seconds against 5.20 for a pickled UDF, and a normal CDF in 0.82 against 6.18; on a string transform the gap was narrower, 2.51 against 6.22, for a reason that turns out to matter later.

What it removed: per-row serialization and per-row function calls. What it left: a rewrite (your function had to speak pandas), and a conversion. Every batch arrived as Arrow and was turned into pandas before your code saw it, and the result was turned back.

What actually crosses the socket

Before going further it's worth seeing what's moving, because every later boundary sends the same thing. Arrow's IPC stream format is a schema message followed by record-batch messages, each framed like this:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Continuation indicator: 0xFFFFFFFF (4 bytes)                │
│ Metadata length (4 bytes, little-endian int32)              │
│ Flatbuffer metadata (Message type, schema or batch header)  │
│ Padding to 8-byte boundary                                  │
│ Message body (data buffers, padded to 8-byte multiple)      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Inside the body, each column is a set of plain buffers: a validity bitmap with one bit per value, the values themselves as a contiguous typed array, and, for variable-length types like strings, an offsets array into one contiguous UTF-8 buffer. For four rows of (name: string, age: int32):

Validity bitmap (age):  [1, 1, 0, 1]      → 0b1011 (bit-packed)
Data buffer (age):      [30, 25, 0, 35]   → 16 bytes (4 × int32)
Offsets (name):         [0, 5, 8, 13, 18] → 5 × int32
Data buffer (name):     "AliceBobCarolDavid" (contiguous UTF-8)

No per-value type tags, no escaping, no framing between values.

The strings are the detail to hold on to: in Arrow, a million strings are one buffer and an array of offsets. In traditional pandas, they're a million separate Python objects.

Boundary three: letting code see Arrow (2022 to 2025)

For four years, every batch API in PySpark handed you pandas, whether you wanted pandas or not.

The first API that let user code see Arrow directly was mapInArrow, added by Hyukjin Kwon, a long-time PySpark maintainer at Databricks (SPARK-37227, with the Python side in SPARK-37228), in Spark 3.3.0 in June 2022. It passes whole partitions as an iterator of pyarrow.RecordBatch objects, and your function yields RecordBatches back:

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

def add_tax_arrow(batches):
    for batch in batches:
        taxed = pc.multiply(batch.column("price"), pa.scalar(1.1))
        yield pa.RecordBatch.from_arrays([batch.column("id"), taxed],
                                         names=["id", "price_with_tax"])

df.mapInArrow(add_tax_arrow, schema="id long, price_with_tax double")

Grouped operations were the obvious remaining gap, and Enrico Minack closed it with applyInArrow (SPARK-40559), which shipped in Spark 4.0.0 in May 2025. Where applyInPandas turns each group into a pandas DataFrame, applyInArrow hands you the group as a pyarrow.Table:

def normalize(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    totals = table.column("total")
    mean, std = pc.mean(totals).as_py(), pc.stddev(totals).as_py()
    normalized = (pa.array([0.0] * len(totals)) if not std
                  else pc.divide(pc.subtract(totals, pa.scalar(mean)), pa.scalar(std)))
    return pa.Table.from_arrays([table.column("order_id"), totals, normalized],
                                names=["order_id", "total", "normalized"])

orders.groupBy("location_id").applyInArrow(
    normalize, schema="order_id long, total double, normalized double")

The same idea reached the other direction in 4.0 too: the new Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076) lets a custom source written in Python yield pyarrow.RecordBatch objects instead of tuples (SPARK-48493), so data read by Python code can enter Spark as Arrow instead of being built up one Python tuple at a time.

I haven't benchmarked the grouped or data-source paths myself, so I'll leave numbers out of this section; the mechanism is the same as everywhere else, and the benefit should be largest where the pandas conversion is most expensive, which is strings.

What it removed: the forced detour through pandas, for anyone willing to write Arrow code. What it left: that condition. Most PySpark code is plain @udf functions that nobody is going to rewrite.

Boundary four: the network (2023)

Spark Connect started as a proposal from Martin Grund at Databricks in June 2022 (SPARK-39375): separate the client from the server, so an application talks to Spark over gRPC instead of living inside the driver's JVM. Once there's a network between you and the engine, the format results travel in stops being an optimization and becomes the protocol.

The answer was Arrow.

The client sends unresolved logical plans as Protocol Buffers; the server optimizes and runs them and streams the results back as Arrow record batches over the same channel. That's what makes a JVM-free Python client possible at all: the pyspark-client package is a 1.6 MB wheel of pure Python. The same columnar format that moves data between executors and Python workers now moves data between a remote cluster and a laptop.

Boundary five: the UDFs nobody rewrote (2023 to 2026)

Every boundary so far helped people who changed their code. Arrow-optimized Python UDFs (SPARK-40307, Spark 3.5.0, September 2023) took the opposite approach: keep your plain @udf exactly as written, and swap the transport underneath it. Batches cross as Arrow; Python unpacks each batch and still calls your function once per value.

Xinrong Meng's 2023 Databricks post measured about 1.6x over pickle for a single UDF and 1.9x for three chained ones on a 32 GB dataset, and my benchmark agrees in spirit: useArrow=True took the arithmetic workload from 5.20 to 2.23 seconds and the CDF from 6.18 to 2.94. Real, and cheap to get, but nothing like the pandas UDF numbers, because the per-row function call is still there.

That call is my benchmark's ceiling.

Turning this on by default took two tries. It was merged for Spark 4.0 (SPARK-48516) and reverted in March 2025 before the release; it finally shipped as the default in Spark 4.2, along with Arrow for toPandas() and for Python UDTFs, and a minimum PyArrow of 18.0. On 4.2, then, every existing @udf gets Arrow transport without anyone touching it.

It's also where I made the mistake that best illustrates how confusing this boundary is. My benchmark's "Arrow" variant of the plain UDF flipped spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled, which governs toPandas() and createDataFrame() and has nothing to do with UDFs. The setting that actually moves a UDF onto Arrow is spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled, or useArrow=True on the decorator. So my "Arrow" row was the pickled UDF measured twice, and its near-identical result was an accidental A/A test.

Three settings are named for Arrow, and they control three different boundaries.

What it removed: pickle, for everyone, with no code changes. What it left: the function call per row, which is the part no transport format can fix.

Boundary six: Arrow as the execution format (2025)

The last step turned Arrow from the way data travels into the way your code computes. Ruifeng Zheng's SPARK-53014, "Make Arrow UDF public," shipped in Spark 4.1.0 on December 16, 2025, almost ten years after McKinney's ticket. An Arrow UDF receives pyarrow.Array values and returns one, and it's meant to be written with pyarrow.compute, whose functions are C++ kernels operating directly on Arrow buffers:

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import arrow_udf

@arrow_udf("double")
def add_tax(price: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.multiply(price, pa.scalar(1.1))

@arrow_udf("string")
def clean_email(email: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.utf8_trim(pc.utf8_lower(email))

Line the UDF types up by what happens to the data and the progression is plain:

UDF type Data path Format conversions
Pickle @udf JVM → pickle → Python value → pickle → JVM pickle both ways, per row
Arrow-optimized @udf JVM → Arrow → Python value → Arrow → JVM Arrow ↔ Python objects, per row
@pandas_udf JVM → Arrow → pandas → Arrow → JVM Arrow ↔ pandas, per batch
@arrow_udf JVM → Arrow → your function → Arrow → JVM none on the Python side

In my benchmark, @arrow_udf was the fastest Python option everywhere, but the margin over pandas UDFs depended almost entirely on the data type. On arithmetic and the CDF it was only 5 to 9% faster; on the string transform it was 1.6x faster at both 50M and 100M rows (1.55 seconds against 2.51 at 50M).

That's the strings detail from the socket section paying off. A numeric pandas Series is a NumPy array underneath, so converting from Arrow is cheap; a string column in traditional pandas is an array of Python objects, so converting means building millions of them. pyarrow.compute skips all of that and works on the one contiguous buffer.

What it removed: the last conversion on the Python side. What it left: Spark's side.

Taken together, the choice today comes down to what your function can receive:

The pipe itself

Everything above changes what goes through the socket. Hyukjin Kwon's SPARK-51688, shipped in Spark 4.1.0, changes the socket: instead of TCP over loopback, which runs every byte through the full TCP/IP stack even though it never leaves the machine, the JVM and Python workers can talk over a Unix domain socket, which goes straight through a kernel buffer.

It's opt-in (spark.python.unix.domain.socket.enabled, whose default comes from the PYSPARK_UDS_MODE environment variable) in 4.1 and 4.2, and that's unchanged on the 4.3 branch, which instead adds another transport option: pipelined, asynchronous transfer of UDF batches between the JVM and Python (spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled, off by default).

Spark 1.x:  pickle format  + TCP loopback        slow format over a slow pipe
Spark 2.3:  Arrow format   + TCP loopback        fast format over a slow pipe
Spark 4.1:  Arrow format   + Unix domain socket  fast format over a faster pipe (opt-in)

One boundary at a time

As of Spark 4.2, Arrow is the format at every place data crosses between the JVM and Python:

Boundary Arrow's role Default
toPandas() / createDataFrame() replaces pickle for driver data collection yes, since 4.2
@udf (plain Python UDFs) replaces pickle transport yes, since 4.2
@pandas_udf, mapInPandas, applyInPandas batch transport, converted to pandas always
@arrow_udf, mapInArrow, applyInArrow transport and execution format always
Spark Connect results the result protocol always
Python Data Source API source data format when the source yields RecordBatches

The last boundary

What's left is on Spark's side of the wall. Inside the JVM, Spark still executes on its own row format (UnsafeRow, from the Tungsten project), and Arrow exists at the edges, so every crossing still begins and ends with a conversion between Spark's rows and Arrow's columns. Engines like Velox and DataFusion show that a query engine can execute on Arrow-format data directly; Spark doesn't, and closing that gap is a much bigger change than any of the boundaries above.

The 4.3 branch, which hasn't been released yet (its first release candidate failed its vote on September 6, and there's no new date), has two small signs of movement at exactly this edge. One is an Arrow format for Spark's in-memory cache (ArrowCachedBatchSerializer, SPARK-57268), part of a proposal to make Spark better on a single machine: the first time Arrow shows up as a storage format inside Spark itself rather than at a door.

The other goes around the boundary instead of through it: experimental transpilation of Python UDFs into Spark expressions (SPIP SPARK-54783), so a simple enough Python function never has to cross into Python at all. It's off by default, classic-mode only, and requires ANSI mode, but it's the one approach that could get under my benchmark's ceiling, because it removes the per-row Python call rather than making the trip to it cheaper.

The pandas side is moving too, more slowly than you'd expect. pandas 3.0, released in January 2026, made a PyArrow-backed string type the default, which should shrink exactly the string-conversion cost that separates pandas UDFs from Arrow UDFs. But PySpark doesn't support pandas 3 yet, not even on the 4.3 branch: it still pins pandas below 3.0, and the umbrella ticket for supporting it (SPARK-55139) is open.

When Wes McKinney filed SPARK-13534 in 2016, he was asking for one method to stop pickling. Ten years later, every door he could have named uses Arrow, the defaults finally say so, and the conversion that remains is the one Spark performs on itself, between its own rows and everything outside it.

That's the last boundary, and it was never a Python problem.

title: Most PySpark Tuning Advice Starts in the Wrong Place
description:
When I benchmarked PySpark's UDF types earlier this year, I ran the same three workloads (trivial arithmetic, a string transform, a normal CDF) at five scales, from 100 thousand rows to 100 million. At 100 million rows, the default row-at-a-time Python UDF took about 10 seconds for arithmetic that a built-in function finished in under a fifth of a second. At 100 thousand rows, the same UDF was the fastest Python option I tested.

Both results are true, and between them they're most of what you need to know about PySpark performance: the cost is almost never in your function. It's in how many times, and in what shape, your data crosses from the JVM into Python, and whether that crossing is large enough to matter at all.

My argument is that there is really one PySpark performance technique, applied at different places: cross the JVM/Python boundary less often, move less across it, or stop paying for a JVM where you don't need one. The changes worth making are ordered by how much of that crossing they remove, and the biggest one, not crossing at all, is also the most often skipped.

The history of how Arrow came to carry that crossing is in Arrow in PySpark, 2016 to 2026, and the full benchmark is in Stop Blaming Serialization for Slow Python UDFs. This post is the practical version: what to change, in what order, and what each change actually removes.

Where the time goes

PySpark is a Python client for a JVM engine. DataFrame operations build a plan in Python (through Py4J, which only ever carries control messages, never bulk data) and the JVM executes it; df.filter(col("x") > 5).groupBy("y").count() never puts a row into Python, which is why it runs at the same speed as Scala. The data only leaves the JVM when your own code needs it:

Everything outside arrows ① and ② happens at native speed. Every change below makes those two arrows smaller, rarer, or unnecessary, and I've ordered them by how much they took off the arrows in what I measured, or, where I haven't measured, by what they remove.

Don't cross at all: built-ins and SQL UDFs

The largest win isn't a better UDF; it's no UDF. Built-in functions run inside the JVM as Catalyst expressions, fused by whole-stage code generation into tight loops, and never serialize anything.

What surprised me more is that SQL UDFs get the same treatment. Spark 4.0 added SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057), and their bodies are inlined into the logical plan, so the optimizer can see straight through them:

CREATE FUNCTION classify(score INT) RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
    WHEN score > 90 THEN 'excellent'
    WHEN score > 70 THEN 'good'
    ELSE 'needs_improvement'
END;

In my benchmark (median wall-clock time, 50M rows, Spark 4.1.0 through Spark Connect on one machine), the SQL UDF was indistinguishable from the built-ins, and every Python option cost several times more:

arithmetic string normal CDF
built-in functions 0.107 s 0.486 s 0.176 s
SQL UDF 0.095 s 0.477 s n/a
fastest Python UDF (@arrow_udf) 0.725 s 1.545 s 0.762 s
default Python UDF (@udf, pickle) 5.199 s 6.216 s 6.183 s

So the first question for any UDF is whether it needs to be Python. Plenty of "we need a UDF" logic is a CASE expression, a string function, or a date calculation that already exists in pyspark.sql.functions. Python earns its place when you need a library (scikit-learn, a parser, a C extension) or logic that genuinely can't be expressed in SQL. Everything after this point is about paying less for that choice.

Cross once per batch, not once per row

If it has to be Python, the next biggest lever is how often Spark calls your function. A regular @udf is called once per row; @pandas_udf and @arrow_udf are called once per batch of rows. That difference showed up as a hard ceiling in my runs: every row-at-a-time UDF, whatever it computed, topped out at roughly 8 to 10 million rows per second, which is roughly the rate at which CPython can be entered and exited. The batched UDFs weren't bound by it.

50M rows arithmetic string normal CDF
@udf (pickle, per row) 5.199 s 6.216 s 6.183 s
@udf(useArrow=True) (Arrow transport, still per row) 2.228 s 4.430 s 2.942 s
@pandas_udf (per batch, pandas.Series) 0.789 s 2.512 s 0.819 s
@arrow_udf (per batch, pyarrow.Array) 0.725 s 1.545 s 0.762 s

Two things in that table decide what to change. Moving a per-row UDF onto Arrow transport helps, 1.4x to 2.4x here, and on Spark 4.2 you get it for free: 4.2 finally flipped spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled (and its UDTF counterpart) to true by default, after the same change was merged for 4.0 and reverted before release (SPARK-48516).

But rewriting to a batched UDF is worth several times more again, because it removes the per-row call rather than making the trip to it cheaper.

Between the two batched options, the choice mostly comes down to strings: @arrow_udf was only 5 to 9% faster than @pandas_udf on numeric work, but about 1.6x faster on the string transform, because pandas has traditionally stored strings as individual Python objects while Arrow keeps them in one contiguous buffer.

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import arrow_udf

@arrow_udf("string")
def add_suffix(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.binary_join_element_wise(pc.utf8_upper(x), pa.scalar("_SUFFIX"), "")

One warning, because I learned it the expensive way: spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled is not the UDF setting. It governs toPandas() and createDataFrame(), and it's the one my benchmark originally toggled for its "Arrow" case, which is why I once reported that Arrow transport changes nothing for UDFs. It was the same pickled UDF, measured twice. (On 4.2 that setting is also on by default, so the confusion matters less for new code than for anyone reading old tuning advice.)

And the scale caveat from the opening is real. At small sizes, fixed costs dominate, and the ordering can flip:

arithmetic, median seconds built-in @pandas_udf @udf(useArrow=True) @udf (pickle)
100K rows 0.073 0.181 0.212 0.161
10M rows 0.074 0.299 0.568 1.092
100M rows 0.147 1.400 4.188 10.139

If your job touches a few hundred thousand rows, rewriting its UDFs is unlikely to be what makes it faster.

Don't produce the data: Python data sources with pushdown

After calling Python less, the next thing to remove is data that never needed to exist. Built-in sources like Parquet already push filters down and skip row groups that can't match; for most of Spark's history, custom sources that could do the same had to be written in Java or Scala. Spark 4.0 added the Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), and Spark 4.1 added filter pushdown for it (SPARK-51271), so a source written in Python can now turn WHERE status = 'active' into a query parameter, a database predicate, or a skipped file block, and never send the rest.

When I went back over my own notes on this feature to write this post, the example I'd written was wrong, and checking it against Spark's source turned up something I hadn't known: pushdown for Python sources is off by default. It's governed by spark.sql.python.filterPushdown.enabled, an internal setting added in 4.1 whose description says enabling it costs "running Python worker one additional time during planning"; without it, your pushFilters() is never called.

The method also has a less obvious contract than I'd assumed. It returns the filters Spark must still apply after the scan, not the ones you accepted, and each filter's attribute is a column-path tuple:

from pyspark.sql.datasource import DataSourceReader, EqualTo

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.python.filterPushdown.enabled", "true")  # off by default

class ApiReader(DataSourceReader):
    def __init__(self, options):
        self.url = options.get("url")
        self.pushed = []

    def pushFilters(self, filters):
        # Filters arrive ANDed together; yield the ones Spark must still apply.
        for f in filters:
            if isinstance(f, EqualTo) and f.attribute == ("status",):
                self.pushed.append(f)          # handled at the source
            else:
                yield f

    def read(self, partition):
        import requests
        params = {f.attribute[0]: f.value for f in self.pushed}
        for row in requests.get(self.url, params=params).json():
            yield (row["id"], row["name"], row["status"])

Only conjunctions are pushed (a filter like a = 1 or b = 2 arrives as an empty list), and a reader can also yield pyarrow.RecordBatch objects instead of tuples, which the Spark docs say can improve performance by "up to one order of magnitude."

I haven't measured either path, so this is the one change on the list I'm ranking by what it removes rather than by what I saw: for a source backed by an API or a database, rows that are never fetched are the cheapest rows there are.

Skip pandas for grouped work

Per-group logic (normalize within each location, fit a model per customer) has long meant applyInPandas, which converts every group from Arrow into a pandas DataFrame and back. Spark 4.0 added applyInArrow (SPARK-40559), and each group now reaches your function as a pyarrow.Table, in the format it crossed the boundary in:

def normalize(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    totals = table.column("total")
    mean, std = pc.mean(totals).as_py(), pc.stddev(totals).as_py()
    normalized = (pa.array([0.0] * len(totals)) if not std
                  else pc.divide(pc.subtract(totals, mean), std))
    return pa.Table.from_arrays([table.column("order_id"), totals, normalized],
                                names=["order_id", "total", "normalized"])

result = orders.groupBy("location_id").applyInArrow(
    normalize, schema="order_id long, total double, normalized double")

This is the same trade as step 2, one level up: it removes a conversion, not a crossing, so the payoff should track what that conversion cost in my UDF numbers (little for numeric groups, more for string-heavy ones, more for larger groups). I haven't benchmarked the grouped APIs, so I won't put a number on it.

Take the JVM out of the client

Spark Connect is on this list for a different reason than the others. It doesn't make a query faster; it removes the JVM from every client process. Classic PySpark embeds a full Spark driver in each notebook, scheduled job, and CI container. With Connect, the client sends unresolved plans over gRPC and gets Arrow batches back, and the thin pyspark-client package has no JVM and needs no JDK. When I measured it for my own Connect demos on 4.2, the numbers were less dramatic than the pitch:

pyspark (full) pyspark-client
PyPI artifact 429.28 MB 1.60 MB
installed pyspark/ 481 MB 19 MB
Spark JARs on the client 456 MB, 276 files none
virtual env with Connect dependencies 820 MB 359 MB

The last row is the honest one: pyarrow, pandas, and numpy are required dependencies, so the environment shrinks by less than half.

What you actually get is a client with no JVM to start, no JDK to install, and no way for a crashed notebook to take the driver down with it. What you give up is anything that needs the JVM on your side: RDDs, SparkContext, custom accumulators. ML on Connect has been supported since 4.0 and generally available since 4.1, so that's no longer on the list of reasons to stay classic.

Give Python the memory it actually uses

The last change is the one that turns slow jobs into failed ones when it's wrong. Python workers live outside the JVM heap, so the settings most Spark tuning advice is about don't cover them:

The rule is that the container has to fit the heap, the overhead, and the OS, and that Python's share has to come out of the overhead. If you use toPandas() or pandas UDFs, spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.selfDestruct.enabled frees Arrow buffers as they're converted, so the same data doesn't sit in memory twice.

Beyond that, the usual advice still holds: let Adaptive Query Execution size shuffle partitions at runtime (it's been on by default since 3.2, and 4.1 extended it to stateless streaming, SPARK-53941, which can change a streaming query's behaviour after an upgrade), and broadcast small dimension tables instead of shuffling them. None of that is specific to Python, which is why it's last on a list about Python.

What's coming in 4.3

The 4.3 branch hasn't been released (its first release candidate failed its vote on September 6, and there's no new date), but it shows where the boundary is heading, and it confirms the order above.

The most interesting change goes around the boundary instead of through it: experimental transpilation of Python UDFs into Spark expressions (SPIP SPARK-54783, spark.sql.experimental.optimizer.transpilePyUDFs). A simple enough Python function would never cross into Python at all, which is change number 1 done for you. It's off by default, requires ANSI mode, and only works in classic mode, not Connect, but it's the only approach on the branch that could get under the per-row ceiling rather than lowering the cost of hitting it.

Alongside it are smaller changes to the crossing itself: pipelined, asynchronous transfer of UDF batches (spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled, SPARK-56642, off by default) and a cap on bytes per UDF batch (SPARK-57593). A proposal to make Spark better on a single machine also adds an Arrow format for Spark's in-memory cache (SPARK-57268).

Two things haven't moved. PySpark still doesn't support pandas 3, even on the 4.3 branch; it pins pandas below 3.0, and the ticket to support it (SPARK-55139) is open, so the PyArrow-backed string type pandas 3 made the default in January won't help pandas UDFs yet. And Real-Time Mode in 4.3 gains stateful operators, but still can't run Python UDFs (SPARK-57237 is open).

Housekeeping to plan for: 4.2 raised the minimum PyArrow to 18.0.0 and dropped PyPy, and 4.3 drops Python 3.10 (SPARK-56889).

I opened with a UDF that took 10 seconds at 100 million rows and was the fastest Python option at 100 thousand. The reason is the same one behind every change on this list: your function was never the expensive part.

The crossing was, and the best PySpark optimization is still the one that decides the data doesn't need to cross.

title: Stop Blaming Serialization for Slow Python UDFs
description:
The benchmark that tested the wrong Arrow

Earlier this year I built a benchmark to answer a question that comes up constantly: if you need custom Python logic in Spark, which kind of UDF should you write, and what does it cost? It compared seven options across three workloads (trivial arithmetic, a string transform, and a normal CDF) at scales from 100K to 100M rows.

The result my write-up leaned on hardest was a pair of rows that came out almost identical: a plain @udf ran at 48.5x the cost of the equivalent built-in function at 50M rows, and the same @udf "with Arrow turned on" ran at 48.9x (69.2x against 69.0x at 100M). I called it the key insight: switching transport from pickle to Arrow buys nothing when your function still executes one row at a time.

The conclusion about per-row execution is right, but the evidence wasn't what I thought. This is the setting the benchmark toggled:

# What my benchmark flipped for its "@udf + Arrow" case:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
# ...which only governs DataFrame.toPandas() and createDataFrame(pandas_df).
# It never touches Python UDFs.

# What actually moves a regular Python UDF onto Arrow:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled", "true")   # session-wide
@udf(DoubleType(), useArrow=True)                                        # or per UDF
def f(x): ...

The PySpark documentation is explicit that arrow.pyspark.enabled controls pandas conversions. So my two nearly identical rows were the same pickled UDF measured twice, and the gap between them (under 1%) is just how much two runs of the same thing vary.

I had built an A/A test by accident, in a benchmark that existed precisely because Spark's "Arrow" naming is easy to confuse.

That mistake is the best evidence I have for the actual thesis: the cost of a Python UDF is decided far more by what your function receives (a single value, a pandas Series, or an Arrow array) than by whether Arrow carries the bytes, and because "Arrow" names several different mechanisms, it's easy to flip the switch that sounds right and optimize nothing. Here is what each of them actually does:

What you set What it controls Affects your UDF?
spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled toPandas() and createDataFrame(pandas_df) conversions No
@udf(useArrow=True) or spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled Moves a regular UDF to Arrow batches (ArrowEvalPython); your function still gets one scalar per call. On by default since Spark 4.2 Yes, 1.4x to 2.4x
@pandas_udf Arrow batches; your function gets a pandas.Series per call Yes, vectorized
@arrow_udf (Spark 4.1+, SPARK-53014) Arrow batches; your function gets a pyarrow.Array per call Yes, vectorized, no pandas

Three choices hiding behind every decorator

Every Python UDF call makes three independent choices: how data crosses from the JVM to the Python worker (transport), which physical operator Spark plans (BatchEvalPython or ArrowEvalPython), and what your function receives once the data arrives (the execution model). The last one determines how many times Python has to be entered.

UDF type Operator Transport Calls into your Python Receives
@udf (default, pre-4.2) BatchEvalPython pickle once per row scalar
@udf(useArrow=True) ArrowEvalPython Arrow once per row scalar
@pandas_udf ArrowEvalPython Arrow once per batch pandas.Series
@arrow_udf ArrowEvalPython Arrow once per batch pyarrow.Array

This is the exact code the benchmark ran for the arithmetic workload (x * 2 + 1):

@udf(DoubleType())                    # once per row, pickle
def py_arith(x):
    return float(x) * 2 + 1 if x is not None else None

@udf(DoubleType(), useArrow=True)     # once per row, Arrow batches
def use_arrow_arith(x):
    return float(x) * 2 + 1 if x is not None else None

@pandas_udf(DoubleType())             # once per batch, pandas.Series
def pandas_arith(x):
    return x * 2 + 1

@arrow_udf(DoubleType())              # once per batch, pyarrow.Array
def arrow_arith(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.add(pc.multiply(x, 2), 1)

And for the string workload (upper(x) + '_SUFFIX'), where the two vectorized options separate:

@pandas_udf(StringType())
def pandas_string(x):
    return x.str.upper() + "_SUFFIX"

@arrow_udf(StringType())
def arrow_string(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    upper = pc.utf8_upper(x)
    suffix = pa.array(["_SUFFIX"] * len(upper), type=pa.string())   # see note below
    return pc.binary_join_element_wise(upper, suffix, "")

What the measurements show

Median wall-clock seconds at 50M rows, with the multiple of the built-in time in parentheses (the mislabeled "Arrow config" row is omitted, since it was a second run of the default @udf):

arithmetic string normal CDF
built-in functions 0.107 0.486 0.176
SQL UDF 0.095 (0.9x) 0.477 (1.0x) n/a
@arrow_udf 0.725 (6.8x) 1.545 (3.2x) 0.762 (4.3x)
@pandas_udf 0.789 (7.4x) 2.512 (5.2x) 0.819 (4.7x)
@udf(useArrow=True) 2.228 (20.8x) 4.430 (9.1x) 2.942 (16.7x)
@udf (default, pickle) 5.199 (48.5x) 6.216 (12.8x) 6.183 (35.1x)

And at 100M rows:

arithmetic string normal CDF
built-in functions 0.147 0.910 0.267
@arrow_udf 1.332 2.904 1.333
@pandas_udf 1.400 4.743 1.449
@udf(useArrow=True) 4.188 8.735 5.658
@udf (default, pickle) 10.139 12.212 12.060

Three things stand out, and each one follows from the execution model rather than the transport.

Arrow batching helps a row-at-a-time UDF, but only about 2x. useArrow=True took arithmetic from 5.20s to 2.23s and the CDF from 6.18s to 2.94s, because ArrowEvalPython moves data in efficient batches instead of pickling rows. It still calls your function once per value, though, and that per-call cost is a hard ceiling: across every workload and scale, the row-at-a-time UDFs topped out at roughly 8 to 10 million rows per second (50M rows in 5.2s; 100M in 10.1s), which is about the rate at which CPython can be entered and exited no matter what's computed inside.

The vectorized UDFs cross into Python once per batch instead, and they were about 3x faster again than useArrow=True on arithmetic.

Between the vectorized options, the gap is almost entirely strings.

@arrow_udf speedup over @pandas_udf arithmetic string CDF
50M rows 1.09x 1.63x 1.07x
100M rows 1.05x 1.63x 1.09x

That split is what you'd expect from how the two libraries lay out data. A numeric pandas Series is a NumPy array underneath, so converting from Arrow is cheap and the arithmetic is the same vectorized arithmetic either way. Strings are different; pandas has traditionally stored them as an array of Python objects, each its own heap allocation, while Arrow keeps them in one contiguous buffer plus an array of offsets. Converting to pandas means building millions of Python objects, and every operation afterwards walks memory scattered across the heap.

If anything the benchmark understates the gap, because my @arrow_udf string function builds a Python list of suffixes the length of every batch before joining them, which is exactly the per-element Python work pyarrow.compute exists to avoid. The CDF case is close for the opposite reason: pyarrow.compute has no erf, so my "Arrow" CDF converts to NumPy and calls SciPy, just like the pandas version does.

Scale changes which choice matters. Arithmetic workload, median seconds (the @arrow_udf column is blank below 50M because it wasn't a separate case in those earlier runs):

rows built-in @arrow_udf @pandas_udf useArrow=True @udf (pickle)
100K 0.073 0.181 0.212 0.161
1M 0.077 0.200 0.248 0.258
10M 0.074 0.299 0.568 1.092
50M 0.107 0.725 0.789 2.228 5.199
100M 0.147 1.332 1.400 4.188 10.139

At 100K rows every Python UDF was within 2x to 6x of the built-ins, and the plain pickled @udf was actually the fastest Python option on arithmetic, because fixed costs (starting Python workers, setting up batches) dominate everything at that size. The tiers only separate cleanly somewhere around 10M rows.

If your job processes a few hundred thousand rows, UDF type is unlikely to be what's making it slow.

Why I'd trust the seconds over the multipliers

There's a second correction to my own write-up, and it applies to almost any benchmark reported as "Nx slower." My report said row-at-a-time UDFs showed superlinear growth, from 48.5x at 50M to 69.2x at 100M. That's true of the ratio and false of the thing you care about:

default @udf, arithmetic 50M 100M growth for 2x rows
@udf absolute time 5.199s 10.139s 1.95x (linear)
built-in absolute time 0.107s 0.147s 1.37x
ratio 48.5x 69.2x "superlinear"

The ratio grew because its denominator grew slowly; the built-in at this scale is mostly fixed overhead.

The baseline has another problem I can't fully explain away. SQL UDFs, which compile to the same plan as built-ins, came out slightly faster than them at every scale (0.64x to 0.98x). The likeliest cause is ordering: the built-in case always ran first in each workload and may have absorbed start-up cost despite the warmup. If so, every multiplier here is somewhat inflated. An earlier set of my own 50M runs, before I raised driver memory, had the built-in at 0.25s and the pickled @udf at about 22x, while the @udf's own time moved only about 10%.

The headline multiplier more than doubled on the strength of the baseline alone.

What has changed, and what I didn't measure

Spark 4.2 turns Arrow optimization on by default for regular Python UDFs, after an attempt to do the same for 4.0 was reverted (SPARK-48516). On 4.2 a plain @udf should therefore behave like my useArrow=True rows, a free 2x for anyone who never touches the setting; I haven't rerun the benchmark on 4.2, so that's an expectation, not a measurement.

I also only benchmarked scalar UDFs. The partition-level APIs mapInPandas and mapInArrow, and the grouped applyInPandas and applyInArrow, follow the same logic about what your function receives (the Arrow variants skip pandas conversion entirely), and they're the right tools when you need to change the number of rows or see a whole partition or group at once. I have no measurements for them, and I'd rather say so than borrow numbers.

The benchmark's own limits:

  • One machine, local[*], via Spark Connect; hardware not recorded.
  • Synthetic, low-cardinality data (spark.range plus two derived columns, short strings), cached in memory before timing.
  • Each case materialized with a count, not written anywhere.
  • One warmup, median of three timed runs, no variance recorded.
  • The 100K to 10M runs predate the 32GB driver setting and the separate @arrow_udf case, so there's no genuine @arrow_udf data below 50M.

None of this changes the ordering, which held everywhere, but the exact multipliers are specific to this setup.

Choosing, based on what was measured

Whichever you choose, check which "Arrow" your setting actually refers to. Mine didn't, and I wrote a benchmark about exactly this.

Further reading

  • SPARK-53014: Arrow UDF public API (@arrow_udf).
  • SPARK-40307: Arrow-optimized Python UDFs (useArrow), Spark 3.5.0.
  • Benchmark code and raw results: spark-udf-benchmark (Spark 4.1.0, Spark Connect, local[*]).

title: Reading a locked Pet Index: verifying 199 Roblox pets without unlocking them
description:
Steal An Egg is a Roblox game where you steal eggs, hatch pets, and the pets earn money every second. How much a pet earns depends on its base income, its weight and its mutations, so players keep asking the same question: what does this pet make?

I built a small calculator site to answer that. The code was the easy part. Most of my time went into a different question: which numbers can I actually trust?

A note on process: AI agents did a lot of the legwork here, reading the in-game index, logging slots, writing the build and the tests, while I set the rules and checked the results. The verification approach is the part I think is worth sharing.

The problem with the numbers I found

When I started, the sources disagreed with each other, and some numbers didn't come from anywhere I could trace:

  • The community wiki keeps pet data in two Lua data modules, and they didn't always agree. One listed Light Dove at $225/s, the other at $225K/s. For 18 pets from limited eggs, the "rarity" field held the egg's group name ("Monster", "Brainrot") instead of an actual rarity.
  • Guides published in August and September listed the Golden mutation as ×2. The wiki said ×2.5.
  • One existing calculator shipped preset pets whose names and incomes don't match any slot in the game's own Pet Index. A pet earning $9/s, for example, would need a slot with a $900 reward, and there isn't one.
  • Nobody had published how multiple mutations stack. One tool simply adds them together, and I couldn't find a source for that either way.

None of this is surprising for a game that updates every few weeks. But a calculator that multiplies an invented input by a correct formula still gives you a confident, wrong number. I wanted every value on the site to say where it came from.

Two sources, one rule

I used two sources:

  1. The Steal An Egg Wiki on Fandom (CC BY-SA). Its data modules give names, rarities, base incomes and base weights for 198 pets, plus 8 names for the newest biome. Every page on the site credits the wiki in the footer.
  2. The game itself. On 2026-10-09 I went through the in-game Pet Index on a fresh account, logged all 184 slots to a CSV (112 in the World tab, 72 in Limited) and kept screenshots.

When they conflict, the order is: in-game reading > official page > wiki > newer third-party source. The CSVs are frozen in the repo, and the build script only ever reads them.

The trick: locked slots still show their reward

On a fresh account the Pet Index is almost all "???". I had unlocked exactly one pet, a Chicken. But every locked slot still shows three things: its rarity, the cash reward for discovering it, and a speed reward.

The Chicken earns $1/s and its slot rewards $100. So the hypothesis was simple: discovery reward = 100 × base income.

If that holds, I don't need to unlock anything. For each slot there should be exactly one wiki pet in the same tab, with the same rarity, whose income × 100 equals the reward. If the rule were wrong, the slots wouldn't line up.

There was one wrinkle. The game abbreviates big numbers to one decimal and truncates instead of rounding, so a $18.5K/s pet shows a reward of "$1.8M", not "$1.9M". The site uses the same formatter as the game (simplified here):

var UNITS = ['', 'K', 'M', 'B', 'T', 'Qa', 'Qi', 'Sx', 'Sp', 'Oc', 'No', 'Dc'];

// In-game abbreviation: one decimal, truncated not rounded ($1.75B -> $1.7B)
function formatCompact(n) {
  if (n < 1000) return String(Math.round(n * 100) / 100);
  var i = 0;
  while (n >= 1000 && i < UNITS.length - 1) { n = n / 1000; i++; }
  var t = Math.floor(n * 10 + 1e-9) / 10;
  return t.toFixed(1).replace(/\.0$/, '') + UNITS[i];
}

The result: outside the newest biome, every slot was claimed by exactly one pet. In the World tab, 102 of 104 slots matched exactly, and the other 2 only differed because of truncation. In the Limited tab, 71 of 72 matched exactly, plus one more truncation case.

The same pass also fixed things:

  • 19 rarities. The 18 limited-egg pets where the wiki used the group name have real rarities in the game (Tung Tung Sahur is Rare, Crawler is Cosmic), and Octophant is Divine, not Eternal.
  • Light Dove and Flame Sprite. The slot reward is $22.5M, so the income is $225K/s, not $225/s.
  • 22 wiki pets have no slot at all: event pets, fusion results and a few others. That fits with them coming from outside the normal eggs, so the site labels them as not in the index instead of guessing.

The limits, honestly:

  • This matches values, not names. The Angels & Demons tab has 8 pairs of pets with identical income, so I can confirm both pets of a pair exist, but not which slot is which.
  • The newest biome has names on the wiki but no incomes, so 7 of its 8 pets can't be matched yet. They're left out of the calculator.

One Golden Chicken settled ×2 vs ×2.5

The index gives base incomes, but mutations needed a live reading. The pet panel doesn't show weight, but the label floating above a pet in your base does. My only pet was a Golden Chicken, and its label said 61 kg, $9/s.

The wiki's size formula (for weight ratios up to 125):

ratio  = weight / baseWeight      // 61 / 8 = 7.625
size   = ratio ^ (37/60)          // ≈ 3.50
income = base × size × mutation
  • With Golden ×2.5: 1 × 3.50 × 2.5 = 8.75. The game pays whole dollars, so it shows $9. Match.
  • With Golden ×2: 1 × 3.50 × 2 = 7.00, which would show $7. No match.

Weight is displayed as a whole number, so I re-ran it for 60.5 to 61.5 kg. Same conclusion. The cash counter agreed too: over about 1,095 seconds my money went up by $9,856, and over another 745 seconds by $6,711. Both work out to $9.00 per second, not $8.75, which is why I think payouts are rounded to whole dollars.

It's one pet at one weight, so I'm careful about what it proves. It rules out ×2 (that would need a base weight around 5 kg instead of 8), and it's consistent with the wiki's formula and the 8 kg base weight. It says nothing about how two mutations stack. I still don't know that, so when you pick more than one, the calculator shows both the added and the multiplied result instead of choosing for you.

That reading is now a pair of unit tests:

test('Golden Chicken: $1/s base, 8 kg base, 61 kg, Golden x2.5 -> 8.75, shown as $9', () => {
  const r = SAE.compute({ base: 1, weight: 61, baseWeight: 8, variant: 2.5, mutations: [], count: 1 });
  near(r.perSec.multiply, 8.75, 0.005, 'per second');
  assert.equal(SAE.gameDisplayPerSec(r.perSec.multiply), '$9');
});

test('Golden x2 would NOT match the in-game $9/s reading', () => {
  const r = SAE.compute({ base: 1, weight: 61, baseWeight: 8, variant: 2, mutations: [], count: 1 });
  assert.equal(SAE.gameDisplayPerSec(r.perSec.multiply), '$7');
});

Another test runs the size formula against three weight and income readings for a different pet that a games site published. All three land within $0.1M.

The build: static HTML, no framework

The site is plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JS. Everything, from the build scripts and browser code to the checks and tests, is about 2,800 lines of JavaScript. No framework, no CDN, and no client-side rendering of the data.

  • data/ holds the frozen CSVs. build/ reads them and writes dist/: the pages, a pets.json for the calculators, the sitemap and robots.txt.
  • Every value table is rendered into the HTML at build time. A small post-processing step adds data-label="<column name>" to every <td>, so on narrow screens CSS can turn each row into a labelled card instead of a table that scrolls sideways.
  • Each pet gets a label from its check status: Verified in-game, Estimated (income derived from the index reward) or Unverified. The label logic lives in the build, and a test makes sure nothing still marked as pending can show up as verified.

Tests and the overflow check

npm test runs 18 node:test cases: the Golden Chicken reading, the size formula on both sides of the 125× breakpoint, the truncating formatter, mutation stacking, input validation (it must never produce NaN), and checks on the built output such as "no external scripts" and "every table cell has a data-label".

npm run check adds two more:

  • An SEO check: title, description, H1, canonical URL, and no dead internal links.
  • A layout check. It starts a clean headless Chrome (fresh profile, no extensions), talks to it over the DevTools Protocol using the WebSocket built into Node 22, so no Puppeteer, and opens all 10 pages at 360, 400 and 768 px. It fails if the page is wider than the viewport and lists the elements sticking out. It also fails on any console error or warning, uncaught exception or failed request.

The measurement itself is tiny:

const w = window.innerWidth;
const sw = Math.max(document.documentElement.scrollWidth, document.body.scrollWidth);
// sw > w means horizontal overflow: report the elements whose right edge is past w

Tables with five or six columns are the usual way a page like this breaks on a phone, so I made overflow a hard failure instead of something to eyeball.

Deploy

Cloudflare Pages runs npm run build and serves dist/. The first build took about two minutes, and the site was live on its own domain about ten minutes after I pushed.

Result

Of the 199 pets with a known base income, 176 match a slot in the in-game Pet Index by rarity and reward. 22 have no slot, and 1 is matched by rarity only and still marked as pending. It's all on Steal An Egg Calculator, where each pet shows whether its numbers were checked in-game or come from the wiki.

What I'd do differently

  • Read the game first. I compared third-party sources against each other before I opened the Pet Index. About 40 minutes in the game settled most of those disagreements.
  • Turn every reading into a test. A screenshot is easy to forget. A failing test isn't.
  • Write down what you can't verify. "Stacking unverified, here are both readings" is more useful than a confident guess.

If you've done something similar for another game, working out the numbers from what the UI gives away, I'd like to hear how you approached it.

title: I built an app to duel your past self in push-ups and pull-ups!
description:
I always quit at the exact same point. Somewhere around rep 15, my brain decides "that’s enough" — and a normal counter just sits there watching.

So I built RivalRep, a web app that counts your push-ups and pull-ups through your phone camera and gives you someone to actually compete against:

Your Ghost: An exact replay of your personal best. Not just a static number, but every rep and pause played back in real time. You literally watch your past self pull ahead.

Bots that learn your weak spots: An adaptive bot studies your past sets and intentionally speeds up right where you usually fade. It’s annoyingly effective.

Live Duels: Send a friend a quick link and go head-to-head in real time. They don’t even need an account to join.

3 Challenge Modes: Classic (most reps in 1 min), Survival (one rep every 5 seconds or you’re out), and Time Trial.

It also includes a training plan that automatically adapts to your feedback and progress!

Quick FAQs:
Is it free? Yes, completely free.

Do I need to download an app? No. It runs directly in your browser (iPhone, Android, or laptop webcam). You can also add it to your home screen like an app.

Privacy / Camera usage? Pose detection runs 100% locally on your device. No video or image data is ever uploaded anywhere.

Do I need an account? No. You can start training immediately. Accounts are only required for saving backups or dueling friends.

It’s a solo project, so it’s definitely not perfect yet!

Thats why i’d love your honest feedback about it!
What didn't worked? What wasn't as clear as it had to be? Were there any bugs or errors you found? Please tell me for improving my app!

Try it here: https://rivalrep.com/

title: Focus Friend: An Executive Assistant Built for My Overwhelmed Friend Rahul
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend

What I Built

For my close friend rahul, opening Slack and email in the morning isn't just routine—it's an obstacle course of cognitive friction. rahul has ADHD, and when a 4-paragraph rambling email or a 15-person chaotic Slack thread lands in their inbox, Task Paralysis sets in. The brain gets overwhelmed trying to separate social fluff and emotional subtext from actual deliverables. The notification gets minimized, and the task gets forgotten.

Existing AI tools (like ChatGPT or Claude) often make this worse: they are conversational, chat-heavy, and require sending sensitive work emails to third-party cloud servers—a major privacy violation for work communications.

Focus Friend is a minimalist, local-first executive function companion built specifically to conquer this problem. It distills chaotic walls of text into three digestible data points in high-contrast Neo-Brutalist cards:

  1. 🔵 THE VIBE (Cyan Card): A one-sentence plain-English emotional temperature reading (e.g., "The boss is pleased with progress and only asks for a routine slide polish"). This immediately disarms rejection sensitivity and anxiety.
  2. 🔴 THE DEADLINE (Coral Card): Isolates the exact calendar date or delivery window from atmospheric fluff.
  3. 🟢 THE ACTION ITEM (Lime Card): A single, imperative-verb bullet point (e.g., "Review slide 7 metrics and reply with confirmation"). 1-click copy into Todoist or Slack so rahul can take action and close the app.

Demo

  • Live Full-Stack App on Render: focus-friend.onrender.com
  • GitHub Repository: github.com/ezabhishek1/Focus-Friend (Anyone can test it instantly in their browser with the embedded Zero-Cloud Heuristic Engine and Overwhelm Presets, or run it locally connected to Microsoft Phi-3 via Ollama).

Code

ezabhishek1 / Focus-Friend

**Focus Friend** is a local executive function assistant that uses open-weight AI to distill "walls of text" (emails, Slack threads) into three digestible data points: **Tone, Timeline, and Task.** By running locally, It ensures total privacy for sensitive work communications and provides a zero-latency experience to prevent focus-drift

⚡ Focus Friend — Local-First Executive Function Assistant

Submission for Hacktoberfest 2026: "Build for a Friend" Challenge
Dedicated to Alex ("The Overwhelmed Professional") and everyone navigating ADHD, neurodivergence, and cognitive overload in modern work environments.

🎨 Aesthetic Neo-Brutalism UI

Focus Friend is built with an unapologetic Neo-Brutalism UI Design System:

  • High-Contrast Geometry: Stark black borders (3px/4px), tactile hard geometric drop shadows (box-shadow: 5px 5px 0px #121212), and zero blur.
  • Visual Clarity for ADHD: Bold color-coding eliminates reading fatigue
    • 🔵 The Vibe (Cyan #38BDF8): Emotional context & tone to disarm rejection sensitivity.
    • 🔴 The Deadline (Coral #FF6B6B): Isolates the true calendar milestone from noise.
    • 🟢 The Action Item (Lime #A3E635): Single imperative bullet point for instant task initiation.
  • Calm Micro-Interactions: Non-startling auditory feedback synthesized entirely in-browser with the Web Audio API (warm major chords, soft click, pop) and focus-friendly breathing progress…
View on GitHub

Stack & Architecture Highlights:

  • FastAPI & Uvicorn (REST API v1): Scalable Python backend with versioned endpoints (/api/v1/extract, /api/v1/health, /api/v1/models, /api/v1/presets), threadpool concurrency, and global exception handlers.
  • Local Inference via Ollama & Microsoft Phi-3: Runs open-weight phi3:mini (2.3GB) strictly over localhost:11434 with zero cloud telemetry.
  • Dual-Layer Zero-Cloud Heuristic Engine: Deterministic regex and sentiment rules in both Python and client-side JavaScript, ensuring 100% functionality even when offline.
  • Aesthetic Neo-Brutalism UI: High-contrast 4px borders, hard drop shadows, ADHD color coding, and calm Web Audio API sound synthesis (no audio files downloaded).
  • Centralized Reactive State Store: Observable pub/sub architecture with selector-based subscriptions and dedicated action dispatchers.

How I Built It

Focus Friend was engineered around local-first open weights, deterministic safety fallbacks, and sensory-friendly UX:

▼ [ExtractionService (FastAPI)] ├─► Tier 1: Local Ollama Daemon (Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct) via localhost:11434 └─► Tier 2: Zero-Cloud Heuristic NLP Engine (Deterministic Regex & Sentiment) │ ▼ [Structured 3-Card Distillation: The Vibe · The Deadline · The Action Item]

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open-weight models and open innovation matter profoundly for applications that interact with the physical world:

  1. Uncompromised Privacy for Living Spaces: Urban exploration starts right from where you live—your apartment block, dorm, or neighborhood street. Proprietary closed APIs demand that you pipe your daily geographic context, walking routines, and photos to third-party corporate servers. With open-weight models, 0 bytes of personal habit data leave your device.
  2. Offline Resilience on Trails & Alleys: Real-world walks often take you into city parks, subway underpasses, or trail segments with poor cellular coverage. Closed API apps immediately fail when connection drops; open models running locally continue functioning in airplane mode.
  3. No Metered Billing Anxiety: Overcoming burnout shouldn't come with token quotas or surprise API bills. Open models empower builders to deliver free, resilient community utilities that anyone can run forever.

My Agent Session

This project was pair-programmed with Google DeepMind's Antigravity agentic coding harness, using the DevRelay gateway and official Agent Skills to inspect guidelines, establish the Neo-Brutalist design system, and manage deployment workflows.

Prize Categories

  • Overall Open-Source AI Challenge
  • Best Use of Render: Deployed on Render using a native Blueprint (render.yaml) as a Node.js web service running the Next.js App Router and dynamic server-side AI routes.
  • Best Use of Gemma: Utilizes Google's open-weight gemma:2b / gemma2:2b via Ollama for lightweight, low-footprint quest distillation.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: Used throughout the component modularization and test suite implementation.

Team Submissions: Built by @ezabhishek1.

title: Invalidating a Code Snapshot Cache on the Thing That Should Invalidate It
description:
A fintech ops lead in London pastes the same incident report into the diagnosis tool twice, three days apart. Same file, same line, same confidence score, same proposed fix — except the schema changed on Tuesday and the fix is now wrong. Nobody lied to the system. The system did exactly what it was built to do. That is the uncomfortable part.

Corporate AI 365 caches its root-cause analysis against a hash of three things: the issue text, a snapshot of the code, and the model version. Same hash, same answer, every time — that is what makes an approval gate defensible instead of a coin flip. But a cache is only as honest as the thing that is supposed to invalidate it, and in a system that never connects to a live database, one of those invalidators is a file someone has to remember to re-export.

The cache key is smaller than it feels

When an engineer in Berlin imagines the input to a diagnosis, they picture the whole repository and the whole database. The cache key doesn't see either. It sees the source tree as committed, and a scripted schema export — a dump of tables, columns, constraints, and views that your own developer generates and checks in or uploads. No connection string, no query against production, ever. That's the non-negotiable we design around.

The consequence is that the hash is a function of two artifacts that move at different speeds. Code changes on every push; the diagnosis engine sees that immediately because it reads the repository directly through your GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps connector. The schema export changes only when someone runs the export again. If a migration adds a column in staging and the team forgets to regenerate the scripted schema, the code snapshot looks fresh, the hash looks fresh, and the cached diagnosis is served with full confidence — pointing at a column that no longer means what the analysis thinks it means.

This is not a bug in the caching strategy. It is the honest cost of refusing to hold a live connection. We could make the schema "always fresh" by letting the AI query production directly — and we have deliberately not built that, because the moment an AI reasoning engine can read live rows, your security review stops being a conversation and becomes a liability audit. So the trade-off stands: reproducibility and a clean trust boundary, in exchange for a manual step that has to be someone's job.

Why the manual step is the real risk in a lean team

That trade-off is tolerable when there's a senior engineer who owns schema hygiene as a matter of habit. It is a real exposure when there isn't one. Across European SMEs and mid-market firms right now, a large share of teams — on the order of six in ten by some recent industry surveys — report they simply cannot find qualified developers to fill open roles. A Dublin logistics company or an Amsterdam retailer running production support with three generalists instead of a platform team isn't being negligent when the schema export goes stale for two sprints. There's no spare capacity to own that discipline full-time.

That matters because the cost of a wrong diagnosis is not symmetric. Enterprise downtime has been estimated by industry research at a median in the region of US$9,000 per minute for large organisations — and a diagnosis that confidently points at the wrong column doesn't just fail to fix the incident, it burns the first twenty minutes of the incident on the wrong hypothesis. In a lean team without a senior engineer to sanity-check the AI's output on sight, that twenty minutes is the whole difference between a contained incident and an escalated one.

What we actually invalidate on, and what we deliberately don't

Given that, the design answer isn't to pretend the schema is always current. It's to make staleness visible instead of silent:

  • The cache entry records the export timestamp alongside the hash, so a diagnosis can be shown next to "schema last scripted: 11 days ago" rather than presented as uniformly fresh.
  • Any manual schema re-export forces a new hash and a new diagnosis run — it is treated exactly like a code change, not a side artifact.
  • Where the AI needs to confirm a live fact — row counts, actual values, current index usage — it writes a read-only query for a developer to run by hand. The result comes back to a human, not to our cache, which keeps the live-data boundary intact even when the stakes are high.
  • We deliberately don't hash at the whole-repository level for large monorepos; the key is scoped to the files and schema objects actually implicated, so an unrelated commit elsewhere in the codebase doesn't force a re-diagnosis that produces nothing new — and, just as importantly, a relevant change doesn't get buried in repository-wide noise.

None of this makes the schema export automatic. It can't be, without the live connection we won't build. What it does is turn "the diagnosis was wrong" into "the diagnosis was wrong and here is exactly which input was stale and when it was last updated" — which is the difference between a system you can audit and one you have to take on faith. For a team in London, Berlin, Amsterdam, or Dublin running production support without a bench of senior engineers, that audit trail is the thing that lets a junior developer trust the output enough to act on it, and lets a manager explain the decision afterward without hand-waving.
