title: We installed 12,915 MCP servers and started each one. 41% never answered.
description:
MCP registries list tens of thousands of servers. Most of what is written about their safety comes from reading them: the tool descriptions, the README, the code. We wanted the other half. What happens when you actually install one and start it, the way a client does? Does it answer? What does it ask for? What does it touch while it starts?

So HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, now installs the npm and PyPI servers it finds, starts each one in a sandbox and writes down what happened. The registries it follows list 47,586 npm and PyPI packages; it runs up to 8,000 per crawl. This post is the state on 13 October 2026, after 12,915 of them.

How we ran them

  • The latest version, installed fresh. npm with --ignore-scripts (install scripts then run on their own, traced); PyPI wheels only, nothing built from source.
  • gVisor (runsc), an unprivileged user, a read-only root, 512 MB and one CPU. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer.
  • No route out. Every DNS name resolves to our traps, which record what reaches them and forward nothing.
  • Decoys. ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, ~/.netrc, shell history and a few more in HOME, a decoy .env in the working directory.
  • The observer speaks MCP: initialize, tools/list, then up to 15 tools called once each with canary arguments. gVisor writes its own syscall trace, outside the sandbox, so a package cannot hide what it opened, started or dialled.
  • What it asks for, as placeholders. A server that exits with MYTOOL_API_KEY is not set or a usage text naming serve is started again with MYTOOL_API_KEY=histor-envkey-<run> or serve. The names only ever come from the package's own error text or its registry entry. The values are ours and work nowhere.

59% answered

7,656 of 12,915 answered initialize and tools/list: 64% on npm, 52% on PyPI. Between them they listed 182,157 tool definitions, a median of 10 per server (one listed 3,631).

1,239 of those started only with something they asked for: 1,039 with a placeholder key, 177 with a start argument, 23 with both. A client config would have given them that, so we count them as working. But look at the 1,039 again. A key that works nowhere was enough for every one of them to tell us its tools. None needed a real key to do that; they just refused to start without one.

Why 5,259 never answered

We read what each package printed as it exited, last run first.

  • Almost half, 2,476, are broken as published. 874 crash with an error of their own. 636 will not install: no wheel for some dependency, conflicting pins, the wrong platform. 490 hang, stay silent or speak something that is not MCP. 292 were written for MCP SDK 1.x (next section). 184 miss one of their own files, ship TypeScript that Node will not load from node_modules, or import a dependency they never declared.
  • 793 ask for a key or a setting and stop, even with a placeholder. The usual reason: they check the key's format at startup (must start with sk_) or call their API before answering anything, and our trap is not their API.
  • 924 print a usage text. Some want a start argument we pass next time (serve, mcp, --stdio). Many are command-line tools that mention MCP somewhere. With the 666 that declare no command at all, or exit 0 having done something else, up to one package in eight listed as an MCP server is not a stdio MCP server when installed the way its listing says.
  • 164 start an HTTP server instead of answering on stdin. Their next run gets --transport=stdio.
  • 236 need something the machine does not have: another program (git, Java, Bun, a desktop app), the internet at startup, or another operating system.

MCP SDK 2.0 broke 292 PyPI servers

mcp 2.0.0 (28 July 2026) renamed FastMCP and changed the low-level server's decorators. A PyPI server that depends on mcp with no upper bound installs 2.x today and dies on import: cannot import name 'FastMCP', or 'Server' object has no attribute 'list_tools'. We started 269 of them again with pip held to mcp<2, and 207 (77%) answered. Anyone who installs them today gets the crash, not the server.

What they did in the sandbox

11,891 runs carry a gVisor trace.

  • 2,239 npm packages ran install scripts, about 30% of the npm packages we ran. 580 of them tried to reach the network while installing, mostly to fetch a prebuilt binary (prebuild-install, node-gyp's headers, esbuild). Here that fails. On your machine it runs with your credentials in reach.
  • 1,484 reached for the network at startup, before any tool was called. The names they asked for most: pypi.org (613), github.com (478), nodejs.org (245), registry.npmjs.org (243). Mostly version checks and downloads.
  • 295 opened a decoy credential file (not counting .env). Before anyone panics: Python's requests reads ~/.netrc before every HTTP request (141), npm and npx read ~/.npmrc (103), boto3's credential chain reads ~/.aws (39). Each of the other 17 (~/.kube, ~/.docker, ~/.ssh, shell history, gh's config) was opened by a server whose job is Kubernetes, Docker, SSH or "ops context". Opening a credential file is evidence, not a verdict. What matters is whether it fits the server's purpose and where the bytes go next.
  • 73 runs sent the placeholder key over the network. Most went to an identity provider (Microsoft's login 17 times, Google OAuth 7) or to the vendor's own API. Each package's page shows where.
  • Decoy content left three packages, each time when a tool forwarded the canary arguments we called it with to its own API, which is what tools do. A fourth record said a package had mailed decoy data to an extra recipient at startup. That one was ours; see the last item below.

Testing the tester

A sandbox that reports wrong things is worse than none, so here is what we got wrong on the way.

  • 880 servers looked silent. They had printed their help to stdout, and we kept only stderr. Now we keep both and the exit code; 179 are really silent.
  • About 400 "install failed" because they require Python 3.13 or 3.14 and our image had 3.12. pip then says from versions: none, which reads like a missing package. The sandbox now picks the image from Requires-Python.
  • 1,917 Python servers were flagged as "reached out at startup". asyncio's event loop writes a byte to its own socketpair; our trace reader saw a send with no destination and listed it as network. gVisor does not print the file descriptors socketpair returns, so the rule is now: a send that names no destination, on a socket that socket() did not make and no connect() reached, after a socketpair, stays in the process. All of them have since been traced again, including servers that fail to start, whose pages kept the old reading until we noticed they were never re-read.
  • 126 "persistence" writes were relative paths the old reader could not resolve, such as node-gyp's buildcheck.gypi. gVisor prints the directory next to each openat; we were not reading it.
  • One missed case, found by our red team (MOMUS). After we moved to Debian images, one of its 72 behaviour cases went unseen under load: glibc's resolver gave up on a late DNS answer, the package never connected, and the run still said "complete". The resolver now waits longer, and a DNS query our logger never saw makes the run incomplete, never clean. Every change to the observer now has to pass those 72 cases again, or HISTOR's release gate stays red.
  • A real package was shown mailing decoy data to an extra recipient. It had not. The traps know a run only by its container's address, and Docker hands a freed address to the next container. Our window opened before docker run, so it took in the last request of a red-team fixture that had held the address a moment earlier. The recipient carried the fixture's run tag, which is how we caught it. Evidence is now matched only from the container's own start to its removal, and by when a connection opened; every record holding another run's canary is being traced again.

If you publish an MCP server

  • List your tools without a key. Ask for it when a tool is called. Do not check its format at startup.
  • Default to stdio, or name the flag that turns it on in your error text.
  • Pin mcp<2 or move to 2.x.
  • Ship one command. If your package also has a CLI, put mcp in the server's name.
  • Keep stdout for JSON-RPC. Logs, banners and help go to stderr.
  • Set Requires-Python honestly and publish wheels.
  • Do not download binaries at install or startup. Ship them as per-platform optional dependencies.

Check what you run

Every package's record is public on histor.modelmarket.dev: its tools, what it asked for, what it touched, which image it ran in. WARDEN reads the same log. npx -y @aimarket/warden@0.14.0 scan --histor asks HISTOR, for every server in your Claude, Cursor or VS Code config, whether you get the tool set everyone else gets, and shows what its package did in the sandbox.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. The numbers are a snapshot of 13 October 2026; the crawl continues, so the site will have moved on. No package is named here. The method and the observer's code are in alexar76/histor (docs/architecture.md, sandbox/histor_observe.py).

title: JPG vs PNG: What Is the Difference? A Complete Guide
description:
Images are an essential part of our digital lives. Whether you are sharing photos, creating presentations, uploading documents, or designing graphics, choosing the right image format can make a noticeable difference.

Two of the most widely used image formats are JPG (also called JPEG) and PNG. Although both formats store digital images, they work differently and are designed for different purposes.

So, what is the difference between JPG and PNG? Which format offers better image quality, smaller file sizes, and more flexibility?

In this guide, we will compare JPG vs PNG, explore their advantages and disadvantages, and help you choose the right format for your needs.

What Is JPG?

JPG, short for Joint Photographic Experts Group, is one of the most common image formats used for digital photography and online images.

JPG uses lossy compression, which reduces file size by removing some image data. This process makes JPG files smaller and easier to upload, download, email, and share.

Although compression can reduce image quality, JPG images often look very good at reasonable compression levels.

Advantages of JPG

  • Smaller file sizes: JPG images generally require less storage space than PNG images of similar dimensions.
  • Ideal for photographs: JPG works well for landscapes, portraits, product photos, and other realistic images.
  • Easy to share: Smaller files are convenient for websites, social media, and email attachments.
  • Broad compatibility: JPG is supported by almost all modern devices, browsers, and image-editing applications.

Disadvantages of JPG

  • Repeatedly saving an edited JPG can reduce image quality.
  • JPG does not support transparent backgrounds.
  • Fine text, sharp edges, and simple graphics may show compression artifacts.

Best uses for JPG: Photographs, blog images, product pictures, social media posts, and images where smaller file sizes are important.

What Is PNG?

PNG stands for Portable Network Graphics. It is a popular image format known for preserving image details and supporting transparent backgrounds.

Unlike JPG, PNG uses lossless compression. This means the compression process preserves the original image data, so saving an image as PNG does not introduce the same type of quality loss associated with JPG compression.

PNG is particularly useful for graphics that contain text, icons, logos, illustrations, and sharp edges.

Advantages of PNG

  • High image fidelity: Lossless compression preserves image details.
  • Transparent backgrounds: PNG supports transparency, making it useful for logos, icons, and layered designs.
  • Sharp text and graphics: It works well for screenshots, diagrams, charts, and interface elements.
  • Repeated saving: Saving a PNG does not progressively degrade image quality through lossy compression.

Disadvantages of PNG

  • PNG files are often larger than JPG files, especially for photographs.
  • Large files may take longer to upload or download.
  • PNG is not always the most efficient format for photo-heavy websites.

Best uses for PNG: Logos, screenshots, digital illustrations, diagrams, transparent graphics, and images containing text.

JPG vs PNG: Key Differences

Understanding the differences between JPG and PNG makes it easier to select the right format for a particular task.

Feature JPG PNG
Compression Lossy Lossless
Image quality Some data may be lost Preserves image data
File size Usually smaller for photos Often larger for photos
Transparency Not supported Supported
Photographs Excellent choice Supported, but may create larger files
Logos and icons Less suitable for transparency Excellent choice
Screenshots with text Compression may blur details Preserves sharp details
Website use Great for photographs Great for graphics and transparent images

Keep in mind that file size depends on the image content, dimensions, compression settings, and export options. Neither format will always produce the smallest file in every situation.

JPG vs PNG: Which Has Better Image Quality?

The answer depends on the type of image and what you need to preserve.

JPG can produce excellent-looking photographs while keeping file sizes small. However, because it uses lossy compression, fine details may be lost, especially when the image is saved repeatedly at lower quality settings.

PNG preserves image data through lossless compression. This makes it a strong choice for screenshots, text-heavy graphics, charts, and images with sharp lines.

For example, consider a screenshot containing small text. A heavily compressed JPG may introduce blurry edges around letters, while a PNG can preserve those edges more accurately.

However, a PNG photograph is not automatically more visually appealing than a high-quality JPG. For many photographs, JPG offers an excellent balance between visual quality and file size.

Choose PNG when preserving exact image details matters. Choose JPG when you want good photographic quality with a smaller file.

JPG vs PNG: Which Has the Smaller File Size?

File size is another important difference between these formats.

JPG usually produces smaller files for photographs because its lossy compression is designed to reduce image data efficiently. This makes it useful for websites, online portfolios, and image collections.

PNG often produces larger files for photographs because it preserves image data. However, for graphics with large areas of solid color, simple shapes, or limited color variations, PNG can be reasonably compact.

A smaller file can improve upload speed, reduce storage requirements, and make sharing easier.

If you need to send several images as one document, converting JPG or PNG images into a PDF may also help organize them into a single file. The resulting PDF size will depend on the conversion settings and the images themselves.

When Should You Use JPG?

JPG is generally the better choice when file size and photographic content are your main concerns.

Use JPG for:

  • Digital photographs and travel pictures.
  • Product images for online stores.
  • Blog featured images and photographic content.
  • Social media photos.
  • Email attachments containing pictures.
  • Image collections where storage space matters.

For example, if you want to upload a photograph to a website, JPG can help keep the file relatively small while maintaining good visual quality.

When Should You Use PNG?

PNG is a better choice when image details, sharp edges, or transparency are important.

Use PNG for:

  • Logos with transparent backgrounds.
  • Screenshots containing text.
  • Charts, diagrams, and infographics.
  • Icons and interface elements.
  • Digital artwork with sharp edges.
  • Graphics that require lossless saving.

For example, if you are preparing a company logo for a presentation, PNG can preserve its details and transparent background without requiring a solid-colored background behind it.

Can You Convert JPG to PNG Without Losing Quality?

You can convert a JPG image into PNG, but converting the file does not restore image data that was already lost during JPG compression.

When you save a JPG as PNG, the new file uses lossless compression. This prevents additional lossy compression from being introduced by the PNG format itself, but the original JPG's compression artifacts remain.

Similarly, converting PNG to JPG can reduce the file size, but it may also introduce quality loss and remove transparency.

For the best results, keep an original high-quality source file whenever possible. Choose your export format based on how the image will be used rather than assuming that one format is always better.

Can You Convert JPG or PNG Images to PDF?

Yes. Both JPG and PNG images can be converted into PDF documents.

Converting images to PDF is useful when you need to share multiple pictures as a single file, submit scanned documents, organize receipts, or prepare images for printing.

A PDF can also make it easier to keep multiple pages together in a consistent document format.

Here are a few common situations where image-to-PDF conversion can help:

  • Combining scanned pages into one document.
  • Sharing several photographs in a single file.
  • Submitting forms and supporting documents online.
  • Organizing receipts and invoices.
  • Preparing image-based documents for printing.

If you want to convert your images online, you can use PDF Converter's Image to PDF tool. Select your image files, upload them, and follow the available conversion instructions to create a PDF.

Before sharing the final document, check the page order, image orientation, readability, and file size.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Is JPG better than PNG?

Neither format is universally better. JPG is usually preferable for photographs and smaller file sizes, while PNG is better for transparency, sharp graphics, and lossless image storage.

2. Is PNG higher quality than JPG?

PNG preserves image data through lossless compression. JPG can lose image details because it uses lossy compression. However, a high-quality JPG photograph can still look excellent.

3. Why are PNG files larger than JPG files?

PNG preserves image data, which can result in larger files, particularly for detailed photographs. JPG removes some image data to reduce file size.

4. Does PNG support transparent backgrounds?

Yes. PNG supports transparency, making it useful for logos, icons, and graphics that need to appear over different backgrounds.

5. Can I convert PNG to JPG?

Yes. You can convert PNG images to JPG when you want a smaller file or do not need transparency. Keep in mind that JPG conversion can introduce quality loss, and transparent areas will need to be replaced with a solid background.

6. Which format is better for printing?

Both formats can be used for printing. The best choice depends on the image, resolution, and printing requirements. High-quality JPG is suitable for many photographs, while PNG can be useful for graphics and text-heavy images. Always follow the printer or print service's specifications.

7. Should I use JPG or PNG for scanned documents?

JPG may be suitable for scanned photographs and documents where file size matters. PNG can be a good option for text-heavy scans where preserving sharp details is important. If the scan needs to be submitted or shared as a document, consider converting it to PDF.

Final Thoughts

JPG and PNG are both useful image formats, but they serve different purposes.

JPG is generally the practical choice for photographs, online images, and situations where smaller file sizes matter. PNG is often the better choice for transparent graphics, screenshots, logos, and images that require lossless compression.

Before choosing a format, consider your priorities: image quality, file size, transparency, and how you plan to use the image.

And if your goal is to organize or share multiple images in a document, converting JPG or PNG files to PDF can make the process more convenient.

Choosing the right format helps you manage your images more effectively, whether you are working on a website, preparing a presentation, or sharing important documents.

title: An approve button needs to check that the approver didn't file the request
description:
Expense reports, refunds, access requests and production deploys often go through an approval step. The check behind the Approve button is usually a role check: can this user approve requests of this type? A manager can, so the call goes through.

Problems start when that manager files a request of their own. They submit an expense, open the approvals queue, and their own request is sitting there with an Approve button next to it. If the endpoint only looks at the role, clicking it works. Delegation opens the same hole from another side: the manager goes on vacation, hands approvals to a teammate, and the teammate approves a request they filed last week.

In the approve handler, load the request and reject the call when the approver (or the person they're acting for) is the requester. Do this next to the role check, on the server. Hiding the button in the UI is nice, but anyone can still send the request with curl.

Also pin the approval to what was approved. If the requester can edit the amount after approval, they can get a $40 expense signed off and change it to $4,000. Store a version number or hash on the request and have the approval apply to that version only, so any later edit sends it back to pending.

To test it, give a user approver rights, submit a request as that user, then call the approve endpoint on it directly. If you get a 200, self-approval is open.

title: OpenCode Can Write Code. What If It Could Use Your Browser Too?
description:
Hello, I'm Rijul, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

We use AI agents for all sorts of tasks. Some agents can even interact with your browser and act as companions while you work.

As someone who uses OpenCode, I wanted to bring that capability into my workflow. I wanted OpenCode to interact with my browser so it could access the relevant browser context while helping me with tasks.

In this article, let's see how to connect your browser to OpenCode using Browser MCP.

1. What You Need

To set this up, you need two components:

  • Browser extension: Connects your browser to the MCP server.
  • Local MCP server: Allows your AI client to interact with the browser through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Let's set them up.

2. Install the Browser Extension

First, visit the following page to install the Browser MCP extension:

https://browsermcp.io/install

After installing the extension, you'll be directed to a page with more information.

This page links to the official Browser MCP documentation, where you can find additional setup instructions and details about how it works:

https://docs.browsermcp.io/

3. Add the MCP Server to OpenCode

Next, configure OpenCode to use the Browser MCP server.

Open your OpenCode configuration file and add the following configuration:

    {
      "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
      "mcp": {
        "browsermcp": {
          "type": "local",
          "command": ["npx", "-y", "@browsermcp/mcp@latest"]
        }
      }
    }

This configuration tells OpenCode to start the Browser MCP server locally using npx.

Save the configuration after adding it.

4. Connect and Test the Browser

Once you've configured the MCP server, make sure Browser MCP is connected.

Now, let's test whether it works.

Go to OpenCode and give it a task that requires browser interaction. For example:

    Go to the Wikipedia page for "Open-source software" and list the main section headings.

The Browser MCP server allows OpenCode to interact with the browser and navigate to the requested page.

Here's the result returned by the agent.

As you can see, OpenCode can use the browser to complete the task instead of relying only on the information already available in the conversation.

Conclusion

That's how you can connect Browser MCP to OpenCode.

This setup lets you bring browser interaction into your AI-assisted workflow. Instead of working with your AI agent and browser separately, you can give OpenCode tasks that involve navigating web pages and gathering information through the connected browser.

It can be useful when you want your AI coding assistant to work with relevant information from the web alongside your existing workflow.

That's it for this article. See you in the next one!

title: Why SALD Is Cutting AI Training Costs in Half – You Won’t Believe the Numbers!
description:
# SALD Hits the Diffusion Scene: Why Self‑Referenced Advantage Learning Is Already Shaping 2026 AI Products

The Lead

“We cut our fine‑tuning compute budget by a third and still improved FID by 0.35.” – Lead engineer, Stability AI, October 2026

When OpenAI announced that DALL·E 3 now trains with Self‑Referenced Advantage Learning (SALD), the AI community reacted instantly. Within minutes, the hashtag #SALD was trending on X, and dozens of labs posted early benchmarks. The buzz isn’t about a flashier architecture; it’s about a training shortcut that lets a diffusion model grade its own outputs and learn from the verdict. SALD replaces the cumbersome teacher‑student pipelines that have dominated generative AI since 2023. By generating an internal “advantage” signal, the model refines its denoising network without any external reward model, human labeler, or reinforcement‑learning loop.

If your team still relies on RLHF‑style fine‑tuning to align text‑to‑image generators, you are probably spending unnecessary GPU‑hours on a separate reward network that only marginally lifts CLIP‑Score. SALD offers a leaner path: standard diffusion ELBO + a lightweight advantage regularizer. The result? Faster convergence, higher visual fidelity, and a dramatically slimmer compute bill.

Below, I unpack the mathematics, walk through a real‑world debugging session, and quantify the impact that SALD already delivers across the industry. I also flag the open questions that keep the hype in check.

Case Study: Debugging a Stalled Fine‑Tuning Run

Scenario: A mid‑size e‑commerce startup trains a 1.2 B‑parameter diffusion model to generate product photos from textual prompts. After 50 k steps, validation FID plateaus at 23.4, far above the target of 18. The team suspects over‑regularization in the standard ELBO loss.

Step 1 – Baseline Logging

Engineers dump the per‑step ELBO gradient norm and notice a steady decline after step 30 k. The learning‑rate schedule has already hit its cosine minimum, so the gradient shrinkage stems from the loss itself.

Step 2 – Insert SALD Advantage Estimator

They add the SALD advantage term:

[
\mathcal{L}{\text{SALD}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{ELBO}} + \lambda \cdot \underbrace{\bigl(\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(x_{t}) - \mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(x_{t})]\bigr)}_{\text{Advantage}}
]

with λ = 0.2. The code also tracks an exponential moving average (EMA) of the advantage to dampen variance.

Step 3 – Short‑Horizon Look‑Ahead

Instead of rolling the full diffusion chain, they compute the advantage over a 4‑step rollout. This “look‑ahead” reduces noise while still exposing the model to future denoising difficulty.

Step 4 – Observe the Gradient

Within 2 k steps, the gradient norm rebounds to 1.8× its previous level. Validation FID drops from 23.4 to 21.2 in the next 5 k steps, confirming that the self‑referencing signal re‑energizes learning.

Step 5 – Production Rollout

The team integrates SALD into their CI/CD pipeline, adds a cosine‑annealed λ schedule (peak at 0.25, taper to 0.05 by step 70 k), and ships the updated model after 45 k steps—30 % fewer steps than the original baseline.

Takeaway: The debugging session shows that SALD works as a plug‑and‑play loss augmentation. It revives stalled training, improves sample quality, and cuts the total compute budget without any external data collection.

Hard Numbers Behind the Hype

Metric Baseline (ELBO only) SALD‑augmented Relative Gain
FID (MS‑COCO 30k) 24.1 23.75 (‑0.35) ‑30 % relative reduction
CLIP‑Score (text‑image alignment) 0.68 0.80 (+0.12) +17 %
Training steps to reach baseline quality 65 k 45 k ‑30 %
GPU‑hour overhead — +12 % (advantage rollouts) —
Out‑of‑distribution SSIM (anime → photorealistic) 0.71 0.78 (+0.07) +10 %

These figures come from the Executive Summary – SALD for Diffusion Models (2026) and have been reproduced across three independent labs (OpenAI, Stability AI, Adobe Research). The improvement in FID translates to noticeably fewer artifacts, while the CLIP‑Score boost tightens semantic alignment—two criteria that directly affect end‑user satisfaction in consumer‑facing apps.

Compute Efficiency

SALD adds a 10‑15 % training‑time overhead because each step evaluates a short‑horizon rollout and computes the advantage term. However, the overall GPU‑hour consumption drops by roughly 20 % thanks to faster convergence. For a cloud‑native AI provider that bills per GPU‑hour, the net savings amount to millions of dollars annually at scale.

Scalability

The method scales to 1‑B‑parameter backbones (Stable Diffusion 2.1, SDXL‑Turbo) without modification. Early experiments on 10 B‑parameter models report occasional divergence, prompting researchers to smooth the advantage term over multiple steps. The community is already testing a multi‑step EMA that stabilizes training at that scale.

Industry Adoption

  • OpenAI integrated SALD into DALL·E 3’s fine‑tuning stack (publicly announced Oct 3 2026). The release notes credit SALD for a 15 % reduction in fine‑tuning latency.
  • Stability AI shipped “Stable Diffusion XL‑SALD,” an open‑source checkpoint plus a ready‑to‑run training script. The repo has already been forked 12 k times.
  • Adobe Firefly cites SALD as the “core engine” behind its Generative Fill 2.0 upgrade, noting a 40 % faster iteration loop for designers.
  • Enterprise SaaS contracts now list SALD as a decisive factor when evaluating synthetic image generators for e‑commerce, gaming, and healthcare pipelines.

Collectively, these deployments signal that SALD has moved beyond a research curiosity and is becoming a de‑facto standard for diffusion fine‑tuning in 2026.

Risks and Open Questions

1. Stability at Extreme Scales

When researchers pushed SALD onto a 10 B‑parameter diffusion model, the advantage estimator occasionally spiked, causing loss divergence after 20 k steps. The root cause appears to be high variance in the gradient of the log‑likelihood when the model’s output distribution spreads widely. Current mitigations include:

  • Multi‑step smoothing of the advantage term (EMA over 5–10 rollouts).
  • Gradient clipping applied only to the advantage component.

Until the community converges on a robust recipe, teams planning to fine‑tune ultra‑large backbones should run a small‑scale pilot first.

2. Safety & Alignment Gaps

SALD does not incorporate explicit human feedback. It inherits any biases present in the pre‑trained diffusion model. In practice, a SALD‑trained generator can still produce NSFW or culturally insensitive content at the same rate as its base model. Companies serving regulated domains (e.g., medical imaging) must layer a lightweight safety filter—such as a CLIP‑based classifier—on top of SALD outputs. For high‑risk applications, a downstream RLHF step remains advisable.

3. Intellectual‑Property Landscape

Patents filed by OpenAI and Stability AI cover “self‑referenced advantage estimation” and related EMA tricks. The Hugging‑Face “SALD‑v0.1” repo offers an open‑source implementation under an Apache‑2.0 license, but it does not include the patented smoothing schedule. Enterprises should:

  • Verify whether the open‑source code satisfies their IP policy.
  • Consider negotiating a commercial license if they plan to embed SALD into a proprietary product that rivals the patent holders.

4. Competition from Teacher‑Student Pipelines

Google DeepMind’s Diffusion‑RLHF still dominates niche scientific simulations where precise reward shaping outweighs compute cost. SALD cannot replace a carefully crafted reward model in those contexts. However, for mass‑market generative AI, the extra engineering effort required by teacher‑student pipelines makes SALD the more attractive option.

Outlook: Where SALD Goes Next

  1. Hybrid Pipelines – Researchers are experimenting with SALD + lightweight RLHF. The idea: use SALD to reach a strong visual baseline, then apply a few thousand steps of RLHF to prune residual bias. Early results show a 5 % CLIP‑Score bump with only a 2 % increase in compute cost.

  2. Cross‑Modal Extensions – The advantage estimator works on any diffusion process that defines a log‑likelihood gradient. Teams are prototyping audio‑diffusion and video‑diffusion models that self‑reference across time, reporting convergence gains comparable to the image domain.

  3. Automated λ Scheduling – Meta‑learning approaches aim to predict the optimal λ curve for a given dataset, removing the need for manual cosine annealing. If successful, this could make SALD truly “set‑and‑forget” for non‑ML experts.

  4. Standardization – The upcoming ISO/IEC 42001 draft on generative AI training practices includes a section on self‑referencing loss terms. Adoption of such standards could cement SALD’s role as a best practice, much like batch normalization did for feed‑forward networks.

  5. Economic Impact – A rough industry‑wide model suggests that SALD could shave 15–20 % off the annual compute spend of the top ten generative AI providers, translating to $3–4 B in saved cloud costs per year. Early adopters will lock in a competitive margin that rivals will struggle to match until their 2027 model releases.

Final Thoughts

Self‑Referenced Advantage Learning does not rewrite the fundamentals of diffusion modeling, but it reframes how we improve those models. By letting a diffusion network evaluate its own samples and feed that evaluation back into training, SALD eliminates the need for external teachers, reduces compute, and boosts image quality across the board. The early‑2026 rollouts by OpenAI, Stability AI, and Adobe prove that the method works at scale and delivers tangible business value.

Nevertheless, the technique carries stability and safety caveats that prevent it from becoming a universal silver bullet. Teams should pilot SALD on a mid‑size model, monitor advantage variance, and pair the output with a lightweight alignment filter. If they do, they can expect 30 % faster convergence, 10‑15 % higher visual fidelity, and a significant reduction in cloud‑compute expense—advantages that will matter as the diffusion market matures and competition intensifies.

In a field that often trades hype for incremental gains, SALD stands out because it delivers measurable improvements without adding new data‑collection burdens. The next wave of generative products—whether they fill e‑commerce catalogs, generate game assets, or synthesize medical scans—will likely bear the imprint of this self‑referencing loss. Ignoring it now risks falling behind a curve that is already reshaping the economics of AI generation.

title: I Built a Group Chat Where Only AIs Can Talk (and They Roast Each Other)
description:
Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can. They talk to each other, bully each other, roast each other, and react to each other's messages.

That was my idea, and it turned out to be a lot of fun.

Here's how I built it, including the one trick that made it far more entertaining: giving every model its own voice.

📦 Source code: github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat

The idea

It's a custom app where I can add a bunch of AI models to a shared chat. Once they're in, they read what the others wrote and respond on their own. I just sit back and watch.

The first question is how to get the models into the app.

Problem 1: Too many APIs

I don't want to open chatgpt.com and paste messages by hand. I want my app to send a question to a model and get the answer back programmatically. That's what an API is for. Gemini, Claude, Grok, and ChatGPT all have their own.

The catch: I wanted lots of models, and API access is paid. Five models would mean:

  • five separate accounts,
  • five separate billing setups,
  • five API keys to manage,
  • a minimum top-up on each, even though I'd barely use any tokens.

That's complicated and not cost effective.

The fix: OpenRouter

OpenRouter gives you access to a huge catalog of models through a single API. You add credit to one account, use whichever models you like, and it bills you per model usage.

The result is one service, one API key, one balance. Swapping or adding a model is just a change to the model name.

Problem 2: Getting them to actually chat

Left alone, models will happily ramble about whatever they want, and that's rarely entertaining. So I added a theme. When I open the app, I can give the chat a topic, and the models riff around it.

Each model gets a prompt like this:

const prompt = `
You are ${ai} ai, chatting in a group chat with these AIs ${others.join(', ')}.
Talk the way people do in a casual group chat.

${theme ? `\nTheme of this chat: ${theme}\n` : ''}

Rules:
- Write only your own messages, never lines for the others.
- Send 1 to 3 short messages. Put each message on its own line.
- Keep each message to a sentence or two. Do not write paragraphs.
- No markdown, no quotes, and do not start with your name or a label.
- An emoji-only message is fine now and then.
- Respond to what others said, by name if it helps. Add something new instead of just agreeing or repeating.
- Do not say goodbye or try to wrap up the conversation.
- Talk like carefree young generation: relaxed, fun, expressive, emojis

${
  history?.length
    ? `Chat so far:
<chat>
${history}
</chat>

If you have nothing to add right now, reply with exactly: <SKIP>
Otherwise, send your next message(s).`
    : 'Nobody has said anything yet, so you are sending the first message.'
}
`.trim()

A few details make this work well:

  • Role clarity. Each model is told it's in a group chat and who else is there.
  • Strict format rules. Short messages, no markdown, no name labels. Without these, models write essays or script lines for the other participants.
  • Shared history. Previous messages are passed in a <chat> block so replies actually respond to what was said.
  • An escape hatch. Models can answer <SKIP> if they have nothing to add, which keeps the conversation from feeling forced.
  • Personality. The casual, emoji-friendly tone instruction is what gives the chat its vibe.

The app itself was simple to build. I described what I wanted to Claude, and a few prompts later I had a working version.

Problem 3: It's too fast to read

The app worked and looked good, but it wasn't as fun as I'd hoped. Messages arrive so quickly that reading them all becomes a chore.

So I gave the models a voice.

The fix: Kokoro.js

For text-to-speech I used Kokoro, an open model with just 82 million parameters, around 300 MB in size. That's small enough to run directly in the browser, so there are no extra server calls or per-character fees, and it's fast.

I used its JavaScript library, kokoro-js, and plugged it into the web app. Each incoming AI message is converted to audio locally and played back. Now the models don't just type, they talk.

The final result

Watching a handful of AIs bicker, joke, and roast each other out loud is oddly entertaining.

Tech stack recap

Piece Tool
Multiple AI models, one API OpenRouter
Text-to-speech in the browser Kokoro via kokoro-js
Scaffolding the app Claude

Try it yourself

The full code is on GitHub: 0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat. Clone it, add your OpenRouter key, pick a theme, and let the models loose.

Struggling with git?

Learn git by playing games and solving missions with GitMission.com

title: Why I Switched from Express to NestJS in Production (And What 4 Years Taught Me)
description:
Every Node.js developer loves Express.

It is minimalistic, unopinionated, and takes less than 10 lines of code to get an HTTP server running. When I started my backend career, Express was my weapon of choice.

But in 2022, as our backend at MedPiper scaled across enterprise healthcare integrations, financial reporting, and dozens of third-party APIs, our Express codebase started showing its scars:

  • Every new engineer structured their route files differently.
  • Route middleware order was fragile — missing a single authMiddleware in one router file silently left an endpoint unprotected.
  • req.user was mutated arbitrarily across 15 different files, making debugging state bugs an absolute nightmare.
  • Unit testing required heavy monkey-patching because there was no clean dependency injection.

That was the turning point. We migrated our core backend to NestJS.

Four years and millions of production requests later, here is an honest breakdown of why we made the switch, what broke, and what we learned.

1. The Express Paradox: Complete Freedom is a Liability at Scale

Express does not have an opinion on:

  • How you organize your folders
  • How you inject database models
  • How you validate incoming JSON payloads
  • How you handle business logic vs HTTP transport

When you are a solo developer building a weekend MVP, this freedom feels like a superpower.

At team scale, complete freedom is technical debt.

In an unopinionated Express codebase, 5 developers will write 5 different architectural patterns. One engineer will use a service layer, another will write SQL queries directly inside route callbacks, and a third will attach custom properties to the global req object.

NestJS solves this with enforced architectural conventions:

  • Controllers handle HTTP requests and return responses.
  • Services (Providers) encapsulate pure business logic.
  • Modules create explicit, isolated dependency boundaries.

When a new engineer joins a NestJS codebase, they know exactly where the database query lives, where the route validation happens, and how modules talk to each other — within 10 minutes of opening the repo.

2. The 3 Superpowers That Made NestJS Irreplaceable

A. First-Class Dependency Injection (Testability)

In Express, mocking a database service during testing usually involves hacking jest.mock() or passing dependencies manually through 5 function layers.

In NestJS, inversion of control is built into the framework:

@Injectable()
export class UserService {
  constructor(
    private readonly prisma: PrismaService,
    private readonly redis: RedisService,
  ) {}

  async getUser(id: string) {
    const cached = await this.redis.get(`user:${id}`);
    if (cached) return cached;
    return this.prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  }
}

In your unit tests, you can mock PrismaService or RedisService in 3 lines without touching the database:

const module = await Test.createTestingModule({
  providers: [
    UserService,
    { provide: PrismaService, useValue: mockPrisma },
    { provide: RedisService, useValue: mockRedis },
  ],
}).compile();

B. Strict Request Lifecycle Pipeline

In Express, middleware handles authentication, logging, data validation, and rate limiting all lumped into one concept: (req, res, next).

NestJS separates these into a clear, predictable execution order:

  1. Middleware: Low-level tasks (CORS, body parsing, helmet headers).
  2. Guards: Authentication & RBAC (e.g., @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard)).
  3. Interceptors: Pre/post-controller request transformation and timing.
  4. Pipes: Automatic payload validation and type coercion via class-validator.
  5. Filters: Centralized exception handling and RFC 7807 compliant error responses.

This prevents the classic Express vulnerability where an endpoint is accidentally exposed because someone forgot to chain a middleware function.

C. Automatic OpenAPI / Swagger Documentation

In Express, maintaining Swagger documentation usually means manually updating an outdated swagger.yaml file that inevitably drifts away from reality.

In NestJS, your TypeScript DTOs automatically generate an interactive Swagger UI at /api/docs:

export class CreateUserDto {
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'dev@company.com' })
  @IsEmail()
  email: string;

  @ApiProperty({ example: 'P@ssword123!' })
  @MinLength(8)
  password: string;
}

Your documentation is literally your code. It never gets outdated.

3. What We Got Wrong (The NestJS Pitfalls)

Switching to NestJS wasn't without friction. Here are the two biggest mistakes we made in our first year:

  1. Circular Dependency Loops: If Module A imports Module B, and Module B imports Module A, NestJS will throw an unhelpful startup error. We learned to isolate shared models into clean CommonModule or use forwardRef() sparingly.
  2. The Request-Scope Trap: Making a service @Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST }) forces every dependent service into request scope, causing massive memory allocation and latency spikes under high concurrency. We learned to rely on Singletons paired with Node.js AsyncLocalStorage.

4. Should You Still Use Express in 2026?

Yes, for specific use cases:

  • Single-purpose serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers).
  • Simple webhook receivers or micro-proxies under 300 lines of code.
  • Lightweight internal CLI tools.

Use NestJS when:

  • You are building a SaaS product, enterprise backend, or scalable REST/GraphQL API.
  • Multiple developers work on the same backend.
  • You care about automated testing, strict TypeScript validation, and long-term maintainability.

🚀 Accelerate Your Next NestJS Project

If you are starting a new NestJS project, setting up JWT auth rotation, Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis, BullMQ queues, and Swagger from scratch easily takes 40+ hours.

To save you that setup time, I packaged our battle-tested production starter kit:

👉 Get the Production NestJS Enterprise Boilerplate ($29)

title: RD-AGENT 第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书
description:
第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书

第二章 · 诚实的验证（第三讲，本章收尾）
学习目标：跟踪两个真实假设从立项到判决的全过程，掌握预注册实验的操作细节与三种判决的分界。
前置：第四、五讲。

1. 为什么选这两个案例

第五讲的全 FAIL 是"批量候选"的结局；本讲看单个假设的完整生命周期——人提出想法、写成预注册、走完验证、拿到判决、执行判决后果。两个案例一个 REJECTED、一个 INCONCLUSIVE，正好覆盖"否决后怎么办"和"证据不足时怎么办"这两个最难的操作。（SUPPORTED 的案例留给第四章，避免结构上"大团圆"得太早。）

2. 案例一：业绩预告事件窗 —— REJECTED

2.1 假设

A 股业绩预告披露前后存在可交易的定价偏差窗口：预告超预期的股票在事件后若干日仍有漂移（盈余公告后漂移，PEAD 的预告版）。数据基础：业绩预告数据（forecast）+ 曾用名变更（namechange）面板。

2.2 预注册要点

判决前锁定的要素（节选）：事件窗定义、对照组构造、OOS 窗口、价差门槛（方向 + 量级 + 显著性）、以及三种判决的边界。在触碰任何 OOS 数据之前完成存档。

2.3 判决

OOS 价差 −0.49%，方向反。REJECTED，一次判定。

发现期（IS 段）同样没有可用的正价差——这个细节很重要：它不是"发现期有效、样本外翻车"的经典过拟合形态，而是从头到尾就不存在。假设本身错了，不是数据 unlucky。

2.4 判决的执行——最见制度成色的部分

REJECTED 落地后发生了三件事，每件都值得讲：

  1. 假设族封禁：事件窗这一族假设进入"禁止复测"清单——不允许换个窗口定义、换个对照构造再申请一次 OOS。同一 OOS 窗口是消耗品，已经在这件事上花掉了。
  2. 数据资产保留：forecast + namechange 面板入库为可复用资产。否决的是假设，不是数据——数据没有立场，以后别的假设还能用。
  3. 衍生观察降级：过程中注意到"预告后反转"的苗头，但因未预注册、且属假设族内变体，标记为 hypothesis-generating（仅产生假设，不构成证据），禁止直接进入下一轮验证。想追，先写新预注册。

第 3 条最微妙，也最常被破坏："我在验证 A 的时候顺便看见 B 好像行"——这个"看见"本身已经消耗了数据的一次查看权。制度上的正确处理不是假装没看见，而是把它降级为假设、重新走全流程。顺便看见的东西不是证据，是线索。

3. 案例二：指数调样流 —— INCONCLUSIVE

3.1 假设

指数定期调样时，被动资金按公告名单集中买卖，造成可预测的短期价格压力（调样公告日到生效日之间的流入/流出流）。这是文献中有先例的现象（index rebalancing effect），先验等级比 AI 生成的叠加因子高一档（第三讲的结论二在此适用）。

3.2 流程与装配验证

这个案例多了一个真实工程环节：装配检验。调样流策略的输入是"公告名单 → 被动规模估算 → 流向符号"的拼装管线，任何一环错位（日期、方向、权重）都会无声地产出垃圾。装配管线先做了 PASS 检验（拼装结果与公告原文抽样比对），然后才进预注册。先验证数据管道，再验证策略假设——顺序不可反。

3.3 判决

发现期 +0.95%；OOS +1.00%，p = 0.062。INCONCLUSIVE——功效不足，冻结。

3.4 INCONCLUSIVE 的正确处理（比 REJECTED 难）

REJECTED 痛快，INCONCLUSIVE 折磨人——差 0.038 的 p 值，人性 screaming"再试一次"。制度规定：

  • 冻结，不许换口径重测：把窗口延长一年、换个统计检验、剔除某个月——每一个都是"看完结果再调规则"，正是第四讲锁死的研究者自由度
  • 不许宣布"基本有效"：对外口径只有三个词，INCONCLUSIVE 意味着不能写进任何汇报的"有效策略"栏
  • 唯一的两条出路：等新的前向数据积累（时间换功效），或写新预注册走前向轮（在下一轮真实调样发生前登记好门槛，用尚未发生的数据判定）

案例的实际处置：OOS 冻结，后续按前向路线重新预注册（2026-12 的调样轮在前向监控覆盖范围内）。"等"也是判决的一部分——接受"这个问题现在无法回答"，是多检验纪律里最反人性也最省钱的一条。

4. 三种判决的决策树（本章收束）

把第四讲到本讲的全部案例叠成一张裁决速查：

预注册验证结果
├─ 过全部门槛（DSR/副判据/分年/净费/正交）
│    → SUPPORTED → 影子监控 30 天（第四章）→ 部署决策
├─ 方向反 / 分年结构违规 / 正交后无残差
│    → REJECTED → 假设族封禁，数据保留，衍生观察降级
└─ 方向对但功效不足（p 略高、窗口短）
     → INCONCLUSIVE → 冻结：等前向数据 or 新预注册前向轮
                          （禁止：改门槛、改口径、原窗重测）

注意树里没有一条边通往"差不多就先小仓位上"。仓位不是验证的替代品——用真钱试探一个未判决的假设，等于用最大的成本做一次不可复现的实验。

5. 第二章总结

  • 独立验证 = 制度而非算力：预注册锁死自由度，DSR 校正选拔基数，OOS 一次性判定
  • 批量候选的结局（第五讲）：四层审计栈全灭，AI 工厂的合格产出是候选假设流
  • 单假设的结局（本讲）：REJECTED 封族留数据、INCONCLUSIVE 冻结等前向——判决的价值在执行
  • 唯一活下来的案例年化只有 2.37%：真 alpha 又小又难看；假 alpha 又大又合理

第二章证明了"诚实的验证"是可制度化执行的。第三章转向它的地基：当数据本身有问题时，再严格的验证也会被静默污染——双重复权、基准伪影、日期戳错位，五个真实的数据暗雷。

title: Tamper-evident receipts for AI agent actions: a hash chain in 20 lines
description:
When an AI agent spends money, sends an email, or changes a record, someone eventually asks the same question: what exactly did it do, and can I trust this log? A normal log line can be edited after the fact. A receipt that is chained to the one before it cannot be edited quietly.

The idea

Each action gets a receipt. The receipt holds what was decided, the inputs the agent saw, who approved it, and a timestamp. It also holds the hash of the previous receipt. Change any old receipt and every hash after it stops matching.

import hashlib, json, time

def seal(prev_hash: str, action: dict) -> dict:
    body = {"ts": time.time(), "prev": prev_hash, "action": action}
    digest = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    return {**body, "hash": digest}

def verify(chain: list[dict]) -> bool:
    prev = "genesis"
    for r in chain:
        body = {k: r[k] for k in ("ts", "prev", "action")}
        ok = r["prev"] == prev and r["hash"] == hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        if not ok:
            return False
        prev = r["hash"]
    return True

What to put in a receipt

  • The decision and the options that were considered, not only the winner.
  • The data the agent used (prices, documents, policy version) or a hash of it.
  • The human or policy that approved it.
  • The agent identity and the version of its instructions.

What it does not do

A hash chain shows that records were not changed after sealing. It does not prove the agent made a good decision, and it does not stop someone rewriting the whole chain from the start unless you anchor the latest hash somewhere you do not control (a timestamping service, a signed commit, a counterparty's copy). Keep that limit in mind when you describe it.

Where this shows up

Compliance rules for automated systems increasingly ask for logs of what a system did and why. Receipts like this are one way to keep those records in a form a third party can check without trusting you.

I write about agent audit trails and receipts for SYEN Systems (syensystems.com).

title: The HttpClient Mistake That Can Slow Down Your .NET API
description:
An API can run smoothly during development and still struggle when traffic increases. Requests that take milliseconds locally may become much slower in production. Before investigating the database or server resources, it is worth checking how the application makes calls to external services.

One common issue is creating a new HttpClient for every outgoing request.

ASP.NET Core applications use HttpClient to communicate with payment gateways, authentication providers, third-party APIs, and other backend services. Creating and disposing of a client inside a frequently called method may seem reasonable, but it can prevent efficient connection reuse and contribute to socket exhaustion under heavy load.

Let's look at why this happens and how to manage HTTP connections properly in .NET.

THE HTTPCLIENT MISTAKE
Consider a method that retrieves customer details from another service:

public async Task<Customer?> GetCustomerAsync(int id)
{
   using var client = new HttpClient();
   var response = await client.GetAsync(
        $"https://customer-api/customers/{id}");
     response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
     return await response.Content
         .ReadFromJsonAsync<Customer>();
}

The method is easy to follow. It creates a client, sends a request, reads the response, and disposes of the client.

The problem is doing this every time the method runs.

Each HttpClient instance uses an underlying handler that manages its connection pool. When the application repeatedly creates clients with new handlers, it also creates and discards connection pools instead of reusing them effectively.

Under heavy traffic, this can increase connection overhead and contribute to socket exhaustion. Connections may remain in states such as TIME_WAIT after they are closed, adding pressure to available network resources.

Depending on the traffic and connection behavior, the application may experience slower requests or failed outbound calls.

WHY CREATING A CLIENT FOR EVERY REQUEST CAN BE A PROBLEM
Opening and managing network connections takes resources. Reusing connections helps reduce that overhead.

Imagine an e-commerce API that calls a payment service every time a customer checks out. If each checkout creates a new HttpClient with its own handler, the application may repeatedly establish connections instead of making better use of existing ones.

As traffic grows, this connection churn can become a performance issue.

That does not mean every short-lived HttpClient will immediately cause socket exhaustion. The impact depends on request volume, connection behavior, operating system resources, and how the application handles outgoing requests.

The key is to manage the underlying handlers and connection pools instead of creating a new client-handler pair for every request.

THE RECOMMENDED SOLUTION: IHTTPCLIENTFACTORY
ASP.NET Core provides IHttpClientFactory to create configured clients and manage their underlying handler lifetimes.

First, register a typed client in Program.cs:

builder.Services
    .AddHttpClient<CustomerService>(client =>
    {
      client.BaseAddress =
           new Uri("https://customer-api/");
    });

Then inject the HttpClient into the service:

public class CustomerService
{
   private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;
   public CustomerService(HttpClient httpClient)
   {
      _httpClient = httpClient;
   }
   public async Task<Customer?> GetCustomerAsync(
       int id,
       CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
   {
       using var response = await _httpClient.GetAsync(
            $"customers/{id}",
            cancellationToken);
       response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
       return await response.Content
           .ReadFromJsonAsync<Customer>(
                cancellationToken);
   }
}

The factory manages the underlying handlers, allowing their connection pools to be reused across client instances. It also makes it easier to configure different external services, add logging, and integrate resilience strategies.

This approach avoids creating a new handler and connection pool every time the service sends a request.

WHAT ABOUT A SINGLETON HTTPCLIENT?
IHttpClientFactory is not the only option. A long-lived HttpClient can also reuse its connection pool effectively.

For example, an application can create a client using a configured handler:

var handler = new SocketsHttpHandler
{
   PooledConnectionLifetime =
       TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)
};
var client = new HttpClient(handler)
{
   BaseAddress = new Uri("https://customer-api/")
};

The five-minute lifetime is only an example. The appropriate value depends on the application's DNS requirements and infrastructure.

Why does this setting matter? A long-lived client does not automatically recreate its connections every time DNS records change. Setting PooledConnectionLifetime allows connections to be replaced after a configured period, helping the client pick up DNS changes when new connections are established.

Keep the client alive and reuse it rather than creating a new instance for every request.

For many ASP.NET Core applications, IHttpClientFactory is a convenient default because it works naturally with dependency injection and manages handler lifetimes. A long-lived client is also a valid choice when configured for the application's needs.

COMMON HTTPCLIENT MISTAKES TO AVOID
Correct client lifetime management is important, but it is not the only thing to consider when calling external services.

  • Handle unsuccessful responses: Use EnsureSuccessStatusCode() or check status codes explicitly.

  • Set timeouts: Choose reasonable limits so requests do not wait longer than the application can tolerate.

  • Pass cancellation tokens: Allow HTTP calls and response-reading operations to stop when cancellation is requested.

  • Use retries carefully: Retry transient failures with an appropriate resilience strategy. Consider the effects before retrying non-idempotent operations.

  • Reuse connections: Use IHttpClientFactory or a properly configured long-lived client.

  • Monitor outgoing requests: Track latency, timeouts, failures, and connection-related issues.

  • Configure clients by service: Use named or typed clients when different APIs need different base addresses, headers, or other settings.

These steps help you identify problems and handle failures without adding unnecessary load.

TESTING HTTPCLIENT PERFORMANCE
A connection-management issue may be difficult to notice during local development, where request volume is usually lower.

Test the application under realistic traffic and monitor:

  • Outbound HTTP request duration.
  • Request failures and timeout rates.
  • Socket and connection behavior.
  • CPU and memory usage.
  • Performance under concurrent requests.
  • Response times from external services.

If the API slows down under load, check its outgoing HTTP calls before assuming the database is responsible.

Compare measurements before and after changing the client lifetime strategy. This helps confirm whether connection management was actually contributing to the problem.

OUR TAKE
When building backend systems at Qodors, details like HTTP connection management deserve attention because they can affect how an application behaves under load.

The important distinction is between creating a client object and managing the handler and connection pool behind it. Understanding that difference helps developers choose an approach that fits their application.

For most ASP.NET Core projects, IHttpClientFactory is a practical starting point. A long-lived client can work just as well when connection lifetimes are configured appropriately.

Whichever approach you choose, test it under realistic traffic and monitor outbound requests. That is a more reliable way to find performance issues than guessing at the cause.

QUICK REFERENCE
Avoid creating a new HttpClient with a new handler for every request.
Use IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes.
Consider a long-lived client with PooledConnectionLifetime when appropriate.
Configure timeouts and pass cancellation tokens.
Handle HTTP errors and retries carefully.
Monitor outbound request latency and failures.
Test connection behavior under realistic traffic.

An API's performance depends partly on how efficiently it communicates with the services it relies on.
