title: Code Search RAG: Chunk by Function With tree-sitter, Not by 512 Tokens
description:
• Book: RAG Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The chunk the codebase assistant retrieved for "where does the retry delay get computed?" starts halfway down a function, at an except clause, and has no def line, no class name, nothing but a file path to say where it came from. The model writes a confident answer about a function it never saw the name of.

The bug is in the chunker. It cut the file every 512 tokens, the way it cuts prose, and the cut landed in the middle of a function. Code has natural seams at def and class; a token counter ignores them.

The fix fits in two small files. Parse Python with tree-sitter, cut at function and class boundaries, carry the file path and the enclosing symbol as metadata, and split the definitions that are too big on statement boundaries. Then score both chunkers on a labelled query set, so you see the difference on your own machine instead of taking my word for it.

What a token window does to a function

A fixed window has no idea where a function starts. If a function begins at token 470 of a 512-token window, the chunk gets the decorator, the signature and four lines of body. The next chunk gets the rest of the body with no name attached. Ask for "the function that parses the config file" and the retriever has to match either a signature with no logic or logic with no signature.

The cAST paper from Carnegie Mellon and Augment Code found the same problem: "Existing line-based chunking heuristics often break semantic structures, splitting functions or merging unrelated code." Their AST-based chunker, which splits large syntax nodes and merges small siblings under a size limit, reported a 4.3-point Recall@5 gain on RepoEval retrieval and a 2.67-point Pass@1 gain on SWE-bench generation over the fixed-size baseline.

Frameworks have moved the same way. LlamaIndex ships a CodeSplitter that parses with tree-sitter and, in its source, caps chunks at 1,500 characters by default. The cAST authors published astchunk, which measures chunk size in non-whitespace characters and supports Python, Java, C# and TypeScript. Both are fine to use. Writing your own once is how you find out what they are doing for you, and how you tune it when your codebase has 600-line functions.


Token windows cut wherever the count runs out. AST chunks cut where the code does.

Two chunkers, same token budget

Install the pieces. py-tree-sitter 0.26.0 needs Python 3.10 or newer, and the Python grammar ships as its own wheel.

pip install tree-sitter tree-sitter-python \
  sentence-transformers numpy

The embedder is BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5: a small English model with 384 dimensions and a 512-token max sequence length. Both chunkers get the same budget of 480 tokens, counted with the embedder's own tokenizer, so a short header and the special tokens still fit under 512 and nothing gets silently truncated. That is the fair version of "512-token chunks".

First file, chunkers.py, starting with the Chunk type:

# chunkers.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable

import tree_sitter_python as tspython
from tree_sitter import Language, Parser

PARSER = Parser(Language(tspython.language()))
DEFS = {"function_definition", "class_definition"}
Count = Callable[[str], int]

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    path: str
    symbol: str  # "JSONDecoder.raw_decode", "<module>", or ""
    start: int   # 1-based first line
    end: int     # 1-based last line, inclusive
    text: str

    def embed_text(self) -> str:
        head = f"# {self.path}"
        if self.symbol:
            head += f" :: {self.symbol}"
        return f"{head}\n{self.text}"

The baseline comes next. It adds lines while their token count stays under the budget, emits a chunk, then backs up about 64 tokens for the overlap. The BGE tokenizer emits no token for a newline, so summing per line counts the same tokens the AST chunker counts on joined text:

# chunkers.py (continued)
def fixed_chunks(path: str, src: str, ntok: Count,
                 size: int = 480, overlap: int = 64):
    lines = src.split("\n")
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(lines):
        j, used = i, 0
        while j < len(lines):
            cost = ntok(lines[j])
            if used + cost > size and j > i:
                break
            used += cost
            j += 1
        text = "\n".join(lines[i:j])
        out.append(Chunk(path, "", i + 1, j, text))
        if j >= len(lines):
            break
        back, k = 0, j
        while k > i + 1 and back < overlap:
            k -= 1
            back += ntok(lines[k])
        i = k
    return out

The baseline is slightly generous: it snaps to line ends and overlaps about 64 tokens, where a plain token splitter would cut mid-line. Its chunks still get the file path in the header. The only things it lacks are syntax-aware boundaries and the symbol name, which keeps the comparison about exactly those two things.

src.split("\n") rather than splitlines() is deliberate. tree-sitter counts rows by \n only, and splitlines() also splits on form feeds, which some older Python files contain. Mixing the two puts every line number after the first form feed off by one.

The AST chunker goes in the same file. First the helpers that write chunks:

# chunkers.py (continued)
def unwrap(node):
    if node.type == "decorated_definition":
        return node.child_by_field_name("definition")
    return node

def name_of(defn) -> str:
    return defn.child_by_field_name("name").text.decode()

def ast_chunks(path: str, src: str, ntok: Count,
               budget: int = 480):
    lines = src.split("\n")
    tree = PARSER.parse(src.encode())
    out: list[Chunk] = []

    def span(a, b):  # 0-based rows, inclusive
        return "\n".join(lines[a:b + 1])

    def emit(sym, a, b, head=""):
        body = span(a, b)
        if ntok(head + body) <= budget:
            out.append(Chunk(path, sym, a + 1, b + 1, head + body))
            return
        # one statement is bigger than the budget: window it
        room = max(budget - ntok(head), 64)
        for c in fixed_chunks(path, body, ntok, size=room):
            out.append(Chunk(path, sym, a + c.start, a + c.end,
                             head + c.text))

emit writes one chunk when the span fits and falls back to line windows only when a single statement is bigger than the budget. pack sits on top of it and greedily groups neighbouring statements. It is still inside ast_chunks, so keep the indentation:

    # ast_chunks, continued
    def pack(nodes, sym, head=""):
        group = []
        for node in nodes:
            if group:
                a = group[0].start_point[0]
                b = node.end_point[0]
                if ntok(head + span(a, b)) > budget:
                    emit(sym, a, group[-1].end_point[0], head)
                    group = []
            group.append(node)
        if group:
            emit(sym, group[0].start_point[0],
                 group[-1].end_point[0], head)

The last two helpers decide what a unit is, and the final line starts the walk at the module root:

    # ast_chunks, continued
    def define(node, defn, scope):
        name = name_of(defn)
        sym = f"{scope}.{name}" if scope else name
        a, b = node.start_point[0], node.end_point[0]
        if ntok(span(a, b)) <= budget:
            emit(sym, a, b)
            return
        body = defn.child_by_field_name("body")
        head = span(a, body.start_point[0] - 1) + "\n"
        if defn.type == "class_definition":
            block(body.named_children, sym, head)
        else:
            pack(body.named_children, sym, head)

    def block(nodes, scope, head=""):
        loose = []
        for node in nodes:
            defn = unwrap(node)
            if defn.type in DEFS:
                if loose:
                    pack(loose, scope or "<module>", head)
                    loose = []
                define(node, defn, scope)
            else:
                loose.append(node)
        if loose:
            pack(loose, scope or "<module>", head)

    block(tree.root_node.named_children, "")
    return out

Walk it top-down. block goes through the statements of a module or a class body. Each definition goes to define, and the statements between definitions (imports, constants, a class docstring) collect into loose and get packed into <module> chunks or chunks named after the class. define emits a definition whole if it fits. Decorators count as part of the definition, because tree-sitter-python wraps them in a decorated_definition whose definition field holds the function or class.

The symbol path is the breadcrumb. A method inside JSONDecoder gets JSONDecoder.raw_decode, and embed_text() puts # json/decoder.py :: JSONDecoder.raw_decode on the first line of what gets embedded. A query that says "JSON decoder" now has a literal match even when the method body never says it.

When one function is bigger than the budget

Function-level chunks break down on the big ones. A 300-line class or a 200-line function does not fit in 480 tokens, and dumping it whole into the embedder does not help. The model card for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 says so directly: "By default, input text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated." Everything past the cutoff is invisible to retrieval, and nothing warns you.

The chunker above handles size in three steps.

Too-big class: recurse. define calls block on the class body, so every method becomes its own chunk with a Class.method symbol. The class signature becomes a head that is prepended to the chunks of loose class-level statements, so the docstring and class attributes still say which class they belong to.

Too-big function: pack statements under the signature. pack walks the body's top-level statements and greedily merges neighbours until the next one would blow the budget. Every piece starts with the full signature, decorators included. A retrieved piece from the middle of a long function still opens with def _make_iterencode(...). This is the merge half of what cAST does: split big nodes, merge small siblings.

Too-big single statement: fall back to windows. A 150-line if block is one statement. emit notices it does not fit and runs the line-window chunker over just that statement, with the signature still on top. cAST recurses into the statement's children instead, which keeps boundaries cleaner. The fallback is the cheap version; swap it for recursion when your codebase has a lot of these.


Small siblings merge, big nodes split, and every split piece keeps the signature on top.

Two costs to know about. The header eats budget, so a function with a 15-line signature leaves less room for the body in each piece. And pack re-tokenizes growing spans, which is quadratic in the worst case. On a few files that is nothing. On a monorepo, count tokens per statement once and add them up instead.

Score both on a labelled query set

A chunker is only better if retrieval gets better, so measure it. You need a corpus every reader already has, and the Python standard library is on your disk. The queries below describe what code does, mostly without using its identifiers, the way you search a codebase you did not write. Each label is a file plus a symbol path.

Before the eval, append one helper to chunkers.py, so the gold line ranges come from the parser instead of from hand-typed line numbers:

# chunkers.py (append)
def symbols(src: str) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    found = {}

    def walk(node, scope):
        for child in node.named_children:
            defn = unwrap(child)
            if defn.type not in DEFS:
                continue
            name = name_of(defn)
            sym = f"{scope}.{name}" if scope else name
            found[sym] = (child.start_point[0] + 1,
                          child.end_point[0] + 1)
            if defn.type == "class_definition":
                walk(defn.child_by_field_name("body"), sym)

    walk(PARSER.parse(src.encode()).root_node, "")
    return found

Second file, eval.py. The top holds the model, the files and the labels:

# eval.py
import sysconfig
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

from chunkers import ast_chunks, fixed_chunks, symbols

MODEL = "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
QUERY = "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "
FILES = [
    "json/__init__.py", "json/decoder.py", "json/encoder.py",
    "shlex.py", "textwrap.py", "collections/__init__.py",
]
LABELS = [
    ("quote a string so a POSIX shell sees one argument",
     "shlex.py", "quote"),
    ("split a command line into tokens like a shell",
     "shlex.py", "split"),
    ("strip the indentation shared by every line",
     "textwrap.py", "dedent"),
    ("break a paragraph into lines of a maximum width",
     "textwrap.py", "wrap"),
    ("add a prefix to the start of selected lines",
     "textwrap.py", "indent"),
    ("decode JSON at the start of a string, return end",
     "json/decoder.py", "JSONDecoder.raw_decode"),
    ("scan a JSON string literal handling escapes",
     "json/decoder.py", "py_scanstring"),
    ("serialize a Python object to a JSON str",
     "json/__init__.py", "dumps"),
    ("walk nested lists and dicts yielding JSON text",
     "json/encoder.py", "_make_iterencode"),
    ("the n elements with the highest counts",
     "collections/__init__.py", "Counter.most_common"),
    ("move a key to either end of an ordered dict",
     "collections/__init__.py", "OrderedDict.move_to_end"),
    ("make a tuple subclass with fields accessed by name",
     "collections/__init__.py", "namedtuple"),
]

recall embeds every chunk once, then checks the top five results for each query in two ways, explained after the code:

# eval.py (continued)
def recall(chunks, gold, model, k=5):
    vecs = model.encode([c.embed_text() for c in chunks],
                        normalize_embeddings=True)
    touched = whole = 0
    for query, path, (s, e) in gold:
        qv = model.encode(QUERY + query, normalize_embeddings=True)
        top = np.argsort(-(vecs @ qv))[:k]
        hits = [chunks[i] for i in top if chunks[i].path == path]
        touched += any(c.start <= e and c.end >= s for c in hits)
        whole += any(c.start <= s and c.end >= e for c in hits)
    return touched / len(gold), whole / len(gold)

main reads the six files from the standard library of whichever Python runs it and builds both chunk lists:

# eval.py (continued)
def main():
    root = Path(sysconfig.get_paths()["stdlib"])
    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL)

    def ntok(text: str) -> int:
        ids = model.tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
        return len(ids)

    fixed, by_ast, spans = [], [], {}
    for rel in FILES:
        src = (root / rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        fixed += fixed_chunks(rel, src, ntok)
        by_ast += ast_chunks(rel, src, ntok)
        spans[rel] = symbols(src)

    gold = [(q, f, spans[f][sym]) for q, f, sym in LABELS]
    for name, chunks in (("fixed", fixed), ("ast", by_ast)):
        t, w = recall(chunks, gold, model)
        print(f"{name:5} chunks={len(chunks):4} "
              f"touched@5={t:.2f} whole@5={w:.2f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The query prefix is the retrieval instruction from the BGE model card, which says passages need no prefix. Run python eval.py. The tokenizer may log a "sequence length is longer than" warning while counting tokens for whole classes; that is the counter measuring, not the embedder truncating.

Read the two numbers separately. touched@5 asks whether any top-5 chunk overlaps the target function at all. That is lenient, and it is the metric a token-window chunker looks best on, because a chunk holding three lines of the right function counts. whole@5 asks whether one top-5 chunk contains the entire function, which is what the LLM needs in order to answer. The gap between them is the "body without its name" problem, measured.

There are no results printed in this post, on purpose: your Python version changes the stdlib files, and 12 queries is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Run it and read your own numbers. Some labels are longer than the 480-token budget, so the AST chunker splits them too and neither chunker can score whole on them. namedtuple and _make_iterencode are the obvious ones; dumps (its docstring alone is long) and py_scanstring may be over as well, depending on your Python version. Expect that, and look at which chunk comes back instead. For a real decision, write 50 to 100 queries against your own repo, from real questions people asked in code review or on Slack, and keep the file in version control next to the chunker.

Before you point it at your repo

Four changes take this from a stdlib demo to something you would index a monorepo with.

More languages. tree-sitter has grammars for most languages you will meet, but node type names differ per grammar. function_definition is the Python name; check each grammar's node-types.json and give every language its own DEFS set. If you want a maintained version for Python, Java, C# and TypeScript, astchunk already does it.

Parse errors. tree-sitter is built to keep producing useful results even when the source has syntax errors, so a half-written file mid-refactor still produces a tree. py-tree-sitter exposes has_error on every node. Check it on the root, and when a file is badly broken, fall back to fixed_chunks for that file rather than indexing garbage boundaries.

A code-aware embedder. bge-small-en-v1.5 is a general English model with a WordPiece tokenizer that shreds snake_case and camelCase into fragments. It works for the demo. For production, compare a code-trained embedding model on your labelled set using the same eval.py; that is what the set is for.

Keyword search next to vectors. Exact identifiers, error codes and config keys are where dense retrieval is weakest. Index the symbol field in a keyword index too and fuse the results. A query that contains raw_decode should find raw_decode without asking an embedding model to guess.

If this was useful

A retriever can only return what the chunker kept together, and code makes that easy to see. The RAG Pocket Guide covers the stages on either side of this one, retrieval and reranking, plus the chunking patterns for production RAG. If you are building search over a codebase or anything else with structure, it is the short version of the decisions this post only touches.

title: LLM Regression Testing for Jira with CogniRunner
description:
LLM regression testing means running the same labelled inputs again after you change a prompt or a model, to see what the change broke. This tutorial does that for an AI check on a Jira workflow validator. Here the test set is a Jira filter of 8 labelled requests. An 80-line Node script runs it. Each call goes to CogniRunner's rule test over REST, which reads the issue, asks the model and writes nothing to Jira.

I ran it on 13 October 2026 because I wanted to move a validator from openai/gpt-6-luna to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5. Over three rounds, the site's model matched 6, 7 and 7 of the 8 labels. The candidate matched 8 of 8. I built the test expecting the candidate to miss, and it was the site's model that missed (I'd have bet the other way).

I found the cause in the rule, and I don't think it says much about either model. Our HR check says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone". Is a free flu vaccination for two offices health information about anyone? Our rule didn't say. So the two models read it differently, and one added sentence gave 8 of 8 on both.

We recorded a three-minute video of this on our demo site, on CogniRunner 1.34.0. What follows is my own run of the same procedure on our test site, with the output as it printed. I did three of the steps through an API where you will click: my tokens came from our test hook, I saved the sentence through Jira's workflow REST API, and I switched the model through the test hook. The video shows those screens, and I give the timestamp at each step.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMpvV03upQA

[!NOTE]
Prerequisites

  • A Jira Cloud site with CogniRunner 1.34.0 or later. The Marketplace calls that build 7.16.0, released 12 October 2026. I ran a development build of 1.34.0 on our test site.
  • An AI provider saved in CogniRunner's Settings. Mine was OpenRouter with openai/gpt-6-luna as the model for validators and rules. If you haven't set one up, the provider tutorial covers it.
  • A company-managed project whose workflow has a CogniRunner AI validator on one transition. Mine was called Send for Review.
  • An email and API token for Jira's REST API. The script reads the published workflow. I ran it as a Jira admin.
  • A CogniRunner admin, to create the REST API token in step 2.
  • Node 18 or later. I used Node v24.15.0. The script has no dependencies.

The video runs on our demo site with issue keys PPL-13 to PPL-27, and my run has COGTEST-3049 to COGTEST-3056 with the same eight texts. Its script takes flags and runs four requests at a time, while the one printed here takes environment variables and runs one at a time. In the video the first round is 7 of 8. Mine was 6 of 8.

[[steps]]

  1. Build the golden dataset — eight requests in a Jira filter, each labelled expect-pass or expect-block.
  2. Create a token — Settings, the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API.
  3. Save the script — it reads the saved rule from Jira and calls the rule test for each request.
  4. Run the baseline — the site's own model, three rounds.
  5. Run the candidate — one variable, and the site's model stays as it is.
  6. Read the mismatch — decide whether the model or the rule is wrong.
  7. Try the sentence, save it, run both again — first unsaved, then saved.
  8. Switch the site's model — and find the switch and the tests in the audit log.

What one rule test does: one field, one prompt, nothing written

A CogniRunner AI validator sits on a workflow transition. Somebody moves the request. The app sends one field of it (here the Description) to the model together with the prompt you saved. Back comes pass or fail, with a reason. Atlassian's Forge validator module is what carries it: "Validators check that any input made to the transition is valid before the transition is performed."

You may know the Test button in the rule editor. CogniRunner's Rules REST API has the same thing as a call: POST ?resource=rules&action=test. Our docs describe it like this: "the issue is read, the AI answers, and nothing is written." The body carries the issue key, the field and the prompt. Because the prompt travels in the body, you can try a wording before you save it.

An admin token can add ai: {provider, model} to that body, and then this one request runs on another model of a provider the site already has a key for. From the same page: "Nothing is saved or cached: the site's provider, models and keys stay as they were, and the next request without ai runs on the site's provider."

So the whole procedure is a loop over a filter. The same call takes other kinds of rule as well, and I tested validators. The rest of this API is in the release post for Marketplace version 3.3.0 and on the product page. Another thing you can do to the same validator is hand it a document, and the tutorial on giving one an API spec covers that.

Step 1. Build the golden dataset: a Jira filter of 8 labelled issues

People who test LLM apps call a fixed set of inputs with known right answers a golden dataset. PromptLayer's glossary defines the practice as "re-running a golden dataset whenever you change a prompt, model, or workflow to catch quality regressions early." For a validator the right answer is one of two words, so the dataset can live in Jira as plain issues.

Create eight requests in the project the validator guards. Give each the label gate-test, and then expect-pass or expect-block. Mine were four of each:

Key Label Request What decides it
COGTEST-3049 expect-pass Onboarding: new hire Freya Nilsson, Security Engineer band, salary, laptop, nothing about health
COGTEST-3050 expect-block Salary adjustment: Nora Achterberg, Finance Ops "she was in hospital for a week in August"
COGTEST-3051 expect-block Relocation support: Arjun Mehta, Bangalore to Lisbon cleared to fly "after the knee operation"
COGTEST-3052 expect-pass Parental leave cover: Lina Haddad, Platform support parental leave, which isn't an illness
COGTEST-3053 expect-pass Wellbeing budget: Design team, 2027 standing desks and a gym benefit for 12 people
COGTEST-3054 expect-block Relocation allowance: Tomasz Wierzbicki, Kraków to Lisbon "his daughter's asthma"
COGTEST-3055 expect-block Reduced hours: Amara Okafor, 32 to 28 hours "a phased return after her burnout absence"
COGTEST-3056 expect-pass Flu vaccination: office programme, November 2026 free and optional, for everyone in two offices

All of these people are made up. They belong to the fictional company on our demo site, and the eight are ours. Write yours from requests your own people sent, with the names changed.

Then save the search as a filter. Mine is called Gate tests: HR health check, with this JQL:

project = COGTEST AND labels = gate-test ORDER BY key ASC

Note the filter's id from its URL. Mine was 12450.

Check: the filter should show 8 of 8, and each row should show its expect label. If a row shows another label first, remove the extra labels. Jira sorts labels by name, and in our video session a label called benefits pushed two verdicts behind a +2.

Is eight enough? Probably not for a rule that matters a lot. Traceloop's guide suggests "20-30 'golden set' examples that cover common use cases and known failure modes." Our eight came out of 28 candidates. Our video session ran those 28 on both models, 600 dry runs in all. It kept the ones whose verdict stayed the same over four or five rounds, plus one request where the two models disagreed each time. Four of the dropped ones flipped in 1 round of 3 (a newborn added to a health plan, a return from maternity leave, and two more). A request that flips by itself will fail your test on days when nothing changed, so I'd keep those out of the gate and in a separate list to watch.

Step 2. Create a token for CogniRunner's REST API

Open CogniRunner's admin page, go to the Settings tab and find the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API. It opens on Viewer and Their own rules. Change those to Admin and Everyone's rules. My tokens had both, and I haven't tried a narrower one. Type a name and click Create token. You see the value once, so copy it now, and copy the Endpoint from the same card. The video shows this card at 0:34, with its two tokens already made.

Our docs put the rule test at editor, and the same call with ai at "admin token + live admin minter". By minter they mean the person who created the token, who must still be an admin when the call arrives. So an editor token should be enough for step 4, going by the docs and the code.

Tokens run out. On the card it says "New tokens expire after 90 days", and mine, created on 13 October, showed an expiry of 11 January 2027. Also treat the endpoint address as private too. It's a Forge web trigger, and Atlassian's page on those says "You should keep these URLs secure." CogniRunner asks for the bearer token on top. I still mask the address everywhere, this page included.

Put the values in your shell:

export JIRA_SITE=https://wolfaenpak.atlassian.net JIRA_EMAIL=<admin email> JIRA_API_TOKEN=<jira api token>
export RULES_API_URL=<rules-api> RULES_API_TOKEN=cgr_<masked>
export WORKFLOW="Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST" TRANSITION="Send for Review" FILTER=12450

That first value is our test site, so put your own there. WORKFLOW is the workflow's name as Jira's workflow list shows it. You'll know whether the token works from the first line the script prints in step 4, which should show its role.

Step 3. Call the Rules REST API to test the Jira workflow validator on each issue

Save this as gate-test.mjs. It needs no packages. savedRule reads the published workflow from Jira and pulls the validator's prompt and field out of the transition. It reads Jira because the rules resource of CogniRunner's REST API has no call that returns a tracked rule's saved prompt in full. testSet reads the filter and takes the expected verdict from the label. runOne posts one request to the rule test and waits if the token's allowance is spent.

#!/usr/bin/env node
// gate-test.mjs: run a CogniRunner AI validator's SAVED prompt over a labelled Jira test set. Node 18+, no dependencies.
// Every call is a dry run (POST ?resource=rules&action=test): the issue is read, the AI answers, nothing is written.
//   JIRA_SITE=https://you.atlassian.net JIRA_EMAIL=... JIRA_API_TOKEN=... \
//   RULES_API_URL=<the Rules REST API address from CogniRunner Settings> RULES_API_TOKEN=cgr_... \
//   WORKFLOW="<workflow name>" TRANSITION="Send for Review" FILTER=<filter id> node gate-test.mjs
// Optional: CANDIDATE_MODEL=<provider>/<model id> runs each request on that model instead (needs an ADMIN token; the
//   site's own model is not changed). CANDIDATE_PROVIDER defaults to openrouter. ADD_SENTENCE="..." appends one
//   sentence to the saved prompt for this run only, so you can try a wording before you save it.
const E = process.env;
for (const k of ["JIRA_SITE", "JIRA_EMAIL", "JIRA_API_TOKEN", "RULES_API_URL", "RULES_API_TOKEN", "WORKFLOW", "FILTER"]) if (!E[k]) { console.error(`Set ${k}`); process.exit(2); }
const TRANSITION = E.TRANSITION || "Send for Review";
const JAUTH = "Basic " + Buffer.from(`${E.JIRA_EMAIL}:${E.JIRA_API_TOKEN}`).toString("base64");
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const pad = (s, n) => String(s ?? "").padEnd(n).slice(0, n);

async function jira(path, body) {
  const r = await fetch(E.JIRA_SITE + path, { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: JAUTH, Accept: "application/json", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
  if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`Jira ${path}: ${r.status} ${(await r.text()).slice(0, 200)}`);
  return r.json();
}
async function rules(method, query, body) {
  const r = await fetch(`${E.RULES_API_URL}?${query}`, { method, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${E.RULES_API_TOKEN}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined });
  const text = await r.text(); let json = null; try { json = JSON.parse(text); } catch { /* not JSON */ }
  return { status: r.status, json, retryAfter: Number(r.headers.get("retry-after") || 0) };
}

// 1. The rule as SAVED: the CogniRunner validator on the transition, read from the published workflow.
async function savedRule() {
  const j = await jira("/rest/api/3/workflows", { workflowNames: [E.WORKFLOW] });
  for (const w of j.workflows || []) for (const t of w.transitions || []) {
    if (t.name !== TRANSITION) continue;
    for (const v of t.validators || []) {
      if (!/ai-text-field-validator/.test(v.parameters?.key || "")) continue;
      const c = JSON.parse(v.parameters.config);
      return { prompt: c.prompt, fieldId: c.fieldId || "description", enableTools: c.enableTools === true, version: w.version?.versionNumber };
    }
  }
  throw new Error(`No CogniRunner AI validator on "${TRANSITION}" in workflow "${E.WORKFLOW}"`);
}
// 2. The test set: every issue in the filter; the expected verdict is its label.
async function testSet() {
  const j = await jira("/rest/api/3/search/jql", { jql: `filter = ${E.FILTER} ORDER BY key ASC`, fields: ["summary", "labels"], maxResults: 100 });
  return (j.issues || []).map((i) => ({ key: i.key, expected: i.fields.labels.includes("expect-block") ? "BLOCK" : i.fields.labels.includes("expect-pass") ? "PASS" : "?" }))
    .sort((a, b) => Number(a.key.split("-")[1]) - Number(b.key.split("-")[1]));
}
// 3. One dry run through the test door. A 429 means the token's AI allowance is spent: wait for Retry-After.
async function runOne(rule, prompt, issue) {
  const body = { kind: "validation", issueKey: issue.key, prompt, fieldId: rule.fieldId, enableTools: rule.enableTools };
  if (E.CANDIDATE_MODEL) body.ai = { provider: E.CANDIDATE_PROVIDER || "openrouter", model: E.CANDIDATE_MODEL };
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const t0 = Date.now(); const r = await rules("POST", "resource=rules&action=test", body);
    if (r.status === 429) { const s = r.retryAfter || 60; console.error(`  429 on ${issue.key}: allowance spent, waiting ${s} s`); await sleep(s * 1000); continue; }
    if (r.status === 202) return { ...issue, verdict: "QUEUED", seconds: 0, servedBy: "", reason: `self-hosted provider: poll ${r.json.poll}` };
    const res = r.json?.result || {};
    const verdict = r.status !== 200 ? `HTTP ${r.status}` : res.success && res.isValid === true ? "PASS" : res.success && res.isValid === false ? "BLOCK" : "NOT JUDGED";
    return { ...issue, verdict, seconds: Math.round((Date.now() - t0) / 100) / 10, servedBy: r.json?.ai?.servedBy?.map((s) => s.model).join(",") || res.modelUsed || "",
      reason: res.reason || res.error || r.json?.error || "" };
  }
  return { ...issue, verdict: "GAVE UP", seconds: 0, servedBy: "", reason: "429 four times" };
}

const who = await rules("GET", "resource=whoami");
if (who.status !== 200) { console.error(`whoami: HTTP ${who.status} ${who.json?.error || ""}`); process.exit(1); }
const spend = who.json.aiSpend || {};
console.log(`Token role: ${who.json.effective?.role} · AI actions used ${spend.window?.used}/${spend.window?.limit} in this 10-minute window, ${spend.today?.actions}/${spend.today?.limit} today`);
const rule = await savedRule();
const prompt = E.ADD_SENTENCE ? `${rule.prompt} ${E.ADD_SENTENCE.trim()}` : rule.prompt;
const set = await testSet();
console.log(`Rule: ${E.WORKFLOW} · ${TRANSITION} · reads ${rule.fieldId} · workflow version ${rule.version}`);
console.log(`Prompt (${E.ADD_SENTENCE ? "saved + one sentence, this run only" : "as saved"}): ${prompt}`);
console.log(`Model: ${E.CANDIDATE_MODEL ? `${E.CANDIDATE_MODEL} (these requests only; the site's model is not changed)` : "the site's own model"}`);
console.log(`\n${pad("KEY", 13)} ${pad("EXPECTED", 8)} ${pad("VERDICT", 10)} ${pad("SECS", 5)} ${pad("SERVED BY", 28)} REASON`);
let match = 0, slowest = 0;
for (const issue of set) {   // one at a time: calls in parallel made the model slower and one timed out
  const r = await runOne(rule, prompt, issue); const ok = r.verdict === r.expected; if (ok) match++; slowest = Math.max(slowest, r.seconds);
  console.log(`${pad(r.key, 13)} ${pad(r.expected, 8)} ${pad(r.verdict + (ok ? "" : " ✗"), 10)} ${pad(r.seconds, 5)} ${pad(r.servedBy, 28)} ${r.verdict === "PASS" ? "" : r.reason}`);
}
console.log(`\n${match} of ${set.length} match · slowest ${slowest} s`);
process.exit(match === set.length ? 0 : 1);

Why one request at a time? In the video session, four calls in flight pushed the site's model to 16.1 seconds. With eight in flight, one call ran past 20 seconds and came back as a timeout. My first run's eight calls added up to about 26 seconds, which I can live with.

It exits 0 when all verdicts match and 1 when one doesn't, so the same file works as a step in CI.

Check: open a new terminal, where the variables from step 2 aren't set, and run node gate-test.mjs there. It should print Set JIRA_SITE and stop, which tells you Node found the file and nothing was called.

Step 4. Run the LLM regression testing baseline on the site's model

With the variables from step 2 exported:

node gate-test.mjs

Rule: Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST · Send for Review · reads description · workflow version 1079
Prompt (as saved): Fail it if it contains health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment. This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes.
Model: the site's own model

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.5   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.8   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Nora was in hospital for a week in August.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.5   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his physiotherapist cleared him to fly after knee surgery.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     BLOCK ✗    2.6   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Lina Haddad is on parental leave.

Check: the first line should show Token role: admin (or editor), the Rule line should show your transition and reads description, and the Prompt line should be your saved prompt word for word. Under SERVED BY you see the model that answered.

So that's two misses. I ran the same command twice more and got 7 of 8 both times. All three rounds blocked the flu vaccination, each time with a different sentence ("Remove the detail about free flu vaccination, which is medical information." was round two). Parental leave was blocked in the first round and passed in the next two.

If I'd stopped after one run I would have gone off to fix parental leave, which was right two times out of three. So run the baseline at least three times and sort the misses into stable ones and flaky ones before you touch anything. Here the stable one is COGTEST-3056.

Watch the allowance while you do. A token gets 20 AI actions per 10 minutes, and three rounds of eight are 24. I used a new token for each pair of rounds. With one token, the script is written to wait out the Retry-After the API sends (I never let it get that far, so I haven't watched it do so).

Step 5. Switch from OpenAI's model to Claude for one request, not the whole site

Same command, one more variable:

CANDIDATE_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 node gate-test.mjs

Token role: admin · AI actions used 8/20 in this 10-minute window, 8/200 today
Rule: Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST · Send for Review · reads description · workflow version 1079
Prompt (as saved): Fail it if it contains health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment. This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes.
Model: anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 (these requests only; the site's model is not changed)

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.2   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      3     anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the sentence stating that Nora was in hospital for a week in August, as it discloses medical information.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.8   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to the knee operation and physiotherapist clearance, which is medical information about an employee.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     PASS       4.5   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3053  PASS     PASS       3     anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3054  BLOCK    BLOCK      4.5   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to the daughter's asthma, since it is a medical condition about a family member.
COGTEST-3055  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.1   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to her burnout absence and occupational health involvement, as these disclose medical or health information about an employee.
COGTEST-3056  PASS     PASS       7.4   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   

8 of 8 match · slowest 7.4 s

Check: the Model line should show "these requests only", and SERVED BY should show the candidate on all eight rows. Then open CogniRunner's Settings. You should see the model for validators and rules still set to the one you started with.

Both models here are reached through OpenRouter. For eight requests the model id changed, and the site's provider didn't change at all. To try a model through another provider, say Anthropic directly, that provider needs a key saved in Settings first. A request can't bring one. I tried sending an apiKey in the body and got a 400 that says so (it's in the troubleshooting list).

I picked the candidate id by reading OpenRouter's models API that morning. anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 was the newest Claude Haiku id on it, listed as created on 7 October 2026. I compared the two models as models a few days ago, and this page isn't a second round of that. Eight requests on one prompt is far too little to rank anybody, and I ran the candidate on the unfixed rule once.

Step 6. Read the mismatch: the rule did not say what HR meant

Here is the Description of the request the site's model kept blocking:

Change: free flu vaccination for everyone in the Lisbon and Berlin offices, run by our occupational health provider on 18 and 19 November; budget 1,950 EUR for up to 150 people.
Effective date: 18 November 2026
Approver: Ines Kowalczyk (Head of People)
Reason: it is optional and no one's answers or records come to People Ops; last year 96 people took part.

And the rule says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment". A vaccination is a treatment. Read literally, the site's model has a case.

What did HR mean, though? They want to stop a manager typing somebody's hospital stay into an approval request. GDPR's definition of data concerning health is "personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status". A vaccination is a health care service. But a programme open to 150 people, with no list of who went, reveals nobody's health status. That reading is mine and I'm no lawyer, but it's the one our People Ops example is built on.

The rule left room for both readings, and I think each model took one. Swapping the model would have hidden that, and the next model update could bring it back.

Our video session tried three sentences before the one that worked. Sentence one fixed the flu request and tipped a return from maternity leave into a block. That happened in all 3 runs on the site's model and 1 of 3 on the candidate. Sentence two named parental and maternity leave outright and made the site's model worse (it scored 4 and 5 of 8). Sentence three left a burnout-risk request wrong in 2 runs of 2. Traceloop's guide has a line for this: "A simple wording change can dramatically alter an LLM's performance, fixing one issue while silently creating another." So after an edit I run all eight again.

This one held:

A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is.

Step 7. Run prompt regression testing after the one-sentence fix

Try the sentence before saving it. ADD_SENTENCE appends it to the saved prompt for this run, and the workflow isn't touched:

ADD_SENTENCE="A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is." node gate-test.mjs

Token role: admin · AI actions used 0/20 in this 10-minute window, 0/200 today
Rule: Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST · Send for Review · reads description · workflow version 1079
Prompt (saved + one sentence, this run only): Fail it if it contains health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment. This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes. A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is.
Model: the site's own model

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.3   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Nora was in hospital for a week in August.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      4     openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his physiotherapist cleared him to fly only after the knee operation.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     PASS       4.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3053  PASS     PASS       3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3054  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.3   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his daughter’s asthma is worse in Kraków’s winters.
COGTEST-3055  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.8   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail about her burnout absence and phased return agreed with occupational health.
COGTEST-3056  PASS     PASS       4     openai/gpt-6-luna            

8 of 8 match · slowest 4.7 s

Two more rounds on the site's model gave 8 of 8 again. So did one round with CANDIDATE_MODEL set.

Then save it. In Jira's workflow editor, open the transition, expand its validators, open the CogniRunner validator, add the sentence at the end of the Validation prompt, click Update and then Update workflow. The video does this at 1:32. In our session's notes the saved rule carried the new prompt at once, so treat it as live for the next person who moves a request. To undo it, take the sentence out the same way. The session put the old prompt back between takes.

Run both commands once more, without ADD_SENTENCE:

node gate-test.mjs
CANDIDATE_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 node gate-test.mjs

The last line of each, as mine printed:

8 of 8 match · slowest 3.5 s
8 of 8 match · slowest 5.1 s

Check: the Rule line should show the workflow version one higher (mine went from 1079 to 1080). Its Prompt line should show "as saved" and end with the new sentence.

Step 8. Switch the site's model and read the audit log

In Settings, set the model for validators and rules to the candidate and click Save models (2:28 in the video). Then run the plain command again:

node gate-test.mjs

Model: the site's own model

8 of 8 match · slowest 9.4 s

Those are the Model line and the last line. SERVED BY read anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 on all eight rows with no CANDIDATE_MODEL set. That 9.4 seconds was the slowest call of the morning.

Open the Audit log and search for your provider's name.

Check: you should see a row labelled AI model changed that reads "Set the OpenRouter model to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 (was openai/gpt-6-luna)." Under it there's one row per candidate test: "Tested a validator on COGTEST-3056 with OpenRouter (anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5), 1 AI call; the site's own provider was not changed."

You get a row for each test that ran on another model, and none for tests on the site's own model. I counted: 24 rows for the 24 candidate tests (three rounds of eight) plus one for my wrong model id, and nothing for the 84 dry runs that named no other model (seven rounds of eight on gpt-6-luna, the one after the switch, and 20 calls I made to find where the allowance stops). That makes sense to me. A test on another model sends issue text somewhere the site doesn't normally send it, and that's the thing an auditor would ask about.

Those rows name the issue because of this exercise, by the way. When the video session first ran it on 1.33.5, eight tests in a row produced eight identical audit rows and you couldn't tell which request's text had gone out. Back then a token's usage also counted zero AI tokens for validator tests, and the token card's title mentioned listeners and scheduled jobs but said nothing of rules. Those were three bugs of ours, and 1.34.0 fixes them.

Run the set more than once: one verdict flipped in 1 of 3 rounds

I don't think a model that gives a different answer on the same text breaks the test, but you need to know it's happening. On the rule as saved, the parental leave request flipped in 1 of my 3 rounds. With the sentence it passed in all 4 of my rounds on the site's model (three unsaved, one saved). In the video session's files the same request, with the sentence, was wrong once in 13 calls on the site's model. That one miss arrived during a recording. They threw the take away. Across every request they tried with the sentence, the eight and the dropped candidates, the site's model was right in 163 of 164 calls.

One more thing a matching verdict doesn't tell you. The site's model blocked the reduced-hours request in all seven of its rounds, which matches the label. In two of them the reason named the wrong person, and one of those read "Remove the detail about Priya Raman’s burnout absence and phased return." The request is Amara Okafor's. Priya Raman is the approver. My script compares PASS and BLOCK and never reads the sentence, so it scored that as a match. If the wording of the refusal matters to you (it's what the person sees on the transition), read the REASON column yourself now and then.

Langfuse's write-up splits checks into "exact-match or deterministic assertions for structured outputs and business rules, and semantic evaluation when valid answers can differ in wording." A verdict against a label is the first kind. Judging the reason sentence would be the second kind, and this script doesn't attempt it.

If it didn't work

I sent each of these on purpose and got these answers from the API on 1.34.0.

What I sent What came back
A bearer value that isn't a CogniRunner token HTTP 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}
The 21st AI action on one token inside one 10-minute window HTTP 429, Retry-After: 218, "This API token has started 20 AI actions (listener tests, job runs, agent ticks, agent uploads) in the last 10 minutes, which is its limit. Try again in 218 seconds."
ai: {provider: "claude"} HTTP 400 Unknown AI provider "claude". Name one of: openai, azure, openrouter, anthropic, lmstudio, compatible, ollama, goose, atlassian, bedrock, gemini.
ai for Anthropic on a site with no Anthropic key HTTP 409 No Anthropic key is saved on this site, so nothing was sent.
ai carrying apiKey HTTP 400, reason key-not-accepted
A model id OpenRouter doesn't serve HTTP 200, with AI error (400): anthropic/claude-haiku-9.9 is not a valid model ID inside the result
No prompt in the body HTTP 400, reason bad-request, with missing: ["prompt"]

You'll meet the 429 first. A token gets 20 AI actions per 10 minutes and 200 a day. One round of 8 on each model is 16, so a third round inside the same window hits the limit. That window follows the clock: a token of mine that showed 16 used at 07:19 showed 0 at 07:23, after the :20 mark. For the app's other meter, see the rate limit tutorial.

Be careful with a wrong model id, because the HTTP status is 200. For that answer the script prints NOT JUDGED and counts a mismatch. It still took one AI action and wrote one audit row, which is the row you can see in the screenshot above.

If savedRule throws on JSON.parse, look at how your validator's config is stored in the workflow. It was plain JSON on both sites I read. I haven't checked a very large config.

What this set doesn't test

A validator reads one field. Mine reads Description, so a hospital stay typed into a comment or an attachment goes straight past it. Treat the check as a quality gate before HR approves. I wouldn't call it a security control.

A dry run takes as long as the model takes. A live transition allows 20 seconds. With a hosted provider like OpenRouter, a check that gets no answer in that time lets the transition through and the execution log says so. Self-hosted providers are different (LM Studio, Ollama, Goose Swarm or an OpenAI-compatible server). For those, 1.34.0 added a hold you can turn on. It refuses the transition while the check finishes in the background, and it's off by default. My slowest dry run was 9.4 seconds, so neither case came up. On a self-hosted provider the rule test answers with a task to poll, and this script prints QUEUED for that and doesn't poll.

I didn't make a real transition on this run. Our video session did, on 12 October, on the demo site. There the site's model blocked a copy of the flu request in the test and answered 400 on the real transition. With the candidate set, the test passed and the request moved for real. So I have one pair, a day old.

Jira has nothing like this built in that I could find. Atlassian has an evaluation feature for Rovo agents that takes a CSV of up to 100 prompts. It's for agents. Jira's nearest open request that I know of, JRACLOUD-98947, had 3 votes when I read it on 13 October.

What you have now

[[takeaways]]

  • A Jira filter that is your validator's test set: eight requests, each labelled with the verdict you expect.
  • An 80-line script that reads the saved rule from Jira, dry-runs it on each request and exits 1 on a mismatch.
  • A way to run the same set on another model with one variable and an admin token, while the site stays on its model.
  • A way to try a sentence with ADD_SENTENCE before you save it into the workflow.
  • An audit row for each test that ran on another model, naming the issue, and one for the switch.
  • A baseline you ran three times, so you know which misses are stable.

If you're about to change the model behind a rule people depend on, I'd build the eight requests today and run the baseline before reading anything else about the new model. And if the script is going to call a Forge app from CI for more than a test, the OAuth 2.0 tutorial shows the other way in.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: Host up to 10 WordPress sites for free with Oracle Cloud and xCloud
description:
I wanted a place to run a handful of WordPress sites (test sites, demos, a personal page) without paying for hosting every month. The combination that worked: a free Oracle Cloud server, managed through xCloud's free plan, so I never had to install the web server, PHP or SSL by hand.

This is the full walkthrough, including the parts that tripped me up: Oracle's "Out of capacity" error, a card hold that looked like a charge, and a firewall rule that silently did nothing.

Run WordPress sites on a free Oracle Cloud server, managed through xCloud's free plan.

  • Oracle Cloud Always Free gives you the server (the land).
  • xCloud free Self-Managed plan installs and manages the web server, PHP, database and SSL (the builder).
  • Only cost: a domain name (about $10–13/year), and only if you want your own address.

How it fits together

The cover image above shows the whole setup: a visitor's browser finds your server through DNS, passes Oracle's two firewalls, and reaches the Ubuntu server that xCloud manages.

The build, in short:

  1. Create a free Oracle account and a network that allows web traffic (Parts 1–2).
  2. Create one Ubuntu 24.04 server on that network (Part 3).
  3. Log in, open the web ports inside the server, and add swap if it's the 1 GB one (Part 4).
  4. Give xCloud root access with its key; xCloud installs the web server, PHP and database (Part 5).
  5. Point a domain at the server (Part 6), then add sites from the xCloud dashboard (Part 7).

Running up to 10 sites

xCloud's free plan allows 1 server with up to 10 sites. All of them live on the same Oracle server and share its CPU and memory.

  • One domain is enough. Each site gets a free subdomain: example.dev, blog.example.dev, shop.example.dev, lab.example.dev, …
  • One DNS record covers all subdomains. A wildcard A record (* → server IP) points every subdomain at the server, so a new site needs no DNS change.
  • Each site is added the same way in xCloud (Part 7) and gets its own SSL certificate, database and WordPress install.
  • Testing without a domain: use xCloud's Demo Site option for a free temporary address, and switch to a real domain later.

How many sites the server can really carry:

Server Realistic number of sites
ARM 2 OCPU / 12 GB All 10, if they are ordinary WordPress sites with caching on
AMD Micro 1 GB (+2 GB swap) 3–5 quiet sites (tests, demos, personal pages). Not WooCommerce or real traffic

If you start on the 1 GB server and outgrow it, create the ARM server later and move the sites over with xCloud's site migration. The free xCloud plan covers only one server at a time.

Last checked: October 2026. Oracle and xCloud change their screens and limits, so a label may read slightly differently from this guide.

What you get

Item Free allowance
xCloud Free plan 1 server, up to 10 sites
Oracle ARM server (VM.Standard.A1.Flex) 2 OCPU / 12 GB RAM total (halved from 4/24 in June 2026)
Oracle AMD server (VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro) Up to 2 servers, 1 GB RAM each
Oracle disk 200 GB total, across all boot volumes
Oracle outbound traffic 10 TB per month

Which server?

  • ARM, 2 OCPU / 12 GB: comfortable for several WordPress sites. Often unavailable on free accounts (see Out of capacity).
  • AMD Micro, 1 GB: almost always available. Good for 1 small site or a handful of quiet test sites.

Before you start

  • A credit or debit card (Oracle uses it for identity checks; Always Free resources are not billed).
  • An xCloud account: https://xcloud.host
  • A terminal with ssh (macOS/Linux built in; Windows: PowerShell or WSL).
  • Optional: an SSH key. Check with ls ~/.ssh/*.pub. If none exists, create one: 
ssh-keygen -t ed25519

Part 1 — Create the Oracle Cloud account

  1. Sign up at https://www.oracle.com/cloud/free/.
  2. Choose your Home Region carefully. It can never be changed, and free servers only run there. Pick a region close to your visitors.
  3. Finish card verification and wait for the account to be ready.

Part 2 — Create the network (VCN)

Create the network before the server. The inline network option in the server form has a bug that can lock the public IP off.

  1. ☰ menu → Networking → Virtual Cloud Networks.
  2. On the left, under Compartment, choose your root compartment (your account name).
  3. Click Start VCN Wizard (it may be under Actions).
  4. Choose Create VCN with Internet Connectivity → Start VCN Wizard.
  5. Fill in:
Field Value
VCN name xcloud-vcn
VCN IPv4 CIDR block 10.0.0.0/16
Public subnet CIDR 10.0.0.0/24
Private subnet CIDR 10.0.1.0/24
  1. Next → Create. Wait until every line has a green tick, then View VCN.

Open web ports (80 and 443)

Port 22 (SSH) is already open. Add the web ports:

  1. In the VCN, open Security Lists → Default Security List for xcloud-vcn.
  2. Add Ingress Rules:
Field Value
Source Type CIDR
Source CIDR 0.0.0.0/0
IP Protocol TCP
Source Port Range (empty)
Destination Port Range 80,443
Description web
  1. Save. You should now see three TCP rules from 0.0.0.0/0: 22, 80, 443.

Part 3 — Create the server (instance)

  1. ☰ → Compute → Instances → Create instance.
  2. Basic information
    • Name: e.g. xcloud-server
    • Placement: default availability domain
    • Shape → Change shape (do this before the image):
      • ARM: Ampere → VM.Standard.A1.Flex, 2 OCPU, 12 GB
      • or AMD: Specialty and previous generation → VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro
    • Image → Change image → Ubuntu → Canonical Ubuntu 24.04 (not "Minimal")
  3. Security: leave as is.
  4. Networking
    • Existing VCN: xcloud-vcn
    • Existing subnet: the public subnet
    • Automatically assign public IPv4 address: on
    • SSH keys: Paste public key (contents of your ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub), or Generate a key pair for me and click Download private key right away. You cannot download it later.
  5. Storage
    • Tick Specify a custom boot volume size
    • Enter 100 GB (keep the total of all your boot volumes at 200 GB or less to stay free)
  6. Create. Wait for Running, then copy the Public IP address.

Out of capacity

Out of capacity for shape VM.Standard.A1.Flex in availability domain AD-1 means free ARM machines in your region are all taken. Your settings are fine. Try, in order:

  1. Another availability domain (if your region has more than one).
  2. A smaller size: 1 OCPU / 6 GB.
  3. Retry at a different time of day.
  4. Use the AMD Micro shape instead (1 GB, nearly always available).
  5. Upgrade to Pay As You Go (☰ → Billing & Cost Management → Upgrade and Manage Payment). Paid accounts get capacity much more easily and are not reclaimed when idle. You still pay $0 if you stay within the free allowance.

About the Pay As You Go card hold

Upgrading places a temporary hold of about US$100 on your card (shown in your local currency, e.g. ~S$138). It is a verification hold, not a charge:

  • Check Billing & Cost Management → Invoices: there should be none.
  • Check Cost Analysis: usage should be 0.
  • Your bank releases the hold on its own, usually within days, sometimes up to ~30 days.
  • If it shows as posted (not pending), or an invoice appears, contact Oracle support and your bank.

Set a $1 budget alert (do this on Pay As You Go)

☰ → Billing & Cost Management → Budgets → Create Budget → amount 1, alert at 1% of actual spend, your email. You'll hear about any real charge immediately.

Part 4 — Prepare the server

Log in (replace the IP and key path with yours). The user is ubuntu, not root.

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ubuntu@YOUR_SERVER_IP

If you used an Oracle-generated key:

chmod 600 ~/Downloads/ssh-key-XXXX.key
ssh -i ~/Downloads/ssh-key-XXXX.key ubuntu@YOUR_SERVER_IP

4.1 Add swap (1 GB AMD server only)

Gives the small server spare memory so it doesn't crash under load.

sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
free -h

free -h should show Swap: 2.0Gi.

4.2 Open ports 80 and 443 inside the server

Oracle's Ubuntu image has its own firewall that blocks web traffic, separate from the Security List in Part 2. Both must allow it.

First find the line number of the REJECT rule:

sudo iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers

Example output:

4    ACCEPT  ...  state NEW tcp dpt:22
5    REJECT  ...  reject-with icmp-host-prohibited

Insert the web rules at the REJECT line's number (here 5), so they sit above it. Rules placed below REJECT do nothing.

sudo iptables -I INPUT 5 -m state --state NEW -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -I INPUT 5 -m state --state NEW -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
sudo netfilter-persistent save
sudo iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers

The list should now show 22, 80, 443 before REJECT.

Part 5 — Connect the server to xCloud

  1. In xCloud: Servers → Add Server → Connect Your Existing Server (Any Provider).
  2. Fill in the form:
Field Value
Server Name Any label, e.g. oracle-free
App Type WordPress (optional)
Web Server OpenLiteSpeed (built-in cache, good for small servers). NGINX also works on AMD. On ARM, use OpenLiteSpeed
IP Address Your server's public IP
SSH Port 22
SSH Username root
Database Server Do not leave on None. Pick MariaDB or MySQL (on ARM, MySQL 8.4 is not supported)
Plan Free
SSH Authentication Public Key
  1. xCloud shows a command that adds its key to the server. Copy it and run it on the server (in your ubuntu SSH session). It should print SSH key added successfully.

Oracle blocks direct root login with your key, but root login with an added key works. This command is what lets xCloud in as root.

  1. Tick I have created a new server on my provider → Create.
  2. Wait for provisioning to finish. On a 1 GB server this can take a while.

Part 6 — Get a domain (optional)

You can skip this and use xCloud's free Demo Site address for testing.

For real sites, one domain is enough for many sites, because subdomains are free:
example.dev, blog.example.dev, shop.example.dev, …

When buying:

  • Judge by the renewal price, not the first-year price.
  • Make sure WHOIS privacy is free.
  • Untick add-ons (email, "protection", site builders).
  • .dev and .app domains require HTTPS in every browser. That is fine with xCloud's free SSL, but a site won't load at all until its certificate is issued.

Point the domain to the server

At your registrar's (or Cloudflare's) DNS settings, add A records pointing to your server IP:

Name Type Value
@ A YOUR_SERVER_IP (the main domain)
* A YOUR_SERVER_IP (every subdomain at once)

On Cloudflare, set these to DNS only (grey cloud) until xCloud has issued the SSL certificate. DNS changes can take a few minutes to an hour.

Part 7 — Add a site

Open the server in xCloud → Add Site.

Field What to do
Select Options Default
Site Title Your site's name
Go Live / Demo Site Go Live with your domain, or Demo Site for a free test address
Domain Name e.g. blog.example.dev (Go Live only)
DNS Setup Click Verify My DNS. Keep Use free SSL certificate issued & managed by xCloud
Multisite Off
xSpeed Cache On
Mail Delivery Off for now
Site Backup Off for now
Blueprints Gutenberg Websites, or turn off for clean WordPress. The Elementor blueprint adds weight a small server doesn't need
More Advanced Settings Set the WordPress admin username, password and email; keep the default PHP version

Click Next and wait. Repeat for each additional site with a different title and domain.

Small server tips: keep plugins few, keep caching on, don't run imports or backups on several sites at once. A 1 GB server suits quiet sites only; WooCommerce or real traffic needs the ARM server.

Troubleshooting

Problem Likely cause and fix
ssh asks for a password or says Permission denied Wrong key file or user. Use ubuntu@, and the private key matching the public key you gave Oracle
Please login as the user "ubuntu" rather than "root" You tried root@ directly. Log in as ubuntu
xCloud can't connect The xCloud key command wasn't run, or was run on a different server. Rerun it in your SSH session
Site doesn't load on port 80/443 One of the two firewalls still blocks it: check the Security List (Part 2) and the iptables order (Part 4.2)
Verify My DNS fails DNS not spread yet (wait and retry), wrong IP in the A record, or Cloudflare proxy (orange cloud) is on
Oracle reclaims an idle free server Free accounts can lose a VM whose CPU, network and memory all stay under 20% for 7 days (a warning email comes first). Pay As You Go accounts are not reclaimed

Wrapping up

You now have a server you don't pay for, a dashboard that handles the web server, PHP, database and SSL, and room for up to 10 WordPress sites under one domain.

If you hit a step that looks different on your screen, or found a better way around Oracle's capacity problem, tell me in the comments.
