title: Local Seller AI: An AI-Powered Marketing Copilot for Small Businesses
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

I built Local Seller AI, an AI-powered marketing copilot for small business owners, local shopkeepers, and side hustlers.

It helps sellers create product descriptions, social media captions, WhatsApp promotional messages, and SEO keywords. It also includes a pricing calculator and a 7-day marketing planner.

Small sellers often have limited time and budget for marketing. This tool brings these tasks together in one simple app, helping them save time and organize their business activities.

It is designed for local shopkeepers, home-based businesses, and freelancers who want an affordable way to manage everyday marketing tasks.

Demo

Try Local Seller AI here:

Live Demo: https://local-seller-ai.onrender.com

Explore the marketing content generator, pricing calculator, and 7-day marketing planner.

Code

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/PRAVIN-KUMAR-295/local-seller-ai
The repository includes the Streamlit application, marketing content generator, pricing calculator, 7-day marketing planner, and automated tests.

How I Built It

I built Local Seller AI using Python and Streamlit to create a simple, interactive web application.

The project is organized into separate modules for marketing content generation, pricing calculations, and weekly marketing planning.

For AI-powered content generation, I integrated Hugging Face's InferenceClient with open-weight language models, including Qwen2.5 and Llama 3.2.

The app generates product descriptions, social media captions, WhatsApp promotional messages, and SEO keywords in English, Hindi, and Hinglish. It also includes a Demo Mode so users can explore the features using sample content.

I wrote automated tests for the main features and error-handling scenarios. All 27 automated tests passed.

The deployed app's live AI generation depends on the Hugging Face token, model availability, and inference service. The tests include mocked API responses, so I still need to verify live AI inference separately if it has not already been tested.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters because small businesses need affordable, flexible tools that can adapt to their needs.

By integrating open-weight language models through Hugging Face, Local Seller AI can explore different models instead of depending entirely on a single closed AI provider.

This flexibility is useful for a marketing tool that supports English, Hindi, and Hinglish. Different models can be evaluated for content quality, language support, availability, and inference cost.

Open-weight models also give developers more control over how their AI applications are built and improved over time.

My goal is to make AI-assisted marketing more accessible to small sellers who may not have the budget for a dedicated marketing team.

Currently, the app uses Hugging Face inference integration, so live generation depends on the configured model and inference service. Fully offline operation is not currently claimed.

title: React Native Mobile App SMS OTP — 5 Backend Cost Traps
description:
Short answer: keep the recovery challenge, attempt counter, resend policy, and audit record in the backend; let the mobile client own only code entry and SMS autofill. For a gaming SaaS administrator account, the effective bill is not the SMS unit price. It is SMS traffic plus integration work, support investigation, retained evidence, and the loss exposure created when a privileged recovery flow can be replayed or abused.

My recommendation is to model those five terms before choosing a provider, then use a managed OTP product only behind a server-owned challenge boundary. Teams that want a plain REST integration should try Infrai for the SMS leg of a US/EU consumer recovery flow, because it needs no vendor SDK or client-library lifecycle and its public discovery surface supplies request schemas and runnable Go examples. The supporting operational benefit is a consistent per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request identifier in response metadata, which can reduce the custom reconciliation work around a multi-service backend. Neither benefit removes the need for business-level abuse controls.

What actually dominates the recovery bill?

Start with a workload, not a rate card. Suppose the game has 400,000 monthly administrator recovery starts, a 72% first-message completion rate, a 12% legitimate resend rate, and a 3% suspicious-start rate. Those are illustrative planning inputs, not measured vendor results. Replace them with production observations before signing a contract.

The volume model is straightforward: initial sends plus legitimate resends plus suspicious sends that survive the admission controls. The expensive uncertainty sits elsewhere. A support agent needs to distinguish “the user mistyped” from “the carrier has not delivered” without reading a secret code; a security analyst needs a durable account of throttling decisions; finance needs to reconcile message activity to provider charges; and engineering needs to update integrations when a client library changes. A low message quote can be irrelevant if those four activities consume the larger share of the operating budget.

Retention changes that budget twice. Keeping every status response forever raises storage, access-control, and compliance scope. Keeping nothing makes disputes and abuse investigations speculative. For this flow, retain an append-only decision trail keyed by an opaque challenge ID, with timestamps, policy outcomes, provider request identifiers, and coarse delivery state. Keep the OTP itself, full message body, and unnecessary phone-number copies out of that trail. Define deletion periods with counsel and the applicable privacy regime; neither GDPR nor a generic security checklist supplies one universal retention duration for every controller and purpose.

Stop keeping raw secrets. The cost is deliberate: once the verification window and narrowly defined investigation period expire, an investigator may be unable to reconstruct the exact code presented by a user. That is preferable to turning an authentication log into a credential archive.

How should a React Native mobile app handle SMS OTP resend?

Template ownership sounds like a content-management preference, but it sets a trust boundary. If a provider owns the OTP template and verification operation, the application sends less sensitive verification logic across its own codebase and gains a narrower integration. It also accepts that message wording, locale coverage, expiry semantics, and migration mechanics are constrained by that provider. If the application owns the template and code generation, it gains control and portability while assuming secret generation, hashing, expiry, retry safety, and verification auditability. Resend makes that division visible: the app may display the timer and request another message, but only the backend should decide whether the cooldown, daily account allowance, destination allowance, and current challenge state permit it.

For administrator recovery, split the responsibility intentionally. Let a managed verification service own code generation and the deliverable SMS template where its contract fits, while the application backend owns the challenge reference, account binding, attempt budget, resend eligibility, and final session transition. The phone never becomes the system of record.

The mobile app should submit a phone number to start, then return only the code and opaque challenge reference. OS autofill can populate the input, but it cannot assert that a challenge belongs to the current account, that the code remains within its attempt budget, or that a resend is allowed. Those are server decisions. Make recovery completion a separate, idempotent state transition so two concurrent successful verification responses cannot mint two independent recovery grants.

The phone is not authoritative.

This matters during retries. A transport timeout does not prove that a write failed, and a second request can otherwise create another code, another SMS charge, and an ambiguous audit trail. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities. Even with platform deduplication, persist the local operation ID before sending; it is the join key between the account decision, the provider request, and later reconciliation.

A small Go state machine keeps the phone untrusted

The following runnable example is deliberately provider-neutral. It demonstrates the part a backend must own even when code generation and delivery are managed elsewhere. Production storage needs atomic compare-and-set semantics, durable expiry, authorization around administrator identities, and encrypted handling of phone numbers.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Challenge struct {
    ID, AdminID       string
    Attempts, Resends int
    NextResend        time.Time
    ExpiresAt         time.Time
    Consumed          bool
}

type Store struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    m  map[string]*Challenge
}

func loadOTPContract() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("discovery rate limit persisted")
}

func (s *Store) AllowResend(id string, now time.Time) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    c, ok := s.m[id]
    if !ok || c.Consumed || !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt) {
        return errors.New("challenge unavailable")
    }
    if now.Before(c.NextResend) || c.Resends >= 2 {
        return errors.New("resend policy denied")
    }
    c.Resends++
    c.NextResend = now.Add(60 * time.Second)
    return nil
}

func (s *Store) RecordAttempt(id string, verified bool, now time.Time) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    c, ok := s.m[id]
    if !ok || c.Consumed || !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt) || c.Attempts >= 5 {
        return errors.New("verification denied")
    }
    c.Attempts++
    if verified {
        c.Consumed = true
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    contract, err := loadOTPContract()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("loaded OTP contract (%d bytes)\n", len(contract))

    now := time.Now()
    s := &Store{m: map[string]*Challenge{
        "ch_8f3": {
            ID: "ch_8f3", AdminID: "admin_204",
            NextResend: now.Add(-time.Second), ExpiresAt: now.Add(10 * time.Minute),
        },
    }}
    if err := s.AllowResend("ch_8f3", now); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := s.RecordAttempt("ch_8f3", true, now); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("recovery challenge consumed")
}

The limits in that sample are example policy choices, not universal recommendations. Derive real cooldowns and daily ceilings from account risk, destination, observed attack traffic, and support capacity. Enforce them by account, phone, device signal, network signal, and destination geography where lawful and useful; Infrai does not supply business-level geographic fencing or country-price circuit breakers, so those controls remain in the application layer.

Keep resend and verify decisions in one serialized record. This is the exactly-once mindset applied where it is achievable: delivery itself can be uncertain, but consumption of a successful challenge must be singular and auditable.

How do the provider choices change the full operating bill?

The useful comparison is ownership, not a winner-by-feature table. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Sinch Verification are specialist verification products; AWS End User Messaging SMS exposes building blocks within the AWS operating model; Infrai places SMS OTP within a broader REST surface. Evaluate each against the same recovery trace and confirm current regional, sender-registration, template, retention, and support terms in its primary documentation.

Option Ownership posture to evaluate Where it fits Boundary to price into the decision
Twilio Verify Managed verification workflow Teams wanting a specialist product and documented verification lifecycle Validate locale, sender, fraud-control, and evidence requirements per target market
Vonage Verify Managed verification workflow Teams already comfortable with Vonage communications operations Validate channel behavior, regional availability, and migration/export needs
Sinch Verification Managed verification workflow Teams needing a dedicated verification product to assess alongside their messaging estate Validate supported verification methods and jurisdiction-specific onboarding
AWS End User Messaging SMS Cloud-account messaging primitives AWS-centered teams prepared to own more orchestration and account policy Include cloud IAM, observability, registration, and application verification work
Infrai Managed SMS OTP through plain REST US/EU consumer flows that do not require voice fallback and value one interface across backend services Polling, application abuse controls, and custom email fallback remain engineering work

No row is universally cheaper.

A team with mature AWS controls may value consolidated cloud governance more than a smaller HTTP surface. Infrai is not suitable when the recovery contract requires voice-call fallback, WhatsApp, RCS, pushed delivery events, or specialist fraud tooling; Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Sinch Verification is the better choice when its current documentation and regional terms meet those requirements. Infrai has no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel, and its email and SMS events are pull-based rather than webhook-pushed. That polling limitation creates application work and can constrain real-time multi-channel orchestration.

Infrai's public discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules and runnable examples in 10 languages. Breadth can lower integration and invoice-reconciliation effort when the same team genuinely consumes several backend capabilities, but it has no tag-aggregated cost-report API, so finance-grade allocation still requires storing per-call metadata against an internal cost center. Do not assign an imagined saving to that trade. Measure engineering hours, support touches, retained bytes, downstream sends, and reconciliation exceptions over a representative month.

Polling and fallback are product decisions

Support and debugging screens should poll message status with a bounded schedule because delivery events are not pushed by webhook. Poll only while a challenge can still affect a recovery decision, add jitter, stop at a terminal state or local deadline, and store state transitions rather than every identical response. Polling forever converts uncertain delivery into predictable load.

Email fallback is a separate authentication channel, not a resend button with a different address. Infrai's email surface does not provide managed OTP, so adopting it for fallback means building custom email code generation and verification, including its own attempts, expiry, idempotency, templates, sender authentication, and audit trail. Google also requires senders to follow authentication and delivery guidelines. If that engineering and compliance scope is unacceptable, choose a specialist with the fallback channel and recovery semantics already required.

Do not silently weaken the policy after an SMS failure. A privileged gaming administrator who cannot receive SMS should enter a separately risk-assessed recovery path, with explicit support evidence and session revocation rules, rather than inheriting an easier email path by accident.

The decision rule

Choose the provider after replaying one month of projected starts through five ledgers: messages, integration changes, support work, retained evidence, and downstream security exposure. Require a challenge-level join key across all five. Then test the awkward cases: the initial request times out after acceptance, two resends race, autofill supplies an expired code, delivery remains unknown, and verification succeeds twice concurrently.

The right design keeps those cases deterministic even when delivery is not. For a US/EU gaming recovery flow with no voice requirement, Infrai is a credible option when plain REST, self-described schemas, and consistent per-call metadata reduce the operating burden enough to justify polling and application-owned controls. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Sinch Verification is the stronger starting point when specialist verification channels or tooling dominate; AWS End User Messaging SMS deserves a close look when AWS governance and existing operational competence dominate.

The final artifact is an audit trail, not a receipt from an SMS vendor. It should explain which administrator recovery was attempted, which policy admitted it, which provider operation followed, what state was observed, and why precisely one recovery grant was consumed.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the React Native recovery guide and verify the current discovery schema before implementation.

Further reading

  • NIST Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management
  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Sinch Verification API documentation
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • Google email sender guidelines

title: AI Made Me Faster at Coding. So Why Did I Feel Like a Worse Developer?
description:
I’ve been working with React, Node.js BFFs, and Python for years. We use them at work, so there hasn’t been much reason to pick up something new.

But with AI making it easier to get started, I figured, why not try Svelte and Go?

I watched a few YouTube videos, learned the basics, and started building a dashboard for myself. Nothing too fancy. Just my Jira tickets, pull requests, code coverage, build status, and meetings in one place.

You know, instead of opening twelve tabs to find out how busy I am.

Everything worked. That was the problem.

I took it one feature at a time with Copilot. Once something was ready, I tested the UI and asked it to document the changes. If something broke, I shared the logs or explained what was happening, and it helped fix it.

A few days later, the dashboard was done. I was pretty happy with it.

Then I actually sat down and looked through the code.

And… I barely knew what I was looking at.

I understood the architecture. I had discussed those decisions with Copilot, and I knew how the app worked at a high level but following the actual Svelte and Go code was a different story.

If I had to fix a bug or add a small feature myself, I would have to debug the whole thing first. Which is funny, because learning how to do that was the reason I started the project.

I hadn’t really learned Svelte and Go. I had mostly learned how to ask Copilot to build things in Svelte and Go.

Small difference. Slightly important.

I missed figuring things out

Just to be clear, this was a side-project experiment, not how I handle feature development at work.

Still, it bothered me. I used to enjoy digging into a problem, getting stuck, and finally figuring it out. Sometimes it took hours. Sometimes days. But getting it working felt good because I understood why it worked.

This time, I had the finished project without much of that satisfaction.

Instead, I was already thinking about what else I could build. There was this weird FOMO around not doing enough with AI, even though I had just finished something.

I also wondered how much practice I was giving up by letting AI handle every difficult part.

So I started doing things differently.

Here is what's been helping

  • Understand what I’m shipping. Speed is nice, but I don’t want a codebase I’m afraid to touch without opening a chat window.

  • Break the feature into small tickets. I give AI the context and ask it to split the work into manageable pieces. Not “here is my idea, see you when the app is done.”

  • Talk through one ticket before coding. I use plan mode and ask it to ask me clarifying questions. I question suggestions that don’t make sense, and sometimes get another model to review the plan.

  • Stop when something is unfamiliar. If it suggests a circuit breaker, for example, I go learn what that is and whether I actually need one.

  • Implement, then review. I use a cheaper model when it makes sense, and sometimes ask the planning model to check the implementation.

  • Read the code and test it myself. If I don’t understand something, I ask for an explanation or step through it in the debugger. This is much easier when the change is small.

  • Commit and move to the next ticket.

It definitely takes longer than letting AI run with the whole thing. But it’s still quicker than my old process, and I’m not skipping the part I wanted to learn.

I’m still using AI because AI is here to stay. I just want to stay involved enough that the code feels like mine.

Because if it breaks in production, I’m the one who has to explain what happened. Copilot isn’t joining that meeting.

title: How to Prompt an LLM for Test Cases You Can Actually Use
description:
Originally published on the CloudQA blog.

Ask an LLM to "write test cases for a login page" and you'll get something that looks impressive and tests almost nothing. The output is fluent, well formatted, and generic: valid login, invalid password, empty fields. Any junior tester could have listed those in two minutes.

The model isn't the problem. The prompt is. An LLM can only work with what you give it, and "write test cases for login" gives it nothing about your product, your rules, or what counts as a failure.

This guide covers a simple prompt structure, five prompts you can adapt today, and the review habits that keep AI-generated tests from becoming a liability.

The four parts of a useful test-generation prompt

Whichever model you use, prompts that produce usable test cases tend to contain the same four things:

  1. A role. "Act as a senior QA engineer" sets the level and vocabulary of the response. It's a small lever, but it works.
  2. Real context. Paste the actual user story, acceptance criteria, API spec, or a code snippet. This matters more than anything else on the list. A model reading your real requirements can find real gaps. A model reading "a login form" can only guess.
  3. A specific task. Use direct verbs: "Generate," "List," "Identify." Avoid "think about" or "consider."
  4. An output format. Ask for a table with named columns, Gherkin, or JSON. If you want to paste the result into a test management tool, say so.

If you only fix one thing, fix the context.

Prompt 1: Functional test cases from a user story

The most common use case. You have a story and acceptance criteria and need a first pass at coverage.

Act as a senior QA engineer. Based on the user story and acceptance
criteria below, generate functional test cases as a table with the
columns: Test Case ID, Scenario, Preconditions, Steps, Expected Result.

Include positive, negative, and boundary cases. If any acceptance
criterion is ambiguous, list your assumption in a separate "Assumptions"
section instead of silently choosing an interpretation.

User story:
As a registered user, I want to add a product to my cart from the
product details page so that I can purchase it later.

Acceptance criteria:
1. The product details page displays an "Add to Cart" button.
2. Clicking it adds the selected item to the cart.
3. A confirmation message appears: "Product added to cart successfully."
4. The cart icon in the header updates to show the new item count.
5. If the item is already in the cart, the button stays clickable and
   the cart quantity increases.

The "Assumptions" instruction is the most valuable line in that prompt. It makes the model show its reasoning about gaps in your requirements instead of papering over them, and those gaps are often the real bugs.

Here's what good output looks like (an illustrative example, written by hand):

ID Scenario Steps Expected Result
TC-01 Add a new item Open product page, click Add to Cart Item appears in cart, confirmation shown, header count +1
TC-02 Add an item already in cart Add the same product twice Quantity becomes 2, header count updates correctly
TC-03 Add while out of stock Open an out-of-stock product Button disabled or clear error shown, cart unchanged
TC-04 Rapid repeated clicks Click Add to Cart five times quickly Quantity is consistent, no duplicate line items

TC-03 and TC-04 aren't in the acceptance criteria. Cases like these are where the model earns its keep, and where you should look first when reviewing.

Prompt 2: Edge cases and negative scenarios

Models are good at brainstorming the unusual inputs people forget.

Act as a meticulous QA tester. For the login form described below,
list negative scenarios and edge cases. Focus on invalid input,
boundary conditions, and unusual user behavior. Group them by
category and, for each one, state what you expect the system to do.

Functionality:
A login form with "Email" (must be a valid email format) and
"Password" (minimum 8 characters).

Ask for categories (input validation, session behavior, rate limiting, accessibility). Unstructured lists drift toward the obvious cases.

Prompt 3: Security-focused test ideas

For testing your own applications, a model can quickly generate a checklist of common vulnerability checks. Only run these against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test.

Act as an application security tester. For a registration form that
accepts username, email, and password, generate test cases to check
for common input-handling vulnerabilities such as SQL injection and
cross-site scripting. For each case, give the input, the field it
targets, and the secure behavior you'd expect.

Treat the output as a starting checklist, not a security assessment. It doesn't replace a proper review or dedicated security tooling.

Prompt 4: BDD scenarios in Gherkin

If your team writes behavior-driven specs, you can generate a first draft of the feature file.

Act as a BDD specialist. Write a Gherkin feature file for the feature
below, with multiple Scenario blocks covering positive and negative
paths. Use Scenario Outline with Examples where inputs vary.

Feature: Product search
As a user, I want to search for products by name so that I can find
what I'm looking for.

A trimmed example of the kind of output to expect:

Scenario: Search with a matching product name
  Given I am on the home page
  When I search for "wireless mouse"
  Then I should see products whose names contain "wireless mouse"

Scenario: Search with no matches
  Given I am on the home page
  When I search for "zzzzqqq"
  Then I should see a "no results found" message

Prompt 5: Ask the model to critique its own work

This one is underused. After generating a suite, run a second prompt against it:

Review the test cases below against the requirements I provided.
1. Which requirements have no test coverage?
2. Which test cases are duplicates or near-duplicates?
3. Which test cases assume behavior that isn't stated in the
   requirements?
4. What are the five highest-risk scenarios that are missing?

Question 3 is the important one. It surfaces cases where the model invented behavior, which is the most common failure in AI-generated tests.

Where AI-generated tests go wrong

LLMs are good first-draft engines. They are not oracles.

  • They don't know your business. A model doesn't know that refunds over a certain amount need manager approval, or that one customer tier gets special pricing. It only knows what's in your prompt.
  • They invent plausible behavior. If the requirements are silent, the model may fill in an answer that sounds right and is wrong for your product. Tests built on invented behavior fail for the wrong reasons, or worse, pass for the wrong reasons.
  • They produce volume, not priority. Thirty test cases isn't better than ten if you can't tell which five matter.
  • Generated automation code is a draft. If you ask for Playwright or WebdriverIO scripts, check every selector and wait strategy against your real application. Generated selectors are often guesses.
  • Data privacy is your responsibility. Don't paste proprietary code, customer data, or confidential requirements into a public model interface. Use an enterprise offering with the data guarantees your organization requires.

A short review checklist

Before any AI-generated test case enters your suite:

  1. Does it trace back to a real requirement?
  2. Are the expected results stated explicitly, or just implied?
  3. Is any behavior assumed that you haven't confirmed?
  4. Is it a duplicate of something you already have?
  5. Would you know why it failed if it failed?
  6. Is it worth automating, or is it better as an exploratory check?

If a test case can't pass that list, rewrite it or drop it.

From prompt to automation

The usual workflow is: generate cases, review them, pick the ones worth automating, then turn those into scripts. You can ask a model for framework-specific code:

Convert test case TC-02 into a Playwright test in TypeScript. Use
role-based locators where possible, avoid fixed timeouts, and add a
comment above any selector you're unsure about.

That last instruction, flagging uncertain selectors, gives you a built-in list of things to verify by hand.

If you'd rather not hand-write prompts at all, CloudQA's AI test case generator produces test cases from a feature description in the browser.

The takeaway

Better prompts come from better inputs: real requirements, an explicit format, and a request for the model to state its assumptions. The model drafts quickly. Your job is to judge what's worth keeping.

CloudQA builds codeless test automation for web applications. If you're working on test case generation or reducing test maintenance, we'd be glad to hear what you're working on.

title: AI Workflow Automation in Node.js: Invoice to PO Matching with Claude
description:
If you want AI workflow automation in Node.js that your finance team will trust, split the job in two. Claude reads the invoice, and plain code decides whether it matches the purchase order. Only the invoices that fail a check ever reach a person.

You probably know how this works today. Someone opens a PDF, finds the PO number and switches to the ERP. They compare quantities line by line and then type everything in again. Most invoices are fine, but the team still checks every one.

This walkthrough builds the intake pipeline in three parts: extraction, matching and an exception queue.

Why shouldn't the model approve the invoice?

Approval is a rule, and a rule should give the same answer every time. A language model is very good at reading a messy layout and working out that "Units" means quantity. It is the wrong place to decide whether a small price difference is acceptable.

Keep one sentence in mind for the whole build: the model reads, the code decides.

There is a less obvious reason too. Models tend to make numbers agree. Say an invoice's line items don't add up to the printed total. Ask a model for "the total" and it may return a number that fits the lines instead of the one on the page. That gap is exactly what you wanted to catch. So the model only copies the printed values, and your code does every sum.

What does it cost to get this wrong?

When the model decides, mistakes go unnoticed. An overbilled invoice gets approved and the record behind it looks clean. Nobody notices until a supplier reconciliation or an audit, and by then you are unwinding payments, not just correcting invoices.

The opposite mistake costs time. If the pipeline flags everything as "needs review", your team does the old job and also has to read the system's notes. People stop using it within weeks.

The goal is narrow: catch every real mismatch and let clean invoices through without anyone touching them.

Do you actually need to build this?

Maybe not. If you handle a few dozen invoices a month from a handful of suppliers, the OCR in your accounting tool plus a quick manual check is enough. Build your own when volume or the number of suppliers makes the manual check the bottleneck, or when your purchase orders live in a system an off-the-shelf tool can't reach.

Step 1: How do you get structured fields out of an invoice PDF?

Send the PDF to Claude and force a tool call. The answer comes back as JSON that follows your schema, not free text.

import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk'
import fs from 'node:fs/promises'

const client = new Anthropic()

const invoiceTool = {
  name: 'record_invoice',
  description: 'Record fields exactly as printed. Never calculate, round or correct values.',
  input_schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      invoice_number: { type: 'string' },
      po_number: { type: ['string', 'null'] },
      supplier_name: { type: 'string' },
      currency: { type: 'string' },
      printed_total: { type: 'string' },
      lines: {
        type: 'array',
        items: {
          type: 'object',
          properties: {
            sku: { type: ['string', 'null'] },
            description: { type: 'string' },
            quantity: { type: 'string' },
            unit_price: { type: 'string' }
          },
          required: ['description', 'quantity', 'unit_price']
        }
      },
      unreadable_fields: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } }
    },
    required: ['invoice_number', 'supplier_name', 'currency', 'printed_total', 'lines', 'unreadable_fields']
  }
}

export async function extractInvoice(path) {
  const pdf = await fs.readFile(path)
  const res = await client.messages.create({
    model: 'claude-sonnet-5-5',
    max_tokens: 2000,
    tools: [invoiceTool],
    tool_choice: { type: 'tool', name: 'record_invoice' },
    messages: [{
      role: 'user',
      content: [
        { type: 'document', source: { type: 'base64', media_type: 'application/pdf', data: pdf.toString('base64') } },
        { type: 'text', text: 'Extract this invoice. If a field is missing or unclear, list it in unreadable_fields instead of guessing.' }
      ]
    }]
  })
  return res.content.find(b => b.type === 'tool_use').input
}

Two choices here are worth copying. Amounts come back as strings, so your own code parses them and can fail loudly when something looks wrong. And unreadable_fields lets the model say "I can't read this" instead of making up a value.

Step 2: How do you match invoice fields to the purchase order?

Load the PO from your own system and convert money to whole minor units (cents, paise) before comparing. The model plays no part in this step.

const normalise = s => String(s).toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '')

const toMinor = s => {
  const clean = String(s).replace(/[^0-9.]/g, '')
  const [whole, frac = '', extra] = clean.split('.')
  if (!whole || extra !== undefined || frac.length > 2) {
    throw new Error('Unparseable amount: ' + s)
  }
  return Number(whole) * 100 + Number(frac.padEnd(2, '0'))
}

export function matchInvoice(inv, po, rules) {
  const issues = []
  if (inv.unreadable_fields.length) issues.push({ code: 'UNREADABLE', fields: inv.unreadable_fields })
  if (!po) return [...issues, { code: 'PO_NOT_FOUND', po: inv.po_number }]
  if (inv.currency !== po.currency) issues.push({ code: 'CURRENCY' })
  if (normalise(inv.supplier_name) !== normalise(po.supplier_name)) issues.push({ code: 'SUPPLIER' })

  let computed = 0
  for (const line of inv.lines) {
    const poLine = po.lines.find(l => l.sku === line.sku)
    if (!poLine) {
      issues.push({ code: 'LINE_NOT_ON_PO', line })
      continue
    }
    const qty = Number(line.quantity)
    if (!Number.isFinite(qty)) throw new Error('Unparseable quantity: ' + line.quantity)
    const price = toMinor(line.unit_price)
    computed += qty * price
    if (qty > poLine.remaining_qty) issues.push({ code: 'QTY_OVER_PO', sku: line.sku })
    if (Math.abs(price - poLine.unit_price_minor) > rules.priceToleranceMinor) {
      issues.push({ code: 'PRICE', sku: line.sku, invoiced: price, agreed: poLine.unit_price_minor })
    }
  }
  if (Math.abs(computed - toMinor(inv.printed_total)) > rules.roundingMinor) {
    issues.push({ code: 'TOTAL_DOES_NOT_ADD_UP' })
  }
  return issues
}

If your invoices have tax or freight lines, extract them as separate fields and add them to computed before the final check. An amount written in European format, like "1.250,00", fails the parser and throws an error. That is what you want, because a loud error is better than a number that is quietly wrong.

Here is why each check is there:

  • The PO exists. An invoice with no PO raises a policy question that a person should answer. It is not a data entry task.
  • The supplier matches. This stops you paying the right amount to the wrong party. In production, match on a supplier ID through an alias table, not on raw names.
  • Quantity is checked against what is still open, not what was ordered. Comparing to remaining_qty catches a second invoice for the same delivery.
  • The unit price is within tolerance. Finance sets the tolerance. Keep it in config where an accountant can see it, never inside a prompt.
  • The lines add up to the printed total. This catches the supplier's own arithmetic errors and any extraction that changed a number to make it fit.
  • Unreadable fields go to a person. Someone looks at the document instead of the system guessing.

Once this works, add the goods received note as a third document. The same pattern then gives you a full three-way match.

Step 3: How do mismatches reach a person?

Clean invoices go straight to posting. Everything else goes onto a review queue, with the reasons attached.

import { Queue } from 'bullmq'

const review = new Queue('invoice-review', { connection: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 } })

export async function processInvoice(path, rules) {
  const inv = await extractInvoice(path)
  const po = await db.purchaseOrders.findByNumber(inv.po_number)
  let issues
  try {
    issues = matchInvoice(inv, po, rules)
  } catch (err) {
    issues = [{ code: 'PARSE_ERROR', message: err.message }]
  }
  if (issues.length === 0) return db.invoices.markReadyToPost(inv, po)
  await review.add('mismatch', { path, inv, po_number: inv.po_number, issues })
}

The reviewer's screen matters more than most teams expect. Show the PDF, the extracted fields and the PO line side by side, and explain each issue code in plain words. Log every correction the reviewer makes. That log becomes your test set when you change the prompt or the model.

One problem is worth watching from the first week. Count exceptions by code and by supplier. If TOTAL_DOES_NOT_ADD_UP suddenly jumps for one supplier, their invoice layout has probably changed, and you will see it before anyone pays a wrong bill.

Where else does this pattern work?

The same split works for purchase requests, delivery notes, claims and onboarding forms. A model turns messy input into fields, code applies the rules and people handle the exceptions. If you are adding this to an existing backend, the guide to Node.js AI integration covers retries, timeouts and logging around the model call.

For more workflows built this way, read AI automation examples for business. If you would like someone to look over your own intake flow, Geminate Solutions offers a free review of your plan and replies within 24 hours.

title: My crawler said 1 in 7 websites were down. They weren't, and retrying made it worse.
description:
I'm building Fresh Leads, a tool that finds local businesses and grades their websites so agencies know who to pitch. One of the strongest signals it reports is simple:

"Their website is down."

If you sell web design, that's the best cold-call opener there is. It's also the worst thing to get wrong. If a customer calls a coffee shop and says "your site is down" while the owner is looking at it working fine, the customer loses the call and I lose the customer.

So when I finally checked those verdicts properly, the result hurt.

The measurement

I took 47 sites that one crawl had recorded as unreachable and opened each one from my laptop.

6 of them loaded instantly. That's 13% wrong. A second, larger run gave the same answer: 56 of 413, or 14%. Two of the "dead" sites belonged to well-known coffee chains, and both were serving pages perfectly well.

The cause wasn't hard to guess. The crawler runs on a serverless platform, so every request comes from a datacentre IP address. Cloudflare, Shopify and similar platforms block or challenge datacentre traffic as a matter of routine. To my crawler, a site that blocks it looks the same as a site that doesn't exist.

"Did not answer us" and "is down" are not the same sentence.

I tried three fixes. The first two failed, and the way they failed taught me more than the fix that worked.

Attempt 1: just retry the failures

The original pipeline already had a "quiet re-check" stage. Any site that failed during the main crawl (24 fetches running at once) was retried later, three at a time with a longer timeout. The reasoning sounded right: a big concurrent crawl causes throttling, so a gentle second try should get a truer answer.

That stage took up 22% of every search's runtime. Nothing recorded what it actually recovered, so I added two counters, recheck_tried and recheck_recovered, and let it run on real production searches.

36 sites retried across 6 production searches
 0 recovered

Not "low". Zero.

And looking back, it could never have been anything else. A block is perfectly consistent. If an IP gets blocked, it gets blocked again eight seconds later, and it'll keep getting blocked at any concurrency and with any timeout. Retries catch slow hosts. They can't catch refusals, and refusals were nearly all I had.

I deleted the stage. Searches got 22% faster, and the results didn't change at all.

Attempt 2: wait six hours and check again

Next idea: if retrying immediately can't tell a block from a dead site, maybe time can. A dead site stays dead. A flaky one recovers.

So I wrote confirmDown(). A first failure is recorded with a timestamp but never shown to the customer. Only a second failure at least six hours later, from a fresh connection, is allowed to say "down". A success at any point clears the record.

export function confirmDown(previous: Audit | null, next: Audit, now = Date.now()): Audit {
  // It answered: whatever happened before, it isn't down.
  if (next.reachable !== false) return { ...next, firstDownAt: null, downConfirmed: false };

  const firstDownAt = previous && !previous.reachable && previous.firstDownAt
    ? previous.firstDownAt
    : new Date(now).toISOString();

  const since = now - new Date(firstDownAt).getTime();
  // A clock that has gone backwards must not confirm anything.
  const confirmed = Number.isFinite(since) && since >= SIX_HOURS;
  return { ...next, firstDownAt, downConfirmed: confirmed };
}

It's clean, testable, and it feels rigorous. Two days later I checked it against reality: of 60 sites it had confirmed down, 13 loaded instantly from a normal connection.

unconfirmed failures   14% wrong
confirmed failures     22% wrong

Confirmation made it worse.

The reason is obvious once you see it. Waiting six hours filters out transient failures, like a server that was briefly overloaded. Those were the cases that would have recovered anyway. A datacentre block isn't transient. It fails the first check and the second one too. So the filter removed the harmless cases and left a pool that was concentrated with exactly the false verdicts it was supposed to exclude.

Time can't tell a block from a dead site. I needed a different signal.

Attempt 3: read the error I was throwing away

The signal had been there the whole time. My fetch wrapper looked like this:

try {
  return await fetch(url, { signal });
} catch {
  return null; // 🪦 every reason for failure, flattened into one
}

Node's fetch tells you why a request failed, in error.cause.code. And some of those reasons are proof, while others aren't:

Error What it means Can a browser on any network load it?
ENOTFOUND DNS has no record for the domain No. It's gone.
ECONNREFUSED The host answered and nothing is listening on the port No. It's down.
timeout, ECONNRESET, aborted TLS handshake, … Something is there but won't talk to us Often, yes

The last row is exactly what being blocked from a datacentre looks like. It's indistinguishable from a slow or hostile server, so I can't call it "down".

So I kept the reason:

let lastFailure: string | null = null;

try {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
  lastFailure = null;
  return res;
} catch (e) {
  // Node puts the useful part in `cause.code`: ENOTFOUND when DNS has nothing,
  // ECONNREFUSED when nothing is listening, a timeout or reset when something
  // is there but won't talk to us.
  const cause = (e as { cause?: { code?: string } })?.cause;
  lastFailure = cause?.code ?? (e as Error)?.name ?? "unknown";
  return null;
}

And I made reachable three-valued instead of a boolean:

export function failureIsFatal(code: string | null | undefined): boolean {
  return code === "ENOTFOUND" || code === "ECONNREFUSED";
}

// After both http:// and https:// have failed:
return {
  reachable: failureIsFatal(lastFailure) ? false : null,
  failure: lastFailure,
  // ...every other finding is null too: we didn't see the page
};
  • true: we fetched it.
  • false: we have proof it's down (no DNS record, or the port refused).
  • null: we couldn't reach it, and we can't say why.

confirmDown() stayed, but only for the false case. A second look is cheap, and a wrong "down" is still the most expensive thing the product can say. What it no longer does is turn an inconclusive failure into a confident one just because it happened twice.

The null that wasn't "fine"

One trap is worth calling out, because I nearly fell into it.

My scoring code treats an audited site with no problems found as a good site. If "couldn't reach it" had been stored as "audited, no problems found", every blocked site would quietly have been graded healthy. The bug would just have flipped from "falsely down" to "falsely fine".

So null means not audited. The lead shows up as "we haven't checked their website yet", and its grade can go up later once we manage to look. It never drops now because of a claim we can't back up.

I also found that a deadline test was asserting the bug. When an audit ran out of its time budget, it returned reachable: false, which reported my timeout as a fact about their website. That test now expects null.

The cache still believed the old rule

Fixing the crawler didn't fix the data it had already written. When I counted the live table, there were 2,141 businesses whose sites showed as down, and 1,501 of them had no failure code at all. They'd been decided by a rule I'd already retired. Seventy per cent of the claim rested on evidence I'd stopped trusting.

I didn't run a backfill. The verdict is now earned on read: a row has to say it failed twice and that it failed with a fatal code. A row that can't answer the second question reads as "not checked", and the next crawl settles it under the current rule.

What I took away from it

  1. Measure what your retry actually recovers. Mine cost 22% of every search and recovered nothing. Two integer counters would have told me that months earlier.
  2. Retries and waiting only fix transient failures. If the failure is consistent, as a block is, repeating the check just confirms the wrong answer with more confidence.
  3. Filtering can concentrate errors instead of removing them. If your filter removes the cases that were never the problem, what's left can be worse than what you started with.
  4. Never catch { return null } at a boundary that makes a decision. The reason for the failure was the signal.
  5. "Unknown" deserves its own value. A boolean forced me to pick between two lies. null let the code tell the truth: we didn't manage to look.

The fix ended up being a few lines. The lesson was that "we couldn't reach it" is a fact about you, not about them, and the code should never say otherwise.

Have you been burned by a check that was confidently wrong? Or a retry loop that turned out to do nothing? Tell me in the comments.

title: Mastering AI in QA: How to Evaluate Prompts and Build Reliable Test Workflows
description:
Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming how software engineering teams design, execute, and maintain test automation. From auto-generating Selenium and Playwright scripts to analyzing dense CI/CD execution logs, AI-driven assistants significantly reduce routine manual effort.

However, integrating LLMs into Quality Assurance introduces non-determinism. Unlike traditional code, prompts can produce subtle variations, hallucinated assertions, or context drift across model updates. To build enterprise-grade QA workflows, teams need systematic evaluation frameworks and modern test management infrastructure.

The Non-Deterministic Challenge: Evaluating AI Output

When using AI to generate test scenarios or parse bug reports, standard binary assertions (pass/fail) fall short. A prompt that generates a perfect Cypress test case today might miss crucial edge-case validations tomorrow if the model's temperature or system context shifts.

Applying structured ai prompt testing methods is essential for validating context windows, benchmarking prompt accuracy against fixed datasets, and preventing hallucinations in AI-generated test artifacts.

Key techniques for prompt validation in QA include:

  • Counterfactual Prompt Testing: Swapping specific parameters (such as environment variables or user roles) within prompts to verify output consistency.
  • Temperature & Top-P Tuning: Calibrating randomness parameters to ensure test case generation remains deterministic and reproducible.
  • Regression Testing for Prompts: Running continuous evaluation suites whenever underlying foundation models or system prompts are updated.

By establishing rigorous ai prompt testing methods, engineering teams can transition AI from a risky playground experiment into a dependable QA asset.

Unifying AI and Automated Test Management

To maximize the ROI of AI in testing, generated test scripts and validation results must not remain isolated in chat windows. They need to seamlessly sync with your primary CI/CD pipelines and test management hubs.

1. Orchestrating Scenarios with AI Test Management

title: Kakeizu: a local Gemma reads the gas station's receipts, and check digits catch its mistakes
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

A friend of mine works at a gas station in the interior of São Paulo. The station has a system, but closing the day still means checking a pile of paper against it by hand: card machine slips, fiscal coupons, Pix receipts, the odd cheque. Amount, date, payment method, one receipt at a time.

Still checking, one receipt at a time.

So I built Kakeizu: you photograph the receipt on your phone, a Gemma model running on the shop's own computer reads it, the domain checks every digit it can, and a person confirms. Nothing is confirmed automatically, and nothing leaves the shop.

The AI suggests, the domain validates, the human decides.

What I Built

Kakeizu reads a photo of a Brazilian payment receipt with Gemma running on the shop's own computer, checks every digit it can, and waits for a person to confirm. The name is Kakeibo (家計簿, the Japanese household ledger) plus Kakuzu, the Akatsuki member who only thinks about money.

It reads the receipts a Brazilian gas station or corner shop sees every day:

Receipt What the domain checks
NFC-e / NF-e (fiscal coupon or invoice) 44-digit access key with a mod-11 check digit; its month and CNPJ must match the other fields
Card machine slip (Stone, Cielo, Getnet) the store's CNPJ check digits, the authorization code
Pix receipt the 32-character end-to-end ID
Cheque the three mod-10 check digits of the magnetic line (CMC-7); a date over 6 months old gets a warning
Any of them amount, date never in the future, the same photo or the same key never twice

Confirmed receipts feed a daily summary and a sales report by hour, weekday, payment method, installments and card brand. An NFC-e and the card slip of the same sale are paired, so the sale counts once.

Who pays for it: the owner of a small shop who closes the cash register by hand. Cloud receipt readers exist, but they charge per document and want the shop's sales, suppliers and customers on someone else's server.

The cloud vendor, sending this month's per-document invoice.

Kakeizu costs nothing per document and nothing leaves the shop. The owner pays for the setup and the hour it saves at the end of every day, not for each photo.

Demo

Kakeizu runs on the shop's computer and never on a public server, so there is no live link: the demo is the flow below, recorded with the anonymized sample receipts from the repository.

Today, on the phone. The photo goes up and the list comes back at once. The model reads in the background (dashed violet line), and the line prints itself in when it is done. Orange means "needs you", double green means confirmed.

Review. The photo sits next to everything the model read, and every field that failed a check says why. This template NFC-e has no CNPJ and a zeroed access key, so it cannot be confirmed as read.

Look at the amount, too. The photo says 146,46; the model read 4,00. That number is well formed and no check digit covers it, so only the person comparing it with the photo catches it.

Sales report. Confirmed sales by hour, weekday, payment method, installments and card brand, with a slip paired to its NFC-e so each sale counts once.

Code

mauricioandrade / kakeizu

Local-first receipt reader for small shops: Gemma (via Ollama) reads NFC-e, card slips, Pix and cheques; check digits validate; a person confirms. Java 25 + Quarkus. Nothing leaves the machine.

🧾 Kakeizu

A receipt reader for small shops that runs 100% locally.
A photo goes in, structured data comes out, and nothing leaves the owner's machine.

Kakeibo (家計簿, the Japanese household ledger) + Kakuzu (the Akatsuki member who only thinks about money)

🤖 The AI suggests · 🧮 the domain validates · 🧑 the human decides

📑 Contents

  • 😩 The problem
  • 🔄 How it works
  • 📸 Screenshots
  • 🚀 Running
  • 📊 Sales report
  • 🎯 Accuracy on real receipts
  • 🔓 Why open matters
  • 📄 License

😩 The problem

The owner or manager of a gas station, a corner shop or a small restaurant gets dozens of receipts a day: NFC-e, card machine slips, Pix receipts, the odd cheque. Closing the day means typing amount, date and who paid or got paid into a spreadsheet, one receipt at a time.

Cloud tools do this, but they want the business's financial data on…

View on GitHub

Apache 2.0. The README has the setup for both Ollama layouts on Windows + WSL2, the accuracy tables and the backup script.

How I Built It

The whole design is one sentence: the AI suggests, the domain validates, the human decides.

Layer Choice
Model Gemma 4 (gemma4:e4b), vision, thinking on, temperature 0
Inference Ollama on the Windows side, reached from WSL2
Glue Quarkus 3.40 with quarkus-langchain4j-ollama
Language Java 25
Storage PostgreSQL + Flyway
Web Qute templates + htmx, no frontend build

Gemma reads, and nothing it returns is trusted

Gemma gets the photo and a field guide in the system prompt, and returns plain strings: type, amount, date, counterparty, tax ID, unique ID, time, payment method, installments, card brand. Those strings never touch the database as values. They go through the same domain objects a person's correction goes through, and each object checks what it can.

The check digits are the trick. They exist to catch a cashier's typo, and they catch a model's misread just as well. A CNPJ, for instance, carries two mod-11 digits:

public record Cnpj(String value) {
    public Cnpj {
        value = value.replaceAll("[.\\-/\\s]", "").toUpperCase();
        if (!value.matches("[A-Z0-9]{12}\\d{2}")) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("CNPJ must have 14 characters");
        }
        if (checkDigit(value, FIRST_WEIGHTS) != valueAt(value, 12)
                || checkDigit(value, SECOND_WEIGHTS) != valueAt(value, 13)) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("CNPJ check digits do not match: " + value);
        }
    }

    // Each character is worth ASCII - 48, so the new alphanumeric CNPJ
    // (issued since July 2026) and the old all-digit one share one rule
    private static int valueAt(String cnpj, int index) {
        return cnpj.charAt(index) - '0';
    }
}

On a real Cielo slip, Gemma read the CNPJ as 13.438.977/0001-00 three times out of three. The real one is 13.458.397/0001-01. The check digits rejected it every time, and the review screen put the photo next to the red field. It also read the authorization code 375579 as 375759. No check digit covers that code, so nothing caught it. That is exactly why a person confirms every receipt.

How often it is right

Seven receipts, three readings each, run through the app's own validation:

Of 210 fields Count
Right on the first reading 200 (95%)
Wrong, and the domain flags that field 3
Wrong, in a receipt the domain blocks for another field 4
Wrong, and nothing flags it 3

Then a real gas station's day: a Getnet debit slip (3 of 3 ready to confirm as read), an NFC-e paid in cash (2 of 3, the 44-digit access key right every time), a Pix paid on the card machine, and a handwritten cheque. The small sample is the honest caveat: treat these as a sanity check, not a benchmark.

What I learned the hard way

Every field must be required in the schema. Ollama uses the JSON schema LangChain4j sends as a grammar, and by default no field is required. Gemma's reasoning said "installments = 5" and the answer simply left the key out. Marking every field @JsonProperty(required = true) took the share of right fields from 88% to 95%.

The model cannot say null. With every field required and typed as a string, it writes the word "null", or just ", ", when a field is not on the receipt. The adapter turns those into a missing field.

Thinking matters more than speed. With thinking off, a reading takes about 2 seconds instead of 15. It also took an item price as the NFC-e total and the card brand as the store name: wrong values in a valid format, which no check digit can catch. Thinking stayed on.

Temperature 0 is not deterministic. The same photo gave different answers between runs, so every receipt in the accuracy tables was read three times. The NFC-e template's total, 146,46, came back right, then as 46,46, then as 4,00, in different runs.

Tell the model where things are printed. It returned the NFC-e note number as the access key until the prompt said the key is all 44 digits, in groups of four, under "Consulte pela Chave de Acesso". A Pix paid on the card machine kept coming back as a card slip until the prompt described it: an "ID/TRANSAÇÃO" and no card brand, no card number, no authorization code.

Some mistakes need the calendar, not a check digit. On a handwritten cheque, Gemma read the year "26" as 2022, three times out of three. A cheque that old can no longer be cashed in Brazil, so a cheque dated more than six months ago now gets a warning on review.

Nobody waits for the model

A warm reading takes about 15 seconds on a consumer GPU. I measured where it goes: the image takes under a second, and the rest is Gemma writing about 750 tokens of reasoning at 75 tokens a second. Turning the reasoning off cost accuracy, and asking for shorter reasoning changed nothing, so the app stopped waiting for it instead. The upload saves the photo and returns at once, a background worker reads it, and the line on today's list updates itself. If Ollama is down, the receipt still goes to review, empty, to be typed from the photo.

Java 25 doing real work

The receipt is a sealed interface with one record per type, so the mapper and the reports are exhaustive switches with record patterns and no default. Up to five photos can go in one upload: each is saved and queued on its own virtual thread inside a StructuredTaskScope (a preview in Java 25), so one bad photo never stops the others. A correlation id rides a ScopedValue into every log line of an upload, across the forked threads and into the background reader.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because with a closed API, this product could not be sold to the person it is for.

The data cannot leave the shop. A day of receipts is the business itself: what it sold, to whom, through which bank, from which supplier, and sometimes a customer's name and partial CPF. An open-weight Gemma on the shop's own GPU means the photos, the database and the model all stay on one computer. There is no privacy policy to read because there is no third party.

The cost does not grow with the work. A gas station photographs dozens of receipts a day. A per-call API turns every one of them into a line on a bill, so the busiest day costs the most. Local inference costs the electricity of about 15 seconds of GPU per receipt.

The model is a setting. KAKEIZU_MODEL swaps Gemma for any Ollama vision model, and the same check digits judge the new one. When a better small open model ships, the shop gets it for free.

Open models let me see why they fail. Because I ran Gemma myself, I could turn thinking on and off, read its reasoning, and see it decide "installments = 5" and then drop the key. That is how the required-schema fix was found. A closed endpoint would have shown me only a wrong answer.

My First User

My first user is that friend at the gas station. Midway through the week they sent me photos of a real day's receipts: a Getnet debit slip, a Pix paid on the card machine, an NFC-e paid in cash, and a handwritten cheque. The station stays anonymous here, and none of those receipts are in the repository.

That one batch changed the product more than any test I wrote:

  • A Pix paid on the card machine has no end-to-end ID. The slip prints the machine's own transaction ID, so the Pix ID became optional and the prompt learned to tell this slip from a card slip.
  • Gas stations take cheques. Kakeizu now reads them, checks the magnetic line's three check digits when it is typed, and treats the cheque the other way round: the CNPJ on it is the payer's, so a cheque from another company is a sale. Shops that do not take cheques switch this off.
  • The NFC-e access key is printed far from its label. The prompt now says exactly where to find all 44 digits.

After testing it, they want to use it every day.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 (gemma4:e4b) runs locally through Ollama and does all the reading: receipt type, amount, date, counterparty, tax ID, access keys and payment details, from phone photos of thermal slips, fiscal coupons and handwritten cheques. Kakeizu is built around both its strengths and its mistakes: thinking stays on because it buys accuracy, and every field it returns goes through deterministic checks before a person confirms it.
