title: Idempotency keys done right: exactly-once effects over at-least-once networks
description:
Why "just retry" creates duplicate payments, and a PostgreSQL-backed design for idempotency keys that survives double clicks, timeouts, crashes and concurrent retries.

Key takeaways

  • Networks give you at-least-once delivery at best. Exactly-once delivery isn't achievable in general; exactly-once effects are, if the receiver de-duplicates.
  • An idempotency key identifies a user intent, not an HTTP attempt. Generate it once, when the user decides, and reuse it for every retry.
  • Store the key in the same transaction as the side effect. If the key and the effect can commit separately, you've only moved the race.
  • Fingerprint the request. Same key + same body = replay the stored response; same key + different body = reject with an error.
  • Handle in-flight duplicates explicitly (return 409 or wait), and make keys recoverable after a crash.
  • External calls need phases or an outbox. You can't put a payment gateway inside your database transaction, so design recovery points around it.

I'm Mohammadreza Alamnejad, a programmer and network security professional, UI/UX designer and developer, and the founder of Arka Studio in Tehran. In the café and restaurant operations platform my studio built, NABZA, several behaviours that users experience as "it just works" are idempotency underneath: a completed order becomes a sale once and only once even with a second click, duplicate payments or payments above the outstanding balance are rejected, a stock count can't be posted twice, and an offline order is submitted exactly once after reconnecting.

I mentioned idempotency briefly in a pre-launch checklist I published earlier. This post goes all the way down: the theory, the failure modes, a schema, the request lifecycle, concurrency, crash recovery and external side effects. The code is a reference implementation in TypeScript and PostgreSQL, not NABZA's source.

1. The problem: you can't tell "lost request" from "lost response"

Consider a client calling POST /payments and getting a timeout.

 Client                      Network                     Server
   │  POST /payments ───────────►│                          │
   │                             │ ───────────────────────► │  charge + commit ✔
   │                             │ ◄─────────────────────── │  201 Created
   │                    ✖ connection drops                  │
   │  (timeout)                  │                          │
   │  retry? ─────────────────── ?                          │

From the client's side, three different worlds look identical:

  1. The request never reached the server.
  2. The server processed it, and the response was lost.
  3. The server is still processing it.

This is a practical cousin of the classic Two Generals' Problem: over an unreliable channel, no finite number of messages lets both sides be certain they agree. The consequence for APIs is simple. If the client never retries, you lose operations in world 1. If it always retries, you duplicate operations in world 2. Neither is acceptable for money or stock.

The way out is to make retries safe: at-least-once delivery + de-duplication at the receiver = exactly-once effect.

2. What HTTP already gives you

RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods: sending the same request several times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once. POST and PATCH are not idempotent by definition.

Two notes:

  • "Idempotent by method" is a contract you have to implement. A PUT handler that appends to a log on every call breaks it.
  • Most business operations ("create a payment", "complete an order", "post a stock count") are naturally POST. You need an explicit mechanism.

That mechanism is the idempotency key: a client-generated unique value sent with the request. The pattern was popularised by public payment APIs (Stripe documents it, and Brandur Leach wrote a well-known public post about implementing it on PostgreSQL), and there's an IETF HTTPAPI working group draft standardising an Idempotency-Key request header field. I'll use that header name below.

3. Rule one: one key per intent

The single most common bug I see: the key is generated inside the retry loop.

// ✖ Wrong: a new key per attempt = no de-duplication at all
async function pay(amount: number) {
  return retry(() => fetch('/payments', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': crypto.randomUUID() },
    body: JSON.stringify({ amount }),
  }));
}

The key must be created when the user decides, and then reused by every attempt, including attempts after a page reload or an app restart.

// ✔ Right: key belongs to the intent, persisted with it
type PendingIntent = { key: string; body: unknown; createdAt: number };

export function createPaymentIntent(body: unknown): PendingIntent {
  const intent = { key: crypto.randomUUID(), body, createdAt: Date.now() };
  savePending(intent);            // IndexedDB / localStorage / device queue
  return intent;
}

export async function submit(intent: PendingIntent) {
  return retry(
    () => fetch('/payments', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Idempotency-Key': intent.key },
      body: JSON.stringify(intent.body),
    }),
    { retries: 6, baseMs: 300, maxMs: 10_000 },
  );
}

On the UI side, a disabled button is a nice-to-have, not the guarantee. The guarantee is that two clicks that represent one decision share one key.

Retries with backoff and jitter

Retrying immediately and in lockstep from many clients turns a brief outage into a self-inflicted overload. Use exponential backoff with jitter:

export async function retry<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<Response>,
  { retries, baseMs, maxMs }: { retries: number; baseMs: number; maxMs: number },
): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      const res = await fn();
      // Retry only on outcomes that might succeed later.
      if (res.status !== 409 && res.status !== 429 && res.status < 500) return res;
      if (attempt >= retries) return res;
    } catch (e) {
      if (attempt >= retries) throw e;   // network error / timeout
    }
    const cap = Math.min(maxMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
    await sleep(Math.random() * cap);    // "full jitter"
  }
}

Don't retry 400/422: those are deterministic. Do retry network errors, 5xx, 429 (honouring Retry-After) and 409 in-progress (see below).

4. The server side: a key is a small state machine

A key isn't just "seen / not seen". It moves through states:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> started: first request (INSERT)
    started --> completed: effect committed + response stored
    started --> started: crash / timeout (recoverable)
    completed --> [*]: expires after retention window
    note right of started
      concurrent duplicate → 409 (in progress)
    end note
    note right of completed
      duplicate with same fingerprint → replay response
      duplicate with different fingerprint → 422
    end note

Schema 

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  tenant_id        uuid        NOT NULL,
  actor_id         uuid        NOT NULL,       -- keys are scoped to who sent them
  key              text        NOT NULL CHECK (length(key) BETWEEN 8 AND 255),
  method           text        NOT NULL,
  path             text        NOT NULL,
  request_hash     bytea       NOT NULL,       -- sha256 of canonical body
  status           text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'started'
                     CHECK (status IN ('started', 'completed')),
  recovery_point   text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'started',
  locked_until     timestamptz,
  response_status  int,
  response_body    jsonb,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, actor_id, key)
);

CREATE INDEX idempotency_keys_gc ON idempotency_keys (created_at);

Design decisions worth calling out:

  • Scope. The primary key includes the tenant and the actor. A key from user A must never replay user B's response. In a multi-tenant system, that's a data leak, not just a bug.
  • Method and path. The same key sent to a different endpoint is a client bug; reject it rather than replaying an unrelated response.
  • request_hash. A fingerprint of the canonicalised body. Canonicalise (stable key order, normalised numbers) before hashing so semantically identical retries match.
  • recovery_point. Where a crashed request should resume. More in section 7.
  • locked_until. A lease, so a request that died mid-flight doesn't block the key forever.

5. The happy path, in one transaction

For operations whose side effects are all inside your database (create a sale, post a stock count, record a payment you've already confirmed), the whole thing fits in one transaction. That's the case to aim for.

import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

const canonical = (v: unknown): string =>
  JSON.stringify(v, (_k, val) =>
    val && typeof val === 'object' && !Array.isArray(val)
      ? Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(val).sort(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b)))
      : val);

export async function idempotent<T>(
  ctx: Ctx, req: { key: string; method: string; path: string; body: unknown },
  effect: (tx: Tx) => Promise<{ status: number; body: T }>,
) {
  const hash = createHash('sha256').update(canonical(req.body)).digest();

  return db.tx({ isolationLevel: 'read committed' }, async (tx) => {
    // 1. Try to claim the key. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes this race-safe.
    const claimed = await tx.oneOrNone(
      `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (tenant_id, actor_id, key, method, path, request_hash, locked_until)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, now() + interval '30 seconds')
       ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
       RETURNING key`,
      [ctx.orgId, ctx.userId, req.key, req.method, req.path, hash],
    );

    if (!claimed) {
      // 2. Someone has this key. Lock the row and decide.
      const row = await tx.one(
        `SELECT * FROM idempotency_keys
          WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND actor_id = $2 AND key = $3
          FOR UPDATE`,
        [ctx.orgId, ctx.userId, req.key],
      );
      if (row.method !== req.method || row.path !== req.path || !row.request_hash.equals(hash)) {
        return { status: 422, body: { error: 'idempotency_key_reused_with_different_request' } };
      }
      if (row.status === 'completed') {
        return { status: row.response_status, body: row.response_body, replayed: true };
      }
      return { status: 409, body: { error: 'request_in_progress' } };
    }

    // 3. We own the key: do the work in the SAME transaction.
    const result = await effect(tx);

    // 4. Store the response; commit makes key + effect visible together.
    await tx.none(
      `UPDATE idempotency_keys
          SET status = 'completed', response_status = $4, response_body = $5,
              locked_until = NULL, updated_at = now()
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND actor_id = $2 AND key = $3`,
      [ctx.orgId, ctx.userId, req.key, result.status, result.body],
    );
    return result;
  });
}

What happens in each failure scenario:

Scenario Outcome
Response lost after commit; client retries Row is completed, fingerprint matches → stored response replayed
Server crashes before commit Transaction rolls back: no key, no effect. Retry starts fresh
Two identical requests arrive concurrently One inserts; the other's INSERT … ON CONFLICT blocks until the first transaction commits, then sees a completed row → replay. (In the phased design of section 7, where a started key is committed before the effect finishes, the duplicate gets 409 request_in_progress instead.)
Same key, different amount 422; the client has a bug and should not be "helped"
Effect throws a business error (e.g. insufficient stock) Whole transaction rolls back. Decide whether deterministic 4xx outcomes should be stored so retries get the same answer (I usually store them; see below)

Should errors be stored? For deterministic failures (validation, "payment exceeds balance"), storing the response gives retries a consistent answer and prevents a later retry from succeeding after state changed, which would surprise the user. For transient failures (5xx, lock timeouts), don't store; let the retry try again. To store a 4xx, catch the business error inside the transaction, write the response, and commit.

6. Idempotency is not only keys: guard your state transitions

Keys de-duplicate requests. Your domain should also refuse to apply the same transition twice, because duplicates can come from places that don't carry your key: a second device, a background job, an admin tool.

-- Completing an order converts it to a sale exactly once.
UPDATE orders
   SET status = 'completed', completed_at = now()
 WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2 AND status = 'served'
RETURNING id;
-- 0 rows → already completed (or not ready): don't create the sale.

-- One sale per order, enforced by the database.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX sales_one_per_order ON sales (tenant_id, order_id);

-- Payments can't exceed the outstanding balance (check inside the tx, with a lock).
SELECT total, paid FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE;

Think of these as defence in depth: the key handles retries of one request; conditional updates and unique constraints handle every other path to a duplicate. Natural keys (one sale per order, one count posting per count) are often stronger than any header.

7. External side effects: phases and recovery points

Things get harder when the effect includes a call you can't roll back: a bank gateway, an SMS provider, an email, a webhook to a partner. You can't hold a database transaction open across a network call to someone else's system, and you can't undo an SMS.

The approach: split the request into atomic phases, each its own transaction, and record a recovery point after each phase.

 Phase A (tx)                 External call              Phase B (tx)
 ┌─────────────────────┐      ┌───────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ claim key           │      │ gateway.charge│          │ record charge result │
 │ create payment row  │ ───► │ (idempotent   │ ───────► │ mark invoice paid    │
 │  status=pending     │      │  key = ours)  │          │ store response       │
 │ recovery=created    │      └───────────────┘          │ recovery=finished    │
 └─────────────────────┘                                 └──────────────────────┘

Rules that make this safe:

  1. Pass an idempotency key downstream. Many payment and messaging APIs accept their own idempotency key or a client reference. Derive it deterministically from yours (for example payment:${paymentId}), so a resumed request reuses the same downstream key.
  2. If the provider has no idempotency support, store enough to ask it ("what happened to reference X?") before trying again. Bank gateways typically have a verify/inquiry call; use it on recovery instead of charging again.
  3. On a retry of a started key whose lease expired, resume from recovery_point instead of starting over. 
async function resumePayment(ctx: Ctx, row: KeyRow) {
  switch (row.recovery_point) {
    case 'started':
      await phaseCreatePayment(ctx, row);              // tx: payment row + recovery='created'
    // fall through
    case 'created': {
      const p = await loadPayment(ctx, row);
      const r = await gateway.charge({ amount: p.amount, reference: `payment:${p.id}` });
      await phaseRecordResult(ctx, row, p, r);         // tx: result + recovery='finished'
    }
    // fall through
    case 'finished':
      return loadStoredResponse(ctx, row);
  }
}

Outbox for everything downstream

For effects that can happen after the response (notifications, webhooks, analytics, search indexing), use the transactional outbox pattern: write an event row in the same transaction as the business change, and let a separate worker deliver it.

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id          bigserial   PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id   uuid        NOT NULL,
  event_id    uuid        NOT NULL UNIQUE,   -- consumers de-duplicate on this
  type        text        NOT NULL,
  payload     jsonb       NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at     timestamptz
);

// Worker: at-least-once delivery, with SKIP LOCKED so several workers can run.
const batch = await tx.any(
  `SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL
    ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,
);
for (const e of batch) {
  await deliver(e);                                  // may be retried → include event_id
  await tx.none(`UPDATE outbox SET sent_at = now() WHERE id = $1`, [e.id]);
}

The outbox moves the problem rather than eliminating it: the worker may deliver twice (crash after deliver, before UPDATE). That's fine, because each event carries event_id and the receiver de-duplicates. Which brings us to the other side.

Inbox: idempotent consumers

If you receive webhooks or queue messages, keep an inbox table and process each event_id once:

CREATE TABLE inbox (
  source     text NOT NULL,
  event_id   text NOT NULL,
  received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (source, event_id)
);

await db.tx(async (tx) => {
  const fresh = await tx.oneOrNone(
    `INSERT INTO inbox (source, event_id) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING 1`,
    ['gateway', event.id],
  );
  if (!fresh) return;              // already processed
  await applyEvent(tx, event);     // same transaction as the inbox insert
});

Producer outbox + consumer inbox is how you get exactly-once effects across a pipeline built on at-least-once delivery.

8. Offline queues are idempotency in slow motion

An offline-capable client is a client that retries hours later. The same rules apply, plus one more:

  • The key is created when the user taps "submit", stored with the queued item, and survives app restarts.
  • Items are submitted in order, and each is removed from the queue only after a definitive response (2xx or a stored 4xx).
  • The server re-validates business rules at submission time. A cached price on the device is not the truth. In NABZA's case, if a price changed while the order sat in the offline queue, the order is held for review rather than silently repriced. The key de-duplicates; the re-validation keeps the result correct.

9. Operational details that bite later

Retention. Keys can't live forever, and they can't expire too early. The retention window must be longer than the longest realistic retry horizon, including offline queues. Stripe, for example, documents that keys may be pruned once they are at least 24 hours old; offline POS clients may need a longer window. Clean up with a periodic job on the created_at index.

Key format. Accept opaque strings with length limits; recommend UUIDs (v4, or v7 for time-ordered locality). Never derive keys from guessable data like orderId + amount on the client side if a collision could merge two legitimate intents.

Response size. Store what you need to replay. If responses are large, store a reference (the created resource ID) and re-render it, accepting that the replay reflects current state.

Observability. Count replays, 409s and 422s per endpoint. A spike in 422 means a client generates keys incorrectly; a spike in replays may mean a network or timeout problem upstream.

Security. Treat keys as scoped identifiers, not secrets, but scope them to tenant and actor so they can't be used to fetch someone else's stored response. Don't store secrets or full card data in response_body.

10. Trade-offs and alternatives

Approach Strength Weakness
Idempotency key table (this post) Works for any POST; replays exact responses Extra write per request; retention to manage
Natural unique constraints Simple, enforced by the DB, covers all paths Only where a natural key exists
Conditional state transitions Protects the domain regardless of entry point Doesn't replay the original response
Client-chosen resource IDs + PUT Idempotent by method semantics Exposes ID generation to clients; not every operation is a "put"
Message de-duplication in a broker Offloads work Usually bounded windows; doesn't cover your DB writes

In practice you combine them: keys at the API edge, natural constraints and guarded transitions in the domain, outbox/inbox between services.

11. A test suite for idempotency 

it('replays the original response for a duplicate', async () => {
  const key = crypto.randomUUID();
  const a = await post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 100_000 }, key);
  const b = await post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 100_000 }, key);
  expect(b.status).toBe(a.status);
  expect(b.body).toEqual(a.body);
  expect(await countPayments(invoiceId)).toBe(1);
});

it('rejects the same key with a different body', async () => {
  const key = crypto.randomUUID();
  await post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 100_000 }, key);
  const b = await post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 200_000 }, key);
  expect(b.status).toBe(422);
});

it('handles concurrent duplicates', async () => {
  const key = crypto.randomUUID();
  const results = await Promise.all(
    Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 100_000 }, key)),
  );
  expect(await countPayments(invoiceId)).toBe(1);
  expect(results.every((r) => [201, 409].includes(r.status))).toBe(true);
});

it('does not replay another user\'s response', async () => {
  const key = crypto.randomUUID();
  await post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 100_000 }, key, userA);
  const b = await post('/payments', { invoiceId, amount: 100_000 }, key, userB);
  // The handler sets `Idempotent-Replayed: true` on replays; user B must never get one.
  expect(b.headers['idempotent-replayed']).toBeUndefined();
});

Add a chaos test: kill the server process between the effect and the response (or inject a fault after commit), then retry and assert a single effect.

Closing

Exactly-once isn't a property of the network; it's a property of your system's bookkeeping. Generate one key per intent, claim it in the same transaction as the effect, fingerprint the request, guard your transitions, and treat every external call as something that may need to be resumed or asked about. The reward is a product where a nervous double tap, a dropped connection or a crashed server never turns into a second charge.

Further reading (public): RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, section on idempotent methods); the IETF HTTPAPI draft "The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field"; Stripe's public API documentation on idempotent requests; Brandur Leach's public article "Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres"; and descriptions of the transactional outbox pattern, for example on microservices.io.

About the author

Mohammadreza Alamnejad is a programmer and network security professional, a UI/UX designer and developer, and the founder of Arka Studio, a design and development studio in Tehran. He built NABZA, a café and restaurant operations SaaS, along with Avenya, Natureio and Radepa. He studied Computer and IT at Sharif University of Technology and Iran University of Science and Technology. More on his founder page at Arka Studio.

title: Quality video on local hardware: the Elsewhere Unfolds workflow
description:
Local models can produce beautiful shots. A finished film needs more: a world that stays coherent, movement that feels intentional, music that holds together, and an edit worth watching. This is the production method we have been developing with Elsewhere Unfolds.

An early Elsewhere Unfolds cut had an attractive world, a complete timeline, and a successful render. It also had water that barely moved and clouds that stayed fixed while the camera drifted past them.

The shot manifest was satisfied. The scene did not feel alive.

That correction changed how we produced the next passages. We separated camera movement from environmental movement, tested short motion clips at normal speed, and watched them before committing to the rest of the film. The improvement came from a clearer creative requirement and a smaller review loop.

Elsewhere Unfolds makes fantasy and cosmic visual journeys with instrumental music. This guide explains the reusable production method behind that work, from the first visual promise to a finished master and vertical excerpts.

The boundary matters: our established motion, music, editing, and finishing pipeline uses local resources. Some starting images were made with a hosted image tool. That makes those productions hybrid. For an entirely local version, supply your own photographs, drawings, local 3D renders, or images from a model running on your machine. The workflow below starts with those local image files. It does not require a hosted video generator.

The examples use the Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B and ACE-Step v1 stack from our production recipes. They are a concrete baseline, not a claim that every newer model has been evaluated or that these settings suit every GPU.

The production loop

Work in three sizes: one shot, one short sequence, then the complete film. Each answers a different question.

Size What you are learning What to review
One native motion take Can the intended action work? Geometry, feet, motion direction, unwanted objects
A 30 to 60 second sequence Do the shots and music belong together? Orientation, pacing, transitions, emotional tone
The complete film Does the experience hold up over time? Repetition, later continuity, score joins, ending

Our longer episodes have used an 8:01 format. That is an editorial choice, not a recommended starting assignment. Begin with a 30-second film you can finish, inspect, and revise. Padding a weak minute into eight minutes only gives you more weak material to fix.

What needs to run locally

You do not need a cluster. You need a machine that can run the chosen model, space for its weights and intermediate files, and a way to edit and review the result.

Job Our established tool or method Output to keep
World and shot planning Written brief, storyboard, reference images Selected brief and shot list
Starting artwork Approved image files; source can vary Original plate and provenance
Image-to-video motion Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B Native take, prompt, seed, settings
Instrumental music ACE-Step v1 3.5B Raw WAVs and selected arrangement
Assembly and finishing Python orchestration and FFmpeg Edit decisions, review copy, final master
Inspection FFprobe, frame samples, normal playback Technical results and review decisions

Wan's documented single-GPU TI2V-5B example targets at least 24 GB of VRAM with model offloading and the text encoder on CPU. Treat that as the reference for that command, not a universal minimum or a guarantee of success. CPU RAM, free VRAM, software versions, and the selected settings still matter. Check the official Wan setup instructions against your hardware before downloading a large checkpoint.

For a first project, keep motion generation and music generation sequential. A background model can consume memory that a video job needs. If the GPU is shared, agree on an available window; do not terminate somebody else's work to make room. A waiting job is cheaper than losing an accepted take or disrupting another workload.

Initial installation and model downloads need network access. Local inference means the generation runs on your equipment. It does not make electricity, storage, setup time, or retakes free.

Record the model revision, source revision, environment, settings, and input image for each run. A seed helps repeat an experiment, but it does not guarantee identical output across different software and hardware.

1. Write the experience before writing prompts

A useful brief explains what the viewer will experience and what will change. “Beautiful cinematic fantasy, ultra detailed” cannot do that work.

Here is an illustrative brief for a small film:

We board a floating garden before it leaves a quiet dock. A gardener crosses the terrace. The gap behind us widens, and a pale arch appears at our destination. Copper, emerald, and pearl remain the visual palette. The mood is calm anticipation. The final image resolves the journey rather than introducing another location.

Turn it into a few fixed decisions:

  • The promise: a garden really leaves one place for another.
  • The route: boarding terrace, departure view, onboard path, destination.
  • The continuity anchors: the same moon placement, architecture, clothing, and direction of travel.
  • The movement: leaves and water move; the dock recedes; a person performs one readable action.
  • The exclusions: no crowds, complicated hand exchanges, or unexplained new landmarks.

Make the thumbnail and first shot agree about the film's promise. If the packaging promises a moving island, establish that island and its departure early. A long logo introduction spends attention before delivering the thing the viewer selected.

For Elsewhere, a recognizable route matters more than a collection of unrelated beautiful locations. Each shot should tell us where we are, what has changed, or where we are going.

2. Build a world that survives the next camera angle

Call the approved starting image for a shot its plate. Keep a small set of reference plates that establish materials, light, landmarks, and any recurring people.

Review the plates together before animating them. A contact sheet makes inconsistencies easier to see: a second moon appears, the destination moves behind the traveler, or a bridge no longer connects to the same terrace.

We have caught all of those classes of problem during production. One reverse view placed another complete moon outside a doorway even though the camera was already inside that moon. Another reference combination duplicated the sun. Attractive individual images can still describe an impossible route.

Use a compact shot table:

Shot Purpose Action Must remain stable
Terrace wide Establish the world Water ripples and leaves move Island silhouette, moon position
Gardener profile Establish habitation One walk from left to right Clothing, ground contact, path
Stern view Prove departure The distant dock recedes Foreground rail, open gap
Bow view Reveal destination Gentle camera reveal Travel direction, destination arch

Simplify a plate when it asks too much of motion generation. Give a walking person visible feet, clear ground, and empty space ahead. Separate actions that would otherwise compete. A close hand exchange, turning crowd, and moving camera in the same five seconds create several opportunities for failure.

If you want the whole process to stay local, this is where you choose your image source. A scene rendered in a local 3D application or a drawing you made yourself is a valid plate. A local image model is another option, but it is a separate tool to qualify. We are not claiming that substituting one reproduces our hosted artwork automatically.

3. Generate one motion take with a clear job

For image-to-video work, let the plate describe the appearance. Use the motion prompt to describe the action, camera, and things that must stay stable.

An illustrative prompt:

Locked medium-wide side view. One gardener walks naturally from left to right along the level stone path. Both feet remain visible and contact the ground. Leaves move gently in the background. Preserve the copper railing, architecture, clothing, and lighting. No additional people, no camera orbit, no cuts.

After following the upstream installation instructions and downloading the TI2V-5B checkpoint, this is the shape of a run from the Wan source directory. Replace the example input and checkpoint paths with your local files. Use a new output filename for each attempt.

python generate.py \
  --task ti2v-5B \
  --size '1280*704' \
  --ckpt_dir ./Wan2.2-TI2V-5B \
  --image ./inputs/gardener.png \
  --prompt 'Locked side view. One gardener walks left to right on a level path. Feet remain visible. Leaves move gently. Preserve the railing and clothing. No extra people or cuts.' \
  --frame_num 121 \
  --sample_steps 50 \
  --sample_solver unipc \
  --sample_shift 5.0 \
  --sample_guide_scale 5.0 \
  --base_seed 42 \
  --offload_model True \
  --convert_model_dtype \
  --t5_cpu \
  --save_file ./gardener-take-01.mp4

These controls follow the upstream command-line interface and our established recipe. This is an adapted example, not a fresh performance benchmark. It does not enable a hosted prompt-expansion service.

At 24 fps, 121 encoded frames occupy about 5.04 seconds. An exact five-second edit uses 120 frames. Check the generated file's actual dimensions and timing: our image-conditioned production outputs have included 1248 × 704, despite the 1280*704 size setting. Do not infer the output raster from the command alone.

Watch the native take before slowing, enlarging, or stitching it. Check the start, middle, and end, then play the entire clip. Look for foot sliding, changing faces, bending rails, sudden foreground figures, and movement in the wrong direction. If the action fails, simplify the action or repair the plate before launching a large batch.

4. Treat three kinds of motion separately

Camera motion changes the viewpoint. Environmental motion changes water, mist, foliage, light, and other scene elements. Performed action is a person walking, turning, or doing something.

An image can have a convincing camera move while its waterfall remains frozen. A scene can have moving fog while its traveler slides without taking a step. Review each kind independently.

For a calm environmental shot, forward slow motion can be useful if it still looks natural. For walking or other recognizable human actions, start with native speed. Watch any interpolation for doubled limbs, smeared edges, and unstable occlusions.

Five seconds of generated movement do not become twenty seconds of new action because the editor can repeat or slow them. A reverse loop can make a person walk backward; a repeated wave or bird can reveal the loop. If a passage needs more time, generate a distinct take, cut to another angle, or shorten the passage.

Continuing from the last frame of a previous take can help connect movement, but it can also carry defects forward. Inspect that frame before making it the next input. Stop a continuation when geometry starts to drift instead of extending the error through the film.

5. Finish a short opening before expanding the film

Assemble a 30 to 60 second proof with real motion, representative music, and the intended edit rhythm. A slideshow of selected plates cannot answer whether the finished motion works.

The proof should contain the hard part. If departure is the central promise, include departure. If a recurring traveler makes the world feel inhabited, include a real walking shot. An easy landscape does not qualify a harder action later.

Review the sequence without pausing first. Does it make sense? Does the first shot deliver the promise? Is there a reason to keep watching? Then examine technical defects and individual transitions.

Once a sequence is accepted, keep its exact files and settings. Expand around it. We preserve accepted openings while generating later passages so a new render cannot silently replace the part that already worked.

Keep a simple project layout:

film/
  brief.md
  shots.csv
  plates/
  motion/raw/
  motion/selected/
  music/raw/
  music/selected/
  edit/
  review/
  exports/

The labels are less important than the separation. Raw sources stay intact; selected sources are explicit; review exports are disposable derivatives. Save a rejection reason beside a failed take so the next attempt changes something useful.

6. Compose and review the soundtrack as a whole

Our established music recipes use ACE-Step v1 3.5B locally. Keep the version explicit: a later release may have different installation, controls, and behavior. Use the project's documentation for the environment matching your selected release.

A music brief should describe the experience and the arrangement. For this style, we ask for warm, spacious instrumental ambience, gradual harmony, and sparse melody. We also describe what would break the mood: lyrics, voice-like passages, a strong beat, abrupt motifs, or a trailer-style crescendo.

Start with a short audition against the opening. Choose where the cue enters and whether it leaves enough space for the imagery. Then review the full arrangement, including every join and the final tail. An attractive first minute does not establish a clean ending.

Keep lossless WAV sources. Build an arrangement from selected cues with measured overlaps, deliberate fades, and enough headroom. The finished duration is the sum of the cue durations minus their overlaps. The same arithmetic applies to overlapping video transitions.

Measure the generated audio rather than assuming a requested duration is exact. We encountered a cue that was roughly 73 milliseconds short because of the installed model's duration grid. The composition had succeeded. The useful response was to preserve it, diagnose the precise discrepancy, and make a small documented finishing correction. That is different from concealing a missing passage with silence.

Check the playback path before removing noise

When static is reported, compare the original WAV, the finished export, and playback in another native player or device. In one later Elsewhere review, native Windows playback sounded correct while the WSL playback path did not. Filtering the accepted source would have changed music that was already satisfactory.

For a different batch of Shorts, a gentle cleanup was accepted after direct comparison. This was the filter used for that case:

ffmpeg -n -i source.wav \
  -af 'afftdn=nr=6:nf=-48:tn=0:gs=8' \
  -c:a pcm_s24le audition-clean.wav

Treat this as an audition candidate, never an automatic mastering preset. FFmpeg documents these controls under afftdn. Denoising can soften wanted texture. Compare original and cleaned versions at comparable listening levels, preserve both, and choose by listening. Waveform similarity and successful decoding cannot establish that something sounds good.

7. Edit to a timeline, not a requested runtime

Give every shot an editorial purpose and an explicit frame allocation. At 24 fps, an 8:01 film contains 11,544 presentation frames. Resolve transitions and overlaps in that frame budget rather than rounding each shot independently.

For a first 30-second exercise, prepare six accepted five-second shots at 24 fps, all with matching dimensions, codec settings, and no audio. Put the filenames in edit/shots.txt, relative to that list:

file '../motion/selected/shot-01.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-02.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-03.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-04.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-05.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-06.mp4'

From the project root, assemble a straight-cut picture track:

ffmpeg -n -f concat -safe 0 -i edit/shots.txt \
  -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v copy edit/picture.mp4

This simple stream-copy path requires compatible, independently prepared clips. Mixed time bases, encoders, or track layouts need normalization in your editing stage; a concat command is not a general repair tool. Keep crossfades out of the first exercise so its duration stays easy to audit. See the concat demuxer documentation.

After preparing a 30-second score with its entrance and ending already shaped, make a review export:

ffmpeg -n -i edit/picture.mp4 -i music/selected/score-30s.wav \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 \
  -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 \
  -movflags +faststart exports/review-30s.mp4

Both sources must cover the intended duration. Avoid adding -shortest as a reflex: it can hide an unexpectedly short input by cutting the other track. Inspect the result and listen to its ending.

Keep the native generation size distinct from the delivery size. A 3840 × 2160 export made from lower-resolution motion is an upscale. It can be a useful delivery format, but enlarging a warped railing makes a larger warped railing. Finish motion and continuity before paying for a high-resolution encode.

8. Make quality control answer specific questions

Automated checks are useful when they tell you exactly what they established. Use FFprobe to inspect the exported file:

ffprobe -v error -count_frames \
  -show_entries 'stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,width,height,avg_frame_rate,nb_read_frames,duration,sample_rate,channels:format=duration' \
  -of json exports/review-30s.mp4

For the exercise, expect 720 video frames at 24 fps and the planned audio channels and sample rate. AAC/container timing can differ slightly from the exact picture duration; investigate meaningful mismatches instead of treating every reported duration as identical.

Decode the entire export, including audio:

ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i exports/review-30s.mp4 \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -f null -

A clean decode establishes readable media. It does not establish pleasing images, good pacing, or acceptable sound. Complete three reviews:

Review Questions
Technical Does it decode? Are the streams, dimensions, frame count, and duration correct?
Visual Does the world stay coherent? Do feet, rails, water, and transitions behave?
Listening Are cue joins, noise, dynamics, and the ending acceptable on real playback?

Sample frames around transitions and at the middle of procedural effects, not just the first and last frames. We caught a highlight problem at the peak of a light treatment: an 8-bit color calculation exceeded its valid range and wrapped. The endpoints looked fine. The fix was in the finishing calculation, not another generation attempt.

When replacing one part of an accepted film, verify that the parts meant to stay unchanged did stay unchanged. File hashes identify exact copies. Decoded-frame comparisons can check preserved picture across a container change. Neither substitutes for watching the new result.

9. Expand, recover, and keep the good work

A long render has more than one kind of success. Generation can finish even if a later copy, collection, or resource-restoration step fails. Inspect the output before rerunning the expensive part.

Save completed takes as they arrive. Record the input plate, prompt, seed, model revision, native output, and selected derivative for each shot. If a job is interrupted, resume from the missing work instead of regenerating everything that already passed review.

On shared hardware, record what resource settings you changed and restore those settings after the run. Check that restoration separately from the video artifact. A good clip does not prove the machine was returned to its previous state.

Agents and scripts are helpful for preparing shot packets, tracking outputs, making contact sheets, checking files, and assembling review pages. Give them explicit limits on retries, durations, and replacement scope. Keep creative selection with the person watching and listening. A process reporting success cannot decide that a walk feels natural.

The useful efficiency measure is accepted footage per production session. A faster model that creates more unusable takes may cost more time overall. Track rejected takes and the reasons for rejection before changing models or increasing concurrency.

10. Derive Shorts from the accepted film

Choose excerpts that contain a complete visual idea: a reveal, an arrival, a short action, or a change in the world. Reframe deliberately for vertical output. A centered crop can remove the destination, the feet, or the object that makes the action understandable.

Elsewhere's vertical edits reuse the accepted picture and soundtrack. Review the new crop, text placement, entrance, and ending as a separate edit. Keep a clean version as well as any version carrying a short hook or invitation to the full film. Captions belong where there is speech or useful context; an instrumental film does not need invented narration.

Watch the export at phone size with the platform's interface area in mind. Keep the important action visible, and listen to the actual exported audio. A short excerpt can expose a rough music boundary that was unnoticeable inside a longer cue.

Publication adds another review: correct file, title, thumbnail, links, visibility, processing, and playback. Follow the platform's current disclosure requirements. Local generation and an original prompt do not settle every source or usage question; retain the provenance and applicable licenses for the material you use.

Measure the audience response separately from production quality. Compare retention and traffic sources at similar release ages where possible. A Short's views do not prove that viewers continued to the full film, and a small audience sample does not establish why one opening performed differently.

Your first local film

Make the first deliverable small enough to finish:

  1. Write one paragraph describing a place, an action, and an ending.
  2. Select a small set of locally sourced plates that agree about the world.
  3. Prove the hardest action in one native motion take.
  4. Build six distinct five-second shots with consistent technical settings.
  5. Select or compose a local 30-second soundtrack and shape its ending.
  6. Assemble, probe, decode, watch, and listen to the complete export.
  7. Preserve the accepted version before trying a longer film or a vertical cut.

The lasting part of the Elsewhere workflow is the ability to inspect and revise each decision. You can replace a model, change an editor, or improve the hardware while keeping that method: define the experience, test its hardest part, preserve what works, and judge the film that the viewer will actually see.

Originally published on danmercede.com.

title: Two new x402 APIs: web-cache-poisoning probe + deep CORS preflight trace (2026-10-14)
description:
Two new $0.0005 USDC x402 endpoints shipped today in the URL Metadata API catalog.

/api/cache-poisoning-vulnerability

Active probe for the well-known web-cache-poisoning vector class. Sends 5 unkeyed-header variants (X-Forwarded-Host + X-Original-URL + X-Forwarded-Prefix + X-Host + X-Forwarded-Server + X-Forwarded-For + X-Forwarded-Proto + X-Original-Host + X-Rewrite-URL), 4 cachebuster-query probes (cb + nocache + utm_source + gclid), and 4 web-cache-deception path probes (robots.txt + .css + .js + .png). Compares body-hash against a baseline fetch and flags any divergence without matching Vary disclosure. Returns web_cache_poisoning_score 0-100 A-F and a verdict.

Tested on stripe.com: 5 poisoned headers detected without Vary disclosure. score=40 grade=D verdict=high_poisoning_risk. On example.com: score=100 grade=A no_poisoning_detected. Distinct from cdn-cache-key-collision (c139) and request-smuggling-evidence (c129): this one invokes the well-known poisoning payloads themselves.

/api/preflight-cors-trace

Deep CORS preflight OPTIONS audit. 6 sequenced probes (baseline GET + simple-Origin preflight + post+contenttype+auth + multi-header x-custom-1/x-custom-2 + credentials + DELETE-method). Per probe captures the full Access-Control-* response set (ACAO + ACAC + ACAM + ACEH + ACEX + ACMA + ACPN) plus Vary. Aggregates method_allowlist_observed + header_allowlist_observed across probes. Returns cors_preflight_score 0-100 A-F + a credential_risk matrix.

Optional &origin= parameter overrides the test origin (default https://example.com). Distinct from cors-policy (c89 single-shot one Origin): this sweeps the actual allowed-headers enumeration.

title: Why Doki Doki Literature Club Bet on Ren'Py and Python: The Niche Engine Behind a Free Horror Phenomenon
description:
Doki Doki Literature Club! should not have scared anyone. A free cute dating sim, made in a Python visual-novel engine most Unity developers have never opened, with static 2D sprites and no voice acting — yet it became one of the most discussed psychological horror games of the decade, spawned endless memes, and earned a premium console sequel.

The short answer for developers is this: the 2017 original was built by Team Salvato, led by Dan Salvato, in Ren'Py, the free and open-source Ren'Py Visual Novel Engine. That niche choice did more than save money. It made the horror possible.

This article explains what Ren'Py actually is, why Python fit a tiny horror experiment, and what I think the rest of us miss about transparent engines, file-system horror, and the cost of leaving niche tech.

Who this is for

You are an indie or hobbyist developer choosing a stack, or a technically curious DDLC player wondering why you had to delete a character file in Explorer to finish the game. You do not need to know Python. You do need to care about scope: a tiny team, about two years, a 350 MB free download.

Scope as verified in October 2026: original DDLC released worldwide September 22, 2017 for Linux, macOS and Windows as freeware, first on itch.io then on Steam. Developer is Team Salvato, designer/programmer/writer/composer is Dan Salvato. Engine is listed as Ren'Py for the original and Unity for Plus!. The game is single-player, visual novel, and explicitly breaks the fourth wall.

What Ren'Py actually is — and how niche it is

Ren'Py is a visual novel engine — used by thousands of creators — that helps you use words, images, and sounds to tell interactive stories that run on computers and mobile devices. It is open source and free for commercial use, with the latest stable 8.5.3 released May 15, 2026.

Under the hood it is deliberately narrow:

  • Written in Python and Cython, built on Pygame which is built with Python on SDL, with FreeType and MIT licensing. The SDK itself is about 115 MB.
  • Script language looks like a screenplay, with label, say, scene, show, menu and Python blocks. A minimal game is literally: 
label start:
    "Sylvie" "Hi there! How was class?"

plus define s = Character('Sylvie', color="#c8ffc8"), scene bg meadow, show sylvie green smile. You get save/load, rollback, preferences and transitions without writing them.

  • Built-ins for the genre: branching stories, save systems, rollback, scene transitions, DLC, movie playback for sprites, in-engine animation via ATL, and full UI customization via Screen Language. Scripts can also include Python blocks for advanced features, and tools are included to obfuscate scripts and archive assets.
  • Platforms are PC and mobile: Windows 10+, macOS 10.10+, Linux, Android 5.0+, iOS 11+, and beta HTML5/WebAssembly. Notably, Ren'Py is not directly supported on game consoles — console ports require porting to another engine such as Unity.
  • Scale: Ren'Py has been used to create over 8,000 visual novels and games, discoverable on VNDB, Itch.io and SteamDB. It has been recommended by PC Gamer and The Guardian and used in classes at Carnegie Mellon, but it remains a single-genre tool compared to Unity, Unreal or Godot.

That is the niche-plus-popular contrast: a Python visual-novel-only framework powering a free horror phenomenon with positive critical attention, memes and a large online following.

Why Python fit a tiny dating-sim-that-isn't

DDLC credits tell the story: Dan Salvato — writing, coding, music; Satchely — character art; Velinquent (VelinquenT) — background art. Salvato was previously known for modding work on Project M, and built DDLC in an estimated two-year period inspired by mixed feelings toward anime and a fascination for surreal, unsettling experiences.

Ren'Py fit that team for three boring, practical reasons:

  1. No engine to build. Dialogue, choices, poem minigame, saves and rollback already exist. Salvato could spend two years on writing, music and horror twists instead of UI framework. The built-in tutorial demonstrates dialogue scripting, images, transitions, music, branching choices — exactly DDLC Act 1.

  2. Screenplay syntax plus Python escape hatch. Act 1 is pure visual novel: first-person narration, static 2D sprites, text without voice acting, occasional choices, and a poem-composition minigame where each girl has different word preferences. That is native Ren'Py. When the game needs to glitch text into mojibake, distort sprites, erase save files, or make Monika talk indefinitely, Python blocks and Screen Language let you break the rules without leaving the engine.

  3. Free and tiny. DDLC is 100% free to play on itch.io, free on Steam with 350 MB storage, 1.8 GHz dual-core, 4 GB RAM and integrated graphics. No license fees, no 10 GB editor, no revenue share to negotiate. For a freeware horror experiment, zero cost is a feature.

My inference, labeled as such: Ren'Py did not just lower cost, it lowered psychological cost. When your engine assumes cute dating sims, subverting it feels transgressive to you as a developer, not just to players. You are misusing a cozy tool. That misuse is creative fuel.

Transparent files as horror mechanic: my deep analysis

Here is where verified facts end and my analysis begins. I label it clearly.

Verified: At a certain point the player must manipulate the game's files to advance the narrative. Monika is revealed as a self-aware character who can manipulate code, deletes Yuri's and Natsuki's character files, confesses love to the real-life player rather than the protagonist, and can only be stopped when the player deletes her character file from the game directory. She then restores the game excluding herself. The game also erases all previous save files when Sayori dies and restarts without her.

Why Ren'Py made this scarier than Unity would have:

Ren'Py games ship as folders players can see. Characters are files like monika.chr, saves and persistent data sit in plain directories, scripts are .rpy text unless you deliberately obfuscate them. Players already browse those folders to install mods or back up saves. DDLC weaponizes that literacy.

In a Unity IL2CPP build, deleting a character would mean hex-editing an AssetBundle or save JSON — technical, abstract, forgettable. In Ren'Py, you open game/characters, see four familiar names, watch two vanish when Monika deletes them, then you yourself right-click-delete monika.chr while she talks to you. It feels like murder, not debugging. The engine's transparency turns OS file operations into moral actions.

My provocation: DDLC proves that legibility is scarier than fidelity. No ray tracing, no jump-scare physics — just the realization that the cute engine you trusted leaves its organs exposed, and the villain knows it. Ren'Py's rollback, persistent data and script obfuscation tools assume a cooperative author. Monika is an uncooperative author living inside those systems.

Three open questions I cannot resolve from public sources alone, and I leave them open deliberately:

  • Did Salvato disable Ren'Py's obfuscation/archiving on purpose to keep files readable, or did readability simply survive because DDLC is Python? Either way, what would horror mean in an engine that encrypts everything by default?
  • How much of the glitch aesthetic — illegible text, distorted sprites, forced watching of Yuri's decomposition over a weekend — is ATL/Screen Language versus raw Python? The docs show both paths, but only source access would tell.
  • If persistent memory tracks you across restarts, at what point does a visual novel stop being a game and start being spyware with consent? DDLC asks this without answering. I think future cozy-tech horror should ask it louder.

If you design narrative horror, ask: what does your engine expose that players already trust? DDLC's answer was: everything.

The console price: 350 MB to 3 GB

Niche tech has a tax, and DDLC paid it visibly.

Because Ren'Py has no console support, the expanded Doki Doki Literature Club Plus!, released June 30, 2021 for Switch, PS4/PS5, Xbox One/Series X/S and PC, was rebuilt in Unity and published with Serenity Forge. The Plus! Steam page lists 3 GB storage versus 350 MB for the original, 6 new side stories, 100+ unlockable images, 26 music tracks, a music player and Full HD art.

Crucially, Plus! replaces actual file manipulation with a virtual desktop that simulates it, plus side stories about friendship and club formation. Reviews praised side stories and console play but noted lack of changes to the core.

My take: this is the honest cost of niche success. Ren'Py got DDLC to viral free release with almost no overhead. Unity got it to consoles and paid sustainability, but at 8.5x disk size and with simulated transgression. A fake OS inside a Unity game is clever; deleting a real file in Windows Explorer is unforgettable. When you port cozy tech to mainstream tech, you gain reach and lose danger. Is that trade always worth it? For Team Salvato, probably yes — free cannot fund forever. For your prototype, maybe not yet.

What would you preserve if you had to rewrite your Ren'Py/Python game in Unity tomorrow? Make a list now, before you need to.

Moddability as accident and engine

Ren'Py scripts are human-readable text. The quickstart shows you edit script.rpy in VS Code, define characters, show images, add menus and Python. That means any player can open DDLC, read dialogue, find flags, and spoil or extend the horror in hours. Datamining is not hacking; it is reading.

This cuts two ways. Spoilers leak fast when horror lives in plain text — Act 2 twists were documented within days. But mods bloom fast too: gender-swaps, new routes, Monika-after-story continuations, poem-word analyzers. Ren'Py's 8,000-game community already knows how to fork a visual novel. DDLC inherited that literacy for free.

My question for you: did Team Salvato choose Ren'Py because it was moddable, or did moddability emerge and then amplify the meme following? I suspect the latter, and that is the lesson. Pick a stack where fans can extend you without permission. If your engine requires an SDK, NDA or encrypted bundle to add one line of dialogue, you are taxing your evangelists.

A warning I do mean rigorously: Ren'Py's ease also eases cruelty. DDLC carries mature content: self-harm, suicide, suggestive themes, and a front-page warning that it is not suitable for children or those easily disturbed. Transparent files plus dark themes plus young anime aesthetics is a volatile mix that led to real-world controversy in the UK. Niche accessibility does not remove responsibility. If you subvert cozy tech, label the horror, provide resources, and do not hide behind freeware innocence.

What to steal (and what not to copy)

Steal this if you are solo or small:

  • Choose genre-native boring tech. Ren'Py removed save systems, rollback, transitions and dialogue UI from your backlog. What would your game's Ren'Py be — Twine, Bitsy, PICO-8, LibGDX?
  • Keep one Python escape hatch. 95% screenplay, 5% code for the moments that break genre. DDLC's ratio is instructive.
  • Ship small and free if horror needs trust. 350 MB and zero dollars made trying DDLC effortless. Fear needs low friction.
  • Design one OS-level interaction. Not ten mechanics — one file deletion players will tell friends about.

Do not romanticize:

  • No console, no 3D, no complex physics. Ren'Py assumes 2D sprites and text. If you need consoles day one, budget a Unity rewrite like Plus! did.
  • Python readability leaks story. If your twist depends on secrecy, you need obfuscation, server flags, or acceptance that spoilers are marketing.
  • Cute plus horror plus accessibility risks harm. Content warnings, age gates and crisis resources are part of the stack, not PR.

Verdict

DDLC did not succeed despite Ren'Py and Python. It succeeded because a niche visual-novel engine let a tiny team ship a convincing dating sim in months, then spend remaining time corrupting it from inside with Python. The official pitch still smiles: welcome to the Literature Club, chit-chat and fun with Sayori, Natsuki, Yuri and Monika — will you promise to spend the most time with Monika? That smile is engineering as much as writing.

If you are starting a narrative experiment in 2026, ask the DDLC question: what does your engine expose that you could betray? If the answer is nothing — everything encrypted, sandboxed, cloud-saved — maybe your horror needs a more honest, more niche machine.

What cozy tool would become terrifying if it hated you just a little? I do not have a rigorous answer. I think the question is more useful than any benchmark.

Sources and verification date

Core facts verified October 14, 2026 via direct English primary-source retrieval. English Bing queries were attempted for Ren'Py, DDLC interviews and sales, but returned generic dictionary, DAN and browser-game noise, so verification relies on primary pages below. Analysis and provocations are my own and labeled as such.

  • Ren'Py purpose, free commercial use, platforms and 8,000+ works
  • Ren'Py Python/Cython, Pygame/SDL, MIT, ATL/Screen Language, branching/rollback/Python blocks, console limitation
  • Ren'Py repo, Python modules and MIT contribution policy
  • Ren'Py script language, characters, scene/show, menus and Python statements
  • DDLC official site: premise, team teaser and content warning
  • DDLC itch.io: free, staff credits and warning
  • DDLC Steam: free, mature note, 350 MB system requirements
  • DDLC reference: Ren'Py vs Unity engines, Sept 2017 release, Team Salvato two-year/Project M background, freeware itch-to-Steam, metafictional fourth-wall horror, poem minigame, file manipulation, Monika self-awareness and deletions, memes/large following, Plus! June 2021 premium and virtual desktop
  • Plus! Steam: side stories, images, tracks, HD upgrade, 3 GB requirements and mature descriptors

title: How to choose a Cloudflare Queues jurisdiction before production
description:
The jurisdiction choice belongs in queue provisioning

If a customer contract says messages must stay in the EU, US, or a specified government environment, decide where the queue lives before your production publisher starts sending jobs. Cloudflare Queues now lets you create a queue with a jurisdiction restriction. The setting is fixed when the queue is created: Cloudflare says you cannot add, change, or remove it later.

That makes this an infrastructure decision, not a runtime toggle. Put the jurisdiction in the reviewed environment configuration, name queues so operators can identify their role and location, and verify the setting before connecting production traffic. If a requirement changes, plan to create a replacement queue and move application traffic deliberately. Do not assume an existing queue can be relabeled in place.

Know exactly what the restriction covers

Cloudflare’s Queues data-location documentation says the default is to store and process messages across its global network. A jurisdiction-restricted queue limits where Queues stores and processes those messages. Workers can still produce to and consume from the restricted queue from any location.

That last sentence is an important boundary. Queue residency does not, by itself, establish that the Worker running your code, the database it calls, your logs, analytics, backups, or every other copy of a payload is in the same jurisdiction. Treat the queue setting as one control in a larger data-flow design. Trace the message from the moment your application creates it through retries, dead-letter handling, downstream services, and deletion. Keep personal or regulated data out of fields that do not need it, and confirm the rules for each system that receives a copy.

Conceptual illustration: queue messages are stored and processed within the chosen jurisdiction while a Worker can connect from elsewhere.

Cloudflare lists three jurisdiction values: eu for the European Union, us for the United States, and fedramp for FedRAMP-Moderate data centers. Select the value required by your actual contract and deployment policy. A region name that sounds plausible is not a supported value, and choosing eu should not be represented as a guarantee of legal compliance by itself.

Create the queue with the intended value

Cloudflare documents a --jurisdiction flag for queue creation. For example:

cf queues create --queue-name invoices-eu --jurisdiction eu

The same field is available on the Create Queue REST endpoint. Keep the choice alongside the queue name in the deployment runbook or infrastructure-as-code input, then make the creation step repeatable for each environment. Avoid creating production queues manually from an engineer’s personal dashboard if your team needs a reviewable record of the selected value.

Before deploying publishers and consumers, check the queue in the Cloudflare dashboard and confirm the displayed jurisdiction. Make that check part of a release checklist, just as you would verify a database target or a production secret binding. The key question is not only “did queue creation succeed?” but also “did this environment create the queue with the policy this tenant and payload require?”

If you use several queues, document the purpose and jurisdiction of each one. A single application may have an EU queue for one customer workflow and a US queue for another, but only if the data-flow and access rules make that separation real. Do not route a message into a queue based only on a user-selected preference unless the server validates that choice against the customer’s account policy.

Plan for the setting you cannot edit

Because the jurisdiction cannot be changed after creation, a wrong choice requires a migration plan. First, create a new queue with the correct jurisdiction and verify it. Next, deploy consumers that can safely handle messages from the old and new queues while you switch producers. Use stable job IDs or idempotency keys so that a message delivered from both paths cannot create a duplicate charge, email, or other side effect.

Then choose a cutover strategy that matches your delivery guarantees. You might stop new writes to the old queue, let its backlog drain, and switch producers once the remaining work is handled. Or you may need a controlled application-level replay into the replacement queue. Cloudflare’s jurisdiction documentation does not promise that changing a setting moves existing messages for you, so do not treat queue creation as an automatic data migration. Preserve enough operational records to reconcile what was sent, completed, retried, or deliberately discarded.

Keep the old queue available only as long as your retention and operational policy allow. Confirm that no publisher can still write to it, no consumer is silently relying on it, and its dead-letter path is accounted for before retiring it. A migration checklist should include the source and destination queue, jurisdiction, producer deployment, consumer deployment, backlog and retry state, idempotency behavior, and the person who verifies the cutover.

Keep the dead-letter path in the same design

A dead-letter queue is part of the message lifecycle, not an unrelated cleanup destination. Cloudflare’s documentation says a DLQ must use the same jurisdiction as its source queue. If you provide a DLQ name that does not exist, Cloudflare automatically creates it in the source queue’s jurisdiction.

Include that behavior in your infrastructure plan and verify the resulting queue after provisioning. If the DLQ already exists, ensure its jurisdiction matches the source before attaching it. Also include replays and manual inspection in your data-flow review: an operational tool that exports or copies a failed message can create a new data location even when the queue itself is correctly restricted.

Conceptual illustration: a dead-letter queue is paired in the same jurisdiction as its source queue.

Test the real path before sending customer data

Start with synthetic messages that contain no personal data. Verify that the expected queue exists, the dashboard shows its jurisdiction, the publisher can send, and the consumer can process. Exercise retries and the DLQ as well as the success path. Confirm what your application logs when a send fails and whether an operator can inspect payloads from a different system.

For production, record a small set of release facts: which policy selected the jurisdiction, which queue and DLQ were created, which application version is bound to them, and who approved the data flow. Recheck those facts when adding a new producer or downstream service. If the message schema changes to include more sensitive fields, repeat the review rather than assuming the old queue decision covers the new data.

If your queue starts accumulating work, residency is only one part of the operating model. Our guide to queue backpressure on an owned backend covers refusing bursts before downstream capacity is exhausted. If you are building the product UI around that workflow, the SaaS Dashboard kit is an optional $99 editable starting point for an app shell and data tables; it does not include Cloudflare Queues or jurisdiction configuration.

Sources

  • Cloudflare, Queues now supports EU, US, and FedRAMP jurisdictions — announced October 12, 2026.
  • Cloudflare, Queues data location — checked October 14, 2026.
  • OTF, SaaS Dashboard kit — optional UI/source starting point; checked October 14, 2026.
