title: 43 days, 17,040 AI signals: four things the data says that trend lists won't tell you
description:
I've been running a small pipeline that collects AI signals from public sources for 43 days now — 17,040 items, ~398 a day. I built it to power a daily digest, but the dataset turned out to be more interesting than the digest, mostly because of what it can't tell me.

Here are the four findings I'd want to know before building anything on top of AI trend data.

1. Only 23 of 1,493 tracked models have enough history to compute a trend

This is the big one. My collector snapshots trending lists — GitHub trending, Hugging Face trending, and so on. Those lists rotate. A model that's #4 today may be gone tomorrow, taking its history with it.

The result:

tracked ranked with ≥20 days of history
Hugging Face models 1,493 228 23
GitHub repos 63 63 14

So when a tool shows you "momentum" for an AI model, ask what its baseline is. If the entity was only observed twice, a "trend" is two points and a straight line.

I chose to publish unranked with the reason rather than fill the gap with something plausible — every row in my JSON either has a derivable number or an explicit "not ranked, here's why". That decision cost me a lot of "wow" numbers. It's still the right one: an invented rank is indistinguishable from a real one to whatever consumes it downstream.

The fix, if you're building this yourself: track a fixed set (top N by a stable metric, every day) in addition to the rotating trending lists. Rotation gives you discovery; a fixed set gives you a time series. Without the second one you have neither.

2. Top entities are boringly stable — the interesting signal is churn

I expected the leaders to move. Over 48 days of daily snapshots:

  • Biggest Hugging Face download change: −11.7% (moonshotai/Kimi-K3)
  • Biggest increase in the same column: +7.6% (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1)
  • Everything else in the top 8: −5% to −10%
  • GitHub stars, top repos: +0.08% to +0.54% over 48 days

So the leaderboard is nearly static, and most large models slowly decay in downloads. Growth is the exception, not the norm.

Meanwhile, a single day's deltas (2026-10-12 → 2026-10-13) looked like this: 2 models entered, 41 were not seen again, 201 changed rank. That's where the motion is — at the edges, not the top.

If you're building alerts, alert on entry and exit, not on rank movement at the top. "This model appeared for the first time / this one vanished" carried far more information than "+3 places".

3. Most of the volume is one source, and it isn't the interesting one

Over 43 days, by source:

source items share
hot-topic aggregation 6,455 38%
arXiv 2,551 15%
Hugging Face 2,107 12%
arena boards 2,041 12%
silicon-valley news 1,198 7%
hardware/chips 1,089 6%
GitHub 860 5%
YouTube 739 4%

The aggregation source alone is more than a third of everything. It's cheap to collect and it mostly duplicates what you already have from the primary sources.

The four sources that actually produce the digest (GitHub, Hugging Face, YouTube, Silicon Valley news) are 29% of the volume. If you rank sources by item count, you'll optimize for the loudest one instead of the useful one. I ended up tracking per-source yield and dedup rate, not raw volume — volume is the metric that makes a pipeline look productive while producing nothing.

4. Derive numbers from raw snapshots, or don't publish them

Every derived number I publish (rank, rank change, 7-day momentum, position in an arXiv category) is recomputed from raw snapshots by an automated audit, and the audit also reconciles the rendered pages against the JSON endpoints. If the two disagree, that's a failure, not a rounding difference.

Two reasons this matters more than it sounds:

  1. Derived numbers drift silently. A rank computed at write time and stored is a claim from the past; recomputed, it's a claim you can defend.
  2. It catches your own bugs. The audit has caught things like a "content quality" check passing on pages whose body was actually empty, and mismatch between a daily edition and the API response for the same date.

I'd rather ship a boring number I can re-derive than an exciting one I can't.

What I'm doing with this

The pipeline is unattended (collects 4×/day, one published edition/day, self-audited daily). The data is public and free:

  • Daily dataset (CC BY 4.0): github.com/jiangzhangcc-glitch/ai-signals-daily — plus a bulk signals.jsonl (all 17,040 rows) on the releases page
  • Today's signals as JSON: https://data.jiangzhang.ca/signals4/api/today.json
  • What changed since the previous snapshot: .../api/changes.json
  • Ranked models/repos with citations: .../api/models.json, .../api/repos.json
  • As MCP tools for Claude/Cursor: signals-api-mcp

One gotcha worth passing on: if you call the API with a bare Python-urllib User-Agent (or none), you'll get a 403 from the CDN, at the edge — your request never reaches the server, and the server's logs show nothing. It looks exactly like an API that's down. requests, httpx, aiohttp, Go, node-fetch, axios and curl are all fine. Set a User-Agent in examples.

If you need more than the free tier — 8 sources instead of 4, four updates a day, and full history behind a stable key — that's the paid feed: what it includes.

And if you're building something similar: I'd genuinely like to know how you handle the rotating-list problem. It's the part I underestimated most.

title: Backend Error Capture: 5 Lightweight Checks for Exception Tracking Without Replay
description:
Short answer: choose a lightweight capture API when a logistics checkout team can diagnose each server-side failure from a small, scrubbed event and can prove that contract with evals; choose a full exception-tracking suite when the team needs source-mapped stacks, release correlation, or an established incident workflow.

The decision is really about signal quality versus noise. A browser replay can show a frustrated click, but it cannot explain why inventory reservation for shipment shp_1842 lost a race. A raw stack can expose implementation detail yet omit the operational facts that settle the incident: checkout stage, carrier mode, retry count, deployment, and a stable error code. For backend routes, I would make those facts the center of the design and treat the collector as plumbing.

This is a narrow recommendation. It isn't a claim that fewer features always win.

1. How should backend routes capture exceptions without sourcemaps or replay?

Start at the failure boundary. A Next.js checkout route catches an exception after normal business recovery has failed, translates it into a controlled response, and emits one event to an internal HTTPS endpoint. The collector validates the event, removes fields it doesn't accept, computes a stable fingerprint, and writes to a searchable sink. An alerting job then works from grouped event rates rather than firing once for every request.

That data flow is deliberately boring:

  1. The route creates a request ID and carries it through downstream calls.
  2. Expected outcomes, such as a declined payment or an unavailable delivery window, remain normal application results unless they violate an invariant.
  3. Unexpected exceptions become structured events with a bounded set of dimensions.
  4. The collector groups repeated events and retains a count, first-seen time, last-seen time, and one sanitized example.
  5. Alerts evaluate impact and novelty, not raw exception volume alone.

The event should answer a concrete question without reconstructing the user's session. For a logistics checkout, useful fields include error_code, checkout_stage, route_template, deployment, carrier_mode, retry_count, and request_id. Avoid the raw URL, address, cart contents, authorization headers, and arbitrary exception locals. Route templates matter: /checkout/[id]/confirm is a bounded label, while a URL containing every checkout ID creates an ever-growing label set.

Prometheus makes the same general instrumentation point: every unique label combination creates a new time series, so unbounded labels such as user IDs should not be labels. The storage system here may not be Prometheus, but the design pressure is identical. High-cardinality dimensions raise query cost and make grouping less useful. Keep request IDs in event details for lookup, not in aggregate labels.

No replay means less behavioral context. No sourcemaps means a minified client stack is of little diagnostic value. Neither omission prevents high-quality server capture if the event contract preserves the decision-making context at the route boundary. That is the first check: can an engineer tell which invariant failed, where it failed, and how many checkouts were affected?

2. Run a lean Python collector before choosing a suite

A notebook-to-prod path benefits from a tiny reference implementation. Even when the producer is a Next.js route, a Python collector makes the ingestion contract executable: it accepts only known keys, rejects malformed input, scrubs obvious secrets, and derives a fingerprint from bounded fields. This example uses only the standard library and keeps events in memory, so it is suitable for a local contract test, not production storage.

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
from collections import Counter
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from typing import Any


ALLOWED_FIELDS = {
    "error_code",
    "checkout_stage",
    "route_template",
    "deployment",
    "carrier_mode",
    "retry_count",
    "request_id",
    "message",
}
REQUIRED_FIELDS = {"error_code", "checkout_stage", "route_template", "deployment"}
SENSITIVE_WORDS = {"authorization", "cookie", "email", "address", "token"}
counts: Counter[str] = Counter()
examples: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}


def sanitize(payload: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    event = {
        key: value
        for key, value in payload.items()
        if key in ALLOWED_FIELDS and not any(word in key.lower() for word in SENSITIVE_WORDS)
    }
    missing = REQUIRED_FIELDS - event.keys()
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"missing required fields: {sorted(missing)}")

    event["message"] = str(event.get("message", ""))[:240]
    event["retry_count"] = int(event.get("retry_count", 0))
    if event["retry_count"] < 0:
        raise ValueError("retry_count must be non-negative")
    return event


def fingerprint(event: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    parts = (
        str(event["error_code"]),
        str(event["checkout_stage"]),
        str(event["route_template"]),
        str(event["deployment"]),
    )
    return hashlib.sha256("\x1f".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]


class EventHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self) -> None:
        if self.path != "/events":
            self.send_error(404)
            return

        try:
            length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", "0"))
            if length < 2 or length > 16_384:
                raise ValueError("body size is outside the accepted range")
            raw = json.loads(self.rfile.read(length))
            if not isinstance(raw, dict):
                raise ValueError("event must be an object")
            event = sanitize(raw)
            key = fingerprint(event)
        except (ValueError, TypeError, json.JSONDecodeError) as exc:
            body = json.dumps({"accepted": False, "reason": str(exc)}).encode()
            self.send_response(400)
        else:
            counts[key] += 1
            examples.setdefault(key, event)
            body = json.dumps(
                {"accepted": True, "fingerprint": key, "count": counts[key]}
            ).encode()
            self.send_response(202)

        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, format: str, *args: object) -> None:
        return


if __name__ == "__main__":
    server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8080), EventHandler)
    server.serve_forever()

Send a representative event from another Python process:

import json
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


event = {
    "error_code": "inventory_reservation_conflict",
    "checkout_stage": "reserve_inventory",
    "route_template": "/checkout/[id]/confirm",
    "deployment": "checkout-2026-08-14.1",
    "carrier_mode": "parcel",
    "retry_count": 2,
    "request_id": "req_7f93a1",
    "message": "reservation version changed before commit",
}
request = Request(
    "http://127.0.0.1:8080/events",
    data=json.dumps(event).encode(),
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    method="POST",
)

with urlopen(request, timeout=2) as response:
    print(json.loads(response.read()))

The example intentionally does not ship authentication, durable storage, transport retries, retention controls, or multi-process aggregation. Those are production responsibilities. Its job is smaller: expose the event contract early, while changing a field still takes minutes rather than a migration across several services.

Keep it dull.

3. Preserve checkout evidence, then suppress duplicate noise

Deduplication is where a lightweight system either earns trust or becomes an inbox nobody reads. Fingerprinting only the exception message is fragile because messages often contain IDs or variable text. Fingerprinting only the exception class goes too far in the other direction: two TimeoutError events at payment authorization and label purchase may have different owners and urgency. A useful checkout fingerprint combines a stable error code, stage, route template, and deployment. The example does that, though your mileage may vary if one deployment serves several independently owned flows.

Do not sample the first occurrence of a new fingerprint. Keep the first event, increment an exact counter for its group, and preserve a recent sanitized example. Sampling can begin after the group is known, but a burst should still update aggregate counts. Otherwise, the collector hides the very shape an incident responder needs.

Alerts need a second layer of judgment. A single inventory_reservation_conflict followed by a successful retry is evidence, not necessarily a page. The same code affecting several checkout stages or continuing after the retry budget is exhausted deserves more attention. I initially want one threshold because it is easy to explain; an eval set usually shows why that is too blunt. Novel failures, sustained failure ratios, and exhausted recoveries are different signals.

This is also where browser performance telemetry must stay in its lane. Core Web Vitals describe loading, interactivity, and visual stability through LCP, INP, and CLS, evaluated at the 75th percentile. Those measurements can reveal a poor checkout experience, but they do not identify a server-side reservation invariant. Join the two kinds of evidence through a privacy-reviewed request or trace correlation strategy; don't pretend one replaces the other.

4. Test signal quality with an eval set, not a feature checklist

Before picking a full suite or a self-serve capture API, build a small labeled corpus from synthetic checkout failures. Twenty carefully chosen fixtures can be more informative than a long feature grid. Include a payment decline that should not page, a retryable carrier timeout, a repeated inventory conflict, malformed input that should remain a client error, and an unknown exception that must be retained. For each fixture, record the expected fingerprint, retained fields, redactions, severity, and alert decision.

Then score both paths against the same questions. Did two instances of the same operational failure group together? Did unrelated checkout stages remain separate? Did an email, address, token, or raw payload survive sanitization? Can the event be tied to a deployment? Does the pipeline retain evidence when the alert threshold is not crossed? How many events and bytes does one synthetic order generate?

That last question is prompt-cost aware in spirit: count before optimizing. An AI-assisted incident summary should consume a compact, validated incident bundle, not thousands of near-identical stack traces. Measure grouping precision first, then decide whether a model adds useful synthesis. I'm not sure a universal alert threshold exists for checkout systems; traffic shape, retry policy, and fulfillment deadlines change the cost of a false positive. A shadow deployment with labeled synthetic failures is what resolves that uncertainty.

The pass condition should be explicit. For example, every secret-bearing fixture must redact the secret, every novel invariant failure must remain searchable, and expected business outcomes must not trigger an urgent alert. The numbers in that test are policy choices, not universal benchmarks. Version the fixtures beside the route contract and run them whenever event fields, grouping logic, or retry behavior changes.

Now the vendor decision is much less theatrical. The winning category is the one that passes the checkout eval with the least operational machinery your team is prepared to own.

5. Know when lightweight capture is the wrong boundary

A lightweight endpoint is a good fit when the scope is server routes, the team already operates a searchable event store, the on-call group can maintain ingestion and retention, and structured domain context matters more than reconstructed source or browser behavior. Its advantage is control: the event schema mirrors the checkout state machine, and a notebook can exercise the same contract used in deployment.

The catch is ownership. A collector that accepts events but lacks durable buffering, access control, retention policy, alert delivery, and an audited redaction process is not an exception-tracking service; it is one small component. Do not choose the lean path merely to avoid setup. Choose it only when those surrounding responsibilities already have clear homes.

Stick with a full exception-tracking suite when engineers need source-mapped stacks across frequent frontend releases, release health, browser breadcrumbs or replay, mature issue assignment, or integrations that the team would otherwise have to build and operate. It is also the better boundary when several teams need consistent workflows and no team owns the capture pipeline. More collected context can increase privacy review and noise, so enable it according to policy rather than by habit.

The operational checklist is short enough to say plainly. Re-run the fixture corpus before deployment. Verify redaction at the collector boundary and again at the sink. Watch accepted, rejected, dropped, and grouped event counts using bounded labels. Exercise delivery failure without blocking checkout responses. Review retention and access with the people responsible for customer data. Finally, inspect a sample of grouped events after release and compare the observed alert decisions with the labels in the eval set. If that loop is healthy, the tool choice has done its job.

References

  • https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/
  • https://web.dev/articles/vitals

title: How to Build a LangGraph Agent with FastAPI and SSE Streaming
description:
Building an AI agent is relatively straightforward. Making it accessible through an API, integrating real tools, and streaming execution updates to a client is where the architecture becomes more interesting.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a small, working example that combines:

  • LangGraph for agent orchestration
  • FastAPI for HTTP endpoints
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming responses
  • Open-Meteo as a real external tool

The goal isn't to build a production-ready platform in one tutorial. It's to establish a working foundation and understand the responsibilities of each component.

Source code: LangGraph + FastAPI Example on GitHub

1. Why LangGraph and FastAPI?

LangGraph handles the agent's execution flow.

FastAPI exposes that execution to external clients.

These are different responsibilities, and separating them makes the application easier to understand and extend.

A useful mental model is:

The client shouldn't need to understand how the agent chooses tools or manages its internal execution flow.

It should interact with a clear HTTP interface.

2. Give the agent a real tool

An agent becomes more interesting when it can do something beyond generating text.

In this example, the agent uses a weather tool backed by Open-Meteo.

That introduces a realistic execution path:

  1. The user asks a weather-related question.
  2. The model determines whether it needs the tool.
  3. The tool requests external weather information.
  4. The result returns to the agent.
  5. The agent uses the result to answer.

This is a useful foundation for more advanced agents that interact with APIs, databases, and business systems.

It also introduces concerns that don't exist in a simple LLM completion: network failures, tool errors, latency, and retries.

3. Expose the agent through FastAPI

The next step is making the agent accessible through an HTTP API.

The example demonstrates two response patterns.

Regular JSON responses

The client sends a request and waits for the agent's result.

This approach is appropriate for simple integrations where intermediate execution updates aren't necessary.

Streaming responses

The client receives updates while the request is being processed.

This is useful when agent execution involves multiple operations and the user would otherwise wait without feedback.

Both patterns can be built around the same agent architecture.

4. Why use Server-Sent Events?

Server-Sent Events provide a way to deliver a stream of updates over an HTTP response.

Instead of waiting for one final response, the client can process events as they arrive.

A simplified SSE message looks like this:

event: message
data: {"content":"Processing your request..."}

The example above illustrates SSE formatting, not the exact event contract of the repository.

For AI applications, streaming can improve the experience by making long-running operations more visible.

However, streaming also introduces engineering considerations:

  • What happens when the client disconnects?
  • How are errors communicated after the stream begins?
  • How does the client recognize completion?
  • What happens if a tool fails halfway through execution?

These questions matter when moving from a working demonstration to a reliable service.

5. Keep the agent separate from the API

One important design principle is to avoid mixing agent orchestration with HTTP transport logic.

The agent should own its execution flow and tool interactions.

The FastAPI layer should handle requests, responses, and streaming transport.

That separation makes it easier to test the agent independently, evolve the API, and introduce additional clients later.

It also creates a clearer boundary for future capabilities such as authentication, persistence, and observability.

6. What this example does not solve yet

A working agent API is not automatically production-ready.

Before using this architecture for critical workflows, several additional concerns need attention.

Persistence and checkpointing

Long-running or multi-step agents may need to recover execution state after interruptions.

Retries and idempotency

Retrying a failed operation can be dangerous when tools modify external systems.

For example, retrying a payment operation must not charge the same customer twice.

Checkpointing alone doesn't guarantee idempotency. External side effects need their own protection.

Observability

Production systems need visibility into agent execution, LLM calls, tool inputs and outputs, errors, and latency.

LangSmith is one option for tracing LangGraph applications at the execution, node, and tool-call levels.

Security and operational controls

Authentication, rate limiting, secrets management, structured logging, and deployment configuration need to be addressed according to the environment.

These aren't reasons to avoid building a small example. They're reasons to distinguish a working foundation from a complete production system.

7. Run the example yourself

The public repository contains the implementation and setup instructions.

GitHub: https://github.com/salada-dados/langgraph-fastapi-example

Start with the README, run the example locally, and inspect how the agent, tool integration, FastAPI endpoints, and SSE streaming fit together.

The most useful next exercise is to replace the weather tool with an API relevant to your own application.

That helps expose the operational questions you'll eventually need to solve.

8. From a working example to production

I'm also building a Production LangGraph + FastAPI Starter, focused on reducing the repetitive engineering work involved in taking an agent beyond a local demonstration.

The goal is to provide a production-oriented starting point rather than claim that every deployment concern can be solved by a template.

If you're working on an agent and running into challenges with persistence, retries, observability, or deployment, I'd be interested in hearing what's been hardest.

Interested in the production-oriented Starter? Join the Early Access list.

Read the original tutorial: https://saladadedados.com/en/blog/langgraph-fastapi-sse

Explore the source code: https://github.com/salada-dados/langgraph-fastapi-example

What has been the hardest part of moving your LangGraph agent from a local prototype to a real application?

title: Node.js Structured Logs 2026: SaaS Notification Request Trace and PII Masking
description:
Log one structured event for each notification delivery attempt, attach request and trace context, pseudonymize the customer identifier, and record usage dimensions that explain the attempt's cost. That is the smallest useful design for a customer-support SaaS trying to answer two questions at once: why did this notification fail, and which workflow incurred the spend?

TL;DR: keep request_id, trace_id, and delivery_attempt_id as separate fields; derive a stable, non-reversible actor_key instead of logging a raw user ID; allowlist event fields before serialization; and put cost inputs such as channel, template class, payload bytes, and attempt number on the delivery event. Do not log message bodies, email addresses, authorization headers, or provider responses wholesale. JSON is the transport shape, not the schema.

The tempting first version is console.log({ request, response }). It is quick to ship and expensive to live with. A failed email can leave a customer address, support text, headers, and a large response object in storage, while still omitting the one identifier needed to connect the enqueue request to the delivery worker. The better experiment is narrower: can an operator reconstruct one failed delivery and attribute its resource use from a small, explicit event?

What should a SaaS application log for each structured notification request?

A useful event describes a state transition, not every object available at that line of code. For a delivery attempt, the state transition is straightforward: a queued notification was handed to a channel adapter, which either accepted or rejected it. The log needs enough context to connect that outcome to an incoming support action and enough dimensions to explain resource use.

Start there.

I would start with five groups of fields. Identity includes event_name, delivery_attempt_id, and the notification's internal key. Correlation includes request_id, trace_id, and span_id. Attribution includes workspace_key, actor_key, channel, template_class, and attempt_number. Outcome includes status, duration_ms, and a bounded error_code. Runtime context includes service name, environment, release, and timestamp.

Those IDs do different jobs. A request ID follows one application request and is still useful when tracing is absent. A trace ID joins work across instrumented services and asynchronous boundaries when that context is propagated. A delivery-attempt ID distinguishes retries of the same notification. Combining them into one convenient correlation_id destroys information exactly when a queue retry or fan-out makes the incident interesting.

Keep the vocabulary boring. A log query should not need to remember that one worker calls a workspace tenant, another calls it account, and the API calls it organization. Define the schema once, version it, and reject unknown fields in tests.

The focused Node.js experiment

The example below uses only Node.js built-ins. It deliberately accepts a small input type rather than a request, user, or provider object.

The boundary is the safety feature.

import { createHash, randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type DeliveryOutcome = "accepted" | "rejected";

type DeliveryAttempt = {
  requestId: string;
  traceId?: string;
  spanId?: string;
  workspaceId: string;
  userId: string;
  notificationId: string;
  attemptNumber: number;
  channel: "email" | "sms" | "push";
  templateClass: "case_update" | "agent_reply" | "sla_warning";
  payloadBytes: number;
  outcome: DeliveryOutcome;
  durationMs: number;
  errorCode?: "timeout" | "rate_limited" | "invalid_recipient" | "provider_rejected";
};

const LOG_HASH_KEY = process.env.LOG_HASH_KEY;
if (!LOG_HASH_KEY) throw new Error("LOG_HASH_KEY is required");

function pseudonymousKey(scope: string, value: string): string {
  return createHash("sha256")
    .update(`${LOG_HASH_KEY}:${scope}:${value}`)
    .digest("hex")
    .slice(0, 24);
}

export function logDeliveryAttempt(input: DeliveryAttempt): void {
  const event = {
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    severity: input.outcome === "accepted" ? "info" : "warn",
    event_name: "notification.delivery_attempted",
    schema_version: 1,
    service: "notification-worker",
    release: process.env.APP_RELEASE ?? "unknown",
    request_id: input.requestId,
    trace_id: input.traceId,
    span_id: input.spanId,
    delivery_attempt_id: randomUUID(),
    notification_key: pseudonymousKey("notification", input.notificationId),
    workspace_key: pseudonymousKey("workspace", input.workspaceId),
    actor_key: pseudonymousKey("user", input.userId),
    channel: input.channel,
    template_class: input.templateClass,
    attempt_number: input.attemptNumber,
    payload_bytes: input.payloadBytes,
    status: input.outcome,
    duration_ms: input.durationMs,
    error_code: input.errorCode
  };

  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(event)}\n`);
}

This sample makes one deliberate trade-off: the pseudonymous keys preserve equality for investigation and attribution, but they are still linkable within their scope. Treat the hashing key as a secret, rotate it under a documented policy, and restrict access to the resulting logs. Hashing is not permission to retain arbitrary personal data. If operators do not need cross-event user correlation, use a per-event random token instead.

Also notice what is absent: recipient address, subject, message body, support-case text, raw exception, stack trace, and provider payload. A stack trace can belong in a separate, tightly controlled error event, but copying an unfiltered error object into the main operational stream risks capturing request data. The ship-first choice is an allowlist. Redaction is a second layer for accidental fields, not the primary contract.

Why do request IDs and trace IDs both survive?

An incoming support action may enqueue three notifications and return before any delivery begins. The API can assign a request ID, start or continue a trace, and place both values in the queue message. The worker then records those values without pretending that the queue delivery is the original HTTP request.

W3C Trace Context defines the traceparent format used to propagate trace identity. Preserve valid trace context at service boundaries, but do not manufacture span relationships by copying strings into unrelated jobs. If a queue consumer creates a new processing span, the tracing instrumentation should express the relationship; the application log should report the resulting trace and span identifiers.

There is a practical failure mode here. If request_id exists only in an async-local store inside the web process, it vanishes at the queue boundary. Put the correlation fields in the job envelope explicitly, validate their length and character set, and generate a fresh request ID when an untrusted or missing value arrives. Never let a caller inject line breaks or an unbounded identifier into logs.

No magic here.

Structured logs still need a propagation design, and traces still need application identifiers such as the notification key. One does not replace the other.

Cost attribution without turning logs into a billing ledger

The goal is to explain cost, not calculate an invoice from log lines. For notification delivery, useful cost drivers are channel, attempt count, payload size, template class, outcome, and workspace. They support questions such as: did retries inflate work for SLA warnings, or did one workspace produce a surge of rejected SMS attempts? Consider a notification that times out twice and is accepted on the third try. Three attempt events should share the notification key and attribution dimensions, while each carries its own attempt number, duration, outcome, and delivery-attempt ID. Counting notifications would hide two-thirds of the channel work; counting attempts without the shared key would make the customer-visible action hard to reconstruct. Both views matter, so preserve the raw attempt facts and derive notification-level totals downstream.

Retries are the trap.

Do not put a changing currency price on every event unless the accounting system requires immutable historical rates. Prices and commercial rules change; operational facts such as attempt_number: 3 and payload_bytes: 1840 do not. Join stable usage events to a versioned rate table downstream. That keeps the logging path fast and makes corrections auditable.

The same restraint matters for metrics. Logs can retain a pseudonymous workspace key for a time-bounded investigation, while a metric label carrying every workspace or user would create an unbounded set of time series. Prometheus naming guidance recommends a consistent base unit and explains that labels should represent the same logical quantity across dimensions. For the aggregate counter, use bounded dimensions:

type MetricLabels = {
  channel: "email" | "sms" | "push";
  status: "accepted" | "rejected";
  error_code: "none" | "timeout" | "rate_limited" | "invalid_recipient" | "provider_rejected";
};

function recordDelivery(labels: MetricLabels): void {
  deliveryAttemptsTotal.add(1, labels);
}

delivery_attempts_total is suitable for rate and ratio calculations. workspace_key, actor_key, request_id, and trace_id belong in logs or traces, not metric labels. This split preserves investigation detail without making every customer a permanent metrics dimension.

The controls that make the schema real

A type is helpful, but runtime data ignores TypeScript. Test the serialized output. Feed the logger an email address in every upstream field you control, then assert that the address, authorization tokens, and message text cannot appear. Test that a rejected attempt has a bounded error code, that required correlation keys are present, and that the output parses as exactly one JSON object per line.

Deployment needs two more checks. First, cap field lengths before serialization so a malformed provider message cannot turn one event into megabytes. Second, make stdout backpressure and process termination behavior explicit. Logging should not silently drop the final failure event, but a blocked sink should not freeze notification delivery forever either. The correct buffer and flush policy depends on the loss tolerance of the service; measure it under a slow consumer rather than guessing.

Retention should follow purpose. Delivery investigation, security review, usage aggregation, and billing evidence can require different access and lifetimes. Separate those stores or streams when their controls differ. A single giant index with broad access is operationally convenient until sensitive support context lands in it.

Measure before retaining.

Before copying this design, measure four things in a staging workload: serialized bytes per attempt, events per notification including retries, logging time at the p95 and p99, and the proportion of failed deliveries that can be reconstructed without opening a message body. Then estimate daily volume by channel and retention tier. A schema earns its keep when it answers the failure and attribution questions with fewer sensitive bytes, not when it records the most context.

A small decision rule

Ship the schema when an operator can move from a customer-reported notification to its attempts, see the bounded failure reason, connect the work to the originating request or trace, and attribute usage to a pseudonymous workspace without reading customer content. Delay extra fields until a concrete investigation cannot proceed without them.

That leaves room to evolve. Increment schema_version for a breaking semantic change, run old and new consumers during migration, and keep the event name stable when the business event itself has not changed. The durable asset is the contract.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/

title: Missed Cron Job Monitoring: 4 Heartbeat Signals for Learning Pipeline Failures
description:
The least complex reliable design is to emit four structured checkpoints for every expected nightly cron run: expected, started, failed or completed, and a post-deadline overdue assessment. Store them beside the pipeline's searchable logs, keyed by one stable run ID and one scheduled instant in UTC. That gives an operator enough evidence to distinguish a scheduler miss from a task crash, a slow import, and a notification failure. It works as a healthchecks replacement when the real requirement is searchable incident evidence rather than a bare heartbeat.

Short answer: an error alert alone cannot prove that a scheduled task ran. Treat schedule evaluation as an independent process, record the expected run before execution, and alert from persisted state after a grace period. For an edtech pipeline that imports enrollment and course activity overnight in both the EU and US, this design favors incident reconstruction over an attractive monitoring screen. It also stays portable: the scheduler, log store, and notification transport can change without changing the event contract.

How should heartbeat monitoring detect a missed cron job run?

Start with the question an on-call engineer will ask the next morning: "Did the scheduler fail to dispatch, did the worker fail, or is the job still processing?" A lone success ping answers only one narrow question. Its absence collapses several different states into the same silence, which makes failure alerts hard to trust during reconstruction.

Silence is ambiguous.

The data flow is small. A schedule evaluator writes an expected event for each region and scheduled instant. A worker claims that run ID and writes started, then either completed or failed. After the allowed completion window, a separate evaluator reads the event stream and writes overdue only when no terminal event exists. The alert sender consumes failed and overdue; it is not the source of truth.

Use these four checkpoints because each closes a specific gap:

  1. expected proves the schedule existed and supplies the deadline.
  2. started proves dispatch reached a worker.
  3. failed or completed records the terminal outcome.
  4. overdue records the evaluator's decision, including the observation time.

Keep "expected" separate from "started." That distinction is the whole diagnosis when a run never launches.

A small event model you can run

The following Node.js TypeScript uses an in-memory store so the state transition is visible. In production, the EventStore boundary should use durable storage that supports your retention and access requirements. The example doesn't depend on a particular scheduler or alert service.

type Region = "eu" | "us";
type Stage = "expected" | "started" | "completed" | "failed" | "overdue";

type RunEvent = {
  runId: string;
  region: Region;
  scheduledFor: string;
  observedAt: string;
  stage: Stage;
  attempt: number;
  records?: number;
  errorCode?: string;
};

interface EventStore {
  append(event: RunEvent): Promise<void>;
  list(runId: string): Promise<RunEvent[]>;
}

class MemoryEventStore implements EventStore {
  private readonly events: RunEvent[] = [];

  async append(event: RunEvent): Promise<void> {
    this.events.push(structuredClone(event));
  }

  async list(runId: string): Promise<RunEvent[]> {
    return this.events.filter((event) => event.runId === runId);
  }
}

const makeRunId = (region: Region, scheduledFor: string): string =>
  `learning-import:${region}:${scheduledFor}`;

async function assessRun(
  store: EventStore,
  region: Region,
  scheduledFor: string,
  observedAt: string,
  graceMs: number,
): Promise<"pending" | "terminal" | "overdue"> {
  const runId = makeRunId(region, scheduledFor);
  const events = await store.list(runId);
  const terminal = events.some(
    (event) => event.stage === "completed" || event.stage === "failed",
  );

  if (terminal) return "terminal";

  const deadline = Date.parse(scheduledFor) + graceMs;
  if (Date.parse(observedAt) <= deadline) return "pending";

  if (!events.some((event) => event.stage === "overdue")) {
    await store.append({
      runId,
      region,
      scheduledFor,
      observedAt,
      stage: "overdue",
      attempt: 0,
    });
  }
  return "overdue";
}

async function example(): Promise<void> {
  const store = new MemoryEventStore();
  const scheduledFor = "2026-10-12T01:00:00.000Z";
  const runId = makeRunId("eu", scheduledFor);

  await store.append({
    runId,
    region: "eu",
    scheduledFor,
    observedAt: "2026-10-12T00:55:00.000Z",
    stage: "expected",
    attempt: 0,
  });

  const result = await assessRun(
    store,
    "eu",
    scheduledFor,
    "2026-10-12T03:01:00.000Z",
    2 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  );

  console.log(result, await store.list(runId));
}

void example();

The two-hour grace period is example policy, not a universal recommendation. Derive it from the pipeline's normal completion distribution and the point at which stale learning data becomes operationally harmful. A tighter window detects trouble earlier but pages on legitimate long runs; a wider one reduces noise while delaying investigation. The trade-off is detection speed against false alarms. I would ship with a documented conservative window, collect durations, then revise it from observed data rather than intuition.

Notice that retries keep the same runId and increment attempt. If every retry invents a new identity, a log search can make one scheduled import look like several unrelated jobs. Also make append operations idempotent in durable implementations. Evaluators can run twice, notifications can be retried, and duplicate overdue records shouldn't create duplicate incidents. This is a poor fit for sub-minute tasks where writing four durable events costs more than the work itself; a single counter plus an external schedule evaluator is enough there. It is also unnecessary for best-effort maintenance work that has no deadline and creates no incident when skipped.

Preserve time without trusting local clocks

Regional schedules are where a clean-looking design often becomes ambiguous. "Run at 1:00" is not an incident key. Store the scheduled instant as an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, retain the region as a separate field, and keep the configured time zone in schedule metadata. That preserves the operator's intent without making daylight-saving transitions part of every log query.

Don't infer a missed EU run from the US run, even if both import the same classes of records. They are separate obligations with separate run IDs. A delayed EU source can coexist with a healthy US source, and combining them behind one heartbeat destroys that fact.

Clock handling needs restraint. scheduledFor comes from the schedule evaluator; observedAt records when each component saw the event. Ordering by observedAt alone can be misleading if hosts disagree. Reconstruct primarily by the stable run ID and stage transition, then use timestamps to inspect latency. The terminal event should include compact counts such as processed records, but student names, email addresses, raw prompts, and model output do not belong in an operational event.

That last boundary matters in education systems. NIST SP 800-66 Revision 2 is written for implementing the HIPAA Security Rule, so it is not a blanket compliance label for an edtech pipeline. Its treatment of risk analysis, access control, audit controls, and incident procedures is still a useful primary reference when regulated health information is actually in scope. Compliance scope must be established by the organization; a logging pattern cannot establish it.

Query the timeline, not the error string

An incident search should begin with region plus scheduledFor, resolve the runId, and return all four stages in observation order. This is cheaper and more dependable than indexing large payloads just in case they become useful. Keep high-cardinality identifiers where they earn their cost: run ID, attempt, region, stage, and a bounded error code.

The shape of the timeline tells you where to look next:

Observed events Working diagnosis Next evidence
expected, then overdue dispatch was not observed scheduler and queue delivery logs
expected, started, then overdue worker is slow, stuck, or lost worker lease, progress, and dependency logs
expected, started, failed worker reported an error bounded error code and attempt history
expected, started, completed pipeline finished downstream publication or index freshness

These are working diagnoses, not proof of root cause. For example, a worker may finish after the evaluator writes overdue. Preserve both events. Don't rewrite history to make the timeline look tidy; close or downgrade the incident when the late terminal event arrives.

The search experience also has a user-facing cost. If missing nightly data affects pages used by teachers or administrators, correlate pipeline freshness with page performance instead of claiming the pipeline caused a slow page. Core Web Vitals define LCP, CLS, and INP and recommend evaluating the 75th percentile of page loads. Those measurements describe user experience; the run timeline describes data operations. A shared incident view can place them side by side without pretending they are the same signal.

Alert only from durable decisions

Send an immediate notification for a recorded failed event. Send a missed-run notification only after the independent evaluator persists overdue. The persisted decision makes notification retries safe to reason about and leaves evidence when the delivery channel itself is unavailable.

Deduplicate on runId plus alert kind, not on the rendered message. Route EU and US incidents according to ownership, but keep severity tied to business impact: an overdue auxiliary aggregation should not page like a blocked enrollment import. Cost matters here. More log fields, longer retention, and broader full-text indexing all have a bill, while the five compact query keys above usually carry the investigation.

Test silence deliberately. A happy-path test proves too little because the dangerous case is the component that never starts. Cover an absent started, a worker failure, a run that completes just before the deadline, a late completion after overdue, a duplicate evaluator pass, and two regional runs at the same wall-clock time. Inject a notification failure and verify that the decision remains queryable for replay.

Before deployment, read the event contract as an operator rather than its author. Confirm that schedule creation precedes dispatch, timestamps are UTC instants, retries retain identity, terminal writes happen in a finally-aware execution path, and the evaluator cannot depend on the worker it watches. Then run one synthetic schedule per region through the real storage and notification boundaries. The final check is blunt: with the worker disabled, can a person search one run ID and explain the silence without guessing?

Further reading

  • https://web.dev/articles/vitals
  • https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final

title: Rust in 2024: Why This Systems Language Is the Future of Safe, Fast Development
description:
Introduction

Rust has quietly become the darling of systems programming, and 2024 is the year it steps into the mainstream. From embedded devices to cloud services, developers are choosing Rust for its unique blend of performance, memory safety, and modern tooling. In this post we’ll explore why Rust is worth learning today, walk through a few idiomatic code examples, and point you to resources that can accelerate your journey.

1. Memory Safety Without a Garbage Collector

One of Rust’s headline features is its ownership model. Unlike C/C++, Rust guarantees that references are always valid at compile time, eliminating use‑after‑free and data races.

fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    // Borrow v immutably to compute a sum
    let sum: i32 = v.iter().sum();
    println!("Sum: {}", sum);

    // Borrow v mutably to modify it
    for x in &mut v {
        *x *= 2;
    }
    println!("Doubled: {:?}", v);
}

The compiler checks that the immutable borrow (v.iter()) ends before the mutable borrow (&mut v). If you try to mix them, you’ll get a clear compile‑time error.

2. Zero‑Cost Abstractions

Rust’s abstractions compile down to the same machine code you’d write by hand in C. Traits, iterators, and async/await are all “zero‑cost” – you pay only for what you use.

fn fibonacci(limit: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    (0..limit)
        .scan((0u64, 1u64), |state, _| {
            let next = state.0;
            *state = (state.1, state.0 + state.1);
            Some(next)
        })
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", fibonacci(10));
}

The scan iterator builds the Fibonacci sequence lazily, yet the generated assembly is as efficient as a hand‑rolled loop.

3. Concurrency Made Easy

Because the borrow checker knows which threads own which data, writing safe concurrent code is straightforward.

use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

fn parallel_sum(data: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let chunk_size = data.len() / 4;
    let data = Arc::new(data.to_vec());
    let mut handles = Vec::new();

    for i in 0..4 {
        let slice = Arc::clone(&data);
        let start = i * chunk_size;
        let end = if i == 3 { slice.len() } else { start + chunk_size };
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            slice[start..end].iter().copied().sum::<i32>()
        }));
    }

    handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let nums: Vec<i32> = (1..=1000).collect();
    println!("Parallel sum: {}", parallel_sum(&nums));
}

No unsafe blocks, no data races – the compiler guarantees that each thread works on a distinct slice.

4. Tooling That Boosts Productivity

  • Cargo – the built‑in package manager handles dependencies, builds, and tests with a single command.
  • rustfmt – automatically formats code to the community style guide.
  • Clippy – a linter that catches common mistakes and suggests idiomatic alternatives.
  • rust-analyzer – a language server that provides instant diagnostics, refactorings, and in‑editor documentation.

Running cargo new hello_rust && cd hello_rust && cargo run gives you a working project in seconds.

5. A Growing Ecosystem

The crates.io registry now hosts over 100k libraries. Whether you need a web framework (actix-web, warp), a database driver (sqlx, diesel), or a game engine (bevy), there’s a crate ready for you. The community also maintains excellent documentation, tutorials, and a Discord channel where newcomers get fast help.

6. Real‑World Success Stories

  • Mozilla – continues to power components of Firefox.
  • Amazon Web Services – uses Rust for performance‑critical services like Firecracker.
  • Dropbox – rewrote parts of its sync engine in Rust, seeing a 30 % latency reduction.
  • Microsoft – integrated Rust into Windows drivers to mitigate memory safety bugs.

These adopters prove that Rust scales from tiny microcontrollers to massive cloud workloads.

7. Getting Started: A Mini Project

Let’s build a tiny command‑line utility that reads a CSV file, filters rows, and writes JSON. This showcases file I/O, error handling, and third‑party crates.

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufReader, BufWriter};

use csv::Reader;
use serde::Serialize;
use serde_json::to_writer_pretty;

#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
struct Record {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    city: String,
}

fn filter_age(path: &str, min_age: u8) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let file = File::open(path)?;
    let mut rdr = Reader::from_reader(BufReader::new(file));
    let out = File::create("filtered.json")?;
    let mut writer = BufWriter::new(out);

    let mut results = Vec::new();
    for result in rdr.deserialize() {
        let rec: Record = result?;
        if rec.age >= min_age {
            results.push(rec);
        }
    }
    to_writer_pretty(&mut writer, &results)?;
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    filter_age("people.csv", 30)?;
    println!("Filtered data written to filtered.json");
    Ok(())
}

Add the dependencies to Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
csv = "1.1"
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"

Compile with cargo run. The example demonstrates how Rust’s strong type system and explicit error handling make data pipelines robust and easy to reason about.

Conclusion

Rust isn’t a niche language anymore; it’s a pragmatic choice for anyone building fast, reliable software. Its compile‑time guarantees, zero‑cost abstractions, and vibrant ecosystem lower the barrier to writing safe code at scale. If you haven’t tried Rust yet, pick a small project, follow the official "The Book", and let the compiler guide you toward a new way of thinking about ownership and concurrency.

Happy coding!

title: Mastering Modern JavaScript: From ES6 to Async Patterns
description:
Introduction

JavaScript has evolved dramatically since the early days of alert('Hello World'). Today's JavaScript powers everything from tiny widgets to massive server‑side applications, thanks to ECMAScript 6 (ES6) and the ecosystem that grew around it. In this post we’ll walk through the most impactful language features introduced in the last decade, show how they simplify real‑world code, and explore async patterns that every modern developer should master.

1. Let, Const, and Block Scope

Before ES6, var was the only way to declare variables, leading to hoisting surprises.

function legacyScope() {
  var i = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    // i is function‑scoped, not block‑scoped
  }
  console.log(i); // 3, not 0
}

let and const fix that:

function blockScope() {
  const arr = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    arr.push(i);
  }
  // console.log(i); // ReferenceError: i is not defined
  return arr;
}
  • let – mutable, block‑scoped.
  • const – immutable binding, block‑scoped. The value can still be mutable if it’s an object.

2. Arrow Functions and Lexical this

Arrow functions give you a concise syntax and capture the surrounding this value.

// Traditional callback
setTimeout(function() {
  console.log(this); // Window (or undefined in strict mode)
}, 1000);

// Arrow version – inherits lexical this
class Timer {
  constructor() {
    this.start = Date.now();
  }
  log() {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log('Elapsed:', Date.now() - this.start);
    }, 1000);
  }
}
new Timer().log();

Because the arrow function does not create its own this, you avoid the common var self = this pattern.

3. Template Literals

String interpolation, multi‑line strings, and embedded expressions are now a breeze.

const user = { name: 'Ada', points: 42 };
const message = `
  Hello ${user.name}!
  You have earned ${user.points} points.
  Keep it up!
`;
console.log(message);

No more cumbersome concatenation or \n escapes.

4. Destructuring & Rest/Spread

Pull values out of arrays or objects directly in the declaration.

// Array destructuring
const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
// Object destructuring with renaming
const { title: postTitle, author = 'Anonymous' } = { title: 'JS Tips' };

Rest (...rest) gathers the remaining items, while spread (...obj) expands them:

const defaults = { theme: 'light', layout: 'grid' };
const userPrefs = { layout: 'list' };
const config = { ...defaults, ...userPrefs }; // { theme: 'light', layout: 'list' }

5. Modules (ESM)

Node.js and browsers now support native ES modules (import/export).

// utils.mjs
export function sum(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const PI = Math.PI;

// app.mjs
import { sum, PI } from './utils.mjs';
console.log(`Area of circle: ${PI * sum(3, 4)}`);

No more bundler‑only require/module.exports—you can write clean, tree‑shakable code directly.

6. Classes & Inheritance

Classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance, making OOP feel familiar.

class Shape {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  area() {
    throw new Error('area() must be implemented');
  }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
  constructor(radius) {
    super('circle');
    this.radius = radius;
  }
  area() {
    return Math.PI * this.radius ** 2;
  }
}

const c = new Circle(5);
console.log(`${c.name} area = ${c.area().toFixed(2)}`);

Static methods, getters/setters, and private fields (#value) are also part of the class spec.

7. Async/Await – Writing Asynchronous Code Like Synchronous Code

Promises turned callback hell into manageable chains, but async/await makes the flow even clearer.

async function fetchUser(id) {
  const response = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Network error');
  const user = await response.json();
  return user;
}

(async () => {
  try {
    const alice = await fetchUser(1);
    console.log('User:', alice);
  } catch (e) {
    console.error(e);
  }
})();

7.1 Parallel Execution with Promise.all

When tasks are independent, run them concurrently:

async function loadDashboard() {
  const [stats, recent, alerts] = await Promise.all([
    fetch('/api/stats').then(r => r.json()),
    fetch('/api/recent').then(r => r.json()),
    fetch('/api/alerts').then(r => r.json())
  ]);
  return { stats, recent, alerts };
}

7.2 Cancelable Fetches (AbortController)

Modern APIs let you abort long‑running requests:

async function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), ms);
  try {
    const resp = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
    return await resp.json();
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeout);
  }
}

8. Optional Chaining & Nullish Coalescing

Safely access deep properties without repetitive guards.

const config = { db: { host: 'localhost' } };
const port = config.db?.port ?? 5432; // 5432 if undefined or null

The ?. operator short‑circuits when a value is null/undefined, while ?? only falls back on nullish values (not 0 or '').

9. TypeScript Integration (A Quick Note)

While this post focuses on vanilla JavaScript, most production teams pair it with TypeScript for static typing. The features we covered today map one‑to‑one in TS, giving you compile‑time safety without sacrificing runtime performance.

10. Putting It All Together – A Real‑World Mini‑Project

Let’s build a tiny Todo API client using the modern features we’ve discussed.

// todoClient.mjs
export class TodoClient {
  #baseUrl;
  constructor(baseUrl) {
    this.#baseUrl = baseUrl.endsWith('/') ? baseUrl.slice(0, -1) : baseUrl;
  }

  async #request(path, options = {}) {
    const url = `${this.#baseUrl}${path}`;
    const resp = await fetch(url, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, ...options });
    if (!resp.ok) {
      const err = await resp.text();
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${resp.status}: ${err}`);
    }
    return resp.json();
  }

  getAll() {
    return this.#request('/todos');
  }

  add(todo) {
    return this.#request('/todos', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(todo) });
  }

  delete(id) {
    return this.#request(`/todos/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' });
  }
}

// usage.mjs
import { TodoClient } from './todoClient.mjs';

(async () => {
  const api = new TodoClient('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com');
  const todos = await api.getAll();
  console.log('First 3 todos:', todos.slice(0, 3));

  const newTodo = await api.add({ userId: 1, title: 'Learn async/await', completed: false });
  console.log('Created:', newTodo);

  await api.delete(newTodo.id);
  console.log('Deleted newly created todo');
})();

Notice:

  • Private fields (#baseUrl, #request).
  • async/await for clear flow.
  • Spread operator for request options.
  • Template literals for URL construction.
  • export/import for modularity.

Conclusion

JavaScript’s rapid evolution has turned it from a quirky browser scripting language into a robust, full‑stack powerhouse. Mastering let/const, arrow functions, destructuring, modules, and async/await equips you to write cleaner, more maintainable code today. Keep experimenting with the newest proposals (e.g., Array.prototype.at, Temporal) and remember that the language’s flexibility is both its strength and its responsibility—use the right tool for the right job.

Happy coding! 🚀

title: Config precedence in Python: why your resolver shouldn't know what "CLI" means
description:
Most config systems I've written have the same shape. A function that looks at the environment, looks at the command line, looks at a YAML file, and decides which one wins. Something like this:

def load_config():
    if cli_args.timeout:
        return cli_args.timeout
    if os.getenv("TIMEOUT"):
        return os.getenv("TIMEOUT")
    return yaml_config.get("timeout", 30000)

Multiply that by every setting and you get a function that's 200 lines long, impossible to test in isolation, and impossible to change precedence on without editing every branch.

The version I've been working on separates two things the if/else version fuses together. What order sources apply in. And how they merge. Once those are separate, precedence stops being code and starts being structure.

The resolver doesn't know what "CLI" means. Here's the merge function in full:

def resolve_config(sources: Iterable[SourceSpec]) -> dict:
    merged_config = {}

    for spec in sources:
        try:
            config = spec.source.get_config()
        except Exception as error:
            if spec.failure_policy == FailurePolicy.REQUIRED:
                raise
            logger.warning(
                "Optional configuration source %s failed: %s",
                spec.source.__class__.__name__,
                error,
            )
            continue

        merged_config = {**merged_config, **config}

    return merged_config

Read that and notice what it doesn't do. It doesn't check whether a source is a CLI source, an env source, or a YAML source. It doesn't sort anything. It doesn't decide that one kind of source should win over another kind. It takes a list of sources, merges them left to right, and returns the result.

The last source in the list wins. That's the entire precedence rule.

That's not a limitation. It's the design. The moment the resolver knows what "CLI" means, it can start making decisions it shouldn't. It can start reordering. It can start special-casing. And once it does that, you can't test precedence without also testing the resolver's opinions, and you can't change precedence without reading the resolver's code.

Precedence is a list. That list comes from a builder:

def build_standard_pipeline(file_path: str, env: Environment, cli_args=None) -> list[SourceSpec]:
    yaml_source = YAMLSource(file_path, env)
    env_source = EnvSource()
    cli_source = CLISource(args=cli_args)
    return [
        SourceSpec(source=yaml_source, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=env_source, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.OPTIONAL),
        SourceSpec(source=cli_source, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.OPTIONAL),
    ]

YAML first. Env second. CLI last. Since the resolver merges left-to-right and later sources override earlier ones, CLI wins over env wins over YAML. That's the whole precedence system, and it's expressed as three lines of a list.

If you want to change precedence, say you decide env should beat CLI, you change the order of that list. Nothing else changes. No if branches to hunt down. No settings that read precedence from a config file. Just the order of the list.

The tests are where the pattern earns its keep, because they lock in behaviors, not implementation details.

First test. Later source wins.

def test_1_later_source_wins():
    source_a = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium"})
    source_b = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "firefox"})
    source_c = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=source_a, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_b, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_c, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    result = resolve_config(specs)
    assert result["browser"] == "webkit"

That's the base contract. Merge is left-to-right, last write wins. It's obvious in isolation and it's the thing every other behavior depends on.

Second test. Reordering changes result.

def test_2_reordering_changes_result():
    source_a = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium"})
    source_b = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "firefox"})
    source_c = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=source_c, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_a, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_b, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    result = resolve_config(specs)
    assert result["browser"] == "firefox"

This one looks trivial and isn't. It proves the resolver has no hidden opinion about which source should win. If someone ever helpfully adds logic to the resolver that reorders sources, say putting CLI sources last regardless of where they appear, this test fails. That's the category of mistake it prevents. Someone trying to make precedence smarter inside the merge.

Third test. The resolver doesn't sort.

def test_3_resolver_does_not_sort():
    # Simulate a logically reversed order: CLI-like -> YAML-like -> ENV-like
    # The resolver should NOT know these names mean anything.
    cli_like = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})
    yaml_like = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium"})
    env_like = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "firefox"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=cli_like, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=yaml_like, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=env_like, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    result = resolve_config(specs)
    assert result["browser"] == "firefox"

This is the one I'd defend hardest. It uses three sources named after the standard precedence chain, CLI, YAML, ENV, but passes them in a deliberately wrong order. The resolver's job is to merge them in the order given, not to fix it.

If you ever find yourself wanting to add precedence knowledge to the resolver, this test is the one that will stop you. That's the point. Tests aren't just assertions about current behavior. They're arguments against future versions of yourself who will have worse ideas.

There's a subtle thing in the resolver that's easy to miss.

try:
    config = spec.source.get_config()
except Exception as error:
    if spec.failure_policy == FailurePolicy.REQUIRED:
        raise
    logger.warning(...)
    continue

Each source carries its own failure policy. YAML is required. If the file is missing or malformed, the pipeline fails. Env and CLI are optional. If they fail to load, the pipeline continues with what it has.

This is deliberately a separate concern from precedence. A source can be last in precedence, highest priority, and optional, failing silently. A source can be first in precedence, lowest priority, and required. The two axes are independent.

def test_5_failure_policy_remains_independent(caplog):
    valid_yaml = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium", "timeout": 30000})
    failing_env = FailingSource()
    valid_cli = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=valid_yaml, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=failing_env, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.OPTIONAL),
        SourceSpec(source=valid_cli, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    with caplog.at_level("WARNING"):
        result = resolve_config(specs)

    assert result["browser"] == "webkit"
    assert result["timeout"] == 30000
    assert "Optional configuration source" in caplog.text

Env fails. The pipeline continues. CLI still overrides YAML. Timeout from YAML still applies because nothing else set it. Precedence and failure handling do their jobs without interacting.

Fusing these two concerns is the most common mistake I see in config systems. It looks natural. If the CLI arg is missing, fall back to env, which falls back to YAML. But it collapses two orthogonal decisions into one tangled function. Keeping them separate makes each one testable in isolation and changeable without touching the other.

One more test, because it's the one that guards the whole design:

def test_7_resolver_remains_unchanged():
    sig = inspect.signature(resolve_config)
    params = list(sig.parameters.values())
    assert len(params) == 1
    assert params[0].name == "sources"

This asserts that resolve_config takes exactly one parameter. Nothing else. No pipeline name, no environment, no flags. Just the list of sources.

It sounds pedantic, and it is, deliberately. Six months from now, someone (probably me) will want to pass an Environment into the resolver so it can adjust precedence based on the environment. This test makes that change fail loudly, which forces a conversation about whether the resolver should know anything about environments. The answer is almost always no. But without the test, the answer quietly becomes yes, one small change at a time.

What this pattern buys you.

Precedence is a list. Changing it means reordering a list, not editing logic.

The resolver does one thing. It merges dictionaries left to right. That's it. It's 20 lines and it doesn't know what a CLI is.

Failure handling is orthogonal. Each source declares whether it's required or optional. The resolver respects that declaration without conflating it with priority.

Tests lock behaviors, not implementations. Each test asserts something category-level about what the system should never do, not just what it currently does.

None of this is novel. It's the same pattern behind a dozen config libraries. But the version where precedence is structure, rather than a decision buried in a conditional, is the version I've found easiest to live with. Because the day you need to change precedence is the day you least want to be reading the resolver's code.

title: To Borrow or To Clone: The Rust Struct Exposure Dilemma
description:
Every Rust developer eventually hits a crossroads when trying to expose private struct fields cleanly. Here is a breakdown of the common approaches, their hidden costs, and how to strike the right balance.

1. The Brute-Force Route: Making Fields Public

The most direct fix for visibility issues is simply marking fields pub. While this instantly grants access, it sacrifices encapsulation and can introduce dangerous side effects. Giving outside callers full access means anyone can mutate internal state or even move values out of the struct entirely, risking broken invariants.

2. The Convenience Trap: Overusing Clone

Another route is writing getter methods that return cloned instances. It is frictionless enough that developers sometimes abuse it purely as an escape hatch to silence the borrow checker.

The downside? Cloning performs a deep copy of the underlying memory. If you are exposing large data structures, frequent cloning introduces hidden CPU overhead and memory bandwidth pressure.

3. The Idiomatic Choice: Strategic Borrowing

The high-performance solution is leveraging references and lifetime annotations. Although lifetimes can steepen the learning curve for developers coming from garbage-collected languages, borrowing is vastly more efficient than cloning. No matter how massive the original type is, a reference only copies a pointer-sized footprint.

Yet, zero-cost abstractions demand careful design. Combining complex lifetime bounds with multi-threaded safety and thread-pool concurrency can escalate quickly. Ultimately, writing production-grade Rust comes down to balancing clean borrowing strategies with minimizing resource contention.
