title: Your Docker Container Is Running… So Why Is Your Application Down?
description:
A practical guide to debugging Docker containers like a real DevOps engineer.

Imagine this situation.

You deploy your application using Docker. Everything looks perfect.

docker ps

Output:

CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          STATUS
a1b2c3d4       my-app:latest  Up 10 minutes

Your container is running. Docker reports no problems. You feel confident.

Then someone messages you:

"Hey, the application is down. Can you fix it?"

You check the container again.

Still running.

You restart it.

Still broken.

You rebuild the image.

Still broken.

Welcome to the real world of DevOps. 😅

A running container does not necessarily mean a healthy application.

Let's learn how to troubleshoot Docker like an engineer instead of randomly restarting containers.

🧠 1. Understand the Difference Between Running and Healthy

Docker can tell you whether a container's main process is running. It cannot automatically guarantee that your application is working correctly.

For example, your container might be running while:

  • The application cannot connect to its database.
  • The API is returning HTTP 500 errors.
  • The application is listening on the wrong port.
  • A required environment variable is missing.
  • The application is responding too slowly.
  • A dependency has crashed.

Think of it like this:

Docker container: RUNNING ✅
Application:       BROKEN  ❌
Database:          UNREACHABLE ❌
Users:             ANGRY 😭

Your job as a DevOps engineer is to discover where the actual failure is happening.

🔍 2. Start With the Logs

Never begin by randomly restarting everything. First, investigate.

Check the application logs:

docker logs my-app

Follow logs in real time:

docker logs -f my-app

Show the latest 100 lines:

docker logs --tail 100 my-app

Include timestamps:

docker logs -t my-app

Look for errors such as:

Connection refused
Database connection failed
Address already in use
Permission denied
Missing environment variable

Pro tip: Logs are often the fastest way to identify the root cause. Read them before changing anything.

🛠️ 3. Inspect the Container

Sometimes the problem is not visible in the logs.

Inspect the container configuration:

docker inspect my-app

Check its state:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}}' my-app

Check its exit code:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' my-app

Check whether Docker reports it as healthy:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' my-app

Note: The last command requires a health check to be configured. Without one, Docker may return an empty value.

Inspecting a container helps you investigate its configuration, state, network settings, mounts, and other runtime details.

🌐 4. Check Port Mapping

Your application might be listening on port 8080 inside the container, but you may have exposed a different port—or forgotten to publish it.

Check published ports:

docker port my-app

Start a container with the correct mapping:

docker run -d \
  --name my-app \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  my-app:latest

The mapping follows this pattern:

-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT

For example:

Your browser
     |
     v
localhost:8080
     |
     v
Docker host port 8080
     |
     v
Container port 8080
     |
     v
Application

Remember: publishing a port does not make an application listen on that port. Your application must actually be listening on the expected interface and port.

💾 5. Check Whether the Container Is Running Out of Resources

An application can become slow or crash when it runs out of memory or struggles with CPU usage.

Check resource consumption:

docker stats

Example:

CONTAINER     CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT
my-app        95%       480MiB / 512MiB
database      15%       300MiB / 1GiB

In this hypothetical example, my-app is consuming almost all its memory limit.

Investigate further before changing resource limits. A memory leak, excessive traffic, or inefficient application code could be the real problem.

Useful commands:

docker ps -a
docker system df
docker events

These help you inspect container states, Docker disk usage, and Docker events.

Important: Avoid running docker system prune -a as a routine troubleshooting step. It can remove unused images and other resources you may still need.

❤️ 6. Add a Docker Health Check

Here's one way to improve your container monitoring.

A health check lets Docker periodically test whether an application is responding to a defined check.

Example Dockerfile:

FROM nginx:alpine

COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s \
  --timeout=5s \
  --start-period=10s \
  --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/ || exit 1

This example uses a lightweight Nginx image and checks whether its HTTP endpoint responds successfully.

Check the health status:

docker ps

A configured health check can report statuses such as:

starting
healthy
unhealthy

But remember: a health check is only as good as the test you define. A successful HTTP response does not necessarily mean every feature of your application is working.

🔗 7. Investigate Network and Database Problems

Suppose your application depends on a PostgreSQL database.

Your application container is running, but database connections keep failing.

First, inspect your Docker networks:

docker network ls

Inspect the network used by your containers:

docker network inspect my-network

If both services need to communicate, make sure they share an appropriate network.

With Docker Compose, services on the same default network can usually reach each other using their service names.

Example:

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:password@db:5432/appdb
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb

Here, db is the database service name.

Important: This is a learning example, not a production-ready configuration. Use secrets rather than hardcoded passwords, persistent storage for database data, and application-level retry logic. Also, depends_on alone does not guarantee that PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.

🧪 8. Build Your Own Docker Troubleshooting Checklist

When an application goes down, follow this order:

  1. Check the state: docker ps -a
  2. Read the logs: docker logs my-app
  3. Inspect configuration: docker inspect my-app
  4. Check resource usage: docker stats
  5. Verify port mapping: docker port my-app
  6. Investigate networking: docker network inspect my-network
  7. Test the application endpoint: use curl or an appropriate health check.
  8. Apply a fix: change the configuration or code based on evidence.
  9. Verify recovery: repeat the relevant tests and check the logs.

The goal is not simply to make the error disappear.

The goal is to understand why it happened and how to prevent it from happening again.

🚀 9. Take It Further: Build a Container Monitoring Project

Want to turn this knowledge into a portfolio project?

Build a small Docker monitoring stack using:

  • Docker Compose to run the services.
  • Prometheus to collect metrics.
  • Grafana to visualize performance.
  • cAdvisor to expose container resource metrics.
  • Alerting to notify you about important failures.

A simplified architecture:

Docker Containers
       |
       v
    cAdvisor
       |
       v
   Prometheus
       |
       v
     Grafana
       |
       v
 Dashboards & Alerts

Track CPU usage, memory consumption, container restarts, and application availability.

Document one simulated failure, your investigation, the root cause, and the fix. That gives you a concrete project to discuss during DevOps interviews.

🎯 Final Thoughts

Docker makes packaging and running applications easier, but it does not eliminate production problems.

Good DevOps engineers do not blindly restart containers. They collect evidence, understand system behavior, identify root causes, and verify their fixes.

The next time someone says, "The container is running, but the application is down," you'll know where to start.

Your challenge: Run a Docker container, inspect its logs, configure a health check, and deliberately introduce a failure in a local test environment. Can you diagnose the problem without immediately restarting the container?

Share what you discover in the comments! 👇

📚 Keep Building Your DevOps Skills

If you want structured resources to help you learn these tools, explore my guides:

  • 🐳 Docker Mastery
  • ☸️ CKA Complete Study Guide
  • 🏗️ Terraform Associate (003) Exam Crash Course
  • 🚀 DevOps Complete Pack

Learn by building, break things in a safe lab, and become better at fixing them.

title: Custom Domain Transactional Email API Beats Unified Messaging for 1 Realtime Receipt
description:
A NodeJS API sending transactional welcome email and payment receipts from a custom domain has one decisive constraint: how quickly must the support stack react to delivery trouble? That answer decides this comparison.

TL;DR: choose a dedicated email API such as Postmark, Resend, or SendGrid when a receipt must trigger near-real-time automation from delivery, bounce, or complaint webhooks. Choose a unified REST surface such as Infrai when polling is acceptable and integration effort matters more: application code uses one key and one contract, and later messaging capabilities do not require another SDK. For a US/EU SaaS sending routine receipts after payment settles, the unified option is practical. For a strict realtime workflow, the dedicated option wins.

That is the decision. DNS still comes first in either case. Set up a branded sending domain, publish the records the provider gives you, and verify DKIM before moving production receipts. SPF identifies permitted senders; DKIM signs the message; DMARC tells receivers how to handle alignment failures. None of this is glamorous, but it matters more than a polished template editor.

How should a NodeJS API send transactional welcome email?

The first implementation question is not “Which email API has the nicest logo?” It is “How late may the support system learn that a receipt bounced?”

Count it.

Infrai exposes delivery, bounce, and complaint events through listing and retrieval rather than webhook pushes. A worker polling every minute may be fine for a receipt archive, a daily support queue, or a welcome campaign. It is a poor foundation for an automation that must branch as soon as a complaint lands. Polling also creates state: the worker needs a cursor, deduplication, retry rules, and monitoring. Glue accumulates fast.

The dedicated products take different shapes. Postmark documents delivery webhooks and separates transactional and broadcast traffic with message streams. Resend documents webhook events and offers a Node SDK as well as an HTTP API. SendGrid documents an Event Webhook and has a much broader email platform surface. AWS SES exposes delivery events through AWS destinations such as SNS and EventBridge, which fits an existing AWS estate but adds cloud-specific wiring. Those are real architectural differences, not a feature-count contest.

Here is the compact comparison I would use before opening an account:

Option Integration shape Best fit Boundary that matters here
Postmark Dedicated transactional email API Teams prioritizing transactional email and pushed delivery events Another vendor contract if SMS or unrelated backend modules arrive later
Resend Email API with first-party Node tooling Small TypeScript teams optimizing time to first send Still a dedicated email integration
SendGrid Mature email platform with API and event webhook Teams needing a broad email-specific toolset More email configuration surface to evaluate
AWS SES AWS-native email service and event destinations Workloads already operated inside AWS IAM and AWS event plumbing become part of the integration
Infrai Plain REST API spanning 295 capabilities in 20 modules Teams accepting pull-based email events and valuing one contract No SMTP relay or email-event webhooks

I benchmark integration effort with a crude metric: count the secrets, packages, callback handlers, and durable cursors needed for the first production path. It is not a performance benchmark, and I would not pretend otherwise. It does expose config bloat early. A dedicated API usually adds a vendor SDK and webhook receiver; the unified surface needs no SDK for email, but its polling cursor is real work.

The smallest send path

The risky move is guessing a request body from a blog post. Infrai's public discovery surface returns the current JSON Schema and runnable examples without a key, so generate RECEIPT_EMAIL_PAYLOAD from the live email.send capability before running this script. Keep customer data and the API key out of source control.

The script below performs one write route, uses an idempotency key tied to the settled payment, honors Retry-After, applies exponential backoff on HTTP 429, and surfaces non-success bodies. It runs on Node 20 or newer.

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const apiBaseUrl = process.env.EMAIL_API_BASE_URL;
const rawPayload = process.env.RECEIPT_EMAIL_PAYLOAD;
const paymentId = process.env.PAYMENT_ID;

if (!apiKey || !apiBaseUrl || !rawPayload || !paymentId) {
  throw new Error(
    "Set INFRAI_API_KEY, EMAIL_API_BASE_URL, RECEIPT_EMAIL_PAYLOAD, and PAYMENT_ID",
  );
}

const payload: unknown = JSON.parse(rawPayload);
const idempotencyKey = createHash("sha256")
  .update(`receipt:${paymentId}`)
  .digest("hex");

const sleep = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

async function sendReceipt(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/v1/email/send`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
      const delay = retryAfter
        ? Number.parseFloat(retryAfter) * 1_000
        : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await sleep(Number.isFinite(delay) ? delay : 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      continue;
    }

    const body: unknown = await response.json();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${JSON.stringify(body)}`);
    }

    return body;
  }

  throw new Error("Email send remained rate-limited after 5 attempts");
}

const result = await sendReceipt();
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`);

Create reusable welcome and account templates before wiring the payment handler, then pass per-user variables from the backend. Do not let the browser send transactional mail. The backend owns the payment event, the idempotency key, and the recipient data.

There is a useful second-order benefit to the unified approach. The public discovery endpoint reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules, with request and response schemas plus examples in 10 languages. If the support workflow later needs SMS, storage, or scheduling, the authentication and REST conventions stay consistent. That breadth is the reason to consider it. Price is not.

No SDK required.

What I would change at scale

The one-file script is a probe, not an architecture. At scale I would put the settled-payment event on a durable queue, derive the idempotency key from the immutable payment ID, and let a worker own sending. Template IDs and versions belong in configuration with a review trail. Domain verification belongs in deployment checks, not in the request path.

For pull-only events, I would store a high-water mark, overlap each polling window, and deduplicate by event identity. The overlap matters because a crash between processing and checkpointing must not lose a bounce. I would also alert on poll age rather than only worker errors; a quiet stalled poller looks healthy until support asks where the events went.

Keep suppression handling close to sending. Complaints and hard bounces should stop later transactional attempts according to the product's policy and legal requirements. For US/EU SaaS traffic, domain authentication and suppression are baseline operational controls, while the exact retention and consent rules need review with counsel for the actual product and jurisdictions.

Email OTP changes the boundary again. Infrai does not provide a managed email OTP endpoint, so an email fallback requires application-owned code. SMS has a managed OTP path, but email does not. If managed email OTP or instant cross-channel branching is central, select a provider whose verified feature set matches that flow instead of stretching a receipt integration beyond its design.

The trade-off I would accept

For an ordinary receipt after payment settlement, I would accept event polling to reduce vendor and SDK sprawl, provided the support requirement is measured in minutes rather than seconds. The broad API surface then pays off: another capability is another endpoint under the same key and billing contract, not another package, secret, and invoice.

I would not accept that trade for fraud controls, immediate journey branching, or a support promise tied to live delivery state. Postmark, Resend, SendGrid, and AWS SES all deserve evaluation there because they document pushed event mechanisms. Run a small proof with the actual DNS domain and record three numbers: time to first authenticated send, time from provider event to application receipt, and the amount of application state required. No synthetic leaderboard can replace those measurements.

The choice is conditional but not vague. Dedicated email APIs win the realtime receipt workflow. A unified API wins the lower-glue workflow when pull-based events are enough.

Sources

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
  • Postmark Webhooks
  • Resend Webhooks
  • SendGrid Event Webhook
  • Amazon SES event publishing

title: A Reproducible Test Contract for Character-Like Voice Pickers
description:
The product problem is a review problem

A voice picker can expose many candidates and still leave a production team unable to explain why one take was accepted. “It felt right” is not a useful event log. It does not tell the next editor which script, scene role, mix, or timing made the decision.

For character-like voices, the UI should preserve the question being tested. The candidate is only one variable. The fixture, visual beat, output state, and publication boundary matter just as much.

Define a fixture before generating audio

Use a small fixed set of lines rather than a full script:

  1. a status line that establishes the speaker;
  2. an information line containing one important noun or number;
  3. a reaction line that follows a visible event;
  4. an announcement line with a clear result.

For a high-status animated persona, the Stewie Griffin AI Voice candidate can be assigned to the status fixture. That assignment is a test input, not an assertion about private model behavior or an official performance. The acceptance question is observable: does the line communicate its role before the cut?

Keep the fixture immutable while comparing candidates. If the script changes at the same time as the voice, the review cannot identify the cause of the difference.

type SceneRole = "status" | "information" | "reaction" | "announcement";

type VoiceFixture = {
  id: string;
  role: SceneRole;
  script: string;
  mustRemainAudible?: string;
  visualBeatMs?: number;
};

type ReviewState =
  | { kind: "draft"; fixture: VoiceFixture }
  | { kind: "preview"; fixture: VoiceFixture; candidateId: string }
  | { kind: "accepted"; fixture: VoiceFixture; candidateId: string; note: string }
  | { kind: "blocked"; fixture: VoiceFixture; reason: string };

This type is a design proposal for a reviewable interface. It is not a claim about VideoAI’s internal implementation.

Separate expressive direction from content clarity

The second fixture should be deliberately ordinary: “The next round starts at seven.” Test it without music, then with the rough mix. If “seven” disappears, changing to a more dramatic candidate is not automatically the right fix. Shorten the line, move the word earlier, or lower the competing layer first.

A creature-oriented Stitch AI Voice candidate can be useful in a reaction fixture because the product question is different: does the response arrive after the visual beat, or does the voice explain the joke before the viewer sees it? The same script should be auditioned in a calm, surprised, and interrupted context. Store the direction as metadata instead of rewriting the line for every candidate.

Model a game-style cue as an event handoff

Game announcer energy is often implemented as a sequence of events rather than one long paragraph. A matchup label, a countdown, and a result cue each have different timing requirements.

For that workflow, the Super Smash Bros AI Voice candidate can be attached to a short announcement fixture. The acceptance contract might be:

  • the matchup is understandable before the animation changes;
  • the result begins after the visual reveal;
  • the final noun is not masked by the sound effect;
  • the line can be replayed without changing the scene’s meaning. 
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft
    Draft --> Preview: fixed fixture + candidate
    Preview --> Review: audio and rough cut available
    Review --> Accepted: required beat is audible
    Review --> Blocked: missing word, early reaction, or unclear role
    Blocked --> Draft: revise one variable
    Accepted --> PublishedCheck: rights and destination review
    PublishedCheck --> [*]

The state diagram keeps creative evaluation separate from a rights or publishing decision. A preview can pass a timing check and still require a separate review of permissions, source material, and platform policy.

Make the comparison repeatable

Every review record should include:

  • fixture ID and script version;
  • candidate ID and direction note;
  • whether music and effects were enabled;
  • the visual timecode under review;
  • one observed failure or reason for acceptance.

Avoid a score that hides the failure. “8/10” is less actionable than “the location name is lost under the transition.” A structured note allows the writer, editor, and audio owner to change different layers without guessing what the previous reviewer meant.

Add a failure taxonomy instead of a star rating

Most preview failures fall into a small set of categories:

  • content loss: a name, number, or action is not intelligible;
  • role mismatch: the line sounds like an announcement when the scene needs a reaction;
  • timing collision: the voice enters before the visual beat or ends under a transition;
  • mix collision: music or effects mask the required word;
  • handoff ambiguity: the reviewer cannot tell what changed between two takes.

This taxonomy makes the next action more deterministic. Content loss suggests rewriting or shortening the sentence. Timing collision suggests moving a cut or adding a pause. Mix collision suggests changing the sound bed. Handoff ambiguity suggests improving the review record. A candidate swap should be one of the later experiments, not the default response to every failure.

For a multi-character or roster-style interface, add a stable candidate ID and a human-readable direction note. Do not use the display label as the only identifier: labels can be edited, localized, or reused in a new fixture. The review record should answer which candidate was selected, which script version was rendered, and which single variable changed.

Evidence boundary

This is an interface-level testing method. It does not measure voice quality, latency, licensing, or production reliability, and it does not reveal private architecture. Those claims require separate evidence. The useful engineering outcome is narrower: a voice picker becomes easier to review when the scene job and the acceptance condition are explicit.

title: Asking Trained Among Us Bots Why They Moved
description:
My Among Us bots can explain themselves. Every time a crewmate picks a room to walk to, the replay records why, and the exported videos show it as a thought bubble over the player: "→ Admin: next task: Swipe Card (Admin); avoiding Pink (I suspect them) in Weapons". For the crew, the arithmetic behind those captions is exact to about fourteen decimal places. The captions were still wrong in three different ways, and one of them made a collapse in training look, on video, like normal play.

Why the explanation can be exact

The bots are trained by self-play, in leagues: each league is a roughly ten-hour training run that starts from the bots the previous league ended with. A crewmate's walking network does not output a choice directly. At each step it is offered the neighbouring rooms, and staying put. Each option is described by the same dozen inputs, such as how much closer it gets to the next task, how many people are visible there, how suspected the most suspected person there is, and how much closer it gets to fixing a running sabotage. The network looks at what the crewmate has seen and outputs one weight per input. Each option's score is the plain weighted sum of its inputs, and the highest score is the most likely pick.

That structure makes "why A and not B" a question with an exact answer. If option A scores s_A and the runner-up B scores s_B, then:

s_A − s_B = Σ_i (input_A,i − input_B,i) × weight_i

So the lead A has over B splits into one part per input, and the parts add back up to the lead with nothing left over. The caption takes the two largest positive parts and turns each into a phrase. There is no approximation step and no separate model of the bot's behaviour, which most explanation methods for neural networks need. (The impostors' walking adds a learned map term that is not a sum over named inputs, so their captions lump that part together as "what it has learned about the map". Everything below about exactness is about the crew.)

To check that the split really is exact in the code and not just on paper, I wrote a probe. It plays 30 games with a league's saved bots, using a fixed random seed so the run repeats exactly, and for every crew move decision it compares the score gap with the sum of the parts:

crew decisions largest error in the split, in score units
league 3 80,550 7.11e-15
league 4 40,433 7.11e-15
league 6 34,226 1.42e-14

The median gap between the chosen option and the runner-up was between 6.3 and 9.8 in the same units, depending on the league, so these errors are floating-point rounding. The arithmetic was never the problem.

Wrong way one: the sign of the weight

The first captions had one phrase per input, chosen when that input's part was large and positive. For the suspicion input the phrase was "keeping an eye on Red". That reads as "I am going where my suspect is", and it is only true if the weight on suspicion is positive.

For the league 3 crew it mostly was not. Over 19,085 decisions with a suspected player in view, its weight on suspicion averaged -3.94 (10th percentile -6.73, 90th -0.45), so it was negative in at least nine decisions in ten: a lean away from people it suspected. That lean was usually outweighed by other inputs, such as the next task. Where the chosen room and the runner-up differed in suspicion, the crew picked the more suspicious one 11,041 times and the less suspicious one 3,348 times. But whenever the weight was negative, a positive suspicion part meant the chosen room was less suspicious than the runner-up, so "keeping an eye on Red" was saying the opposite of what the number meant. The caption now checks the sign, and says "avoiding Red (I suspect them) in Weapons" when the weight is negative.

Wrong way two: relative is not a direction

Fixing the sign was not enough. The part for an input is a difference between two options, and a caption reads as an absolute statement about one.

My fifth league collapsed: its impostors learned to sabotage the reactor every game, and its crew stopped fixing it (written up separately). The replays from that league were full of crewmates "fixing the reactor" while walking the other way. Four replays survive from the end of that run, at games 57,500, 60,000, 62,500 and 65,000; one of them never had a reactor sabotage. In the other three I counted every crew move captioned "fixing the reactor" while a reactor sabotage was running. For each one I compared how many rooms the destination was from the reactor with how many the crewmate's starting room was:

destination compared with where it stood moves
closer to the reactor 6
the same distance 10
farther from the reactor 45

Forty-five of 61 "fixing the reactor" moves went farther away. The explanation was right every time: once its weight is applied, the chosen room did beat the runner-up on the "closer to the fix" input. That can happen in two ways. Either the weight had turned negative, or the runner-up was even farther from the reactor than the chosen room, and I did not count which. Either way, "better than the runner-up" and "toward the reactor" are different claims, and a person watching the video reads the second. That is how a crew that had stopped fixing sabotage looked, in the replays, like a crew that was fixing it.

There are four "closer to X" inputs: the next task, a sabotage fix, the lights fix, and the emergency button. Their captions now say "away from the reactor fix" (and so on) whenever the weight is negative. That covers the first way and not the second: a crewmate that picks the less bad of two moves away from the reactor is still captioned "fixing the reactor". The collapse itself was confirmed by measuring the weight directly, not by reading captions.

Wrong way three: what the bot saw is not what was there

The impostors explain their door sabotage too, and these captions used to give a headcount: "shut the Cafeteria doors", followed by how many crewmates were inside. The morning I found the collapse, I had changed the simulator so that impostors choose doors using only the crewmates they can see, after noticing they had been choosing with knowledge of every room's true headcount. The decision was now right, and the caption still stated what the impostor saw as a fact about the room. It now says "I can see 5 crewmates in there".

Counting across the current replays from the sixth league: 39 door captions give a headcount. In 38 of them the number equals what the impostor could see from where it stood; in 13 the room actually held more crewmates than that. In the game at the end of the run, Yellow shuts the Cafeteria doors at tick 240 (a tick is about half a second) with "I can see 5 crewmates in there", and there are 7. The same rewording went into the crew's "nobody in engine hall", now "I can't see anyone in engine hall", and the impostors' "Lime is alone in Admin", now "I can see only Lime in Admin".

What I would check in any explanation like this

All three failures were in the last step, turning a number into words, and none of them would show up in a test of the arithmetic. An exact attribution still has three hidden qualifiers: it is relative to a specific alternative, it is signed, and it is conditioned on what the agent observed. A caption that drops any of them makes a different claim from the one the numbers support. The check that caught the second failure was the cheap one. Take the words literally, write down what would be true in the world if they were right (the crewmate gets closer to the reactor), and count how often it was.

The simulator, the explanation code and the probes were written by Claude Code at my direction. The reactor captions came to light because I was watching the replays, and the bots' explanations did not match where they were walking. The code is not public. The probes are single scripts over saved leagues and replays, and every figure above is their output.

title: Node.js Kitchen Order Transitions: Publish to 2 Read-Only Kiosks
description:
An order board becomes a security problem the moment a browser can choose what it watches. For an e-commerce kitchen display, publish a deliberately small projection after the authoritative order change, bind the connection to one store on the server, and treat the browser's location parameter as untrusted input. The same capability boundary applies when a checkout flow creates a video room: the issued token should name one room and a limited action set, rather than become a general-purpose credential because a client supplied a nearby identifier.

Short answer: split the system into an authoritative write lane and a display-only delivery lane. The write lane commits an order transition and records a durable event; the delivery lane gives a kiosk only its assigned store's display projection. A reconnect may restore that projection, but it must not broaden the kiosk's authority.

This is a small distinction with a large failure domain. A screen that goes stale is an operations problem. A screen that receives another store's customer details is a boundary failure.

How should a Node.js service publish kitchen order transitions to a read-only kiosk?

Start with a bounded production scenario before debating transports: a kiosk is carried away while still authenticated, reconnects within five minutes, and tries a different store identifier in its first message. The acceptable result is boring: it sees only the projection for the store embedded in its server-issued session. It cannot turn a reconnect into a store selector.

The invariant is specific enough to test: possession of a display credential permits observation of one store's display projection and no state mutation. The storage concern here is less about the socket than about what has been persisted. If the session record stores store_id, display_id, expiry, and a display-only role, every later delivery decision can be derived from server state. If the server instead accepts store_id from each client message, the access check is distributed across call sites and will eventually be skipped.

The browser should never receive the full order row merely because its UI renders three fields. A display event might contain an opaque order label, a named transition, an event ID, and the server-accepted timestamp. It does not need payment status, customer contact data, internal notes, or fulfillment controls.

The same rule survives a change in medium. WebRTC 1.0 defines browser APIs for real-time communication; it does not decide which video room a participant may join. Room membership and permitted actions remain an application authorization decision, just as store membership remains one for a kitchen display.

Publish a projection after the commit

The preventative path starts at the database boundary. Write the accepted transition and an outbox record in one transaction, then have a worker fan out the display event. That makes the event durable before delivery is attempted, which matters when a process dies after commit and before it reaches a connected screen. The worker may retry and publish an event more than once, so the display contract needs a stable event ID and idempotent application.

Here is the part reviewers should be able to point at: authorization happens when the subscription is established, and later fan-out uses the stored scope rather than a client-provided store field.

package display

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrForbidden = errors.New("display session may not receive events")

type Session struct {
    DisplayID string
    StoreID   string
    CanView   bool
}

type Transition struct {
    EventID   string    `json:"event_id"`
    OrderView string    `json:"order_view"`
    State     string    `json:"state"`
    ChangedAt time.Time `json:"changed_at"`
}

type SessionStore interface {
    FindDisplaySession(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) (Session, error)
}

type Fanout interface {
    PublishToStore(ctx context.Context, storeID string, event Transition) error
}

func PublishAcceptedTransition(
    ctx context.Context,
    sessions SessionStore,
    fanout Fanout,
    sessionID string,
    event Transition,
) error {
    session, err := sessions.FindDisplaySession(ctx, sessionID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !session.CanView {
        return ErrForbidden
    }

    // StoreID comes from the server-side session, never from a browser message.
    return fanout.PublishToStore(ctx, session.StoreID, event)
}

The function is intentionally narrow. In an implementation, the transaction that changes the order writes an outbox row; a separate consumer constructs Transition and calls the fan-out interface for authorized sessions or channels. The source of truth for the store is the committed order and the session, not the screen.

There is no universal freshness promise hiding in that pattern. Define one a kitchen can use, such as an accepted transition becoming visible on a connected authorized display within 2 seconds. Then measure commit-to-publish latency, outbox age, reconnect count, authorization denials, and the age of the last rendered event per display. An average across every store can look healthy while one busy location misses its window.

Two delivery lanes make failure behavior legible

The write lane accepts commands, validates the actor, applies the state transition, and appends an outbox record. The display lane reads only display projections, begins with a scoped snapshot, then receives newer events. A cursor or monotonically increasing sequence lets the server decide whether a display can catch up or needs a new snapshot; a timestamp from the browser cannot make that decision reliably.

Duplicates happen.

For a screen, a tiny receipt table keyed by event ID is often enough to make applying the same transition harmless. Retain those IDs for at least the reconnect and replay window that the product promises. Storage capacity follows from that chosen window: active displays multiplied by event rate multiplied by retention, plus headroom for bursts. This is capacity planning, not a transport feature.

Approach What the display receives Operational burden Boundary to verify
Scoped event stream A store-specific projection and cursor Connection lifecycle, replay, slow consumers Server binds scope at subscription time
Filtered snapshot polling The current projection at an explicit interval Repeated reads and accepted staleness Filter is enforced before data leaves the service
Direct record access A broad domain object Schema coupling and a much larger blast radius The display has no accidental mutation or cross-store path

WebSocket's protocol gives a bidirectional channel; Server-Sent Events provide a one-way stream over HTTP. Neither protocol supplies the authorization model, replay semantics, or SLO. A read-only kiosk normally benefits from a one-directional contract because its job is visible state, not a second administrative client. Use a bidirectional channel only when the display has a separately authorized need such as an explicit health signal.

How should a team choose the fan-out layer?

Choose from the recovery contract first, then from the on-call contract. The queue or log must preserve enough information to rebuild a display projection after a consumer or network failure, and the team must be prepared to operate its retention, backpressure, access controls, and upgrades. A managed transport can reduce runtime work while adding an external dependency and integration boundary. A self-operated transport keeps more control in-house while making patching and capacity review part of service ownership.

Option Useful property Cost the team owns Exit condition
Redis Streams Consumer groups and explicit pending entries Retention policy, memory pressure, recovery procedures Replay contract is tested independently of the client library
NATS JetStream Persisted streams with consumer delivery state Stream sizing, replication choices, operator knowledge Event schema remains portable outside the broker
Apache Kafka Partitioned durable logs and consumer offsets Cluster operations, partition planning, longer operational runway Ordering assumptions are explicit per partition key

Those are different operational shapes, not a ranking. For a modest board with a stated stale-data tolerance, filtered polling can be the most honest choice and may avoid a persistent connection fleet altogether. For high transition volume, isolate slow consumers so a stalled screen cannot delay the outbox worker or widen memory queues without a bound.

A persistent stream also has a clear limitation: it is a poor fit when the kitchen cannot support connection monitoring, replay testing, and bounded slow-consumer behavior. In that case, a filtered snapshot at a declared interval is the appropriate design because it turns freshness into an observable promise instead of an assumption. Direct record access is likewise a poor fit for a kiosk because it couples a display to the broader order schema and enlarges the authority that must be defended.

Video rooms follow the same decision rule: issue a short-lived, server-validated capability for a specific room and permitted media actions; do not let the client exchange a broad identity for a room name of its choosing. The mechanism differs, but the trust calculation does not.

Where this boundary is the wrong abstraction

A display projection is the wrong interface for a workflow that needs to acknowledge preparation, change an order, expose payment state, or search across stores. Give those actions their own command interface, actor authorization, audit trail, and failure handling. Folding them into the convenience channel turns a kiosk into a control plane.

It is also the wrong optimization when the system cannot state a recovery expectation. Before adding fan-out infrastructure, decide whether the kitchen needs a 2-second visible-state objective, a 30-second refresh interval, or something else the operation can observe. The smallest authority that meets that objective is the design to defend.

Sources

References:

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/
  • https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream
  • https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/

title: Prisma 8 Postgres connection pools: replace connection_limit with pg.Pool
description:
A new application replica can quietly multiply its database connections.

With Prisma ORM 8, the old connection-pool URL limit is no longer the setting to rely on. You must know which pool you are configuring, how many copies can run, and what happens when all its connections are busy.

What changed in Prisma ORM 8

Prisma’s 12 October issue roundup describes the fix for a long-standing PostgreSQL connection-slot error. Its entry for issue #7120 says Prisma 8 no longer uses the engine pool or the connection_limit URL parameter. The runtime uses node-postgres pg.Pool; you can tune the pool through the documented options or construct and size a pool yourself. The roundup says the listed behavior was checked against 8.0.0-rc.16, released on 7 October, and labels Prisma 8 a release candidate.

That last detail matters. Treat the change as an RC feature until Prisma declares general availability. Verify the package versions and current reference docs in the exact project you are upgrading; the example below illustrates the documented shape, not a promise that the API will remain unchanged.

The practical consequence is simple: connection capacity is now a driver-level budget you need to make explicit. A URL parameter that used to look like a universal cap is not a substitute for sizing the pool that your app processes actually create.

Separate pool size from pool timeouts

Pool size and timeout answer different questions.

The size limit is how many database connections one pool may hold at once. With a custom pg.Pool, that is the driver's max setting. A connection timeout limits how long a request waits to obtain or open a connection. An idle timeout controls how long an unused connection stays open.

Prisma’s poolOptions are for timeout settings on a pool Prisma creates from a URL. They do not set the custom pool’s max. If your concern is “how many PostgreSQL slots can these app processes consume?”, set max on the pg.Pool you pass into Prisma, then budget every running process.

Create one bounded pool per process

For a Node service using the Prisma 8 PostgreSQL runtime, a custom pool makes the cap visible in application code:

import postgres from '@prisma/orm-postgres/runtime';
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import type { Contract } from './contract.d';
import contractJson from './contract.json' with { type: 'json' };

const max = Number(process.env.PG_POOL_MAX ?? '5');
if (!Number.isInteger(max) || max < 1) {
  throw new Error('PG_POOL_MAX must be a positive integer');
}

const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
});

const db = postgres<Contract>({
  contractJson,
  pg: pool,
});

// On graceful shutdown:
await db.close();
await pool.end();

The value 5 is only an example. Choose a cap from the database budget, not from the snippet. The pool is created once at module or process scope and shared by requests. Do not construct a new pool inside a route handler: one pool per request defeats the limit because every request brings another set of possible connections.

Passing your own pool also means your code owns its lifecycle. Close the Prisma client and then end the pool during graceful shutdown. Do not close it after each request. In serverless environments, keep the pool at module scope so warm invocations can reuse it, and account for the fact that each live instance can own a separate pool.

If you do not need to choose a custom maximum, you can let Prisma create the pool from the URL and use poolOptions for timeout behavior:

const db = postgres<Contract>({
  contractJson,
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  poolOptions: {
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
  },
});

This controls waiting and idle lifetime; it does not make connection_limit=5 work again. If you need a deliberately bounded maximum, use a custom pool and set its max.

Budget across replicas before deployment

A safe per-process value depends on how many processes can exist at the same time. Write down the database’s connection ceiling, reserve room for migrations, monitoring, administration and other services, then divide the remaining application budget across the maximum number of replicas.

For example, suppose the database can spare 24 connections for this service after those reservations. If autoscaling can start six processes, a per-process maximum of four uses the entire app budget: 6 × 4 = 24. That leaves no burst room, so a lower setting or a separate pooler may be safer. This is arithmetic for an example, not a recommended universal limit. Count workers, scheduled jobs and deployment overlap too; a rolling deploy may briefly run old and new replicas together.

Do not calculate from the number of database clients in one process and stop there. The database sees the sum across all live processes. A pool cap of ten can be harmless for one long-lived process and excessive when dozens of short-lived instances each create their own pool.

Keep transactions and slow work from pinning the pool

A bounded pool can still feel exhausted if each request holds a connection for too long. Keep database work inside a short query or transaction. Do not check out a connection, call a slow external service, then hold the same connection while waiting for that service. Finish the database operation and release its connection before doing unrelated network work.

Give acquisition a finite timeout so overload produces a visible failure instead of an unbounded queue of requests. Log pool-wait timeouts separately from SQL errors; they point to different fixes. A timeout is not extra capacity, though. Increasing it can make callers wait longer without creating another PostgreSQL slot.

For a broader checklist covering Postgres pool budgets, poolers and saturation canaries, see the production connection-pooling guide. This article focuses on the Prisma 8-specific change: where the cap now lives and how to keep the sum of pools inside the database budget.

Test the limit you intend to run

Before moving production traffic, verify the exact Prisma RC and driver versions in staging. Confirm the old URL parameter is not being treated as your cap, confirm the custom pool’s max is applied, and exercise more concurrent requests than the pool can serve. The test should show that active database connections stay within the combined process budget and that excess work waits only up to the configured timeout.

Then test the deployment shape, not just one local process. Start the maximum expected number of replicas, include background workers, and observe the database connection count while they run. Repeat with rollout overlap if the platform can run old and new versions at once. If the observed total exceeds the budget, lower each pool maximum, cap concurrency, or add an appropriate pooler before launch.

Also check the paths that use a database connection outside normal requests: migrations, admin tools and long-running jobs may need a separate connection strategy. Keep those connections in the reserved portion of the database budget instead of silently letting them compete with request traffic.

What the OTF kit does and does not provide

The SaaS Dashboard kit is an optional editable Postgres app and UI starting point. Its data layer uses Drizzle; it does not include Prisma ORM 8 or this pool configuration. You would add and validate the Prisma integration yourself. Check current pricing before choosing a kit.

The durable takeaway is not a magic pool number. In Prisma ORM 8, choose the pool you intend to own, put the maximum on that pool, and multiply it by the largest number of processes your deployment can run. Test that total against the database’s available slots before the first production spike.

Sources

  • Prisma ORM 8: We closed 330 of your most-requested issues (published 12 October 2026; entry #7120; behavior checked by Prisma against 8.0.0-rc.16).

Conceptual migration illustration: supply a separate pool rather than relying on the old engine-managed pool.

Conceptual illustration: set the maximum on the custom pg.Pool; use poolOptions for timeouts.

The SaaS Dashboard is an optional editable UI starting point; it does not include this Prisma integration.

title: Reading DDIA, Day 1: Data Systems, Reliability, and Why a Fault Isn't a Failure
description:
I've started reading Designing Data-Intensive Applications (DDIA), and I'm going to write up what I learn each day as I go. My original handwritten notes go on GitHub, and this is the cleaned-up version.

Day 1 covers the building blocks of data systems, the questions to ask when you design one, and the first big topic: reliability.

The building blocks

Most data-intensive applications are built from a few standard pieces:

  • Databases: store data so that they, or another application, can find it again later.
  • Caches: remember the result of an expensive operation, to speed up reads.
  • Search indexes: let users search data by keyword or filter it in various ways.
  • Stream processing: send a message to another process, to be handled asynchronously.
  • Batch processing: periodically crunch a large amount of accumulated data.

The lines between these categories are blurry:

  • Some datastores are also used as message queues. Example: Redis.
  • Some message queues come with database-like durability guarantees. Example: Apache Kafka.

A few more tools that show up again and again:

  • Memcached: an application-managed caching layer.
  • Elasticsearch / Solr: full-text search servers.

Questions to ask when designing a data system or service

  1. How do you make sure data stays correct and complete, even when things go wrong internally?
  2. How do you keep performance consistently good for clients, even when parts of your system are degraded?
  3. How do you scale to handle an increase in load?
  4. What does a good API for the service look like?

The three concerns that matter most

  1. Reliability
  2. Scalability
  3. Maintainability

Today was all about the first one.

Reliability

For software, reliability means:

  1. The application performs the function the user expected.
  2. It can tolerate the user making mistakes or using the software in unexpected ways.
  3. Its performance is good enough for the required use case, under the expected load and data volume.
  4. The system prevents unauthorised access and abuse.

In one line: it should work correctly, even when things go wrong.

Faults vs. failures (remember this one)

  • The things that can go wrong are called faults. Systems that anticipate faults and can cope with them are called fault-tolerant or resilient.
  • A fault is not the same as a failure.
    • A fault is one component of the system deviating from its spec.
    • A failure is when the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user.

📌 On my reading list: Netflix's Chaos Monkey.

Types of faults

1. Hardware faults

  • A hard disk crashes
  • RAM becomes faulty
  • The power grid has a blackout
  • Someone unplugs the wrong network cable

Related term: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure).

2. Software errors

  • A software bug that causes every instance of an application server to crash when given a particular bad input.
    • Example: the leap second on June 30, 2012 made many applications hang at the same time, because of a bug in the Linux kernel.
  • A runaway process that uses up a shared resource: CPU time, memory, disk space, or network bandwidth.
  • A service the system depends on slows down, becomes unresponsive, or starts returning corrupted responses.
  • Cascading failures, where a small fault in one component triggers a fault in another component, which then triggers more faults.

Day 1 takeaway

A reliable system isn't one where nothing goes wrong. It's one where faults happen and the system as a whole keeps working anyway.

📓 Original handwritten notes: Github link

See you tomorrow for Day 2. 👋

title: Concurrency Programming (9): BlockingQueue and Channels — Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering
description:
Table of Contents

  • 0. From Shared Memory to Message Passing
  • 1. A Short History of Message Passing
    • 1.1 Dijkstra: Cooperation Through a Shared Buffer
    • 1.2 RC 4000: Messaging Through the Operating System
    • 1.3 Actor Model: Asynchronous Messages and Local State
    • 1.4 CSP: Synchronization Through Communication
    • 1.5 How Do These Approaches Differ?
    • 1.6 Back to Message Passing
  • 2. What Do Message-Passing APIs Guarantee in Each Language?
    • 2.1 Java: BlockingQueue
    • 2.1.1 Which Queue Implementations Does Java Provide?
    • 2.1.2 Two Concurrency Guarantees of BlockingQueue
    • 2.1.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer
    • 2.1.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer
    • 2.1.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers
    • 2.1.6 Blocking and FIFO
    • 2.2 Go: Channels
    • 2.2.1 What Kinds of Channels Does Go Provide?
    • 2.2.2 Channel Communication and Synchronization Rules
    • 2.2.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer
    • 2.2.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer
    • 2.2.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers
    • 2.2.6 Buffered vs. Unbuffered Channels and FIFO
    • 2.3 CPython: queue.Queue
    • 2.3.1 Which Queues Does Python Provide?
    • 2.3.2 Thread Safety and Synchronization in Queue
    • 2.3.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer
    • 2.3.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer
    • 2.3.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers
    • 2.3.6 Blocking, FIFO, and Task Completion
  • 3. Next: How Is Message Handoff Implemented?

0. From Shared Memory to Message Passing

The opening article introduced two common ways for concurrent execution units to exchange data and coordinate work:

  • Shared Memory: execution units access shared state and coordinate through synchronization.
  • Message Passing: execution units communicate by explicitly sending and receiving messages.

The preceding articles followed Shared Memory, showing how Mutexes, atomics, and ReadWriteLock provide Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering.

We now turn to Message Passing. Before examining individual languages, it helps to see how the idea developed.

1. A Short History of Message Passing

1.1 Dijkstra: Cooperation Through a Shared Buffer

In 1968, Dijkstra's Cooperating Sequential Processes explored coordination between sequential processes. One example uses a Producer and a Consumer exchanging data through a shared buffer, with Semaphores controlling access.

The Consumer waits when the buffer is empty; with a bounded buffer, the Producer must also wait when it is full.

1.2 RC 4000: Messaging Through the Operating System

In 1969, Per Brinch Hansen designed the RC 4000 Multiprogramming System around a system nucleus that supported interprocess communication through messages. His 1970 paper The Nucleus of a Multiprogramming System describes that design.

Unlike the shared-buffer example, the RC 4000 nucleus exposes explicit message operations:

  • send message: send a message to a specified process.
  • wait message: wait for and receive a message.
  • send answer: send a reply to the sender.
  • wait answer: wait for the reply.

The nucleus manages message-buffer allocation and queues messages for their recipients.

Applied to a Producer and Consumer:

The Producer submits work with send message. The Consumer receives it using wait message and can then reply via send answer; the Producer retrieves the reply through wait answer.

If the Consumer has not begun receiving, the Producer may still complete its send, provided the system has enough message-buffer resources.

1.3 Actor Model: Asynchronous Messages and Local State

In 1973, Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop, and Richard Steiger presented A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence. In the Actor Model, each Actor owns its state and interacts with others through asynchronous messages. Incoming messages trigger the Actor's behavior.

For a Producer–Consumer scenario, a Buffer Actor could accept work from the Producer and forward it to the Consumer:

This Buffer Actor and its Mailbox illustrate one possible design; they are not mandatory components of the Actor Model.

1.4 CSP: Synchronization Through Communication

Tony Hoare introduced Communicating Sequential Processes in 1978.

CSP describes programs as sequential Processes that communicate through explicit input and output operations. Its characteristic interaction is a rendezvous: a send and its matching receive must meet for communication to complete. A Process in this model is an abstract execution unit, not necessarily an operating-system process.

In the Producer–Consumer example, the Producer cannot hand over a task until the Consumer participates in the communication:

The Rendezvous is a logical communication event, not a central buffer. If the Consumer is not ready, the Producer waits until the operations can pair.

1.5 How Do These Approaches Differ?

These four approaches do not replace one another. They explore communication and cooperation between execution units in different contexts: Dijkstra studied process cooperation and synchronization; RC 4000 provided operating-system messaging; the Actor Model and CSP are more comprehensive models of concurrent computation.

Approach Intermediate Mechanism Data Exchange Primary Concern If the Consumer Is Not Ready
Dijkstra Shared Buffer Direct access to shared storage Synchronization and process cooperation Buffered: write while space remains; wait when full; handoff can be asynchronous
RC 4000 System Message Queue Operating-system messaging interface OS communication mechanism Buffered: write while space remains; wait when full; handoff can be asynchronous
Actor Model Actor Messages sent to Actors Actor identity, state, and behavior Buffered: write while space remains; wait when full; handoff can be asynchronous
CSP Rendezvous Paired Send / Receive Communication events and execution synchronization Unbuffered: wait until the receiver is ready; handoff is synchronous

1.6 Back to Message Passing

Message Passing lets execution units exchange data and coordinate explicitly through send and receive operations. Communication can be buffered or unbuffered: a buffer can temporarily hold messages, allowing the sender and receiver to complete the handoff asynchronously; without a buffer, messages cannot be stored, so both sides must be ready for a synchronous handoff.

We will examine Java BlockingQueue, Go channels, and CPython queue.Queue through three questions:

  • Atomicity: what makes an individual message handoff safe?
  • Visibility: can a receiver observe the data prepared before sending?
  • Ordering: what synchronization order is established between sending and receiving?

2. What Do Message-Passing APIs Guarantee in Each Language?

2.1 Java: BlockingQueue

2.1.1 Which Queue Implementations Does Java Provide?

Java's Queue interface represents a collection of elements awaiting processing. Common implementations can be grouped by whether they support concurrent access and blocking operations:

Category Representative Implementations Supports Concurrent Access Provides Blocking Operations
Ordinary Queue ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue No No
Concurrent Non-blocking Queue ConcurrentLinkedQueue Yes No; poll() immediately returns null when empty
BlockingQueue ArrayBlockingQueue and others Yes Yes; for example, take() waits for an item, and put() waits for space when a bounded queue is full

Some representative BlockingQueue implementations:

Implementation Storage Structure Capacity Retrieval Order Blocking Conditions
ArrayBlockingQueue Array Fixed at construction FIFO put() waits when full; take() waits when empty
LinkedBlockingQueue Linked nodes Optional limit at construction; defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE FIFO put() waits when full; take() waits when empty
SynchronousQueue No element storage 0 Direct pairing between sender and receiver put() waits for a receiver; take() waits for a sender
PriorityBlockingQueue Heap Unbounded By priority; FIFO is not guaranteed for equal priorities put() does not wait for space; take() waits when empty
DelayQueue Priority heap Unbounded Earliest expiration first put() does not wait for space; take() waits when empty or when no item has expired
LinkedTransferQueue Linked nodes Unbounded FIFO put() does not wait for space; take() waits when empty; transfer() waits until the element is received

We will use the typical implementation ArrayBlockingQueue.

Its two relevant operations are:

  • put(e) inserts an element, waiting if the queue is full.
  • take() removes and returns an element, waiting if the queue is empty.

2.1.2 Two Concurrency Guarantees of BlockingQueue

The JDK 25 BlockingQueue documentation states:

“All queuing methods achieve their effects atomically.”

This provides Atomicity. Each enqueue or dequeue is atomic, so concurrent operations do not corrupt queue state.

The same documentation specifies a memory-consistency effect:

Actions before placing an object into a BlockingQueue happen-before actions after another thread accesses or removes that object.

This establishes both Visibility and Ordering.

For Visibility, writes performed before a Producer enqueues a message are visible to the Consumer that retrieves it.

For Ordering, actions before sending, the message handoff, and actions after receiving establish a cross-thread memory order through the transitivity of happens-before.

We will reuse the opening article's count++ example as we progress through SPSC, MPSC, and MPMC:

class Increment {
    int delta;
}

BlockingQueue<Increment> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);

2.1.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer 

// Producer thread
Increment message = new Increment();
message.delta = 1;
queue.put(message);

// Consumer thread
int count = 0;
Increment received = queue.take();
count += received.delta; // count == 1

The relevant execution order is:

Producer                                 Consumer

message.delta = 1
        │
        │ program order
        ▼
queue.put(message)  ───── handoff ───────► queue.take() returns message
                                                  │
                                                  │ program order
                                                  ▼
                                         read received.delta == 1
                                         count = 1

A successful put() inserts a message; take() removes and returns it. That demonstrates the Atomicity of each queue operation, although no competing Producers or Consumers exist yet.

delta is an ordinary field: neither volatile nor an atomic type is needed. Provided no other thread modifies this message after enqueueing it, the Producer's write happens-before the Consumer's read. The Consumer therefore sees 1, as required by Visibility and Ordering.

2.1.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer 

// Producers A and B each execute this in their own thread
Increment message = new Increment();
message.delta = 1;
queue.put(message);

// The sole Consumer thread
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
    count += queue.take().delta;
}
// After both messages have been submitted and processed: count == 2

One possible interleaving:

Producer A              Producer B              Consumer

put(A: +1)
                        put(B: +1)
                                                take() -> +1
                                                count: 0 -> 1
                                                take() -> +1
                                                count: 1 -> 2

Atomicity: concurrent Producers cannot overwrite one another's successfully enqueued messages. If both put() calls complete, the Consumer can retrieve two messages.

Visibility / Ordering: the happens-before guarantee holds independently for each message. Nothing predetermines which Producer enqueues first.

count += delta is not an atomic instruction. It is safe from competing Consumer updates here because only one Consumer modifies count.

2.1.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers

Now add another Consumer. The two Producers still enqueue one +1 message each, but Consumers A and B call take() concurrently:

// Producers A and B each send a distinct Increment instance
Increment message = new Increment();
message.delta = 1;
queue.put(message);

// Consumers A and B each execute once
Increment received = queue.take();
int delta = received.delta;

For example:

Producer A        Producer B        Consumer A        Consumer B

put(A: +1)
                  put(B: +1)
                                    take() -> A
                                                      take() -> B

Atomicity: a successful take() removes one element. Two Consumers cannot both remove the same enqueued message. A and B identify the messages, not fixed assignments to Consumers.

Visibility / Ordering: whichever Consumer receives a message can rely on its Producer's preceding writes. FIFO dequeue order does not imply that Consumers finish their business logic in that order.

There is an important boundary. If both Consumers later update the same ordinary counter:

// Counter shared by both Consumers
class Counter { int count; }
Counter sharedCounter = new Counter(); // Created before starting them

// Each Consumer executes this in its own thread
int delta = queue.take().delta;
sharedCounter.count += delta;

Both messages can be removed safely while the final count is still 1 because of a lost update. BlockingQueue protects the atomicity of message handoff, not arbitrary business operations after the handoff.

2.1.6 Blocking and FIFO

All three scenarios also inherit two behaviors of ArrayBlockingQueue:

  • Blocking: take() waits when the queue is empty; put() waits when its capacity of 2 is exhausted.
  • FIFO: items leave in their actual enqueue order. Concurrent Producers have no predetermined insertion order, and multiple Consumers need not finish processing in dequeue order.

2.2 Go: Channels

Unlike Java, Go does not primarily expose a family of standard concurrent queues. It provides channels as a language construct for communication between Goroutines.

2.2.1 What Kinds of Channels Does Go Provide?

The Go Language Specification distinguishes channels by buffering:

Type Declaration Behavior
Unbuffered make(chan int) No stored messages; sends and receives pair directly
Buffered make(chan int, 2) Fixed-capacity buffer; a sender can enqueue before a receiver is ready

Channel types can also constrain direction:

Direction Type Allowed Operations
Bidirectional chan T Send and receive
Send-only chan<- T Send only
Receive-only <-chan T Receive only

Direction and buffering are independent: a buffered channel can be passed to a function as chan<- T if that function should only send.

We will use a buffered channel with capacity 2:

type Increment struct {
    delta int
}

jobs := make(chan Increment, 2)

The two operations we need are:

  • ch <- value sends a value, waiting when the buffer is full.
  • value := <-ch receives a value, waiting when the buffer is empty.

2.2.2 Channel Communication and Synchronization Rules

The Go Language Specification allows any number of Goroutines to send to or receive from one channel without additional synchronization.

That rule provides Atomicity at the communication boundary: concurrent Sends and Receives exchange messages safely. Each successful Receive corresponds to one sent message, which cannot be received again by another Consumer.

The Go Memory Model, Channel Communication also states:

“A send on a channel is synchronized before the completion of the corresponding receive from that channel.”

This establishes Visibility and Ordering.

For Visibility, writes completed before the Producer's Send are visible to the Consumer after its matching Receive.

For Ordering, actions before sending, the channel's Send / Receive, and actions after receiving establish a happens-before relationship through synchronized-before and program order.

As with Java, the examples reuse the opening article's count++ example, building from SPSC through MPSC to MPMC.

2.2.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer 

// Producer Goroutine
message := Increment{delta: 1}
jobs <- message

// Consumer Goroutine
count := 0
received := <-jobs
count += received.delta // count == 1

The handoff establishes this order:

Producer                                 Consumer

message.delta = 1
        │
        │ sequenced-before
        ▼
jobs <- message  ─────── handoff ────────► received := <-jobs completes
                                                  │
                                                  │ sequenced-before
                                                  ▼
                                         read received.delta == 1
                                         count = 1

A successful Send delivers one value to a successful Receive. No competing senders or receivers are involved yet.

delta is an ordinary field. Here, the channel carries an Increment value, and the send is synchronized-before the corresponding receive completes. The Consumer can therefore read 1, satisfying Visibility and Ordering.

2.2.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer 

// Producers A and B each execute once in a separate Goroutine
jobs <- Increment{delta: 1}

// The sole Consumer Goroutine
count := 0
for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
    received := <-jobs
    count += received.delta
}
// After both messages have been sent and processed: count == 2

One possible interleaving:

Producer A              Producer B              Consumer

send(A: +1)
                        send(B: +1)
                                                receive -> +1
                                                count: 0 -> 1
                                                receive -> +1
                                                count: 1 -> 2

Atomicity: concurrent Sends cannot overwrite successfully sent messages; two successful Sends can be matched by two Receives.

Visibility / Ordering: each message independently establishes a Send/Receive synchronization relationship. Neither Producer is guaranteed to send first.

2.2.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers 

// Producers A and B each execute once in their own Goroutine
jobs <- Increment{delta: 1}

// Consumers A and B each execute once in their own Goroutine
received := <-jobs
delta := received.delta

For example:

Producer A        Producer B        Consumer A        Consumer B

send(A: +1)
                  send(B: +1)
                                    receive -> A
                                                      receive -> B

Atomicity: each successful Receive obtains the value of one matching Send; the same message is not delivered to two Consumers. A and B label messages, not predetermined receivers.

Visibility / Ordering: the receiving Consumer gets the synchronization guarantees associated with that message, but reception order does not determine processing-completion order.

What if both Consumers then modify a shared counter?

// Incorrect: two Consumers update the same ordinary counter
received := <-jobs
sharedCounter.count += received.delta

Even though both Receives succeed, concurrent writes to sharedCounter.count introduce a data race and can lose an update. Channels protect message handoff; they do not automatically protect shared state after receiving.

2.2.6 Buffered vs. Unbuffered Channels and FIFO

The previous examples use a buffered channel with capacity 2:

  • Waiting: Receive waits when the buffer is empty; Send waits when it is full.
  • FIFO: values are received in the channel's send order. The order of competing Producers is not predetermined, nor is the completion order of multiple Consumers.

Go also supports unbuffered channels:

jobs := make(chan Increment)

With no storage, the Send cannot complete until a corresponding Receive participates. The Go Memory Model provides an additional rule: the matching Receive is synchronized-before the unbuffered Send completes. A buffered Send, in contrast, can finish before the receiver starts.

The next article will examine how the Go runtime parks Goroutines waiting for communication and resumes them when the conditions are met.

2.3 CPython: queue.Queue

Unlike Go, Python does not offer channels as language syntax. Instead, its standard library offers queue mechanisms for different concurrency models.

2.3.1 Which Queues Does Python Provide?

Python provides different queues for different execution units:

Module Representative Types Communicating Units Waiting Behavior
queue Queue, SimpleQueue and others Threads within one process Blocks the calling thread
asyncio asyncio.Queue Asynchronous Tasks within one event loop Suspends the calling Task, allowing other Tasks to run
multiprocessing multiprocessing.Queue Separate processes Blocks the caller

queue provides thread-safe queues. asyncio.Queue is designed for asynchronous Tasks and is not thread-safe. multiprocessing.Queue supports interprocess communication and serializes the objects it transfers.

Our scope is CPython Threads, so we will focus on the standard library's queue module. The Python documentation lists several implementations:

Implementation Capacity Retrieval Order Default Blocking Conditions Task-Completion Tracking
queue.Queue Configurable; unbounded by default FIFO put() waits when full; get() waits when empty Supported
queue.LifoQueue Configurable; unbounded by default LIFO put() waits when full; get() waits when empty Supported
queue.PriorityQueue Configurable; unbounded by default Lowest-valued entry first put() waits when full; get() waits when empty Supported
queue.SimpleQueue Unbounded FIFO put() does not wait for space; get() waits when empty Not supported

Task-completion tracking uses task_done() to mark a task as processed and join() to wait until all enqueued tasks have been processed.

Note: In Python, maxsize <= 0 means the buffer has no preset capacity limit; in Go, a channel with capacity 0 has no buffer.

We will use queue.Queue, whose two primary operations are:

Operation Meaning Default Waiting Condition
put(item) Inserts an item Waits for space when full
get() Removes and returns an item Waits for an item when empty

Both operations block by default. Use block=False for an immediate attempt or timeout to limit the wait. Failure to insert or retrieve an item raises queue.Full or queue.Empty, respectively.

2.3.2 Thread Safety and Synchronization in Queue

The Python queue documentation states:

“The Queue class in this module implements all the required locking semantics.”

This supports Atomicity at the queue boundary. Multiple threads may call put() and get() concurrently; internal locking protects queue state, so two Consumers cannot remove the same enqueued item.

For Visibility and Ordering, the Producer prepares a message before put(), and the Consumer reads that message after get() returns. CPython coordinates the handoff using the queue's internal locks and condition variables, making the prepared data available to the receiving thread.

We will reuse the opening article's count++ example, building from SPSC through MPSC to MPMC:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from queue import Queue

@dataclass
class Increment:
    delta: int

jobs = Queue(maxsize=2)

2.3.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer

One Producer sends +1; one Consumer receives the message and updates count:

# Producer thread
message = Increment(delta=1)
jobs.put(message)

# Consumer thread
count = 0
received = jobs.get()
count += received.delta  # count == 1

The relevant handoff is:

Producer                                 Consumer

message.delta = 1
        │
        ▼
jobs.put(message) ── internal queue sync ─► jobs.get() returns message
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                         read received.delta == 1
                                         count = 1

A successful put() inserts a message; get() removes and returns it. At this point there is no contention among multiple Producers or Consumers.

delta is an ordinary attribute. Provided no thread continues mutating this message after it is enqueued, the Consumer can read the value 1 following the queue handoff. This comes from Queue synchronization, not from a blanket guarantee that the GIL protects every shared object.
