Unlike the earlier Shared Memory example, no separate shared ready flag is needed: get() waits for a message if the queue is empty.

2.3.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer

Add a second Producer. Each submits a +1 message; the only Consumer accumulates both:

# Producers A and B each execute this in a separate thread
jobs.put(Increment(delta=1))

# The sole Consumer thread
count = 0
for _ in range(2):
    received = jobs.get()
    count += received.delta
# After both messages have been submitted and processed: count == 2

One possible interleaving:

Producer A              Producer B              Consumer

put(A: +1)
                        put(B: +1)
                                                get() -> +1
                                                count: 0 -> 1
                                                get() -> +1
                                                count: 1 -> 2

Atomicity: the two Producers can enqueue concurrently without overwriting each other's successfully enqueued items; the Consumer can retrieve both.

Visibility / Ordering: each message is handed off through the queue's synchronization. The order in which concurrent Producers enqueue is not predetermined.

count += received.delta remains a compound operation, but only the sole Consumer modifies count.

2.3.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers

Now let two Consumers call get() concurrently while two Producers each enqueue +1:

# Producers A and B each run once in their own thread
jobs.put(Increment(delta=1))

# Consumers A and B each run once in their own thread
received = jobs.get()
delta = received.delta

For example:

Producer A        Producer B        Consumer A        Consumer B

put(A: +1)
                  put(B: +1)
                                    get() -> A
                                                      get() -> B

Atomicity: a successful get() removes one item; two Consumers cannot both remove the same enqueued item. A and B only distinguish the messages, not predetermined assignments.

Visibility / Ordering: whichever Consumer gets a message can read the data prepared before enqueueing it through the queue's thread synchronization. Dequeue order still says nothing about when the Consumers finish their work.

If both Consumers subsequently update the same shared counter:

# Incorrect: both Consumers share the same counter
counter = {"value": 0}  # Shared before starting either Consumer

# Each Consumer executes this
received = jobs.get()
counter["value"] += received.delta

Correctly dequeuing both messages does not guarantee that two counter["value"] += 1 operations cannot lose an update. Do not rely on the GIL to make this compound operation atomically safe; that assumption is especially unsafe with free-threaded CPython.

2.3.6 Blocking, FIFO, and Task Completion

The three scenarios also share these queue.Queue behaviors:

  • Blocking: with a capacity of 2, put() waits by default if the queue is full; get() waits if it is empty. A maxsize of 0 means no capacity limit, not a Go-style unbuffered rendezvous.
  • FIFO: items are removed in actual enqueue order. Concurrent Producers have no predetermined arrival order; multiple Consumers need not finish processing in dequeue order.
  • Task completion: get() reports only that a task has been removed. task_done() marks processing complete, while join() waits until the unfinished-task count reaches zero. Receiving and finishing are different events.

The next article will examine how CPython implements this behavior with Locks and Condition variables.

3. Next: How Is Message Handoff Implemented?

At the language level, Java BlockingQueue and Go channels provide explicit communication and memory-synchronization rules. CPython queue.Queue provides safe handoff through its standard library's thread synchronization.

Next, we will trace Java ArrayBlockingQueue, Go channels, and CPython queue.Queue through synchronization primitives, runtime implementations, the operating system, and ultimately the CPU.

This article was first published on ThinkerQAQ's personal blog and syndicated here by the author. The original article may be revised over time; please refer to the personal blog for the latest version.

title: The Longest Transaction in Your Low-Code Platform Is the One Nobody Designed
description:
The first message was three words long: "Saving is frozen."

It came from a production planner at a components manufacturer, forwarded by her IT lead with no commentary. She had opened a work order, changed one quantity, and pressed save. The button had been spinning for eleven minutes. She tried it three times, then stopped, because the second attempt made her nervous.

By the time we got on a call, two things were true. Her save had not failed — it was still running. And nobody else in the plant could edit that work order, or the four records downstream of it. The system was not down. It was busy in a way that looked exactly like being down.

The cause took an afternoon to find and four seconds to explain. The work order's automation recalculated a bill of materials, looping over every component line and calling a partner API for current pricing. Nine hundred lines, roughly three seconds per call. Forty-five minutes of work, wrapped in a single database transaction, holding locks the whole time, because of a boundary nobody had ever drawn.

The transaction is bigger than the drawing

In our platform, the transaction boundary is not something the builder chooses.

An automation is one transaction. All of it. The documentation is unambiguous — a complete automation runs inside a single transaction, and if anything throws, or the flow is stopped, the whole thing rolls back. It goes further: the before-create event, the creation, and the after-create event of a single step are also one transaction, so aborting anywhere in that chain discards the creation itself. The listener model matches. Listeners — the rules that fire on record creation, on data change, on user action — execute in the same transaction as the thing that triggered them. A listener that throws rolls back the form submission that woke it up.

None of that is wrong. Atomicity is not a bug. But look at what it means in a visual builder. The person who drew that recalculation was drawing logic — sequence, branches, API responses. They were not drawing a transaction, and nothing on the canvas told them they were. The transaction is inferred from the shape of a graph they built for an entirely different reason.

The graph is precise. The transaction is a side effect.

The number nobody computes

Our own documentation contains the clearest illustration of this failure I have read, and it is offered as friendly advice.

The example is two data tables, two thousand records each, and a nested loop with an HTTP request at the innermost level. Average request time: three seconds. The documentation does the arithmetic honestly — two thousand times two thousand times three seconds is more than thirty hours — then says what you would expect, that a flow like this running frequently is a disaster for the system, and recommends estimating execution time before you build.

That paragraph is correct and I am glad it exists. It is also a confession. A thirty-hour transaction is not something the platform prevented. It is something the platform documented. The canvas renders a nested loop as a modest little box, the same size as a single API call. There is no meter, no warning, no estimate, no ceiling. We outsourced the work of noticing to the person with the least information about what it costs.

There is a transaction timeout in the API — thirty seconds, if you set it — but you can only set it from script. Which brings us to the real problem.

Everything that governs a transaction lives where the builder cannot see

Our script API for transactions is more complete than I remembered. Seven propagation modes, including nested and requires-new. Isolation levels from read-uncommitted up to serializable. A timeout. A read-only flag. Transaction synchronizations — hooks that fire before commit, after commit, after completion — exactly the mechanism you would use to send a notification after the data is safe rather than inside the lock.

There is even a name for the transaction, and the documentation explains its purpose: a name helps developers identify and track transactions in logs and monitoring tools.

Count how many transactions in a real customer application have names. Approximately none. Not because the feature is missing, but because there is no moment in the visual workflow where a transaction becomes a thing a person is asked to think about. It is a constructor you must know exists before you can name it, in a document you only read after something has already gone wrong.

The one hint that reliably reaches builders is a tip telling them to paste three lines of script if they want a step to open a new transaction — a curious way to teach someone that they were inside one all along.

The scheduler has one lane, and it deletes the future

Transactions do not only come from user actions. They come from scheduled work, and the scheduling model has the same shape of problem.

Scheduled tasks fire at one-minute precision, and at any given moment exactly one is running. Consider a job configured every five minutes that takes six to finish. The run scheduled for minute five does not queue and does not wait. It is cancelled. A slow job does not merely finish late; it quietly accumulates runs that never happened. And after an outage, the misfire policy offers two choices: execute everything that was missed, or throw all of it away. Neither answers the question, which is whether a job that runs long should be allowed to run long, run chunked, or run at all.

The first time I watched a nightly reconciliation silently lose two cycles because one cycle was slow, I stopped thinking of schedules as triggers and started thinking of them as a single-lane road with no shoulders.

Termination is a person, and it is a destructive act

The runtime page does try. It lists what is executing right now — scripts, scheduled jobs, automations, API calls — and lets you terminate one by hand. The documentation names the reasons you would need to. Long-running tasks. Slow execution. Infinite loops. Database deadlocks.

Read that list again as a design document. Those are the system's own admitted failure modes, and the remedy for all four is a human noticing and clicking a button. Now consider what the button does. It does not pause and it does not checkpoint. It rolls back — which can mean discarding forty-five minutes of calculation, plus every record a colleague created inside a listener that shared the transaction, plus the save the user believed had succeeded.

A platform whose only answer to "this is taking too long" is "have someone destroy it" has not finished designing the feature.

Abort is the only word we gave you for no

Because listeners share the trigger's transaction, the way you implement a business rule at the data layer is to abort. Rule violated, flow stopped, everything rolls back. There is no vocabulary for reject this field but keep the record, no partial acceptance. The state machine has two states: it all happened, or none of it did. Builders who need a third state invent it outside the platform, and the validation they were asked to implement quietly becomes a reliability hazard instead of a guardrail.

And when a script reaches across to an external ERP over a raw JDBC connection, holds it in manual-commit mode, writes to both systems, and commits once — there is no coordinator. Two databases, one commit call, no two-phase protocol. The transaction that spans two systems is the most optimistic object in the building.

The uncomfortable conclusion

Every other finite resource here has a visible number. Storage is gigabytes. Tables have row counts. Usage points are metered and show up on an invoice. Customers can see the ceiling and argue about where it should be.

Transaction duration has no number at all, because on the canvas a transaction is not a thing that exists. It is a consequence of a diagram. So the most expensive decision in the system — how long we hold a lock on your data, and therefore how many other people are standing behind you — is a decision nobody is ever asked to make.

We moved application development up the stack, into a canvas a process analyst can read. Transactions stayed down in milliseconds and isolation levels and lock waits. We never built the bridge.

Which is why "why is saving frozen?" took an afternoon to answer out of pieces that were all in the documentation. The platform knew.

The most expensive thing in a low-code platform is not a feature you chose not to build. It is a duration you never knew you were choosing.

title: Designing a quiz result that shows its limits
description:
A result page can be mathematically consistent and still invite the wrong conclusion. A large label at the top of a political quiz makes a convenient screenshot, but it can hide the choices that produced it.

12 Axes Test is a free example of a different presentation: twelve separate scores across government, diplomacy, economy and society. It offers 36, 60 or 288 statements and calculates scores in the browser without requiring an account. Here are three design questions that this kind of interface raises.

What is the primary output?

A label compresses a vector into a name. That compression loses information. Two people can receive the same closest label while disagreeing on several dimensions. If the interface only gives the label visual emphasis, readers have little reason to inspect those disagreements.

For a multidimensional quiz, the scores should be readable before the comparisons. Axis names need visible endpoints, and a reader should be able to explain what a high or low value refers to. A compact chart is useful, but text labels still need to carry the meaning.

What does a comparison claim?

A nearest match is relative to the comparison set. It does not establish that the match is objectively correct, that its examples are exhaustive, or that the user agrees with every policy associated with a person or country.

12 Axes Test includes comparisons to ideologies, countries and public figures. These profiles are editorial estimates. They are discussion aids, not scientific diagnoses or voting advice. Placing that qualification close to the result helps readers understand the output before they share it.

What happens when a result is shared?

Scoring in a browser and sharing a result are different operations. A result link is designed to let another person view an output; anyone who receives the link may see the encoded scores. A share control should make that consequence understandable. Local calculation alone is not a blanket promise about analytics, every network request, or every future use of a shared link.

A useful review exercise is to ask a reader to describe a result without using its ideology label. Can they identify two strong dimensions, one mixed dimension and one question they would answer differently after discussion? If they can, the interface has given them more than a badge.

You can try the quiz and use its methodology and result explanations to examine these trade-offs. This article introduces the product and a design perspective; it does not validate the questionnaire as a scientific assessment.

title: Stop asking AI to “write tests for this” — 5 prompt changes that make generated tests catch bugs
description:
AI coding tools can write a test file in seconds. Most developers have also noticed the catch: the tests are green, coverage goes up, and a real bug ships straight through them.

That usually isn’t the model being bad at testing. It’s the prompt leaving out everything that makes a test valuable. Here are five changes I now make to every testing prompt — in Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT or Copilot Chat — and why each one matters.

1. Give it the intent, not just the code

If the only input is the implementation, the implementation becomes the spec. The model reads what the code does and asserts exactly that — including any bug.

Add one or two sentences of intent, in your own words:

What this code is supposed to do:
prorate() returns the charge for the unused part of a billing period,
rounded half-up to cents. It never returns a negative amount.

Now the model has something to test against. If it notices the code can return a negative amount, it has a reason to flag it instead of pinning it.

2. Ask for a plan before any code

“Write tests” invites volume. Ask for a behaviour inventory and a case table first:

Before writing any code:
1. List every observable behaviour (return values, errors, side effects, branches).
   Mark anything that looks like a bug with [SUSPECT].
2. For each behaviour, list cases: happy path, boundaries (empty, zero, one, max,
   off-by-one), invalid input, error paths.
Show me both. Then write the tests.

A case table takes ten seconds to review. If the boundaries or error paths are missing, you see it immediately — instead of discovering it in 300 lines of generated code.

3. Attach one existing test file

Describing your conventions (“we use Vitest, factories live in tests/factories, we name tests like…”) works poorly. Showing them works well:

Conventions to copy: tests/billing/invoice.test.ts
Match its imports, helpers, file location and naming.

This one line stops most of the “new assertion library, different folder, duplicate fixtures” problems.

4. Write the rules the model would otherwise break

Models take the shortest path to green. State the boundaries explicitly:

Rules:
- Do not change production code to make tests pass. If the code seems wrong, report it.
- Expected values must be hand-computed literals, not the same formula as the code.
- Only stub true boundaries: clock, randomness, network, third-party APIs.
- No fixed sleeps. Freeze time and seed randomness explicitly.

The second rule alone removes a whole class of “mirror tests” — tests that agree with the implementation by construction and can never fail for the reason you care about.

5. Make it justify every test

End with a self-check:

For each test, state in one line the specific bug it would catch.
Delete any test whose answer is "none" or "same as another test".
List behaviours from the case table that still have no test.

Then do the human version: break the code on purpose (flip a < to <=, return early) and see whether anything goes red. If nothing does, the tests are decoration.

Different jobs need different prompts

The five changes above are the skeleton. The process section should change with the job:

  • Integration/API tests: rank scenarios by risk — contract, validation, auth (including another tenant’s resource), persistence, idempotency, downstream failure — and forbid mocking the database.
  • E2E: separate checkpoints worth asserting from incidental UI, use role/label locators, and ask for an explicit flake review.
  • Legacy code: write characterization tests that pin current behaviour, bugs included, before you change anything.
  • Flaky tests: ask for ranked hypotheses with evidence and a reproduction step. Retries and longer sleeps are not fixes.
  • Coverage: treat the percentage as one input to a risk-based plan, not the goal.

The shape that works

Every good testing prompt I use has the same five parts:

Part Purpose
Role “Senior engineer writing tests a skeptical reviewer will accept”
Context Target, intent/spec, framework, one example test, what not to touch
Process Numbered steps, plan before code
Output contract Exact sections and tables to return
Rules The shortcuts the model must not take

Try it on a function you know well. If the case table finds an edge case you hadn’t written down, it’s working.

I packaged the eight prompts I use for this — unit, spec-first, integration/API, E2E, characterization, flaky diagnosis, coverage planning and mock boundaries — plus two checklists, a Cursor rule and a PDF guide, as the **AI Test Generation Prompt Pack: https://lirenplr.gumroad.com/l/cuofwr. Everything above works without it.

— Pluto · @Mars_Peakul

title: ISTQB CT-PT in Code: The Load Profile, Throughput Math and Script Behind Half the Exam
description:
The ISTQB Performance Testing exam (CT-PT) asks 40 questions in 90 minutes, and 20 of them come from one chapter of the syllabus: Performance Testing Tasks. You pass with 26 points out of 40. So the best use of your study time is to work that chapter once with your own hands: write an operational profile, turn it into a load profile, do the throughput arithmetic, and put the result in a script.

This post does that with one small example. The scripts use k6 because it is free and reads like plain JavaScript. The syllabus names no tool at all, so treat the code as a way to make the ideas concrete, not as exam content.

What does the CT-PT exam look like?

CT-PT is a 40-question multiple-choice exam in ISTQB's Specialist stream, and you need the Foundation Level certificate before you can sit it. The figures below are from the ISTQB page for Certified Tester Performance Testing, read on 14 October 2026.

Item Value
Questions 40
Points 40, one per question
Passing score 26 points (65%)
Time 90 minutes, or 113 if the exam is not in your native language
Prerequisite Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL)
Syllabus v1.0, released in 2018
Fee Not listed by ISTQB. The exam provider you book with sets it

Where do the 40 questions come from?

Half of them come from chapter 4. ISTQB publishes the split per chapter in its Exam Structures and Rules tables (v1.19, August 2026), and the syllabus gives each chapter a minimum training time.

Chapter Questions Training time
1. Basic Concepts 6 60 min
2. Performance Measurement Fundamentals 4 55 min
3. Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle 7 195 min
4. Performance Testing Tasks 20 475 min
5. Tools 3 90 min

The same tables sort the questions by thinking level. Two are K1 (remember), 25 are K2 (understand), 4 are K3 (apply) and 9 are K4 (analyze). Ten of the 13 apply and analyze questions sit in chapter 4.

There is a timing catch in those tables. They allow 1 minute for a K1 question, 2 for K2, 3 for K3 and 4 for K4. For CT-PT that adds up to 100 minutes of nominal work (2 + 50 + 12 + 36) in a 90-minute exam. The only place to win the ten minutes back is the 25 K2 questions, so the definitions have to come fast.

How do you turn usage data into an operational profile?

An operational profile is one distinct pattern of interaction with the application, and you build it in three steps: decide what data you need, gather it, and evaluate it. The syllabus asks for three kinds of data: the user personas and their roles, the generic tasks each role performs, and the estimated number of users for each role per unit of time.

It also tells you where to look. Sources include workshops with product owners and sales managers, functional specifications and user stories, usage logs from the current system, and watching real users work through tasks. The approach is top-down. Start with broad profiles and split one further only if a test objective needs it.

Here is the example used in the rest of this post. It is a made-up ticket shop, not something from the syllabus.

Operational profile One session Think time Volume at peak
Visitor Open the home page, list events, open one event 9 s after each step 100 sessions open at any moment
Buyer Log in, search, add to cart, pay 9 s after each step 19,800 orders an hour

Two profiles are enough. The learning objective for this section is K4, analyze, so be ready to read usage data like this and say which profile matters. The syllabus singles out profiles whose tasks run often, need critical or frequent transactions between components, or move large volumes of data.

How do you build a load profile from the operational profiles?

A load profile says how many instances run each operational profile, and how that number changes over the test. When the instances stand for people, they are called virtual users. The syllabus lists four shapes to combine: ramp-ups, ramp-downs, steps, and predefined distributions that copy a daily or seasonal cycle.

Section 4.2.4 of the CT-PT syllabus builds a stress profile from two parts. A step of 100 virtual users runs the first operational profile for the whole test as background load. A second group ramps up to 220 virtual users, holds for two hours, and ramps down. Added together, they give the system three hours of stress.

In k6 that diagram is two scenarios:

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    background: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',   // a step: all 100 start at once
      exec: 'visit',
      vus: 100,
      duration: '3h',
    },
    stress: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      exec: 'buy',
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { duration: '30m', target: 220 },  // ramp-up
        { duration: '2h', target: 220 },   // hold
        { duration: '30m', target: 0 },    // ramp-down
      ],
    },
  },
};

The syllabus does not print the ramp lengths. Thirty minutes each is my choice, so that the two ramps and the two-hour hold fill the three hours.

How many virtual users give the throughput you planned?

Divide the number of virtual users by the time one pass takes, and you have the throughput. The syllabus writes it like this:

system throughput = virtual users / (processing time + think time)

It then warns that a user count alone is not a measure of load. Its example: 500 users who each run a short query every minute produce 30,000 queries an hour. The same 500 users running one query an hour produce 500. The user count is the same and the load differs by a factor of 60.

Now the ticket shop. A buyer session has four transactions. Say each takes 1 second to process and is followed by 9 seconds of think time. That is 4 seconds of processing and 36 seconds of thinking, 40 seconds a pass.

const targetPerSecond = 19800 / 3600;        // 5.5 orders a second
const pass = 4 + 36;                         // seconds for one session
const users = targetPerSecond * pass;        // 220 virtual users

// The system slows down under stress: 4 s of processing becomes 14 s
const slowPass = 14 + 36;                    // 50 seconds
const actual = users / slowPass;             // 4.4 orders a second
console.log(users, Math.round(actual * 3600));   // 220 15840

The same 220 virtual users now place 15,840 orders an hour, 20% under the plan. This is the sentence in the syllabus that candidates skip: when processing time goes up, throughput can drop even if everything else stays the same. Your stress test eases off at the moment it should push hardest.

The syllabus explains why. A typical test setup is a closed system: the number of users is fixed, so when all of them are waiting for a response, no new user can arrive. Many public systems are open systems, where new users keep arriving while the current ones wait. The k6 documentation describes the same split in its page on open and closed models. To hold the arrival rate steady, swap the executor:

stress_open: {
  executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
  exec: 'buy',
  rate: 11,
  timeUnit: '2s',          // 11 sessions every 2 seconds = 5.5 a second
  duration: '2h',
  preAllocatedVUs: 300,    // 5.5 x 40 s = 220 in flight, 5.5 x 50 s = 275
},

What does the syllabus expect inside a performance test script?

It expects three parts: an initialization section, a main section that can run many times, and a clean-up section. k6 uses different names for the same idea. Its test lifecycle has init code and setup() for initialization, a scenario function for the main part, and teardown() for clean-up.

import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, group, sleep } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { scenario } from 'k6/execution';

// 1. Initialization: load test data and declare metrics. No requests here.
const buyers = new SharedArray('buyers', () => JSON.parse(open('./buyers.json')));
const orderTime = new Trend('order_time', true);
const BASE = 'https://shop.test.example';
const JSON_HEADERS = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' };

export function setup() {
  // Still initialization. A broken system gives no useful load numbers.
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/health`);
  if (res.status !== 200) throw new Error('system under test is not ready');
}

// 2. Main section: one pass is one buyer session.
export function buy() {
  const me = buyers[scenario.iterationInTest % buyers.length];   // parameterization
  let spent = 0;

  group('order', () => {                                         // outer transaction
    let res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/login`, JSON.stringify(me), { headers: JSON_HEADERS });
    check(res, { 'logged in': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    const token = res.json('token');                             // correlation
    const headers = { ...JSON_HEADERS, Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` };
    spent += res.timings.duration;
    sleep(9);                                                    // think time

    res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/events?city=${me.city}`, { headers });
    const eventId = res.json()[0].id;                            // correlation again
    spent += res.timings.duration;
    sleep(9);

    group('add to cart', () => {                                 // nested transaction
      res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/cart`, JSON.stringify({ eventId, seats: 2 }), { headers });
      check(res, { 'two seats in cart': (r) => r.json('seats') === 2 });
      spent += res.timings.duration;
    });
    sleep(9);

    group('pay', () => {
      res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/orders`, null, { headers });
      check(res, { 'order confirmed': (r) => r.json('status') === 'CONFIRMED' });
      spent += res.timings.duration;
    });
  });

  orderTime.add(spent);    // response time of the whole order, think time left out
  sleep(9);
}

// 3. Clean-up
export function teardown() {
  http.post(`${BASE}/api/test-data/reset`);
}

The visit function for the background scenario is left out to keep this short. Five things in the script map to lines of the syllabus:

  • Transactions. A transaction runs from the start of a request to the end of the processing it triggers. Transactions can be nested, so one run measures each step and the order as a whole. That is what the inner groups and the order_time metric do.
  • Think time. The syllabus states that transaction response time plus think time equals elapsed time. The sleep(9) calls are the think time, and the trend records response time only.
  • Timers. Time a meaningful unit of work, such as submitting an order. A protocol-level script like this one measures server and network time only. A script that drives the GUI measures end to end.
  • Result verification. Checking the HTTP return code is the minimum. The check calls look at what came back: two seats, a confirmed order.
  • Scripts are software. Review the script and test it with the whole range of input data before trusting its numbers.

Correlation gets its own paragraph in the syllabus. If you record a session at the protocol level, the recording holds identifiers that were valid once, such as the login token above. They have to become variables that are filled from each response. The syllabus says incorrect or missing correlation is the main reason recorded scripts fail on playback, and the k6 docs carry examples of extracting tokens from responses for JSON and for form fields.

Parameterization is the other half. Run every virtual user with the same name and the same data, and the results mislead in one of two directions. The data may be fully cached, which makes the system look faster than production. Or users may queue on a lock for the same record, which makes it look slower.

That is why the script reads buyers from a file and gives each iteration a different one. The k6 page on data parameterization shows the same pattern with JSON and CSV files.

Why does the report use a percentile and not only an average?

Because the average can be skewed by outliers, and the syllabus says so in those words. It lists four ways to report transaction response time: minimum, maximum, average and a percentile such as the 90th. Ten response times show the problem:

const ms = [180, 190, 200, 210, 220, 230, 240, 250, 2600, 4100];
const avg = ms.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / ms.length;
const pct = (q) => [...ms].sort((a, b) => a - b)[Math.ceil(q * ms.length) - 1];
console.log(avg, pct(0.5), pct(0.9));   // 842 220 2600

Eight of the ten users waited a quarter of a second or less. Two waited seconds. The average of 842 ms describes none of them. The median shows the typical user, and the 90th percentile shows the tail.

The syllabus adds two points that are easy to miss. A goal of 100% compliance is not recommended, because the resources it needs may be too large for a minor gain to users. And you look at the status of the virtual users before anything else. A failed transaction takes far less time than a completed one, so failures can make the transactions-per-second figure look better than it is.

In k6 you write the goal down as a threshold, and the run fails when it is missed. The thresholds reference lists the aggregation methods you can use.

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],     // under 1% failed requests
    order_time: ['p(90)<3000'],         // 90% of orders within 3 s of response time
  },
};

Which test type fits which objective?

The syllabus defines seven types under the umbrella term performance testing, and chapter 1 carries six questions. The first two columns below follow section 1.2. The third column is my shorthand for the load profile each one usually needs.

Type What it focuses on Typical load shape
Load Handling increasing levels of anticipated, realistic load Ramp up to the expected level and hold
Stress Peak loads at or beyond the specified limits, or reduced resources Ramp past the expected maximum
Scalability Meeting future needs, such as more users or more stored data Repeated runs with growing load or data
Spike Sudden bursts of peak load, then a return to a steady state Step up, step down
Endurance Stability over a period that fits the system's use Flat load for a long time
Concurrency Specific actions that happen at the same moment Many users doing one thing at once
Capacity How many users or transactions it supports while meeting its objectives Step up until an objective fails

Endurance testing is the one that finds resource problems which build up slowly. The syllabus gives memory leaks, database connections and thread pools as its examples.

A short video on the exam

ProcessExam's channel has a three-minute video with five preparation tips for CT-PT. It covers the study side that this post leaves out.

How should you split your study time?

Follow the syllabus's own weighting. The five chapters add up to 875 minutes of minimum training time, about 14 and a half hours, and chapter 4 takes 475 of them. A plan that gives chapter 4 half of your hours matches both the training time and the question count.

A split that works in practice:

  1. Chapters 1 and 2 first, in one sitting. They are ten questions, mostly definitions, and they are where you win back time on exam day.
  2. Chapter 4 over three or four sittings, with a keyboard. Build one operational profile, one load profile and one script for a system you know.
  3. Chapter 3 next. Its seven questions are about risk: which performance risks belong to which architecture, and which test activity belongs to which lifecycle phase.
  4. Chapter 5 last. Three questions on tool types and how to judge whether a tool suits a project.

If you want every learning objective in one place to tick off, the CT-PT syllabus topics listed by chapter on ProcessExam work as a checklist.

Finish with ISTQB's own sample exam, which is a free download on the certification page. Time yourself at 90 minutes. The answer sheet gives the learning objective and K-level of every question, so note which level each wrong answer was.

For the weeks before the exam, this CT-PT preparation playbook goes deeper into planning and revision than a code walkthrough can.

Frequently asked questions

1. How many questions are on the ISTQB CT-PT exam, and what is the passing score?

The exam has 40 multiple-choice questions worth one point each, and you need 26 points to pass, which is 65%. You get 90 minutes, or 113 minutes if the exam is not in your native language.

2. Do I need the Foundation Level certificate before taking CT-PT?

Yes. ISTQB states that candidates must hold the Certified Tester Foundation Level certificate to gain the Performance Testing certification.

3. Does the CT-PT exam test a specific tool such as JMeter or k6?

No. The syllabus names no tool. Chapter 5 covers types of tools (load generators, load management consoles, monitoring tools) and how to judge whether a tool suits a project, and it carries 3 of the 40 questions.

4. Which chapter of the CT-PT syllabus has the most exam questions?

Chapter 4, Performance Testing Tasks, has 20 of the 40 questions. Chapter 3 has 7, chapter 1 has 6, chapter 2 has 4 and chapter 5 has 3.

5. Is the 2018 CT-PT syllabus still the current version?

Yes, as of 14 October 2026. The ISTQB certification page offers CT-PT Syllabus v1.0 (2018) as its syllabus download, and the Exam Structures and Rules tables dated August 2026 still list CT-PT with 40 questions and 90 minutes.

Written by the team behind ProcessExam, a practice-test site for process, project and software testing certifications. We are not affiliated with ISTQB.

title: React Server Components Guide: Architecture, Examples, and Best Practices
description:
React Server Components (RSC) introduce a different way to think about rendering React applications. Instead of sending every component's JavaScript to the browser, developers can render selected components on the server and send their results to the client, reducing the amount of JavaScript users need to download and execute.

RSC are especially useful for applications that display database records, product catalogs, dashboards, documentation, or other content that benefits from server-side data access. They also introduce important architectural decisions around component boundaries, data fetching, caching, and client-side interactivity.

In this guide, we'll explore how React Server Components work, how they differ from traditional client components, and how to build a practical example using modern React patterns. We'll also cover common mistakes and best practices that matter when building production applications.

Understanding React Server Components with a Practical Example

What Are React Server Components?

React Server Components are React components that execute on the server and can access server-side resources without exposing that implementation to the browser. Their rendered output is represented through the React Server Component payload, which the framework uses to update the UI.

Unlike traditional server-side rendering, Server Components are not simply components that render HTML on the server before hydrating in the browser. They can remain server-only components, meaning their implementation does not need to become part of the client-side JavaScript bundle.

Server Components vs. Client Components

Server Components are well suited for fetching data, accessing databases, reading files, and rendering content that does not require browser APIs. Client Components are necessary for features such as event handlers, local interactive state, effects, and browser-specific APIs.

In frameworks that support React Server Components, a component is generally a Server Component by default unless it is placed within a client boundary. Adding the "use client" directive at the top of a module marks that module and its transitive dependencies as part of the client-side component graph. It does not mean the component can never be prerendered on the server.

A Practical Product Catalog Example

Imagine building an online store that displays products from a database. A Server Component can retrieve product data directly from a server-side data source and render the catalog without requiring the browser to make a separate request for that initial data.

The following runnable JavaScript example demonstrates the core architecture using a small, framework-independent simulation. It separates server-side product retrieval from client-side interaction and uses console logs to show which responsibilities belong to each layer. It is an educational model of the architecture, not a replacement for React's actual Server Component runtime or transport protocol.

How This Maps to a Real React Application

In a framework such as Next.js App Router, the catalog page can be an asynchronous Server Component that retrieves products directly from a database or backend service. A separate component marked with "use client" can handle filtering, adding products to a cart, or responding to user input.

Keep database credentials, privileged API keys, and server-only dependencies out of client modules. Also remember that props crossing the Server Component to Client Component boundary must be serializable according to React's supported serialization rules; ordinary functions and arbitrary server resources cannot simply be passed as client props.

Important Performance Considerations

Server Components can reduce client JavaScript and simplify secure data access, but they do not automatically make every application faster. Slow database queries, excessive sequential requests, large rendered payloads, and poorly designed caching strategies can still hurt performance.

Fetch independent data concurrently when possible, use appropriate caching and revalidation policies, and keep client boundaries focused on the interactions that genuinely require them. Measure real production performance instead of assuming that moving work to the server always produces a better result.

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: "Wireless Headphones", price: 2499, stock: 12 },
  { id: 2, name: "Mechanical Keyboard", price: 3999, stock: 8 },
  { id: 3, name: "USB-C Hub", price: 1499, stock: 0 },
  { id: 4, name: "Laptop Stand", price: 999, stock: 15 }
];

// Step 1: Simulate a server-side data source.
// In production, this function could query a database or internal API.
async function getProducts() {
  console.log("[SERVER] Connecting to the product data source...");

  // Simulate asynchronous I/O without external dependencies.
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));

  console.log("[SERVER] Product records retrieved successfully.");
  return products.map((product) => ({ ...product }));
}

// Step 2: Implement server-side business logic.
// Keep data access and business rules outside interactive UI code.
async function getAvailableProducts() {
  console.log("[SERVER] Applying availability rules...");
  const allProducts = await getProducts();
  const availableProducts = allProducts.filter(
    (product) => product.stock > 0
  );

  console.log(
    `[SERVER] Found ${availableProducts.length} available products.`
  );

  return availableProducts;
}

// Step 3: Model a Server Component's data preparation.
// This function demonstrates the server-side responsibility only.
async function ProductCatalogServer() {
  console.log("\n[SERVER] Rendering the product catalog...");
  const catalog = await getAvailableProducts();

  // Return plain data that can be consumed by a UI layer.
  return {
    title: "Available Products",
    products: catalog.map(({ id, name, price }) => ({ id, name, price }))
  };
}

// Step 4: Model client-side interaction.
// A real React implementation would use a Client Component with state.
function ProductCatalogClient(catalog) {
  console.log("\n[CLIENT] Initializing catalog interactions...");
  let selectedProductId = null;

  function selectProduct(productId) {
    const selectedProduct = catalog.products.find(
      (product) => product.id === productId
    );

    if (!selectedProduct) {
      console.log("[CLIENT] Product not found in the catalog.");
      return null;
    }

    selectedProductId = selectedProduct.id;
    console.log(`[CLIENT] Selected: ${selectedProduct.name}`);
    return selectedProduct;
  }

  function renderCatalog() {
    console.log(`\n${catalog.title}`);
    console.log("-".repeat(40));

    catalog.products.forEach((product) => {
      console.log(`${product.name} | Rs. ${product.price}`);
    });

    console.log("-".repeat(40));
  }

  return {
    renderCatalog,
    selectProduct,
    getSelectedProductId: () => selectedProductId
  };
}

// Step 5: Run the demonstration from a server-side entry point.
// This standalone program simulates the two responsibilities in one process.
async function main() {
  console.log("=== React Server Components Architecture Demo ===");

  // Prepare data on the server before handing it to the UI layer.
  const catalogData = await ProductCatalogServer();

  console.log("\n[BOUNDARY] Passing serializable catalog data to the client.");
  const clientCatalog = ProductCatalogClient(catalogData);

  // Display the catalog and simulate a user selecting a product.
  clientCatalog.renderCatalog();
  clientCatalog.selectProduct(2);

  console.log(
    "\n[CLIENT] Selected product ID:",
    clientCatalog.getSelectedProductId()
  );

  // An unavailable product is not included in the client catalog.
  clientCatalog.selectProduct(3);

  console.log("\nDemo completed successfully.");
}

// Step 6: Handle unexpected failures without hiding the error.
main().catch((error) => {
  console.error("Demo failed:", error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Conclusion

React Server Components provide a useful foundation for building applications that keep data access and rendering on the server while delivering focused interactive experiences to the browser. Their biggest architectural advantage is the ability to separate server-only responsibilities from client-side behavior instead of treating every component as browser code.

The most effective implementations use Server Components for data-intensive UI and Client Components for focused interactions. In real applications, frameworks such as Next.js handle the React Server Component payload, routing, and rendering integration, so developers should follow the framework's conventions rather than attempting to recreate that infrastructure themselves.

Start by moving data-fetching components that do not need browser interactivity to the server, then introduce client boundaries only where state or event handling is required. Combine that approach with sensible caching, parallel data fetching, clear security boundaries, and performance measurement to build React applications that remain maintainable as they scale.

title: Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies
description:
title: "Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies"
published: true
published_at: "2026-12-18T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [api, backend, webdev, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of rest apis architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Idempotent Http Methods (Get: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Delete) Vs Non-Idempotent (Post: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Patch): Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Url Structure Nouns Over Verbs: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: REST APIs Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Idempotent HTTP methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) vs non-idempotent (POST, PATCH), URL structure nouns over verbs, URI vs Header versioning, and RFC 7807 Problem Details."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: tuning tokio thread pool to cut latency spikes in high‑throughput services
description:
in a recent microservice that ingests 200k requests /s, we saw occasional latency outliers up to 200 ms while the 99th‑percentile stayed under 5 ms. the spike source turned out to be the tokio runtime's default thread‑pool configuration, which silently oversubscribes the CPU and induces cache line contention.

The Bottleneck

tokio builds a work‑stealing scheduler on top of a fixed number of worker threads. by default it uses the number of logical cores, which on a hyper‑threaded 8‑core box means 16 workers. each worker pulls tasks from a shared deque; when many short tasks compete, the deque's head pointer is updated concurrently, causing false sharing on the cache line that holds the queue metadata. the result is a series of cache‑miss stalls that amplify latency under load.

A Minimal Fix

pinning the runtime to a core‑count that matches physical cores and padding the deque structures eliminates the false sharing. the code below shows a tuned builder that also raises the stack size to avoid guard‑page faults when deep recursion occurs.

use tokio::runtime::{Builder, Runtime};

let rt: Runtime = Builder::new_multi_thread()
    .worker_threads(8)               // match physical cores, not logical
    .max_blocking_threads(32)        // bounded blocking pool
    .thread_stack_size(2 * 1024 * 1024) // 2 MiB stacks for heavy recursion
    .enable_all()
    .build()
    .expect("failed to build runtime");

The runtime now creates exactly eight workers; each worker’s local queue resides in its own cache line because the scheduler pads the queue header to a full 64‑byte line. this reduces inter‑worker cache traffic and brings the 99th‑percentile back to sub‑5 ms even under sustained peak load.

Trade‑offs & Edge Cases

  • More workers → higher parallelism but also more context switches and larger total stack memory (8 workers × 2 MiB ≈ 16 MiB). on memory‑constrained containers this can push the RSS close to limits and trigger OOM.
  • Increasing max_blocking_threads helps when legacy blocking I/O is unavoidable, yet each extra thread adds a kernel scheduler overhead that can negate the latency gains.
  • Thread affinity: on Linux you can bind each worker to a distinct physical core via taskset or numactl. without it, the OS may migrate workers across cores, re‑introducing cache line bounce.
  • Hyper‑threading: keeping workers equal to physical cores avoids the “two‑threads‑per‑core” contention, but if your workload is I/O bound you might benefit from the extra logical threads; profiling is the only way to decide.

When It Still Fails

if latency spikes persist, look for hidden blocking calls inside async tasks (e.g., std::fs::read_to_string). such calls fall back to the blocking pool, which can starve the worker pool if max_blocking_threads is too low. also verify that the executor’s yield_now is used in long loops to give other workers a chance to steal work.

how do you balance thread‑pool size, stack allocation, and cache‑line padding in your high‑throughput async services? share the configuration that gave you the most stable latency curve.

title: Writing tests in python?
description:
from colorama import init, Fore
from duration import *

def print_pass(the_data, i):
print(f'{Fore.GREEN}Test {i} with {the_data} passed')

def print_fail(the_data, i):
print(f'''{Fore.RED}*** Test {i} with {the_data} failed.''')

def print_tests():
_test_default = Duration(60)
_test_minutes = Duration(10, "m")
_test_hours = Duration(2, "h")
_test_sec = Duration(120, "s")

print('''

Test #1 - simple declarations
-----------------------------''')
test_objects = (
_test_default,
_test_minutes,
_test_hours,
_test_sec
)

test_print_out = (
    "60.00 s",
    "600.00 s",
    "7200.00 s",
    "120.00 s"
)

test_repr_out = (
    "Duration(60.00, 's')",
    "Duration(10.00, 'm')",
    "Duration(2.00, 'h')",
    "Duration(120.00, 's')"
)

for i, test_obj in enumerate(test_objects):
    try:
        assert str(test_obj) == test_print_out[i], f'Expected {test_print_out[i]} received {str(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'print of {test_obj}', i+1)
        assert repr(test_obj) == test_repr_out[i], f'Expected {test_repr_out[i]} received {repr(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'repr of {repr(test_obj)}', i+1)

    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, i+1)
        continue

def add_tests():
print('''

Test #2 - Addition
------------------''')
_test_default = Duration(60)
_test_minutes = Duration(5, "m")
_test_hours = Duration(1, "h")
_test_list = [Duration(10), Duration(2, 'm'), Duration(1, 'h')]
_test_inc = Duration(60)

test_objects = (
    _test_default + _test_minutes,
    _test_default + 30,
    sum(_test_list),
    15 + _test_minutes
)

test_add_out = (
    "Duration(360.00, 's')",
    "Duration(90.00, 's')",
    "Duration(3730.00, 's')",
    "Duration(5.25, 'm')"
)

for i, test_obj in enumerate(test_objects):
    try:
        assert repr(test_obj) == test_add_out[i], f'Expected {test_add_out[i]} received {repr(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'print of {repr(test_obj)}', i+1)

    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, i+1)
        continue

_test_inc += 30
try:
    assert repr(_test_inc) == "Duration(90.00, 's')", f'Expected Duration(90.00, s) received {repr(_test_inc)}'
    print_pass(f'Incremental test of {repr(_test_inc)}', 1)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, 1)

def sub_tests():
print('''

Test #3 - Test all subtraction cases
------------------------------------''')
_test_default = Duration(120)
_test_minutes = Duration(1, "m")
_test_dec = Duration(100)

test_objects = (
    _test_default - _test_minutes,
    _test_default - 30
)

test_sub_out = (
    "Duration(60.00, 's')",
    "Duration(90.00, 's')"
)

try:
    reverse_sub = 200 - Duration(60, "s")
    assert repr(reverse_sub) == "Duration(140.00, 's')", \
        f"Expected Duration(140.00, 's') received {repr(reverse_sub)}"
    print_pass(f'reverse subtraction: {repr(reverse_sub)}', 6)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, 6)

for i, test_obj in enumerate(test_objects):
    try:
        assert repr(test_obj) == test_sub_out[i], f'Expected {test_sub_out[i]} received {repr(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'print of {repr(test_obj)}', i+1)

    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, i+1)
        continue

_test_dec -= 40
try:
    assert repr(_test_dec) == "Duration(60.00, 's')", f'Expected Duration(60.00, s) received {repr(_test_dec)}'
    print_pass(f'Decremental test of {repr(_test_dec)}', 1)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, 1)

def comp_tests():
print('''

Test #4 - Test comparisons between Duration objects
--------------------------''')

_test_comp1 = Duration(60)
_test_comp2 = Duration(1, "m")
_test_comp7 = Duration(100)
_test_comp8 = Duration(101)

count = 1
try:
    assert _test_comp1 == _test_comp2, f'Equality tested failed for {repr(_test_comp1)} and {repr(_test_comp2)}'
    print_pass(f'comparison: {repr(_test_comp1)} = {repr(_test_comp2)} ', count)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, count)

count += 1
try:
    assert not (_test_comp7 > _test_comp8), f'Greater than test failed for {repr(_test_comp7)} and {repr(_test_comp8)}'
    print_pass(f'comparison: {repr(_test_comp7)} not > {repr(_test_comp8)} ', count)
    assert _test_comp7 < _test_comp8, f'Less than test failed for {repr(_test_comp7)} and {repr(_test_comp8)}'
    print_pass(f'comparison: {repr(_test_comp7)} < {repr(_test_comp8)} ', count)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, count)

def exception_tests():
print('''

Test #5 - Test Exceptions
-------------------------''')
count = 1
try:
Duration("abc")
print_fail(f'Value error not thrown when value is string', count)
except ValueError as msg:
try:
assert str(msg) == "Value must be a number", f'Value error does not have correct message. Received {msg}'
print_pass(f'Value error thrown with message: {msg} as expected', count)
except AssertionError as test_data:
print_fail(test_data, count)
count += 1

try:
    Duration(-10)
    print_fail(f'Less than zero exception not thrown when value is negative', count)
except DurationLessThanZeroException as msg:
    try:
        assert str(msg) == "Duration cannot be negative", f'Exception does not have correct message. Received {msg}'
        print_pass(f'Negative-value error thrown with message: {msg} as expected', count)
    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, count)

count += 1
try:
    Duration(10, "abc")
    print_fail(f'Incorrect unit exception not thrown', count)
except TimeUnitNotDefinedException as msg:
    try:
        assert str(msg) == "Unit cannot be used", f'Exception does not have correct message. Received {msg}'
        print_pass(f'Unit error thrown with message: {msg} as expected', count)
    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, count)

if name == "main":
init(autoreset=True)
print_tests()
add_tests()
sub_tests()
comp_tests()
exception_tests()

title: I built a free static analyzer for Solana programs — here's what it catches and how it's built
description:
Solana exploits keep hitting the same bug classes: missing signer checks, arbitrary cross-program invocations, unchecked account deserialization, integer overflow. These aren't exotic — they're the same patterns that have drained hundreds of millions of dollars from on-chain programs, and they're detectable with static analysis before code ever gets deployed.

So I built SolAudit: a free, MIT-licensed static analyzer for Anchor/Solana Rust programs. 0.2.0 shipped this week.

Try it in 10 seconds: npx solaudit ./your-program

What it does

Point SolAudit at a directory of .rs files and it applies 11 security rules, then gives you a report grouped by severity — no RPC calls, no wallet, no build step:

Severity Examples
CRITICAL Missing signer checks on token transfers/mints
HIGH Arbitrary CPI (caller-controlled program IDs), unchecked deserialization, type cosplay, insecure manual account closure, missing bump canonicalization
MEDIUM Integer overflow on balance math, insecure account init, missing rent-exemption checks
LOW Missing owner checks

Each finding includes the exact line and a concrete remediation hint. Exit code is 1 on any CRITICAL/HIGH finding, so it drops straight into CI as a gate.

Three ways to use it

CLI — npx solaudit ./program, or bun add -g solaudit. Outputs human-readable, --json, or --sarif.

Web app — solaudit-web.vercel.app. Paste a public GitHub repo URL or upload a single .rs file. No install.

GitHub Action — on the Marketplace. Ten lines of YAML and every push gets scanned, with findings uploaded to your repo's Security tab as code-scanning alerts:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: blueeyez425-art/solaudit@main
  with:
    path: ./programs

On accuracy — honest numbers

On the committed labeled benchmark suite, the engine scores 93.8% precision, 100% recall, 96.8% F1 on rule-covered categories.

Those numbers describe that suite, not general effectiveness. One known gap remains: duplicate mutable accounts. I built a "distinctness" heuristic for it, it produced false positives on common legitimate patterns (e.g., a deposit instruction's user/vault token accounts of the same type), so I didn't ship it. A scanner that cries wolf gets uninstalled; I'd rather have a smaller rule set people trust.

Supply chain: verify the build yourself

A security tool that asks you to trust its binaries shouldn't exist. Every npm publish of SolAudit goes through GitHub Actions trusted publishing with signed Sigstore provenance — the package on npm is cryptographically bound to an exact commit and workflow run in the public repo. There's no "someone's laptop" in the loop. npm displays the provenance badge on the package page.

The dogfooding story

The repo's own CI runs SolAudit against its intentionally vulnerable example program on every push. Setting that up immediately caught a real bug — in my own Action: when a consuming repo had a local workspace package named solaudit, npx would resolve the local package instead of the pinned npm release, and the scan silently ran... nothing. The fix: install the pinned CLI into a temp dir and invoke it directly. Self-scanning found a distribution bug before any user did. That's the loop working as advertised.

What's next

  • Closing the duplicate-mutable-accounts gap with a smarter heuristic that survives the false-positive review
  • More rules from post-mortems of real exploits
  • Reentrancy-via-CPI-callback detection

Links

  • Repo: https://github.com/blueeyez425-art/solaudit (⭐ if useful)
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/solaudit
  • Action: https://github.com/marketplace/actions/solaudit-security-scanner
  • Demo: https://solaudit-web.vercel.app/

Feedback, false positives, and rule requests are all welcome as GitHub issues. SolAudit is free and will keep being built either way — development doesn't depend on tips. That said, if it saved you real time or caught a real bug, there's a tip link in the README, and it's genuinely appreciated.

Built by an independent security researcher. SolAudit is a first-pass scanner, not an audit — it doesn't replace manual review for anything holding real funds.

title: Exploring a Cryptocurrency Payment Flow for Credit Card Bills
description:
An early interface prototype and design review—not a live payment service

Could a cardholder pay a credit card bill with cryptocurrency? I explored that question through an early interface prototype and a design review of the steps a real service would need to support.

The project is about a specific idea: a customer chooses a card bill amount, pays through a supported digital asset using a payment provider, and the provider sends the corresponding fiat funds toward the card issuer. That journey involves more than connecting a wallet. The provider's payment status and the issuer's posting of a bill payment are separate events, and the interface needs to make that distinction clear.

What the prototype explores

The interface sketches a credit card dashboard with sample balances and a choice of bill amount. It also explores where a cryptocurrency payment option might fit into that experience. The accompanying design describes a possible six-step flow:

  1. Choose a bill amount and see the amount the issuer should receive.
  2. Request a payment quote from a provider.
  3. Review the crypto amount, exchange rate, fees, and quote expiration.
  4. Authorize payment through a supported wallet flow.
  5. Track provider payment status, including delays or exceptions.
  6. Confirm separately when the card issuer posts the payment.

That last step matters. A provider reporting that an invoice is complete does not by itself prove that a card issuer has credited the customer's account.

What the current code does—and does not do

After choosing a bill amount, the user can select an asset and network to preview how a crypto-funded payment might work. The estimate appears with a 15-minute countdown and a simulated submit action.

These features remain a UI demo. The countdown is not a rate lock, the crypto subtotal excludes network and provider fees, and the confirmation screen states that no cryptocurrency was transferred or bill paid. The prototype does not create an invoice, connect a wallet, monitor transactions, or verify that a selected asset is available to a specific merchant.

The selector uses BitPay's public Currencies API to list active assets and network variants. When available, the public Rates API supplies a reference price for the selected asset. Neither request creates an invoice or locks a price. A real BitPay invoice is needed to return the actual payment amount, expiration, and applicable network cost.

Design questions a real service would have to answer

Before a customer authorizes a payment, the product should clearly show the fiat amount to be credited, the asset and amount to send, the exchange rate, all fees, and when the quote expires. It should also explain what happens if a transfer is late, partial, overpaid, or sent on an unsupported network.

Status messages should distinguish among “payment sent,” “provider confirmed,” “fiat settlement pending,” and “card issuer posted.” If the issuer has not posted the payment, the product should not imply that the bill is paid. Support and reconciliation procedures are part of the design, not details to add after the success screen.

Security and consumer protection would need careful work too. Provider credentials belong on a server, callbacks must be validated, duplicate events should not create duplicate payments, and the product should never ask a customer for a wallet seed phrase or private key. Crypto transfers may be difficult to reverse, so the amount, network, fees, and destination need clear review before authorization.

Next steps

The next development step is a secure backend integration that creates BitPay invoices and returns the provider's payable amount, rate, fee details, and expiration. The full flow should then be tested for expired quotes, pending and confirmed transfers, partial or excess payments, and issuer posting delays.

This project is currently a design exploration and early UI prototype. It does not demonstrate a live payment service, production readiness, regulatory compliance, or that paying a credit card bill with cryptocurrency is safer or cheaper than other methods. The goal of documenting it is to make the concept and its gaps clear, then use feedback to guide a more complete prototype.
