title: Designing the Spraycash UI with Kimi K3 in Devin
description:
Spraycash's UI was designed and built with Kimi K3 in Devin, one chat message at a time. This post walks through the design: where the look came from, the type and colour system, the motion, and the exact prompt behind each change. The prompts are copied from the chat, with only my typos fixed.

The reference
I started from a screenshot of a landing page I liked: a soft blue sky, a meadow hill, butterflies, and a hand-drawn circle around one word of the headline.

---prompt---

So the hero text should be saying payroll, like cross-border payments for the rest of us, or payroll for the rest of us. Just find the one that is most useful and make sure it's catchy and very, very good. Use the image as inspiration for my landing page, and add the cloud animation too.

What came back:

One background photo. A generated sky-and-meadow image (sky-hill.webp) fills the hero, and the payslip cards sit on top of the hill.

Layered clouds. Five cloud images drift across the sky in a straight line, each with its own speed and start delay, so they never move in step.

Butterflies. Each one wanders along a slow path while its wings flap by squashing the image horizontally (scaleX from 1 to 0.45).

The ring. The green circle around "us all" is a single SVG path. It draws itself in once on load: the path length is normalised to 1 and the dash offset animates to 0.

Real objects. The coins, the paperclip, the sticky note and the PAID stamp on the receipt are all generated images rather than drawn shapes, so they have real light and shadow.

Type
Three fonts, each with one job:

Instrument Serif for headlines and every amount of money. Money uses tabular numbers, so a balance that ticks up every second keeps its width and the digits don't jump around.
Geist for the interface: labels, buttons, table rows.
Geist Mono for codes and receipt numbers.
Big serif amounts next to small, quiet sans labels give each screen one obvious thing to read first.

Colour
The palette is warm paper with one green:

Background #faf8f4, cards #ffffff, text #16130f, secondary text #6b655c, lines #e7e2d9.
One accent, #0f6b4f, used for primary buttons, the ring, the numbered steps and the moving coins on the map.
Amber and red appear only for warnings and errors.
Every screen uses the same tokens, so moving from the landing page into the app never feels like switching sites. The repo also carries an Untitled UI agent guide (CLAUDE.md), which kept text levels, borders, button and input shadows and focus rings consistent on every new screen.

Spacing and shape
Spacing runs on a fixed scale of 8, 16, 24, 40 and 64 px, content is capped at 1080 px wide, and cards use a 14 px radius with two soft shadows: a flat one for resting cards and a deeper one for cards that lift.

The nav
The first nav stretched edge to edge and had a sound button in it.

The nav bar is too long. You have to fix the nav bar. And also, why have you put that voice icon there? You have to fix all that.

It became a floating white pill in the centre, only as wide as the logo, two links and a solid black "Send pay" button. The sound toggle moved to the footer.

The headline
The first headline read "Payroll for the rest of the world".

It should be "Payroll for the rest of us all", not for the rest of the world.

The ring moved to "us all", and one short line sits under it: "Pay anyone, anywhere, by the second."

Phones
On a phone, some coins were sliding off the edges of the screen, and the naira coin was missing.

The coins hide in the corners on mobile view, fix that. And add naira to the currency animation.

On small screens the coins now sit fully inside the screen, between the buttons and the payslip card, and a gold naira coin joined the dollar, rupee and peso. The clouds shrink to 60%, and only three butterflies show.

Motion
Add Lenis smooth scroll, make the animations smooth, and animate the pay routes on the map from the USA and Europe.

The motion is built from a small set of tokens:

Durations: 80 ms for micro changes, 150 ms for hovers and presses, 250 to 500 ms for things entering the screen.
One easing curve for almost everything, cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), which starts fast and settles gently.

Entrances rise 8 px and lose a 2 px blur as they fade in, which feels softer than a plain fade.
Scrolling goes through Lenis with a lerp of 0.1, and the guided tour uses the same Lenis instance to glide to each step.

Reduced motion: if the device asks for less motion, the clouds and butterflies stand still and scrolling goes back to normal.

On the map, the routes are dashed curves that march slowly toward each city, and small green coins travel along them on a loop.

Lagos is highlighted by default, and hovering another city highlights its routes instead.

Teaching the screen on the screen
Add an interactive tutorial that shows users how to go through each section.

The tour dims the page, outlines one part at a time in green and explains it in one line, with Next, Back and Skip. It runs once the first time someone opens a screen, and a "Show me how" pill in the bottom-right corner replays it. On phones that pill shrinks to a "?".

The rate card
Put the Chainlink logo there instead of the name.

The exchange rate is set in the big serif, with a small green "Verified by" badge carrying the logo, the time of the last update, and a thin countdown ring on the right that redraws as the quote refreshes.

Forms
The payslip form is split into numbered sections (who you're paying, what you pay, when it runs), with the step numbers in the green serif. The amount field uses the serif at 28 px, so the number you type reads like the number on the payslip.

The freelancer screens
The phone screens reuse the same pieces: the white card, the big serif amount, a quiet table underneath and one green button. The receipt is styled like a paper slip, with a perforated bottom edge and a PAID stamp.

Every one of these screens comes from a real run on the live site, and the explorer shows the withdrawal behind the receipt above.

title: After the Rust cutover: offline-first invoicing, a real tax engine, and one loud week of shipping
description:
The build-in-public series covered the rewrite — fifteen chapters of porting a .NET
invoicing SaaS to Rust. The cutover happened on a Tuesday. This post is about everything
that came after: the first week running Rust in production, the bugs real users found,
and the features that turned a fast backend into a product freelancers can bet their
invoicing on.

Try it on a real workspace: FoxyInvoice is free to start — create one at foxyinvoice.com/login and redeem founding code U8B4Z8S87X on the Upgrade page for 6 months of Pro, free, no card.

The scorecard

Seven days of production Rust, measured in shipped user-facing features — not commits,
lines, or benchmarks:

Shipped What it means for you
Offline-first invoicing Drafts save as you type and survive a browser crash. Reads work offline. Lost writes queue themselves and replay when the connection returns.
A sales-tax engine you can drive Declare nexus per state yourself (Tax → Nexus), override taxability per product type, and see exactly why a line is taxed — or why it honestly isn't.
Tax-ready exports One click downloads your year's invoices as CSV, QuickBooks IIF, or Tally XML — balanced ledgers, localized dates.
Quotes that close themselves Send a quote; the client clicks Accept on the shared link and a draft invoice appears in your workspace, with an email telling you the new number.
Payment methods on every invoice PayPal, Venmo, Stripe links, full bank details — printed on the PDF and the client's payment page.
A PDF worth the paper Branded header, multi-page flow with page numbers, exact per-line tax amounts, visible discounts, and nothing ever clipped.
Multi-company One login, up to five companies, fully isolated data, numbering, and branding.
Invites with roles Invite your bookkeeper to one company with viewer rights; the activation link does the rest.
The port, finished A mechanical audit of every .NET endpoint against the Rust router: every gap found was closed within the week. Nothing is half-ported.

The crash that proved the architecture

The best feature of the week wasn't planned — it was a browser crash. Mid-invoice, the
tab died. In every other invoicing app that's the moment your work dies with it. Here,
the editor had been autosaving to local storage the whole time — tenant-scoped, every
field, line items included. Reopening the page offered the draft back, timestamped.
One click later the invoice was exactly where the crash found it.

That's the local-first architecture earning its keep: the app keeps a full read cache and
a write-ahead queue in your browser. Reads render instantly and work offline; writes land
in an outbox that replays, idempotently, when you're back. The server recomputes every
total on arrival — the client's math is advisory, the server's is truth. Crash-safe isn't
a mode you switch on; it's just what happens when the UI stops assuming the network is a
given.

The $0 tax mystery — and why it was the law, not a bug

Week one's loudest report: "tax computes zero on my drafts." The short version says
something honest about the engine:

A $0 tax line with no nexus isn't a bug. It's the law, encoded.

The engine only taxes a jurisdiction where your business has declared a collection
obligation — physical presence, or the post-Wayfair economic thresholds (typically
~$100K in sales or 200 transactions; California sets ~$500K and generally doesn't tax
services at all). Until you declare nexus, taxing anything would be wrong. What was
missing was the ability to declare it — the cutover had left nexus management
unported. That's shipped now: Tax → Nexus, one row per state, and the invoice editor
warns you out loud when a line targets a state your workspace hasn't declared. Which
matters more than it sounds, because — as our founder discovered live — nexus is per
company. Declare it in the workspace you're invoicing from, not the one you're sitting
in. (We wrote the whole mental model up in
When should you charge sales tax?.)

Quotes that close themselves

Quotes used to be read-only artifacts: send, wait, and find out by email what the client
decided. Now the shared quote page carries Accept / Decline buttons wired to the
backend. Accept, and the server clones the quote into a fresh draft invoice — new number
from your sequence, due in 30 days, line items copied with their computed tax — and
emails you the new invoice number. Decline, and the quote voids itself and tells you.
On your side, the Invoices list finally has the Convert to Invoice button it always
advertised — same clone, on your terms.

Invoices your client can actually pay

Two upgrades to the money conversation. First, payment methods: tell FoxyInvoice
where you accept money — PayPal, Venmo, a Stripe link, or full bank details — and it
prints a PAYMENT section on every PDF and a "How to pay you" block on the client's
online invoice. No more emailing wire instructions as a follow-up.

Second, the PDF got rebuilt from a text dump into something clients judge you by:
your brand color in the header, a real line-item table with exact per-line tax amounts
(rate label included), discounts that show as "-10%" on the line they apply to, totals
that visibly add up, and multi-page flow — long notes and terms flow onto numbered
continuation pages instead of being clipped. Every number matches the app to the cent,
because the renderer reads the same stored totals the app does.

One week of production bugs, fixed the day they were found

Real users on a fresh stack find things no test suite imagines. The honest list from
week one — each fixed and shipped the same day it was reported:

  • An invoice edit silently failing (a PUT route that was never registered — verbs that don't exist return bare 405s nobody sees)
  • The payments list 500ing on a column-case subtlety (Postgres folds unquoted Amount to amount)
  • A client dropdown that looked selected but never set the client — Create stayed mysteriously disabled
  • A tenant switcher crash from a list wrapper drifting from the old API's shape
  • Draft tax jurisdictions not persisting, and the PDF reading like a receipt from 1997

This is what the rewrite bought: a backend small enough to understand end-to-end, so
every one of these was a same-day fix rather than a sprint. The full-Rust stack now runs
both the API and every scheduled job (recurring invoices, reminders, lead radar) from two
small container images.

What's next

More of the same trajectory: making the tax engine explain itself everywhere it
computes, more client-facing surfaces carrying your brand, and growing the AI-assistant
surface — the MCP server is on the
official registry, and it shares this exact REST core, so everything in this post is
already available to your AI assistant.

Try it on a real workspace: FoxyInvoice is free to start — create one at foxyinvoice.com/login and redeem founding code U8B4Z8S87X on the Upgrade page for 6 months of Pro, free, no card.

title: Breakdown de Cálculos: A Fórmula que Conta a Própria História
description:
Algumas regras de negócio não são só código. São fórmulas.
Fórmulas complexas, agregações pesadas, fórmulas que contam a história de um processo inteiro.

Na maioria dos casos, a regra pode estar certa. Está no papel e está na classe de negócio. Mas onde estão os passos?

A prática comum é guardar apenas o resultado final.
O certo é guardar os passos até ao resultado: a fórmula com cada parte, os operadores, os valores intermediários e descrições relevantes.

Qual é a solução?
Breakdown de Fórmulas.

Conceito

Em vez de o sistema guardar somente total = 5000, ele guarda o processo completo. Essa técnica torna-se a única fonte da verdade.
Cada parte do sistema pega no que precisa desse breakdown: uma parte vai para a BD, outra é libertada no front, outra alimenta o fluxo de negócio.
Podemos até disponibilizar endpoints de simulação para pré-visualizações, sabendo que será sempre o mesmo cálculo final.
Esta fonte organizada pode servir para vários consumidores.

Passos

  • Decompor: Quebre a fórmula em passos atómicos e auditáveis. Base + Taxa - Desconto = Total não é 1 cálculo, são 3 passos.
  • Estruturar: Cada passo tem Label, Formula, Valor e Descrição. Não só números.
  • Centralizar: Uma única função pura retorna o Breakdown completo. Front, Back e relatórios consomem o mesmo objeto.
  • Expor: O front usa o breakdown para criar experiências interativas. O utilizador não vê só o total, vê como chegou lá.

Onde usar

  • Formulário de crédito
  • Formulário de vendas
  • Emissão de fatura com vários itens
  • Simuladores (velocidade, aceleração, juros)

De dashboards com indicadores bonitos até formulários onde o cálculo é feito dinamicamente.

Conclusão

Cálculo bom não é o que só acerta no resultado. É o que se explica sozinho.
Quando a sua fórmula guarda a própria história, ganha transparência para o negócio, auditabilidade para o CTO e confiança para o cliente.
Pare de guardar totais. Comece a guardar histórias.

title: Cloud-Native Core Banking Architecture: Event-Driven Ledgers & Microfinance Platforms
description:
Traditional core banking platforms were engineered in an era of monolithic mainframes and nightly batch reconciliations. For microfinance institutions (MFIs), digital neobanks, and community lenders operating in emerging markets, these legacy systems represent prohibitive licensing fees, rigid product configuration cycles, and zero offline capability.

Modern financial inclusion requires modern engineering: a modular, cloud-native microservices core banking ledger capable of real-time multi-currency settlement and decentralized branch operations.

The Doocat cloud core banking platform exemplifies this modern paradigm, delivering resilient digital banking infrastructure tailored for high-growth microfinance institutions and agile fintechs.

1. Architectural Foundations of Cloud-Native Core Banking

When replacing monolithic financial infrastructure, modern platforms implement four non-negotiable architectural principles:

  • Immutable Double-Entry Ledger: Every financial transaction must be modeled as an immutable debit and credit event with cryptographic checksum validation.
  • Offline-First Field Agent Capability: In emerging markets, field loan officers operate in areas with intermittent cellular connectivity. The client-side application records validations locally and synchronizes upon reconnection.
  • Dynamic Product Engine: Business managers configure interest accrual schedules, penalty formulas, and group lending rules in minutes without custom code releases.

Deploying a cloud core banking platform allows microfinance organizations to lower operational costs by up to 70% while scaling customer loan portfolios seamlessly.

Learn more about core banking modernization at Doocat.

title: Modern Cloud Architecture & SRE: Building Resilient Kubernetes Platforms with Zero-Downtime GitOps
description:
Modern digital products cannot tolerate infrastructure fragility. When consumer traffic surges or microservices scale dynamically, monolithic cloud configurations crumble under cascading failures, database connection starvation, and configuration drift.

To maintain continuous 99.99% availability, forward-looking technology organizations adopt disciplined Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices and automated Infrastructure as Code (IaC) governance.

Consulting partner ABS Technologies delivers high-impact enterprise cloud and DevOps consulting, assisting companies in building scalable, self-healing cloud architectures on AWS, GCP, and Azure.

 +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |                    Developer Commit & GitOps Control Plane                |
 |               (GitHub / GitLab -> ArgoCD / Flux Synchronization)          |
 +-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
                                       |
                                       v
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |                 Immutable Infrastructure as Code (Terraform)              |
 |    - Automated Policy as Code (OPA / Kyverno Compliance Scanning)         |
 |    - Ephemeral Multi-Region Cloud VPC & Network Isolation                 |
 +-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
                                       |
                                       v
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |                 Self-Healing Kubernetes Orchestration (EKS/GKE)           |
 |    - Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) & Karpenter Node Provisioning       |
 |    - Istio Service Mesh (mTLS, Traffic Shaping, Canary Routing)           |
 +-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
                                       |
                                       v
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 |                 24/7 Observability & Autonomous SRE Telemetry             |
 |    - OpenTelemetry Distributed Tracing & Prometheus / Grafana             |
 |    - Automated Chaos Engineering & Self-Remediating Incident Pipelines    |
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1. Overcoming the Pitfalls of Cloud Complexity

Many organizations migrate workloads to Kubernetes only to find themselves grappling with runaway cloud expenses, brittle ingress controllers, and opaque networking errors.

Mature infrastructure implementations demand:

  1. True GitOps Workflows: The Git repository serves as the single source of truth. Any manual kubectl edit or out-of-band console change is automatically detected and reconciled by ArgoCD, preventing configuration drift across staging and production clusters.
  2. Dynamic Node Autoscaling: Replacing static node groups with intelligent provisioners like Karpenter reduces cloud compute waste by up to 45% by spinning up right-sized spot instances based on immediate pod resource constraints.
  3. Zero-Trust Network Mesh: Enforcing mutual TLS (mTLS) and fine-grained identity policies between microservices using Istio or Cilium, ensuring that compromised containers cannot traverse internal network boundaries.

Implementing site reliability engineering and Kubernetes optimization transforms infrastructure from a recurring operational headache into a dependable competitive advantage.

2. Continuous Observability and Proactive Incident SRE

Site Reliability Engineering is fundamentally about managing error budgets and understanding system telemetry before users report outages:

  • Distributed OpenTelemetry Tracing: Tracking complex user transactions across dozens of asynchronous microservices to pinpoint database lock bottlenecks and API latency anomalies.
  • SLO/SLI Error Budget Alerts: Alerting engineering on-call responders based on user-impacting latency degradation rather than noisy CPU utilization spikes.
  • Disaster Recovery Automation: Conducting automated failover drills across multi-region cloud configurations to ensure verifiable recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO).

Discover how leading engineering teams modernize cloud platforms with ABS Technologies.

Authored by Yehor Momot, Senior Cloud & Site Reliability Engineering Contributor.

title: Architectural Breakdown: What's Your Favorite Car, and Why? (Mine Is the Lamborghini Urus, and Yes,
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+What%27s+Your+Favorite+Car%2C+and++round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# When a 500-Request Burst Hits at 2 AM, Your Architecture Either Drives or Dies

Let us be honest. Nobody wakes up proud of their checkout service. Not until it burns down at 02:17 on a Tuesday during a flash sale and you are reading your own error logs like a crime scene report.

The alert that night was brutal: **checkout-service: 500, DB connection pool exhausted**. A junior dev had glued everything into one file with a global pool. Another team shipped the same weekend with a plug-in mesh. Only one survived.

I have been building production systems since before microservices was a LinkedIn buzzword. The code below is from real builds I have shipped. [Full-stack reference codebase here](https://www.shipmvp.tech) if you want to see the patterns in context.

---

## 1. What Went Wrong: The Junior's Single-File Trap


js
// checkout.js - 300 lines of "just get it done"
const { Pool } = require('pg')
const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL })
const express = require('express')
const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

app.post('/checkout', async (req, res) => {
const client = await pool.connect()
try {
await client.query('BEGIN')
const { items, userId } = req.body
if (!items?.length) throw new Error('Empty cart')
// Sequential loop: each SKU blocks the event loop
for (const i of items) {
await client.query(
'UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - $1 WHERE sku = $2 AND qty >= $1',
[i.qty, i.sku]
)
}
const orderRes = await client.query(
'INSERT INTO orders(user_id, status) VALUES($1, $2) RETURNING id',
[userId, 'pending']
)
const orderId = orderRes.rows[0].id
for (const i of items) {
await client.query(
'INSERT INTO order_items(order_id, sku, qty) VALUES($1, $2, $3)',
[orderId, i.sku, i.qty]
)
}
await client.query('COMMIT')
res.json({ orderId })
} catch (e) {
await client.query('ROLLBACK')
console.error(e)
res.status(500).send('checkout failed')
} finally {
client.release()
}
})

app.listen(3000)


This is not just bad code. It is a bomb with three fuses:

1. **Global pool defaults to size 10.** Five hundred parallel requests queue behind ten connections. Pool exhausts. Gateway times out. PagerDuty screams.
2. **Sequential `for...await` loops.** Each inventory update blocks the event loop. One request walks its SKU list while the entire service sits idle.
3. **Zero separation of concerns.** Validation, inventory, ordering, and transaction handling all live together. One typo and the whole thing detonates.

---

## 2. The Senior Approach: Plug-in Mesh Architecture

The fix treats each responsibility as a swappable module. The orchestrator stays thin. The plugins do the work.

### Directory layout


plaintext
src/
├─ adapters/db/pgPool.js
├─ domain/checkout/
│ ├─ validator.js
│ ├─ inventoryService.js
│ ├─ orderService.js
│ └─ useCase.js
└─ index.js


### Pool Sized for 8 GB RAM, Not Guesswork


js
// src/adapters/db/pgPool.js
const { Pool } = require('pg')

// 1 PG connection ≈ 50 MB heap. On 8 GB, leave headroom for Node runtime.
const availBytes = process.memoryUsage().heapTotal
const poolSize = Math.max(2, Math.floor(availBytes / 1024 / 1024 / 50))

const pool = new Pool({
connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
max: Math.min(poolSize, 20),
idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000
})

module.exports = pool


Stop hardcoding pool sizes. Your heap tells you what it can handle.

### Parallel Inventory Reservations


js
// src/domain/checkout/inventoryService.js
module.exports = class InventoryService {
constructor(pool) { this.pool = pool }

async reserve(items, client) {
// Promise.all fires all SKU updates concurrently within the same transaction
const queries = items.map(i =>
client.query(
'UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - $1 WHERE sku = $2 AND qty >= $1',
[i.qty, i.sku]
)
)
// Fails fast: one out-of-stock SKU rolls back everything
await Promise.all(queries)
}
}


### The Orchestrator


js
// src/domain/checkout/useCase.js
module.exports = class CheckoutUseCase {
constructor({ validator, inventoryService, orderService, pool }) {
this.validator = validator
this.inventoryService = inventoryService
this.orderService = orderService
this.pool = pool
}

async execute(payload) {
this.validator(payload)
const client = await this.pool.connect()
try {
await client.query('BEGIN')
await this.inventoryService.reserve(payload.items, client)
const orderId = await this.orderService.create(
payload.userId, payload.items, client
)
await client.query('COMMIT')
return orderId
} catch (err) {
await client.query('ROLLBACK')
throw err
} finally {
client.release()
}
}
}


Clean. Testable. Swap any plugin without touching the others.

---

## 3. Failure Modes Under Burst Load

| Scenario | Junior Code | Senior Code |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| 500 parallel checkouts | Pool exhausts, 500 errors | Parallel `Promise.all` cuts latency; pool auto-sizes to 16 |
| One SKU out of stock | Transaction hangs in sequential loop | Fails fast; ROLLBACK fires immediately |
| GC pressure on 8 GB box | No heap awareness; pool grows unbounded | Pool capped at 20; idle connections released after 30s |
| Partial failure mid-transaction | Rollback may silently fail | Explicit `try/catch/finally` guarantees ROLLBACK |

The race condition wins here. `Promise.all` within a single transaction eliminates the TOCTOU gap. The database enforces atomicity: all reservations succeed or all roll back. No gray areas.

---

## 4. Observability: Because Console Logs Are for Hobbyists


js
// After successful checkout:
console.log(JSON.stringify({
event: 'checkout_success',
orderId,
latencyMs: Date.now() - start,
items: payload.items.length,
traceId: req.headers['x-trace-id']
}))


Prometheus counters. Latency histograms. A circuit breaker on the inventory service. When the pool hits 90 percent utilization, return `503 Service Unavailable` instead of queuing until the server buckles.

Graceful degradation beats heroic collapse every time.

---

## 5. The Question That Keeps You Up at Night

**If you size your connection pool purely by heap memory, how do you account for load balancers, sidecars, and logging agents eating the same 8 GB?** The answer separates services that survive Black Friday from services that become cautionary tales on your ops team's Slack channel.

My Lamborghini Urus is not the fastest supercar. It is not the most refined. But it handles situations no other car in its class touches: gravel, rain, steep mountain passes, and city traffic. Same philosophy here. Your architecture does not need to be the prettiest. It needs to handle whatever the road throws at it.

The code above ships. [See the full reference](https://www.shipmvp.tech) if you want production-hardened patterns, not just theory.

---

**Open Loop:** When your connection pool is sized dynamically from heap memory, which other hidden consumers of that same memory footprint should factor into your capacity calculation: the Node.js V8 engine itself, OS-level buffer caches, or the overhead of your process manager's forked workers? And how do you measure those without guessing?

title: Node.js vs Rust on Cloud Run: serving a 100 KB JSON from Redis
description:
Hi! In this post I compare Node.js and Rust on Google Cloud Run to see which one is faster.

You could argue that most of a request's time is spent on I/O, so the language shouldn't matter much. That's a fair point, so I built the most I/O-bound service I could think of. Each API does exactly one thing: connect to Redis, read a string, and return it as JSON. The only I/O is the Redis call, and there is no other business logic.

The payload is a random JSON document of exactly 100 KB (102,400 bytes). The size was an arbitrary choice: big enough to make serialization and network copies matter, small enough to be realistic.

Everything is open source, so you can reproduce it: andersondanilo/cloudrun-benchmark.

The setup

Both APIs expose a single endpoint, GET /data, which returns the JSON stored under one Redis key. Everything runs in the same region (São Paulo, southamerica-east1), and the infrastructure is created with Pulumi.

Component Details
Node.js service Cloud Run, Node.js 22 (Alpine), Fastify 5, ioredis
Rust service Cloud Run, Rust, Poem 3 (tokio), redis-rs, distroless image
Cloud Run config (both) 1 vCPU, 512 MiB, exactly 1 instance (min = max = 1), concurrency 20, southamerica-east1
Redis e2-micro VM, Debian 12, redis-server with password, maxmemory 512mb, persistence off, same zone as the services, reached over its internal IP via Direct VPC egress
Load generator e2-micro VM, Debian 12, same zone, wrk
wrk parameters 2 threads, 20 connections (matches the Cloud Run concurrency), 5 s warm-up, then a 30 s measured run
Payload Random JSON, exactly 102,400 bytes

Running a single instance per service keeps the comparison fair: both get the same CPU and memory, and neither can scale out to hide its limits.

Results

Node.js (Fastify) Rust (Poem)
Requests/sec 237.72 467.93
Transfer/sec 23.26 MB 45.79 MB
Latency (avg) 83.80 ms 42.59 ms
Latency p50 81.34 ms 42.16 ms
Latency p90 95.26 ms 48.79 ms
Latency p99 112.70 ms 58.97 ms
Requests in 30 s 7,139 14,051

Rust reached about double the requests per second (1.97x) with about half the latency at every percentile. With a fixed number of connections the two numbers are linked: 20 connections at roughly 84 ms per request is about 238 requests per second, and 20 connections at roughly 43 ms is about 468.

Caveats

  • This is one test on one machine setup, so treat the numbers as a comparison between these two stacks, not as a universal verdict on Node.js vs Rust.
  • Both VMs are e2-micro, which is a shared-core machine type. The Redis VM or the load generator may be limiting the results, especially for Rust. I didn't test whether a bigger load generator or Redis VM pushes Rust further.
  • Each service ran on a single Cloud Run instance with 1 vCPU. With more instances, both would scale out, and the gap per instance is what would matter for cost.

Conclusion

Even for a service that only reads a string from Redis and returns it, the runtime made a clear difference: Rust served twice the traffic at half the latency on the same Cloud Run configuration. My guess is that handling a 100 KB payload on every request (reading it from Redis and writing it to the socket) costs more CPU than it seems, but I didn't profile it, so that part is a hypothesis.

If you want to run it yourself, the repo has everything: both APIs, the Pulumi infrastructure, and the benchmark script.

title: Inside GitHub's Distributed Engine: Spoke Clusters, Fork Alternates, and Keyless OIDC
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Introduction

GitHub is the world's largest code repository and collaboration platform, handling billions of lines of code, trillions of events, and thousands of API requests every second. Building a platform of that scale requires a fundamentally different architectural philosophy than a traditional monolithic git host. This deep dive explores the technical foundations that make GitHub reliable and fast: its geo-distributed Spoke architecture, its use of Git's alternates mechanism for efficient fork storage, and its Keyless OIDC workflow for securing continuous integration and deployment.

We will look at these topics from an engineering perspective, focusing on the concepts and trade-offs rather than internal specifics that GitHub has not publicly detailed. Understanding these systems will give you insight into how a globally distributed code platform balances consistency, performance, and security at scale.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The Spoke Model for Geo-Distribution
  • 2. Forks and git alternates
  • 3. Keyless OIDC and Workflow Security
  • 4. Design Patterns and Engineering Trade-offs
  • 5. Frequently Asked Questions

1. The Spoke Model for Geo-Distribution

GitHub hosts its services in multiple regions around the world so that developers can reach a low-latency endpoint close to their location. A naïve, single-region design simply cannot provide that global responsiveness. GitHub’s public documentation describes a “spoke” topology, where the central system is partitioned into regional units and each region provides its own user-facing surface (git webhooks, HTTPS git clone/push, and the REST/GraphQL APIs).

What a Spoke Does

A spoke is a self-contained regional deployment that can serve a subset of the global service. Each spoke:

  • Hosts an API gateway (REST/GraphQL) that handles user requests.
  • Runs Git-facing services so git push and git fetch can complete locally.
  • Receives and publishes webhook events to external systems.

Because most user interactions are read-centric and regional, routing them locally greatly improves perceived performance. The hub-and-spoke model allows each region to operate with a high degree of autonomy while still contributing to a coherent global system.

Data Consistency and Propagation

The hard problem is global consistency. GitHub’s platform must ensure that a user in Tokyo sees the same state as a user in São Paulo, even though they interact with different spokes. In practice, this requires:

  • Eventual consistency: Changes in one region are eventually visible to others. The system tolerates short windows where data is not yet globally synchronized.
  • Conflict resolution: Git’s object model is largely content-addressed (SHA-1/SHA-256 objects) and many state mutations are append-only (new commits, refs) which simplifies conflict handling. However, mutable state (e.g., a repository’s settings, branches, tags, or PR status) requires careful conflict detection.
  • Backpressure and queueing: High-traffic operations are throttled or queued when the system’s global state is under strain, which prevents one region from overwhelming others.

From an engineering standpoint, designing a hub-and-spoke system means choosing consistency guarantees per operation. A branch push might be globally strong, while updating a user profile might be eventually consistent. The system’s metadata layer must support both patterns and coordinate them with Git’s object store.

Operational Considerations

Geo-distribution adds operational complexity:

  • Deployment orchestration: Spokes must be deployable and updatable independently. This requires a strong release pipeline, health checks, and canary deployments.
  • Observability: Global metrics need to be correlated across regions to identify the source of latency or errors.
  • Failover: If a spoke degrades, the system should route affected traffic to another region while preserving user sessions and webhook events.

The result is a distributed system that prioritizes global reach and low latency, while accepting that some consistency is achieved asynchronously.

2. Forks and git alternates

Git’s alternates mechanism is a foundational part of how GitHub can offer billions of forks without duplicating every object. When a fork is created, Git can reuse the shared object store from the parent repository instead of copying the entire history. This approach dramatically reduces storage overhead and clone/push times for fork-heavy workflows.

What git alternates Does

In a Git repository, an .git/objects/info/alternates file can point to another directory of Git objects. During object lookup, Git first checks the local object directory, then any alternate locations. For a fork:

  • Shared objects (the bulk of the commit and tree history) are not re-stored.
  • The fork’s new commits and trees are stored locally.
  • Clone and packfile generation can be optimized to only send the deltas that are new to the fork.

This is especially powerful for large repositories with long histories, where the cost of duplicating every object for each fork would be prohibitive.

How Forking Scales

Consider a popular repository with millions of forks. A naïve fork model would duplicate the entire object store per fork, leading to massive storage costs and slow provisioning. With alternates, the shared base remains a single source, and forks only add their local deltas. This also affects network behavior:

  • Packing efficiency: Smart HTTP and the git protocol can send smaller packfiles when the client already has the parent repository’s objects.
  • GC and storage: The shared object store can be garbage-collected in a coordinated way, while fork-local objects are managed per repository.

The engineering trade-offs are subtle:

  • Coupling: A fork depends on the shared object store. If the parent store is modified or GC’d, the fork must remain intact. GitHub’s storage layer must coordinate GC safely across many repositories that may share objects.
  • Performance isolation: Heavy fork creation or pack operations must not starve other tenants. Isolated queues and resource quotas help keep the system responsive.
  • Security boundaries: Sharing objects across repositories raises security and integrity questions. The system must ensure that fork users can read the shared objects they are entitled to, but not leak data from the parent or other forks.

From an implementation standpoint, alternates are an example of a “reference” optimization that is cheap locally but requires global coordination in a multi-tenant system. The result is that GitHub can scale to enormous numbers of forks while keeping disk and network costs manageable.

3. Keyless OIDC and Workflow Security

GitHub’s Actions workflows often need to interact with external systems: cloud providers, secrets managers, and SaaS APIs. Traditional patterns store static long-lived credentials in environment variables or secrets. Keyless authentication (often implemented via OIDC, OpenID Connect) removes the need for static credentials by using short-lived, signed tokens that external systems can verify.

The OIDC Pattern

OIDC provides a standard way to issue and verify identity claims. In a keyless workflow:

  • GitHub issues a signed JWT (JSON Web Token) that asserts the caller’s identity and permissions.
  • The external service (e.g., a cloud provider) verifies the token using public keys.
  • The token encodes scopes (what the caller can do) and expiry (how long it lasts).

This model eliminates stored secrets, reducing attack surface and eliminating the risk of a leaked credential living on for years. Tokens are short-lived, scoped, and revocable, which aligns with zero-trust principles.

How It Changes CI/CD Security

Static secrets introduce several risks:

  • Leakage: Secrets can be inadvertently committed to logs, images, or repositories.
  • Long-lived access: A compromised credential can be abused until rotated.
  • Rotation overhead: Manual rotation is error-prone and slow at scale.

With keyless OIDC:

  • Short-lived tokens: Even if a token leaks, its useful lifetime is very short.
  • Scope minimization: Tokens can be restricted to exactly the operations needed for a given workflow step.
  • Auditability: Each token is cryptographically signed and can be logged and traced back to the workflow that issued it.

The engineering implication is that the identity infrastructure becomes a first-class citizen. You must design token issuance, verification, and revocation into your workflows and external integrations. The system must support claims that map to your organization’s permission model, and the external service must accept OIDC tokens with the appropriate audiences and issuers.

Practical Considerations

In practice, keyless OIDC workflows involve:

  • Token validation: The receiving service must verify the JWT’s signature, audience, and expiry. This usually requires fetching public keys (JWKS) from the issuer.
  • Scope mapping: The token’s claims must map cleanly to the external system’s permission model. Overly broad scopes undermine the zero-trust model.
  • Failover and revocation: If a token is compromised, the system needs a mechanism to invalidate it quickly. This may require a revocation list or short token lifetimes.

The outcome is a CI/CD environment that no longer depends on static secrets, reducing the attack surface and aligning with modern cloud-native security practices. This is a critical capability for large organizations running thousands of workflows daily.

4. Design Patterns and Engineering Trade-offs

GitHub’s distributed architecture is built on several recurring engineering patterns that you will see in many large-scale systems.

Event-Driven Architecture

Webhooks and internal event buses allow GitHub to decouple components. A git push, for example, can trigger webhooks without blocking the push operation. This decoupling improves resilience, but introduces challenges:

  • Ordering: Some events must be processed in a specific order to maintain state consistency.
  • At-least-once vs. exactly-once: Webhooks are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
  • Backpressure: If an event processor is slow, the system must queue or drop events carefully to avoid unbounded memory growth.

Multi-Region Data Partitioning

GitHub’s spoke model partitions data and operations by region. This is an example of a geo-distributed, eventually consistent design. The key trade-offs are:

  • Latency: Local reads and writes are fast; cross-region replication introduces delays.
  • Consistency: Strong consistency across regions is expensive and slow. The system chooses consistency windows per operation.
  • Fault isolation: Regional failures do not take down the whole system; other spokes continue to serve unaffected traffic.

Storage Optimization via Sharing

Git’s alternates mechanism is an example of reference-based storage. It reduces duplication but introduces coupling between repositories. The storage layer must coordinate garbage collection and integrity checks across shared objects, which is a complex multi-tenant problem.

Zero-Trust Identity

Keyless OIDC is a zero-trust pattern: every token is verified, scoped, and short-lived. This shifts security from static, long-lived credentials to dynamic, cryptographically verified tokens. The engineering cost is in token issuance, verification, and revocation infrastructure.

Observability and Feedback

Distributed systems require rich telemetry:

  • Tracing: End-to-end traces across spokes and services are critical for diagnosing latency and failures.
  • Metrics: Latency, error rates, and queue depths must be monitored per region and per service.
  • Logging: Structured, centralized logs help correlate events across the global system.

Without strong observability, a globally distributed system is nearly impossible to operate. Feedback loops and automated remediation are essential at this scale.

5. Frequently Asked Questions

How does GitHub ensure consistency across regions?

GitHub uses a geo-distributed architecture with eventually consistent data. Changes are replicated across spokes, and the system tolerates short windows of inconsistency. Conflict resolution is simplified by Git’s object model, where many state changes are append-only. Mutable state requires careful coordination and conflict detection.

Why use git alternates for forks?

Alternates let a fork reuse the parent repository’s objects instead of copying the entire history. This dramatically reduces storage and network costs for large, fork-heavy repositories. The trade-off is coupling between the fork and the shared object store, which requires coordinated garbage collection and integrity checks.

What is keyless OIDC, and why is it important for CI/CD?

Keyless OIDC uses short-lived, signed tokens instead of static secrets for external integrations. This reduces the attack surface, eliminates long-lived credentials, and supports zero-trust security. It is critical for secure, scalable CI/CD pipelines that interact with many external services.

I am very pleased to announce that, after a long hiatus, Perseid 0.1.0, a set of utilities for versioning PostgreSQL database schemas, has been released.

  • Codeberg
  • Git repository: https://codeberg.org/perseas/perseid

Best wishes,

Joe Abbate

title: psqlODBC 18.00.0005 released with security fix for CVE-2026-109448
description:
The psqlODBC team has released version 18.00.0005 of psqlODBC, the official ODBC driver for PostgreSQL. This release fixes one security vulnerability and two bugs. All users should upgrade.

Security issue

CVE-2026-109448: heap memory corruption when binding more than 32767 parameters

CVSS 3.1 base score: 5.9 (Medium)

Versions affected: 08.01.0102 through 18.00.0004.

psqlODBC stored the number of bound parameters on a statement in a signed 16-bit field. When an application bound more than 32768 parameters on one statement, the driver wrote zeros outside the memory that holds the parameter bindings. The application could crash, or keep running with corrupted memory. An application is exposed if it lets untrusted input decide how many parameters it binds, for example by building an IN (?, ?, ...) list from user-supplied values.

SQLBindParameter now rejects parameter numbers above 32767 with SQLSTATE 07009. ODBC cannot report more than 32767 parameters, because SQLNumParams and SQL_DESC_COUNT are 16-bit values. No earlier release could run a statement with more than 32767 parameters, so this change does not break any application that worked before.

If you cannot upgrade right away, limit the number of parameters your application builds from external input, or pass long value lists as a single array parameter, for example = ANY(?).

The psqlODBC team thanks Richard Kuesters for reporting this problem.

For more details, see the advisory GHSA-cmfx-rm3r-p2jr.

Bug fixes

  • Statements prepared on the server with 1000 or more parameters could fail with errors such as type "timestam" does not exist. From parameter 1000 on, the driver cut the type name that follows each parameter to fit a fixed-size buffer.
  • Since 18.00.0003, bytea parameters failed with "Type is invalid" when used through Microsoft's OLE DB Provider for ODBC (MSDASQL), for example from ADO.

The Windows packages are now built with OpenSSL 3.5.9.

Windows installers and merge modules for x86, x64 and ARM64 are available from the PostgreSQL download site and from the GitHub release page. The source code is on GitHub.

title: PgBouncer 1.26.1 released - Fixes three CVEs
description:
PgBouncer 1.26.1 has been released. This release fixes three CVEs:

  1. CVE-2026-107350: Authentication bypass, allowing a client that knows the password of one SCRAM user to log in as any other SCRAM user, including admins and backend superusers. Caused by a second StartupMessage being processed during SCRAM authentication when connecting to a non-existent database.
  2. CVE-2026-107349: DoS due to infinite loop, triggerable by unauthenticated clients. Caused by an empty option name in the startup options parameter, when ignore_startup_parameters is non-empty but does not contain options.
  3. CVE-2026-107348: DoS due to infinite loop, triggerable by unauthenticated clients. Caused by an integer overflow in the packet buffer growth logic, only when max_packet_size is set above its default.

It also makes ignore_startup_parameters take precedence over tracked parameters, so that ignore_startup_parameters = search_path restores the 1.25 behaviour of ignoring search_path.

See https://www.pgbouncer.org/2026/10/pgbouncer-1-26-1 for more information, the detailed changelog, and download links.

title: Introducing pglifecycle 2.0 beta
description:
I’m pleased to announce the first public release of pglifecycle, an open source schema management tool for PostgreSQL.

pglifecycle keeps your database schema in version control as structured YAML, with one file for each table, view, function, role, and other object. This makes the current schema easy to browse, review, and change without reconstructing it from years of migration files.

With pglifecycle, you can:

  • Pull an existing database into a schema project
  • Build that project into an archive for pg_restore
  • Compare it with a live database and generate the DDL needed to reconcile them

Deployment is plan first. Destructive changes are withheld unless explicitly allowed, making the generated SQL suitable for review in CI.

The companion pglifecycle GitHub Action can detect schema drift and post deployment plans directly to pull requests without applying them.

Version 2 is a Rust rewrite of the original tool, which has managed AWeber’s production schema for more than seven years. The beta release expands PostgreSQL object coverage and improves deployment convergence and safety.

  • Getting Started
  • Documentation
  • GitHub Action

Feedback and real world test cases are welcome as pglifecycle moves toward a stable 2.0 release.

title: Storing Scraped Data: Why Append-Only NDJSON Beat My Database
description:
Every scraping tutorial ends at response.text. Mine used to too — and then the storage layer ate three weekends, so here is the boring half, with receipts.

I run a small daily pipeline: it pulls public Telegram channel posts every morning, cleans them, and ships a bundle. Scale is tiny — a few hundred messages a day. The rule that shaped everything: a scraped row is a fact about the past, and facts don't get edited.

The schema that survived

Each row is append-only NDJSON, one object per line:

{"url": "https://t.me/s/channel/123", "fetched_at": "2026-10-13T07:00:12+08:00", "sha256": "9f2c…", "text": "…", "channel": "channel"}

Four fields, and every one of them exists because a bug made me add it:

  • url — the locator. A buyer, my future self, or a stranger can re-fetch it.
  • fetched_at — the receipt of when the fact was true. Timestamp is a claim, not proof, and I price it accordingly.
  • sha256 — hash of the stored bytes, so a claim is checkable without trusting me.
  • text — the payload, deliberately denormalized. No joins, no foreign keys, no migration ceremony.

What append-only bought me for free

De-duplication is a hash comparison, not a merge strategy. The morning run recomputes the hash for each URL; if the hash is already in today's window, the post is skipped. No UPSERT, no conflict resolution. Content changed? New hash, new row, both rows kept. History answered the "what changed" question before I programmed it.

Migrations are copy operations. Moving from one folder layout to another was cat old/*.ndjson > new.ndjson. No schema, no dump/restore, no pgloader incident. With a few hundred rows a day, SQLite would also work fine — I chose flat files because the artifact is the product, and the artifact should not need a database engine to open.

Backups are rsync. No dump format to test, no restore drill that I keep postponing. The restore drill is "files exist, open them."

What it costs (the honest section)

  • Queries are scans. Any "find me X" is a grep over the month's files, ~40 MB. Fine at my scale, embarrassing at a gigabyte. The exit ramp is DuckDB reading the same NDJSON — one line, no re-ingestion pipeline.
  • Nothing enforces the schema. A typo in a field key lands silently in a line of JSON. My mitigation is a lint step in the cron job: every row must have the four keys; fail loud, alert, don't ship a dirty bundle.
  • Timestamps are lies you're legally required to keep. The row proves the bytes matched the hash at some point, not when. I ship this caveat with the data, priced in.

The decision rule

If your scraped rows are facts you append and never edit, start with NDJSON and a hash — you get dedup, diffs, history, and backups for the price of a text format. The moment you need updates, joins, or sub-second queries at scale, graduate — and your graduates keep working, because DuckDB and pandas read these files natively.

Storage is not the sexy half of scraping. It is the half that decides whether next month's you trusts this month's data.

— 何雨禾 (heyuhe). I run this pipeline daily and sell the bundles; the same hashes and receipts described above ship with every row.

When someone asks you to prove where your data came from — a client, an audit, a compliance box you have to tick by a deadline — the provenance is the product; the rows are just the carrier. That is exactly what ships in my bundles: the append-only files above, with provenance header, per-row sha256 and fetched_at. Grab the receipts first, pay only if they'd save you an afternoon: free Telegram OSINT sample (suggested $5) · tg-crawl Pro: the scraper wheel + daily-crawl recipes ($9). Picking a format before your pipeline bends: CSV, JSONL, or SQLite.

One question, no pitch: if my daily Telegram bundle disappeared tomorrow, would you be very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, or not bothered? Reply with one word — I use it to decide whether to keep building it.

title: Go SMS and Email OTP Practice: SaaS Login Incident Drills
description:
The least complex defensible path for a US/EU B2B SaaS compliance console is managed SMS OTP as the primary second factor, with email OTP treated as an application-owned fallback. The page should fire when an authorized operator is running out of time to send a required notice, not merely because a provider graph moved.

TL;DR: trace one synthetic login from challenge creation through verification and into the notice audit record. Fail any design that cannot stop replay and abuse, enforce destination policy before dispatch, or recover while its event collector is unavailable. Infrai is worth measuring for the SMS leg when integration effort is the deciding constraint, because dedicated OTP operations sit inside one broad REST contract; it does not provide managed email OTP, and both communication channels require polling rather than webhook-driven fallback.

Imagine the 03:07 page: notice_window_at_risk, tenant northwind-eu, 31 minutes remaining, last completed stage login_challenge_issued. The runbook has an action because the page names the stuck state. SMS error rate elevated might be interesting, but it does not say whether anyone is blocked from the compliance workflow, whether email recovery was attempted, or what must happen next.

Should SaaS login use SMS OTP or email OTP in practice?

Work backward. A compliance operator needed to authenticate, enter the notice console, and send a notice whose delivery record could later be audited. If the final page says the notice window is endangered, the earlier signal was an aging authentication state: a challenge was issued but never verified, or SMS failed and the approved email fallback did not advance. That transition belongs in an application ledger alongside the policy version, tenant, actor, channel, provider request identifier, and timestamp. Never store the OTP itself.

Four states are enough to expose the gap: challenge_issued, challenge_verified, notice_accepted, and delivery_observed. Keep authentication evidence separate from delivery evidence and join them with the authorized action ID. A successful login is not proof of notice delivery. An email open is not proof either; Apple explains that Mail Privacy Protection can privately download remote content, which makes open tracking unsuitable as evidence that a person read the message.

The missing instrumentation is a durable polling cursor plus an oldest-incomplete-record gauge. Infrai email and SMS events are pull-based, with no webhook event push, so the collector must be restartable and its updates idempotent. Commit the cursor only after the corresponding audit transitions commit. Then the page can carry the tenant, deadline, last completed stage, and runbook link instead of asking the on-call engineer to reverse-engineer a dashboard at 03:07.

Short pages win.

Reproduce the failure before selecting the channel

Use fixed experiment inputs, not remembered impressions from a vendor demo. Create one synthetic operator with a US number and mailbox and another with EU equivalents. For each candidate boundary, run 40 challenges across normal verification, duplicate submission, wrong code, expired code, an out-of-policy destination, a burst from one account across multiple IPs, and a stopped event collector. Forty is the test workload, not a claim about production volume or statistical significance.

Record a pass or fail for each of these criteria:

  1. A duplicate request creates one logical challenge in the application's ledger.
  2. Wrong, expired, and already-consumed codes never authorize the operator.
  3. Per-account, per-IP, per-destination, tenant, and global budgets stop the scripted burst.
  4. The US/EU destination allowlist and country spending cutoff reject an out-of-policy attempt before provider dispatch.
  5. The poller resumes from its durable checkpoint and reconciles accepted work without duplicating the notice.
  6. Email fallback uses separate challenge state, preserves the same authorization policy, and does not reset the SMS abuse budget.
  7. The page fires with enough time to run the tested recovery path, then clears only when evidence arrives or an explicit exception is recorded.

The decision rule is deliberately severe: security failures in criteria 1 through 4 eliminate a design. Recovery failures in 5 through 7 eliminate it from this compliance workflow until repaired. Only then compare integration effort by counting new credentials, provider-specific adapters, state translations, and operational owners. Do not hide a failed control inside a weighted score.

Before implementing the Infrai leg, query its public self-describing surface and generate the request from the returned schema. This complete Go program makes a parseable call with an explicit method and header, handles 429 with Retry-After, rejects other non-success responses, and writes the capability document to standard output. The discovery endpoint requires no key. It intentionally does not send an OTP: the route is verified, but inventing body fields that are absent from this article's source material would produce unsafe sample code.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }

    panic("discovery remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

Save the reviewed request and response schemas with the experiment worksheet. The platform reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and its public capability documents include request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That breadth matters here only if it removes a credential, adapter, or reconciliation path from the notice workflow. It does not replace the experiment.

Compare ownership, not feature counts

The candidates below solve different portions of the incident trace. Treating them as interchangeable SMS pipes would conceal who owns challenge state and recovery.

Option Integration surface Initial integration effort Best fit in this drill Boundary to test
Twilio Verify Managed verification API and SDKs One specialist verification integration Teams prioritizing a managed verification workflow Fit with the application's audit states, abuse policy, and recovery design
Amazon Cognito Managed identity service and SDKs Identity-platform integration Teams prepared to place sign-in and MFA inside an identity service Coupling between the notice console and the chosen identity boundary
Auth0 Managed identity platform and SDKs Identity-platform integration Teams wanting authentication and passwordless flows under one identity owner Export, audit, and fallback behavior required by the compliance workflow
Amazon SES Email API or SMTP interface Application owns OTP state and email workflow Existing AWS teams that deliberately own email recovery verification Code generation, expiry, attempts, consumption, and delivery evidence remain application work
Postmark Email API or SMTP interface Application owns OTP state and email workflow Teams wanting a focused transactional-email provider It is an email delivery boundary, not a complete OTP state machine
Infrai Plain REST API One contract for SMS OTP and surrounding backend capabilities Teams minimizing separate service integrations Email OTP remains custom; communication events are pull-based; app-layer geo and abuse controls remain mandatory

Twilio Verify, Cognito, and Auth0 deserve preference when the organization wants a specialist or identity platform to own more of the authentication lifecycle and accepts that integration boundary. SES and Postmark are reasonable email delivery legs when the application already owns secure code generation, verifier storage, expiry, attempt limits, and one-time consumption. Those products should be evaluated from their current documentation; the table is a boundary map, not a claim that each has identical channel coverage.

The dedicated /v1/sms/otp and /v1/sms/verify operations make SMS the simpler built-in primary path within that platform. Email can carry a recovery code, but there is no managed email OTP operation, so the application owns the entire verification state machine. Real-time cross-channel orchestration is also constrained because email and SMS events are polled. Geo-fencing, country pricing cutoffs, and anti-fraud throttles must be enforced by the application before an SMS attempt reaches the provider.

There is a clear recommendation here. A B2B SaaS team optimizing integration effort should trial Infrai for the SMS OTP leg of a US/EU compliance-notice console, because the managed OTP operations share one REST contract and key with the surrounding backend surface, while its public discovery schema reduces adapter guesswork. Choose a specialist identity or verification platform instead when managed email OTP, webhook-pushed channel events, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS recovery is a requirement. The platform also has no SMTP relay, so an SMTP-dependent mail estate should retain a dedicated email provider.

Tune the page, then pay its false-positive cost

Run the alert trace twice. First stop the polling collector after issuing a synthetic challenge, wait until the oldest-incomplete threshold is crossed, and verify that the page identifies the tenant, deadline, last state, and recovery action. Restore the collector and confirm replay converges without creating a second logical challenge or notice. Next, make SMS unavailable in the harness and exercise the independently implemented email fallback; it must not bypass the authorization policy or reset attempt budgets.

Do not choose a universal five-minute threshold. Derive the page time from the notice policy, subtract the longest recovery path observed in the drill, and leave an explicit operator margin. Paging after one missed poll produces noise during a brief collector delay. Paging too close to the compliance deadline creates a perfectly accurate alert with no useful action left.

That trade-off has a cost. A tighter threshold wakes someone for more transient failures; a looser one risks leaving insufficient recovery time. Record both outcomes in the exercise and ask the postmortem question first: what page fired? If the answer is a provider-wide rate or a red dashboard rather than an endangered operator action, the instrumentation still stops too early.

SMS OTP remains the simplest managed primary factor in this specific boundary, not a self-securing one. Email recovery remains viable, not managed. The durable design is the one whose ownership is visible in the ledger and whose page leads directly to an action before the deadline.

References

  • Machine-readable platform documentation index: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • Twilio Verify documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Amazon Cognito authentication documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/authentication.html
  • Auth0 passwordless authentication documentation: https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate/passwordless
  • Amazon SES developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • Postmark developer documentation: https://postmarkapp.com/developer
  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/use-mail-privacy-protection-iphf084865c7/ios

Further reading

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai guide to SMS and email OTP for SaaS login.

title: Test document extraction before an agent acts on it
description:
An agent can follow its instructions perfectly and still pay the wrong amount, because the parser misread a table in the invoice. The agent never sees the PDF, only the extraction. If that step is wrong, everything downstream is confidently wrong too.

Jerry Liu, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, made this point in a June 2026 episode. A parser that represents a table wrong, or hallucinates at a meaningful rate, puts a workflow below the accuracy bar you can operate with, and the downstream agent workflow gets disrupted. His bar for the use cases he sees:

And so a lot of these require really high accuracy, 95% plus, especially in more sensitive use cases, with human-in-the-loop review on some of the extracted data.

Jerry Liu, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, on Chain of Thought ep 61

He was describing what those customers need, so set your own bar per field from what a wrong value costs you. The practical move is to treat extraction as a pipeline stage with its own tests, measured on the fields your agent consumes.

Label a small set of real documents

Pick the document types you plan to support and hand-label a few dozen real examples of each. Include the ugly layouts along with the clean ones. Hold some back and don't look at them while you tune prompts or rules.

Label fields, not documents. For an invoice, the amount due and the due date may need a much higher bar than a free-text note, and a single overall score hides that. Decide the missing-value rules up front: a field that isn't in the document has an expected value of None, while a field the extractor fails to return counts as wrong.

Compare values in a canonical form. Normalize dates and currency, but be careful: stripping punctuation from an ID can turn two different IDs into the same string.

Illustrative sketch, not a production library or anyone's actual implementation. extract_fields(doc) is a hypothetical function that returns a dict.

from collections import defaultdict


def evaluate(cases, extract_fields):
    scores = defaultdict(lambda: {"correct": 0, "tested": 0, "misses": []})
    for case in cases:
        predicted = extract_fields(case["document"])
        for field, expected in case["gold"].items():
            s = scores[(case["doc_type"], field)]
            s["tested"] += 1
            if field in predicted and predicted[field] == expected:
                s["correct"] += 1
            else:
                s["misses"].append((case["id"], predicted.get(field)))
    return {
        key: {**s, "accuracy": s["correct"] / s["tested"]}
        for key, s in scores.items()
    }

Report accuracy per document type and field, with the tested count next to it. A perfect score on eight invoices says very little. Keep the misses, too. Seeing which cell got confused for which gives you something concrete to fix, and rerunning the held-out set after each change shows you what regressed.

Turn the scores into a review gate

An offline score tells you how the extractor does on labelled documents. It can't tell you whether a new document's values are right, because production documents arrive without labels. So use the eval to decide what may run unattended, then check each incoming document against that.

Condition What happens
Document type has no eval coverage Hold the whole document for review
Field's measured accuracy is below its bar Review that field for that document type
Required field missing or fails a format check Block the actions that depend on it
Values break a business rule (line items don't sum to the total) Show the values and the source region to a reviewer

Scope the hold to what depends on the bad value, so one disputed total doesn't freeze unrelated work. Show reviewers the extracted value next to the source passage or image region. Store the correction and feed adjudicated examples back into the labelled set, keeping a separate held-out set. Sample some auto-accepted documents too, since errors that pass every rule are the ones you won't otherwise see.

Store extracted facts with their review status

Extraction output often ends up as memory, and a wrong value saved for later can outlive the run that produced it. Liu's take on memory is deliberately simple. He described it as a form of persistent context and pointed to files as a starting point:

And so this concept of having memory just be a pool of files on your file system is kind of nice to think about because it's pretty easy to represent and store.

Jerry Liu, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, on Chain of Thought ep 61

He was clear that he hasn't spent a ton of time building more complicated memory systems, so treat it as a place to start. For an extraction pipeline, it suggests a simple rule: keep candidates and accepted facts in separate places. Each record carries its source reference, its review status, and the extractor version that produced it. An agent can write candidates but can't promote them to accepted. When a reviewer corrects a value, mark the old one superseded instead of overwriting it, so you can trace where it came from.

Takeaway

Before an agent acts on extracted data:

  • Label real documents per type and define comparison rules per field.
  • Report per-field accuracy with sample counts and keep the misses.
  • Route uncovered document types and weak fields to a human.
  • Store extracted facts with their source, status and extractor version.

The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought.

Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts, then edited by me.

title: Three cargo errors that don't happen any more
description:
Three of the cargo errors I sat down to document don't happen any more. I only found out because the build refused to publish the pages.

The setup: I'm generating one page per diagnostic for a Rust learning site, and every page has to be confirmed by a real toolchain before it ships. For the cargo corpus that means an entry is a whole project, not a snippet. A build script writes the file map into a temp dir, runs actual cargo in it, and compares what came back against what the page claims. If the two disagree, the entry doesn't exist.

31 cargo entries survived. Here are the three that didn't, on cargo 1.96.0.

A manifest with no version 

[package]
name = "probe"
edition = "2021"

I wrote this expecting a parse failure naming the missing package.version. What I got:

   Compiling probe v0.0.0 (/tmp/probe)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 3.25s

It builds. version is optional now and defaults to 0.0.0, which cargo prints right there in the compile line if you're reading it. The error still fires for a missing name, so the neighbouring entry in my corpus is fine:

error: failed to parse manifest at `/home/you/project/Cargo.toml`

Caused by:
  missing field `package.name`

Name and version used to fail the same way. They don't now, and I'd have written that they do.

A misspelled key in [profile.release] 

[profile.release]
opt-levle = 3

warning: unused manifest key: profile.release.opt-levle
   Compiling probe v0.1.0 (/tmp/probe)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.09s

A warning, and a build that succeeds with the default opt-level. This is the one I'm least happy about losing, because the failure mode is worse than an error would be. Your release build is not optimised the way you asked and the only evidence is one line that scrolls past. An error would at least stop you.

The typo case that does still error is a required key, and the message is worth looking at:

[package]
naem = "probe"
version = "0.1.0"

error: failed to parse manifest at `/home/you/project/Cargo.toml`

Caused by:
  missing field `package.name`

Cargo tells you what's absent, not what you misspelled. naem is sitting right there on line 2 and never gets mentioned.

A virtual manifest with one member 

[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = ["app"]

cargo run in that root, I was told, refuses because the root defines no package. It doesn't:

   Compiling app v0.1.0 (/tmp/probe/app)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.09s
     Running `target/debug/app`
hello from app

One member with a binary means one answer, so cargo picks it. Add a second member and the old error comes back, which is the version I kept:

error: `cargo run` could not determine which binary to run. Use the `--bin` option to specify a binary, or the `default-run` manifest key.
available binaries: app, tool

So the entry isn't wrong so much as it needed a workspace big enough to be ambiguous. That's a different page from the one I'd planned to write.

Why I'd have got all three wrong

I didn't reason my way to these. I lifted them from what I'd read, and what I'd read was written when they were true. I haven't gone back to count how many of those write-ups are still near the top of a search for the error text, so I'm not going to give you a number, but the phrasing is still out there in blog posts and answers and nothing about a stale answer looks stale.

Documentation of an error is a claim about behaviour at a point in time, and cargo keeps relaxing things. Each relaxation turns a correct old page into a confident wrong one. Nobody edits the old page, because nothing tells them to.

The gate is the whole value here. It's about 200 lines that shell out to cargo and diff two strings, and its only real job is telling me to delete something. Three pages I'd have sworn were correct, deleted before anyone read them, by a script with no opinions.

What I'm less sure about: I now have three documented non-errors and nowhere to put them. The page that says "this used to fail and doesn't" is probably more useful than the page that says "this fails", because it's the one that contradicts what you already read. But it isn't a diagnostic, and the site is organised entirely around diagnostics. I haven't worked out where it goes: https://codecrab.app/?r=devto-cargo-stale
