title: High-Availability Distributed Sagas via Active-Active Topologies
description:
In tier-1 core banking systems, system availability is not merely an operational metric—it is a regulatory mandate. Outages in mission-critical business capabilities like Payment Execution or Position Keeping trigger immediate regulatory scrutiny, massive financial penalties, and systemic reputational damage.

Historically, banks relied on Active-Passive (Disaster Recovery) infrastructure topologies. In these setups, a primary data center handles all live traffic while a secondary data center sits idle, asynchronously replicating state. However, during a catastrophic regional failure (e.g., a total cloud region outage or physical fiber cut), Active-Passive failover mechanisms incur unacceptable recovery costs:

  • Non-Zero RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Asynchronous replication logs lag behind live transactions, resulting in lost financial writes upon failover.
  • High RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Manual or semi-automated DNS cutovers, database promotion scripts, and cache warm-ups take minutes—if not hours—to execute safely.
  • In-Flight Saga Corruption: Distributed transactions mid-execution during a regional collapse are left in indeterminate states, leading to orphan holds on customer accounts or uncompensated ledger debits.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, high-availability banking platforms eliminate single-region failure risks by deploying Multi-Region Active-Active Topologies for distributed Saga orchestrators (such as Temporal) backed by Distributed SQL engines (such as CockroachDB or Google Cloud Spanner). This paper evaluates the architectural patterns, state fencing mechanisms, consensus latency mathematics, and automated DR runbooks required to achieve RPO = 0 and RTO < 1s across regional disasters.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain HA & SLA Matrix

Not all BIAN Service Domains demand identical disaster recovery profiles. Engineering active-active consensus across multi-region WANs introduces network latency trade-offs that must be categorized by domain criticality.

BIAN Service Domain Criticality Tier Target RPO Target RTO Multi-Region Topology Pattern Database Consensus Strategy
Payment Execution Tier-1 (Critical) 0 (Zero Loss) < 1 Second Multi-Region Active-Active (3+ Regions) Serialized Quorum Consensus (Raft/Paxos)
Position Keeping Tier-1 (Critical) 0 (Zero Loss) < 1 Second Multi-Region Active-Active (3+ Regions) Multi-Region Row-Level Lease Pinning
Credit Assessment Tier-2 (High) < 1 Second < 10 Seconds Dual-Region Active-Active (Follow-the-Leader) Asynchronous Cross-Region Group Replication
Customer Onboarding Tier-2 (High) < 5 Seconds < 30 Seconds Active-Active with Regional Sharding Eventual Consistency / Asynchronous Outbox
Historical Reporting Tier-3 (Standard) < 1 Hour < 1 Hour Active-Passive (DR Read Replica) Asynchronous Batch Snapshot Hydration

Mathematical Model: Multi-Region Consensus Latency vs. Availability

Achieving zero RPO across active-active regions requires synchronous consensus (e.g., Raft or Paxos). A transaction cannot be acknowledged to a client until a quorum of regions confirms state persistence.

The minimum commit latency Tcommit​ for a distributed Saga step executing across a multi-region deployment spanning M regions (where M≥3 to prevent split-brain tie votes) is governed by the round-trip time (RTT) to the closest majority quorum:

Tcommit​=Tlocal-execution​+max(RTTregion-local,RTTregion-quorum-1)+Tfsync​

Where RTTregion-quorum-1​ represents the network latency to the geographically closest peer region required to form a majority quorum ( ⌊M/2⌋+1 nodes).

The composite system availability Asystem​ across M independent active-active regions, assuming an individual region unavailability probability of Pregion-fail​ , is expressed as:

Asystem​=1−k=0∑⌊M/2⌋​(kM​)⋅(Pregion-fail​)M−k⋅(1−Pregion-fail​)k

By deploying across 3 geographically distinct active-active regions with independent power grids and cloud control planes, system availability reaches 99.999% ("five nines"), guaranteeing continuous execution even during the complete destruction of an entire cloud region.

Active-Active Multi-Region Saga Architecture Topology

In a Xenon active-active architecture, application workers and Saga orchestrators run simultaneously in all active regions. Traffic is routed via Global Anycast DNS or BGP Anycast routing.

                           MULTI-REGION ACTIVE-ACTIVE TOPOLOGY

                      +------------------------------------------+
                      | Global Anycast DNS / Cloudflare Route    |
                      +--------------------+---------------------+
                                           |
                ┌──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
                │ 33% Traffic              │ 33% Traffic              │ 33% Traffic
                v                          v                          v
  +--------------------------+ +--------------------------+ +--------------------------+
  | REGION A (us-east-1)     | | REGION B (us-west-2)     | | REGION C (eu-central-1)  |
  |                          | |                          | |                          |
  | [ App / Temporal Worker] | | [ App / Temporal Worker] | | [ App / Temporal Worker] |
  |            │             | |            │             | |            │             |
  |            v             | |            v             | |            v             |
  | [ CockroachDB Node 1 ]   | | [ CockroachDB Node 2 ]   | | [ CockroachDB Node 3 ]   |
  +------------+-------------+ +------------+-------------+ +------------+-------------+
               ▲                            ▲                            ▲
               └────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘
                                Multi-Region Raft Quorum
                                (Synchronous State Replications)
  1. Global Traffic Management: Requests enter through Anycast BGP routing, directing client traffic to the closest operational region.
  2. Stateless App / Saga Workers: Stateless Temporal application workers run in all regions, connecting to the local region's database pool.
  3. Distributed SQL Consensus Layer: CockroachDB or Google Cloud Spanner maintains row-level Raft consensus across regions. A write committed in Region A is synchronously replicated to Region B before acknowledging completion, guaranteeing RPO = 0.

Multi-Region Saga State Persistence & Fencing Mechanics

The primary risk during a network partition between regions is the Zombie Worker Scenario: Region A experiences a transient network partition and is temporarily isolated. Region B assumes Region A is dead and takes over execution of an in-flight Payment Saga. If Region A wakes back up mid-way, both regions might attempt to execute steps or compensations simultaneously, leading to double-spends.

To prevent double execution, Xenon Architecture mandates Epoch Fencing Tokens enforced by distributed database leases.

1. Database Schema for Multi-Region Saga State (sagas_schema.sql) 

CREATE TABLE saga_instances (
    saga_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    bian_domain VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    current_state VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    epoch_token BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    lease_owner_region VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    lease_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) LOCALITY REGIONAL BY ROW;

-- Ensure high-concurrency balance updates execute near primary account region
ALTER TABLE saga_instances CONFIGURE ZONE USING 
    num_replicas = 3,
    constraints = '{"+region=us-east-1": 1, "+region=us-west-2": 1, "+region=eu-central-1": 1}';

2. Idempotent Epoch-Fenced Saga Execution Engine (Go / Temporal SDK)

The Go code below illustrates how a Temporal worker in Region B acquires a lease, increments the epoch_token, and invalidates any lingering execution attempts from Region A:

package sagas

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "go.temporal.io/sdk/workflow"
)

type SagaLeaseManager struct {
    db           *sql.DB
    regionName   string
    leaseTimeout time.Duration
}

func NewSagaLeaseManager(db *sql.DB, regionName string) *SagaLeaseManager {
    return &SagaLeaseManager{
        db:           db,
        regionName:   regionName,
        leaseTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
    }
}

// AcquireOrRenewLease uses conditional CAS (Compare-And-Swap) to fence out old workers
func (m *SagaLeaseManager) AcquireOrRenewLease(ctx context.Context, sagaID string) (int64, error) {
    tx, err := m.db.BeginTx(ctx, &sql.TxOptions{Isolation: sql.LevelSerializable})
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("failed to begin serializable transaction: %w", err)
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    var currentEpoch int64
    var currentOwner string
    var leaseExpires time.Time

    // 1. Read current saga fencing state
    query := `SELECT epoch_token, lease_owner_region, lease_expires_at FROM saga_instances WHERE saga_id = $1 FOR UPDATE`
    err = tx.QueryRowContext(ctx, query, sagaID).Scan(&currentEpoch, &currentOwner, &leaseExpires)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("failed to fetch saga state: %w", err)
    }

    now := time.Now().UTC()

    // 2. Verify if lease is held by another active region
    if currentOwner != m.regionName && now.Before(leaseExpires) {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("lease currently held by active region %s until %s", currentOwner, leaseExpires)
    }

    // 3. Increment Epoch Token to fence out zombie workers from previous region
    newEpoch := currentEpoch + 1
    newExpiry := now.Add(m.leaseTimeout)

    updateQuery := `
        UPDATE saga_instances 
        SET epoch_token = $1, lease_owner_region = $2, lease_expires_at = $3, updated_at = $4 
        WHERE saga_id = $5 AND epoch_token = $6`

    res, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, updateQuery, newEpoch, m.regionName, newExpiry, now, sagaID, currentEpoch)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("fencing update failed: %w", err)
    }

    rows, err := res.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil || rows == 0 {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("CAS fencing failure: epoch token mutated concurrently by another region")
    }

    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("failed to commit lease acquisition: %w", err)
    }

    return newEpoch, nil
}

// PaymentSagaWorkflow executes with cross-region fencing checks
func HighAvailabilityPaymentSaga(ctx workflow.Context, sagaID string, input PaymentSagaInput) error {
    options := workflow.ActivityOptions{
        StartToCloseTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
        RetryPolicy: &workflow.RetryPolicy{
            MaximumAttempts: 3,
        },
    }
    ctx = workflow.WithActivityOptions(ctx, options)

    // Step 1: Claim Lease and Fence Execution Context
    var epochToken int64
    err := workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, AcquireLeaseActivity, sagaID).Get(ctx, &epochToken)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("aborting saga execution: failed to acquire multi-region lease: %w", err)
    }

    // Step 2: Pass Epoch Token to Downstream Microservices for Strict Mutex Checking
    err = workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, ExecuteFencedDebitActivity, input.SourceAccount, input.Amount, epochToken).Get(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        // Run Compensations with Epoch Token
        _ = workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, ExecuteFencedCompensationActivity, input.SourceAccount, input.Amount, epochToken).Get(ctx, nil)
        return fmt.Errorf("saga failed, compensations executed: %w", err)
    }

    return nil
}

Automated DR Runbooks & Failover Mechanics

In an active-active topology, regional failover does not require manual human intervention. Continuous automated health checking at the ingress mesh layer detects regional unresponsiveness and reroutes traffic in sub-seconds.

                    AUTOMATED SUB-SECOND FAILOVER TIMELINE

  T=0ms           T=150ms                     T=300ms                 T=450ms
  Region A        Health Probes Fail          Envoy / Anycast         Region B Workers
  Infrastructure  (3x 50ms Timeout)           Reroutes Traffic        Claim Leases &
  Collapses       ──────►                     to Region B             Resume Pending Sagas
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

Automated Envoy Multi-Region Route Failover Configuration

The following Envoy Proxy configuration snippet illustrates automatic client-side load balancer eviction of a failing active region:

static_resources:
  clusters:
    - name: bian_payment_execution_cluster
      connect_timeout: 0.25s
      type: STRICT_DNS
      lb_policy: ROUND_ROBIN
      common_lb_config:
        healthy_panic_threshold:
          value: 50.0
      health_checks:
        - timeout: 0.1s
          interval: 0.2s
          unhealthy_threshold: 2
          healthy_threshold: 1
          http_health_check:
            path: "/healthz/liveness"
      outlier_detection:
        consecutive_5xx: 3
        interval: 1s
        base_ejection_time: 30s
        max_ejection_percent: 100
      load_assignment:
        cluster_name: bian_payment_execution_cluster
        endpoints:
          - priority: 0 # Local Region Priority
            locality:
              region: us-east-1
            lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address:
                      address: payment-api.us-east-1.internal.xenon
                      port_value: 8443
          - priority: 1 # Failover Region Priority (Sub-second automatic fallback)
            locality:
              region: us-west-2
            lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address:
                      address: payment-api.us-west-2.internal.xenon
                      port_value: 8443

Chaos Engineering, Validation & DR Testing

To verify RPO = 0 and RTO < 1s compliance for regulatory bodies (e.g., Fed, EBA, MAS), core banking architectures must execute continuous, automated chaos injection experiments in staging and production environments.

Chaos Mesh Experiment: Region Isolation Simulation (region_blackhole.yaml)

This experiment drops all network packets between Region A (us-east-1) and the remaining cluster nodes while an active load test of 10,000 TPS payment Sagas is executing:

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata:
  name: simulate-region-a-blackhole
  namespace: xenon-chaos
spec:
  action: partition
  mode: all
  selector:
    namespaces:
      - bian-payment-execution
    labelSelectors:
      topology.kubernetes.io/region: "us-east-1"
  direction: both
  target:
    selector:
      namespaces:
        - bian-payment-execution
      labelSelectors:
        topology.kubernetes.io/region: "us-west-2"
  duration: "5m"
  scheduler:
    cron: "0 2 * * 6" # Run automatically every Saturday at 02:00 UTC

Verification Criteria During Chaos Experiments

During a simulated regional blackout, automated monitoring systems must verify three non-negotiable assertions:

  1. Zero Corrupted States: Database consistency checkers verify that no account balance exhibits a split-brain mismatch or missing ledger transaction (RPO = 0).
  2. Sub-Second RTO: Ingress metrics demonstrate that 99.9% of HTTP/gRPC requests resume successful processing in peer regions within < 850ms of network partition onset.
  3. No Double-Compensations: Temporal history logs verify that no Saga executed compensating actions twice due to race conditions between surviving regions.

Deploying high-availability distributed Sagas via multi-region Active-Active topologies guarantees that core banking platforms survive full cloud-region disasters without data loss or prolonged downtime. By combining distributed SQL Raft consensus, epoch-fenced Saga execution, and automated ingress failover routing, financial systems achieve strict RPO = 0 and RTO < 1s operational compliance across all critical BIAN service domains.

title: Auditing Password Reset Email API 429 Rate Limit Cooldowns
description:
Treat a password-reset request as an auditable recovery workflow, not as a synchronous email send: accept the request without revealing account state, enforce a per-account repeat-request cooldown, and let a durable worker honor Retry-After after an HTTP 429 without creating a second live reset token. The deciding constraint in a customer-support system is that delivery can be uncertain while the security outcome cannot be.

Short answer: return the same generic response for existent and nonexistent accounts, create at most one active recovery challenge for the policy window, and record delivery attempts separately from that challenge. A 429 changes when the next attempt may run; it does not justify generating another link. A permanent bounce or an administratively confirmed invalid address closes the email delivery path and routes the case into the support team's verified account-recovery process.

This distinction gives the system three useful properties at once: users cannot create a retry storm by clicking "resend," workers can crash after a network call without corrupting the recovery state, and support staff can explain why mail stopped without reading secrets or reconstructing events from application logs. Exactly once delivery is unavailable across an HTTP boundary. Exactly once state transition is attainable with uniqueness constraints, conditional updates, and an append-only audit record.

How Should a Password Reset Email API Handle 429 Rate Limits?

The first invariant is non-enumeration. OWASP recommends a consistent message and response time for password-reset requests regardless of whether the account exists, so the public handler should acknowledge the request before exposing any delivery decision. The handler may enqueue internal work only for a matched account, but that branch must not change the observable response.

The second invariant is one usable challenge per account and recovery purpose. Store only a hash of a cryptographically random token, give it an expiry, make it single-use, and invalidate it after a successful reset. A repeated request should normally reference the same unexpired challenge or atomically replace it under a documented policy; blindly minting one token per click leaves several valid credentials in inboxes and makes incident review needlessly ambiguous.

The third invariant is that recipient validity and message delivery are different state machines. An HTTP 429 means the sending endpoint is rate-limiting requests. RFC 6585 says a 429 response may include Retry-After; RFC 9110 defines that field as either delay seconds or an HTTP date. Neither statement says the address is invalid. Conversely, an SMTP enhanced status such as 5.1.1 identifies a permanent address failure, while a temporary 4.x.x status does not justify permanent suppression. Conflating these signals turns a transient capacity event into an account lockout.

Stop there.

For a support organization, suppression also needs provenance. Record whether the evidence came from a permanent delivery status, an authenticated administrative action, or a later address correction; record the event identifier and time; never store the reset token in the audit payload. This is the same discipline expected of a ledger: a current balance is useful, but it is not a substitute for the entries that produced it.

Decision record and failure boundaries

The selected design is a transactional outbox plus a recovery-challenge table, a recipient-status table, and an append-only attempt log. The web transaction creates or finds the active challenge and inserts a uniquely keyed outbox item. A worker claims that item, checks suppression again, performs one remote send attempt, and then records the outcome. Bounce ingestion is a separate authenticated path because it arrives later and has different trust and replay boundaries.

The unit of idempotency is (account_id, purpose, challenge_generation), not an HTTP request ID supplied by a browser. Browser retries, two open tabs, and a support agent's repeat-send action can all represent the same desired effect. A database unique constraint makes that effect durable. Each remote attempt receives its own attempt ID for correlation, while the stable outbox ID is used as the idempotency key if the delivery interface supports one.

The failure boundaries are explicit. Consider one plausible chain rather than an isolated status code: two browser tabs submit a recovery request, the first transaction creates challenge generation 18 and its outbox item, and the second transaction encounters the uniqueness rule and returns the same generic acknowledgement. A worker leases that item and calls the remote endpoint. The connection then closes before a response arrives. No observer can infer from that socket error whether the remote system accepted the email, so the worker lets its lease expire and later repeats the call with the same outbox ID; it does not create generation 19. If the response is a 429, the adapter parses Retry-After and persists a future attempt time. If a permanent mailbox failure arrives afterward, the independently authenticated bounce path records its event ID, changes recipient eligibility, and prevents another delivery attempt. The challenge itself remains unconsumed until it expires or is used. This longer chain is why a single sent boolean is inadequate: rollback, lease ownership, uncertain acceptance, throttling, mailbox validity, and challenge consumption are separate facts, and collapsing them destroys the evidence needed for reconciliation.

Option Integration effort Behavior after an ambiguous timeout Audit quality Decision
Send inside the request handler Low initially Handler or client may duplicate work Split across request logs Rejected for recovery mail
Database outbox and worker Moderate Reclaims the same logical item Attempt history joins to one challenge Selected default
External durable queue plus database state Higher Depends on coordinated deduplication Good with stable cross-system IDs Valid when a queue is already operated

The table is deliberately about integration effort rather than a promise that one transport is intrinsically more reliable. An outbox uses the database transaction already required for the challenge. An external queue can absorb bursts and isolate workers, but introducing it solely for reset mail creates another credential, deployment, retention policy, and reconciliation surface.

Critical path in Go

The worker below shows the boundary that matters. Repository methods are assumed to use conditional updates: Complete, Defer, and Suppress succeed only while this worker owns the lease, and the outbox uniqueness rule prevents two live items for the same challenge generation. The sender accepts a stable idempotency key. Those contracts, rather than an in-memory retry loop, carry correctness across process restarts.

package recovery

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Item struct {
    ID            string
    AccountID     string
    Recipient     string
    ChallengeID   string
    AttemptNumber int
}

type SendResult struct {
    Accepted          bool
    RateLimited       bool
    RetryAfter        time.Time
    PermanentAddress bool
    EvidenceID        string
}

type Sender interface {
    SendReset(ctx context.Context, recipient, challengeID, idempotencyKey string) (SendResult, error)
}

type Repository interface {
    IsSuppressed(ctx context.Context, recipient string) (bool, error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, itemID, evidenceID string, at time.Time) error
    Defer(ctx context.Context, itemID string, next time.Time, reason string) error
    Suppress(ctx context.Context, itemID, recipient, evidenceID string, at time.Time) error
}

type Worker struct {
    repo   Repository
    sender Sender
    now    func() time.Time
}

func (w Worker) Deliver(ctx context.Context, item Item) error {
    suppressed, err := w.repo.IsSuppressed(ctx, item.Recipient)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if suppressed {
        return w.repo.Complete(ctx, item.ID, "suppressed-before-send", w.now())
    }

    result, err := w.sender.SendReset(ctx, item.Recipient, item.ChallengeID, item.ID)
    if err != nil {
        // The outcome may be unknown. Reuse the item and key; do not mint a token.
        return errors.New("delivery outcome unknown; lease may be retried")
    }

    switch {
    case result.Accepted:
        return w.repo.Complete(ctx, item.ID, result.EvidenceID, w.now())
    case result.RateLimited:
        return w.repo.Defer(ctx, item.ID, result.RetryAfter, "rate-limited")
    case result.PermanentAddress:
        return w.repo.Suppress(ctx, item.ID, item.Recipient, result.EvidenceID, w.now())
    default:
        return w.repo.Defer(ctx, item.ID, w.now().Add(time.Minute), "temporary-failure")
    }
}

Parsing Retry-After belongs in the HTTP adapter because it depends on response headers and the adapter's clock. Accept delay seconds and HTTP dates, reject negative or malformed values, and cap the result with an operator-defined maximum so corrupted input cannot park an item indefinitely. If the header is absent, use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. The queue's next_attempt_at timestamp must be persisted; sleeping inside a worker wastes capacity and loses the schedule on restart.

Do not hold a database transaction open across the network call. Claim with a short lease, commit, call the sender, then conditionally write the result. The small window between remote acceptance and local completion is why the stable idempotency key matters. If the receiving interface cannot deduplicate, duplicate email remains a possible presentation outcome, though both messages should point to the same challenge and only one successful consumption can occur.

How should cooldowns and bounces interact?

A repeat-request cooldown is an abuse and workload control, not proof of delivery. It should be checked against the account or normalized recipient rather than the caller's IP alone, because distributed callers can evade an IP-only rule and shared networks can punish unrelated users. Keep the public response generic even during cooldown. Internally, record a cooldown_reused decision so a support investigator can distinguish "no new work was necessary" from "the address was suppressed."

Use separate times for separate claims: challenge_expires_at, next_attempt_at, repeat_request_allowed_at, and suppressed_at. One overloaded status plus updated_at cannot answer whether a link is valid, an email is queued, or the recipient is blocked. This is a common schema shortcut, and it fails precisely when an agent needs a defensible timeline.

Bounce processing must be idempotent too. Deduplicate an authenticated event by its source event ID, retain the raw classification needed for audit under the organization's data-retention policy, and map only well-understood permanent address failures to suppression. RFC 3463 separates persistent 5.x.x failures from persistent transient 4.x.x failures and defines X.1.1 as a bad destination mailbox address. A complaint or policy rejection may require a different action from an invalid mailbox, so do not flatten every failure into invalid_recipient.

Support agents need a narrow control surface: see the non-secret event timeline, correct an address through an authenticated process, and trigger reevaluation after verification. They should not be able to reveal token hashes, bypass the cooldown casually, or remove suppression without leaving an audit event. Compliance limits vary by jurisdiction and company policy; define retention, access, and deletion requirements with the responsible security and legal teams rather than treating an email log as permanent by default.

The rejected shortcut, its limitations, and where it still fits

The rejected option is sending synchronously in the reset endpoint and retrying 429 responses in that process. It is attractive because the integration is small: one handler, one API call, one visible result. It also couples user latency to rate-limit delays, loses durable retry intent on a process restart, and tempts the caller to issue a fresh token after a timeout.

The selected outbox design has limitations as well. It is not suitable for a prototype whose database cannot run conditional updates, and it adds migrations, a worker deployment, lease monitoring, cleanup, and reconciliation work. A team that already operates a durable queue may reasonably accept higher coordination effort and keep scheduling there; a low-risk internal tool with a mail sink may accept synchronous delivery. The trade-off favors an outbox here because production account recovery already needs a transactional challenge record and a support-visible audit trail, not because an outbox guarantees delivery.

It still has a valid use case. An internal prototype with no real accounts, no support workflow, and a disposable mail sink may choose synchronous sending because there is no durable security outcome to protect. The boundary should be written down. Before production, move token creation and outbox insertion into one transaction, add unique constraints and lease recovery, authenticate bounce events, and exercise crash points in tests.

The deployment test matrix should include duplicate browser submissions, concurrent support repeat-send actions, a 429 with both forms of Retry-After, a missing header, worker death before and after the remote call, replayed bounce events, temporary 4.x.x failures, permanent 5.1.1 failures, and an address correction that occurs while an item is leased. Reconciliation then becomes mechanical: every active outbox item has one challenge, every completed item has a terminal attempt, and every suppression has attributable evidence.

Measure queue age, attempts by outcome, lease recoveries, cooldown reuse, and suppressions by classified reason. Alert on age and reconciliation violations, not on raw 429 count alone; a short rate-limit burst that drains within policy is operationally different from a queue whose oldest recovery message keeps aging. Logs should carry opaque account and attempt identifiers, never reset URLs or tokens.

The final decision is modest: make the database authoritative for recovery intent, make retries resumable, and make recipient suppression evidence-based. This costs more integration work than a direct send, but it keeps throttling, invalid addresses, and human support actions from changing security state by accident.

References

  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (Retry-After): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321

title: Next.js 14: Server Components and the Future of React – Like Taking the Red Pill
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Honestly, I was tired of shipping React apps that felt like they were dragging a backpack full of rocks. Every time I added a new feature, the bundle grew, the first‑paint slowed, and I found myself constantly wrestling with data‑fetching waterfalls. I’d fetch something on the client, wait for the API, then render a skeleton, then finally show the UI—repeat for each nested component. It was like playing a RPG where every enemy you defeat spawns two more, and you never get to the boss fight.

I kept asking myself: Is there a way to let the server do the heavy lifting so the browser only gets what it actually needs to show? I’d heard whispers about React Server Components, but the docs felt like ancient scrolls—mysterious, a bit intimidating, and full of “you’ll understand later” vibes. When Next.js 14 landed with stable server components, I knew it was time to grab my sword and see what loot awaited.

The Revelation (The Insight)

Here’s the thing: Server Components aren’t just another way to fetch data on the server. They let you write components that never ship JavaScript to the browser. Think of them as pure‑render functions that live on the server, get the data they need, and return plain HTML (or a lightweight RSC payload) that the client can stitch into the DOM without downloading the component’s code. The client only receives the minimal JavaScript needed for interactive parts—those stay as traditional Client Components.

The biggest mind‑blow for me was realizing that you can mix Server and Client Components freely inside the same tree. A Server Component can render a Client Component as a child, and the boundary is handled automatically by Next.js. No more prop‑drilling of fetch functions or trying to guess where data should live. You just write the UI, tell Next.js where you need interactivity, and the framework does the rest.

Why does this matter? Because the browser now gets less JavaScript to parse, less to download, and the initial paint feels snappier—especially on slower networks or low‑end devices. And you still get the full React ecosystem (hooks, context, etc.) wherever you need it.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

Let’s look at a common scenario: a blog page that lists posts, each with a title, author, and a “like” button that updates optimistically. In the old world (Next.js 13 with getServerSideProps or client‑side fetch), you’d end up fetching the posts on the server, passing them down, and then each post component would fetch its own like count on the client—cue the waterfall.

The Struggle (Before) 

// pages/blog.tsx  (Next.js 13)
import { GetServerSideProps } from 'next';
import PostList from '@/components/PostList';

export const getServerSideProps: GetServerSideProps = async () => {
  const res = await fetch('https://my-blog-api.com/posts');
  const posts = await res.json();
  return { props: { posts } };
};

export default function Blog({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
  return <PostList posts={posts} />;
}

// components/PostList.tsx
import Post from '@/components/Post';

export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map(p => (
        <li key={p.id}>
          <Post post={p} />
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// components/Post.tsx
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export default function Post({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(post.likes);
  const [liking, setLiking] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    // fetch live like count (could be stale)
    fetch(`https://my-blog-api.com/posts/${post.id}/likes`)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(data => setLikes(data.count));
  }, [post.id]);

  const handleLike = async () => {
    setLiking(true);
    const newCount = likes + 1;
    setLikes(newCount);
    try {
      await fetch(`https://my-blog-api.com/posts/${post.id}/like`, {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ likes: newCount }),
      });
    } catch {
      setLikes(likes); // rollback on error
    } finally {
      setLiking(false);
    }
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{post.title}</h2>
      <p>by {post.author}</p>
      <button disabled={liking} onClick={handleLike}>
        {liking ? 'Liking…' : `👍 ${likes}`}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

What’s painful here?

  • The Post component does a client‑side fetch for likes, causing a request per post after the initial HTML arrives.
  • We’re sending the entire Post component code to the browser, even though the title and author never change.
  • The useEffect runs on the client, meaning we wait for the JS bundle to load before we can even start the request.

The Victory (After with Server Components)

Now we split concerns: the static parts (title, author) live in a Server Component, while the interactive like button stays a Client Component.

// app/blog/page.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router)
import PostList from '@/components/PostList';

// ✅ This is a Server Component by default in the app router
export default async function BlogPage() {
  const res = await fetch('https://my-blog-api.com/posts');
  const posts = await res.json();

  // We only pass the data we need; the component itself stays on the server
  return <PostList posts={posts} />;
}

// components/PostList.tsx
import Post from '@/components/Post';

export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
  // Still a Server Component – no client bundle
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map(p => (
        <li key={p.id}>
          <Post post={p} />
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// components/Post.tsx
'use client'; // ← marks this file as a Client Component
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Post({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(post.likes);
  const [liking, setLiking] = useState(false);

  const handleLike = async () => {
    setLiking(true);
    const newCount = likes + 1;
    setLikes(newCount);
    try {
      await fetch(`https://my-blog-api.com/posts/${post.id}/like`, {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ likes: newCount }),
      });
    } catch {
      setLikes(likes); // optimistic rollback
    } finally {
      setLiking(false);
    }
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{post.title}</h2>
      <p>by {post.author}</p>
      <button disabled={liking} onClick={handleLike}>
        {liking ? 'Liking…' : `👍 ${likes}`}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

What changed?

  • app/blog/page.tsx and PostList are Server Components by default. They run on the server, fetch the posts once, and send only the rendered HTML (plus a tiny RSC descriptor) to the browser.
  • The Post file now has 'use client' at the top, telling Next.js to ship its JavaScript to the browser only for the interactive bits (the like button). The title and author never leave the server as JS code.
  • No more per‑post client fetches for static data; the like button still works optimistically because it’s a Client Component with its own state.

Common Traps to Avoid

  1. Forgetting the 'use client' directive – If you add interactivity (state, effects, event handlers) inside a file that’s meant to be a Server Component, you’ll get a runtime error like “Invalid hook call”. Remember: any hook or event handler forces a Client Component boundary.

  2. Passing large objects from Server to Client Components – Anything you pass as a prop crosses the network. If you accidentally pass the entire Post object (including heavy fields like bodyMarkdown) to a Client Component, you’re sending unnecessary data. Keep the prop diet lean: only send what the client truly needs (e.g., id, title, author, likes).

Why This New Power Matters

With Server Components, the line between “static” and “dynamic” blurs in the best way. You can now build pages where the bulk of the work—data fetching, markup generation—happens on the server, delivering a fast first paint, while still enjoying the full React experience for the bits that truly need to be alive in the browser. It’s like getting the best of both worlds: the performance of a traditional SSR site and the richness of a modern SPA.

Imagine building a dashboard where the charts and tables are Server Components (fast, cached, SEO‑friendly) and the filter controls, drag‑and‑drop panels, and live updates are Client Components. Your users see meaningful content instantly, and the interactive parts feel snappy because they’re only loading the JavaScript they actually need.

So go ahead—grab your red pill, step into the Next.js 14 world, and start splitting your UI into server and client pieces like a pro. You’ll be amazed at how much lighter your apps feel, and how much more you can focus on building features instead of fighting bundle bloat.

Your turn: Try converting an existing page to use a Server Component for the data‑heavy part and a Client Component for a single interactive widget. Notice the difference in network waterfall and time‑to‑interactive. Share your findings in the comments—let’s learn from each other’s quests! Happy coding!

title: How to Secure Java Docker Images and Reduce CVE Risk
description:
The Black Forest Commandos' field guide to CVEs, SBOMs, hardened images, attestations, and software supply chain security.

Your Java application can inherit vulnerable dependencies and packages from your base image before you write a single line of application code. Also, scanning your Docker image for vulnerabilities has blind spots, as the SBOM generated after the fact does not give you the full picture. A successful Docker build alone does not tell you what is shipped, how it was built, or whether you can trust it.

Asgard is under attack. Shadow creatures called CVEs have infiltrated the realm, and Thor's hammer is proving surprisingly ineffective. Odin has only one option: summon the Black Forest Commandos.

Behind the mythology is a practical question: How do we build container images that we can inspect, trust, and deploy with confidence?

Let's secure a Spring Boot sample project together, and with the help of the Commandos (CLI commands).

TL;DR

Most of the CVEs come from base images. Just swapping the baseline base image for a Docker hardened base image reduces the runtime inventory—the packages an attacker could actually reach—by 75.5%, with no application dependency changes between the two images.

Fewer number of packages, means less attack surface. Docker Hardened Images are also shipped with near-zero CVEs, non-root user, and no shell or package manager for the production images. So, even if an attacker gets inside your container, they won't have much to play with.

All these considered, swapping your base images won't make your application CVEs go away. That's why you should read the full article!

Start with the Ready-to-Run Sample

Before we start, let's check your toolset:

Checklist

  • Install Git to clone the sample repository.
  • Install and start Docker with Buildx. Check that docker info and docker buildx version work.
  • If not on Docker Desktop, install Docker Scout CLI separately. Check docker scout version.
  • Install Trivy and check trivy --version. The recorded run used 0.75.0.
  • Install Cosign and check cosign version. The recorded run used 3.1.3.
  • Have Bash, curl, and Python 3 available for the demo scripts.
  • Sign in to Docker Hub with docker login for Scout CVE queries.
  • Sign in to Docker Hardened Images with docker login dhi.io.

Docker builds, compiles, and tests the application, so you can follow this walkthrough without installing Java or Maven locally. Use a Bash-like terminal for the commands below.

Check Out the Tested Starting Point

The reference repository has two branches:

  • main, which is the state you will reach at the end of the article.
  • start, is the beginning of the journey.

We will start from there:

git clone --branch start --single-branch \
  https://github.com/ContainerSecurity-dev/dockerize-java-securely.git
cd dockerize-java-securely

You can edit and commit your experiments on this local branch. Base-image tags and vulnerability databases can still change, so your scan results may differ.

The files you'll use are:

  • src/ and pom.xml: the working application and its HTTP integration test.
  • Dockerfile.baseline: the starting image, using the official Maven and Eclipse Temurin images.
  • Dockerfile: the hardened version you'll compare against it.
  • scripts/: helpers to check the HTTP response and save vulnerability reports.

So, let it rip.

1. Build a Baseline You Can Inspect

The Commandos survey the ground before they fight. For us, that ground is a baseline image, built and pushed so it can be inspected.

We use a temporary, loopback-only registry so the audience can practice pushes and attestations without publishing application images to a public registry. This unauthenticated HTTP registry is for local demos only. For a remote registry, use an authenticated namespace you own over HTTPS.

docker run -d --name dockerize-java-demo-registry \
  -p 127.0.0.1:15000:5000 registry:3
export PLATFORM=linux/amd64   # use linux/arm64 on Apple Silicon
export IMAGE_REPO=127.0.0.1:15000/dockerize-java-securely
mkdir -p results

docker buildx build --platform "$PLATFORM" \
  -f Dockerfile.baseline \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  --metadata-file results/baseline-build-metadata.json \
  --push -t "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline" .

scripts/smoke-test.sh "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline"
export IMAGE="$IMAGE_REPO:baseline"

Let's unpack the commands:

  • The docker buildx build command is an extended command for building Docker images using BuildKit.
  • The flag --sbom=true instructs the builder to generate SBOM attestations: SBOM records "attached" to the image.
  • The flag --provenance=mode=max is used to generate provenance attestations. This attestation records more metadata about the build process.
  • As you can see, -f Dockerfile.baseline is used to specify the Dockerfile. So, the only non-optional argument, being the . at the end, is not actually the path to the Dockerfile, it's rather the build context, which is all the files that Docker can access and can potentionally end up in your Docker image.

View book

Also, if you inspect the smoke-test.sh file, it's running the image with the following flags:

docker run --detach --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true -p 127.0.0.1::8080 "$image"

The smoke test should return Hello, Docker Security! as user 10001:10001. The flags are used to run the container in a safer environment.

2. Know Your Enemy: CVEs and SBOMs

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) demonstrated why knowing which dependencies we ship matters. An SBOM, or Software Bill of Materials, is a list of software components in your application. Having this list handy helps you identify your packages in case there is a known exploit in one of them. Having it does not make your application safer by itself.

Rothütle's first mission in Asgard is to discover who lives there. Using Docker Scout, you can check the list using docker scout sbom command:

docker scout sbom "$IMAGE" --format list
docker scout sbom "$IMAGE" --format spdx --output results/sbom.spdx.json

How many packages are listed here?

Output of those commands will mention the SBOM attestation being used. If the attestation is absent from the build, Docker Scout will try to build it by scanning your files.

In the docker buildx build command we ran, we have created an SBOM attestation, and the Docker Scout command picked it up. But, the SBOM only contains packages from the final stage, which is not a full picture. A compromised build-time package can still write a backdoor into your application.

Further reading:

generating-an-sbom-with-docker-scout

3. Hunt the CVEs: Docker Scout and Trivy

Jack, our cybernetic scout, now dressing as Jack-o'-Lantern for Halloween, can detect CVEs hiding inside container images.

docker scout cves "$IMAGE"
docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high "$IMAGE"

Docker Scout is an enterprise offering, free for personal use. Trivy is an open-source alternative and similarly an industry standard.

trivy image --scanners vuln "$IMAGE"
trivy image --scanners vuln --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 "$IMAGE"

The final command should return exit code 1, because there are high and/or critical CVEs in the image. That is a security gate you should add to your workflow.
Let's save machine-readable reports with the repository's helper:

# Saves JSON, summarizes findings, and exits 1 if the gate fails.
scripts/scan.sh "$IMAGE" results/baseline-trivy.json

The scan.sh script runs Trivy under the hood, but also stores the reports and parses them. A similar script would be in your pipeline, e.g., to report the number of CVEs via a pull request comment.

Note that, severity is not the same as exploitability, and malicious software does not necessarily have a CVE. Scanner databases and package matching also differ: the same baseline yielded different totals in Scout and Trivy. Compare images within the same scanner and inspect the affected packages.

4. Include the Build Stage in Your SBOM

Rothütle suspects the inventory is incomplete: some components were present while the application was built, not only while it runs.

The baseline uses a multi-stage build, but --sbom=true alone inventories the final image. Packages used only while compiling the application can disappear from that inventory when the build stage is discarded.

First inspect the baseline's attached SBOM and provenance:

docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline" --format '{{json .SBOM}}' > results/baseline-sbom.json
docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline" --format '{{json .Provenance}}' > results/baseline-provenance.json

Now edit Dockerfile.baseline. Add this argument immediately after the build stage's FROM line:

FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true

Rebuild under a separate tag so you can compare the two inventories:

docker buildx build --platform "$PLATFORM" \
  -f Dockerfile.baseline \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  --metadata-file results/baseline-build-sbom-metadata.json \
  --push -t "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline-build-sbom" .

docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline-build-sbom" --format '{{json .SBOM}}' > results/baseline-with-build-sbom.json

The new output includes an additional sbom-build document alongside the runtime SPDX inventory. The argument adds metadata about the packages from earlier stages, and it doesn't mean those packages end up in the final image.

  • SBOM: What software was inventoried in the image and covered build stages?
  • Provenance: How was the image built, and from which materials?

Use BuildKit secret mounts for credentials. Maximum-level provenance can expose build arguments, so never put secrets in them. Furthermore, an attached attestation is not automatically a trusted cryptographic signature.

Now, how many packages are listed in the SBOM attestations?

Further reading:

the-poisoned-macchiato

5. Harden the Runtime and Measure the Difference

Armor time. Docker Hardened Images are a set of open-source and near-zero-CVE base images, designed to "armor" your Docker image against future attacks. You can check their catalog on dhi.io.

Let's swap the base image for the hardened ones:

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM dhi.io/maven:3-jdk21-dev AS build
ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B verify

FROM dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-alpine3.23
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/app.jar /app/app.jar
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

If you check the sample repo, there is a file .dockerignore there with the following content:

**
!pom.xml
!src/
!src/**
!Dockerfile
!Dockerfile.baseline

This means, everything is ignored by the docker buildx build command (removed from the build context), except for the listed files. This is called an allowlist. So, instead of ignoring a bunch of files, we ignore everything, and allow a bunch of files.

Also, the POM sets finalName to app, avoiding an ambiguous JAR wildcard.

This follows Docker's Java DHI migration pattern, with explicit tests and a non-root runtime user.

docker buildx build --platform "$PLATFORM" \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  --metadata-file results/hardened-build-metadata.json \
  --push -t "$IMAGE_REPO:hardened" .

scripts/smoke-test.sh "$IMAGE_REPO:hardened"
# Also returns 1 for the recorded sample:
scripts/scan.sh "$IMAGE_REPO:hardened" results/hardened-trivy.json
python3 scripts/summarize-scans.py results/baseline-trivy.json results/hardened-trivy.json

It's report time! You can run all of them yourself, or just read through mine!

Observed results: 13 October 2026

Both final application images use Spring Boot 4.0.8 and Java 21. The results are based on runs on Linux Ubuntu (linux/amd64) and Mac Silicon (linux/arm64), yielding identical results. These are Trivy 0.75.0 vulnerability records, grouped by scan target; totals are not counts of unique CVE IDs across all packages.

Scan target Baseline: eclipse-temurin:21-jre Hardened: dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-alpine3.23
OS packages 0 critical, 0 high, 40 medium, 4 low No findings
Java dependencies 3 critical, 5 high, 2 medium 3 critical, 5 high, 2 medium
Other detected binary (pebble) 3 high, 5 medium, 1 low, 4 unknown Not present as a scan target

Docker Scout 1.20.3 reported 5 critical / 13 high / 2 medium / 3 unspecified for the baseline and 3 critical / 5 high / 2 medium for the hardened image. Those are separate scanner observations, not interchangeable with the Trivy counts.

The original Spring Boot 4.0.5 sample had 9 critical / 18 high / 20 medium / 6 low Java findings in Trivy. Updating to 4.0.8 reduced those findings, but did not eliminate them. The remaining Java findings implicated Tomcat and Jackson dependencies. Review the report's fixed-version guidance, update the application dependencies, rerun tests, and rescan before promotion.

Inspect the Blast Radius in Your Dependency Tree

"Update Tomcat and Jackson" is easier said than done, because most of these libraries arrive transitively through the Spring Boot BOM. Inspect what your project actually resolves before you touch a version:

# Full resolved tree (run inside the builder image if you have no local JDK):
./mvnw -B dependency:tree

# Narrow it to the packages the scanner flagged:
./mvnw -B dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-core
./mvnw -B dependency:tree -Dincludes=tools.jackson.core:jackson-core

I can't believe it's 2026 and Maven flags still look like that. Dincludes. Anyway!

The tree shows each artifact's depth and the path that pulled it in. A dependency you declare directly in pom.xml can be overridden there or in a <dependencyManagement> entry; a transitive one usually needs a version override or an updated parent/BOM. After the change, confirm the fix reaches the runtime JAR, rerun mvn verify, and rescan the new digest. If an affected artifact is transitive and has no fix yet, record that in a VEX statement instead of silently suppressing it.

Check VEX Before Comparing Scanners

VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) records whether a particular vulnerability affects a product. One can create VEX records for CVEs that are harmless in their case. One can ship them with their Docker image as "VEX attestations". Docker Hardened Image come with their own VEX attestations.

Docker Scout automatically applies DHI VEX statements and excludes them from the listed CVEs; Trivy needs VEX enabled:

docker scout cves dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:8-alpine3.23

# Configure and download the DHI VEX repository first (see linked instructions).
trivy image --scanners vuln --vex repo dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:8-alpine3.23

For Trivy, enable the docker-hardened-images/advisories repository in its VEX configuration and download it before using --vex repo. Review applicable VEX statements; suppression is an assessment of affectedness, not a dependency fix.

This can sometimes explain differences in reported CVEs without any change to the image. See Docker’s VEX-aware scanning instructions.

The recorded Trivy scans above did not enable VEX. However, the observed difference between Scout and Trivy was in the non-DHI baseline, so it was not coming from VEX attestations.

Both images passed the HTTP smoke test. In the recorded comparison, with build-stage scanning enabled, the runtime SBOM contained 192 packages for the baseline and 47 for the hardened image; the separate build-stage inventories contained 396 and 377, respectively. Hence, just by swapping for a DHI base image, the number of dependencies in the production image is reduced by 75%. Hence the Artemisia bar chart image, as she's squashing the attack surface!

The results report records image digests, versions, and evidence.

docker-hardened-images-are-free

6. Sign Before You Trust: Cosign

Evie is the Commando responsible for cryptographic signatures. She always uses the immutable digest returned by the build, rather than a mutable tag:

export DIGEST_IMAGE="$IMAGE_REPO@$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("results/hardened-build-metadata.json"))["containerimage.digest"])')"
mkdir -p .demo-keys
cosign generate-key-pair --output-key-prefix .demo-keys/cosign
cosign sign --key .demo-keys/cosign.key "$DIGEST_IMAGE"
cosign verify --key .demo-keys/cosign.pub "$DIGEST_IMAGE"

# Scan the same immutable artifact; this sample still fails the gate.
trivy image --scanners vuln --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 "$DIGEST_IMAGE"

Cosign 3.1.3 successfully verifies the signature, claims, and transparency-log inclusion. The vulnerability gate still returns 1. A signed image can contain known vulnerabilities.

Keep the private key out of Git; the sample ignores .demo-keys/ and *.key. Enter a key password interactively and use a disposable key for rehearsal. Default signing publishes signature metadata and the public key to a transparency log. Production verification needs a trusted signing policy, not an arbitrary public key supplied alongside an image.

We sign the image to make sure no one altered it on the way to production. But, the attackers are getting smarter. Read the Shai Hulud family account to learn about the incident that a signed image was altered by the attacker:

taxonomy-of-modern-supply-chain-worms

7. SIP It Before You Ship It

The Shai-Hulud family illustrates why scanning a final image is not enough: malicious packages can target developers and CI before an image exists. AI coding agents are another environment with access to code, tools, and potentially credentials.

SIP: Security Immediate Plan ties the controls together:

  1. Sandbox agents. Isolate execution and restrict credentials, network access, and mounted directories.
  2. Lock down dependencies. Manage Maven dependency and plugin versions, inspect the resolved tree, and review updates. Gradle and npm projects need their own locking and install policies; this Maven sample does not exercise those tools.
  3. Harden builds. Keep compilers and build tools in the build stage, and run the final image without root privileges.
  4. Attest. Generate SBOM and provenance, including relevant build stages.
  5. Scan before promotion. Scan the exact digest, enforce your vulnerability policy, and verify trusted signatures before deployment.

Sandbox → Lock → Harden → Attest → Scan. No single scanner, image, or signature secures the entire supply chain. For agent isolation and ecosystem-specific dependency controls, see the full SIP implementation.

This walkthrough demonstrates three of those controls end to end on a real Java image: Harden (a DHI runtime running as a non-root user), Attest (SBOM and provenance, including the build stage), and Scan (gating the exact digest before promotion). It touches Lock only partially, through the Maven dependency tree and version discipline shown above; full dependency locking for Gradle and npm projects is outside this sample. Sandbox agents—isolating AI coding agents and restricting their credentials, network access, and mounts—is not exercised here at all, so treat it as an additional SIP control rather than something this experiment proved.

Read more about sbx and kits here:

docker-sandbox-kits-tutorial

When finished, remove the dedicated local registry and its temporary data:

docker rm -f dockerize-java-demo-registry

Conclusion

Three findings came out of this run, and they map directly onto the Commando team:

Key takeaways

  • Hardened base images reduce OS-level exposure. The DHI runtime dropped from 192 inventoried packages to 47 (75.5%) and removed all 44 Ubuntu package findings and the pebble binary target, without changing any application dependency.
  • SBOM attestations improve visibility. --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max attaches what shipped and how it was built, and BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true extends the inventory to the build stage.
  • Application dependency remediation remains essential. Tomcat and Jackson kept the same 3 critical and 5 high findings in both images, so hardening and signing never replaced updating libraries.

Hardening the base image and signing the result are necessary, not sufficient. The Commandos' armor kept out the creatures that came with the base image; the ones hiding inside Tomcat and Jackson are a different fight, and it is fought at the dependency level. Fix what you ship, prove how you built it, and scan the exact digest before it reaches production.

Keep Learning: Articles and Tutorials

  • Generating SBOM with Docker Scout — inspect and export software inventories.
  • The Poisoned Macchiato — Java SBOM attestations, Cosign, and OCI artifacts.
  • Docker Hardened Images are Free — hardened base images and vulnerability comparisons.
  • The Shai-Hulud Family — taxonomy of modern supply chain worms.
  • Docker Sandbox Kits: A Hands-On Tutorial — agent isolation and capability controls.
  • Black Forest Commandos: Asgard Mission DIY — a longer, hands-on version of the Commandos' mission.

Official Documentation

  • Docker Scout SBOM CLI
  • Docker Scout CVE CLI
  • Docker BuildKit SBOM attestations
  • Docker BuildKit provenance
  • Trivy
  • Sigstore Cosign
  • Docker Sandboxes

Meet the Black Forest Commandos in My Books

  • Docker and Kubernetes Security. To learn about Linux capabilities (the ones that we dropped here), or secure CI workflows, check this book.
  • Black Forest Shadow. The origin story of Gord, Rothütle, Evie, and the CVE monsters, set in the Black Forest in 1865.
  • Black Forest Commandos: Asgard Mission. The graphic novel behind the Commandos' adventure in Asgard. The story expands the mythology used in my talks and workshops. Do you want to know the ending? Spoiler alert!

SIP it before you ship it.

Mohammad-Ali A'râbi — Docker Captain, author, and creator of the Black Forest Commandos.

Results are a dated snapshot from the linked sample. Review versions, permissions, and security policies and rerun the checks before production use.
