title: Taste is not a design methodology
description:
It has become our favorite answer to AI-generated sameness. The reality is good products come from judgment built on facts, and the agency to use them when the room prefers opinions.

Ask Rick Rubin what he does and he’ll tell you he has “no technical ability” and knows nothing about music. In a 2023 interview with Anderson Cooper, the producer said artists pay him for confidence in his own taste.

https://medium.com/media/1f83a53654c7bc936b099303acddda54/href
“The confidence I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.” — Rick Rubin

Everyone now wants that job.

Just typing this makes me squirm because I believe the field should be research and data driven as much as it can be. With humans even.

“Taste is the new moat” might be the industry’s favorite sentence of 2026: artificial intelligence made competent screens cheap, so the one thing left to sell is the judgment to pick the good one. A ProductLed interview in January went further, telling builders not to validate before they build. It’s about 45 minutes in.

I decided not to show the video inline because it adds fuel to the fire and their use of typography isn’t to my taste.

It’s come up with couple of authors I follow — The taste paradox by Nicole Alexandra Michaelis is a good read over at UX Collective, and Xinran Ma had a interview recently about it in UX — and it’s in the zeitgeist.

My point is that it’s the wrong word.

The moat crowd is right that judgment matters; they’re wrong about where it comes from:

  • Taste is a preference. It comes from what you’ve seen and who you admire, and two people with different taste can disagree with no way to settle it.
  • Judgment is a claim you can check. It rests on principles research has tested, plus evidence about your users, so it can be explained, taught, and shown wrong.

Judgment needs agency too, because someone has to raise those facts when the most senior voice would rather trade opinions. What Nicole Alexandra Michaelis and Xinran Ma are talking about Judgement i.e. experience they can back with facts and experience.

The short rule: if you can’t name the fact or research behind a call, it’s still an opinion, which is otherwise known as taste.

Admit taste is an opinion

In 2001, researchers in Bordeaux and Montpellier gave a panel of 54 tasters a white wine colored red with an odorless dye. The panel described it with the vocabulary of red wine.

Nothing had changed but the color, and that was enough to overwrite their noses.

That’s the trouble with treating taste as a standard: it’s an opinion that feels like a fact. Two skilled designers can look at the same screen, reach opposite conclusions, and neither can prove the other mistaken.

Taste feels like perception, but a lot of it is expectation. Apple Music is probably the best example, it’s Apple, but still a challenging application to use established as fact.

For example, I like driving Audi TTs. A lot.

The proportions, the way one sits on a highway on-ramp, the complete impracticality of the back seat, the beautifully designed cockpit, the race to 110 miles per hour in California.

That last part is just storytelling, really.

I don’t expect any of that to be anyone else’s taste, and nothing is wrong when it isn’t, because my taste in cars only has to satisfy only me. A product has to work for thousands of people who never met me for it to be profitable, and that’s where a preference stops being enough.

My expectation is that Audi TT’s are designed for my taste, and it doesn’t fail me, ever.

Design has its own version of the wine study.

In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura of Hitachi had people rate 26 ATM layouts and found that how usable a layout looked tracked its beauty far more than its inherent usability. The field now calls this the aesthetic-usability effect, and it cuts both ways.

Generative tools make this worse because they turn out polished screens by default, so every option in the review looks finished. That’s the blind spot in the moat argument: the less polish costs, the less polish can tell you.

It reminds me of a conversation I had with Scott Jenson — Generative AI makes a lot of beautifully just above average screens. I made that argument they’re still better than a lot of portfolios I have seen, even if the screens have less depth.

This is why “does it have taste?” makes a weak review question: it has no failure condition other than an opinion.

Ruiqi Zhou called taste unfalsifiable in a February essay named Taste Is the New Moat — And That’s the Problem. It’s a great read, and points out that a standard you can never fail works more like a status marker, and status markers reward whoever already holds status. Usually, that’s product management.

Build judgment on laws that have held for centuries

User experience borrowed its foundations from people who ran experiments, and they had computers in only some cases.

Here are examples:

  • Paul Fitts showed in 1954 that the time to hit a target depends on its size and distance using fighter cockpits for research, and William Edmund Hick showed that decision time climbs as options pile up. Both findings have held up for seven decades.
  • Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich developed heuristic evaluation in 1990, and the ten heuristics are still the default checklist. Each turns an opinion into a checkable claim, like a button too small for a thumb.
  • Dieter Rams and his ten principles took what could have stayed personal taste and wrote it down where other people could use it, which is why teams still audit work against them fifty years on.

They are normative rather than experimental, but a checklist can be argued with. I keep plain-language summaries of Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, Nielsen’s heuristics, and Rams’s principles on ux-guidelines.com, a reference site I maintain. Every law has conditions, and knowing them is part of judgment.

Hick’s Law describes a choice among equally likely options, and a 1985 study of its exceptions found cases where adding choices barely slowed people down. Fitts measured people tapping a stylus between two targets, not a thumb stretching across a phone.

A law applied outside its conditions is just another opinion with a citation.

Principles don’t settle everything.

At Microsoft, Ronny Kohavi’s team reported that only about a third of well-run experiments improved the metric they were designed to move. The laws tell you what’s likely, and testing tells you what happened.

User research earns its place next to the laws for the same reason.

A law is general and your users are specific, so only watching them shows which steps they repeat and where they give up. Teresa Torres makes the cadence the point, defining continuous discovery as weekly contact with customers by the team building the product, rather than a study that lands after the decision.

Test beauty with the people who will use it

None of this means beauty is decoration. The same aesthetic-usability effect explains why users forgive attractive products, and appearance shapes trust and first impressions.

Don Norman gave the effect a mechanism in Emotional Design: a positive mood broadens thinking and makes people more forgiving of small friction. Jony Ive’s teams built the most admired hardware of their era and also shipped the butterfly keyboard, which Apple settled a class action over for $50 million in 2022 after years of complaints.

Taste operating at that altitude still needed someone to check whether the thing worked.

The mistake is assuming the designer’s eye can stand in for the audience’s. Nielsen Norman Group showed the same five screenshots to 229 adults aged 18 to 25 and 228 aged 35 and older,

The results?

  • The younger group rated the flat designs slightly more attractive.
  • The older, slightly less attractive.

Whose taste was right? Each group’s, for itself.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, especially in enterprise software, where the person who admires the demo is rarely the one who lives in the product eight hours a day.

Beauty is a user outcome, so measure it like one.

That’s where the line between fact and opinion falls here. What users report about a screen is a fact about your audience, while a design lead’s verdict is one more opinion, however practiced the eye behind it. The survey used a modified version of the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit, which asks people to pick words that describe what they see from a fixed list.

Score task success and time on task separately from those ratings, so a polished prototype can’t inflate the verdict on whether the thing works.

Teach the principles before the portfolio

In 2009, two researchers who had spent careers on opposite sides of this argument wrote a paper together. Daniel Kahneman had documented how judgment fails, while Gary Klein had defended expert intuition in the field.

Their joint answer on when intuition deserves trust came down to two conditions:

  • The environment has to be regular enough to learn about who they’re designing for
  • The person needs a real chance to learn it

Design taste rarely gets that chance. A designer ships a screen, moves on to the next project, and never finds out whether the choice helped anyone.

Confidence grows with years, but accuracy only grows with feedback.

Tell a designer two years out of school to trust their taste, after a portfolio course, maybe an internship, and very few closed loops between a decision and its outcome. What they have is exposure to showcase sites and admired apps, which produces taste that matches the feed, not the user.

Principles are the shortcut experience can’t hand out, and they come with standing. A junior designer who knows Hick’s Law can push back on a longer menu in her first critique, and a new hire who has studied the heuristics can flag a missing undo before anyone senior does.

Facts give people the agency that seniority usually keeps for itself.

Give everyone the agency to argue from facts

Taste has a politics problem.

When the standard is taste, the taste that counts usually belongs to the most senior person present. Ron Kohavi named it in a 2008 Stanford talk, Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO: the HiPPO is the highest-paid person’s opinion.

A taste culture is a HiPPO culture with better typography.

The fix isn’t to ban taste from the room, it’s to stop one person from owning it without evidence.

Everybody on a team has taste, and the new designer’s is worth as much as the vice president’s, which is exactly why it makes a poor standard: nothing decides whose version wins except rank. Facts don’t work that way, since a law or a session recording says the same thing no matter who reads it out.

Taste cultures have a patron saint they misappropriated: Steve Jobs.

He told BusinessWeek in 1998 that designing by focus group is hard. People, he said, “don’t know what they want until you show it to them.” It gets quoted as permission to skip research, though the same answer described watching trends and studying Apple’s installed base.

But even he met his match in Paul Rand.

When Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT in 1986, he hired Rand, whom he openly called the greatest living graphic designer. The friction came immediately: Jobs asked for a few options, and Rand refused, saying he would solve the problem and Jobs would pay him, and if he wanted options he could hire someone else.

Jobs agreed to the terms and the $100,000 fee. Rand returned with one design, the tilted black cube, presented in a hand-bound booklet that walked Jobs through the reasoning until the logo felt inevitable.

Jobs loved it, and later admitted that you don’t hand a genius a menu.

Because of this, Apple did research all the time and that gave Jobs credibility to make judgement calls. Those that claim they have the same truly understand the company, nor how to combine taste with judgement.

Even Steve Jobs’ famous 2x2 Matrix Strategy is rooted in science — Paradox of Choice.

The larger problem is survivorship bias, another old law. We remember the founder whose certainty paid off and forget the rooms where the same certainty sank the product with dollar amount attached to it.

Agency with receipts is the fix.

Session notes, retention data, and a heuristic all lose to a senior “that feels off,” unless the team agrees that facts outrank opinions.

With that agreement in place, the quietest person in the room can win by naming the law a design breaks or the data point it ignores. Peter Merholz argues that design executives earn that standing by making design their secondary concern.

The fair counterargument belongs to Doug Bowman, Google’s first visual designer.

In 2009 he left and explained why in Goodbye, Google: a team was testing 41 shades of blue, and he had been asked to prove whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide.

His complaint went past the trivia: with nobody senior who understood design, he argued, the company ran out of reasons for its decisions, and data became “a crutch for every decision” that kept anything daring from shipping.

$200 million later. Hard to argue that as an outcome.

Measuring everything is its own way of dodging judgment, so decisions slow to the test calendar, and designers who could settle a border width from a principle leave for places where that counts, as Bowman did.

Aim evidence at the choices that change what users can do. A corner radius needs no significance test, since a law settles it faster.

Choose facts over opinions

Judgment is knowing which facts apply, and where they stop applying: a law, a heuristic, a published study, or research on your own users. Where taste says “this feels right,” judgment points out that the target is too small to tap reliably and that Fitts showed why in 1954.

Agency is saying that out loud in the review, even when it cuts against the most senior opinion in the room.

Judgment tells you which facts matter, and agency is using them when the room prefers an opinion.

The new reality:

  • Generative tools can produce fifty layouts before my morning coffee.
  • Judgment cuts the pile fast, dropping the ones with targets too small to hit, menus too long to scan, and flows that ask people to hold too much in their heads.
  • What’s left goes to research, where users settle what the principles can’t.

Teams that run interviews and usability sessions on a schedule build a store of facts they can reach for in any review, and teams that skip them are left with preferences and a deadline. Dan Maccarone spent a year rebuilding his studio’s process around these tools and found that it didn’t make the work faster, which he counts as the point: what changed was where the thinking had to happen.

Rubin’s approach works because a record has no task to fail. A designer who borrows that job description claims the authority without the conditions that make it hold.

Judgment also improves in a way taste doesn’t, if somebody writes the call down. Jeff Gothelf formalizes that in the Lean UX canvas: state what you believe will happen, then name the evidence that would tell you whether you were right. It’s the equivalent of the Change My Mind meme, and it’s brilliant.

Picture two designers.

  • One moves a filter panel above the results because Hick’s Law favors fewer competing choices on the way to what people came for, predicts lower search abandonment, and checks the numbers six weeks after launch.
  • The other spends the same six weeks studying award-winning screen shots.

Only the first one learned something new about their users, and only their judgment got sharper.

Conclusion

Taste isn’t going away, and it isn’t the real enemy.

Opinions shape style, brand voice, and the small choices no principle covers. The trouble starts when an opinion gets treated as a fact and wins arguments it hasn’t earned.

The moat story is half right.

Artificial intelligence does make average output cheap, and plenty of products will look alike because of it. The scarce skill isn’t picking the prettiest variation, it’s knowing which ones break what the field already knows, which ones deserve a test, and what the result means for the next decision.

The wine panel in Bordeaux wasn’t foolish; its members were human, and so are we. That’s the whole reason design has laws and methods at all.

Human perception drifts toward what it expects to see, and principles are how a field keeps itself honest across decades of new tools.

So learn the laws, read the research carefully, and give your team the agency to use both. Then let your users decide the rest. Judgment you can explain, backed by the nerve to raise it, will outlast taste you can only defend, and teams built on it will ship the products everyone else ends up copying.

Action Items

  • Ask “what fact supports this?” instead of “does it have taste?” In critiques, every significant call should rest on a principle, a study, or something your users did. If nobody can name one, label the call an opinion and flag it for testing.
  • Teach the laws before the look. Give junior designers Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, cognitive load theory, and Nielsen’s heuristics before mood boards. Principles hand them decades of feedback, and the standing to use it.
  • Make it safe to push back with facts. Say plainly that a cited principle or data point outranks a job title, and back the junior designer who uses one against you. Agency that gets punished once rarely shows up twice.
  • Test where the facts run out. Brand feel, new interaction patterns, and cases where two laws conflict all need research. Run a usability session, a few interviews, or a first-click test that week, and log the prediction behind it. Leave the border widths alone.

Taste is not a design methodology was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Amazon ECS adds LiveTaskCount and removes the charge for RunningTaskCount metric
description:
Today, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) announces LiveTaskCount, a new ECS service metric that reports how many tasks are actively running in your service, available to all customers at no additional charge. Additionally, the existing RunningTaskCount metric in Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights no longer incurs a charge.

LiveTaskCount reports the number of actively running ECS tasks across all desired states (ACTIVATING, RUNNING, and DEACTIVATING), including tasks still running while transitioning to a stopped state, for example, tasks undergoing connection draining during a scale-in event. This comprehensive state coverage makes LiveTaskCount well suited for autoscaling policies and capacity planning where a complete view of active, metric-generating tasks is required. It is available at no charge as part of ECS service utilization metrics and does not require opting in to CloudWatch Container Insights. The existing CloudWatch Container Insights RunningTaskCount metric tracks tasks where both the current and desired state are RUNNING, and continues to serve as a health and stability signal for customers who depend on it. With today's update, RunningTaskCount is now available at no additional charge for all CloudWatch Container Insights users.

These updates are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECS is available. No action is required, and the pricing change for RunningTaskCount takes effect beginning October 1, 2026, and applies automatically. To learn more, see ECS CloudWatch metrics and ECS Container Insights metrics. For a pricing example, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing.

title: AWS Lambda durable functions increases durable operation and checkpoint payload limits
description:
Starting today, AWS Lambda durable functions increases the maximum number of durable operations per execution from 3,000 to 30,000, and the maximum checkpoint payload size from 256 KB to 1 MB. Higher operation limits let you safely do more work in a single execution including expanding iterative loops, polling for longer time periods, and building more complex rollback paths that run when a step fails. At 1 MB, checkpoint payloads match the maximum payload size of asynchronous Lambda invocations, and integration services such as Amazon SQS, and Amazon EventBridge, so a workflow can persist a full event from any of these sources in a single operation.

AWS Lambda durable functions helps you build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that execute for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing, automatic retries, and waits that suspend execution without incurring compute charges. Every durable operation counts toward the per-execution limit, including each step attempt, each poll of a wait-for-condition, and each branch of a parallel or map operation. With 30,000 operations, a single execution has more room to coordinate complex, multi-step workflows, iterate across thousands of items, or poll an external system for weeks, without exceeding checkpoint limits.

An agentic application can reason over thousands of model and tool calls, and with 1 MB checkpoints it persists larger conversation histories, model responses, and outputs from tools directly in the checkpoint instead of writing to external storage. For state larger than 1 MB, the JavaScript and Python SDKs include a FileSystem serializer that writes the payload to an Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files mount and checkpoints a pointer instead.

 The new limits apply in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more about these service limits, see the AWS Lambda developer guide.

title: How to photograph a job site for a quote without emailing 12 MB files
description:
When a contractor quotes a repair, the photos matter. They show the customer what you saw, and they protect you later if someone asks what the wall looked like before you started. But phone photos create two practical problems: they are huge, and they often contain more than you meant to share.

Take photos that support the quote

  • One wide shot, then close-ups. The wide shot shows where the problem is. The close-up shows what it is.
  • Put something in the frame for scale, like a tape measure or a hand.
  • Shoot the same angle before and after so the change is obvious.
  • Keep the number small. Six clear photos beat forty similar ones.

Shrink them before sending

A modern phone photo is often several MB. Four of them can bounce an email or choke a text message on a weak connection. Resizing to a width of around 1600 pixels keeps them readable on a phone and brings each one down to a few hundred KB. Most phones and free desktop tools can do this, and the quote tool you use should do it for you.

Check what is in the picture

  • Photos can carry location data in their metadata. Strip it if you share outside the job.
  • Look for the customer's mail, documents, family photos and screens in the background.
  • Keep job photos private to the job. A public link to an image is a link anyone can forward.

Tie the photos to the estimate

The best place for the photos is the estimate itself, so the customer approves the work with the evidence next to the price. One record per job also means you can find the pictures again when a change order comes up.

I build JobNeatly, which lets you attach resized private photos to an estimate and send it as a link the customer can sign from their phone. Estimates are free; the first three approvals are free, then $9 per approval or $19 a month. It does not send automatic reminders. (Disclosure: I'm the maker.)

title: Realtime Event Observability API Boundaries Explained for Go (Live Auction Dashboards)
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API for transport, but make presence, subscription state, authentication, and auction events separate observable signals; clients need stable event identifiers so they can reconcile after reconnecting instead of guessing what they missed.

For a live auction dashboard, presence accuracy is the deciding constraint. A green socket indicator doesn't prove that a bidder is authenticated, subscribed to the right auction, or caught up to the current bid. I would treat those as different states, attach an SLO to each one, and choose an API boundary only after the client and server responsibilities are written down. Infrai is a credible option for the publish boundary when a team expects to add other backend capabilities later: its 295 routes across 20 modules share one REST surface, so the integration does not require another SDK and credential set for every new module. The catch is that this breadth is less important when realtime is the product's dominant technical problem; in that case, evaluate a specialist first.

How should realtime event observability define API boundaries for a live auction dashboard?

Start with four signals, not one catch-all “connected” metric. Authentication answers whether the session may act. Subscription state answers whether the client asked for and received the intended auction channel. Presence answers whether the system currently considers the participant present. Business-event progress answers whether the client has applied the latest known auction event. Mixing these together makes a dashboard look healthy while it is stale — precisely the failure an operator needs the screen to expose.

The boundary should also say who owns recovery. The server returns stable identifiers and publishes events with enough application-level identity for a client to detect duplicates or gaps. The client persists its last applied identifier, reconnects, and reconciles before declaring itself current. Expiry and partial failure are normal states, not exceptional branches hidden behind a generic red badge.

Keep it explicit.

For capacity planning, model reconnects as bursts. If 10,000 viewers lose connectivity at once, the steady-state event rate tells you very little about the resulting authentication, subscription, presence, and replay pressure. The useful SLO is therefore not merely “socket connected”; it is a bound on time from reconnect to reconciled auction state, measured alongside the share of clients whose presence and event cursor agree. The exact target depends on auction rules and traffic shape. I'm not sure a universal number would be defensible without peak concurrency, event rate, and acceptable staleness; those three inputs should resolve it.

Choose the boundary before the vendor

The buy-versus-build decision is mostly an ownership decision. A managed transport can remove infrastructure work, but it cannot decide whether a late bid is valid, define the authoritative auction sequence, or choose what the dashboard shows during reconciliation. Those remain application responsibilities.

Option Setup and credential question What to verify for this dashboard Better fit when
Build and operate the transport Can the platform team own deployment, scaling, and on-call response? Presence semantics, reconnect bursts, replay, and operator visibility Realtime behavior is core intellectual property and lock-in is unacceptable
Pusher How many SDKs and credentials enter the application and CI system? Presence accuracy and reconciliation behavior under the auction's traffic shape A specialist evaluation proves a closer fit than a broad backend surface
Ably How quickly can a Go service produce the first useful event and expose recovery state? Stable identifiers, subscription observability, and reconnect semantics Specialist realtime depth dominates integration consolidation
PubNub Which client and server responsibilities are imposed by the chosen integration? Authentication, presence, and business-event signals can be inspected separately The specialist's contract matches the required presence model
Infrai Can plain HTTP and one key reduce integration and credential sprawl? The publish boundary and presence query meet the application's explicit contract The team values a consistent surface across multiple backend modules

This table is an evaluation runbook, not a benchmark result. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub deserve workload-specific tests before selection; no latency, uptime, or presence-accuracy measurements are asserted here. Stick with a specialist when its realtime model wins those tests or when deep realtime controls matter more than reducing SDK surface. Self-host when the team can afford the on-call load and needs direct control over recovery semantics. Infrai should be tried by platform teams that need a small publish integration now and expect adjacent backend work later, because its broad module set remains accessible through the same plain REST contract. A second practical benefit is discovery: the public discovery surface returns request schema, response schema, billing details, and runnable examples, which shortens the path from a route name to a reviewable integration without committing the codebase to another vendor SDK.

Implement reconciliation as application logic

Do not guess a publish payload from a route name. The small Go program below asks Infrai's public discovery surface for the current metadata, locates the verified realtime publish capability, then retrieves its full request and response schema. It is a read-only first integration: a reviewer can inspect the actual contract before anyone writes transport-specific auction code. The API key is still read from the environment and sent with Bearer authentication, so the HTTP client can be reused when the integration moves from public discovery to an authenticated capability.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type Discovery struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

type Capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(when); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func get(client *http.Client, endpoint, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status=%d body=%s", endpoint, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: retry limit reached after rate limiting", endpoint)
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    body, err := get(client, baseURL+"/discovery", key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var manifest Discovery
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode discovery: %w", err)
    }

    var publish Capability
    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/realtime/publish" {
            publish = capability
            break
        }
    }
    if publish.ID == "" || !publish.Available {
        return fmt.Errorf("realtime publish capability is not available in discovery")
    }

    detailBody, err := get(client, baseURL+"/discovery/"+url.PathEscape(publish.ID), key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var detail Capability
    if err := json.Unmarshal(detailBody, &detail); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode capability: %w", err)
    }

    fmt.Printf("%s %s\nrequest schema: %s\n", detail.Method, detail.Path, detail.Params)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The discovery response exposes capability IDs, methods, paths, availability, and vendor readiness; the single-capability response adds the full request JSON Schema and response schema. Generate the eventual request from that path field and schema, rather than from descriptive prose. After publishing is wired, the application should stop its “current” indicator on an event gap, fetch authoritative state through its own recovery boundary, and replace the cursor only after reconciliation succeeds. Authentication, subscription health, presence, and business-event progress still need separate signals.

The same discipline applies to a live poll during a gaming session. A vote event, participant presence, and permission to vote are related, but they aren't interchangeable. A reconnecting player should not be counted twice merely because the presence view and the applied event cursor recover at different speeds.

Verify the failure modes, not the happy path

The first useful test is a forced disconnect between two consecutive auction events. Record the last stable identifier on the client, reconnect, and verify that the dashboard stays in a reconciling state until its authoritative auction state and event cursor agree. Repeat with an expired credential, a lost subscription, a duplicate event, and an event sequence gap. Each result should land in a distinct metric or structured log field; one aggregate connection error discards the evidence needed during an incident.

Then test the herd. Ramp concurrent reconnects toward the expected peak rather than extrapolating from a single client, and watch the full path: credential issuance, subscription restoration, presence convergence, recovery reads, and business-event application. Capacity should be reserved against that recovery path. Otherwise, a transport that is comfortable at steady state may still miss the only SLO users notice during a network interruption.

There is a standards boundary too. WebRTC defines browser-facing real-time communication primitives, but adopting it does not remove the application-level obligation to distinguish presence from auction state; the recommendation is available at https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/. For a dashboard that only consumes server-published state, don't select a richer media-oriented path without evidence that it improves the required presence and recovery behavior.

Roll back without corrupting auction state

Rollback should switch transport adapters, not auction semantics. Keep the application envelope, cursor storage, and reconciliation rules outside the provider-specific client. During a migration, shadow the candidate path with non-authoritative events and compare stable identifiers, ordering, presence observations, and reconnect completion before moving readers. Avoid dual-authoritative publishing unless the business layer has an idempotent rule for every event; two successful deliveries are still wrong if they apply one bid twice.

Define the abort condition before the test. If presence divergence exceeds the auction's agreed error budget, if reconnect-to-reconciled time breaks its SLO, or if operators cannot separate credential, subscription, presence, and business-event failures, return traffic to the previous adapter and preserve the last authoritative cursor. The dashboard may briefly show “reconciling.” It must never manufacture certainty.

If the shared REST boundary fits your platform roadmap, validate the current contract in the Infrai realtime API documentation before implementing the publisher. No urgency; the workload test should decide.

References

  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • PubNub documentation

title: I built a Claude skill that makes AI design like a senior UX designer
description:
Ask any AI to "design a dashboard" and you get the same thing every time. A KPI row, a line chart, a table. Logistics, HR, healthcare, fintech: they all look identical. And the moment you look closer, there's no loading state, no empty state, no error state. It renders. It doesn't work.

I've spent 14 years designing enterprise SaaS for aviation, logistics, and HR products. So I wrote down how I actually design, and turned it into a Claude skill.

It's free, open source, and MIT licensed: your-ui-ux-designer on GitHub

A logistics shipment dashboard, generated with the skill in HTML.

The core rule: render, don't describe

Most AI output describes good design. "The table should have a loading state." "Buttons should have focus styles."

The skill treats a described state as not delivered. If a rule names an output, that output must appear in the result. So every screen ships with:

  • Default, Loading, Empty, and Error states, as real rendered views
  • Focus rings and working interactions
  • Four responsive breakpoints
  • A prefers-reduced-motion fallback

The same dashboard in its Loading, Empty, and Error states. Built in, not added later.

What it does

It asks before it designs. At the start of a session, it asks 5 questions once: your design system (or it creates one), industry, output target, style, and dark mode. Then it commits.

11 distinct styles. Minimal, Material 3, Bento Grid, Glassmorphism, Liquid Glass, Spatial, Aurora, Neo-Brutalism, plus Neumorphism, Claymorphism, and Skeuomorphic for the narrow cases where they fit. It also warns you when a style is wrong for the context, like Claymorphism for enterprise B2B.

Enterprise navigation. Gmail-style dual nav, a fixed icon rail plus a collapsible secondary panel, that reflows correctly to a mobile top bar and bottom bar.

Bring your own design system. Share tokens, a link, or an image. It adopts them and fills in what's missing.

Multiple output targets. HTML, Figma, Claude Design, or a written spec.

Built-in validation. Before delivering, it checks that charts actually paint, controls actually work, and contrast actually passes.

Same skill, different industry: a fintech landing page with a live dashboard, in HTML.

How it's built

A lean core file, plus reference files that load only when needed. That keeps it fast and stops it from dropping rules on big tasks.

ui-ux-designer/
├── SKILL.md          core spine
└── references/
    ├── styles.md     11 style definitions
    ├── patterns.md   navigation, tables, dropdowns
    ├── mobile.md     touch / gesture / mobile spec
    └── figma.md      Figma auto-layout & variants

Does it work?

I tested it on 30 cases across aviation, transport, and HRM, scored on a 10-point rubric covering screen logic, style fidelity, contrast, grid, states, interaction, and responsiveness.

  • Overall: 86.7 / 100 on Sonnet 4.6
  • HTML on Opus 4.8: 93.0 / 100
  • Figma on Opus 4.8: 88.0 / 100

One lesson from testing: model choice matters. Routing HTML and Figma work to Opus fixed the responsiveness gap. And low reasoning effort drops states, so don't run it on low.

Install in 3 steps

  1. Download ui-ux-designer.skill from the repo or its Releases page
  2. In Claude: Settings → Capabilities → Skills → Upload skill
  3. Select the file. It installs automatically.

It triggers on any UI/UX request, or call it directly with /ui-ux-designer. Works in Claude Chat, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork.

Try it

Paste this after installing:

Design a mobile app screen for a field-service technician: a job list with status, and a job detail view. Output as HTML.

What I learned building it

AI is fast, but it's confidently incomplete. The value isn't in getting AI to generate a screen. It's in encoding the checks a senior designer runs without thinking: what happens when this table is empty? What does a technician see when the network fails? Where does this nav go on a phone?

That's what this skill tries to capture.

If you try it and it gets something wrong, open an issue with the prompt and a screenshot. And if it's useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other people find it.

AI builds. I decide.

title: AWS Outage One Year Later: Lessons From Every Cloud Failure
description:
TL;DR

Every major cloud provider has had a serious outage since mid-2025, each from a different cause, so any single provider is a single point of failure.

  • On October 20, 2025, a DNS race condition in DynamoDB's automation took the DynamoDB endpoint in AWS us-east-1 offline. The event ran about 15 hours and spread to EC2 instance launches and Network Load Balancers.
  • Google Cloud (June 2025, global), Azure Front Door (October 2025, global), Oracle Cloud US East (Ashburn) (March 2026), and an automated Google Cloud action that suspended a customer's production account (May 2026) each failed in a different layer.
  • Failures hit three blast radii: a zone, a region, or a whole provider. Multi-region on one provider covers the first two. It doesn't cover a provider's global control plane, edge network, or account layer.
  • Put a second, independent, already-running path under every layer you can't lose, keep failover off the failing provider, and drill the switch.
  • Control Plane combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one virtual cloud and runs workloads active-active across providers, with a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. During the October 20 outage, no Control Plane customer experienced downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.

What happened in the AWS us-east-1 outage on October 20, 2025?

A latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management system left the DynamoDB regional endpoint in us-east-1 with an empty DNS record, and everything that resolves that name failed. According to the AWS post-event summary, the event ran from 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 to 2:20 PM PDT on October 20 (06:48 to 21:20 UTC on October 20), about 15 hours. The disruption affected dozens of AWS services in us-east-1, and AWS's Health Dashboard event history lists the full set.

AWS's summary splits the impact into three periods:

  • DynamoDB became unreachable (11:48 PM to 2:40 AM PDT). Two automation components, a DNS Planner and DNS Enactors, manage DynamoDB's DNS. One unusually delayed Enactor applied an outdated plan, and another Enactor's cleanup step then deleted that plan, leaving an empty record for dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. Customer traffic and internal AWS services that depend on DynamoDB couldn't connect.
  • New EC2 instances failed to launch (2:25 AM to 10:36 AM PDT). After DNS was restored, internal subsystems that depend on DynamoDB stayed impaired, and AWS throttled some operations while it recovered. Some newly launched instances had connectivity problems until 1:50 PM PDT.
  • Network Load Balancers saw connection errors (5:30 AM to 2:09 PM PDT). Health checks began failing because new instances came into service before their network state had propagated, and automatic health check failover then removed capacity from service. AWS engineers disabled automatic NLB health check failover at 9:36 AM PDT.

AWS said it disabled the DynamoDB DNS automation worldwide until it fixed the race condition and added protections. Recovery that needed new instances was blocked for hours: AWS says Amazon Redshift's host-replacement workflows stalled while EC2 launches were impaired, leaving some clusters unavailable. AWS also notes that customers with DynamoDB global tables could still reach replicas in other regions, though replication to and from the us-east-1 replica lagged. Regional redundancy helped where it was real and tested.

What other major cloud outages happened in 2025 and 2026?

Four more major incidents hit a different provider or a different failure layer. The table lists major incidents from June 2025 to May 2026; it is a selection, and smaller incidents in the same period are not included.

Date Provider What failed Blast radius Duration Source
June 12, 2025 Google Cloud An invalid quota policy with blank fields replicated globally and crashed Service Control, the API management layer Global, all regions About 3 hours (most regions began recovering within 40 minutes; us-central1 took up to 2 hours 40 minutes) Google Cloud incident report
October 19 to 20, 2025 AWS A DynamoDB DNS race condition in us-east-1, cascading to EC2 launches and Network Load Balancers One region, many dependent services About 15 hours AWS post-event summary
October 29 to 30, 2025 Microsoft Azure Incompatible customer configuration metadata crashed the Azure Front Door data plane at edge sites Global edge network About 8.5 hours (15:41 to 00:05 UTC) Azure Front Door post-incident review
March 3 to 4, 2026 Oracle Cloud Infrastructure A network infrastructure issue affecting multiple OCI services in US East (Ashburn); Oracle has not published a root cause One region About 20 hours (13:24 UTC March 3 to 09:18 UTC March 4) Oracle incident record
May 19 to 20, 2026 Google Cloud (account level) An automated Google Cloud action that Railway reports incorrectly suspended its production account One customer's whole production account, cascading to its workloads on AWS and its own hardware About 8 hours Railway incident report
  • Google Cloud (June 2025). Google's report says the policy change replicated globally within seconds, and the failing code path was never exercised during its region-by-region rollout. Google's Cloud Service Health status page was down too, delaying its first incident post by about an hour, and some customers' monitoring running on Google Cloud also failed.
  • Azure Front Door (October 2025). Microsoft's review says this incident was not directly related to an earlier Front Door incident on October 9, although both were broadly related to configuration propagation risk.
  • Oracle US East (March 2026). Oracle describes a network infrastructure issue that caused connection timeouts, errors, and increased latency across multiple OCI services. The Register reported that it disrupted parts of TikTok's U.S. service, which TikTok's U.S. joint venture acknowledged (The Register). Oracle logged a second Ashburn networking incident that began 52 minutes after the first was resolved and ran until 04:40 UTC on March 5.
  • Account suspension (May 2026). Railway's report says the automated action extended to many Google Cloud accounts. Its edge proxies cached routing tables from a control plane hosted in Google Cloud, so when the cache expired, workloads on AWS and on its own hardware became unreachable even though they were still running. Railway takes responsibility for that architecture. Redundant workloads can still share one dependency that decides whether anyone can reach them.

Large systems have shared layers, and shared layers fail, whichever provider runs them.

What is a blast radius in a cloud outage?

A blast radius is the set of workloads that fail together when one thing breaks. Cloud failures fall into three scales, and each needs a different kind of redundancy.

Blast radius Typical cause What it takes out Redundancy that covers it Recent example
Zone A facility, power, cooling, or network fault in one availability zone Workloads placed only in that zone Replicas spread across zones in a region None among the five above; multi-zone designs usually absorb zone faults
Region A regional service, a regional dependency, or regional networking Everything in that region, plus anything that depends on its endpoints Active capacity in more than one region, with data replicated AWS us-east-1 (October 2025), Oracle US East (March 2026)
Provider A global control plane, global edge network, global configuration push, or account-level action Every region of that provider, or your whole account A second, independent provider, including the control path Google Cloud Service Control (June 2025), Azure Front Door (October 2025), the account suspension (May 2026)

Why does multi-region fail during cloud outages?

Multi-region covers regional failures. It doesn't cover failures in layers every region shares. Three of the five incidents above weren't regional. Google's Service Control policy data replicated to every region within seconds. Azure Front Door's crash spread to all edge sites worldwide. The account suspension took down an entire account, which spans every region, and then spread to other clouds through a routing dependency hosted in Google Cloud.

Multi-region plans also fail for quieter reasons:

  • The failover step needs a control plane call (launch an instance, change a route, update a record) in the region that is failing. On October 20, new EC2 launches in us-east-1 failed from 2:25 AM to 10:36 AM PDT.
  • The failover target shares a dependency with the primary, such as a global service, an identity system, or a DNS zone.
  • The monitoring that tells you to fail over runs on the provider that is down. Google's June 2025 report says this happened to some customers.
  • The plan was written but never exercised under load.

AI workloads add their own dependencies: model APIs, GPU capacity from neoclouds, and agents that fail a customer if they die mid-task. Each is another layer that needs a second path. For a regional failure like October 20, tested multi-region capacity is a real defense, but it covers only the regional layer.

How do you keep services up during a cloud outage?

Post-incident reports don't say who stayed up, but they show which preparations would have mattered. Build them before the incident:

  • Keep capacity already running. When instance launches fail, a plan to scale up on demand depends on a control plane that may be struggling. Capacity already serving in another location doesn't.
  • Keep the failover path off the failing layer. Traffic shifting, health checks, and routing decisions should run somewhere independent of the provider or region in trouble.
  • Monitor from outside the provider. Google's report shows what happens when the monitoring stack and the workload share a failure domain.
  • Map hidden dependencies. The account-suspension report shows workloads in three environments and a routing control plane in only one of them.
  • Drill the switch. Teams that rehearse find the stale credential, the missing quota, or the unreplicated dataset on a Tuesday afternoon instead of during an outage.
  • Match redundancy to the cost of downtime. Rank services by business impact and put the strongest design under the ones that cost the most when they stop.

Control Plane builds the first two into the platform: capacity running in every location, and routing that sits above any single provider. For a deeper look at targets and trade-offs, see our guides to high availability, RTO and RPO targets, and what single-region, multi-region, and multi-cloud designs can deliver.

How does Control Plane keep you up when a provider fails?

Control Plane combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one virtual cloud, so you stay up when others are down. You choose the locations for a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC): AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure regions, Kubernetes clusters you already run, and your own servers on premises. Every workload runs active-active in all of them, with replicas already serving in each location. A built-in global endpoint sends each request to the nearest healthy location. When a zone, region, or provider fails, traffic moves to locations that are already running, and autoscaling adds replicas there as load arrives. Nothing has to boot, nobody runs a runbook, and failover doesn't depend on the failed provider's control plane.

The rest of the platform serves the same outcome. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, so nothing needs re-keying when traffic moves. Each location keeps serving the last healthy version until a new release passes its health checks, so a broken update can't take the workload down (docs). Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory to actual usage in every location. None of it needs a platform team to build or operate.

On October 20, 2025, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry (Beyond Backups). For the Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle, and account-level failures above, a GVC that spans more than one provider is designed to route around a failure confined to one.

Control Plane offers a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. No migration is required: existing Kubernetes clusters and your own servers join as locations, so you add failure domains from what you already run.

Next step: watch us recreate the us-east-1 outage live on October 20 at 11 AM PT. Register for the webinar, or talk to the Control Plane team.

Cloud outage resilience checklist

Use this to find the layers you can't recover without. Answer each row for every service that matters to revenue.

Check Question to answer
Single points of failure Have we listed every provider, region, account, DNS zone, identity system, and control plane each service depends on?
Zone spread Are replicas spread across at least two zones?
Region spread Can the service run in a second region without a human launching new capacity?
Provider spread Can the service run on a second provider if a global layer or account fails?
Capacity already running Is the failover location already running enough replicas to carry real load?
Data Is data replicated to the failover location, with an RPO we have actually measured?
Failover path Does traffic shifting work if the primary provider's console, API, and DNS are unavailable?
Monitoring Does alerting run outside the provider we are monitoring?
Account risk Do we have a documented path if the provider suspends or restricts our account?
Credentials Can the failover location authenticate to everything it needs without a manual step?
Drills Have we run a failover in the last quarter and written down what broke?
Communication Does the team know who decides to fail over, and how customers are told?
SLA reality Do we know that provider SLA credits are service credits, not compensation for lost revenue?

Frequently asked questions

What caused the AWS us-east-1 outage in October 2025?

A latent race condition in the DNS management system for Amazon DynamoDB left the regional endpoint in us-east-1 with an empty DNS record, so services that resolve that endpoint couldn't connect. Recovery then continued through EC2 instance launch failures and Network Load Balancer connection errors.

How long did the October 2025 AWS outage last?

AWS's summary gives the event window as 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 to 2:20 PM PDT on October 20, about 15 hours, with three distinct periods of impact.

Which major cloud outages happened in 2025 and 2026?

This post covers Google Cloud's global Service Control outage (June 12, 2025), the AWS us-east-1 outage (October 19 to 20, 2025), the Azure Front Door global outage (October 29 to 30, 2025), the Oracle US East outage (March 3 to 4, 2026), and an automated Google Cloud suspension of a customer's production account (May 19 to 20, 2026). Other incidents happened in the period, so treat it as a selection.

How do you survive a cloud provider outage?

Identify what each service depends on, then give each dependency a second independent path: spread across zones, run active capacity in more than one region, and for critical services run on a second provider. Keep failover and monitoring off the failing provider, keep capacity already running, and drill the switch.

Is multi-region enough to survive an outage?

Multi-region protects against regional failures, such as the AWS us-east-1 and Oracle US East incidents, if failover works without the failing region. It doesn't protect against a failure in a provider's global control plane, edge network, or your account, as in the Google Cloud, Azure Front Door, and account-suspension incidents.

What is the difference between multi-cloud and multi-region?

Multi-region means running in more than one region of the same provider. Multi-cloud means running across more than one provider. Multi-region covers regional failures, and multi-cloud also covers provider-level failures, at the price of more work in networking, identity, and data replication unless a platform such as Control Plane handles them for you.

Is multi-cloud worth it?

It depends on what an hour of downtime costs you. Provider SLA credits are service credits, not compensation for lost revenue. For revenue-critical services, a second provider removes a failure class that regions can't. Control Plane makes a second provider another location in the same GVC, with capacity scaled to demand in each location. Rank services by business impact and give the most critical ones cross-provider redundancy first.

What happened to Control Plane customers during the AWS outage?

During the October 2025 AWS outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry. Control Plane offers a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

  • Google Cloud: Incident report, June 12, 2025
  • Microsoft Azure: Post Incident Review, Azure Front Door (YKYN-BWZ)
  • Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: Incident record, US East (Ashburn), March 3, 2026

title: My German links unfurl in English, and I decided that's OK (for now)
description:
I run a small AI headshot app on my own. React and TypeScript, hosted on Firebase Hosting. No Next.js. It speaks five languages: English, Spanish, French, German and Chinese.

Paste a German link to it into Slack and the preview card comes up in English.

I know exactly why. I wrote a comment explaining it. And I'm leaving it alone. Here's the setup, because I think the tradeoff is more useful to talk about than a tidy fix would be.

Languages live in the query string

There are no /de/ or /fr/ paths. Language is a query param, ?lang=de, picked up by i18next's browser language detector:

detection: {
  order: ['querystring', 'navigator', 'htmlTag'],
  lookupQuerystring: 'lang',
},
supportedLngs: ['en', 'es', 'fr', 'de', 'zh'],

Every page then emits its hreflang set through react-helmet-async:

{supportedLangs.map(l => (
  <link key={`hreflang-${l}`} rel="alternate" hrefLang={l}
        href={`${CANONICAL_BASE}${canonicalPath}?lang=${l}`} />
))}
<link rel="alternate" hrefLang="x-default" href={canonicalUrl} />

I picked query params because it meant zero router changes. I had a custom router already and didn't want to touch every route. Cheap at the time. You'll see what it cost.

Prerendering, the poor man's SSR

A pure SPA ships an empty <div id="root">, which is not what you want crawlers chewing on. So after the build, a script spins up a tiny static server, opens each route in headless Puppeteer, waits, and writes page.content() back into dist/ as a flat HTML file.

Twenty routes, give or take. It sounds trivial. It produced most of my SEO bugs.

Bug one: two of every meta tag. index.html has static fallback <meta> tags for the SPA shell. Helmet adds its own route-specific ones on render, marked data-rh="true", but it only manages tags it created. It never removes the originals. So every snapshot had two description tags, generic homepage one first. Some crawlers read the first and stop. The fix was a post-processing pass in the prerender script: collect every key Helmet declared, then strip the static duplicate of each.

Bug two: the right page with the wrong title. Articles load from Firestore in the browser, and the page's whole <Helmet> block waits on that fetch. Firestore keeps a long-lived connection open, so networkidle2 fired well before the article arrived. I added waitForSelector('article'). Still broken sometimes: the <article> would be in the DOM while Helmet hadn't caught up, so the snapshot had real content under the generic shell <title>.

What finally fixed it was asserting on the output, not the timing:

if (route.startsWith('/articles/') && html.includes(SHELL_TITLE_TAG)) {
  throw new Error('still carrying the generic shell <title>');
}

If a snapshot comes out wrong, that route fails loudly and doesn't get written. The previous good file stays. I'd much rather ship yesterday's page than a quietly broken one.

(There was also a reCAPTCHA thing. App Check can't run headless, so the article query never resolved at all. Now the script pulls published articles through Firestore's public REST API and injects them with evaluateOnNewDocument before the page boots. A whole saga. Another post.)

Where the query string bites

Firebase Hosting rewrites match on path. /?lang=de and /?lang=es and / all get the same file, the English prerendered index.html. The German version only exists after JavaScript runs.

Googlebot runs JavaScript before indexing, so the hreflang signal for search is fine. Slack, iMessage, LinkedIn, Discord and friends don't. They read the raw HTML and get an English og:title.

Fixing it properly means per-locale static output plus a way to route on the query string, and Firebase rewrites can't do that by path alone. That's a build and infra change, not a one-liner. So the decision, as written in the comment above that hreflang block: accept it, and revisit if anyone actually starts sharing non-English links.

If I started over

Path-based locales, /de/..., from day one. The router changes I dodged would have been an afternoon. The workaround has now cost me more than that in comments alone.

And I'd write the "assert on the snapshot" check before the first prerender ever shipped. Timing waits feel like fixes. They're guesses.

The app is Stature AI, if you want to poke at the prerendered pages yourself.

title: AWS Agent Registry now supports custom metadata for registry records
description:
AWS Agent Registry is the centralized, governed catalog for agents, MCP servers, agent skills, gateways, and custom resources within your organization. As organizations scale to hundreds of such resources, a name and description alone are insufficient for effective governance and discovery. Custom metadata lets you extend every registry record with your organization's own structured fields, so both people and automated systems can find and govern resources consistently.

With custom metadata, publishers can record fields like team ownership, data classification, or review status directly on each registry record. You define a schema once per registry with common attributes, then extend it with type-specific fields — such as a model family for agent records. Each field supports free text, a URL, a Boolean, or a choice from a list of allowed values, and the registry validates required fields and values on every record creation or update. You can then filter search results on any custom metadata field from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or the registry's MCP endpoint.

Custom metadata is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation. For detailed setup guidance, see Define a custom metadata schema and Set custom metadata values on a record.

title: I got tired of checking GPU cloud pricing pages by hand, so I built a price index API
description:
Every time I needed to rent a GPU, the workflow was the same: open six provider tabs, squint at pricing pages that all structure their numbers differently, and try to remember whether that H100 price was spot, on-demand, or a 3-year contract rate buried in a footnote.

So I built the thing I wanted: a price index that normalizes GPU cloud pricing into one dataset, where every row says what kind of price it is and links back to the provider page it came from.

Some of what the data shows right now (it refreshes hourly):

GPU Cheapest $/hr Provider Price type
H100 1.37 Vast.ai spot
H200 2.62 CoreWeave spot
A100 1.15 Paperspace 3-yr contract
L40S 0.79 RunPod community cloud
B200 4.26 CoreWeave spot

The price-type column is the part I care about most. A $1.15 A100 sounds cheaper than a $1.37 H100 until you notice one is a 3-year contract and the other is spot. Most comparison content flattens that away; the index doesn't.

The API is live on RapidAPI as GPU Index — there's a free tier (1,000 requests/month) if you want to poke at it: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/gpu-index1

Endpoints are simple: /prices for the full normalized dataset (filter by GPU family, provider, or price type), /summary for the cheapest price per family, /gpus and /providers for what's covered and how fresh each source is.

While I was in there, I built the same pattern for a few other datasets I kept checking by hand:

  • LLM Token Price Index — 458 models, per-token input/output prices normalized across providers. Same model, side by side: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/llm-token-price-index
  • Domain Price Index — registration/renewal/transfer prices per TLD, because renewal pricing is where registrars actually make their money: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/domain-price-index
  • CT Lookup — Certificate Transparency data as JSON, with a watchlist for catching certs issued for your domains that you didn't request: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/ct-lookup
  • Email Deliverability Check — one call returns SPF/DKIM/DMARC/MX/rDNS verdicts for a domain, with fix hints: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/email-deliverability-check

All of them have the same free tier, and every price row in the indexes carries its source URL so you can check my work. If you're building a router, a cost dashboard, or anything that picks compute or models programmatically, I'd rather you call an API than maintain your own scrapers — that was certainly true for me.

Feedback welcome: what provider or GPU family am I missing?
