title: Blazor ErrorBoundary
description:
Blazor is a web UI framework from Microsoft that allows developers to build interactive web applications using C#, .NET, and Razor components.

A Blazor component is a reusable part of a user interface that can contain HTML markup, C# logic, data binding, event handlers, and conditional rendering.

Let's understand this with a simple example of a product details component.

Product Details

<h5>@productName</h5>
<p>Price: ₹@price</p>


    Increase Price

@code {
private string productName = "Wireless Headphones";
private decimal price = 1500;

private void IncreasePrice()
{
    price += 100;
}

In this example:

  • HTML markup defines the structure of the product details.
  • Bootstrap classes such as card, shadow-sm, and btn btn-primary style the UI.
  • C# variables store the product name and price.
  • Data binding using @productName and @price displays variable values in the UI.
  • Event handling using @onclick calls the IncreasePrice() method when the button is clicked.

When the user clicks the button, the price increases by ₹100, and Blazor automatically updates the displayed value.

This example demonstrates how Blazor combines C# logic with HTML markup to build interactive user interfaces.

What Is Bootstrap, and Why Use It with Blazor?

Bootstrap is a CSS framework that provides predefined styling classes for layouts, forms, buttons, cards, tables, badges, and responsive designs.

For example, the product component above uses the card class to create a card-style container, shadow-sm to add a subtle shadow, and btn btn-primary to style the button.

Bootstrap handles the visual presentation, while Blazor handles the application logic and user interactions.

Important: Using Bootstrap CSS classes directly in a Razor component is different from using a dedicated Blazor Bootstrap component library. In this article, we use Bootstrap CSS classes with normal Blazor components.

What Are We Going to Build?

Now that we understand how a normal Blazor component works, let's apply the same concepts to a real-world example: a for a Gym Center and Membership Plan Management System.

The page retrieves membership plans from an ASP.NET Core Web API and displays them using Bootstrap cards.

Product Price Calculator

Price per item: ₹500

Quantity:

Total Price: ₹@(500 * quantity)

@code {
private int quantity = 1;
}

The following example demonstrates how Blazor components, Bootstrap styling, API integration, and event handling work together.

Complete Browse Membership Plans Component

and place the following code inside it. The complete component is included together below, without changing the supplied code.

@page "/gyms/{GymId:int}/plans"

@using System.Net.Http.Json

@inject HttpClient http
@inject NavigationManager navigation
@inject SweetAlertService Swal

<PageTitle>Browse Membership Plans</PageTitle>

<div class="container-fluid py-4">

    <!-- Page Heading -->
    <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-4">
        <div>
            <h3 class="fw-bold">Membership Plans</h3>
            <p class="text-muted mb-0">
                Explore membership plans available at this gym.
            </p>
            <p class="text-muted small mb-0">
                Selected Gym ID: @GymId
            </p>
        </div>

        <button class="btn btn-outline-secondary"
                @onclick="GoBack">
            Back to Gyms
        </button>
    </div>

    <!-- Search -->
    <div class="card shadow-sm mb-4">
        <div class="card-body">
            <label class="form-label">Search Membership Plan</label>

            <input class="form-control"
                   type="text"
                   placeholder="Search by plan name..."
                   @bind="PlanSearch"
                   @bind:event="oninput" />
        </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Loading -->
    @if (isLoading)
    {
        <div class="text-center py-5">
            <div class="spinner-border text-primary" role="status">
                <span class="visually-hidden">Loading...</span>
            </div>

            <p class="text-muted mt-3">
                Loading membership plans...
            </p>
        </div>
    }
    else if (hasError)
    {
        <div class="alert alert-danger">
            Unable to load membership plans.
            Please try again.

            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger ms-2"
                    @onclick="LoadPlans">
                Retry
            </button>
        </div>
    }
    else if (FilteredPlans.Count == 0)
    {
        <div class="card shadow-sm">
            <div class="card-body text-center py-5">
                <h5 class="text-muted">
                    No membership plans found
                </h5>

                <p class="text-muted mb-0">
                    This gym has no matching membership plans.
                </p>
            </div>
        </div>
    }
    else
    {
        <!-- Plans List -->
        <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-3">
            <h5 class="mb-0">Available Plans</h5>

            <span class="badge bg-primary">
                @FilteredPlans.Count plans
            </span>
        </div>

        <div class="row g-4">

            @foreach (var plan in FilteredPlans)
            {
                <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-xl-4" @key="plan.Id">

                    <div class="card h-100 shadow-sm">

                        <!-- Plan Header -->
                        <div class="card-header bg-white py-3">
                            <div class="d-flex justify-content-between
                                        align-items-start gap-2">

                                <h5 class="fw-bold mb-0">
                                    @plan.PlanName
                                </h5>

                                <span class="badge @(IsActive(plan.Status)
                                    ? "bg-success"
                                    : "bg-secondary")">
                                    @plan.Status
                                </span>

                            </div>
                        </div>

                        <!-- Plan Details -->
                        <div class="card-body">

                            <div class="mb-3">
                                <span class="text-muted">Price</span>

                                <h3 class="text-primary fw-bold mb-0">
                                    ₹@plan.Price.ToString("N2")
                                </h3>
                            </div>

                            <p class="mb-2">
                                <strong>Duration:</strong>
                                @plan.DurationInMonths months
                            </p>

                            <p class="mb-2">
                                <strong>Class Sessions:</strong>
                                @plan.ClassSessionsPerWeek per week
                            </p>

                            <p class="mb-3">
                                <strong>Personal Training:</strong>
                                @plan.PersonalTrainingSessions sessions
                            </p>

                            <hr />

                            <h6 class="fw-semibold mb-3">
                                Plan Benefits
                            </h6>

                            <ul class="list-unstyled mb-0">

                                <li class="mb-2">
                                    @if (plan.LockerAccess)
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-success me-2">✓</span>
                                        <span>Locker Access</span>
                                    }
                                    else
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-muted me-2">✕</span>
                                        <span class="text-muted">
                                            No Locker Access
                                        </span>
                                    }
                                </li>

                                <li class="mb-2">
                                    @if (plan.GuestAccess)
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-success me-2">✓</span>
                                        <span>Guest Access</span>
                                    }
                                    else
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-muted me-2">✕</span>
                                        <span class="text-muted">
                                            No Guest Access
                                        </span>
                                    }
                                </li>

                                <li class="mb-2">
                                    <strong>Guest Passes:</strong>
                                    @plan.GuestPasses
                                </li>

                            </ul>

                        </div>

                        <!-- Subscribe Button -->
                        <div class="card-footer bg-white border-0 pb-3">

                            @if (IsActive(plan.Status))
                            {
                                <button class="btn btn-primary w-100"
                                        @onclick="() => Subscribe(plan.Id)">
                                    Subscribe
                                </button>
                            }
                            else
                            {
                                <button class="btn btn-secondary w-100"
                                        disabled>
                                    Plan Inactive
                                </button>
                            }

                        </div>

                    </div>

                </div>
            }

        </div>
    }
</div>

@code {
    // Gym ID comes from the URL:
    // /gyms/1/plans means GymId = 1.
    [Parameter]
    public int GymId { get; set; }

    private string PlanSearch = string.Empty;

    private bool isLoading = true;
    private bool hasError = false;

    private List<MembershipPlanItem> planList = new();

    // Plans displayed after applying the local search.
    private List<MembershipPlanItem> FilteredPlans =>
        planList
            .Where(plan =>
                string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(PlanSearch) ||
                plan.PlanName.Contains(
                    PlanSearch.Trim(),
                    StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            .ToList();

    // Response model used by this page.
    public sealed class MembershipPlanItem
    {
        public int Id { get; set; }

        public string PlanName { get; set; } = string.Empty;

        public int GymId { get; set; }

        public decimal Price { get; set; }

        public int DurationInMonths { get; set; }

        public int ClassSessionsPerWeek { get; set; }

        public int PersonalTrainingSessions { get; set; }

        public bool LockerAccess { get; set; }

        public bool GuestAccess { get; set; }

        public int GuestPasses { get; set; }

        public string Status { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    }

    protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync()
    {
        await LoadPlans();
    }

    private async Task LoadPlans()
    {
        isLoading = true;
        hasError = false;

        try
        {
            // Assumed API endpoint:
            // GET api/MembershipPlan/BrowseMembershipPlans?GymId=1
            var url =
                $"MembershipPlan/BrowseMembershipPlans?GymId={GymId}";

            var response = await http.GetAsync(url);

            if (response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
            {
                var result = await response.Content
                    .ReadFromJsonAsync<List<MembershipPlanItem>>();

                // Keep only plans belonging to the selected gym.
                // The backend should also enforce this filter.
                planList = (result ?? new List<MembershipPlanItem>())
                    .Where(plan => plan.GymId == GymId)
                    .ToList();
            }
            else
            {
                planList = new();
                hasError = true;

                await Swal.FireAsync(new SweetAlertOptions
                {
                    Title = "Unable to load plans",
                    Text = $"The server returned status {(int)response.StatusCode}.",
                    Icon = SweetAlertIcon.Error
                });
            }
        }
        catch (Exception)
        {
            planList = new();
            hasError = true;

            await Swal.FireAsync(new SweetAlertOptions
            {
                Title = "Connection Error",
                Text = "Unable to connect to the gym API.",
                Icon = SweetAlertIcon.Error
            });
        }
        finally
        {
            isLoading = false;
        }
    }

    private static bool IsActive(string status)
    {
        return string.Equals(
            status,
            "Active",
            StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    }

    private void Subscribe(int planId)
    {
        // The subscription page will receive both IDs.
        navigation.NavigateTo(
            $"/subscribe?gymId={GymId}&planId={planId}");
    }

    private void GoBack()
    {
        navigation.NavigateTo("/browse-gyms");
    }
}

Understanding the Main Concepts

1. Route parameters

The route is defined as:

@page "/gyms/{GymId:int}/plans"

The [Parameter] property receives the gym ID from the URL:

[Parameter]
public int GymId { get; set; }

For example, /gyms/3/plans supplies the value 3 to GymId.

This allows the same component to display plans for different gyms.

2. Data binding and search

The search input uses:

@bind="PlanSearch"
@bind:event="oninput"

The PlanSearch variable is updated as the user types. The FilteredPlans property uses LINQ to filter the loaded plans by name without sending a new API request for each keystroke.

3. Bootstrap cards

The component uses Bootstrap classes such as card, card-header, card-body, and card-footer to organize membership information into cards.

The responsive grid uses col-12 col-md-6 col-xl-4 to display one, two, or three columns depending on the screen width.

4. API integration

The LoadPlans() method sends a GET request to the membership-plan endpoint, deserializes the JSON response into MembershipPlanItem objects, and filters the results for the selected gym.

The backend should also enforce the gym filter. Frontend filtering alone is not a security measure.

5. Conditional rendering

The component displays different UI states depending on isLoading, hasError, and the number of filtered plans.

This provides feedback while data is loading, when an error occurs, and when no matching plans are found.

6. Event handling and navigation

The Subscribe button calls Subscribe(plan.Id), which navigates to the subscription page with the selected gym ID and plan ID.

The Back to Gyms button calls GoBack() to navigate to /browse-gyms.

Conclusion: Understanding Blazor Components Through Practical Examples

Blazor components make it possible to combine UI markup, C# logic, data binding, and event handling in a single reusable unit.

We started with a simple product details component and then applied the same concepts to a real-world membership-plans page.

Consider one final small example that demonstrates how a component can display a membership price and calculate a discounted price:

<h3>Membership Price Calculator</h3>

<p>Original Price: ₹@price</p>
<p>Discount: @discount%</p>
<p>Final Price: ₹@FinalPrice</p>

@code {
    private decimal price = 2000;
    private decimal discount = 10;

    private decimal FinalPrice =>
        price - (price * discount / 100);
}

Here, the component uses C# properties and expressions to calculate the final price and display it in the UI. When the underlying values change, Blazor can render the updated result.

The same fundamental approach is used in the Browse Membership Plans component, where data comes from an API and the UI displays prices, benefits, status badges, and subscription actions.

The key takeaway: Blazor manages the component's logic and interactivity, Bootstrap provides the styling, and services such as HttpClient connect the UI to backend data.

These concepts can be applied to many applications, including product catalogs, booking systems, hotel management, employee directories, and subscription platforms.

Thanks for reading! I hope this article helps you understand how normal Blazor components and Bootstrap work together to build practical web applications.

title: Building MoneyMov — A Free Personal Finance Tracker with MERN
description:
I recently built MoneyMov, a free personal finance tracker to help people understand where their money is going.

The idea was simple:

Know where your money moves.

Instead of building another complicated finance application, I wanted to create something simple enough for everyday use.

What Is MoneyMov?

MoneyMov is a personal finance tracker where users can manage their:

  • 💰 Income
  • 💸 Expenses
  • 📊 Spending categories
  • 📈 Investments
  • 🤝 Committees / Bachat
  • 💵 Lending / Loans

The additional modules are optional, so users can use only the parts they actually need.

For example, someone may only want to track expenses, while another person may also want to keep track of investments or money they've lent to someone.

Tech Stack

I built the application using the MERN stack:

  • MongoDB — Database
  • Express.js — Backend API
  • React.js — Frontend
  • Node.js — Backend runtime
  • Axios — API requests
  • Tailwind CSS — UI styling
  • Recharts — Charts and data visualization
  • JWT — Authentication
  • bcrypt — Password hashing

The frontend is deployed on Netlify, while the backend is deployed on Render.

Authentication & Security

One of the things I focused on while building the project was authentication and basic application security.

Some of the things implemented include:

  • Password hashing with bcrypt
  • HTTP-only authentication cookies
  • JWT-based authentication
  • Protected API routes
  • Environment variables for secrets
  • Forgot-password functionality
  • Hashed password-reset tokens
  • Token expiration
  • Helmet
  • Rate limiting
  • MongoDB input sanitization
  • HTTP Parameter Pollution protection
  • User-specific data access

For example, the backend doesn't simply trust the user ID coming from the frontend.

The authentication middleware verifies the token and gets the authenticated user's ID before accessing their data.

Spending Visualization

One of the dashboard features is a category-based spending breakdown.

For example:

Shopping      Rs 400
Food          Rs 1,200
Transport     Rs 500
Bills         Rs 2,000

The data is also visualized using a pie chart so users can quickly understand where most of their spending went.

Some Challenges

Building the application wasn't completely straightforward.

I ran into several issues during development and deployment, including:

  • MongoDB Atlas connection timeouts
  • Render deployment and networking issues
  • SMTP connection problems
  • Authentication cookies
  • CORS configuration
  • Express proxy configuration
  • SPA routing on Netlify
  • Mobile authentication behavior
  • Handling protected routes correctly

These problems were actually a useful part of the project because they forced me to understand what was happening beyond simply writing React components.

For example, deploying a MERN application locally is very different from deploying the frontend and backend separately.

You have to think about how each layer communicates in production:

Frontend
   ↓
API requests
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Database

Each layer introduces its own configuration, security considerations, and potential issues.

Why I Built It

I wanted to build something that was more than just another CRUD project.

While working on MoneyMov, I got to work with:

  • Authentication
  • REST APIs
  • MongoDB
  • Deployment
  • Security
  • Email verification
  • Password reset
  • Data visualization
  • Responsive UI
  • Production debugging

It also gave me a chance to work through problems that don't usually appear when everything is running on localhost.

What's Next?

There are still several things I want to improve.

Some ideas include:

  • Better dashboard analytics
  • More useful financial reports
  • Improved mobile experience
  • Better transaction filtering
  • More visualizations
  • Exporting financial data
  • Additional security improvements
  • Performance improvements

MoneyMov is currently free, and my goal is to keep the core personal finance features simple and accessible.

Final Thoughts

This project started as an idea for a simple expense tracker, but it gradually became a much bigger learning experience.

The biggest thing I learned is that building a real application isn't only about making the UI work.

You also have to think about:

Authentication → Security → APIs → Database → Deployment → Users

That's where a lot of the interesting engineering problems begin.

If you're also building a MERN application, I'd be interested to hear what problems you've run into while deploying your project.

Try MoneyMov

MoneyMov is free to use. Give it a try and let me know what you think!

🔗 Website: https://moneymov.netlify.app

MoneyMov — Know where your money moves.

title: Connect Your App to Your Enterprise Traces
description:
Your customer taps “Place order.” The request crosses your app, an API gateway, a native backend, a payment service and a database. Your operations team needs to see that path in the same tracing system it uses for the rest of the company. Neither the client app nor a compiled Java server should disappear from that picture.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

I wrote a book on debugging, so I am probably more opinionated about this than most people: in 2026, production diagnosis should not depend on somebody searching a pile of logs with grep and guessing which lines belong together.

Logs still matter. At enterprise scale, though, you need to connect work across machines, teams and runtimes, then see whether a failure is isolated or spreading. On a JVM, Java agents can instrument much of that work for us. Once our backend is translated to C and compiled into a native executable, the usual JVM instrumentation hook is gone.

We have to carry that visibility into the binary. OpenTelemetry support started that work last week. The expanded backend API adds metrics and management alongside it. This article follows what happens after you turn them on.

Follow an operation across your systems

Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal behavior from the evidence it emits. OpenTelemetry, usually shortened to OTel, defines APIs, data conventions and transport for producing that evidence. It is not itself the screen where you investigate an incident; a collector and an observability backend handle that part. The OTel primer provides the broader model.

Question Useful evidence
Why did this request take two seconds? A trace connecting its operations
Is database waiting increasing across the service? Metrics over time
What did the application decide at the failure? Logs and events with context

A span records one timed operation. Related spans form a trace. Metrics aggregate behavior across operations: a count, a current value or a distribution such as request duration. Neither replaces the other. A single trace can explain a slow query without telling you how often it occurs.

Our integration exports traces and metrics. It does not turn every application log into an OTLP log record.

Add tracing to your native executable

Put this in the backend's application.properties before building:

cn1.otel.enabled=true

Or use the backend's @OpenTelemetry annotation. The generator installs the tracer, making its implementation reachable to the translator. Without that build-time opt-in, the unused tracing code can be left out. Setting an environment variable after deploying a binary that omitted the tracer cannot add it back.

Once enabled, the runtime records an incoming request span named for its route template. A Web call creates a client span and propagates W3C trace headers. A database statement creates another client span. Incoming traceparent connects the request to its caller.

The native backend propagates context on outbound Web calls. Each receiving service must accept and continue that context. OTel-compatible instrumentation lets those services participate regardless of their implementation language.

Include the client, not just the servers

The client annotation belongs on your app's main class:

import com.codename1.annotations.OpenTelemetry;
import com.codename1.system.Lifecycle;

@OpenTelemetry(
        relay = "https://api.example.com",
        relayToken = "replace-with-your-relay-token",
        serviceName = "orders-app",
        sampleRatio = 0.2,
        requireAnalyticsConsent = true)
public class OrdersApp extends Lifecycle {
}

Replace the URL with your backend and the token placeholder with your relay token. Set the backend's RELAY_TOKEN environment variable to that same value. Enable its relay as shown below, and wire the app's analytics-consent flow before collecting telemetry. The client instruments supported app operations and ConnectionRequest calls, including outgoing trace context. It sends its recorded spans through the backend rather than carrying your collector credentials.

For browser apps, context propagation is limited to the relay host and configured propagateTo hosts. A cross-origin service must allow the tracing headers in CORS. The client tracing walkthrough covers consent, propagation and the supported span types.

That connects the experience on the device to the work behind it. A server-only trace cannot show the client work before the request or after the response. You can investigate that larger path in your enterprise tracing system instead of keeping a separate, disconnected account of what the app did.

Database spans record SQL as supplied, with placeholders intact; bound parameters are not recorded. If an application concatenates a secret into SQL, the resulting text already contains it. cn1.otel.attributes.exclude=db.query.text can exclude that attribute. Parameterized SQL remains the better habit.

WebSocket lifetime is outside this automatic request-span model. An hours-long connection with thousands of messages is not one useful HTTP request duration, and its upgrade is handled before this tracing path.

Send it to the system your team already uses

For an enabled build, configure a collector at runtime:

export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=orders-native
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:4318
export OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
export OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1
./build/Orders

Here Orders is the packaged application's executable. The ratio samples a tenth of newly rooted traces; the parent-based policy respects an upstream sampling decision.

The exporter uses OTLP over HTTP, with protobuf by default and JSON as an option. It does not implement OTLP/gRPC. It appends /v1/traces or /v1/metrics to the base endpoint unless you supply a signal-specific endpoint.

Dynatrace can receive that OTLP data. For traces, its documented ingest endpoint is configured through OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT, with an ingest credential in OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS. This uses explicit telemetry export; the translated server no longer has the JVM hooks used by Java instrumentation agents.

A dedicated exporter thread batches spans. If the collector is slow or unavailable, request handling does not wait indefinitely for it. A bounded queue eventually drops spans and records the drops. That preserves the service at the cost of incomplete telemetry, which is itself a condition to monitor.

Track latency without a metric for every URL

The server records request duration, active requests, open connections, database pool counts and task queue depth. Scheduled jobs report duration and outcome. The default metric export interval is one minute, using cumulative temporality.

Route labels use /orders/{id}, not /orders/81379. Putting each order ID into a metric label would create a new time series for every order. Templates keep the series count bounded by the API's shape.

The application can instrument a method too:

package example;

import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Counted;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Component;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Timed;

@Component
public class QuoteService {
    @Timed
    @Counted
    public int quoteCents(int quantity) {
        if (quantity < 1) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        }
        return quantity * 250;
    }
}

This deliberately small example creates a duration histogram and call counters, including a failure counter. The default instrument names derive from the class and method. The build weaves the measurement into the method, so a call through this is measured too. For a real quote service, validate upper bounds and apply the application's monetary rules.

@ManagedResource, @ManagedAttribute and @ManagedOperation offer a JMX-inspired model for current values and operator actions. Numeric managed getters become gauges. The management transport is the backend's own HTTP API; this is not a JVM JMX server hidden inside the native executable. Follow the management configuration before exposing operational actions.

Let an agent check the running application

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, gives a development tool a structured way to ask the server questions. The backend serves tools for listing routes, inspecting beans, reading recent requests and querying the database. After editing a handler, you can call it and inspect the row it wrote from your development tool.

A practical loop is:

  1. Start the backend on its development profile.
  2. Inspect backend_routes, backend_beans and backend_schema.
  3. Make the edit, then stop and restart the server. There is no hot reload.
  4. Exercise the handler with backend_call.
  5. Check backend_requests, backend_sql and backend_metrics.

The default SQL tool uses a database-enforced read-only transaction unless its caller explicitly requests write access. An application can publish its own methods with @McpTool; the build derives JSON Schema from their supported parameter types and calls them directly.

For a tool of your own, here is a complete bean using the generated dispatch:

package example;

import com.codename1.backend.annotations.McpParam;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.McpTool;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Component;

@Component
public class QuoteTools {
    private final QuoteService quotes;

    public QuoteTools(QuoteService quotes) {
        this.quotes = quotes;
    }

    @McpTool(description = "Returns a quote in cents for a positive quantity.")
    public int quote(@McpParam("quantity") int quantity) {
        return quotes.quoteCents(quantity);
    }
}

It reuses QuoteService above. The description tells an agent when the tool is relevant, and @McpParam supplies a stable argument name independent of compiler parameter metadata. Runtime authentication still has to be configured before serving it outside development.

Development tools are omitted by backendPackage / cn1:backend-package unless deliberately enabled. Outside development, the MCP endpoint requires a bearer token. A tokenless development server is restricted to loopback. Origin checks also matter when a browser can reach that machine. The MCP chapter spells out these boundaries.

Keep collector credentials off the phone

An app can send its own spans through the backend relay. The relay validates the OTLP/JSON payload, applies size and span-count limits, then queues it for export using credentials held by the server.

cn1.otel.relay=true
cn1.otel.relay.token=${RELAY_TOKEN}
cn1.otel.relay.corsOrigin=https://app.example.com

The relay requires the client's relayToken to match RELAY_TOKEN; a missing or different token returns HTTP 401. The CORS setting is for a web app on another origin. An app-carried relay token is not an unextractable secret; the collector's ingest credentials should remain on the backend. A full queue returns 503 so the client can back off.

Start with one real app action that crosses the native backend and an existing enterprise service. Verify that its spans share a trace ID in your collector, then check consent, sampling, queue drops and access to the relay before expanding collection. The goal is to make the app and its native server observable parts of the system your operations team already runs.

title: Architecting Static Comparison Micro-Sites with TypeScript and JSON-LD Schema
description:
When building vertical web applications, separating feature comparisons into standalone, fast-loading micro-sites is an effective way to keep your core application bundle lean while addressing specific user intents.

Recently, while building out supporting comparison pages for an educational test simulator, I designed a reusable data schema in TypeScript to render head-to-head feature matrices and inject structured JSON-LD data automatically.

Here is the architectural pattern and data model used to build these static comparison micro-sites.

1. Defining the Comparison Data Model in TypeScript

Instead of hardcoding HTML tables for each competitor analysis, defining a strict TypeScript interface ensures every micro-site renders consistent evaluation metrics (pricing model, learning format, regulatory updates, and pass guarantees):

export interface ComparisonMetric {
  featureName: string;
  primaryPlatformValue: string | boolean;
  competitorValue: string | boolean;
  highlightAdvantage?: boolean;
}

export interface ComparisonSiteConfig {
  slug: string;
  title: string;
  competitorCategory: 'legacy-portal' | 'career-directory' | 'trade-school';
  lastUpdatedYear: number;
  metrics: ComparisonMetric[];
}

By typing the competitorCategory, the UI components can dynamically adjust the layout depending on whether we are comparing two software tools or comparing digital self-study against an offline curriculum.

2. Live Production Deployments (Built on Lovable)

Using this modular structure, I deployed three separate micro-sites targeting different segments of the HVAC certification space:

  • Demo 1 (Legacy Portal Comparison): HVAC Exam Master vs EPATest.com — EPA 608 Prep Compared (2026) — Compares interactive active-recall testing (Core, Type I, II, and III modules) against static Web 1.0 study guides.

  • Demo 2 (Lead-Gen Directory Comparison): HVAC Exam Master vs HVAC Career Now (2026 Comparison) — Contrasts direct certification utility tools against school lead-generation portals.

  • Demo 3 (Offline Institution Comparison): HVAC Exam Master vs HVAC Technical Institute — 2026 Comparison — Evaluates self-paced digital exam prep ROI against traditional brick-and-mortar tuition costs.

3. Automating FAQ & Comparison JSON-LD Schema

To help search engines and AI answer engines parse the comparison matrices accurately, each micro-site injects a structured FAQPage and WebPage JSON-LD payload into the document head:

TypeScript

export function ComparisonSchema({ title, url, description }: { title: string; url: string; description: string }) {
  const schemaData = {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "WebPage",
    "name": title,
    "url": url,
    "description": description,
    "specialty": "EPA Section 608 Certification Prep"
  };

  return (
    <script
      type="application/ld+json"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(schemaData) }}
    />
  );
}

Key Takeaways for Frontend Builders

  1. Decouple Content from Layout: A shared TypeScript schema lets you spin up multiple comparison landing pages in minutes.
  2. Keep Micro-Sites Focused: Rather than building one massive table comparing ten different business models, isolating each comparison into its own deployment keeps page speed high and user intent clear.

title: Revolutionizing CAD: Why CADCraft is the Open-Source AutoCAD Alternative You Need!
description:
Quick Summary: 📝

CADCraft is an open-source, clean-room reimplementation of AutoCAD, built entirely in Rust. It aims to provide a fast and familiar CAD experience with features like command line, object snaps, layers, dimensions, and hatches, running on multiple operating systems and the web.

Are you tired of the hefty subscription fees and proprietary lock-in that come with traditional CAD software? Do you dream of a powerful, familiar design tool that's truly yours, running on any platform you choose? Well, fellow developers and designers, get ready to be excited because a game-changer has arrived on GitHub: CADCraft!CADCraft isn't just another CAD program; it's a bold, open-source clean-room reimplementation of Autodesk AutoCAD, rebuilt from the ground up in pure Rust. Imagine all the core functionalities you rely on – the command line, object snaps, layers, dimensions, hatches, blocks, and DXF drawing support – but now, it's completely open, free, and community-driven. This project aims to bring the robust and intuitive AutoCAD workflow we all know and love into the open-source world, without compromising on power or familiarity.One of the most exciting aspects of CADCraft is its foundation in Rust. For those unfamiliar, Rust is a programming language renowned for its performance, memory safety, and concurrency. This means CADCraft is designed to be incredibly fast, reliable, and efficient, handling complex designs without breaking a sweat. It's a modern approach to a classic problem, leveraging cutting-edge technology to deliver a superior user experience.And the accessibility? It's phenomenal! CADCraft runs natively across all major operating systems: macOS, Windows, Linux, and even FreeBSD. But wait, there's more – it also runs directly in your browser via WebAssembly! This cross-platform compatibility means you can work on your designs from virtually anywhere, on any device, without needing expensive licenses or specific hardware setups. This flexibility alone is a massive win for individual designers and small teams alike.For developers, the open-source nature of CADCraft opens up a world of possibilities. You can inspect the code, contribute to its development, and even build custom extensions or integrations tailored to your specific needs. This isn't just a tool; it's a platform that you can help shape and evolve. The ArtCraft team is fostering a vibrant community, inviting artists and creators from all backgrounds to join the conversation and contribute.In essence, CADCraft is poised to democratize computer-aided design. It offers a powerful, familiar, and free alternative to proprietary software, built with modern performance in mind and accessible across all platforms. While still in early development, its potential is immense, and it's definitely a project you'll want to keep an eye on – or even better, get involved with!

title: Price first, time second: a limit order book in about 50 lines of Rust
description:
Last week I posted a quiz: three sell orders, one buy order, who gets filled first? Here is the answer, in Rust.

Most order books follow one rule: the better price goes first, and at the same price the earlier order goes first.

rust
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Default)]
struct Book {
    // price -> queue of (id, size), oldest order at the front
    asks: BTreeMap<u64, VecDeque<(&'static str, u64)>>,
}

impl Book {
    fn sell(&mut self, id: &'static str, price: u64, size: u64) {
        self.asks.entry(price).or_default().push_back((id, size));
    }

    // buy `size` units, paying at most `limit`
    fn buy(&mut self, mut size: u64, limit: u64) {
        while size > 0 {
            let Some(mut level) = self.asks.first_entry() else { break };
            let price = *level.key();
            if price > limit { break; }
            let queue = level.get_mut();
            let (id, avail) = queue.front_mut().unwrap();
            let qty = size.min(*avail);
            println!("{id}: {qty} @ {price}");
            size -= qty;
            *avail -= qty;
            if *avail == 0 { queue.pop_front(); }
            if queue.is_empty() { level.remove(); }
        }
    }
}

The BTreeMap keeps prices sorted, so the best price is always first. Each price holds a VecDeque, so the oldest order is always first. There is no timestamp anywhere. The queue is the clock.


Now A, B and C sell, then someone buys 10 with a limit of 100.20:


fn main() {
    // prices are integer ticks: 10010 = 100.10
    let mut book = Book::default();
    book.sell("A", 10020, 5);
    book.sell("B", 10010, 3);
    book.sell("C", 10010, 4);
    book.buy(10, 10020);
}

B: 3 @ 10010
C: 4 @ 10010
A: 3 @ 10020

A arrived first and was filled last. B beat C because both were at 100.10 and B was earlier. And the buyer paid 100.10 on seven units even though the limit was 100.20.

This toy has no cancel, no sell side and no balance check. On Solana the book also has to fit into one account with a fixed compute budget, so the same rule has to work inside fixed slots.

I work on Privora, where the book stays public and the position behind an order stays private (devnet, test funds).

If you have put an order book onchain, which limit hit you first, account size or compute?

Amazon DCV is a high-performance remote display protocol that enables customers to securely access remote desktops and application sessions across Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Amazon DCV 2026.0 includes the following key features and improvements:

  • Support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04, with Linux hosts and sessions running on the modern Wayland display server

  • A new macOS client with gamepad support, and updated Windows and Linux clients

  • Performance improvements, including H.264 frame slice support and slice-based multithreaded decoding on the Linux and macOS clients for lower latency

  • Support for new macOS server versions on Amazon EC2

For more information about the new features and enhancements in Amazon DCV 2026.0, see the release notes or visit the Amazon DCV webpage to learn more and get started.

title: WCAG Color Contrast Explained: AA vs AAA, Large Text, and the Gray That Fails
description:
I used to treat contrast as a box to tick at the end of a project. Then an audit flagged half our secondary text and most of our buttons, and I learned how close "looks fine to me" is to "fails WCAG."

This is what I wish I'd known earlier. The thresholds, the formula, and a small JS contrastRatio() function are in a gist: WCAG Color Contrast Ratio Cheat Sheet. Every number in this post comes from that script.

What the ratio actually means

A contrast ratio compares how bright two colors are, but not the way you'd guess. Each color gets turned into a "relative luminance" between 0 (black) and 1 (white). The formula weights green much more than blue, because our eyes are far more sensitive to green. Then you take (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05).

The result runs from 1:1 (same color) to 21:1 (black on white). So 4.5:1 doesn't mean "4.5 times different" in any intuitive sense. It's just the scale WCAG uses.

Because of that weighting, two colors that look equally "strong" can score very differently. Tailwind's red-600 (#dc2626) behind white text gets 4.82:1, while green-600 (#16a34a) gets only 3.29:1. Green is perceived as much lighter.

AA vs AAA

WCAG 2.x has two levels you'll actually run into:

  • AA is what most laws and contracts point to (ADA cases, EN 301 549 in the EU). Normal text needs 4.5:1.
  • AAA is stricter. Normal text needs 7:1.

I aim for AA everywhere and AAA for long-form body text, like docs, articles, and anything people actually read for a while. Hitting AAA across a whole product is hard and usually not required.

One detail that catches people: the ratio is not rounded. A color at 4.49:1 fails AA. I've seen "4.5" in a design tool that was really 4.47.

Large text gets a discount

Bigger, bolder text is easier to read, so the bar drops: 3:1 for AA and 4.5:1 for AAA. "Large" has a specific meaning: at least 24px regular, or about 18.66px (14pt) bold. A 20px medium-weight heading does not count, even though it feels big.

UI components count too

Since WCAG 2.1 there's a 3:1 rule for non-text things you need to see in order to use the interface: input borders, icons that carry meaning, focus indicators, chart lines, checkbox outlines. This is the one that bit me hardest.

The classic failure is a light gray input border. Tailwind's gray-300 (#d1d5db) on white is 1.47:1. It looks clean, but for a lot of people the field basically isn't there. You don't need a dark border, though. A border that's clearly visible, or a filled background with enough contrast, does the job.

The gray pitfalls

Gray text on white is where most contrast bugs live. These are the ones I check now:

  • #767676 on white is 4.54:1. That's the lightest pure gray that passes AA for normal text. Burn it into your memory.
  • #777777, one step lighter, is 4.47:1 and fails. Same goes for any "close enough" gray.
  • #999999, a very common "muted" color, is 2.84:1. It fails even the large-text bar.
  • Tailwind's gray-500 (#6b7280) is 4.83:1 on white, so it's fine. gray-400 (#9ca3af) is 2.53:1, so it isn't.

Backgrounds matter as much as text. gray-500 passes on white but drops to 4.39:1 on gray-100 (#f3f4f6) and fails. #767676 on #f5f5f5 is 4.16:1. So a gray that passes on your page background can fail inside a light gray card or table row. Check text against the surface it actually sits on.

Brand colors on white

The second big source of failures is the brand color, usually a bright blue or green. Designers want white text on it and it doesn't quite get there:

  • Bootstrap 4's #007bff with white text: 3.97:1. Fine for big buttons, fails for normal text.
  • Bootstrap 5 switched to #0d6efd: 4.50:1. It passes AA, but just barely.
  • Tailwind blue-500 (#3b82f6): 3.67:1. blue-600 (#2563eb): 5.16:1.
  • Tailwind green-500 (#22c55e): 2.27:1. You need green-700 (#15803d, 5.01:1) for white text.
  • Amber/yellow (#f59e0b) with white text is 2.14:1. With black text it's 9.77:1.

My fix is usually to keep the bright brand color for big surfaces and illustrations, and add a darker shade of the same hue for text and buttons. On yellows and oranges, I switch to dark text. It almost always looks better anyway.

How I check now

A simple trick: run a small script in CI that computes ratios for your design tokens (the gist function is enough for this) and fail the build if any text/background pair you actually use drops below the threshold. That catches regressions when someone tweaks a color.

For quick one-off checks while designing, I paste two colors into this colour contrast checker. It runs in the browser and shows AA/AAA pass or fail right away.

Also check the states people forget: hover, focus rings, placeholders, and text over images or semi-transparent overlays. Those are where audits find the leftovers.

Contrast isn't the whole accessibility story, but it's measurable and cheap to fix. Fixing it early beats finding out in an audit.

title: CSS Easing Explained: Picking the Right cubic-bezier() for Enter, Exit and Move Animations
description:
For a long time I wrote transition: all 0.3s ease on everything and moved on. It worked fine. It also made every interface I built feel a little bit off, and I couldn't explain why until I started paying attention to easing.

This post is the mental model I use now. If you only want the values, I keep the full list of curves as CSS variables in a gist: CSS cubic-bezier() Easing Cheat Sheet.

Why easing matters at all

Nothing in the real world moves at a constant speed. A drawer you pull out speeds up and then slows to a stop. A ball you drop speeds up until it hits the floor. When a UI element moves linearly, your brain notices that it's "wrong" even if you can't say why.

Easing is how you describe that change in speed. In CSS, every timing function is really a cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2). The x axis is time and the y axis is progress, both from 0 to 1. Even the keywords are just presets: ease is cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1) and ease-in-out is cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 0.58, 1).

The most useful way to read a curve: a steep part means fast, a flat part means slow. That's really all there is to it.

Enter, exit, move

I use three rules and they cover about 90% of what I build.

Things entering the screen: ease-out. A modal, a toast, a dropdown. It should show up fast and settle gently. Ease-out puts the speed at the start, so the element looks like it reacts to the user right away and then slows down where the eye lands on it. My default is cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1) (easeOutCubic). When I want something snappier, I use easeOutQuint, cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1).

Things leaving: ease-in. Same logic in reverse. The element starts slowly and speeds up as it goes away, which reads as "it's gone." Exit animations should also be a bit shorter than enters. Nobody wants to watch something leave.

Things moving from A to B on screen: ease-in-out. A tab indicator sliding, a card changing position, a carousel. Both ends are visible, so the element should speed up and slow down: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1) (easeInOutCubic).

One thing I avoid is plain ease-in for enter animations. It feels laggy, because the slowest part happens right when the user is waiting for feedback.

.toast {
  transition: transform 250ms cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1),
              opacity 250ms cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1);
}
.toast[data-leaving] {
  transition-duration: 180ms;
  transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0, 0.67, 0); /* easeInCubic */
}

Durations

Easing and duration go together. A good curve at the wrong duration still feels bad. These are the ranges I start from:

  • Hover, press, small color changes: 100–200ms
  • Dropdowns, tooltips, toasts: 150–250ms
  • Modals, drawers, page sections: 250–400ms
  • Big full-screen transitions: up to about 500ms

Bigger elements and longer distances can take a bit longer. On mobile, I go a little shorter than on desktop. If something feels slow, I almost always fix it by cutting the duration, not by changing the curve.

Also, stop using transition: all. List the properties (transform, opacity). It's cheaper to render, and you won't accidentally animate layout properties like width or top.

Overshoot with Back curves

cubic-bezier() lets the y values go outside 0–1 (the x values can't). If y goes above 1, the element shoots past its final value and settles back. That's the "Back" family:

/* easeOutBack: overshoots ~10% then settles */
.badge-pop { transition: transform 300ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); }

I like this on small playful things: a notification badge popping in, a like button, a checkbox tick. I'd never use it on a modal or anything large. On a big surface, a wobble feels sloppy instead of fun. A real bounce or elastic effect, with several wobbles, can't be done with one cubic-bezier. For that you need @keyframes or the newer linear() function.

Respect reduced motion

Some people get dizzy or nauseous from motion on screen, and they turn on "reduce motion" in their OS. Honoring that setting takes a few lines:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

I use 0.01ms instead of none so that transitionend and animationend events still fire and JS that waits on them doesn't break. A softer approach is to keep opacity fades and drop only the transforms (sliding, scaling, parallax). Those cause most of the trouble.

Keep curves in one place

My last tip is to put your curves in CSS custom properties and use only those:

:root {
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1);
  --ease-in: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0, 0.67, 0);
  --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1);
}

Three or four named curves applied consistently do more for how an app "feels" than a dozen hand-tuned ones. The gist has the full Sine through Back set if you want more options.

When I need a custom curve, I drag the handles in a visual editor until it looks right, then copy the four numbers. Lately I've been using this cubic-bezier editor. It runs in the browser and doesn't need an account. Seeing the curve beats guessing numbers every time.

That's it: ease-out to enter, ease-in to leave, ease-in-out to move, keep it short, and respect reduced motion.
